stories.title: Ottawa, Alberta pledge to build 1,460 affordable houses
stories.summary: Ottawa will provide up to $220 million through Build Canada Homes, a federal agency formed to speed up the delivery of the housing, while Alberta will pay up to $165 million.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The federal government and Alberta are pledging to build at least 1,460 affordable housing units across the province.

Ottawa will provide up to $220 million through Build Canada Homes, a federal agency formed to speed up the delivery of the housing, while Alberta will pay up to $165 million.

The governments are expecting to receive $238 million from other sources.

A news release says the 21 planned housing projects will include supportive and transitional housing.

There is a target of building at least 500 homes using modern methods of construction, including off-site and factory-built approaches.

Build Canada Homes and Alberta will also establish a “joint collaboration table” to identify priority projects and coordinate investments.

stories.title: Quebec political leaders to appear in TV interviews on day 14 of election campaign
stories.summary: The leaders of Quebec's five main political parties are continuing on the campaign trail Wednesday ahead of the election set for Oct. 5.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The leaders of Quebec’s five main political parties are continuing on the campaign trail Wednesday ahead of the election set for Oct. 5.

They are heading to Quebec City, where they will face a crucial test this evening with back-to-back interviews on Radio-Canada’s airwaves.

Tariffs, the cost of living, education and language are among the key issues dominating the election campaign so far.

Polls show voters are paying close attention to how leaders are addressing affordability, which has become a central theme in the campaign.

The interviews come at a pivotal moment in the campaign, with many voters still undecided.

The leaders are also scheduled to participate in their first debate on Sept. 15.

stories.title: Report: Maple Leafs’ Gavin McKenna to live with John Tavares
stories.summary: McKenna, 18, is turning pro after one season at Penn State, where he had 15 goals and 51 points in 35 games.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
Posted September 9, 2026 8:10 am.

A former No. 1 pick is taking the NHL’s newest No. 1 pick under his roof.

John Tavares told reporters at the Player Media Tour in Las Vegas that new Toronto Maple Leafs teammate Gavin McKenna will be living with his family this season, according to Michael Traikos of The Hockey News .

McKenna, 18, is turning pro after one season at Penn State, where he had 15 goals and 51 points in 35 games. The Maple Leafs selected the left winger from Yellowknife first overall in the NHL Draft this past June.

Tavares is entering his 18th NHL season and ninth with the Maple Leafs. He was the first overall pick in the 2009 NHL Draft.

According to Traikos, this isn’t the first time Tavares and his wife Aryne have welcomed a young Maple Leafs teammate into their home. Last year, rookie Easton Cowan lived with Tavares’ family as he navigated his first NHL season at age 20.

stories.title: Leaside family home fetches two early bidders
stories.summary: Two-storey house sells for $2.25-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
327 Bessborough Dr., Toronto

Asking price: $1,999,000 (July, 2026)

Selling price : $2.25-million (August, 2026)

Taxes: $10,404 (2026)

Days on the market: Nine

Listing agents: Andrew Ipekian and Sophia Puccetti, Keller Williams Referred Urban Realty

To make this four-bedroom house more inviting to potential buyers, agent Andrew Ipekian had it professionally staged and opened to the public on the last Friday in July. Potential buyers quickly booked private tours and dozens of people roamed through open houses that weekend and the next.

“Generally, before a long weekend, a lot of people leave the city to go up north,” said Mr. Ipekian.

“Sometimes open houses work, sometimes they don’t, but for this house, they drove in a lot of activity.”

The 76-year-old home was at the time one of few available for purchase near Eglinton and Bayview avenues. Two offers came in, one of which added $251,000 to the asking price, free of conditions.

“Historically, the summer months are generally slow for real estate; however, you can realize a great price if there’s low inventory at the same time,” Mr. Ipekian said.

“Leaside is known for fantastic schools, as well as shopping and transit. It’s very family-friendly and highly desirable.”

This two-storey house has a living room with a gas fireplace, a dining area and a remodelled, eat-in kitchen.

There are dens on two levels, including one with access to a back deck, patio and yard on the 35- by 124-foot lot.

Full bathrooms are on each level, including the basement. It also has a fifth bedroom, a laundry room and two entrances. One exits out to the front driveway and attached garage.

“This is a standard-size home for the neighbourhood,” Mr. Ipekian said.

“It was renovated and updated, but there’s always more renovations you could do.”

stories.title: Some home sellers recoil from a lethargic market as Canada-U.S. trade war adds uncertainty
stories.summary: Fall market usually kicks off soon after Labour Day
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
A lethargic August in the Toronto-area real estate market has some potential sellers wondering whether to push ahead with plans to list their property in the fall while others have already spiked their listings.

Havoc created by the trade war between the United States and Canada only adds to the uncertainty as participants prepare for a fall market that typically kicks off soon after Labour Day.

Nutan Brown, real estate agent with Royal LePage Terrequity Realty, often waits until the second or third week of September so she can gauge the pace of sales.

This year, she is being especially attentive to the mood of buyers in the early going.

“I like to monitor from the sidelines,” Ms. Brown says. “I can tell my clients, ‘here’s the activity level.’”

Business was slow last month in the west end of Toronto, where she does much of her business in areas such as Bloor West Village, Baby Point and Old Mill.

The same trend was apparent throughout the Greater Toronto Area, with a few exceptional sales in desirable pockets.

Sales in the GTA dipped 1.3 per cent in August from July on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board. That result halted a run of improving sales for five months in a row.

New listings surged 5.2 per cent in August from July, notes Daren King, senior economist with National Bank of Canada, who figures some sellers were prompted to list when they saw renewed momentum in the previous months.

Overall, active listings gave buyers lots of choice by historical standards, Mr. King says.

Toronto-area home buyers adjust to the new normal

Sales dropped 2.1 per cent compared with August of last year, while new listings fell 14.1 per cent in the same period.

The average price decreased 2.7 per cent in August compared with August, 2025, to $993,410. That marks the second time this year that the average price in the GTA has come in below $1-million.

Ms. Brown worked with one set of buyers who were keen on a house with an asking price in the $1.6-million range.

That price placed it almost out of reach for the buyers, says Ms. Brown, who decided against submitting an offer.

“We didn’t want to be bold enough to put in a really lowball offer,” she says. “It can annoy the seller and backfire on you.”

Ms. Brown continued to monitor the property for a few weeks until the sellers dropped the asking price by $100,000.

“We went in as quickly as we could,” says Ms. Brown, which gave the homeowners little time to drum up another bid.

The buyers offered about 95 per cent of the new asking price, she says, and the sellers accepted.

“If the right house comes, they’re ready to act, but they can be selective,” she says of many house hunters.

After 399 days on the market, price cuts help find a buyer for lakefront condo in Toronto

In another instance, Ms. Brown worked with one client searching for a two-bedroom waterfront condo in the Humber Bay Shores area.

The downsizing client looked at several units but got cold feet and decided to sell her existing property first.

Ms. Brown says that strategy is wise in an uneven market when homeowners are unsure of how much their house will fetch.

“Sometimes you’ll be pleasantly surprised – sometimes you’d better be careful.”

Some sellers of larger condo units around the Humber Bay area are also putting their listings on hold, says Luke Dalinda, real estate agent with Royal LePage Real Estate Services.

“There is a significant demand for larger suites from empty nesters, except the owners of those suites seem to be waiting out the trade uncertainty,” says Mr. Dalinda.

In an area with many recently built condo towers, Mr. Dalinda notes there were 239 active listings heading into the Labour Day long weekend compared with inventory around 197 in the spring.

Fifty units traded hands in August, he says, and 40 of those sold for less than $800,000. The larger suites often sell for upwards of $1-million.

Mr. Dalinda was optimistic Canada and the United States would have a positive outcome to negotiations for a bilateral trade deal. Instead, talks broke down in late August.

“I was telling clients it would be rocket fuel for the market, and all of a sudden it just went boom,” he says. “It creates a black cloud.”

Mr. Dalinda says the owners of suites with 2,000 square feet of living space or more have seen prices come down over the past few years and they are taking a wait-and-see approach. Some plan to hold off selling for two or three years.

Many of the investors who bought micro “shoebox” condo units can’t afford to wait for a rebound, he says, and they are force to list. He is also seeing a rise in the number of “power of sale” listings as lenders take over.

Mr. Dalinda recently listed an investment property in High Park with three renovated units in a converted red brick house.

The triplex at 137 High Park Ave., with an asking price of $3.98-million, might appeal to an investor or a buyer who wants to live in one unit and rent out the others, says Mr. Dalinda.

Just before the long weekend, Mr. Dalinda listed a detached house at 87 Riverview Gardens in the Old Mill neighbourhood with an asking price of $1.799-million.

The house with original wood trim and panelled doors likely needs a renovation, he says, but several potential buyers had booked showings in the first two days.

Mr. Dalinda listed in the opening days of September because he believes there is a window of opportunity before consumers feel the impact of countertariffs on U.S. imports.

“October is traditionally a scary time,” he points out, with that month’s reputation for negative surprises that rattle financial markets.

Meanwhile, the “elbows up” rallying cry has galvanized many Canadians.

“People haven’t been affected economically,” he says. “There’s a lot of belief and support and good will.”

stories.title: El Niño expected to extend fall and delay winter’s arrival
stories.summary: September and October will still bring the usual swings between warm spells and bursts of chilly, stormy weather, The Weather Network’s forecast suggests
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
It’s shaping up to be a mild fall across much of Canada, The Weather Network’s forecast suggests, with a potentially historic El Niño expected to prolong the season and delay winter’s arrival.

September and October will still bring the usual swings between warm spells and bursts of chilly, stormy weather, the network’s three-month outlook says. But the balance is expected to trend milder and, in many regions, drier than normal as the season progresses, said senior meteorologist Doug Gillham.

“Winter is probably going to wait on the sidelines for a while,” he said in an interview.

The main reason is El Niño, the climate phenomenon tied to shifting patches of warm water in the Pacific Ocean, Gillham said.

Several forecasters suggest this could be among the strongest El Niños on record. The global weather disrupter is set to spike temperatures, already elevated due to human-caused climate change, further raising the risk of serious floods, drought and extreme heat in some regions into 2027.

While there will be catastrophic impacts globally, it’s “not all doom and gloom for the fall in Canada,” said Gillham. El Niño tends to shift the storm track south of the border, fill Canada with milder pacific air and limit the ability of cold arctic air to plunge south, he said.

The result could mean fewer classic fall storms, a milder start to winter and fewer Atlantic hurricanes. But an unprecedented El Niño could introduce some surprises and uncertainty into the forecast, Gillham said.

“Don’t be lulled into a sense of, ’oh we’re just going to have a dry fall and we don’t have to worry about any storms.’ Fewer storms doesn’t mean that the storms that occur won’t pack a punch,” he said.

The Canadian Press

While El Niño is the main driver of the fall outlook, conditions vary by region.

British Columbia’s reprieve from summer heat came earlier than in recent years. But warmer, drier conditions are expected to dominate the rest of September and into October, which May be of little relief to wildfire-weary communities in the interior, said Gillham.

“The rest of September into the beginning of October is not good news in that we need more rain than we’ve seen,” he said.

Along the coast, precipitation levels are expected to get closer to normal as the season deepens. A delayed start to winter is expected across the province, but alpine regions May just be cold enough to get a decent start to ski season, Gillham said.

Moving east into Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, the theme is similar. Milder temperatures are expected to dominate, interrupted at times by shots of cold weather. Most of the Prairies will be on the drier side, with the exception of near-normal conditions in southern Saskatchewan and southern Manitoba.

While stormy weather has hampered the start of harvest season in some regions, “the good news is that our backs aren’t up against the wall with the impending arrival of consistent winter weather,” said Gillham.

“Some years, we’ve seen winter weather show up in September and then it kind of takes over. That is not the concern this year,” he said.

Into Ontario and Quebec, the forecast suggests the rest of September into October is expected to feature typical fall weather.

What counts as typical fall conditions has changed in recent decades, especially in the north. Average fall temperatures are now about 2.4 degrees warmer across the country compared to the mid-20th century as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, heats the planet.

The forecast’s baseline, or what’s considered normal, is based on a more recent period between 1991 and 2020.

As recent Ontario thunderstorms have shown, the season will feature some high-impact storms, though possibly fewer than normal, Gillham said. A drier weather pattern is expected to settle in later in the fall and persist into November, potentially welcome news for areas such as Ottawa and Niagara after a summer of record rainfall, Gillham said.

And while Gillham still holds out hope for the ski season in B.C. and Alberta’s alpine regions, he’s much less optimistic about what’s in store for Ontario and Quebec.

“We do not expect consistent cold or early winter weather as we wrap up the fall season,” he said of Central Canada.

The quiet hurricane season is expected to continue in Atlantic Canada, but it only takes one storm to make an impact, Gillham said. The very warm Atlantic Ocean temperatures mean any storm that does track toward the region could keep up its intensity and moisture.

Across the region, the forecast suggests near normal precipitation and temperatures, with a late start to consistent wintry weather.

Northern Canada is also expected to see warmer-than-normal conditions, with exception of near-normal temperatures in Western parts of Yukon and parts of Baffin Island.

Canada is warming nearly twice as fast as the global average, while the Arctic is warming three times faster. Under current climate policies, Canada’s average temperatures are expected to rise by five degrees and Nunavut’s winters could get more than 10 degrees Celsius hotter by the end of the century, a recent federal scientific assessment said.

stories.title: St. Boniface residents raise concerns over proposed aquatic centre
stories.summary: Some St. Boniface residents are concerned the new aquatic park in the Provencher Park area will bring parking and road safety challenges as more people head to the pool.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Some St. Boniface residents are concerned the new aquatic park in Provencher Park area will bring parking and road safety challenges as more people access the facility.

The city of Winnipeg is proposing to build the St. Boniface Outdoor Aquatic Park at the current Provencher Park, according to city agenda documents for Sept. 8.

Provencher Park was chosen as its pool was reaching the end of its lifespan.

“It’s not a matter of end of life cycle. It’s a lack of respect to this community that the City of Winnipeg has given in maintaining upkeeping,” said Tom Scott, a St. Boniface resident.

“It’s a wonderful facility it’s just too large of a footprint for this park,” said Brian Boychuck, a St. Boniface resident.

Watch the video above for the full story.

The city of Winnipeg is proposing to build the St. Boniface Outdoor Aquatic Park at the current Provencher Park, according to city agenda documents for Sept. 8.
Provencher Park was chosen as its pool was reaching the end of its lifespan.
“It’s not a matter of end of life cycle. It’s a lack of respect to this community that the City of Winnipeg has given in maintaining upkeeping,” said Tom Scott, a St. Boniface resident.
“It’s a wonderful facility it’s just too large of a footprint for this park,” said Brian Boychuck, a St. Boniface resident.

stories.title: Canada’s digital defences are lagging. Now what?

stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Earlier this year, Ottawa announced a commitment towards ensuring digital sovereignty, but what exactly does that look like?

More data centres? AI within more government sectors? Modernizing hospital and school board technology?

Host Maria Kestane speaks to David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security to discuss how strengthening our cyber security will improve our digital defence, and how Canadians can show up in the fight for maintaining Canadian digital sovereignty.

stories.title: Krose launches mayoral campaigning to win, not play spoiler
stories.summary: Surrounded by almost 100 supporters, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose shared her vision for London at an event in downtown London to officially launch her campaign.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Surrounded by almost 100 supporters, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose shared her vision for London at an event in downtown London to officially launch her campaign.

“I want to do this for the people who live in London,” Krose told the enthusiastic crowd. “I have gained knowledge and experience over 20 years working in government and politics.

I see how a city can be run. I see how levels of government can come together. I see how results can be delivered and I want to do that for Londoners.”

She highlighted the four pillars in her platform:

A city that feels safe for all

Services that work

Traffic that moves

The taxpayer is respected

Following her remarks to supporters, she was interviewed by CTV News.

Krose pushed back when asked if her campaign might play the role of spoiler on election night, asserting that she’s running to bring her vision to the mayor’s office.

“I’ve never heard of a spoiler campaign in my 20 years in (public affairs), I’m running for me and what my vision is. I’m running for what people are telling me,” she responded.

Krose added, “This is for the City of London. This is for the people I just want to represent. What I’m hearing from people and make sure that we get the change that they’re asking for.”

Krose’ campaign platform also proposes several new initiatives at city hall including:

One city hall experience - Residents and businesses should not have to navigate multiple departments to get an answer. Common interactions will be reviewed to reduce unnecessary hand-offs and create clearer responsibility for resolving a resident’s issue.

Traffic bottleneck program - Identifies, ranks and publicly reports London’s most problematic intersections and corridors and then targets practical improvements where they will have the greatest impact

Risk-rank London’s school zones - Prioritize physical safety improvements where speeding, collision history and pedestrian risks are greatest.

London performance dashboard – Display major spending commitments, project status, expected outcomes and significant cost overruns.

Annual taxpayer value report - Straightforward annual account of what City Hall spent, what programs were reviewed, what savings or efficiencies were identified, which major projects stayed on budget and what needs to improve next.

Also running for mayor are Josh Morgan (incumbent), Susan Stevenson, John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam, and Mustafa Zeboon.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: The Associated Press says it will still refer to Lake Ontario, not Lake America
stories.summary: continue to refer to Lake Ontario by its original name, and not Lake America.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
continue to refer to Lake Ontario by its original name, and not Lake America.

It says that as a global news agency, it must ensure place names are easily recognizable to broad audiences, noting Canada has said it will not be following the name change decreed by U.S. President Donald Trump in an executive order.

The guidance note says staff should refer to the body of water as Lake Ontario, acknowledging and explaining the name Trump has chosen if it’s relevant to a story.

It says no single body determines the names of international bodies of water, although Trump has “wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.”

The note lists other places whose names Trump has sought to change by executive order, including North America’s tallest peak, which he reverted to Mount McKinley from Denali, and the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump said should be called the Gulf of America.

The agency says it now refers to Mount McKinley because it lies solely in the United States and Trump has authority to change federal geographical names, while it continues to refer to the Gulf of Mexico, which forms a shared border between Mexico and the United States.

The agency’s guidance acknowledges the long history of Lake Ontario’s name.

“Lake Ontario has carried that name for more than 400 years. The word ‘Ontario’ is derived from the northern Iroquoian language family,” it says, adding that the province of Ontario took its name from the lake.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Cloudy, muggy Wednesday with showers and thunderstorms possible
stories.summary: A mainly cloudy and muggy day is expected across southern Ontario Wednesday, with scattered showers and thunderstorms possible through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A mainly cloudy and muggy day is expected across southern Ontario Wednesday, with scattered showers and thunderstorms possible through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“We have a front that will be slumping its way southward and that will generate some rain,” Atchison said.

Temperatures will reach 26 C, with southwest winds picking up and gusts possible ahead of the front.

The front will continue moving south overnight, with the chance of showers lingering into Thursday afternoon and evening. Thunderstorms are also possible, with the potential for heavy rainfall.

Atchison says the muggy conditions will last through Wednesday before cooler temperatures arrive Thursday.

Thursday will be mainly cloudy with a high of 22 C, while Friday will bring full sunshine after a cool start with a single-digit low.

Saturday is expected to start with lots of sunshine and a high of 26 C, although conditions will be somewhat unsettled over the weekend.

stories.title: Western Fair returns with new rides, food and ways to save
stories.summary: The 149th edition brings back longtime favourites alongside new attractions and entertainment across the 10-day fair.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
The 149th edition brings back longtime favourites alongside new attractions and entertainment across the 10-day fair.

The Western Fair begins its 10-day run Friday, with new attractions, vendors, rides and returning favourites marking its 149th edition.

“(The Western Fair) has been around for a very, very long time. People have gone since they were kids and have grown up with it . . . There are actual memories that are built from attending this fair and watching your kids see them and experience them, watching your grandkids,” Western Fair spokesperson Angela Hawkins said.

“That’s ultimately what this fair is all about; tradition, having old experiences, but also discovering new experiences with your family.”

Hawkins said the Creative Arts competition has been “beloved for a very long time.” Running for nearly as long as the fair itself, the competition showcases visual arts, baking, crafts, horticulture and more created by people across Southwestern Ontario.

The Animal Barn is another returning favourite offering hands-on agricultural education. Horses, cows, alpacas, sheep and rabbits are among the livestock in the barn.

“No matter how old or young you are, everybody loves to get to the Animal Barn,” Hawkins said.

Simon the camel and micro mini Highland cows, or Mini Moos, from Jersey Ridge are new additions to the Animal Barn.

Simon will be at the fair from Monday to Thursday, while the Mini Moos will be outside the barn from Friday to Sunday on both weekends.

Two new animal activities are free daily pony rides for children and goat yoga at the infield pasture on Saturdays and Sundays.

“There is something for everybody to come here and enjoy and to make memories with their family,” Hawkins said.

Away from the barn, visitors can find the Bathtub Singer roaming the grounds in her clawfoot tub or watch the Hockey Circus Show, featuring acrobatics, juggling and hockey stunts.

Summer is fading. But fall fairs are just getting warmed up

Hometown Specialty: From frontier London fair, to tourism 'powerhouse'

Motorsport performances are included with admission, with monster trucks, FMX, BMX and demolition derbies taking over the Grandstand.

“It’s crazy all the things that we get to experience in a ten-day fair,” Hawkins said. “This is such an important tradition for London. It’s such a good value for your admission and it’s such a good way to experience something outside of our screens and our everyday lives with your family.”

Hawkins said visitors can find more information and plan their trip on the Western Fair website.

There are more than 150 food options from more than 60 vendors across the fairgrounds. Eight new vendors have joined this year, offering everything from tanghulu and cheesecake on sticks to birria tacos, artisan breads and roasted local corn on the cob.

Londoners can also try two new midway rides this year. The Super Miami will take riders 55 feet into the air before plunging back down, while the Downdraft, described as a high-thrill ride, will have riders swinging, spinning and dropping.

Musical performances are included with Western Fair admission, with daily shows spanning a range of genres.

The opening weekend will feature mainly rock music, with The Strumbellas headlining Friday, Wide Mouth Mason on Saturday and Texas Kings on Sunday.

Throughout the week, fairgoers can catch several tribute acts, including the OverKillers, a five-piece Killers tribute, along with Taylor Swift and Chappell Roan tribute performers.

Sept. 19 is dedicated to Latin culture at the Bud Light Music Garden, with authentic food, drinks and live Norteño, mariachi and Latin performances from noon to 10:30 p.m. Los Grandes Del Norte will headline at 8 p.m.

The Western Fair has introduced several ways to save on admission, food and rides.

Hawkins said the best way to save on admission is to plan ahead, with $15 advance tickets or a $50 SuperPass. The SuperPass includes admission and unlimited midway rides for one full day and saves $20 compared with prices at the gate. Advance-ticket and SuperPass sales end Thursday.

Children 10 and under and adults 65 and older can enter the fair for free. Admission is also free for everyone during community hours from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. on opening Friday.

Sept. 16 is We Care Wednesday at the fair. Attendees can donate non-perishable food items at the gate to receive $2 off admission while helping Harvest Hands supply food boxes to the community.

“It’s a really great initiative to not only give back to the community, but also save a little bit of money on the entry,” Hawkins said.

Other ways to save include:

Showing an advance ticket to London Transit drivers for a free ride to and from the Western Fair.

$6 food options at any vendor before 6 p.m.

A family of four can eat for $40 at the J-AAR Expo Centre concession.

On Monday, 75 ride tickets can be purchased for $30.

Two free water stations are available on the fairgrounds for bottle refills.

content_blocks.text: The 149th edition brings back longtime favourites alongside new attractions and entertainment across the 10-day fair.
The Western Fair begins its 10-day run Friday, with new attractions, vendors, rides and returning favourites marking its 149th edition.
What’s returning this year?

“(The Western Fair) has been around for a very, very long time. People have gone since they were kids and have grown up with it . . . There are actual memories that are built from attending this fair and watching your kids see them and experience them, watching your grandkids,” Western Fair spokesperson Angela Hawkins said.
“That’s ultimately what this fair is all about; tradition, having old experiences, but also discovering new experiences with your family.”

Hawkins said the Creative Arts competition has been “beloved for a very long time.” Running for nearly as long as the fair itself, the competition showcases visual arts, baking, crafts, horticulture and more created by people across Southwestern Ontario.
The Animal Barn is another returning favourite offering hands-on agricultural education. Horses, cows, alpacas, sheep and rabbits are among the livestock in the barn.
“No matter how old or young you are, everybody loves to get to the Animal Barn,” Hawkins said.
What’s new at the fair?
Simon the camel and micro mini Highland cows, or Mini Moos, from Jersey Ridge are new additions to the Animal Barn.
Simon will be at the fair from Monday to Thursday, while the Mini Moos will be outside the barn from Friday to Sunday on both weekends.
Two new animal activities are free daily pony rides for children and goat yoga at the infield pasture on Saturdays and Sundays.
“There is something for everybody to come here and enjoy and to make memories with their family,” Hawkins said.
Away from the barn, visitors can find the Bathtub Singer roaming the grounds in her clawfoot tub or watch the Hockey Circus Show, featuring acrobatics, juggling and hockey stunts.

stories.title: Tiff 2026: Expanded Wavelengths program proves outré visions and Hollywood glitz can co-exist
stories.summary: This year’s program features standout biographical works
stories.author: Mark Peranson
stories.content:
Biographical works are a crowd-pleasing staple at the Toronto International Film Festival , and this year they even pervade the festival’s most experimental section, Wavelengths. This edition, audiences are treated to the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance reminiscing and quibbling in Once Upon a Time in Harlem, while a radical Japanese filmmaker, banned from leaving his country for decades due to his support of the Red Army, persists in Masao Adachi Takes a Passport Photo .

In the film that holds the section together, the genial Argentine gadfly Mariano Llinás goes way deep on the Life of Jorge Luis Borges . This is not your typical biography, and Wavelengths, each year, proves far from a typical collection of films.

Thanks to some grousing in outlets such as this one , the program has been slightly expanded this year, consisting of 15 shorts, two mid-lengths and 11 features (up from nine), most of which bowed elsewhere, including Llinas’s three-part, 330-minute digressional epic on the influential Argentine writer, which just launched in Venice.

Life of Jorge Luis Borges proves to be Wavelengths’ linchpin as Llinás’s hunt through the relics of Borges’s past focuses on how, in Borges’s writing, fiction pervades reality or vice versa. Llinás’s quest becomes as much about himself as his subject, a film about a brilliant eccentric made by a brilliant eccentric. It’s not the only film so deeply personal that its autobiographical leanings will be the focus of postscreening discussions. Others, as Llinas teaches us, require some investigation to reveal hidden clues.

Take Llinas’s countrymate, Lisandro Alonso, who returns with one of the most unlikely sequels of all time, Cannes standout Double Freedom . Back is woodcutter Misael Saavedra, whose daily work on Alonso’s father’s estate is again patiently depicted. The original La libertad intermingled fiction and reality so seamlessly that many confused it for documentary. In the intervening decades Alonso embraced artifice, and Double Freedom introduces Saavedra’s sister, Catalina Saavedra – in a Borgesian twist, they aren’t at all related (she’s the Chilean actor from The Maid ).

In a more dizzying confluence of realities, Sebastian Brameshuber’s London can be a considered a sequel to a film made by another director entirely. Bobby (Bobby Sommer), a rideshare driver going back and forth from Vienna to Salzburg on the A1 West Autobahn, plays the same character he did in Jem Cohen’s Museum Hours . A compelling representation of today’s Europe, London is almost entirely shot in studio in a car with rear projection, with improvised dialogues, some more real than others – to add a further layer, in real life Sommer is a driver himself, in charge of the transportation for the Vienna film festival.

Denis Côté has spoken about how Nobody’s Violence , his unsettling story of a euthanizing angel of death in the Quebec countryside, was influenced by his own confrontation with mortality, leading up to and after his kidney transplant. Côté dedicated it to his recently deceased mother, and grieving is also central to John Torres’s transfixing yet mystifying The Remotes , a world premiere that plays like a labyrinthian Filipino remix of David Cronenberg’s Crash . As Borges wrote about Keats, “I do not think I understood the words, but I felt that something was happening to me. It was happening not to my mere intelligence, but to my whole being.”

Likewise, while watching Nicolás Pereda’s amusing, self-reflexive chamber piece Everything Else Is Noise, one doesn’t grasp a fully personal connection. There is the reappearance of Pereda’s stock cast of actors including Teresita Sánchez, who plays a classical musician and composer, and Lázaro G. Rodriguez, as a TV documentarian bumbling through an interview with Sánchez, her friend and her daughter, all musicians. But the genesis of the film was Pereda spending time with his mother, who was the first to establish a group of female composers in Mexico.

Also focusing on womanhood, the British artist Beatrice Gibson plunges into auto-fiction in her atmospheric, 16mm-shot debut At Night : She appears on camera as a director trying to figure out the film she’s making. Dream, reality and fiction intertwine as over the course of one Parisian night she meets heterogenous women also playing versions of themselves. They engage in a handful of frank on-camera discussions about topics such as sexuality, motherhood and race, guided by their own literary figures, including the late American poet Alice Notley.

Llinás doesn’t shy away from Borges’s Peronist and fascist tendencies in his twilight years, and political autobiography invades every frame in two experimental works that see filmmakers confronting problematic elements of their national identities. Both are standouts of a program that reinforces Wavelengths’ tendency to refuse to separate the personal and the political.

For the first time, the Oscar race officially starts at Tiff – at least for student filmmakers

In the world premiere of The Black Box Is Orange , Toronto’s Yuula Benivolski complies a biography of her Israeli hometown in an intelligent way that would impress even Llinás. Her shape-shifting essay in 10 chapters makes trenchant use of photographic archives to uncover the history of Shlomi and its environs, built atop the rubble of the Palestinian village of al-Bassa on the Lebanese border. Patient, complex and absorbing, Benivolski’s debut is a genuine discovery.

An equally unflinching short provides the title for the Wavelengths 2 program, This Suffocating Now. Taking off from a broken wrist playing basketball, Vika Kirchenbauer carefully builds up an analysis of hypocrisy and state oppression she and others continue to experience. Kirchenbauer shows and tells us what it means to speak your truth as an artist in contemporary Germany, a country she describes as failing to learn the correct lessons from its own past, driven home this week by Alternative for Germany’s (AfD) seismic electoral breakthrough. The implicit conclusion, as a Roomba rumbles over the floors of her recently renovated flat, is that her homeland is in dire need of a good house cleaning.

Special to The Globe and Mail

stories.title: One of the giant ships at the centre of Canada’s shipbuilding revival is taking shape
stories.summary: From new military investments to Arctic security and sovereignty, Canada is pouring billions into asserting its presence in the North. In the first instalment of a CTV News series, we go inside the shipyard where the country’s future polar Arctic icebreaker is slowly coming together.
stories.author: Graham Richardson
stories.content:
From new military investments to Arctic security and sovereignty, Canada is pouring billions into asserting its presence in the North. In the first instalment of a CTV News series, we go inside a Vancouver shipyard where the country’s future polar Arctic icebreaker is slowly coming together.

Vancouver – More than 15 years after Ottawa launched its National Shipbuilding Strategy, Canada’s effort to rebuild the industry is taking shape on the West Coast.

Seaspan’s Vancouver shipyard operates around the clock, with much of the work centred on a massive steel structure that will eventually become Canada’s largest-ever polar icebreaker, the Canadian Coast Guard’s 158-metre, 26,000-tonne Imnaryuaq.

Years of design work and planning are now emerging in steel as workers assemble what will become the future flagship of the Canadian Coast Guard’s Arctic fleet.

“It’s a first-in-class vessel. I’m really proud to be a part of this project,” said welder John Starle. “There’s a sense of pride in what you’re building because it is for Canada.”

The contract for the ship alone is worth more than $4 billion.

When it enters service in the early 2030s, the vessel will provide capabilities Canada does not currently have, allowing the coast guard to operate farther north, break through thicker ice and maintain a greater presence in the High Arctic.

“This is huge,” said Jessica Fetterman, Seaspan’s chief engineer for the polar icebreaker project.

“We only build icebreakers in North America once every 40, 50 or 60 years, so this is groundbreaking.”

Fetterman said the ship will be capable of breaking through 2.5 metres of ice and 30 centimetres of compacted snow, nearly three metres in total, while maintaining a speed of three knots for up to 1,800 kilometres without stopping.

Decades of decline in Canada’s shipbuilding industry, combined with aging fleets in the Royal Canadian Navy and Canadian Coast Guard, prompted Ottawa to launch the National Shipbuilding Strategy in 2010.

The strategy’s first major vessel was delivered in 2020. Since then, 11 large ships have been designed in Canada, with most building taking place in Canada.

“The strategic question was whether you buy these ships from another country or try to build them here,” said Dave Hargreaves, Seaspan’s vice-president of strategy and business development.

“The decision was made to build them here, and that has enabled Canada to develop the capability not only to build ships, but to design them as well.”

Seaspan has delivered four vessels under the strategy so far. Two more are under construction, along with the company’s largest and most ambitious project to date, the Imnaryuaq. Seaspan is partnering with a Finnish company on the construction of the Imnaryuaq.

The vessel remains years from completion, but at 158 metres long and 26,000 tonnes, it is expected to become the largest ship in the Canadian Coast Guard’s Arctic fleet.

For workers such as Starle, the polar project, and the other ships, that have been ordered represents long-term employment.

“There’s a lot of longevity here,” he said. “With the contracts we already have and the ones that are coming, there’s an immense amount of work ahead.”

Seaspan is not the only company involved in Canada’s shipbuilding strategy. Chantier Davie Canada Inc., located in Lévis, Que., has been awarded a separate contract valued at more than $3 billion to build another polar icebreaker that will be named the Ccgs Arpatuuq.

The federal government also announced last month that Chantier Davie will lead the construction of six program icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard, which will help maintain year-round trade in Eastern Canada.

That contract is valued at $11.3 billion and is expected to create nearly 5,000 jobs during the construction phase that is set to begin in 2027.

Vancouver – More than 15 years after Ottawa launched its National Shipbuilding Strategy, Canada’s effort to rebuild the industry is taking shape on the West Coast.

Seaspan’s Vancouver shipyard operates around the clock, with much of the work centred on a massive steel structure that will eventually become Canada’s largest-ever polar icebreaker, the Canadian Coast Guard’s 158-metre, 26,000-tonne Imnaryuaq.

content_blocks.alt: Polar icebreaker CCGS Imnaryuaq
content_blocks.caption: Artist's rendition of the CCGS Imnaryuaq. The ship will be capable of breaking through 2.5 metres of ice and 30 centimetres of compacted snow, nearly three metres in total, while maintaining a speed of three knots for up to 1,800 kilometres without stopping.

content_blocks.text: Years of design work and planning are now emerging in steel as workers assemble what will become the future flagship of the Canadian Coast Guard’s Arctic fleet.

content_blocks.alt: Building Imnaryuaq: Canada's biggest icebreaker begins to take shape
content_blocks.caption: Welder John Starle tells CTV News he is 'really proud' to be part of the team putting together Canada’s largest-ever polar icebreaker. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: “It’s a first-in-class vessel. I’m really proud to be a part of this project,” said welder John Starle. “There’s a sense of pride in what you’re building because it is for Canada.”
The contract for the ship alone is worth more than $4 billion.

When it enters service in the early 2030s, the vessel will provide capabilities Canada does not currently have, allowing the coast guard to operate farther north, break through thicker ice and maintain a greater presence in the High Arctic.
“This is huge,” said Jessica Fetterman, Seaspan’s chief engineer for the polar icebreaker project.
“We only build icebreakers in North America once every 40, 50 or 60 years, so this is groundbreaking.”

content_blocks.alt: Building Imnaryuaq: Canada's biggest icebreaker begins to take shape
content_blocks.caption: Seaspan’s chief engineer Jess Fetterman says the new polar icebreaker will be capable of breaking through 2.5 metres of ice and 30 centimetres of compacted snow. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: Fetterman said the ship will be capable of breaking through 2.5 metres of ice and 30 centimetres of compacted snow, nearly three metres in total, while maintaining a speed of three knots for up to 1,800 kilometres without stopping.

Decades of decline in Canada’s shipbuilding industry, combined with aging fleets in the Royal Canadian Navy and Canadian Coast Guard, prompted Ottawa to launch the National Shipbuilding Strategy in 2010.
The strategy’s first major vessel was delivered in 2020. Since then, 11 large ships have been designed in Canada, with most building taking place in Canada.
“The strategic question was whether you buy these ships from another country or try to build them here,” said Dave Hargreaves, Seaspan’s vice-president of strategy and business development.

content_blocks.alt: Building Imnaryuaq: Canada's biggest icebreaker begins to take shape
content_blocks.caption: David Hargreaves, Seaspan’s senior vice-president of strategy and business development, says the shipbuilding industry is 'on the upswing' with thousands of employees and decades of work ahead. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: “The decision was made to build them here, and that has enabled Canada to develop the capability not only to build ships, but to design them as well.”

Seaspan has delivered four vessels under the strategy so far. Two more are under construction, along with the company’s largest and most ambitious project to date, the Imnaryuaq. Seaspan is partnering with a Finnish company on the construction of the Imnaryuaq.
The vessel remains years from completion, but at 158 metres long and 26,000 tonnes, it is expected to become the largest ship in the Canadian Coast Guard’s Arctic fleet.
For workers such as Starle, the polar project, and the other ships, that have been ordered represents long-term employment.
“There’s a lot of longevity here,” he said. “With the contracts we already have and the ones that are coming, there’s an immense amount of work ahead.”

content_blocks.alt: Building Imnaryuaq: Canada's biggest icebreaker begins to take shape
content_blocks.caption: Welder working on what will become Canada’s largest-ever polar icebreaker, the CCGS Imnaryuaq, at Seaspan’s Vancouver shipyard. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: Seaspan is not the only company involved in Canada’s shipbuilding strategy. Chantier Davie Canada Inc., located in Lévis, Que., has been awarded a separate contract valued at more than $3 billion to build another polar icebreaker that will be named the Ccgs Arpatuuq.

The federal government also announced last month that Chantier Davie will lead the construction of six program icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard, which will help maintain year-round trade in Eastern Canada.
That contract is valued at $11.3 billion and is expected to create nearly 5,000 jobs during the construction phase that is set to begin in 2027.

stories.title: One girlfriend survived. One did not: W5 Exclusive
stories.summary: In a W5 Exclusive investigation, a former girlfriend of a Canadian man convicted of femicide in Mexico breaks her silence.
stories.author: Avery Haines
stories.content:
This is part two of a three-part W5 investigation series. Part three will be released Thursday. You can read part one here .

Watch the W5 investigation “If I’m Ever Found Dead” on our CTV News YouTube channel .

Warning: Graphic content.

When 28-year-old Keyana McNeil, of Vancouver, learned that a young Canadian woman had been brutally beaten to death at a resort in Mexico, she nearly passed out.

Her first thought: It could have been, it nearly was, me.

In 2023, the brutalized body of 23-year-old Kiara was discovered in the laundry room of an all-inclusive resort in Playa del Carmen, Mexico. Her boyfriend, Ryan Friesen from Dawson Creek, B.C., was found fast asleep beside her body, his fists swollen. A Mexican court initially found him not guilty of femicide. Early in 2026, the acquittal was overturned with a judge finding Friesen guilty of killing Kiara, a decision he is now appealing while free in Canada.

Keyana dated Friesen before he met Kiara. In an exclusive interview with W5, she says the pattern that ended Kiara’s life is one she survived herself, years earlier.

“I should have spoken up and been loud about it when it happened to me,” she said, “so that people could get an idea of who he truly is.”

‘I accepted my death’

Keyana describes an on-again-off-again relationship that she says escalated from control into repeated, severe physical violence over roughly three years.

“Choking, hitting, pushing,” she said. “He attacked me brutally.”

In one incident, she says, Friesen dragged her by her hair into a bathtub and turned on the shower because she was covered in blood.

“And then he sat there and continuously called me names, told me I was worthless.”

She says she believed in that moment that she might not survive.

“I accepted my death and I gave up trying to fight back. And I just went numb, limp and just said, ‘OK, I might die here.’”

Isolation, manipulation and control

Beyond the physical violence, Keyana describes years of psychological abuse and shared text messages from his phone number describing her as a “waste of skin” and threatening her.

“I was isolated from any support, family, friends,” she said. “He would purposely destroy relationships so that… he was the only person I had.”

Keyana says she barely recognizes the person she was back then.

“I was not me when I was with him,” she said. “I am quite strong as a person, but with somebody like him, you start questioning who you are.”

She calls him “a master manipulator.”

Neighbours who didn’t come

Keyana says that on more than one occasion, people were close enough to hear what was happening and no one intervened.

She says Friesen had two roommates in the house at the time of the bathtub incident.

“I was yelling for help. I was trying to be loud so that they would hear me and nobody came to the door. Nobody checked on me,” she said.

She says Friesen’s status as an athlete May have shaped how people saw him.

“Everybody just thought he was fantastic,” she said. “I was like, ‘What, ‘cause he’s good at hockey?’”

A break-in and a court order

Keyana described one night at her parents’ home when she says she discovered Friesen hiding inside her bedroom closet.

“It looked like he (was) on something.”

Keyana says her father chased Friesen from the house.

Court records show that in 2018, Friesen was charged with assaulting Keyana. She claims Friesen pressured her to tell authorities that she had instigated the physical altercation, in exchange for a promise that he would leave her alone.

“I just wish I was stronger then, to know that I should just stick with what was the truth,” she said.

The charge was ultimately dropped and a no-contact order was issued in 2019. Keyana says Friesen violated that order at least four times, ranging from unwanted contact by phone and on social media to showing up in person. In one instance, she says, he hid in the bed of her father’s truck outside her workplace.

“He jumped out when I had stopped at a stop sign,” she said.

Keyana says she called police every time. “And each time they said there’s nothing we can do.”

The detail that haunts her

Keyana says her life with Friesen mirrors what she’s since learned about Kiara’s.

Both women, she says, were isolated from family and friends. Both described extreme jealousy and control. Both documented their injuries in photographs.

One survived. One did not.

Keyana says the similarity that haunts her more than any other was what she learned about how Kiara died.

She says that after violent episodes, Friesen would simply go to sleep beside her, as though nothing had happened.

“He flipped out. He was violent,” she said, describing one incident. “And then at the end when he was done, he fell asleep right beside me and I stayed up wondering why that happened, wondering if I did something. And he was just asleep.”

Asked if this happened more than once, she said: “Multiple times ... it was like a regular thing.”

Friesen was initially found not guilty in Kiara’s death on Sept. 17, 2024. He immediately returned to Canada.

Just one day after the verdict, Keyana says she received a single-word text from his number: “Hey.”

She didn’t respond. She says the message reignited fears she has tried to move past.

“I even slept with a knife beside my bed for a period of time, once he got back,” she said.

‘I don’t believe he’s changed’

Keyana says the fear has never fully left her, even years removed from the relationship.

“I’ve had moments where I go and check all the rooms in the house in the middle of the night. I sleep with my closet open,” she said.

She describes recurring nightmares: “Feeling like I’m running and can’t get away from him,” she said. “I wake up and I’ll have my heart racing, and I will go make sure everything in the house is OK, all the doors are locked.”

She carries guilt, she says, over not speaking out sooner, a guilt amplified by what happened to Kiara.

“Maybe if I would have said something and been more vocal, somebody would have known and maybe she wouldn’t have been with him.”

Mexico was the first country in Latin America to make femicide a specific crime in the penal code. The crime carries a sentence of between 50 and 80 years’ imprisonment. Under Mexican law, a murder is classified as a femicide if it meets certain criteria, including a history of intimate partner violence against women.

Keyana has one message to the judges in Mexico who are right now deciding whether to uphold Friesen’s guilty verdict.

“He will do it again if he can,” she said. “Somebody like that doesn’t just change. That was proven from my experience to Kiara’s. That’s who he is.”

Friesen has not responded to W5’s request for comment but in a previous statement through his lawyer has maintained his innocence.

There is no timeline on a decision from the Mexican courts on Friesen’s appeal but if the guilty verdict is upheld, the extradition process to return Friesen to Mexico for sentencing would begin.

You can read parts 1 , 2 and 3 of W5’s previous investigative series on Kiara Agnew’s murder, and Part 1 on the legal fight surrounding Ryan Friesen here .

You can also watch W5’s “If I’m Ever Found Dead” on CTV News’ YouTube channel .

W5 is the multiplatform investigative unit of CTV News, continuing its decades-long commitment to covering tough, relevant stories.

stories.title: Ottawa and Alberta pledge to build at least 1,460 affordable houses
stories.summary: Ottawa will provide up to $220-million through Build Canada Homes, while Alberta will pay up to $165-million
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The federal government and Alberta are pledging to build at least 1,460 affordable housing units across the province.

Ottawa will provide up to $220-million through Build Canada Homes, a federal agency formed to speed up the delivery of the housing, while Alberta will pay up to $165-million.

The governments are expecting to receive $238-million from other sources.

A news release says the 21 planned housing projects will include supportive and transitional housing.

stories.title: Born on 9/11: Canadians turning 25 mark a day of both happiness and mourning
stories.summary: 'I never realized the gravity of my birthday until the first time my dad took me to New York when I was 10 years old.'
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
'I never realized the gravity of my birthday until the first time my dad took me to New York when I was 10 years old.'

When Monica Spoletini tells people she was born on Sept. 11, 2001, “Nine times out of 10 I get a look and … nine times out of 10 the second question is ‘on the year? On 2001?’

“And I just smile and (say) yep,” she says.

2026 marks the 25th anniversary of the hijacked airplane strikes on the Twin Towers, the Pentagon, and the crash of a fourth plane in Pennsylvania. All told, the attacks claimed the lives of 2,977 people , including 24 Canadians .

On that same day, as many as 13,238 people were born in the United States. It’s not known exactly how many Canadians also took their first breath Sept. 11, 2011, but Statistics Canada says average daily births in September in that period numbered 1,067 .

Among those Canadians were Monica and her twin brother, born in Chestermere, Alta. Both will turn 25 on Sept. 11. Spoletini now works as a hairdresser in Edmonton, where her family moved when she was 12. (Her brother declined an interview.)

Neither twin has yet visited the 9/11 memorial in New York City; however, they were acquainted with the events of 9/11 from a young age, because their father read them articles about it, says Monica Spoletini.

“(He) wanted to educate us a little bit (about) why everyone knows our birthday so much and why it’s so recognized,” Spoletini says.

One of her most vivid memories is of an old article that her parents framed on the wall, featuring her family. “I would say maybe (we were) eight or nine years old, and we could really understand why” it was so significant.

Christopher Rutkowski was born in Oshawa, Ont. on Sept. 11, 2001.

He says some of his friends believe he is a reincarnated 9/11 victim. “I was born about six hours before the first plane hit. And I have a birthmark on the right side of my face.” His friends theorize that he was initially a financier working in the towers. “I didn’t make it (out alive) — and then, ‘real Christopher’ was born.”

CBC reverses policy against calling 9/11 a terrorist attack without attribution

How Canada's best-known 9/11 widow became a fierce advocate for terrorist victims

Rutkowski has visited the memorial at the site of the World Trade Centre three times, the most recent visit in August.

“I never realized the gravity of my birthday until the first time my dad took me to New York when I was 10 years old,” he says. He also visited on his 15th birthday.

With his father, he went to the Ground Zero museum, which he recalls displayed “steel columns and pillars and escalators (from the site)… and people’s stories and phone recordings.”

Rutkowski, who calls himself a “big reader,” says he has spent years expanding his home library dedicated to 9/11 to properly commemorate the event.

The Spoletini twins, who had planned to visit the site some years ago, were delayed when COVID struck. Now that they lead independent lives, coordination is a bit of challenge, Monica Spoletini admits, adding that “it definitely is something that the two of us want to do together.”

The challenge of being born on 9/11 has been difficult for some.

For instance, “My family pretends it isn’t a thing. My birthday, I mean,” one person wrote on Reddit. “I was born in NYC, actually between the time the first and second towers were hit. My parents were pretty scarred (sic) by it so we just pretend I don’t have a birthday.”

Another posted: “My best friend was born on the date. She gets a lot of sympathy aww’s and, “Oh, honey” comments. She does joke that our high school has an assembly for her birthday every year though so … ”

“My daughter was born on 9/11/2001 a few hours before the 1st plane hit. First few birthdays were rough for the family and we didn’t celebrate day of but by now we do. I think it makes her feel kind of special being born that day. But she shows respect and knows the significance of the tragedy,” wrote one mom.

For his part, Rutkowski believes in balancing both aspects of the date — taking joy at being born, yet honouring the victims of the tragedy: “It’s a double-edged sword in a sense.”

Spoletini feels the sadness too. But she also believes in a purpose: “I was raised religious, so normally… my parents would say: ‘there was a reason God brought you into the world on that day.’ I also believe in God, but I also do believe in the universe as well.

“I do think, you know, the universe or God, or whoever’s outside of us, brought us here on that day too. To… teach us.”

Both have major plans for their birthdays.

For the Spoletinis, it is the time for a family reunion, and, says Monica, “I’m planning … to realize that I’m actually 25 years old and that my brain is fully developed and that I’m grown up.”

Rutkowski, ON his third visit to the site last month, stopped in at Fire Engine Company No. 65, which was among the first to respond to the disaster. Rutkowski met New York firefighters at the station during one of his earlier visits too.

He is also training to run a 5K obstacle course to honour the victims of 9/11 and demonstrate resilience: “(T)his will be my first year doing it.”

And he concludes: “If things are going bad or I’m having a bad day, you know, people have had a lot worse days or the bad doesn’t last forever or there’s always going to be some sort of good in something bad that happens.

“And so, it’s taught me to be patient and full of gratitude.”

stories.title: Jay Baruchel’s fast and furious dream to rocket Canadian film into the stratosphere
stories.summary: Ahead of The Stunt Driver’s Tiff world premiere, the star talks with Barry Hertz about the film he’s been working his entire career toward
stories.author: Barry Hertz, Photography by David Kerr
stories.content:
The plan was simple. Construct a 430-metre ramp on a patch of farmland near Morrisburg, Ont. Then use that ramp to launch a rocket-powered Lincoln Continental across a 1.6-kilometre stretch of the St. Lawrence River, where the vehicle would land safe and snug on the other side of the Canada-U.S. border, a bed of freshly planted roses cushioning its fall. The only challenge: There had to be a person behind the wheel of that Lincoln. And that person would need to survive the ramp, the jump, and, of course, the landing.

In 1976, Ken “The Mad Canadian” Carter planned just such a feat, as much a bid to cement his daredevil legacy as it was to prove to the world that Canadians had just as much heart, courage, and never-say-die tenacity (to say nothing of unhinged audacity) as our neighbours to the south. And now, a half-century and a few cultural-sovereignty crises later, actor Jay Baruchel is immortalizing Carter’s 400-km-an-hour journey in director Michael Dowse’s The Stunt Driver , a wild, hilarious, heartbreaking, and surprisingly timely new movie that only a fellow Mad Canadian such as himself could headline.

“First and foremost, this is just a great entertaining old-school movie. But it is also very much a meditation on the condition of being Canadian. It works on a bunch of different levels and scratches a bunch of different itches. But any Canadian who sees themselves in it, that’s not an accident,” says the Ottawa-born, Montreal-raised, and now Toronto-based actor.

“That’s something we talked about throughout the entire movie, and everything you’re feeling connected to as a Canadian is all deliberate. That is all a bunch of Dowse and I and a bunch of crabby Canadian men of a certain time period getting a lot of stuff out of their system.”

It is a few weeks before The Stunt Driver makes its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, and Baruchel is interrupting his last-gasp-of-summer vacation at his cottage about an hour outside Kingston – a wood-panelled hideaway with mosquitos and spotty Wi-Fi, or about as Canadian a retreat as it gets – to trace the development of what might be the movie that he’s been working his entire career toward .

In the business for more than a quarter-century, starting with roles on such tween-flavoured series as Are You Afraid of the Dark? and Popular Mechanics for Kids , Baruchel spent much of his 20s and 30s keeping one foot in Hollywood, the other at home in Canada.

At a certain point, it might have simply been easier for the actor to migrate south completely like fellow Canadian Seth Rogen, the two actors becoming key players in that now-distant, bygone era when any Judd Apatow-associated comedy ( Knocked Up , This Is the End ) could dominate the box office and discourse for weeks. Instead, Baruchel kept evolving his roster of collaborators – Clint Eastwood to Ben Stiller to David Cronenberg to a pre- Heated Rivalry Jacob Tierney – while increasingly focusing on what he could do within, and for, the Canadian industry.

“I grew up in Montreal and I also grew up in Oshawa at the arse end of the eighties, and it was a pretty bleak time in Canada. I was a TV and movie addict, but I’d go outside in Oshawa and be like, well, I might as well be on Mars because how do you get into that? From here to there?” Baruchel recalls. “The one thing that would tell me I could do it here was the existence of the National Film Board and the CBC. They have been many things to me, but one of them is a beacon. So if we can play even a tiny role in that, that’s a pretty big source of pride.”

Then use that ramp to launch a rocket-powered Lincoln Continental across a 1.6-kilometre stretch of the St. Lawrence River, where the vehicle would land safe and snug on the other side of the Canada-U.S. border, a bed of freshly planted roses cushioning its fall. The only challenge: There had to be a person behind the wheel of that Lincoln. And that person would need to survive the ramp, the jump, and, of course, the landing.

In 1976, Ken “The Mad Canadian” Carter planned just such a feat, as much a bid to cement his daredevil legacy as it was to prove to the world that Canadians had just as much heart, courage, and never-say-die tenacity (to say nothing of unhinged audacity) as our neighbours to the south. And now, a half-century and a few cultural-sovereignty crises later, actor Jay Baruchel is immortalizing Carter’s 400-km-an-hour journey in director Michael Dowse’s The Stunt Driver , a wild, hilarious, heartbreaking, and surprisingly timely new movie that only a fellow Mad Canadian such as himself could headline.

“First and foremost, this is just a great entertaining old-school movie. But it is also very much a meditation on the condition of being Canadian. It works on a bunch of different levels and scratches a bunch of different itches. But any Canadian who sees themselves in it, that’s not an accident,” says the Ottawa-born, Montreal-raised, and now Toronto-based actor.

stories.title: Ontario's new high school grading scheme 'a lot more pressure' for students, teens say
stories.summary: High school students in Ontario are going into the first year of the province's education policy changes, which include mandatory final exams and attendance grading.
stories.author: Kendra Seguin
paragraphs: London·Video
High school students in Ontario are going into the first year of the province's education policy changes, which include mandatory final exams and attendance grading.
· Posted: Sep 09, 2026 5:22 AM EDT | Last Updated: 39 minutes ago

Expectations are changing for high school students in Ontario, who will be the first group to go through the province's new grading scheme, which puts more emphasis on attendance and final evaluations.
Education Minister Paul Calandra announced the changes earlier this year, saying then that the ministry has "heard constantly" from teachers that they need better control of classrooms
"We've been hearing about it all day," said grade 11 student Rowynn Whaley, who attends H.B. Beal Secondary School in London, Ont. "They're making it such a big deal."
Back to school: Everything you need to know about Ontario's education policy changes
Ontario has unveiled mandatory changes for schools, starting this fall. Here's what you need to know
Starting this year, students in grades 9 and 10 will be graded on 65 per cent of class work, 20 per cent on final evaluations and 15 per cent on attendance and participation.
Grade 11 and 12 students will be marked on 65 per cent of class work, 25 per cent on final evaluations and 10 per cent on attendance and participation.
What are students saying about Ontario's new grade breakdown?

"I'm not too happy about it. I don't think any of us are," Whaley said about the new attendance marks. "Not that I skip class a lot, but I just feel like as long as I'm getting my work done and things are getting handed in, showing up shouldn't really matter that much."

According to the province's website, students who miss two classes or fewer and consistently participate in class will receive 80 to 100 per cent of their participation marks. Those who miss more than nine classes and don't participate at all will receive less than 50 per cent of the mark.
Attendance for high schoolers, elementary students is plummeting in Ontario: data
Ontario education minister urges parents not to pull kids from school for sports
Excused absences such as illness or cultural days will not negatively affect a students' marks, the website says.
"It's fair because some people are skipping and don't come to school," said Catholic Central Secondary School student Jana Ibrahim. "I think that it's better."
Several students told CBC News the increased focus on final exams is anxiety-inducing and raises the expectations for high schoolers across the province.
"It's a lot more pressure in that aspect. It's good, but I'm kind of nervous," said Margarita Balbin, who is starting Grade 11 at Catholic Central.
New high school student Bailey Becker said she's staying positive as she starts the next chapter of schooling amid the new changes.
"I feel like some of the changes are a little bit too much, but I think I'll be OK."
Other teenagers said there should be more support for students preparing for exams this year, considering the raised stakes.

"Some teachers ... expect you to put all your focus into their lessons, but they're not accommodating if you need help and I think it's kind of ridiculous that they're going to make our exams 25 per cent," said Grade 12 Beal student Charli Lockhart.
Ragad Ibrahim, who attends Catholic Central, said she thinks final exams should be open book going forward.
"25 [per cent] is a really big number," she said.
However, Grade 12 student Sarina Haghighatnama said she thinks students can succeed with the new grading scheme, so long as they put in the effort.

"I think if you study, you can get a high mark," she said. "If you're just skipping and don't care, then absolutely you'll fail, but if you just focus, [go to] class and do everything, you're going to absolutely get a good mark."

According to the province's website, students who miss two classes or fewer and consistently participate in class will receive 80 to 100 per cent of their participation marks. Those who miss more than nine classes and don't participate at all will receive less than 50 per cent of the mark.

Attendance for high schoolers, elementary students is plummeting in Ontario: data

Ontario education minister urges parents not to pull kids from school for sports

Excused absences such as illness or cultural days will not negatively affect a students' marks, the website says.

"It's fair because some people are skipping and don't come to school," said Catholic Central Secondary School student Jana Ibrahim. "I think that it's better."

Several students told CBC News the increased focus on final exams is anxiety-inducing and raises the expectations for high schoolers across the province.

"It's a lot more pressure in that aspect. It's good, but I'm kind of nervous," said Margarita Balbin, who is starting Grade 11 at Catholic Central.

New high school student Bailey Becker said she's staying positive as she starts the next chapter of schooling amid the new changes.

"I feel like some of the changes are a little bit too much, but I think I'll be OK."

Other teenagers said there should be more support for students preparing for exams this year, considering the raised stakes.

"Some teachers ... expect you to put all your focus into their lessons, but they're not accommodating if you need help and I think it's kind of ridiculous that they're going to make our exams 25 per cent," said Grade 12 Beal student Charli Lockhart.

Ragad Ibrahim, who attends Catholic Central, said she thinks final exams should be open book going forward.

"25 [per cent] is a really big number," she said.

However, Grade 12 student Sarina Haghighatnama said she thinks students can succeed with the new grading scheme, so long as they put in the effort.

"I think if you study, you can get a high mark," she said. "If you're just skipping and don't care, then absolutely you'll fail, but if you just focus, [go to] class and do everything, you're going to absolutely get a good mark."

stories.title: Okamoto, Smith hit home runs to help Blue Jays down Athletics
stories.summary: Toronto (73-73) sits one game back of the Cleveland Guardians (74-72) for the third and final American League wild-card spot.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Posted September 9, 2026 5:21 am.

Kazuma Okamoto and Josh Smith hit home runs, José Soriano worked seven innings of two-run ball, and the Toronto Blue Jays beat the Athletics 4-2 on Tuesday night.

Toronto (73-73) sits one game back of the Cleveland Guardians (74-72) for the third and final American League wild-card spot. The Guardians beat the Baltimore Orioles 9-5 earlier in the day.

The Texas Rangers, who beat the Mariners 10-5 in Seattle on Tuesday, are a half-game behind the Blue Jays.

Smith, who was traded from the Texas Rangers on Aug. 3, opened the scoring in the second inning with a 360-foot shot to give Toronto a 1-0 lead. In his 20 games with the Blue Jays, he has five homers.

Okamoto followed in the next at-bat with the 30th home run of his rookie season. He joins Shohei Ohtani, Hideki Matsui, Seiya Suzuki and Munetaka Murakami as the only Japanese players to complete the feat.

The milestone also marked the first time in major league history that three rookies have hit 30 or more home runs in the same season. Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart is the other.

Okamoto already set the Blue Jays record for most home runs by a rookie in a season when he belted his 25th of the year against the Tampa Bay Rays in August.

Alejandro Kirk hit an RBI single, and Smith capped the scoring by grounding into a one-run double play.

Soriano (12-7), who was traded from the Los Angeles Angels on Aug. 3 as well, struck out three and gave up six hits. Spencer Miles worked two hitless innings for his second save of the season.

Carlos Cortes and Donovan Walton each had home runs for the Athletics.

Athletics starting pitcher Jack Perkins (3-11) allowed all four runs on seven hits while fanning three.

Athletics’ LHP Brady Basso(1-2, 4.32 ERA) takes the mound on Wednesday. The Blue Jays will turn to reliever Braydon Fisher, expected to serve as the opener.
