stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 1 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 1 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 1 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Hadleigh McAlister

Occupation: Full-time city councillor

Family: My wife Samantha, our daughter Maeve and our dog Charlie.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

I live in Ward 1.

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation?

I have and will continue to work full-time as a city councillor.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Housing and homelessness

Infrastructure

Improving city services

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I have the utmost respect for the Mathyssen family. Irene and Lindsay were compassionate and dedicated politicians who served their constituents well. I have had the pleasure of working with both and I endeavour to live up to the high standard of public service they set.

5. What is your vision for London?

I want everyone to be proud to call London their home. To achieve a higher quality of life that Londoners deserve, our city services need to meet the current and future needs of Londoners. It is important that we continue to invest in our recreational facilities, parks, infrastructure, libraries, transit, housing and homeless solutions. I want London to be a safe, accessible, inclusive, and prosperous city for current residents and future generations.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Londoners are faced with many socio-economic challenges right now. Our economy is still sluggish and adapting to volatile markets, housing and groceries have become unaffordable, and we’ve seen high numbers of people experiencing homelessness in our city. Over the last four years efforts have been made to address these important issues at the local level. London cannot solve all the challenges alone and to make real headway we need to have greater co-ordination between all levels of government.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I have recent experience dealing with the current challenges facing Ward 1 and London. When I took office in 2022, I saw what decades of neglect had done to Ward 1. I have worked tirelessly to ensure that the city invests in Ward 1. In four years, I have been able to secure historic investments in our aging recreational facilities and infrastructure. I have also been a vocal advocate for housing affordability, addressing homelessness and dealing with food security in London. I have a proven track record of working collaboratively with community organizations, city staff, my council colleagues, and provincial and federal representatives. I understand the current challenges that our city faces and will continue to be a strong and effective representative for Ward 1 and London.

Name: Roger Caranci

Occupation: Real estate agent

Family : Father of two and grandfather of five.

I will continue working as a real estate agent in a reduced capacity.

Safer streets through support for police, bylaw enforcement, and zero tolerance for tent cities and open drug use. Affordable housing that respects our neighbourhoods and fits the community. Getting back to basics by repairing potholes, plowing snow on time and protecting and maintaining our parks.

At this point, I identify most with my former colleague, the late Tom Gosnell. He built relationships, forged compromise and got things done. He returned to council after some time away and delivered a unique and invaluable perspective. Above all, he earned and maintained the trust of the people who elected him. That is the standard I set for myself when I served before and it is the standard I will bring back.

A well-run city. Currently listed as priority #8 of the City of London’s strategic plan. It should be #1. Cleaner streets and safer neighbourhoods. London should deliver the basics well and reject decline as inevitable. I want a city that supports families, businesses, and people who play by the rules.

Public safety and the condition of our streets and neighbourhoods. Too many people feel the city has lost control of parks, business areas, and open drug use. Basic services have slipped in favour of grandiose projects. It’s time for focus and accountability.

I have already done the job and I am proud of my record. As councillor from 2000 to 2010, I helped deliver the Hale-Trafalgar overpass, the HELP clean water initiative, and the renaming of Airport Road to Veterans Memorial Parkway. As president of Residenza Affordable Housing, our team has built and maintained 300 beautiful affordable homes for seniors, veterans, and low-income families. I bring experience, common sense and a record of results.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 2 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 2 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 2 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Shawn Lewis

Age: a full fledged GenX, 54

Occupation : City councillor & deputy mayor

Family : Single, 1 cat, and a hockey team worth of nephews and their friends.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Yes, I live in Ward 2 and have been proud to call the east end my home for over 25 years.

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation?

Yes and I strongly believe it must be to properly do the job for a city of half a million people.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Every candidate will say homeless and addiction, but that must come alongside a recognition that the city cannot fix that alone, that there are provincial and federal changes needed. Some changes cannot be direct action via property taxes, but advocating with other levels of government and also has to include appropriate measures for community safety and policing.

Ensuring Ward 2 and the east end is getting necessary infrastructure renewal.

Enhancing customer service and efficiency at city hall for Londoners and providing good value for taxes in our services.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I learned a great deal from two women in our city, Cheryl Miller, who was a TVDSB trustee and then a member of council, and Irene Mathyssen, who served as a Member of Parliament who I had the privilege of working directly for. I also developed a great relationship and learned from Mayor Ed Holder in my first term on council.

5. What is your vision for London?

My vision for London is for it to be a vibrant city that competes regionally and globally and offers a wide range of opportunities for work, housing, entertainment, and an excellent quality of life for the people who call it home, a city that is seen as the capital of Southwestern Ontario.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

The biggest challenge facing London today is a problem not of our making, and shared by cities across the province and country, the issue of homelessness and addiction and the safety and economic problems that come from that.

It is a challenge created by the province closing mental health hospitals and providing rates of social assistance too low to help people and by a federal government that failed to match immigration policies to housing, education, health care, and infrastructure capacity to absorb newcomers appropriately. It is a problem that all 3 levels of government, as well as non-profits, charitable, faith organizations and civil society at large need to do their parts to address.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

The difference with me is I don’t tell people what I think they want to hear, I give them an honest answer even if I know they won’t like it. I don’t make grand promises to fix things or do things that a city simply cannot just do. At the same time my record speaks for itself, the promises I made in both my previous elections have been kept, I’ve brought those things forward and delivered results. I’m straightforward and my residents in Ward 2 know they can approach me in the grocery store or at the Malibu or wherever they run into me and chat, because I live, work, and play here, Ward 2 is my home too.

Name : Zack Ramsey

Occupation: Concrete construction worker

Family: I have a wife and two cats (Harvey and Booga)

I do not. I live just on the west side of Highbury Avenue. I chose to run in Ward 2 as it is where I spend a majority of my time and “living” in a ward should be defined as where you spend your awake time not where you sleep.

City council will be my sole occupation. I have worked 40- to 60-hour weeks all my life and I have no plans to slow down in such an important role.

Treat the crisis we face like crisis (homelessness, affordability, housing, etc.)

Organizing London tenants, workers, and communities so Londoners have more power to improve their lives.

Reforest the Forest City. (Expand our canopy coverage, grow more food in public, improve our parks, etc.)

I like a few city politicians but, none enough to say that I identify with them. While I love politics, I am running because I am disappointed in my elected officials. I am disappointed that instead of finding solutions that will improve the quality of Londoners’ lives they continue to make excuses at every opportunity.

I want London to be a place where you have a roof above your head, food in your belly, and the knowledge that your children will have a more prosperous future than yourself! I envision a London where people have free time to live their lives how they like and can be involved in their community!

Affordability: it affects all the other crisis London faces. If folks are paid too little and charged too much it forces them to work longer hours, which disconnects them from their community and their passions. When you have to work more hours you have to spend less time with your kids, less time with your friends, less time spent on your passions, and less time spent improving your city. Many Londoners are forced to make choices between food and rent or food and medication.

I do not believe that any of the problems we face can be solved solely by city council. To solve these large systemic issues it will require the collective effort of every Londoner. I believe the crisis we face are a feature of the system we live in not an accident or mistake. Every crisis that exists only exists because it is not profitable to solve.

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Steve Reed, Alexandria Hames

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 3 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 3 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 3 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Peter Cuddy

Occupation : Ward 3 councillor, City of London

Family: Wife Lisa, 3 children

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

YES. City councillor has been my full-time job since being elected in 2022 and will continue to be my full-time occupation.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Serving the residents of Ward 3 and responding to their needs without delay.

Keep in property taxes in line with inflation or below inflation.

Cutting red tape at city hall.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Bernie MacDonald

5. What is your vision for London?

London has so much commercial and industrial opportunity due to our proximity to international trading partners, transportation infrastructure and our fast-growing economy. I want to build on that vision of economic growth. Revitalizing our downtown, encouraging residential development in our downtown by means of housing our homeless with the assistance of both federal and provincial governments. This will bring long-term sustainable growth to our core. All the while, we need to keep our property taxes in lockstep with inflation or below. Responsible fiscal management and keeping our city’s 4-star Moodys credit rating are critical to London’s growth.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Mental health / addiction, homelessness issues and the housing of our highest acuity are our greatest challenge. For this to succeed, we need to continue to partner with all levels of government to ensure long-term sustainable solutions are implemented.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

My constituents will tell you that I am the hardest working councillor since Bernie MacDonald. That is high praise, as Bernie is a legend in Ward 3, and a role model to me personally. I respond to all residents as quickly as possible, often within the hour of their email or text. I call every resident personally for follow up calls to ensure their concerns have been resolved to their satisfaction. I am conciliatory, working with my colleagues to find solutions in committee and on council. My motions are often passed unanimously, as was the case of the renoviction motion passed in 2024. I speak to my colleagues to ask for their opinions, and ways to improve motions about to come to committee or council.

Name: Ben Durham

Occupation : Creative director, video producer, entrepreneur

Family: Happily married to the most amazing and supportive wife in London.

I live and own a home in Ward 3.

Yes, if elected as Ward 3 city councillor, this will be my sole full-time occupation.

In addition, if I had been at that table, I would have moved two amendments to the proposal:

1. Remove the part-time option entirely (because we are no longer a small city), and

2. Scale back the increase to a more modest, fiscally responsible number, rather than 35%

Smarter traffic, safer streets

Financial accountability

Tackle homelessness now

None. I’m my own person and I don’t pattern myself after other leaders.

My vision of London is one where:

London’s taken a leadership role by learning from successes around the world and adapting them for our city’s specific economic and geographic needs.

Transportation is modernized and allows more options for more people. Congestion is reduced, commutes are pleasant and predictable, and we’ve adapted well to our vibrant mid-sized city of London, Ontario.

The homelessness crisis is a thing of the past and the downtown is a bustling district with a strong pulse. Communities across London all have their own distinct personalities and draws but because of everyone tirelessly fighting for a better London together, we accomplish what many thought to be impossible: a brighter future for London.

Most people say “homelessness” is London’s biggest challenge (when asked).

However, after knocking on thousands of doors across Ward 3 and tallying residents’ concerns, it’s clear to me (with a sample size of thousands) that traffic-related issues such as road work co-ordination, traffic congestion, street safety (speeding), and road maintenance are cumulatively their most major concern.

That’s why, since day one, I’ve made “Smarter Traffic, Safer Streets” the NUMBER ONE PILLAR for my platform.

I’m the charismatic and strategic leader Ward 3 needs right now.

I’m firm but kind and determined to get things done.

No one else can outwork my dedication and time management skills.

I wake up at 7am, work until 3pm, and then tirelessly canvass 3-9pm, and then get the best sleeps of my life. And I have been doing this 6 days per week for the last few months and will continue to do so until October 26th (election day).

Name : Harkirat Kaur

Occupation : Disability support worker

Family: I come from a close-knit family and have built my life in London. My family has taught me the value of hard work, responsibility, perseverance and looking out for the people around me.

Yes. I live in Ward 3.

Yes. If elected, I will treat the role as a full-time responsibility. Being a councillor is more than attending council meetings. It means being accessible to residents, understanding what is happening in the ward, following up on concerns and being prepared to do the work between meetings. I would make serving Ward 3 my priority.

My three priorities are better-connected transportation, safer and stronger neighbourhoods, and more responsive city services. Ward 3 deserves reliable bus service, better cycling and active-transportation connections, and infrastructure that reflects how people actually move around our community. I also want to see safer neighbourhoods and more quality green space, including opportunities for a larger park where our community can gather and families can enjoy the outdoors. Finally, residents should be able to count on city services that are responsive, practical and accountable.

I respect many people who have served London, but I would not say that I model myself after one particular politician. I am running to bring my own perspective and to be an independent voice for Ward 3. I believe good representation starts with listening, asking difficult questions when necessary and making decisions based on what is best for residents – not simply following the way things have always been done.

I want London to be a city where people can build a good life and feel proud of the neighbourhood they call home. That means reliable public transportation, safer streets, accessible cycling and active-transportation routes, quality parks and green spaces, and city services that respond when residents need them. I also want London to grow thoughtfully, with infrastructure and services keeping pace with that growth. My vision is a city that is connected, safe, welcoming and practical – a city that works for families, seniors, students, workers and future generations.

One of our biggest challenges is ensuring that London’s growth keeps pace with the infrastructure and services residents depend on. We cannot measure success simply by how much the city grows. We also have to ask whether people can get where they need to go, whether neighbourhoods feel safe, whether there is enough quality green space and whether residents can get timely, responsive service from the city. Affordability and housing pressures add to that challenge. London needs thoughtful growth that improves quality of life rather than putting additional pressure on the people who already live here.

I am not a career politician, and I believe that gives me a different perspective. I am a working professional and someone who has spent my career working directly with people and understanding the challenges they face. I am not running for a title – I am running because I believe Ward 3 deserves a strong, independent and accessible voice at city hall. I will listen to residents, ask questions, do the work and be accountable for the decisions I make. I may be new to politics, but I am not new to responsibility, service or hard work.

Name : Leroy Osbourne

Age: respectfully decline. I wish for voters to look at my experience and community contributions than my birth year.

Occupation: university staffer

Family: respectfully decline given how divisive politics has been in recent years.

Yes, the council role will be my sole occupation and responsibility after family.

Cost of housing

Cost of living

Infrastructure

Tough to say just one. The personable, charismatic, commitment of Harold Usher. The thoughtfulness and straightforwardness of Jesse Helmer. The articulation and compassion of Sam Trosow and David Ferreira.

A place where people are proud of their city, has top-quality infrastructure, places that create an experience, addresses affordability and improves the quality of life of all of us.

Cost of living – addresses housing, poverty, quality of life.

Breadth of experience; I have seen issues up front for a long time. I have smart, innovative and pragmatic ideas for my ward and our city. From little homes communities, a community wealth fund idea and on-demand mini-buses for unserved areas. I want to look at successful initiatives of other municipalities, not reinventing the wheel or having endless staff and consultant reports. I wish to participate in decisive decisions that move us forward in positive ways.

Name: Zak Rahim

Occupation : I run a political consulting agency that has helped good people get elected to deliver positive results for our community. I believe that the political process is the true vehicle for positive change and I channel this belief into my small business. As a volunteer on the frontline of the homelessness crisis since 2017, I’ve dedicated my time to dealing with the worsening socioeconomic crisis in our community in real time.

Family : I’m unmarried with no kids. Like many young Londoners, the milestone of being married, finding your first home, and having kids is moving further and further away. We are all being impacted by the current socioeconomic crisis. However, the way that this crisis is impacting my generation is making me fearful for those that come after me.

No, I do not own property, and I chose to stay at home outside of the ward to lend my support to my family. My elderly grandfather is dependent on our collective efforts. In a housing crisis, our seniors are choosing between a nutritious meal and paying rent on a fixed income. I’m inspired to run so that seniors, like my grandfather, who’ve worked hard their whole lives don’t have to choose between the two basic necessities of food or shelter.

Yes. The role of a London city councillor should be full time regardless of the pay. It should also be full time considering that council voted themselves a 35% pay raise, which is beyond the rate of inflation. This is quite a lot to ask from Londoners given the economic context. It is council’s responsibility to deliver value for this money, including setting performance standards for committee.

Public accountability starting with who we appoint to our agencies. When council appoints political actors and rubber stamp their budget proposal the result is sky-high tax increases. Instead I’ll appoint experts to hold administration to account and lower taxes.

On taxpayer value, that means cutting wasteful spending across the city and making sure city contracts go towards supporting London jobs & businesses.

The cost of housing has far outpaced income growth, while London’s homelessness numbers have had similar growth. I want density done right, building up instead of endless sprawl, protecting the character of our neighbourhoods while cutting the red tape that slows down the housing, including supportive housing, that is needed yesterday.

Mayor Mike Bradley of Sarnia never shied away from holding Sarnia’s agencies to account by bringing scrutiny to administrations’ proposals, cutting spending to keep more money in the pocket of citizens.

Mayor Ed Holder of London’s leadership during COVID, and in response to the murder of the Afzaal family, embodied strong leadership that brought people together in a crisis to work together to deliver for our community.

Mayor Joe Preston who says “yes is the answer, now what is the question.” Has led to bold developments in alleviating the housing and homelessness crisis and growing the economy in St. Thomas. We need this quality of leadership in London to say yes to bold ideas.

A city that says yes. Yes to housing, Yes to helping the most vulnerable, Yes to fighting the socioeconomic causes of the crime and disorder, and yes to keeping London affordable & vibrant.

London is facing a homelessness crisis that is made worse by our lack of institutional capacity. Yes, we started building more homes, but we remain behind the overall demand. The cost of living remains high, which pushes people to the streets. On the frontlines, I witnessed several people freeze to death in the winter. I spent my nights during the coldest point of winter at the city’s Boyle Memorial Community Centre warming shelter. I saw the city scrambling to effectively stand up its winter response services. Coupled with constantly hearing from Londoners that folks are struggling on our streets, I realized that we are lacking the proper means to give people some level of dignity in their lives.

I attended council throughout this term as an observer and advocated for policy decisions meant to improve the situation on our streets. I understand the cost of living crisis firsthand. I’ve seen the interrelated effects of homelessness. All of this prompts me to work tirelessly on the frontline. I bring a humanitarian perspective and business leadership that will translate into respecting the taxpayer, doing more with less and delivering results for Londoners.

I want to deliver results with compassion for our community in mind to ensure a better London for the next generation.

Name: Peter Cuddy
Occupation : Ward 3 councillor, City of London
Family: Wife Lisa, 3 children
1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?
YES. City councillor has been my full-time job since being elected in 2022 and will continue to be my full-time occupation.
3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?
Serving the residents of Ward 3 and responding to their needs without delay.
Keep in property taxes in line with inflation or below inflation.
Cutting red tape at city hall.
4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?
Bernie MacDonald
5. What is your vision for London?

London has so much commercial and industrial opportunity due to our proximity to international trading partners, transportation infrastructure and our fast-growing economy. I want to build on that vision of economic growth. Revitalizing our downtown, encouraging residential development in our downtown by means of housing our homeless with the assistance of both federal and provincial governments. This will bring long-term sustainable growth to our core. All the while, we need to keep our property taxes in lockstep with inflation or below. Responsible fiscal management and keeping our city’s 4-star Moodys credit rating are critical to London’s growth.
6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Mental health / addiction, homelessness issues and the housing of our highest acuity are our greatest challenge. For this to succeed, we need to continue to partner with all levels of government to ensure long-term sustainable solutions are implemented.
7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

My constituents will tell you that I am the hardest working councillor since Bernie MacDonald. That is high praise, as Bernie is a legend in Ward 3, and a role model to me personally. I respond to all residents as quickly as possible, often within the hour of their email or text. I call every resident personally for follow up calls to ensure their concerns have been resolved to their satisfaction. I am conciliatory, working with my colleagues to find solutions in committee and on council. My motions are often passed unanimously, as was the case of the renoviction motion passed in 2024. I speak to my colleagues to ask for their opinions, and ways to improve motions about to come to committee or council.
Name: Ben Durham
Occupation : Creative director, video producer, entrepreneur
Family: Happily married to the most amazing and supportive wife in London.
I live and own a home in Ward 3.
Yes, if elected as Ward 3 city councillor, this will be my sole full-time occupation.

1. Remove the part-time option entirely (because we are no longer a small city), and
2. Scale back the increase to a more modest, fiscally responsible number, rather than 35%
Smarter traffic, safer streets
Financial accountability
Tackle homelessness now
None. I’m my own person and I don’t pattern myself after other leaders.
My vision of London is one where:
London’s taken a leadership role by learning from successes around the world and adapting them for our city’s specific economic and geographic needs.

Transportation is modernized and allows more options for more people. Congestion is reduced, commutes are pleasant and predictable, and we’ve adapted well to our vibrant mid-sized city of London, Ontario.

The homelessness crisis is a thing of the past and the downtown is a bustling district with a strong pulse. Communities across London all have their own distinct personalities and draws but because of everyone tirelessly fighting for a better London together, we accomplish what many thought to be impossible: a brighter future for London.
Most people say “homelessness” is London’s biggest challenge (when asked).

However, after knocking on thousands of doors across Ward 3 and tallying residents’ concerns, it’s clear to me (with a sample size of thousands) that traffic-related issues such as road work co-ordination, traffic congestion, street safety (speeding), and road maintenance are cumulatively their most major concern.
That’s why, since day one, I’ve made “Smarter Traffic, Safer Streets” the NUMBER ONE PILLAR for my platform.
I’m the charismatic and strategic leader Ward 3 needs right now.
I’m firm but kind and determined to get things done.
No one else can outwork my dedication and time management skills.

I wake up at 7am, work until 3pm, and then tirelessly canvass 3-9pm, and then get the best sleeps of my life. And I have been doing this 6 days per week for the last few months and will continue to do so until October 26th (election day).
Name : Harkirat Kaur
Occupation : Disability support worker
Family: I come from a close-knit family and have built my life in London. My family has taught me the value of hard work, responsibility, perseverance and looking out for the people around me.
Yes. I live in Ward 3.

Yes. If elected, I will treat the role as a full-time responsibility. Being a councillor is more than attending council meetings. It means being accessible to residents, understanding what is happening in the ward, following up on concerns and being prepared to do the work between meetings. Ward 3 deserves reliable bus service, better cycling and active-transportation connections, and infrastructure that reflects how people actually move around our community. I also want to see safer neighbourhoods and more quality green space, including opportunities for a larger park where our community can gather and families can enjoy the outdoors. Finally, residents should be able to count on city services that are responsive, practical and accountable.

I respect many people who have served London, but I would not say that I model myself after one particular politician. I will listen to residents, ask questions, do the work and be accountable for the decisions I make. I may be new to politics, but I am not new to responsibility, service or hard work.

I believe good representation starts with listening, asking difficult questions when necessary and making decisions based on what is best for residents – not simply following the way things have always been done.

content_blocks.text: I want London to be a city where people can build a good life and feel proud of the neighbourhood they call home. That means reliable public transportation, safer streets, accessible cycling and active-transportation routes, quality parks and green spaces, and city services that respond when residents need them. I also want London to grow thoughtfully, with infrastructure and services keeping pace with that growth. My vision is a city that is connected, safe, welcoming and practical – a city that works for families, seniors, students, workers and future generations.

content_blocks.text: One of our biggest challenges is ensuring that London’s growth keeps pace with the infrastructure and services residents depend on. We cannot measure success simply by how much the city grows. We also have to ask whether people can get where they need to go, whether neighbourhoods feel safe, whether there is enough quality green space and whether residents can get timely, responsive service from the city. Affordability and housing pressures add to that challenge. London needs thoughtful growth that improves quality of life rather than putting additional pressure on the people who already live here.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 4 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 4 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 4 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name : Elivis Birindwa

Occupation: Composite specialist

Education (Police foundations diploma and Criminology degree)

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

No I do not live in the Ward 4 I’m running in, I relocated 2 years to Ward 2.

Yes council will be my sole occupation.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

My top three priorities if I’m elected

1. Create a much more safe community through stronger community ties.

2. Investing in our young people and create long-term vision for them.

3. Create better living conditions for tenants, all residents and fight to reduce property taxes.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Olivia Chow the current mayor of the City of Toronto is a particularly interesting politician to study when I’m looking at municipal leadership and campaigning.

1. Strong community connection

2. Progressive municipal platform

3. Coalition building

4. Personal communication style

The one lesson worth studying from Chow is how she connects big city issues to people’s everyday experiences – housing, affordability, transportation, safety and community wellbeing.

5. What is your vision for London?

Safer for everyone to live in, affordable for Londoner’s to live in and more vibrant city for companies to invest in.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

If I were ranking the issues.

1. Affordable housing & homelessness

2. Community safety

3. Cost of living/property taxes

4. Roads, transit & infrastructure

5. Economic development and jobs

Community safety. Residents are concerned about crime, disorder, downtown safety, encampments and the impacts of addiction and mental-health challenges.

Rapid population growth. London is growing quickly, which puts pressure on roads, transit, schools, housing, health care and other infrastructure.

Infrastructure and transportation. Growth creates pressure to maintain roads, bridges, sidewalks and stormwater systems while expanding public transit and active transportation.

Property taxes and affordability. The city has to pay for infrastructure and services while residents are already feeling pressure from housing, food, utilities and other living costs.

Mental health and addictions. This overlaps heavily with homelessness and community safety. London has been expanding highly supportive housing that combines housing with health and social supports.

Economic development and good jobs. London needs continued investment, entrepreneurship and employment opportunities while ensuring that economic growth benefits neighbourhoods across the city.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

What sets me apart is that I am not running to be a politician I am running to be a strong voice for the people of Ward 4. I believe residents deserve a representative who listens, is accessible, and follows through. I want to bring people together, including residents, local businesses, nonprofits, community organizations, and young people, to find practical solutions to the challenges facing our neighbourhoods. I also believe Ward 4 deserves a councillor who will stand up for the ward while working constructively with the rest of city council. Most importantly, I want residents to know that their voice will not stop mattering after election day.

Name: Tom Cull

Occupation: Part-time professor at Western (English and Writing Studies), Full-time community partner specialist at the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority

Family: partner, son, two rascally dogs.

Currently, yes. However, when the new ward boundaries come into effect, I will live just outside the southern Ward 4 boundary.

Yes, council would be my full-time job.

My top three priorities are to

1) Ensure that Ward 4 residents receive timely and efficient city services, including road repair, snow removal, garbage pickup, street light maintenance, etc.

2) Keep Ward 4 residents informed about city planning, infrastructure projects and development, and ensure they understand timelines, impact on their communities, and avenues for input and participation.

3) Work collaboratively and pragmatically with fellow councillors to implement programs and policies that tackle our biggest challenges as a city, including affordability, homelessness, and sustainable city growth, while also attracting investment, innovation, and talent to London.

Long-time councillor and interim mayor Joni Baechler. Joni was approachable and kind, but also razor sharp, principled, and informed. She did her homework (for those who remember, “read the report!”) and she used her power and position to build a city that worked for people. She stepped into the mayor’s seat at a dark time for London politics, steadied the ship and brought integrity back to the office.

I want to help build a London that is designed to maximize the potential of its residents, a city where young people put down roots and raise families, not only because they can get good jobs, but because they see the city prioritizing sustainable development that makes neighborhoods and communities safer and more affordable. The city I’m envisioning takes care of its most vulnerable, has clean air, clean parks, and a healthy river. It is a city where people can get around with ease: on roads, public transit, bikepaths, sidewalks, hiking trails. Finally, I envision a city governed by its people through strong representations at city hall.

Like many mid-sized cities, London is facing significant challenges around affordability, housing, homelessness, public health, high unemployment, and urban decay. We don’t have enough affordable housing, and one in three families are food insecure.

An equal challenge to these more material realities, is the ongoing assault on the idea of a shared truth, and the value of evidence-based politics. The result is growing cynicism and alienation from the democratic process (last municipal election turnout was amongst the lowest ever) and a growing distrust of government. Practicing patient politics in the age of rage bait and echo chambers is no easy task. We need a politics that places faith in truth, people, communities, and the health of the planet.

I don’t set myself apart from anyone. We all have gifts to share – I have been lucky enough to be mentored by some amazing Londoners who showed me what it means to give back to the community and to use your voice and position to bring people together to find common ground and shared purpose. My particular strength is in listening to people and connecting them to what they need: to other people, to opportunities, to a way through or around a problem. When people are connected they build great things and tackle tough challenges.

Name: Mario Jozic

Occupation : Chief Operating Officer for Braxx General Contracting and Railings

Family: Yes, I have a long-term partner and a 6-year-old son. I am also very fortunate to have both of my parents, sister and her family directly involved in my life as we a very are tight-knit family.

Yes, I grew up here and spent my entire childhood in Ward 4. We still own our family home just around the corner from Ed Blake Park.

Absolutely! If I am lucky enough to be elected, serving Ward 4 will be my sole occupation. With councillor compensation increasing to more than $94,000 and the position being recognized as a full-time responsibility, residents should expect their councillor to be fully available and committed to the job.

My priorities are based on a common-sense, neighbourhood-focused approach.

1. Property-tax relief and financial accountability: Scrutinize spending, improve procurement and demand clear, measurable results before approving further tax increases. Eliminate dramatic and unsustainable tax increases of the past 4 years.

2. Safer, stronger neighbourhoods: Improve community safety, property-standards enforcement, road and sidewalk conditions, traffic management and basic municipal services. Create a Ward 4 Portal where residents can give their input on safety, smart development, and other community issues.

3. Housing and homelessness: Accelerate construction on suitable land rather than building high-rise buildings in single-family dwelling neighbourhoods. Focus on permanent housing solutions while connecting people with mental-health care, addiction treatment and employment services. City-funded programs must demonstrate measurable results.

Tough question! Most recently, I would say Mayor Ed Holder. Like me, Ed Holder approached municipal government from a common-sense, business and management perspective. Moreover, directly speaking from personal experiences, he was available and ready to listen to any concerns the downtown business community had while we were struggling with homelessness and other issues. Unfortunately, I can’t say the same of every past representative.

My vision is a safe, affordable and well-managed city where people receive good value for their property-tax dollars. London should support responsible growth while protecting established neighbourhoods, improving transportation connections and ensuring essential services keep pace with development. We need a common-sense and compassionate approach to the homelessness crisis that provides housing, adequate mental health and addiction services while also enforcing laws. Residents should be able to see clearly how decisions are made, where their money is going and what results the city is delivering.

Affordability is London’s most immediate challenge. Residents are being squeezed by housing costs, property-tax increases and the rising cost of everyday life, while homelessness, addiction and neighbourhood safety continue to deteriorate. The city must control its own spending while addressing these problems with co-ordinated, measurable solutions instead of repeatedly funding programs without demonstrating results.

I bring senior management experience, including overseeing budgets, schedules and complex projects. That experience has taught me to examine costs carefully, solve problems directly and hold people accountable for results.

I have also personally knocked on every single door in Ward 4 during this campaign. I am not relying only on reports or social media to understand the ward – I have listened to people at their homes and seen the issues firsthand. If elected, council will be my sole occupation, and residents will have an accessible, independent and neighbourhood-focused representative.

Name : Stephen Orser (ORS)

Occupation: Buy, sell different things from Facebook Marketplace, retired and bored.

Family: Lori my partner of 14 years, my rabbit Maddie daughter my dog George, cat Commander.

I have lived in Ward 4 for 25 years.

I was full time for 8 years in council, this wage increase is greedy and must be rescinded.

I wish to rise up weak off the streets, out of the alleys and encampments, I want to immediately ends open drug use, and lastly I wanna make London safe again and take it back.

Jack Burkhart (editor’s note – sic) hands down, he taught to fight for people and he taught to care for people.

A safe city, where homeless, addicts get their life back on track, I wish to raise up the weak.

Homelessness, addicts and public safety, open drug use.

I can’t be bought, bribe, or buffaloed, I am decorated hero for saving a life and I want to save more. orser.vote

Name: Randi Prunner

Occupation : Registered massage therapist

Family: (Partner) Rylan Waring, (Dog) Balu

While council will be my primary focus, I still plan to maintain my RMT work part-time. This will allow me to connect and serve Londoners across all wards.

Top three priorities on my agenda would be making feasible municipal changes to improve support for unhoused individuals, exploring and expanding renewable natural gas energy sources to positively impact utility bills for residents, and implementing affordable housing options across the city.

While not a municipal politician, I do find a lot of Terence Kernaghan’s work relates to the work I want to do at the municipal level.

I want all Londoners to have reasonable access to core living needs (eg. affordable housing, public transit, support services). I want Londoners to feel encouraged and motivated to engage in their community. I want Londoners to have access to emergency services when they need them, and to feel safe, supported, and heard by their city representatives.

The biggest challenge facing everywhere, London included, is the cost of living. By deprioritizing for-profit developments, pausing approval of those projects, and shifting focus to infrastructure upgrades and non-profit affordable housing options that utilize abandoned/vacant existing structures, we could better support our working class and tackle this challenge.

I am not a politician; I am a regular, working-class Londoner who understands intimately what most of us are living through right now. I am also a people person by trade; my life and work is dedicated to helping as many people around me as I can.

Name: Bob Wright

Occupation : Lawyer/mediator

Family: Spouse – Noel Kingu, Keeper, Patricia – Dogs Gabriel – Cat

Yes, I currently retain my license to practice law but only do so on a very limited part-time basis for friends and family.

1. To provide effective representation for the residents of Ward 4 on council.

2. To assist members of the public in dealing with the bureaucracy at city hall.

3. To ensure that our tax dollars are spent effectively.

Pat O’Brien, councillor ’82-’93, MP ’93-’05. While I do not share his convictions against same sex marriage, I admired that he gave up his position for what he believed in. He was instrumental in helping assist my wife in coming to Canada by cutting through government red tape. He was also my teacher at CCH. I aspire to be his equal as a representative.

A community that cares for its least well off and makes everyone feel like they are part of the community without regard to race, sexual orientation, place of origin or creed.

Coming to grips with how we best deal with residents in need whether it be homelessness, mental health issues, addiction, poverty or any combination thereof.

My career as a mediator. I spent most of my work life trying to help parties resolve their differences or at the very least come to an agreement they could live with. I believe this will be a helpful attribute on council that I hope will benefit my colleagues on council and all of the citizens of our city.

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Bonnie Baleck, Ray Daamen, Alan Lieknins

2) Keep Ward 4 residents informed about city planning, infrastructure projects and development, and ensure they understand timelines, impact on their communities, and avenues for input and participation.

3) Work collaboratively and pragmatically with fellow councillors to implement programs and policies that tackle our biggest challenges as a city, including affordability, homelessness, and sustainable city growth, while also attracting investment, innovation, and talent to London.

Long-time councillor and interim mayor Joni Baechler. Joni was approachable and kind, but also razor sharp, principled, and informed. She did her homework (for those who remember, “read the report!”) and she used her power and position to build a city that worked for people. She stepped into the mayor’s seat at a dark time for London politics, steadied the ship and brought integrity back to the office.

I want to help build a London that is designed to maximize the potential of its residents, a city where young people put down roots and raise families, not only because they can get good jobs, but because they see the city prioritizing sustainable development that makes neighborhoods and communities safer and more affordable. The city I’m envisioning takes care of its most vulnerable, has clean air, clean parks, and a healthy river. It is a city where people can get around with ease: on roads, public transit, bikepaths, sidewalks, hiking trails. Finally, I envision a city governed by its people through strong representations at city hall.

Like many mid-sized cities, London is facing significant challenges around affordability, housing, homelessness, public health, high unemployment, and urban decay. We don’t have enough affordable housing, and one in three families are food insecure.

An equal challenge to these more material realities, is the ongoing assault on the idea of a shared truth, and the value of evidence-based politics. The result is growing cynicism and alienation from the democratic process (last municipal election turnout was amongst the lowest ever) and a growing distrust of government. Practicing patient politics in the age of rage bait and echo chambers is no easy task. We need a politics that places faith in truth, people, communities, and the health of the planet.

I don’t set myself apart from anyone. We all have gifts to share – I have been lucky enough to be mentored by some amazing Londoners who showed me what it means to give back to the community and to use your voice and position to bring people together to find common ground and shared purpose. My particular strength is in listening to people and connecting them to what they need: to other people, to opportunities, to a way through or around a problem. When people are connected they build great things and tackle tough challenges.

My priorities are based on a common-sense, neighbourhood-focused approach.

1. Property-tax relief and financial accountability: Scrutinize spending, improve procurement and demand clear, measurable results before approving further tax increases. Eliminate dramatic and unsustainable tax increases of the past 4 years.

2. Safer, stronger neighbourhoods: Improve community safety, property-standards enforcement, road and sidewalk conditions, traffic management and basic municipal services. Create a Ward 4 Portal where residents can give their input on safety, smart development, and other community issues.

3. Housing and homelessness: Accelerate construction on suitable land rather than building high-rise buildings in single-family dwelling neighbourhoods. Focus on permanent housing solutions while connecting people with mental-health care, addiction treatment and employment services. City-funded programs must demonstrate measurable results.

Tough question! Most recently, I would say Mayor Ed Holder. Like me, Ed Holder approached municipal government from a common-sense, business and management perspective. Moreover, directly speaking from personal experiences, he was available and ready to listen to any concerns the downtown business community had while we were struggling with homelessness and other issues. Unfortunately, I can’t say the same of every past representative.

My vision is a safe, affordable and well-managed city where people receive good value for their property-tax dollars. London should support responsible growth while protecting established neighbourhoods, improving transportation connections and ensuring essential services keep pace with development. We need a common-sense and compassionate approach to the homelessness crisis that provides housing, adequate mental health and addiction services while also enforcing laws. Residents should be able to see clearly how decisions are made, where their money is going and what results the city is delivering.

Affordability is London’s most immediate challenge. Residents are being squeezed by housing costs, property-tax increases and the rising cost of everyday life, while homelessness, addiction and neighbourhood safety continue to deteriorate. The city must control its own spending while addressing these problems with co-ordinated, measurable solutions instead of repeatedly funding programs without demonstrating results.

I bring senior management experience, including overseeing budgets, schedules and complex projects. That experience has taught me to examine costs carefully, solve problems directly and hold people accountable for results.

I have also personally knocked on every single door in Ward 4 during this campaign. I am not relying only on reports or social media to understand the ward – I have listened to people at their homes and seen the issues firsthand. If elected, council will be my sole occupation, and residents will have an accessible, independent and neighbourhood-focused representative.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 5 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 5 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 5 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name : Corrine Rahman

Occupation : City councillor, Former college business professor (10 years), former municipal political staffer, non-profit manager, former TVDSB trustee for Wards 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 from 2018-2022.

Family: Married to Adam, mother of 3 children.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Budget-conscious decision-making

I will continue to push for savings, efficiencies, accountability and transparency across the corporation to ensure your tax dollars are spent wisely.

Smart growth & economic prosperity

I will fight for new developments to maintain neighbourhood compatibility while expanding housing – especially affordable and supportive housing to address the homelessness crisis.

Advocate for council to take on an active role in economic development to attract quality jobs.

Transportation & infrastructure

Push to alleviate congestion and address growth pressures.

Enhance communication and co-ordination for construction projects across the city.

Simplify the traffic-calming process and invest in safer school travel.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Joni Baechler. I appreciated the way she engaged with the community, her level of preparedness for the issues of the day. She was collaborative, well spoken, kind and a real champion for our city. I admired the way she led authentically, with humility, compassion and transparency.

I also admired the way she mentored and supported women in our community. Encouraging them to take on leadership positions. After I was elected, she sent me a note that I still have in my office. It reminds me to “pay it forward,” to mentor young aspiring leaders in our community.

5. What is your vision for London?

I want London to have a strong economy; to be a great place to raise a family; a community that cares for one another, where residents feel heard, valued, and safe. My vision is for Londoners to have ample housing choices and supports. Londoners deserve a city where it’s easy to get around. Our city is anchored by beautiful parks, walking trails, the Thames River, and a strong tree canopy worth protecting. Our mid-size city should feel connected, with a vibrant arts and culture scene, and a thriving downtown; in short, London should feel like a well-planned city.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Homelessness is London’s most pressing challenge. The city has shown leadership through hubs, supportive and affordable housing, micro-shelters, expanded emergency shelter capacity, and housing stabilization (rent stability bank etc.) funding. The province also opened a HART Hub in 2025. Despite these efforts, homelessness in London increased by 19% in 2025, compared with 25% across Ontario.

Addressing this issue requires collaboration across all levels of government and strong partnerships with local service organizations. The city must focus on areas within its control, prepare for funding shortfalls, and ensure limited resources are directed to services that deliver results.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I have a strong record of service in this community. My background in communications, political science, human resources, negotiations and leadership brings unique expertise to council. I’m effective at bringing big issues forward. I am a strong advocate, and dedicated leader who doesn’t shy away from tough conversations. I show up, take extra responsibilities, and work hard to serve my community.

As a ward councillor, I prioritize listening, responsiveness and effective communication. I meet residents at their doorsteps, at ward meetings and community events. I believe public service is a privilege, and I work every day to serve.

Name: Abid Raza

Occupation: small entrepreneur

Family : Married, father of 2 boys.

I am renting a appartment on the border of Ward 5 but I am technically living in Ward 4.

If I’m fortunate enough to be elected as a city councilor, my top three priorities will be enhancing community safety, providing stronger support for local businesses, and improving essential city services like transit, housing, and specifically addressing homelessness in London, Ontario. I truly believe these are the areas that will make the biggest difference in people’s lives.

I really respect the work that Jerry Pribil did as the previous councilor in Ward 5. I feel a strong responsibility to build on his efforts, especially around community safety, small business support, and addressing homelessness. I hope to carry forward that same commitment to the people of Ward 5.

If I’m elected, my focus will be on three main priorities: enhancing community safety, providing stronger support for local businesses, and addressing homelessness right here in London. I’m committed to making a real difference.

The growing issue of affordable housing and homelessness. It’s having a serious impact on many families, and we need effective, long-term solutions to make sure everyone has a safe place to call home.

My deep connection to this community and my hands-on approach. I’m out in the neighborhoods, listening to residents, and ensuring their voices directly shape the decisions I make.

Name : Mary Blake Rose. You may also know me as Mary Blake Bonn.

Occupation: I work for the national office of Citizens’ Climate Lobby Canada, a non-profit, non-partisan, grassroots environmental advocacy organization. I also give private French lessons to public servants whose jobs require proficiency in both of Canada’s official languages.

Family: Married

I live within walking distance of Ward 5, but I live in Ward 7.

Yes, if I am elected, this will be my sole occupation.

Transportation. This includes road safety, as well as transit and active transportation infrastructure. We all deserve safe streets and we all deserve to be able to get around, with or without owning a car.

Housing affordability, affordable housing, and the homelessness crisis. One priority in particular is implementing protections for tenants facing demoviction.

Protecting our natural environment and meeting our Climate Emergency Action Plan targets. This has been treated as a nice to have, but it’s a need to have.

I best identify with Skylar Franke. We both come from the environmental non-profit world, we both prioritize evidence-based solutions, and I think we both have an approach to leadership that involves working toward the changes we need, not just the ones that cynics say are possible.

My vision is for London to be a city where everyone can see a future. This means that London needs to be:

Fairer. Safe streets, transportation options, affordable and attainable housing, and opportunities for life-long Londoners and recent graduates to stay and build a future.

Greener. Whether we like it or not, environmental degradation and climate change are defining issues of our time and climate anxiety is a crisis among Canadian youth.

Undaunted. London is a city that has been known to tread cautiously, but I think that we do our best work here when we’re willing to tackle big problems with bold solutions.

I’m not exactly sure how high-level the answer to this question is meant to be, but I think that the biggest challenge facing London right now is that we’re living with the consequences of decades of downloading from the higher orders of government. With that being said, I’m not running for city council to point fingers, and I think that my experience in the non-profit sector has prepared me to face this challenge. I’m good at doing a lot with a little, and I’ve spent over a decade engaging in advocacy at multiple levels of government, with politicians of all political parties.

In Ward 5, I’m the progressive choice, I’m the green choice, and I’m the forward-thinking choice. I’m also younger than the average city councillor, so I think that I can represent perspectives that are sometimes underrepresented on council. I was a renter until three years ago. I was car-free until two years ago. I’ve experienced London as a student and as a young professional. I think that if elected, I can add a voice to council that’s often missing.

Name: Charles Spina

Occupation : Semi-retired executive, consultant and community board member

Family : Married with children and grandchildren.

Yes. I regard my candidacy as the response to a calling that I can no longer ignore, not as an income opportunity. Having a consulting background, I will continue to make myself available on a limited pro bono business advisory basis to friends and family.

(1) articulate and champion policies that promote well defined, financially sound measures to improve the lived experiences of Londoners of all walks of life, and the visitors who are our guests

(2) advocate for responsible needs-based-as opposed to cost-plus- budgeting, inclusive of realistic target returns on our more than one billion dollars of invested financial assets. I will oppose any tax increase that is not going to deliver better services to Londoners or better conditions for economic growth.

(3) show respect for established neighbourhoods and for small business owners, as reflected in (a) sensible intensification decisions free of preferential treatment of special interests, (b) mobility options that are accessible, safe and reliable, and (c) streets that are free of crime.

Jane Bigelow. Our first female mayor and a member of what was board of control. Elected when I was an undergrad, she struck me as sensible, caring and tough. She also recognized that she couldn’t do it alone. She was courageous, as I think most women are, including Angela Merkel, another one of my heroes.

The restoration of London’s golden age of opportunity, safety and wellbeing for residents of all ages and walks of life. Call it a renaissance, and not coincidently, a pre-condition for certain kinds of investment.

One would never know that we are a rich city financially when you consider the suffering and livability challenges faced by a significant minority of residents, some of whom are now having to make tough aging-at-home decisions simply because of our three-year 20% property tax increase. We also seem to be having a case of creeping streetscape uglification, emerging roadwork quality issues, and an obvious housing/consumer preference mismatch.

We have also somehow let core Dundas East become a graveyard for many young people and small business owners.

Saying that we have work to do is a gross understatement.

Corporate leadership and consulting experience navigating complex operating and people environments. I have also been a Richmond Row business owner.

Governance is supposed to be about achieving defined objectives, finite timelines and fixed resources. As a councillor, I will be guided by that philosophy and discipline

I was also eighteen years on one social agency board here in London and eleven years on the investment committee of a large diocesan fund. I chaired the committee during the most difficult days of the 2007-9 global financial crisis. I am therefore no stranger to crises. Although I steer clear when I foresee them, I know how to confront them and land on the other side when they are forced on me.

Sitting in the chamber gallery, reading city financial and investment reports, and attending GMIS amd development charge meetings, the questions: “why are we doing it this way?” and “why are we delaying action on this?” would occur to me. “We should be doing it this way” would usually be my unexpressed response. If I am elected, I will make such expression my business because I will know that my voice will be my constituents and I have insights that I know can help.

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Simon Sabeesh Karikassery

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 6 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 6 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 6 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name : Ian Sterling Leishman

Occupation: Real estate broker, business association president

Family: Married with a son going to Western

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Ward 6 is where I was born and raised. I grew up on Maitland Street and later Colborne, and attended Banting High School. While I no longer live in the ward, my roots there run deep. I spent much of my life in the community, and my father still lives there.

This will be my full-time job. The responsibility entrusted by residents is significant. This role requires being accessible, truly listening and understanding the issues facing the community, and putting in the time to make informed decisions that are in the public’s best interest.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

AFFORDABILITY: Everything is more expensive. We can’t raise taxes by 26.9% in 4 years again. That kills affordability. We need to stop wasteful spending.

CORE SERVICES: Delivered fast, efficiently and well. Road care & safety/calming, helping those that need it the most, safe parks & downtown for kids and families, development that fits, reliable public transit, etc.

COLLABORATION & ACCOUNTABILITY: Ward 6 deserves a councillor who listens, responds, and works collaboratively to get results. I’ll work with residents, community groups, city staff, and my fellow councillors to find practical solutions and make sure Ward 6 has a strong voice at city hall.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I don’t model myself after any one politician. I admire leaders who build consensus, listen first, and focus on practical results instead of ideology and division. My approach to city hall: Be accessible, accountable, fiscally responsible, willing to work with anyone to deliver the best outcomes for Ward 6 and London, and I won’t make promises I can’t keep.

5. What is your vision for London?

My vision is a London where families can afford to live, the downtown and neighbourhoods are safe, where we look after the less fortunate, and residents feel city hall is working for them. That means delivering excellent core services, making responsible financial decisions like with household spending, supporting smart growth, and building a culture of collaboration instead of division. I want London to be known as a city that gets the basics right first with quality, fast service and plans responsibly for the future.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

The biggest challenge is balancing affordability with growing service demands. Residents are paying more while expecting better roads, safer communities, housing, and infrastructure. The city can’t simply spend more or cut indiscriminately. We need the provincial and federal governments to play a much stronger role in supporting the fight against homelessness, addictions and mental health challenges. We need better priorities, smarter budgeting, and accountability for residents.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I bring real experience managing budgets with 103.1 Fresh Radio, leading organizations like the Old South Business Association and as a real estate broker, and solving problems outside politics. I’m not interested in division or grandstanding. I’ll be an accessible councillor who listens, builds consensus, and focuses on practical solutions. My commitment is simple: work hard, communicate honestly, and make decisions that respect taxpayers while improving the quality of life for Ward 6 residents.

Name: Stephanie Marentette

Occupation: lawyer

Family: my fur child, a Great Dane named Briz

Yes, I live in the ward I am running in.

No, it will not. The most effective councillors are individuals who have had and maintain careers alongside municipal council roles. I do not believe that full-time professional politicians in municipal government have the skills and experience necessary to do this job well. If elected, I will continue with my legal career on a part-time basis to ensure that I am able to dedicate the time and attention that Londoners deserve to do this job well, while also ensuring that I continue to grow professionally in order to provide the best possible service as a councillor to Londoners that I can.

1) Supporting intelligent, responsible development and growth by working with developers, city staff and community partners with respect to infrastructure, affordable housing, alignment with the preexisting character of an area, green initiatives and promoting commercial investment.

2) Better customer service, including addressing service call response times, ensuring usable public spaces such as proper maintenance of parks and roads, and improved delivery of key services such as transit.

3) Keeping property taxes reasonable.

Ed Holder. I have known Mr. Holder for many years, going back to our Parliament Hill days. Something I really admire about Mr. Holder was his ability to reach across party lines as an MP and how he took the same approach as mayor to work collaboratively with his colleagues to get things done in London. A councillor is only one vote, and a cooperative, collaborative approach is essential to making meaningful progress on major issues facing London. I hope to take the same approach if I am elected.

My vision for London is for London to be the city of opportunity. London has two first-class post-secondary education institutions and several major research institutes, is home to corporate headquarters for numerous multinational corporations as well as some incredible home-grown businesses. There is a burgeoning arts community, and our city has been designated a UNESCO music city. London has so much to offer and I would like to see council encourage investment, growth, supports for the arts and local business, as well as caring for our most vulnerable to grow into a vibrant city where there is something for everyone.

The current economic climate. Everything from fuel and food to housing has skyrocketed and people feel it the most at the municipal level, causing increased reliance on food banks, transit, public spaces and essential services. Council may have no influence over national fiscal policy, but it does have control over how London supports its most vulnerable and what steps it takes to attract investment and growth to our city. Both are important in supporting Londoners through this challenging economic climate to ensure no one is left behind while also building a vibrant city full of opportunity.

I am a practicing litigation lawyer. I spend my days engaged in advocacy, whether mediating and negotiating or attending court if needed. If I am elected, I will problem-solve, negotiate and fiercely advocate on behalf of Ward 6 residents and Londoners more broadly, the same as I would for my clients to achieve the best possible result and make true progress on the major issues facing our city.

Name: Naomi Nadea

Occupation : Community advocate

Family: Single

Yes. I live in Ward 6.

This will be not only a dream come true, but I will finally be able to help even more people than I could ever imagine.

My three top priorities are community safety, health care, and creating jobs for people with no education. I want to focus on practical issues that directly affect residents, while ensuring London continues to be a safe, affordable and well-managed city. I believe council should focus on responsible spending, delivering reliable services and listening to residents before making major decisions.

My vision is for a London that is safe neighbourhoods, better care at hospitals and medical industry, affordable living, and stronger bylaws on the lawless tenants where residents can build a good life and businesses have the confidence to invest and create jobs. We need a city that manages growth responsibly, maintains the services people rely on and makes decisions based on long-term value rather than short-term politics. Most importantly, I want residents to feel that city hall listens to them and that their tax dollars are being spent responsibly.

I believe London’s biggest challenge is the illegal opioid crisis. This issue affects residents in very practical ways, and addressing it will require council to work collaboratively with the province, community organizations, businesses and residents. We need to focus on practical solutions, measurable results and responsible use of public funds rather than simply acknowledging the problem.

What sets me apart is relating to the average low-income people of London. I am running because I know I am only 1 missed paycheque from being homeless, and I bring lived experience and relevant street smarts to the role. I am prepared to listen, ask difficult questions and work collaboratively to get results. My commitment is to represent residents first, remain accessible and make decisions based on what is best for the ward and for London as a whole.

Name: Sam Trosow

Occupation : Full-time city councillor and retired UWO faculty member

Family: I live with my spouse Marie (we have no children).

Yes, it is now and will continue to be my sole occupation. I retired from the university in 2023. The council will need to develop more precise definitions and guidelines for what is meant by full-time service, and how this expectation will be reported and enforced.

3. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Gina Barber.

4. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

I continue to see housing and the homelessness crises; transit and mobility; and environmental and planning policies as pressing priority issues the next council must address. Tying together all these concerns is the need for increased civic engagement and public participation.

My vision for London is a city that truly lives up to its name as the Forest City: a place where residents can afford decent, secure housing; where public and active transportation systems are robust and reliable; and where growth is carefully planned, sprawl is minimized, and our parks and trails are beautifully maintained. My aspiration is for a diverse, inclusive community – one that feels like home and ensures safety for people of all ages, incomes, identities, abilities, and backgrounds. Now more than ever, London needs experienced, knowledgeable councillors who possess the political will to make the difficult choices ahead that can bring this vision about.

Our biggest challenge is the affordability crisis. Whether it is escalating costs for housing, food, utilities, health care, transportation, growing debt, taxes or education, this crisis is creating greater hardship and uncertainty about the future for more and more Londoners. An effective city council must identify those factors that can effectively be influenced at a municipal level and prioritize what actions we can undertake given our limited resources and tax-base.

My background and experience, combined with my deep life-long commitment to public service, give me a strong vantage-point to continue addressing the complex issues facing Ward 6 and the broader city.

I have taken a consistent, well-researched and evidence-based approach to issues coming to the council table, and I base my council positions on the long-term implications of policies and decisions, not just current pressures and passing trends.

Being an effective advocate for residents of Ward 6 and across the city often requires asking difficult questions, putting forward creative solutions, and taking risks in making proposals.
