Name : Ian Sterling Leishman
Occupation: Real estate broker, business association president
Family: Married with a son going to Western
1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Ward 6 is where I was born and raised. I grew up on Maitland Street and later Colborne, and attended Banting High School. While I no longer live in the ward, my roots there run deep. I spent much of my life in the community, and my father still lives there.

This will be my full-time job. The responsibility entrusted by residents is significant. This role requires being accessible, truly listening and understanding the issues facing the community, and putting in the time to make informed decisions that are in the public’s best interest.
3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?
AFFORDABILITY: Everything is more expensive. We can’t raise taxes by 26.9% in 4 years again. That kills affordability. We need to stop wasteful spending.

CORE SERVICES: Delivered fast, efficiently and well. Road care & safety/calming, helping those that need it the most, safe parks & downtown for kids and families, development that fits, reliable public transit, etc.

COLLABORATION & ACCOUNTABILITY: Ward 6 deserves a councillor who listens, responds, and works collaboratively to get results. I’ll work with residents, community groups, city staff, and my fellow councillors to find practical solutions and make sure Ward 6 has a strong voice at city hall.
4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I don’t model myself after any one politician. I admire leaders who build consensus, listen first, and focus on practical results instead of ideology and division. My approach to city hall: Be accessible, accountable, fiscally responsible, willing to work with anyone to deliver the best outcomes for Ward 6 and London, and I won’t make promises I can’t keep.
5. What is your vision for London?

My vision is a London where families can afford to live, the downtown and neighbourhoods are safe, where we look after the less fortunate, and residents feel city hall is working for them. That means delivering excellent core services, making responsible financial decisions like with household spending, supporting smart growth, and building a culture of collaboration instead of division. I want London to be known as a city that gets the basics right first with quality, fast service and plans responsibly for the future.
6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

The biggest challenge is balancing affordability with growing service demands. Residents are paying more while expecting better roads, safer communities, housing, and infrastructure. The city can’t simply spend more or cut indiscriminately. We need the provincial and federal governments to play a much stronger role in supporting the fight against homelessness, addictions and mental health challenges. We need better priorities, smarter budgeting, and accountability for residents.
7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I bring real experience managing budgets with 103.1 Fresh Radio, leading organizations like the Old South Business Association and as a real estate broker, and solving problems outside politics. I’m not interested in division or grandstanding. I’ll be an accessible councillor who listens, builds consensus, and focuses on practical solutions. My commitment is simple: work hard, communicate honestly, and make decisions that respect taxpayers while improving the quality of life for Ward 6 residents.
Name: Stephanie Marentette
Occupation: lawyer
Family: my fur child, a Great Dane named Briz
Yes, I live in the ward I am running in.

No, it will not. The most effective councillors are individuals who have had and maintain careers alongside municipal council roles. I do not believe that full-time professional politicians in municipal government have the skills and experience necessary to do this job well. If elected, I will continue with my legal career on a part-time basis to ensure that I am able to dedicate the time and attention that Londoners deserve to do this job well, while also ensuring that I continue to grow professionally in order to provide the best possible service as a councillor to Londoners that I can.

1) Supporting intelligent, responsible development and growth by working with developers, city staff and community partners with respect to infrastructure, affordable housing, alignment with the preexisting character of an area, green initiatives and promoting commercial investment.

2) Better customer service, including addressing service call response times, ensuring usable public spaces such as proper maintenance of parks and roads, and improved delivery of key services such as transit.
3) Keeping property taxes reasonable.

Ed Holder. I have known Mr. Holder for many years, going back to our Parliament Hill days. Something I really admire about Mr. Holder was his ability to reach across party lines as an MP and how he took the same approach as mayor to work collaboratively with his colleagues to get things done in London. A councillor is only one vote, and a cooperative, collaborative approach is essential to making meaningful progress on major issues facing London. I hope to take the same approach if I am elected.

My vision for London is for London to be the city of opportunity. London has two first-class post-secondary education institutions and several major research institutes, is home to corporate headquarters for numerous multinational corporations as well as some incredible home-grown businesses. There is a burgeoning arts community, and our city has been designated a UNESCO music city. London has so much to offer and I would like to see council encourage investment, growth, supports for the arts and local business, as well as caring for our most vulnerable to grow into a vibrant city where there is something for everyone.

The current economic climate. Everything from fuel and food to housing has skyrocketed and people feel it the most at the municipal level, causing increased reliance on food banks, transit, public spaces and essential services. Council may have no influence over national fiscal policy, but it does have control over how London supports its most vulnerable and what steps it takes to attract investment and growth to our city. Both are important in supporting Londoners through this challenging economic climate to ensure no one is left behind while also building a vibrant city full of opportunity.

I am a practicing litigation lawyer. I spend my days engaged in advocacy, whether mediating and negotiating or attending court if needed. If I am elected, I will problem-solve, negotiate and fiercely advocate on behalf of Ward 6 residents and Londoners more broadly, the same as I would for my clients to achieve the best possible result and make true progress on the major issues facing our city.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 7 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 7 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 7 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name : Germán Gutiérrez

Age: I will not provide my age because leadership in Ward 7 should be measured by integrity, competence, and a willingness to listen – not by a number that can overshadow the issues residents are facing. Our community deserves representatives who focus on substance, not stereotypes. I’m open about my experience and the work I’ve done, and I trust voters to evaluate me on that rather than on a detail that doesn’t speak to my ability to serve this ward.

Occupation: College professor, journalist

Family: Wife and two daughters

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

I live and own property in Ward 7

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation?

Absolutely. If I’m elected, serving Ward 7 becomes my day job, my night job, and my weekend job.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

My top three priorities are clear: strive from day one to strengthen community wellbeing, improve how the city listens and responds to residents, and ensure our decisions actually solve problems instead of recycling them. If we get those three right, London becomes a city that works better for everyone.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I don’t model myself after any one politician. I identify with the councillors who read the reports, asked real questions, and remembered who they worked for. That’s the tradition I’m interested in.

5. What is your vision for London?

My vision for London is simple: a city where people feel secure, supported, and heard. A London that solves problems instead of staging them, and builds community instead of crisis.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

London’s biggest challenge right now is a combination of increasing insecurity, deteriorated infrastructure and flawed transit planning, increasing homelessness, and an increasing absence of communication between the city and the people who live here. When residents don’t feel safe, when more neighbours are pushed into crisis, and when communication breaks down, the whole city feels it. Fixing those pressures is essential to restoring trust and stability.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I have not held any position at city hall or with the City of London. I have sat on the board of directors of WIL Employment Connections, London Public Library, Museum London, Reforest London, London & Middlesex Local Immigration Partnership Council (LMLIP), and the City of London’s Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee. I ran for federal parliament in 2011 and 2015.

Name: Sam Hajar

Occupation: Business and zoning co-ordinator with the City of London, rental properties owner, retail business owner, and dance school owner.

Family: Born and raised right in London, and I’ve lived in Ward 7 for about 20 years. My wife and I have been married for 20 years, and we have three kids 2 girls and one boy. All three go to school here in the ward.

I live in Ward 7.

Yes council will be my sole focus for the duration of my term and will be approaching it as a full time position.

My primary priorities would be:

First, addressing housing affordability, homelessness and the growing cost of living.

Second, protecting and improving public services. transit, libraries, recreation, parks, road maintenance, That must keep pace with London’s growth.

Third, creating a fair local economy based on stable employment, living wages, union rights, local procurement and investment in workers’ skills.

I would have to say I mostly identify with the former mayor Anne Marie DeCicco-Best given her work ethic, strong leadership and fiscal responsibility.

My vision for London is a safe, welcoming, and vibrant community where everyone has the opportunity to build a stable and fulfilling life. This includes taking meaningful action to reduce homelessness, increasing the availability of affordable housing, and ensuring that residents can access the services and support they need. I would also like London to remain an affordable place to live, with responsible municipal spending and property taxes kept as low as possible. By supporting local businesses, improving essential services, and encouraging thoughtful growth, London can become an even stronger and more inclusive community for current residents and future generations.

The biggest challenges for the City of London are:

– Addressing the homeless situation by providing affordable housing, and wraparound support.

– Finding efficiencies to reduce the property tax rate.

– Encouraging and supporting small businesses to reduce our unemployment rate.

I am confident that my combination of municipal, policing, business, and property-management experience makes me a highly qualified candidate to represent Ward 7. Having worked within the city for more than 25 years, I understand how the organization operates, where improvements and efficiencies can be implemented, and how to navigate the system to achieve meaningful results for residents.

Name: Waseem Kazzah

Occupation : Chartered professional accountant (CPA) working in banking operations and investment finance at Canada Life.

Family : I come from a close-knit family that rebuilt its life in London after coming to Canada as refugees. My family’s experience taught me resilience, hard work and the importance of giving back to the community.

I do not currently live or own property in Ward 7. I lived in the ward for approximately seven years before temporarily moving to south London.

Yes. If elected, serving as Ward 7 councillor will be my sole occupation, and I will be taking a pay cut to do so. I am not pursuing this position for financial gain but because I believe public service is worth that commitment. Residents deserve a councillor who is fully available, responsive and focused on representing them at city hall. I believe compensation should be benchmarked against comparable municipalities and tied to responsibilities, performance, recruitment needs and taxpayers’ ability to pay.

My first priority is managing growth responsibly by ensuring roads, infrastructure and public services keep pace with development. Second, I will address homelessness, addiction and open drug use through a balanced approach that combines housing, treatment and support services with accountability and safe public spaces. Third, I will protect affordability by bringing discipline, transparency and measurable results to the city’s budget. London must continue delivering essential services while ensuring residents receive meaningful value for every tax dollar.

The city politician I identify with most is my father, who served as mayor and deputy mayor in the suburbs of Damascus for nearly a decade. He taught me that leadership is not about titles, but about serving people. After losing everything during the war, he came to Canada and took whatever work was necessary to rebuild our family’s life. He never lost his dignity, work ethic or commitment to helping others. The values I hope to bring to city hall resilience, compassion, accountability and service come directly from his example.

My vision is for London to be an affordable, well connected, and welcoming city where people flourish and businesses succeed. Growth must be supported by roads, transit, housing, parks and essential services, rather than approving development and addressing the consequences later. I want London to become a destination where people enjoy our parks, neighbourhoods and opportunities. It should plan and govern itself as the major city it is becoming, with transparent decisions, responsible budgeting and reliable services. I want London to be the kind of city where my children and grandchildren can build their lives and thrive for generations.

London’s biggest challenge is managing rapid growth while maintaining affordability, public safety and quality of life. Housing shortages, homelessness, open drug use, traffic congestion and pressure on infrastructure are interconnected. London needs a co-ordinated approach that connects development with infrastructure, expands housing and treatment options, and keeps public spaces safe. These investments must be balanced with responsible budgeting so the burden does not continually fall on homeowners, renters and local businesses.

I bring financial expertise, direct municipal experience, and a younger perspective. As a certified public accountant and former City of London budget analyst employee, I have an in-depth understanding of the need for financial accountability across London’s operating, capital and infrastructure projects. I came to Canada as a refugee, and it was here that I acquired skills to rebuild my life through hard work, listening and participation. London gave my family the opportunity to begin a new life, and now I want to give back to London using the professional capacity and wisdom my community has invested in me.

Name: Dan Meinen

Occupation: Municipal building inspector (On unpaid leave for the duration of the campaign)

Family: Wife, 2 daughters and 2 daschunds.

No. I live right outside the ward, less than 1 km away.

Yes, I cannot work for the municipality and be on its council at the same time. If I am elected, I must resign from my job.

First, spend tax dollars carefully and prove it in public. Council found $9.6 million in internal savings this budget. That discipline should be the norm, backed by a clear public ledger. Second, infrastructure before growth. Ward 7 sits at the centre of the urban growth boundary expansion, and roads, servicing, traffic calming, and transit that works in the northwest have to lead development, not trail it. Third, a homelessness response measured by results. London is spending real money on shelters and supportive housing. I’ll push to measure it by people moved into stable housing, paired with fair provincial cost-sharing.

Tom Gosnell. As mayor, he led the boundary expansion that secured the land London is still growing into today. He was planning for 2026 back in the early nineties. Years later he returned to council as deputy mayor and budget chief, because the work mattered more than the title. He was known for bringing people together, treating every colleague and resident with respect, and quietly delivering results that outlasted his time in office.

A city that plans ahead instead of reacting late. London has real momentum, but we approve growth first and scramble on roads, transit, and services afterward. Residents pay for that gap in congestion, taxes, and frustration. My vision is a proactive city: infrastructure built before the next wave of growth, a budget Londoners can actually follow, a downtown where vacant buildings carry a cost instead of dragging down the core, and a homelessness response measured by people moved into stable housing, not dollars spent. I want results that outlast one council term, for my daughters’ generation and not just the next election.

Jobs, and everything connected to them. London’s unemployment rate was the highest of any major Canadian city this spring, over nine per cent, and we remain well above the provincial and national rates. When people can’t find work, housing becomes unaffordable and more of our neighbours slide toward homelessness. Poor public transit makes it worse, forcing families to carry the cost of a second car just to get to work. Council controls whether London is easy to invest in, build in, and get around. Every decision should pass one test: does this help Londoners work and afford to live here?

I’ve spent my life serving, first my country in uniform, then my community as a tradesperson and now a City of London building inspector. I carry the Sacrifice Medal from my military service, a reminder of what service can cost. I’ve built homes, studied at post-secondary here in London, and today I inspect everything from single-family houses to post-disaster structures. I understand how this city gets built, where projects go sideways, and what growth costs, from the ground up rather than from a briefing note. I’m not a career politician. I’m offering Ward 7 a practical, evidence-first voice.

Name : Djuma Moïse Sharifu

Occupation: Civil engineering technologist, community advocate, and event co-ordinator.

Family: In a relationship, from a large family of 11 siblings. My family background has shaped my values of community, responsibility, and service.

Yes, I live in Ward 7.

Yes, I would treat the role as a full-time commitment. London is a growing city with a growing population, and that requires councillors who are fully dedicated to listening to residents, understanding challenges, and making responsible decisions for the future of our city.

My top three priorities are accountability at city hall, improving infrastructure and city services, and supporting economic opportunities.

Residents deserve a city government that listens, spends tax dollars responsibly, and delivers results. We need practical solutions to challenges like traffic safety, housing pressures, unemployment, and the impact of growth on our infrastructure.

I identify most with politicians who focus on community engagement, accountability, and practical results rather than politics. I believe local government should be about listening to residents, understanding their concerns, and finding solutions that improve people’s daily lives.

My vision is for London to become a city where growth is managed responsibly, residents feel heard, infrastructure keeps pace with development, and opportunities exist for everyone. Growth brings challenges, but with responsible leadership, transparency, and smart investments, London can continue to thrive while maintaining the quality of life that residents value.

London’s biggest challenge is managing rapid growth while ensuring our infrastructure, services, and economy keep up. Issues like housing, homelessness, traffic, and unemployment are connected. Simply identifying problems is not enough; we need practical actions, responsible spending, and accountability to create meaningful improvements for residents.

What sets me apart is my combination of technical knowledge, community experience, and my willingness to listen. As a civil engineering technologist, I understand infrastructure and development. Through my community outreach work with different organizations in the city, I have seen the challenges residents face firsthand. I believe leadership starts with accountability, humility, and delivering practical solutions.

Name: Jonathan Sher

Occupation : Western Law professor, journalist, health advocate and economic development researcher/writer

Family: My wife Antoinette has taught elementary school since 1990. Our children Katie and Alex are in their 20s.

I have lived in and owned our family home since 1998 in a neighbourhood that is in Ward 7 but will be outside that ward with boundary changes that take effect after the election.

Council will be my full-time job; I will honour a commitment I made earlier to teach a single course in 2027 at Western Law, work of about six hours a week for four months.

Seek better value for our property taxes, restore responsible growth that respects our communities and advocate strongly by responding quickly to constituents and acting decisively to tackle our toughest challenges, among them, homelessness, traffic and transit.

Joni Baechler, whom I covered as a journalist from 2000 to 2014 before council appointed her as acting mayor. Joni worked tirelessly, advocated strongly, acted ethically and built coalitions to get things done.

A city that grows responsibly, manages its finances well, provides good services to its residents and works with other levels of government to make life more affordable and care for the most vulnerable.

Growth has outpaced services needed to support that expansion, leaving a gap that hurts our communities and local business. We need more road capacity, effective transit, new recreation facilities and a re-focusing on core services. That gap is hard to close because cities like London have reduced what they collect from new development – a reduction pushed by the Ontario government.

All candidates promise change but I delivered change at city hall for 21 years as a journalist with The London Free Press, persuading council to make the city safer, improve traffic flow and transit and produce value for property taxes. I know how city hall works, when it doesn’t, and how to get things done. As someone who teaches at Western Law and who worked for the Canadian Mental Health Association and the Registered Nurses Association of Ontario, I know how to think critically, collaborate effectively and act decisively.

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Kamrul Ahsan, Bensy Mathew

content_blocks.text: 6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?
content_blocks.html: 6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

content_blocks.text: London’s biggest challenge right now is a combination of increasing insecurity, deteriorated infrastructure and flawed transit planning, increasing homelessness, and an increasing absence of communication between the city and the people who live here. When residents don’t feel safe, when more neighbours are pushed into crisis, and when communication breaks down, the whole city feels it. Fixing those pressures is essential to restoring trust and stability.

content_blocks.text: The city politician I identify with most is my father, who served as mayor and deputy mayor in the suburbs of Damascus for nearly a decade. He taught me that leadership is not about titles, but about serving people. After losing everything during the war, he came to Canada and took whatever work was necessary to rebuild our family’s life. He never lost his dignity, work ethic or commitment to helping others. The values I hope to bring to city hall resilience, compassion, accountability and service come directly from his example.

content_blocks.text: My vision is for London to be an affordable, well connected, and welcoming city where people flourish and businesses succeed. I want London to become a destination where people enjoy our parks, neighbourhoods and opportunities. It should plan and govern itself as the major city it is becoming, with transparent decisions, responsible budgeting and reliable services. I want London to be the kind of city where my children and grandchildren can build their lives and thrive for generations.

These investments must be balanced with responsible budgeting so the burden does not continually fall on homeowners, renters and local businesses.

Years later he returned to council as deputy mayor and budget chief, because the work mattered more than the title. He was known for bringing people together, treating every colleague and resident with respect, and quietly delivering results that outlasted his time in office.

content_blocks.text: A city that plans ahead instead of reacting late. London has real momentum, but we approve growth first and scramble on roads, transit, and services afterward. Residents pay for that gap in congestion, taxes, and frustration. My vision is a proactive city: infrastructure built before the next wave of growth, a budget Londoners can actually follow, a downtown where vacant buildings carry a cost instead of dragging down the core, and a homelessness response measured by people moved into stable housing, not dollars spent. I want results that outlast one council term, for my daughters’ generation and not just the next election.

content_blocks.text: Jobs, and everything connected to them. London’s unemployment rate was the highest of any major Canadian city this spring, over nine per cent, and we remain well above the provincial and national rates. When people can’t find work, housing becomes unaffordable and more of our neighbours slide toward homelessness. Poor public transit makes it worse, forcing families to carry the cost of a second car just to get to work. Council controls whether London is easy to invest in, build in, and get around. Every decision should pass one test: does this help Londoners work and afford to live here?

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 8 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 8 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.

stories.content:
We asked Ward 8 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name : Osam Ali

Occupation: Business intelligence specialist and college professor (+19 years of Canadian experience), worked for Ontario Health, Western University, London Health Sciences Centre, Fanshawe College, and non-profit organizations

Family: Husband and Dad of two sons and a daughter

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Yes. I am a proud resident of Ward 8, where I have lived for many years. I have called London, Ontario, home for approximately 20 years and have developed a strong connection to the community.

Serving as city councillor would be my full-time priority, and I would give the role the time, commitment, and attention it requires. Teaching part-time is a passion of mine because it allows me to share knowledge and help others develop their skills. If permitted, I would consider continuing on a very limited basis, provided it did not interfere with my council responsibilities or create any conflict of interest. If the position requires council to be my sole occupation, I would fully respect that requirement.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

If elected, my top three priorities would be:

1. Affordability and responsible financial management: I will work to respect taxpayers by carefully reviewing city spending, limiting unnecessary property tax increases, improving efficiency, and ensuring residents receive strong value from every municipal dollar. I will also support affordable housing and responsible development that respects established neighbourhoods and ensures infrastructure keeps pace with growth.

2. Safer and healthier communities: I will support practical and compassionate action on homelessness, mental health, addiction, crime, and public safety. This means working with police, emergency services, health providers, nonprofits, businesses, and residents to connect vulnerable people with appropriate support while keeping our streets, parks, and neighbourhoods safe.

3. Better transportation, infrastructure, and accountable city services: I will advocate for improved traffic flow, reliable public transit, well-maintained roads and sidewalks, and clearer planning for construction projects. I will also promote transparency, meaningful public consultation, and modernized city services so residents can easily understand decisions, access services, and hold council accountable.

My goal is to help make Ward 8 and London safer, more affordable, better connected, and more responsive to the people who live and work here.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Honestly, I respect all public servants and leaders, past and present, who listen carefully, act with integrity, manage public resources responsibly, and work collaboratively despite differences of opinion.

My goal is to learn from the strengths and experiences of others while developing my own leadership approach, guided by the needs and priorities of Ward 8 residents and the best interests of London as a whole.

5. What is your vision for London?

My vision is for London to be a safe, affordable, inclusive, and prosperous city where every resident feels heard, respected, and connected to their community. I want London to grow responsibly, with attainable housing, reliable transportation, strong infrastructure, thriving local businesses, vibrant neighbourhoods, and compassionate solutions to homelessness, mental health, and addiction. I also envision a transparent and accountable city hall that manages taxpayers’ money responsibly, embraces innovation, and works closely with residents and community organizations. Together, we can build a stronger London that offers opportunity, security, and a high quality of life for everyone.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

I believe the biggest challenge facing London right now is managing rapid growth while keeping the city affordable, safe, and livable. Rising housing costs, homelessness, pressure on property taxpayers, traffic congestion, and increased demand for public services are all connected to this challenge. London needs responsible development that increases housing supply while respecting established neighbourhoods, stronger co-ordination of housing and support services, infrastructure that keeps pace with population growth, and careful management of public funds. Addressing these issues requires practical planning, co-operation among all levels of government, and transparent decisions that balance compassion, fiscal responsibility, and the needs of the entire community.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

What sets me apart is the combination of community leadership, professional experience, education, and a genuine commitment to public service that I bring to this role. As a leader within ethnocultural & nonprofit organizations and a part-time educator, I understand the importance of listening to diverse voices, bringing people together, and helping others succeed. I also bring a practical, results-focused approach to responsible financial management, technology, process improvement, and transparent decision-making. I am not running simply to hold a position; I am running to be an accessible, collaborative, and accountable representative who listens carefully and works diligently to turn residents’ concerns into meaningful action for Ward 8 and London.

Name: Steve Lehman

Occupation: City councillor

Family: Married with 2 boys.

Yes. I have treated this role as full time since being elected in 2018.

Public safety, affordability (ie property tax, housing), traffic

There are four prior city politicians that I identify with – Tom Gosnell, Cheryl Miller, Nancy Branscombe, Phil Squire

London is the largest city in Southwestern Ontario. We need to lead the region in economic growth, transportation, arts/entertainment and overall quality of life.

Over the last number of years London has been one of the fastest-growing cities in Ontario as many people are discovering the advantages our community has to offer and are relocating here. The biggest challenge facing London is handling this significant growth (ie traffic, affordable housing, public safety, homelessness, mental health/addiction).

I have over 35 years of business experience and have served on city council for 8 years. This combined experience gives me the pragmatism and solution-oriented outlook to respond to the many challenges faced by Londoners. My ability to navigate the departments and services within the City of London ensures that I can deliver rapid solutions for my constituents.

Name: Coralia Esterra Tudor

Occupation: Philanthropist, I donate my time and money to various causes throughout the city and broader community.

Family: Married (Husband: Dr. Jeremy Keller; Children: Luciana, Michael and Elaina)

Yes, but I will continue serving on the boards of directorship as well as my other philanthropy work so long as there is no conflict of interest.

Like everyone in this city, I want to address the downtown core including, the homelessness crisis and high vacancy rate.

I want to tackle the lack of affordable and subsidized housing while addressing urban sprawl.

Additionally, I want to solve our high unemployment rate by drawing more businesses to London.

Hazel McCallion, she began as a city councilor and brought innovative thoughts, new businesses, and revolutionized the City of Mississauga into what it is today; a booming, thriving, city and economy with it’s own distinctive character.

A place with its own charm and character, where people can work, live and play, feeling comfortable and safe, all while becoming an innovative, and dynamic city.

Cost of living. Everything is expensive, (housing, food, taxes, rent, etc.) As council we need to address these matters, as well as increase employment opportunities. It’s important to grow as a city in a balanced manner so that there is both work, affordable homes, and quality of life for people.

I bring with me a multitude of life experiences. I understand everyone’s perspective and can empathize, while still seeing the pathway to success. I also bring with me an openness to listen to all sides of a matter, research and mediate the situation. I bring with me innovative thought and a voice that won’t shy away from doing what’s right.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 9 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 9 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 9 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Tammy Abi-Khalil

Occupation: My work has always centred on helping people navigate difficult moments and systems that can feel overwhelming. Today, I work in a constituency office, helping residents access programs, services, and solutions. Earlier in my career, I supported seniors and people living with Alzheimer’s, as well as children with special needs. Those roles taught me patience, compassion, and how important it is to listen before acting. My family’s restoration business has also given me insight into small business, trades, and the pressures facing employers. Across every role, the common thread has been service, problem-solving, and helping people move forward.

Family: My family and I have been blessed to call Lambeth home for the past nine years. We are raising four active children involved in sports and community activities, while our oldest proudly serves in the military. One of our sons has autism, and another lives with chronic health challenges that sometimes require hospital care. Those experiences are part of our family’s life, but they do not define our children. They have deepened my understanding of the patience, uncertainty, and advocacy many families quietly carry every day. Our home is busy, resilient, and grounded in love, service, and neighbours helping neighbours.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Yes. My family and I own our home in Ward 9 and have owned property in the ward for the full nine years we have lived here.

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation ?

Yes. If elected, serving Ward 9 will be my full-time occupation and my first professional responsibility. Residents deserve a councillor who is accessible, prepared, and present, not only at council meetings, but throughout the ward. I will maintain regular communication with residents, respond promptly to neighbourhood concerns, and work proactively with city staff and community organizations. A full-time salary should come with full-time accountability.

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

First, I want to bring community back into city hall. Politics has become too divisive and too quick to assume the worst in people. A councillor should lower the temperature, listen across differences, and help residents find common ground. Second, I want to modernize how London moves people. This is bigger than routine traffic fixes, and I will have more to say about it soon. Third, I will work with council and community partners to strengthen safety by pairing safe public spaces with practical pathways from homelessness and addiction into treatment, recovery, stable housing, and reintegration.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

I identify with outgoing St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston. I respect the way he brings people together at city hall and keeps the focus on solving problems rather than assigning blame. His approach to homelessness, addiction, and mental health balances compassion with practical action, including housing, treatment, community partnerships, and public safety. His record as a Conservative MP and as mayor also shows that clear principles do not prevent leaders from working constructively across differences. That combination of unity, accountability, and results is the kind of municipal leadership I hope to bring to Ward 9.

5. What is your vision for London?

My vision is a London where residents feel heard, neighbourhoods become stronger, safer, and better connected, and city hall focuses on practical results. Growth must be responsibly managed so roads, services, and infrastructure are not overwhelmed, while thoughtful development respects the character of our communities. I want a city that supports local businesses, protects parks and green spaces, and offers transportation that responds to how people actually live. City hall should respect residents’ time and money by communicating clearly, managing projects responsibly, and delivering reliable everyday services. London can move forward without losing the community character that makes it home.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

London’s biggest challenge is the homelessness, addiction, and mental health crisis, although its effects look different across the city. Some neighbourhoods see encampments and visible decline. In Ward 9, residents may feel it more through property crime, break-ins, and safety concerns. Not every crime has the same cause, but our systems too often manage crisis instead of helping people move beyond it. City hall does not control health care, treatment, or every solution, but it can champion London’s needs and work with other governments and community partners. Real compassion means pursuing recovery and stability while protecting homes, businesses, parks, and public spaces.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

My experience is grounded in helping people through real-life challenges. I have supported seniors, people living with Alzheimer’s, and children with special needs, and I currently help residents navigate government services through my work in a constituency office. As a mother, Ward 9 resident, and member of a small-business family, I understand the pressures facing families and employers. I bring compassion, practical judgment, and a strong service ethic. I listen first, do the homework, and focus on solutions that produce visible results for residents.

Name: Anna Hopkins

Occupation : City councillor, Ward 9

Family : 3 sons and 3 grandchildren

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in? (Please include your address; it will not be published, only used to verify your answer)

The new Ward 9 boundary now is Springbank Drive and not the River. Therefore, I live a stone throw from the Ward 9 boundary.

Balanced growth – Ward 9 is growing quickly. My focus is on building strong neighborhoods with local parks, schools, and essential amenities while protecting our green spaces, heritage, and farmland.

Better mobility – More homes mean more traffic. I am working to upgrade existing roads and expand transit options to keep traffic moving smoothly as our community expands.

Holding taxes – Recent 6% tax increases aren’t sustainable. I’m committed to keeping city spending in check to offer real relief for first-time buyers, seniors, and families on fixed incomes.

There are many as they are all unique and have influenced me but two that come to mind would be Gina Barber and Joni Baechler. They both showed me the importance of doing my homework and being open to being convinced I may have it wrong.

Building a city where we all belong.

Housing affordability and homelessness

Every resident in our community deserves a safe, affordable place to call home, whether you’re buying your first place, renting, or looking to age in place. That’s why I’m advocating for more funding from the province for day-to-day wraparound supports that make highly supportive housing successful including mental health and addictions supports

My engagement with constituents, experience as a councillor and my openness to continuing to learn, position me best to deliver results for our Byron, Lambeth and Riverbend neighbourhoods.

Name: Matt Millar

Occupation: Farmer / IT specialist / software developer

Family: 3rd generation of a farming family

No. I won’t give up the family farm to become a full-time politician, and I’m opposed to pinning council salary to more than what 70% of full-time working Londoners earn. That’s why I drafted the Pay Accountable to City Taxpayers (PACT) bylaw. Making council a career discourages the kind of people this job actually needs: those who understand what it’s like to run a business, meet a payroll, or work a trade, because they’re still doing it. Staff already do the day-to-day work of the city. Council’s job is to set direction and represent the will of their constituents.

1) Making sure every single tax dollar extracted from hard-working Londoners is treated with the respect it deserves.

2) Getting traffic flowing efficiently through the city and planning for construction intelligently.

3) Rein in the ever-expanding government tentacles and redirect that energy into the core functions that Londoners really care about.

None, really. That’s the reason I’m running. I’m not here to become part of the status quo. I’m here because we need something different at city hall.

My ideal London spends every dollar in the budget like it belongs to a taxpayer, because it does. It’s a city where crossing town doesn’t mean cursing strings of red lights and rerouting around construction on every alternate route. Families don’t have to worry about strangers prowling their neighbourhoods for vehicles and yards to loot. City hall does its core job well, and then it gets out of the way and lets residents prosper, along with the entire city.

Getting city hall to listen to what Londoners actually want instead of trying to coerce Londoners into what city hall thinks we should want.

I’ve lived on the same Ward 9 property my whole life, as a family farmer and IT specialist.

Specific to this election, I’ve actually drafted a bylaw that I intend to introduce if elected. The PACT bylaw is on GitHub for anyone to read, version by version, before they decide whether to support it. I also built a public tracker at ward9.online asking every council and mayoral candidate in London, not just Ward 9, to put their position on PACT on the record.

Name: Luke Thomas

Occupation: Founder of Healthy Eats, a London-based meal-prep company that uses local ingredients to provide fresh, healthy meals to families.

Family: Proud member of the Thomas family.

I will continue to operate Healthy Eats. Running a small business has taught me how to deliver results on a budget. I will bring that discipline to city hall and remain connected to the community I serve.

1. Keep property taxes low by delivering core city services reliably and efficiently and saying no to BRT and other wasteful spending.

2. Protect the character of Byron, Lambeth and Riverbend by opposing ultra-high-density projects that don’t belong here and redirecting growth to London’s core.

3. Restore public safety through strict bylaw enforcement and real action on addiction and mental health, while protecting our parks, farmland, and the Thames River.

I most identify with Joe Preston. As a fellow small-business owner who later served as both an MP and mayor of St. Thomas, he showed that you can run a government by applying successful business principles. Stay focused on the basics, work co-operatively with council and staff, and good things will happen. That is the practical approach we need.

A city that grows smarter, not just bigger. I want neighbourhoods that keep their character, families that can afford to stay, and a downtown that gets the investment it needs. Ward 9 should remain a place of tight community and beautiful parks, not high-rise towers. London will succeed when we protect what works and stop wasting money on ideas that don’t.

The combination of rising taxes, declining basic services, and an addiction crisis that is being enabled rather than solved. We need to solve this crisis on the streets of downtown and Old East Village before it expands elsewhere. We need to double down on what’s working and hold those accountable who are not delivering on their commitments.

I am a lifelong Ward 9 resident who grew up in Lambeth, a small-business owner who meets payroll, and a volunteer coach who works with local kids. I am not a career politician. I bring a fresh perspective with local roots. I will outwork everyone to protect the character of our community and deliver the fundamentals.

Name : Veronica Warner

Occupation: Salon owner 30 yrs

Family: 4th generation Londoner

I have owned a property and a business for 30 years in Byron

Becoming a Ward 9 counselor is not a formal requirement to be fulltime, although the job is viewed as being full time. However, I would treat this job as full-time continuing my current position part-time on weekends as I am in the service industry that keeps me engaged with the community. Staying active with the public opinion is a great asset with hands-on communication.

The top three parties in London are homelessness, traffic and infrastructure.. I would like to see the emergency threshold temperature for emergency warming centers be at -10 C and -15 C wind chill. I will support this and if required I will make a motion for these changes.

I find it difficult to name just one politician that I look, or have looked up to. Coming from four generations of Londoners. I have had a few leaders and mentors in my family. Being a useful member of my community is important to me. Being kind, thoughtful and engaging is an important part of being a leader of our community. We must keep the public informed on changes coming and public participation meetings.

My vision for London – safe streets. I vision a plan that focuses more on sustainability looking to the future and continuing to plan for more growth as we continue to welcome more people into our beautiful Forest City. London is a place to live forever. We must keep our taxes competitive in relation to other large municipalities. Communication is key. This weekend is “Shine The Light” I would endorse and help plan for better lighting on our streets. We need to make changes in how we can help people navigate in the dark.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 10 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 10 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 10 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Steven Edwards

Occupation: Business owner

Family: Married, 3 children. Oldest son is serving in the Canadian Navy. Middle son is a restaurant manager. Youngest daughter is school age.

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

1) Financial transparency and responsibility in government

2) Voicing our Ward 10 neighbours’ concerns to city hall, as sometimes this ward feels neglected.

3) To actively participate in City of London decisions for both our own neighbourhood as well as the City of London as a whole.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

Unfortunately I do not feel particulary connected to any past or present city politicians. Change is needed.

5. What is your vision for London?

To be a safe, liveable city for families young and old.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Lack of transparency and accountability of decisions made at city hall.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I am running a Zero Impact Grass Roots campaign. No election materials, no donations, no waste. Just talking with neighbours and allowing them to express their concerns. As my platform is financial responsibility I believe it should start with my campaign and this is why a Zero Impact Grass Roots campaign is what sets me apart the most.

Name : Alex Moore

Occupation: Sales manager and business owner

Family: Married to my high school sweetheart, and together we’ve raised three children. We lost our oldest son in 2023.

We own our home at the border of Ward 9 and 10.

Yes, I intend to do the job full time.

A) Housing /homelessness / addiction issues: The need for increased resources (provincially and federally) and innovative approaches to associated petty crime.

B) Infill: Limiting high rises in neighbourhoods that can’t support them. Managing urban growth responsibly by addressing vacant buildings and restricting sprawl into surrounding communities.

C) Affordability: We are being taxed by each level of government more than ever before. Municipal taxes can only increase with the level of inflation

Gina Barber was always very accessible and deeply connected to the community and I could trust what she said. And Harold Usher, of course. His integrity and commitment to mentoring is well known and I admire that. I know you aren’t asking about trustees, but they are part of our city elections. I’ve watched my wife Sherri Moore fight for students and families for the past 5 years. I see her put in long hours to fight for what’s right and that’s the level of commitment and integrity that I aspire to. That’s the bar that we set.

– I believe that London has what it takes to be in Canada’s top 10 cities; we can live up to our potential as a great Ontario city and the heart of Southwestern Ontario.

– We need to bring a lot more investment to London with the help of our provincial and federal partners.

– We deserve a city council that works together productively for what’s best for London residents.

– Above all, I want the people that elect me to feel connected to the decisions that are made at city hall and that their voices are heard and valued.

Everybody brings different skills and values to the table, and one of my key strengths is finding where these skills and values intersect to try and reach truly collaborative decisions. I believe that consensus is better than a majority vote. Also, I have a solid reputation of bringing determination and a strong work ethic to everything I do As Ward 10 city councillor, I’ll bring that same commitment to serving the people of London every day.

Name : Paul Van Meerbergen

Occupation : Advanced manufacturing manager (recently retired)

Family: Married – Four adult children – Five grandchildren

Yes, I live in Ward 10 and have done so for 40 years.

3) Homelessness

Former London Mayor Tom Gosnell. I was privileged to serve with Tom for one term on council. Tom had a deep understanding and appreciation for economic development in London. He knew the importance of business – particularly manufacturing – to the health and prosperity of our city. He was found of saying, “You can have your opinion but you can’t have your own facts!” Tom also had a terrific sense of humour!

A prosperous Ward 10 and London.

Getting things done: Widening and improving roads, homelessness and open drug use, cleaning up the downtown.

I have a balance of over 30 years in business coupled with over 19 years in governance. This brings real perspective and therefore better decision making on city council.

Name: Lois Ward

Occupation : Registered massage therapist

Family: Yes, lots of family!

I intend to continue working one half day, three weeks out of each month as a registered massage therapist to provide continuity of care for my patients with the greatest complexity of need. This will also allow me to maintain my license so that, should I return to my practice after my term as city councillor, I will not have to complete re-training. I will periodically reassess this decision.

Increasing quality of life, which is impacted both directly and positively through: 1. truly affordable housing to decrease the risk of low income earners sliding into homelessness; 2. reliable, accessible and dependable public transit to reduce the burden of car traffic across the city and improve safety for all commuters; and 3. functional green space that is close at hand, safe and accessible to people of any income level. These three priorities improve mental and physical health outcomes, which decreases the burden on our health care system and significantly reduces the risk of homelessness, mental health crises and drug dependency.

This is a weird question for me. I do not generally compare myself to others in that way. I do have role models, if that is what you are asking, but there is no individual city politician, past or present with whom I closely identify. I see a few current councillors being consistently engaged and honest with all the citizens of London which I find honourable since that is what they have been hired to do: Sam Trosow, Skylar Franke, Hadleigh McAlister, Anna Hopkins, and David Ferreira.

People feel safe and at ease as they walk, bike, use e-transportation, bus or drive anywhere. Neighbourhoods have character, are attractive, and people feel pride of place. Parks, environmentally significant areas, mature shade trees, rain gardens, community gardens, food forests, urban farms, rooftop gardens, blue roofs, and native plant gardens in all parts of the city: to cool our heat island, soften summertime heat domes, absorb torrential rainfall, feed us and our non-human kin, and reduce the possibility of wildfire in our city. Business is bustling, creativity is thriving, and people feel happy because they have what they need.

Affordability and the erosion of quality of life. People say again and again that they are losing hope that it will ever get better.

I am all in to work with any partner who wants to see this vision come to life, for a future that we call all love!

Candidates who did not respond to the survey or did not provide a way to reach them: Juman Al-Jumaili

I see a few current councillors being consistently engaged and honest with all the citizens of London which I find honourable since that is what they have been hired to do: Sam Trosow, Skylar Franke, Hadleigh McAlister, Anna Hopkins, and David Ferreira.

People feel safe and at ease as they walk, bike, use e-transportation, bus or drive anywhere. Neighbourhoods have character, are attractive, and people feel pride of place. Parks, environmentally significant areas, mature shade trees, rain gardens, community gardens, food forests, urban farms, rooftop gardens, blue roofs, and native plant gardens in all parts of the city: to cool our heat island, soften summertime heat domes, absorb torrential rainfall, feed us and our non-human kin, and reduce the possibility of wildfire in our city. Business is bustling, creativity is thriving, and people feel happy because they have what they need.
Affordability and the erosion of quality of life. People say again and again that they are losing hope that it will ever get better.
I am all in to work with any partner who wants to see this vision come to life, for a future that we call all love!

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 11 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 11 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 11 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name: Denise Brown

Occupation: Self-employed

Family : Mother, grandmother, great grandmother

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Many issues need to be addressed including but not limited to homelessness and addiction, housing and infrastructure, city finances and spending.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

5. What is your vision for London?

A vibrant, affordable city with a healthy downtown and no homelessness.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

Residents face different challenges. Some is homelessness, others drug addictions, others safety and affordability. Each is a priority.

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

I am approachable and a problem solver. I do not work 9 to 5. I am available when constituents need me.

In addition, when elected, the 35% wage increase council voted themselves will be donated back to local charities.

Name : Skylar Franke

Occupation : City councillor

Family: I love them 🙂

Yes, I live in Old South and I used to live in the Coves – both are part of Ward 11.

I’ve taken my role as councillor as my main priority over the past four years, and will continue to treat it as my full-time occupation.

My top three priorities, if re-elected, are housing & homelessness, affordable and safer communities, and environmental action. To me, the solution for all three is creating a resilient city that addresses these intersecting issues.

For example, building inwards and upwards along transit routes is one solution to many issues. It offers more housing, economic growth, and a larger tax base, along with reducing emissions and creating a city that people can navigate more easily. It also reduces urban sprawl, which is costly, bad for the environment, and creates long-term maintenance issues. Integrated solutions that address multiple issues at the same time are the most affordable option for residents.

Joni Baechler.

I want London to be a city that works for everyone. A city that’s easy to navigate; that residents can afford; with good jobs; that is vibrant with arts, music and culture; and is resilient to the oncoming climate crisis. I want to live in a city with a successful downtown and walkable neighbourhoods.

I believe that great cities are built by great neighbourhoods, and London has amazing neighbourhoods that need to continue thriving. Overall, I want all London residents to be proud to live in a city that feels safe and welcoming.

The biggest challenge facing London – and many other cities across Canada – is affordability, and the heart of which is housing. We see the effects of inadequate affordable housing every day: people choosing between paying their rent and putting food on the table, and more people experiencing homelessness. In London, for every new unit of affordable housing built, we lose 19 units. Keeping people housed means long-term savings for taxpayers and the government.

More than 30% of Londoners experience food insecurity, above the Ontario average. Addressing affordability requires action on several fronts. With strong community partnerships and co-operation from other levels of government, we can make meaningful progress on these challenges.

My demonstrated approach to community building and collaborative leadership means that I spend time actively listening to the concerns of Ward 11 residents, and advocating for their needs. As a councillor, I’ve moved motions that directly funded more services, supported better policies to address homelessness, and expanded transit service. I’ve pushed council to plan for winter response earlier and better protections for tenants from being displaced. When I ran in 2022, I said I wanted to see London get serious about housing, climate change and helping the people our city was leaving behind. Four years later, I still do – and now I know how to get it done.

Name: Harinder Kumar (Harry)

Occupation : Real estate professional

Family : Married with two daughters

Yes, I live and own property in Ward 11.

Yes. Serving the residents of Ward 11 on city council will be my sole focus and full-time commitment. My background as a real estate professional gives me both the operational discipline and practical problem-solving skills required to dedicate myself fully to municipal governance. Ward 11 deserves accessible, full-time representation that listens to neighbors and holds city hall accountable.

1) Safe streets and accountable social investments: Restore safety in commercial corridors and parks, counter rising property crime, and enforce strict performance tracking and financial transparency for city-funded social hubs following recent federal funding cuts.

2) Smart infrastructure and road maintenance: Repair deteriorating Ward 11 secondary streets and potholes, synchronize traffic signals along key avenues, and mandate strict scheduling on central construction projects to ease gridlock.

3) Support for small businesses and balanced housing: Protect local storefronts using tax predictability and commercial vacancy mechanisms, while championing entry-level housing supply that respects neighborhood character.

⁠I identify with leaders who focus on grassroots neighborhood priorities rather than rigid political agendas, delivering real measurable results for local families.

My vision is a safe, vibrant, and practical London built on a strong economic foundation, accessible infrastructure, and secure public spaces. I envision a city where rapid growth is managed intelligently – where families feel safe in local parks, small businesses can expand with tax predictability, and housing supply grows without overwhelming existing municipal infrastructure or neighborhood character.

Managing rapid growth while maintaining public safety and fiscal responsibility. With homelessness surging, local taxpayers are facing increased pressure. London’s key challenge is delivering metric-driven accountability for social hubs and infrastructure so growth pays for growth without burdening residents.

I am not a political insider or someone who has spent years working alongside city bureaucrats – I am a neighbor and real estate professional running to be a genuine people’s voice for Ward 11. My background brings practical, technical, and financial discipline to city hall. Rather than pushing a rigid political agenda, I focus on real neighborhood priorities – from repairing deteriorating roads and easing gridlock to restoring public safety and supporting local small businesses. I listen first and focus on delivering measurable results for our community.

stories.title: London municipal election: Ward 12 candidates in their own words
stories.summary: We asked Ward 12 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
We asked Ward 12 candidates in London’s 2026 municipal election to answer a survey to help voters evaluate the people running for the job. Here are their answers.

Name : Alexander Main

Occupation: Self-employed

Family : Yes

1. Do you live or own property in the ward you are running in?

Yes, actually two properties. One which I live in, the other my daughter does with her boyfriend and grandmother.

2. The base salary for councillors elected in October will be boosted to more than $94,000, with a recommendation that council should be treated as a full-time job as a result. Will council be your sole occupation?

3. What are your top three priorities, if elected?

Community safety, affordability and enforcement.

4. Which city politician, past or present, do you best identify with?

As I said when I ran for mayor way back when I best reflect Joe Swann (editor’s note – sic), when he started his political career. Most people running for local office have it in their mindset to help make positive change within the community and that is why they run. Along the way many get lost in the bureaucracy of trying to make that change, but for me in business I have learned how to make things happen.

5. What is your vision for London?

London deserves a council that not only listens, but acts. For all too long council has been a place of back and forth between city staff and the elected officials vs. making real change in a timely fashion. The world around us is moving faster with every waking day and we need leadership that moves just as fast, not waiting for reports or another meeting because sadly that is how we fall behind which is something we have all seen in the numbers. Action, not just words.

6. What is the biggest challenge facing London right now?

The current council

7. What sets you apart from other candidates?

Of the two other people running in my ward, what separates me is my life skills. At the age of 16 I was homeless, just another statistic and destined to become another person people passed on the street, however I was lucky. Through the kindness of a family who brought me in, gave me a job, a place to live and it was there that I began my journey of giving back to those around me. I have had to work for everything in my life, often alone however it has given me the chance to understand the world around me and the challenges we all face which is why I am running, to give back to a community that has given me so much.

Name: Elizabeth Peloza

Occupation: Full-time Ward 12 city councillor (museum conservator and arts administration – cultural management by training).

Family: Proud mom of 3.

Yes, I have lived in Ward 12 for 17+ years.

I dedicated myself full-time to my council duties when I was elected in 2018, again in 2022 and I will continue to do so if re-elected.

Current and future Londoners deserve elected officials who puts them first and focuses full-time on the issues at hand and plans for a safe, prosperous, and affordable city.

Community safety and wellbeing:

Continue advocating for responsive policing, safe community spaces, environmental stewardship, and affordable housing.

Infrastructure and transportation:

Efficient infrastructure and reliable transit keep our local economy moving and growing. I will continue to push for intersection and traffic signal upgrades, active transportation networks, essential LTC service, including to industrial areas.

Accountable and accessible leadership:

To ensure I continue pressing for action on the issues that matter most to residents; I am committed to continuing to host ward meetings, newsletters, and community events.

I prefer looking to past and present colleagues for best practices. Is there something they are doing to serve residents, through newsletters, events, town halls, social media, or something else that would help me to engage with my constituents.

From my observations, I’ve expanded from town hall meetings into hosting a community skate or swim. Evolving from community feedback, I hosted a community pancake lunch with staff and community partners on hand for residents to engage with. Each event served a purpose and attracted different segments of the community allowing me to connect with more people and hear their concerns.

I vision a London where residents have a family doctor, attend adequately funded educational institutes, partake in stable employment and experience city services and facilities they are proud of and out of town visitors are a tad envious of.

I recognize the above vision requires investment from all levels of government to become a reality. I’m will advocate, work across party lines and relationship build to advance the needs of current and future Londoners.

Homelessness. Everyone deserves a place to lay their head and a place to call home.

It’s going to take communities across the province making meaningful steps to house residents, and provide wrap around supports when required, and long-term investment from ALL levels of government to make an impact. Affordable/ rent geared to income housing, community and co-operative housing, tiny homes, additional residential units, emergency shelters and new housing construction all have a place. When housing is coupled with adequate access to food, mental health, addiction, job and skill training supports we have succeeded.

I have 8 years of proven leadership on council for the residents of Ward 12. I’ve gained experience serving as audit chair, budget chair, and as a member on all the cities standing committees. I’ve served with Dearness Home, Elgin Water Board, Tourism London, Western Fair, Museum London, KCCA, MLHU, and London Public Library. For the past decade I’ve helped to create community celebrations by volunteering with the Community Concill of White Oaks planning the South London Canada Day celebrations.

Name : Ribal A. Zebian

Occupation : Civil engineering student at Western University, Schulich Leader Scholar, inventor, three-time author and entrepreneur. I am the founder of Generous Homes and have developed civic technology focused on housing and improving municipal services.

Family: My family’s story in Canada began approximately 70 years ago. Generations of my family have had the opportunity to build their lives in this country, and I was raised with the belief that opportunity comes with a responsibility to give back. London is where I have grown, studied, built my projects and chosen to serve. That history has shaped my belief that our responsibility is not simply to benefit from what previous generations built, but to leave our city stronger, more affordable and full of greater opportunity for the generations that follow us.

Yes. I live in Ward 12.

If elected, representing Ward 12 will be my primary professional responsibility while I complete my civil engineering degree at Western University. I believe public service should also be demonstrated through action. I have committed to redirecting the 35% increase in councillor compensation toward scholarships for graduating London students. Rather than personally benefiting from that increase, I want those additional dollars reinvested into the next generation, rewarding students who demonstrate excellence in STEM, innovation, leadership and vision.

My first priority is housing and affordability: cutting unnecessary red tape and getting more homes built faster. Second is economic opportunity and fiscal responsibility, including advancing my Work for Wages proposal to create stronger pathways from assistance into employment while protecting taxpayers. Third is modernizing municipal services and infrastructure. I have already developed civic technology addressing permitting, road maintenance and community safety. Across all three priorities, my approach is the same: identify measurable problems, develop practical solutions, use technology where it genuinely improves outcomes and ensure Londoners can see whether their government is delivering results.

I don’t model myself after one particular politician. I entered this race because I believe London needs a different approach to municipal leadership. I respect leaders who challenge conventional thinking, make difficult decisions and measure success through results rather than rhetoric. My own approach comes largely from engineering, invention and entrepreneurship: understand the problem, challenge assumptions, develop a practical solution and measure the outcome. I am not running to reproduce somebody else’s approach to city hall. I want to demonstrate what a new generation of innovative, accountable and results-driven municipal leadership can contribute to London.

My vision is for London to become Canada’s model mid-sized city: affordable, innovative, economically competitive and built for the next generation. I want young people to be able to afford homes and build their futures here, businesses to see London as a place to invest, and residents to know where their tax dollars are going and what results they are producing. London has exceptional universities, health care institutions, businesses and talent. City government should match that potential by embracing innovation, removing unnecessary barriers to growth, maintaining fiscal discipline and measuring success by tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

London’s greatest challenge is ensuring our infrastructure, housing and public services keep pace with our growth. Housing affordability, homelessness, infrastructure pressures, public safety and rising municipal expenditures are interconnected challenges that cannot be solved simply by spending more each year. We need structural solutions: build housing faster, create stronger pathways into employment, modernize municipal processes and maintain infrastructure proactively before problems become more expensive. London does not lack potential. Our challenge is turning that potential into measurable results while ensuring growth improves affordability and quality of life rather than leaving residents with higher costs and slower services.

I am 19, but my candidacy is defined by what I have already done, not my age. I have physically built an affordable home and developed civic software designed to cut red tape and accelerate permitting, licensing and zoning. I understand both sides of getting homes built: the administrative process and what it takes to actually put hammer to nail. I have developed policy proposals and solutions before taking office, not promises waiting for election day. I am also proposing a public Progress and Promises Report, which I will be the first to sign, documenting my commitments and creating a clear framework for public accountability.

content_blocks.text: London’s greatest challenge is ensuring our infrastructure, housing and public services keep pace with our growth. Housing affordability, homelessness, infrastructure pressures, public safety and rising municipal expenditures are interconnected challenges that cannot be solved simply by spending more each year. We need structural solutions: build housing faster, create stronger pathways into employment, modernize municipal processes and maintain infrastructure proactively before problems become more expensive. London does not lack potential. Our challenge is turning that potential into measurable results while ensuring growth improves affordability and quality of life rather than leaving residents with higher costs and slower services.
