stories.title: Bob Aaron: A B.C. court just sent a loud message to anyone who’s ever eyeballed a neighbour’s tree
stories.summary: Never assume that because a neighbour has said go ahead and "trim the trees," everyone agrees on what those words mean.
stories.author: Bob Aaron
stories.content:
A British Columbia homeowner has learned the hard way that lopping off a neighbour’s trees without permission can be a costly mistake.

Jacalyn Hays and five members of the Fenton family own adjacent cottage properties in Sicamous, B.C., overlooking Shuswap Lake.

In July 2021, Alan Fenton asked Hays for permission to trim or top her trees to improve his view of the lake. Hays claimed she gave him limited approval to trim just small saplings provided they were no more than three inches in diameter and six or seven feet in height.

The problem was that the parties had very different ideas about exactly what had been authorized. Unfortunately some much larger trees were cut and topped, and one 50-foot tree was completely felled.

That turned a neighbourhood tree-trimming exercise into a lawsuit for trespass. Judge George Leven of the B.C. Provincial Court issued his decision last month, following hearings in May.

As is so often the case in property disputes, the problem was not simply what somebody said. It was proving what had actually been said.

Hays told the court that her property had once been a “shaded oasis” and was now “unbearable” since it was exposed to direct sunlight for much of the day.

Fortunately for Hays, she had recorded an important conversation in which Fenton admitted, “I have to take responsibility.”

The judge used the recording to conclude that Hays had not consented to the cutting of the larger trees.

The defendants, including the unlicensed and uninsured tree cutter, were held liable in trespass.

The judge noted that the defendants had ample opportunity to phone or email Hays to confirm exactly what could be cut. Instead, the defendants proceeded without obtaining first-hand confirmation.

All of the defendants were found liable.

The next question was damages. For Hays, the loss of the trees meant loss of shade. She sought compensation for expenses resulting from her losses, including replacement trees, installation of a shade structure, new air conditioning, professional reports and a shelter for a propane tank.

The judge considered what expenses reasonably flowed from the trespass and tried to arrive at an award that was fair to both sides, but he refused to award the full cost of replacing the trees themselves.

The damages, however, did not end with out-of-pocket expenses.

The court also recognized something homeowners instinctively understand: trees can be part of the enjoyment of a property. Their removal can affect privacy, appearance, shade and comfort.

Hays complained about the increased heat caused by the lost shade, the appearance of the property and concern over the stability of the slope where the trees had stood.

The judge awarded $35,000 damages as compensation for the trees and diminished enjoyment of the property. That amount is the maximum permitted monetary jurisdiction of the provincial court.

Although this was a British Columbia decision and does not bind Ontario courts, the warning for Toronto homeowners is clear. Never assume that because a neighbour has said go ahead and “trim the trees,” everyone agrees on what those words mean.

Is permission being given to remove one branch? To prune everything extending over the property line? To reduce the height of a tree? Or to cut it down? Those are all very different things.

In Ontario, the issue can be even more complicated when a tree trunk grows on the boundary between two properties.

Under Ontario law, every tree whose trunk grows on the boundary between adjoining properties is the common property of the two owners. Injuring or destroying a boundary tree without both owners’ consent is an offence.

Toronto has another layer of protection. Under the city’s tree bylaw, trees on private property with a diameter of 30 centimetres (12 inches) or more are generally protected against injury or removal without a permit. The city also cautions homeowners dealing with a neighbour’s overhanging branches that they cannot trespass onto the neighbour’s property to remove them, and cannot damage the neighbour’s tree.

The practical lesson from Hays is simple. If neighbours agree that tree work can be done, put the agreement in writing. Identify the tree. Take photographs. Mark the branches that can be removed. Specify whether the work involves pruning, topping or removal.

And make sure an arborist sees the written agreement before the chainsaw starts.

A five-minute email or call between neighbours could have prevented the B.C. litigation.

Trees can survive for a century. Unfortunately, a neighbour’s oral permission May have a much shorter life expectancy.

stories.title: Ontario’s new school year starts with major curriculum changes and one big labour question. Here’s what you need to know
stories.summary: Ontario teachers and school support staff start the year without a contract, leaving uncertainty around labour peace.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
The province’s new family support offices are opening in every school board. Kindergarten students will learn a revamped curriculum, there are new history lessons in Grade 7, 8 and 10 — a grade where teens will also have mandatory financial literacy lessons, with a must-pass test . High schoolers will be marked on attendance and participation, and have to write exams in almost all courses.

But there’s one big question no one has the answer to as this school year begins: Will there be labour peace?

The answer is: for now. But with talks in limbo as everyone awaits a labour board ruling, the year begins with many unknowns.

“The first few days are really exciting, and that’s the first thing on their minds, and they then have (bargaining issues) in the back of their minds,” said René Jansen in de Wal, president of the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association, referring to the teachers.

René Jansen in de Wal President of Oecta with the union’s new ad campaign at Union Station.

The unions have appealed to the board after an early disagreement with the government, which is seeking to add items for provincial negotiations that they feel are better suited for local units and boards to hammer out under Ontario’s two-tier bargaining system.

While waiting for that decision, the five big education unions — representing 275,000 public, Catholic and French elementary and secondary teachers, as well as support staff — have planned an in-school day of solidarity and rallies while watching and waiting for the labour board decision.

No strike votes have been planned as yet and no possible job action can happen until there have been meaningful negotiations.

“This could drag on for a few months before we get much indication which way it’s going to go,” said Rob Kristofferson, a labour studies expert at Wilfrid Laurier University.

Education union leaders at the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario headquarters in downtown Toronto.

Education Minister Paul Calandra is optimistic a deal can be reached without labour strife, saying “everything that we’re doing is about putting student achievement first. Every teacher I talk to, every educator I talk to, has the exact same mission.”

He said the changes coming this fall “aren’t revolutionary changes. Some of these things bring us back to a time when we were having better student achievement, better outcomes, and teachers have better control of their classroom, and I am confident that our educators can deal with the changes.”

On the labour front, he said he was “heartened” to hear David Mastin, president of the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, say there will be no job action early on.

David Mastin, president of the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario, and Martha Hradowy, president of Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, at a union press conference in June.

“I fully expect that there is an opportunity for the government and the unions to come to an agreement,” Calandra said. “We’ll be working hard on that. I don’t expect any labour challenges; I think students will be in school for a number of months going ahead ... It behooves us to work together to come to an agreement so students stay in the classroom. And I still remain optimistic.”

But for Stephanie Ross, a labour studies expert at McMaster University, “the fact that we have not gotten to some meaningful discussions yet, and that we’re still dealing with process, that means people should be paying close attention.”

She believes “the likelihood of disruption is greater than the last time because of the strategies of the unions to be more united,” adding that doesn’t necessarily mean a strike down the road, but “there could be various kinds of pressure techniques that are used.”

Indeed, in a recent memo to members obtained by the Star, the Catholic teachers’ union advised it “is actively planning and preparing for the next steps, should they become necessary.”

Martha Hradowy, president of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, said “families have dealt with alot of uncertainty in public education over the last several years, and nobody wants another school year to be dominated by labour negotiations — I would say our members don’t want that either.

“But the best way to create stability is to bargain, to sit down, to deal seriously with the issues, find compromises where we can, and to get agreements.”

She said her union is “asking the government to work with us on three fundamental things: better supports for students, meaningful investment in public education, and respect for teachers and education workers. I think if we start there, I think that there’s a path forward.”

Among the other changes this year are $750 spending cards for teachers, who began ordering in an online Staples portal Sept. 1, with a list of 200-plus items to start. A number of teachers reported finding lower prices at the retail site, leading Staples to say it will price match.

The province is also spending $16.8 million over three years for experienced teachers who help mentor younger educators.

Meanwhile, the new policy that ties attendance to marks for high school students — 15 per cent of final marks in Grades 9 and 10, and 10 per cent in grades 11 and 12 — has led to some confusion, with Ontario principals seeking clarification. They are hoping to meet with Calandra soon.

stories.title: Stevens scores 3 TDs as Riders beat Bombers in OT
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan Roughriders earned some breathing room in the CFL's West Division standings with a thrilling 32-26 overtime victory over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sunday.
stories.author: Jeff DeDekker
stories.content:
Regina – The Saskatchewan Roughriders earned some breathing room in the CFL’s West Division standings with a thrilling 32-26 overtime victory over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sunday.

The victory improves the Roughriders’ record to 8-4, good for second place in the West Division behind the Edmonton Elks who have an 8-3 record heading into Monday’s game in Calgary against the Stampeders. The Bombers slipped to 6-6 after Sunday’s loss.

The Riders had the first possession in overtime and scored on a one-yard run by quarterback Tommy Stevens. It was the third touchdown of the game for Stevens, who now has 15 rushing touchdowns on the year. The ensuing two-point conversion attempt failed, opening the door for the Bombers.

The Riders, however, sealed the victory by stopping the Bombers on a third-and-six attempt from the Saskatchewan 31-yard line.

Trailing 16-13 heading into the fourth quarter, the Riders took a 20-16 lead on a one-yard touchdown run by Stevens at the 11:21 mark.

The Bombers pulled to within one point on Sergio Castillo’s fourth field goal of the game, coming with 5:44 remaining.

The Riders replied on their next possession, going 70 yards on five plays, culminating with a three-yard touchdown run by Stevens.

The Bombers forced overtime when quarterback Zach Collaros hit Dorian Singer on a five-yard touchdown pass on the final play of regulation.

First downs were hard to come by early with Saskatchewan getting the first of the game with five minutes left in the first quarter on its fourth possession. Winnipeg got its opening first down three minutes into the second quarter on its sixth possession of the game.

With Saskatchewan holding a 5-3 lead after the first quarter, the Riders got into the end zone at the 12:20 mark of the second quarter when quarterback Trevor Harris connected with Quali Conley on a seven-yard scoring pass.

After Castillo cut the deficit to 12-6 with his second field goal of the game, the Bombers took a 13-12 lead when Collaros hit Kevens Clercius on a 12-yard touchdown pass with 38 seconds left in the half.

Harris passed Doug Flutie for 10th spot on the CFL’s all-time passing list with a 72-yard completion to Daniel Wiebe early in the second quarter. Harris entered the game with 41,228 passing yards, 127 yards behind Flutie, who had 41,355 passing yards.

After passing for 341 yards on Sunday, Harris now has 41,590 passing yards and trails Matt Dunigan who occupies ninth place with 43,857 yards. Anthony Calvillo is the all-time passing yardage leader with 79,816 yards.

Blue Bombers: Host the Saskatchewan Roughriders on Saturday, Sept. 12.

Roughriders: Visit the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Saturday, Sept. 12.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Indigenous actor and filmmaker Georgina Lightning dies at 63
stories.summary: Lightning was the first Indigenous woman in North America to direct a major feature film with her 2008 debut, Older Than America
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Georgina Lightning, the Cree actor, director and screenwriter who broke barriers for Indigenous women in the film industry, died Saturday after an incident at an Indigenous equestrian championship west of Edmonton. She was 63.

Ms. Lightning was shooting a documentary about the three-day Indian Relay event at the Enoch Rodeo Grounds when the incident occurred, according to friends and family.

Police responded at 6:40 p.m. after a horse veered off track and struck a woman standing in a designated media area, said Alberta RCMP public information officer Corporal Mathew Howell. Emergency medical services attended and declared the woman deceased on the scene, Cpl. Howell said. Occupational Health and Safety, Alberta’s workplace-safety regulator, will be taking over the investigation.

“She was doing what she loved, where she loved, and with who she loved,” Edmonton-Rutherford MLA Jodi Calahoo Stonehouse, a close friend of Ms. Lightning’s, said in an interview.

Born in Edmonton and a member of the Samson Cree Nation, Ms. Lightning moved to Los Angeles in the 1990s with her three young children to attend the American Academy of Dramatic Arts and pursue a career in film. Her acting credits included Blackstone , The West Wing and DreamKeeper .

She eventually expanded into producing, directing and screenwriting, becoming an advocate for Indigenous peoples to have a greater role not only in front of the camera but in deciding which stories are told.

Ms. Lightning became the first Indigenous woman in North America to direct a major feature film with her 2008 directorial debut, Older Than America , about the intergenerational effects of U.S. residential schools, which went on to win more than two dozen festival awards. The film was dedicated to her father, George De Jong, who died by suicide after years of struggling with the effects of his experience in the Canadian residential school system.

Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse said Ms. Lightning had spent years working on the film about the Indian Relay, which was in its final stages of shooting.

“Georgina wanted to show not just the excitement of the race, and the joy it brings to the nations as it travels around, but also the healing of the horse spirit, the effect that it has on the families and the riders,” she said.

Indian Relay is a traditional horse race in which participants race bareback around a track at high speed, switching horses after each lap. The sport grew out of centuries-old Indigenous horse cultures after the animals were reintroduced to North America in the late 15th and early 16th centuries.

Presented with the option of shutting down the event after Saturday’s incident, Ms. Lightning’s family said both the race and her work should continue. Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse was at the racetrack on Sunday, finishing Ms. Lightning’s final interviews.

Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse described her friend as a firecracker who held those in power to account, but also had “a tremendous amount of love for people.” She was deeply spiritual, grounded by her faith and connection to ceremony, and devoted to mentoring young people across North America. She was also fiercely proud of her three children and grandchildren.

“Last night when her children and I sat down, we said we have to finish what she started because she was just so determined to tell these stories that no one was telling,” Ms. Calahoo Stonehouse said. “She’s been so determined to take up space where there are no First Nations peoples’ voices being heard.”

Danielle Paradis, a Métis freelance journalist who was working with Ms. Lightning on a documentary about climate change in the Prairies, said the filmmaker was always fighting to show the “bigger picture” in her work.

“She wanted to make sure that whoever was working on [the documentary] understood the complexities of resource extraction in Indigenous communities, because that’s often presented as one of the only ways out of poverty for these communities,” Ms. Paradis said.

“And so, what’s the real conversation about that? Because you’ve got to have money and jobs to feed your family, but you also have to have water and land. It was brave. We’re in an age when so many people are cowardly to talk about that sort of stuff.”

Ms. Paradis said Ms. Lightning was most passionate about fighting for Indigenous women, ensuring that there is a clear path for them and that they are recognized for the work that they do.

She added that she was moved by Ms. Lightning’s humility, despite her many accolades.

“Her answer was always, ‘Teach me,’” she said. “It was such a rare and humble way of approaching things.”

The Enoch Cree Nation said it is mourning the loss of a community member and that the chief and council extend their condolences to the family.

“Our community is grieving, and we are holding them in our thoughts and prayers,” the nation said in a statement issued Saturday.

stories.title: One dead after Cape Breton floods prompt state of emergency, cut power for thousands
stories.summary: Body of 46-year-old woman found on Saturday afternoon after she was reported missing, RCMP say
stories.author: Sophia Bertuzzi
stories.content:
Torrential rains and high-speed winds hammered Cape Breton Island and parts of the northeastern mainland of Nova Scotia over the weekend, flooding and damaging roads, cutting off power to tens of thousands of residents, and leaving one person dead.

Environment and Climate Change Canada issued a severe weather warning for all of Cape Breton on Saturday morning while 200 millimetres of rain poured over the region. A state of emergency was declared for the counties of Inverness, Richmond and Victoria.

In Richmond County, first responders recovered the body of a missing 46-year-old Cape Breton woman, the RCMP said. Crews started searching for her after she was reported missing earlier that morning when her vehicle was found parked near her home on a flooded bridge in the community of Cleveland, N.S. In a news release, the RCMP said the death was not considered suspicious.

On Sunday, Environment Canada ended its weather alerts, but Nova Scotia’s Department of Emergency Management said roads across the region continued to be affected by flooding.

Jacqueline Cassel-Cramer and Arthur Cramer, who have been road-tripping around Nova Scotia for the past week in a rented camper van, said the rain and windy conditions picked up around Friday evening.

The Winnipeg-based couple in their 60s pulled into a campground near Baddeck, N.S., ON Cape Breton’s Bras d’Or Lake on Friday night unaware of any weather advisories. Ms. Cassel-Cramer said they had told the campground owners of their plan to visit the Fortress of Louisbourg National Historic Site on the southeastern coast of the island the next day.

“They said, ‘There’s a massive storm. You’re not going to be able to go anywhere.’ They really tried to talk us out of it,” Ms. Cassel-Cramer said.

Throughout the night, the weather turned inclement, she said, recalling the camper van rocking back and forth from the wind, and heavy rain seeping into parts of the van.

“That was pretty intense, and it got rather scary. I was starting to feel a little bit afraid,” Ms. Cassel-Cramer said.

These conditions continued Saturday throughout the day and evening, before ameliorating Sunday morning.

“We could see a little bit of blue sky trying to break through the clouds,” she said on Sunday.

The couple has since made their way west along Highway 105, which was clear despite washouts on the shoulders toward the Canso Causeway, the crossing that connects Cape Breton Island to the mainland of Nova Scotia.

On the other side of Bras d’Or Lake, near Dundee, N.S., Sophie Symonds woke up around 4 a.m. on Saturday morning when her downstairs neighbours called her because their apartment had flooded.

In a hurry, Ms. Symonds and her neighbours scrambled to salvage what they could from the ground-floor apartment while losing power in the process. Outside, the water on the street reached their knees. If they ventured out, the strong current would have swept them away, she said.

“The whole road kind of looked like we were on a river. We had no road left.”

Ms. Symonds’ apartment is about a 15-minute walk away from Dundee Resort and Golf Club, where she and her neighbours work. In truckloads, Ms. Symonds and about 10 other employees managed to make it to the resort that morning – where they have been hunkered down since.

Despite the storm, guests and employees of the resort made the most of being stranded.

“Everybody was gathering and laughing and talking, and just trying to make the best of the situation. It was nice to have everybody in one spot,” she said.

On the Western coast of Cape Breton, the village of Inverness was also battered with high-speed winds and buckets of rain.

“It was unbelievable. I thought the roof was going to come off my house, seriously,” Ruth Skinner, an Inverness local, said.

Earlier this morning, Ms. Skinner and her friend of 50 years, Ray Walker, the owner of Dusky Diamonds Bed & Breakfast, drove down to the beach to get some fresh, salty air.

Ms. Skinner’s house and Mr. Walker’s bed and breakfast had suffered power outages beginning in the early hours of Saturday morning – among the 40,000 homes and businesses that lost power, according to Nova Scotia Power.

“We wanted to have a look at the waves, and because there’s no power, hard to get any work done at the Dusky,” Ms. Skinner said.

Since then, the power has returned to Mr. Walker’s bed and breakfast. They have a full house this evening.

On their evening plans: “Turn the heat up, get it nice and warm, and relax,” Ms. Skinner said.

stories.title: Trade talks remain frozen as Canadian countertariffs set for Tuesday
stories.summary: Ottawa has pledged to impose levies on $28-billion worth of U.S. imports
stories.author: Marieke Walsh
stories.content:
Talks between Canadian and American officials remained at an impasse Sunday, with Ottawa saying that there have been no formal meetings to avert the imposition of fresh retaliatory tariffs .

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has pledged to impose levies on $28-billion worth of U.S. imports effective 12:01 a.m. Tuesday. The policy will hit a range of products from steel and aluminum to textiles, stoves and hundreds of other goods.

The planned tariffs are a response to new 50-per-cent levies that President Donald Trump imposed on Canada after Mr. Carney withdrew from trade talks on Aug. 21.

In the lead-up to those U.S. tariffs, Canadian and U.S. officials held near-daily meetings as they tried to strike a deal to avert the levies and reduce others that the White House had previously imposed. This time though, there has been no last-minute rush to avoid additional economic pain from the new Canadian tariffs.

Instead, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is spending the Labour Day weekend back in his home province of New Brunswick, a federal official said. Mr. LeBlanc, the official said, has had no formal talks with his U.S. counterparts this weekend and none are scheduled.

The official said that the last time any formal talks took place was Aug. 21 – the day the negotiations in Washington fell apart.

Similarly, Canada’s top trade negotiator, Janice Charette, has had no formal talks with her American counterparts and none are planned, a second official said.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the officials, who were not authorized to release the information.

Mr. Carney’s office said the Prime Minister has not spoken with the President since the week formal trade talks ended.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne’s office said Canada’s plan for countertariffs remains whole and they will come into effect as planned on Tuesday.

The new tariffs are aimed at shoring up the domestic market for Canadian companies hit by U.S. tariffs while also ramping up political pressure south of the border.

But the tariffs can also hurt Canadian businesses that rely on imported material and products from the U.S.

Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters, an industry group representing manufacturers of all sizes, has repeatedly warned that countertariffs will increase costs for businesses reliant on American inputs, particularly smaller manufacturers with little ability to quickly change their supply chains.

The association has called for the federal government to continue providing tariff remission for companies that cannot competitively source other input alternatives.

“The ultimate objective must remain the removal of U.S. tariffs and a durable agreement that restores certainty for manufacturers and workers on both sides of the border,” said Dennis Darby, president and CEO of CME, last week.

The Trump administration has already pledged to retaliate if Canada goes ahead with its countertariff response.

On Friday, The Globe reported that White House officials are hoping to hit back against Canada’s retaliation no later than Wednesday. The Trump administration is considering banning imports of Canadian alcohol, dairy products, and possibly steel, The Globe reported based on a source.

Debate continues within the Trump administration on how tough the measures should be, with some in the President’s orbit calling for even more punitive actions. What those would consist of remained unclear.

Late last week, Mr. Trump suggested in a social-media post that the trade war between the two countries would lead to Canada’s economic collapse. The ramifications will be “worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian Politician. Just watch!” he threatened.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump and his officials continued to attack and deride Canada. The President’s social-media page again posted about the renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent compared Canada to a “yippy dog.”

He argued that Canada’s countertariffs will have a negligible effect on U.S. prices.

“It is not much of a hit to us, if any,” he told Fox News.

In the past few weeks, the Prime Minister has repeatedly said Canada will only return to the negotiating table when the U.S. changes its attitude.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Mr. Carney said on Sept. 1.

U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters last week that he was confident the trade war would ultimately end with a negotiated deal.

“That’s where this is going to wind up – the sooner, the better,” Mr. Johnson said.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are increasing political pressure on Republicans by targeting industries in states that are vulnerable in this fall’s midterm elections.

For example, the state likely to suffer the single biggest hit from Canada’s tariffs is Republican-run Ohio , where Democratic candidates are mounting competitive gubernatorial and senate campaigns.

Canadian unions, in particular, have been vocal supporters of Mr. Carney’s tariff countermeasures, saying that Canada should fight back against Mr. Trump’s tariffs, which are designed to target Canada’s industrial base, and force concessions.

“The Canadian countertariffs are a good first response, but we need to take action at home to keep workers on the job by fast-tracking procurement dollars, implementing national industrial strategies, and calling on corporate Canada to step up and Buy Canadian,” said Lana Payne, Unifor’s national president, in a statement on Aug. 25.

With reports from Vanmala Subramaniam, Adrian Morrow and Mark Rendell

stories.title: Sikh community targeted with death and hate messages amid holy procession
stories.summary: The Sikh community is disappointed after seeing death threats spray painted on several signs along their procession route in downtown Winnipeg ahead of the event on Sunday.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Winnipeg’s Sikh community is disappointed after seeing death threats spray-painted on several signs along their procession route downtown ahead of the event on Sunday.

Nagar Kirtan is an annual event celebrating Sikhism’s holy scripture. It features a procession carrying the Guru Granth Sahib, the religion’s holy book, along with songs of faith.

An image of the graffiti circulating on social media shows a death threat against Indians and a swastika on a transit sign advising of road closures for the event. Winnipeg police confirmed several signs were tagged with hate messages.

“I don’t know why people hate, or something like that, because nowadays the racism has gone beyond the lines,” said Jagmeet Brar, an attendee.

The president of the Sikh Society of Manitoba said the community is staying strong and keeping a positive attitude.

“It’s (hate) everywhere in the world,” said Harbans Singh Brar, the society’s president. “Don’t worry. Come here and enjoy yourself. We will pray for the whole community.”

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew condemned the hateful graffiti.

“There is no place for racism against Sikhs. There’s no place for hate for Punjabi people, and there’s no place for hate in that sort of activity in this province,” he said.

Const. Claude Chancy said police increased their presence at the event. The graffiti is being investigated as a hate crime.

Hate-motivated crimes more than doubled, rising from 44 in 2024 to 112 in 2025, according to the Winnipeg Police Service’s 2025 statistical report.

stories.title: Indigenous filmmaker Georgina Lightning mourned by family, friends: ‘Shattered’
stories.summary: RCMP confirmed a woman died after a horse veered off the track and struck a woman. Her family confirmed it was Lightning who was hit.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Friends and family are remembering an Indigenous filmmaker and actor described by her family as a trailblazer after she died at an Alberta rodeo.

Georgina Lightning was at the Enoch Park race track on Saturday night when she was hit by a horse.

RCMP confirmed a woman died after a horse veered off the track and struck her. Lightning’s family confirmed the filmmaker was the victim.

“I am shattered in every way possible,” Crystle Lightning, Georgina’s daughter, said on Facebook late Saturday. “I have lost my mother, my sons Kohkum, my matriarch, my role model, my confidant. That’s all I can say right now. I’m wrecked.”

Lightning was in a designated media area when the incident happened, police said. She died at the track.

Enoch Cree Nation said in a statement that the community was in mourning following the loss of one of its members during the evening’s Indian relay event at the Enoch Rodeo Grounds on Saturday.

“Chief and Council extend our most sincere condolences to the family,” a statement from the office of Chief Cody Thomas. “Our community is grieving, and we are holding them in our thoughts and prayers.”

The nation also said it was working with authorities as they conduct their investigation.

Lightning was at the track for an upcoming documentary.

The 63-year-old filmmaker was a member of Samson First Nation, about 100 kilometres south of Edmonton.

Janine Windolph, director of Indigenous Arts at the Banff Centre, said in a post on Facebook she was shocked to hear about Lightning’s death.

“She was an amazing talent, a matriarch and a supportive woman,” Windolph said. “No words… doesn’t feel real. Sending love and prayers to everyone who loved Georgina.”

Windolph recalled hosting Lightning for “Decolonizing the Narrative,” a conversation series held at the Banff Centre. She said Lightning was also a graduate of the Digital Constellations Residency: Production and Post-Production.

Tributes have been pouring in on social media for Lightning.

“Heartbroken to hear this news,” said MLA Janis Irwin (NDP – Edmonton-Highlands-Norwood). “I wish I had the right words. Rest easy, Georgina.”

Jennifer Podemski, a writer, showrunner, producer, director and member of the Muscowpetung Saulteaux Nation, said on Instagram that Lightning was her first role model.

“When I got into the business I knew something was broken and early in my journey I came upon the legend that was Georgina,” Podemski wrote. “This tragic and sudden loss has rocked the entire Indigenous arts and cinema community to its core.”

One of Lightning’s friends, Roberto Mukaro Borrero, called the filmmaker a “true soul sister.”

He said they met in 2015 and immediately connected.

“Georgie was a shining star—a brilliant and courageous Cree storyteller, filmmaker, actor, producer, mentor, and tireless advocate for Indigenous Peoples,” Borrero wrote. “She broke barriers, opened doors, and used the power of storytelling to speak truths that too many had tried to silence. Yet beyond all she accomplished, Georgie was simply a beautiful and genuine human being: loving, spirited, funny, fierce, and unforgettable.”

RCMP confirmed Alberta Occupational Health and Safety has taken over the investigation.

The relay races are planned to go ahead on Sunday, with a tribute to honour Lightning and her family.

stories.title: Here's what you need to know about London's new centre-running bus lanes
stories.summary: London's Express Route 90 bus, which runs between White Oaks Mall and Masonville Place, is now driving on a short section of the city's first centre-running bus lane.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London's Express Route 90 bus, which runs between White Oaks Mall and Masonville Place, is now driving on a short section of the city's first centre-running bus lane.
· Posted: Sep 06, 2026 6:05 PM EDT | Last Updated: 23 minutes ago
How do London's new centre-running bus lanes work?
London's Express Route 90 bus, which runs between White Oaks Mall and Masonville Place, is now driving on a short, completed section of the city's first centre-running bus lanes.
As of Sunday, September 6, the bus now runs down the centre of Wellington Road along its dedicated red-painted lanes, between Simcoe Street and Grand Avenue.
Some commuters said they were excited to experience the new route.
"Let's see," said Tariq Alyousif as he waited to board the bus. "I'm thinking it's going to be faster, easier and more safe for people to use the bus in the middle lane."

For riders getting on or off Route 90 at the Wellington at South stop, this means they will no longer wait at the curb, but rather on the new protected platforms in the centre of the road, which are accessible from the crosswalk.
Only Route 90 is using the new platforms for now, and Routes 1 and 13 will still stop at the curb.

The new transit lanes mean changes for drivers, too. Drivers can no longer make left-hand turns into driveways or onto side streets along that stretch of Wellington, so they will have to continue to the light and make a U-turn.
Drivers can no longer turn left in some driveways and onto some streets along the new centre-running bus lanes. Instead, they can carry on to the light and make a U-turn. (City of London)
Centre-running bus lanes are new for both London riders and bus drivers, said Kelly Paleczny, the general manager at London Transit Commission (LTC), who sees this is an opportunity for a trial run.

"We looked at it and said, 'Let's start utilizing it and gain some experience,'" she said. "Then if there are any issues that we encounter, we can incorporate any necessary changes into the next stops as they're being completed."
LTC staff will be present in the area during the first week to help riders navigate the new system and answer any questions, she added.

The new centre-running lane are a part of the larger Wellington Gateway project — part of London's Bus Rapid Transit System — which is scheduled to begin full operations in 2029. The East London Link project is expected to be finished and operational earlier, beginning sometime in 2027.
The latter saw its first major milestone last year when LTC began using new contraflow lanes on King Street, with buses running in both directions on the one-way street.
Buses will travel in both directions on King Street starting today

According to LTC, Londoners will see more Rapid Transit stations located on the centre-running lanes opening as construction wraps up and they become safe to operate. Riders can check for more updates on the LTC website.

stories.title: Moving in! 6,000 first-year students arrive at Western University
stories.summary: It was move-in time for 6,000 first-year students at Western University this weekend. Reporter Ryan Goodison spoke with a handful of them.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
It was move-in time for 6,000 first-year students at Western University this weekend. The school has an on-campus population of about 7,100 students across 12 residence buildings, with another first-year residence under construction and set to open in 2027. Lfp’s Ryan Goodison caught up with some of the newcomers and asked them what they’re most excited about and why they chose Western.

18-year-old Matilda Sciullo from Markham is the first in her family to come to Western University , entering her first year in media communications. She says she’s excited for the year ahead, especially with some familiar faces coming along.

“My best friend is here, so I’m excited to have that experience with her,” she said. “We’ve been friends ever since we were in Grade 1, so it’s a big change now.”

Sciullo plans to go into teaching after her undergraduate degree and says her program gives her enough options if she changes her mind.

18-year-old Olivia Boyle was greeted by a singing chorus of Western’s upper-year students, known as sophs, as she got out of the car with her family. From Oakville, Boyle is entering her first year of engineering at Western and says she is excited to meet her fellow classmates.

Boyle’s older sister also attends Western and she is excited about attending the school with her.

“I just love the environment (at Western), and I just like the community feel,” she said.

18-year-old Mackenzie Corscadden was busy on Sunday decorating her residence room ahead of her first year studying psychology. From Midland, Corscadden says she is most looking forward to meeting new people at Western.

Her father also attended Western, graduating with a teaching degree in 1998, but that wasn’t the reason she chose to go to school in London.

“When I toured Western, I just really liked it. The campus is just absolutely gorgeous,” she said.

From Mississauga, 18-year-old Parin Patel is looking forward to everything Western has to offer ahead of his first year in engineering.

“I’m excited to meet people, go to different events, and obviously go to a bunch of different classes,” he said.

Patel decided Western was the right choice after touring campus and already has some friends at the university.

From Pembroke, just north of Ottawa, 18-year-old Harmony Fowler came to Western to study engineering, hoping to eventually go into environmental engineering after her first general year.

“I’m excited for the introduction of this new community that I’m going to have for the next four years,” she said. “Definitely meeting new people, starting this new journey and finding my community here.”

Fowler says she became intrigued by Western after seeing what they had to offer on social media. When she visited campus, she said she was sold that Western was the place for her.

paragraphs: It was move-in time for 6,000 first-year students at Western University this weekend. The school has an on-campus population of about 7,100 students across 12 residence buildings, with another first-year residence under construction and set to open in 2027. Lfp’s Ryan Goodison caught up with some of the newcomers and asked them what they’re most excited about and why they chose Western.

18-year-old Matilda Sciullo from Markham is the first in her family to come to Western University , entering her first year in media communications. She says she’s excited for the year ahead, especially with some familiar faces coming along.
“My best friend is here, so I’m excited to have that experience with her,” she said. “We’ve been friends ever since we were in Grade 1, so it’s a big change now.”
Sciullo plans to go into teaching after her undergraduate degree and says her program gives her enough options if she changes her mind.

18-year-old Olivia Boyle was greeted by a singing chorus of Western’s upper-year students, known as sophs, as she got out of the car with her family. From Oakville, Boyle is entering her first year of engineering at Western and says she is excited to meet her fellow classmates.
Boyle’s older sister also attends Western and she is excited about attending the school with her.
“I just love the environment (at Western), and I just like the community feel,” she said.

18-year-old Mackenzie Corscadden was busy on Sunday decorating her residence room ahead of her first year studying psychology. From Midland, Corscadden says she is most looking forward to meeting new people at Western.
Her father also attended Western, graduating with a teaching degree in 1998, but that wasn’t the reason she chose to go to school in London.
“When I toured Western, I just really liked it. The campus is just absolutely gorgeous,” she said.
From Mississauga, 18-year-old Parin Patel is looking forward to everything Western has to offer ahead of his first year in engineering.
“I’m excited to meet people, go to different events, and obviously go to a bunch of different classes,” he said.
Patel decided Western was the right choice after touring campus and already has some friends at the university.
From Pembroke, just north of Ottawa, 18-year-old Harmony Fowler came to Western to study engineering, hoping to eventually go into environmental engineering after her first general year.

“I’m excited for the introduction of this new community that I’m going to have for the next four years,” she said. “Definitely meeting new people, starting this new journey and finding my community here.”
Fowler says she became intrigued by Western after seeing what they had to offer on social media. When she visited campus, she said she was sold that Western was the place for her.

stories.title: Frechette holds mid-campaign cabinet meeting ahead of counter-tariffs
stories.summary: The meeting comes as Canada prepares to impose retaliatory tariffs on a wide range of U.S. goods on Sept. 8 in response to President Donald Trump's own 50 per cent tariffs.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette has called a special cabinet meeting for Monday, putting her election campaign on hold one day before Canadian retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods are set to take effect.

Fréchette’s office confirmed Sunday that the cabinet meeting will be held virtually at 6 p.m., but the agenda for cabinet meetings is not disclosed in advance. Such meetings are relatively rare during an election campaign, when Fréchette is simultaneously serving as premier and campaigning as CAQ leader.

The meeting comes as Canada prepares to impose retaliatory tariffs on a wide range of U.S. goods the following day. The tariffs, which will range from 15 to 50 per cent, will apply to products including dairy, steel, copper and some beauty products.

They are in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, ranging from hockey sticks to honey.

Rhetoric over the looming tariffs continued through the long weekend, with Trump posting on social media Sunday that the Canadian dollar’s exchange rate with the U.S. has been “unacceptable … for years — but no longer.”

Trump did not elaborate on his concerns, though the weaker Canadian dollar makes Canadian exports cheaper in the U.S. and American goods more expensive for Canadians.

Several of Fréchette’s political opponents accused her Sunday of using the tariff dispute for political gain during the provincial election campaign.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard accused Fréchette of putting on “a play” by calling her ministers together on the eve of the tariffs taking effect.

“We’re going to have a news conference, flags, long faces, people lined up around a table telling us they’re there for Quebecers and that they’ll do everything they can to save Quebec,” Milliard said during a campaign stop in Gatineau.

He argued the CAQ government has failed to prepare Quebec businesses for the tariff war.

2:01 Counter-tariffs on U.S. ‘measured, targeted and strategic’: Canada’s finance minister

“This government has been there for eight years, not eight weeks,” Milliard said. “So to be told now that we’re going to be there for Quebecers, we’re going to be there for workers, we’re going to hand out this cheque and that tax credit, I find that astonishing.”

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime also criticized the decision to convene cabinet, remarking on it during a campaign stop in Pont-Rouge, about 40 kilometres west of Quebec City.

“We all understand this is a CAQ marketing operation that is trying to exploit the tariff crisis to hide its record,” Duhaime said.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said in a written statement that “fear is not an economic strategy.”

He accused Fréchette of using “the Trump bogeyman” in recent days in the hope that voters will look away from the Caq’s record and the other parties’ proposals.

Speaking later in Montmagny, about 80 kilometres east of Quebec City, St-Pierre Plamondon said that strategy should not be “an excuse not to campaign and to lack transparency with Quebecers.”

He also called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to directly keep all Quebec party leaders informed of developments in the event of further U.S. retaliation.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal acknowledged that Fréchette remains premier and is holding the meeting in that capacity.

“What I’m asking her is: what is she proposing when it comes to tariffs for workers?” Ghazal said after a campaign announcement outside the legislature in Quebec City.

The cabinet meeting comes as Ottawa is also preparing for the latest escalation in the trade dispute.

On Friday, the federal government briefed its advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations about the looming tariffs and planned support for workers and businesses.

The meeting included a briefing from Canada’s chief U.S. trade negotiator, Janice Charette, as well as ministers in charge of finance, industrial policy and U.S. trade.

“The discussion also highlighted the importance of a unified Team Canada approach, with governments, industry, labour and other partners working together to ensure Canada’s response reflects national priorities and promotes long-term economic growth,” reads a Sept. 4 news release.

Fréchette is not the first political leader to temporarily step away from an election campaign because of the tariff dispute.

During the 2025 federal election, Prime Minister Mark Carney paused his campaign three times to resume his official duties as the federal government prepared its response to the trade war with the United States.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa and Thomas Laberge in Gatineau

stories.title: Healing and history at Canada’s saltiest body of water, Little Manitou Lake
stories.summary: Manitou Beach has water up to 5 times saltier than the ocean and is said to have healing abilities. Indigenous people were the first to use the water medicinally centuries ago.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
Just outside the small community of Watrous, Saskatchewan, Manitou Beach sits on the so-called “Dead Sea of Canada.”

“Little Manitou Lake, carved out by glaciers exposing bedrock and minerals that have been absorbed by water over time,” said Jeff Siegfried, community enhancement director of the Watrous Manitou Beach Marketing Group. “It’s called a terminal lake meaning water flowing into it has no way to escape and so the minerals that are in the bed of the lake leach into the water.”

The water is up to five times saltier than the ocean and said to have healing properties. The name Manitou means spiritual force or mysterious being.

Indigenous people first used the water for its healing abilities. Oral tradition suggests the water was used to treat ailments such as smallpox.

“I guess in their day, because they had to move to follow the buffalo,” said Lionel Sproule, Watrous Manitou Beach Heritage Centre chairman. “They left these ill people behind… they would come back by this way a month later and there would be the ill people healed and then carry on with life.”

Sproule, who managed the spa in Manitou when it opened, has many other stories of the healing waters, including a lady named Lydia from the southern part of Saskatchewan.

Lydia came to Manitou Beach not being able to walk by herself. She soaked in the water over 10 days and by the end of it, she was able to take small stiff steps.

She moved to Watrous and lived there the rest of her life.

But the water isn’t the only thing Manitou Beach is known for. The land is rich with history and more than 3,000 artifacts have been found along the shore, left by Indigenous people over centuries.

It’s also home to The Salty Cinema Drive-In Theater, one of just three remaining in the province.

“Drive-ins are you know not as in vogue, but it is just another experience that goes on here at Manitou that makes us unique and people are willing to travel for it,” said Lane Manson, overseer of the drive-in.

Just outside the theatre sits a combine from the original Twister movie.

The Manitou Beach attractions bring in people from all over Canada and beyond, with the area seeing about 150,000 visitors a year.

“I recovered from my hip injury, but I come out here for the water and you know the magnesium in the water, it’s really good and I find that it really works well. I mean last year when I was here with my arm injury, I was in the water and I could do things with my arm I couldn’t do before,” said Bob Dobko from Rocky Mountain House, Alberta.

Watch the video above to learn more about Canada’s saltiest body of water.
paragraphs: Just outside the small community of Watrous, Saskatchewan, Manitou Beach sits on the so-called “Dead Sea of Canada.”

“Little Manitou Lake, carved out by glaciers exposing bedrock and minerals that have been absorbed by water over time,” said Jeff Siegfried, community enhancement director of the Watrous Manitou Beach Marketing Group. “It’s called a terminal lake meaning water flowing into it has no way to escape and so the minerals that are in the bed of the lake leach into the water.”
The water is up to five times saltier than the ocean and said to have healing properties. The name Manitou means spiritual force or mysterious being.
Indigenous people first used the water for its healing abilities. Oral tradition suggests the water was used to treat ailments such as smallpox.

“I guess in their day, because they had to move to follow the buffalo,” said Lionel Sproule, Watrous Manitou Beach Heritage Centre chairman. “They left these ill people behind… they would come back by this way a month later and there would be the ill people healed and then carry on with life.”
Sproule, who managed the spa in Manitou when it opened, has many other stories of the healing waters, including a lady named Lydia from the southern part of Saskatchewan.
Lydia came to Manitou Beach not being able to walk by herself. She soaked in the water over 10 days and by the end of it, she was able to take small stiff steps.
She moved to Watrous and lived there the rest of her life.
But the water isn’t the only thing Manitou Beach is known for. The land is rich with history and more than 3,000 artifacts have been found along the shore, left by Indigenous people over centuries.
It’s also home to The Salty Cinema Drive-In Theater, one of just three remaining in the province.

“Drive-ins are you know not as in vogue, but it is just another experience that goes on here at Manitou that makes us unique and people are willing to travel for it,” said Lane Manson, overseer of the drive-in.
Just outside the theatre sits a combine from the original Twister movie.
The Manitou Beach attractions bring in people from all over Canada and beyond, with the area seeing about 150,000 visitors a year.

“I recovered from my hip injury, but I come out here for the water and you know the magnesium in the water, it’s really good and I find that it really works well. I mean last year when I was here with my arm injury, I was in the water and I could do things with my arm I couldn’t do before,” said Bob Dobko from Rocky Mountain House, Alberta.

stories.title: Quebec Premier Fréchette calls cabinet meeting ahead of tariffs
stories.summary: Meeting comes as Canada prepares to impose retaliatory tariffs on a wide range of U.S. goods the following day
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette has called a special cabinet meeting for Monday, putting her election campaign on hold one day before Canadian retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods are set to take effect.

Fréchette’s office confirmed Sunday that the cabinet meeting will be held virtually at 6 p.m., but the agenda for cabinet meetings is not disclosed in advance. Such meetings are relatively rare during an election campaign, when Fréchette is simultaneously serving as premier and campaigning as CAQ leader.

The meeting comes as Canada prepares to impose retaliatory tariffs on a wide range of U.S. goods the following day. The tariffs, which will range from 15 to 50 per cent, will apply to products including dairy, steel, copper and some beauty products.

They are in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, ranging from hockey sticks to honey.

Rhetoric over the looming tariffs continued through the long weekend, with Trump posting on social media Sunday that the Canadian dollar’s exchange rate with the U.S. has been “unacceptable … for years – but no longer.”

Trump did not elaborate on his concerns, though the weaker Canadian dollar makes Canadian exports cheaper in the U.S. and American goods more expensive for Canadians.

Several of Fréchette’s political opponents accused her Sunday of using the tariff dispute for political gain during the provincial election campaign.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard accused Fréchette of putting on “a play” by calling her ministers together on the eve of the tariffs taking effect.

“We’re going to have a news conference, flags, long faces, people lined up around a table telling us they’re there for Quebeckers and that they’ll do everything they can to save Quebec,” Milliard said during a campaign stop in Gatineau.

He argued the CAQ government has failed to prepare Quebec businesses for the tariff war.

“This government has been there for eight years, not eight weeks,” Milliard said. “So to be told now that we’re going to be there for Quebeckers, we’re going to be there for workers, we’re going to hand out this cheque and that tax credit, I find that astonishing.”

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime also criticized the decision to convene cabinet, remarking on it during a campaign stop in Pont-Rouge, about 40 kilometres west of Quebec City.

“We all understand this is a CAQ marketing operation that is trying to exploit the tariff crisis to hide its record,” Duhaime said.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said in a written statement that “fear is not an economic strategy.”

He accused Fréchette of using “the Trump bogeyman” in recent days in the hope that voters will look away from the Caq’s record and the other parties’ proposals.

Speaking later in Montmagny, about 80 kilometres east of Quebec City, St-Pierre Plamondon said that strategy should not be “an excuse not to campaign and to lack transparency with Quebeckers.”

He also called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to directly keep all Quebec party leaders informed of developments in the event of further U.S. retaliation.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal acknowledged that Fréchette remains premier and is holding the meeting in that capacity.

“What I’m asking her is: what is she proposing when it comes to tariffs for workers?” Ghazal said after a campaign announcement outside the legislature in Quebec City.

The cabinet meeting comes as Ottawa is also preparing for the latest escalation in the trade dispute.

On Friday, the federal government briefed its advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations about the looming tariffs and planned support for workers and businesses.

The meeting included a briefing from Canada’s chief U.S. trade negotiator, Janice Charette, as well as ministers in charge of finance, industrial policy and U.S. trade.

“The discussion also highlighted the importance of a unified Team Canada approach, with governments, industry, labour and other partners working together to ensure Canada’s response reflects national priorities and promotes long-term economic growth,” reads a Sept. 4 news release.

Fréchette is not the first political leader to temporarily step away from an election campaign because of the tariff dispute.

During the 2025 federal election, Prime Minister Mark Carney paused his campaign three times to resume his official duties as the federal government prepared its response to the trade war with the United States.

stories.title: Otto Jelinek, a former cabinet minister and world-champion figure skater, dead at 86
stories.summary: Jelinek died peacefully in hospital on Saturday after living with Parkinson’s disease for nearly 20 years, his family says
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Otto Jelinek, a former world-champion figure skater and federal cabinet minister, has died at the age of 86.

The Jelinek family says he died peacefully in hospital on Saturday after living with Parkinson’s disease for nearly 20 years.

Jelinek was born in Prague and his family escaped communism in Czechoslovakia when he was a young boy.

Jelinek and his sister Maria went on to represent Canada in figure skating at the 1960 Winter Olympics in California.

He then entered federal politics, representing the Oakville, Ont. area for two decades and serving as national revenue minister under then prime minister Brian Mulroney, as well as portfolios in sport and multiculturalism.

He left politics after considering running for leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party, and was later appointed Canadian Ambassador to the Czech Republic.

stories.title: Ex-mayor sole Liberal leadership candidate for P.E.I., provincial party says
stories.summary: Dan Kutcher resigned as mayor of Summerside, P.E.I., last month to run in the Liberal leadership race
stories.content:
The Liberal Party of Prince Edward Island says it has only one leadership candidate.

The party says in a news release that Dan Kutcher was the sole approved candidate when the nomination period closed.

Kutcher resigned as mayor of Summerside, P.E.I., last month to run in the Liberal leadership race.

He was elected mayor in 2022, and previously said he wouldn’t run again in the municipal election this November.

He has also told local media he would seek the Liberal nomination for a provincial district that covers part of the eastern side of the city.

The Liberal Party says Kutcher will continue to engage with Islanders ahead of the party’s leadership convention on Sept. 13.

stories.title: Trump says Canada-U.S. dollar 'imbalance is unacceptable'
stories.summary: Donald Trump was posting about Canada's dollar and the renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America in the U.S. Sunday on Truth Social.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump took a few swings at Canada during a spate of AI-generated posts to his Truth Social platform on Sunday afternoon, including a complaint about the value of the Canadian dollar.

“Canada’s (currency) Dollar imbalance with the U.S. is unacceptable,” he wrote in the morning. “It has been that way for years – but no longer!”

Trump didn’t elaborate.

'We're taking it very personally': Republican mayor from Lake Ontario city rejects Trump's 'Lake America'

Letters: Pull the plug on Trump's 'Lake America'

The U.S. is set to be hit with Canada’s retaliatory tariffs Tuesday, adding to the tension of an already complicated and costly trade war.

Early Sunday afternoon, after sharing AI-generated images of himself with George Washington — one in the Oval Office with this cabinet, another of the pair astride horses — the president posted another image of himself writing America over Ontario on a map of the suddenly disputed lake.

In his salvo against Canada 10 days ago, Trump ordered the U.S. Geographic Names Information System to change the hydronym, after which Google Maps said it would make the change for users in the U.S. Apple followed suit last week.

On Friday, Trump said Bing Maps, a Microsoft product, has also made the change.

“People, especially Patriots from the United States of America, love the name change of Lake Ontario to Lake America,” he wrote. “The support has been overwhelming, including affirmation from Google Maps, Apple Maps, and Microsoft’s Bing Maps.”

Trump claimed business on the U.S. side of the border has been “booming” since the change.

National Post has contacted Microsoft for confirmation and comment.

Amid his flood of posts on Sunday, Trump shared a graphic reading: “If you have a problem with Lake Ontario being renamed Lake America just remember, the Left renamed the following.”

His list of things include various renamed U.S. military bases, commercial products, as well as the Nfl’s Washington Commanders (formerly Redskins) and the MLB’s Cleveland Guardians (formerly Indians).

Later, while he didn’t mention Canada specifically, he posted three separate graphics explaining “Non-tariff cheating” and the “8 hidden tricks by foreign countries.”

Some of the examples of “cheating” include banning U.S. food, cheapening their money and applying “weird tests” to make it hard for American firms to enter their market.

stories.title: Legendary film producer René Malo helped introduce Quebec film to the world
stories.summary: Considered ‘one of the great pillars’ of cinema in the province, he championed an unlikely hit that received Canada’s first Oscar nomination in international film
stories.author: Alexander Hackett
stories.content:
René Malo, who died on Aug. 23 at the age of 84, was a driving force behind what many consider to be a before-and-after event in Canadian cinema: the production of Denys Arcand’s 1986 bedroom comedy-drama The Decline of the American Empire.

The film was an unlikely success story and runaway hit, earning Canada’s first-ever Oscar nomination in the Best International Feature Film category. On a more fundamental level, it was a wonderful window into the uniqueness and vitality of Quebec culture for audiences in English-speaking Canada and around the world.

A serious-themed comedy of manners often compared to movies like The Big Chill and Annie Hall, it followed a group of talky, bourgeois intellectuals and libidinous academics from the University of Montreal as they navigated love, sex and relationships. Full of bawdy humour and many a verbose monologue, it touched on everything from adultery, prostitution and Bdsm to homosexuality, the Aids epidemic and the nature of love in an era of middle-class stability and prosperity. It was proof that Canadian films could be different, highbrow and entertaining all at once. Audiences loved it.

Along with the Oscar nomination, it won nine Genie Awards, including Best Motion Picture; the International Critics Award at Cannes; and the People’s Choice Award at Tiff. To this day, few Canadian films have equalled its performance. From a budget of $1.8-million, the film grossed $30-million worldwide. It paved the way for further success for Mr. Arcand, who garnered another Academy Award nomination for Jesus of Montreal (1989) and a win for The Decline ’s sequel, The Barbarian Invasions (2003) – Canada’s first and only Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film/Best International Feature Film.

Not many people would have bet on Mr. Arcand’s edgy script, but Mr. Malo understood its potential.

“René was absolutely instrumental in getting the film made,” said co-producer Roger Frappier, a 50-year veteran of the Quebec and Canadian film industries who has worked with the likes of Denis Villeneuve, Jane Campion and Don McKellar.

“At the time there was a resistance within the National Film Board toward fictional films – they preferred documentaries. So I said I would do the movie in collaboration with the private sector. I sent the script to René and he loved it. He went to Telefilm Canada and he was responsible for the foreign sales.”

Despite the push, Telefilm Canada was initially unimpressed.

“It’s funny, because at the time, Telefilm Canada did not like the movie. They thought it would not make a penny,” Mr. Frappier said.

Mr. Malo was undeterred. His flair for business kicked in and, knowing audiences would respond positively after a series of advance screenings in France, he devised a plan to generate buzz for the film in Montreal.

“René had this very daring and risky idea: he opened The Decline of the American Empire in only one theatre at first – the Crémazie theatre, high up on Saint-Denis Street,” Mr. Frappier said. “He said ‘People from [northern suburb] Laval will come down to see it, and people from Montreal will go up.’ This was the intelligence of René Malo.”

Enthusiastic word-of-mouth led to sold-out screenings, with people scrambling to find tickets. The movie stayed at the Crémazie theatre for a full year.

The tactic was typical of Mr. Malo’s approach, according to Quebec screen legend Micheline Lanctôt, who worked with him for her directorial debut L’Homme à Tout Faire and its follow-up, Sonatine, which won the Silver Lion Award at the Venice Film Festival in 1984.

“I first met René in California, when he was there to discuss a deal with Warner Brothers to get the exclusive VHS rights for distribution in Quebec,” Ms. Lanctôt said. “I had written a screenplay, and René loved it. I had no intention of directing it, but he thought it was too personal to give to someone else, so he asked me to direct it, and I said, Why not? That was pretty bold.”

“He had a very well-supplied address book,” she continued. “I owe him everything, actually. He launched me, in a way. He got the film financed, and it ended up in the Director’s Fortnight at Cannes in 1980. We were flabbergasted. We had a really good time. He was lavish.”

René Malo was born in the small town of Joliette, Que., ON March 7, 1942, the eldest son of a seamstress and a factory worker for the Joliette Steel Company. He attended a Collège Classique programme at the Séminaire de Joliette, firmly in the Jesuit tradition, where he was exposed to the arts, philosophy and a European-style education. It was an important influence on René, who came of age just as Quebec was shaking off centuries of religious conservatism, culminating in the Quiet Revolution of the 1960s.

“My dad had humble beginnings,” said his daughter Fanny-Laure Malo, who followed in her father’s footsteps and works in the film industry. “Growing up, he had to sleep on the couch, while his younger brother and sister shared the bedroom. But he was part of the generation that brought [modern rock] music and arts to small towns in Quebec.”

Rénald Paré, a childhood friend who lived in the apartment above the Malo family, was born only 14 days after René. They became business partners and remained lifelong friends.

“René was very extroverted,” Mr. Paré said. “He was admired by all the young women, and respected by all the young men.”

This extroversion led him and some friends to start their own boîte à chansons, or nightclub, in Joliette called Le Cabastran, from 1963 to ’66. While studying at the University of Montreal – which he quit after two years – he and the group organized summer concerts at Le Cabastran for Quebec impresario Guy Latraverse.

“At first, René was mostly drawn to theatre, but in those years he put on shows for people like Charles Aznavour, Johnny Hallyday and Robert Charlebois,” Mr. Paré said. “He became close with artists like Jean-Pierre Ferland and Claude Dubois and really helped their careers. Already by the age of 18, in the early sixties, he was deep into the world of show business. René was very warm, very generous. He was a great communicator and an excellent negotiator.”

“We’d start around Saint-Jean-Baptiste holiday [June 24], and have shows up until Labour Day,” Mr. Paré continued. “Then we’d take our profits and go down to Cape Cod for a week.”

At Expo 67 in Montreal, he was named director of variety shows for the Youth Pavillion, putting on a further 1,450 hours of concerts and shows – everything from jazz to rock, pop and French-language chansonniers , as well as debates, experimental theatre and audio-visual presentations.

In 1971, he founded his first film production company, Corporation Image M&M, which was followed by Malofilm Distributions in 1973 and Malofilm Communications Inc. in 1983. From 1971 onwards, Mr. Malo was involved in every aspect of the film business, from production and distribution, to promotion and international sales.

At its peak, Malofilm Communications Inc. boasted annual sales of $50-million, becoming one of Canada’s leading entertainment companies. Mr. Malo’s deft hand at running a company and turning profit was confirmed after he sold the company in 1996 for $21-million. Within three years, following an attempted rebrand and a series of financial losses, new owner Richard Szalwinski dismantled the company and sold its parts.

In his later years, diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease, Mr. Malo turned to philanthropy and founded the Fondation René Malo, supporting childhood health initiatives, and the René Malo chair at the University of Quebec at Montreal to help young filmmakers. He was a staunch defender and promoter of Quebec and Canadian cinema, playing an active role in the enactment of the Quebec Cinema Act, and the establishment of Telefilm Canada’s distribution and feature film funds.

“He was the first person to modernize the [film distribution] industry in Quebec,” Mr. Frappier said. “He was one of the great pillars of our cinema.”

Among the many honours he received in his life were the Air Canada prize for contributions to the Canadian film industry and the Prix Jutra-Hommage in Quebec. Mr. Malo was made a Knight of the National Order of Quebec in 2013.

“My father was the most intelligent person I’ve ever met,” his daughter said. “He was always optimistic about our filmmakers and had a will to fight for our culture. His vision was always grand. He was the protector.”

Mr. Malo leaves his wife, Marie Gagnon; their children, Fanny-Laure and Laurent Emmanuel Malo; his sister, Reine Malo; two nieces and two nephews.

stories.title: Quebec Premier calls cabinet meeting ahead of tariffs
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette has called a special cabinet meeting for Monday, putting her election campaign on hold one day before Canadian retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods are set to take effect.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette has called a special cabinet meeting for Monday, putting her election campaign on hold one day before Canadian retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods are set to take effect.

Fréchette’s office confirmed Sunday that the cabinet meeting will be held virtually at 6 p.m., but the agenda for cabinet meetings is not disclosed in advance. Such meetings are relatively rare during an election campaign, when Fréchette is simultaneously serving as premier and campaigning as CAQ leader.

The meeting comes as Canada prepares to impose retaliatory tariffs on a wide range of U.S. goods the following day. The tariffs, which will range from 15 to 50 per cent, will apply to products including dairy, steel, copper and some beauty products.

They are in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, ranging from hockey sticks to honey.

Rhetoric over the looming tariffs continued through the long weekend, with Trump posting on social media Sunday that the Canadian dollar’s exchange rate with the U.S. has been “unacceptable … for years — but no longer.”

Trump did not elaborate on his concerns, though the weaker Canadian dollar makes Canadian exports cheaper in the U.S. and American goods more expensive for Canadians.

Several of Fréchette’s political opponents accused her Sunday of using the tariff dispute for political gain during the provincial election campaign.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard accused Fréchette of putting on “a play” by calling her ministers together on the eve of the tariffs taking effect.

“We’re going to have a news conference, flags, long faces, people lined up around a table telling us they’re there for Quebecers and that they’ll do everything they can to save Quebec,” Milliard said during a campaign stop in Gatineau.

He argued the CAQ government has failed to prepare Quebec businesses for the tariff war.

“This government has been there for eight years, not eight weeks,” Milliard said. “So to be told now that we’re going to be there for Quebecers, we’re going to be there for workers, we’re going to hand out this cheque and that tax credit, I find that astonishing.”

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime also criticized the decision to convene cabinet, remarking on it during a campaign stop in Pont-Rouge, about 40 kilometres west of Quebec City.

“We all understand this is a CAQ marketing operation that is trying to exploit the tariff crisis to hide its record,” Duhaime said.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said in a written statement that “fear is not an economic strategy.”

He accused Fréchette of using “the Trump bogeyman” in recent days in the hope that voters will look away from the Caq’s record and the other parties’ proposals.

Speaking later in Montmagny, about 80 kilometres east of Quebec City, St-Pierre Plamondon said that strategy should not be “an excuse not to campaign and to lack transparency with Quebecers.”

He also called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to directly keep all Quebec party leaders informed of developments in the event of further U.S. retaliation.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal acknowledged that Fréchette remains premier and is holding the meeting in that capacity.

“What I’m asking her is: what is she proposing when it comes to tariffs for workers?” Ghazal said after a campaign announcement outside the legislature in Quebec City.

The cabinet meeting comes as Ottawa is also preparing for the latest escalation in the trade dispute.

On Friday, the federal government briefed its advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations about the looming tariffs and planned support for workers and businesses.

The meeting included a briefing from Canada’s chief U.S. trade negotiator, Janice Charette, as well as ministers in charge of finance, industrial policy and U.S. trade.

“The discussion also highlighted the importance of a unified Team Canada approach, with governments, industry, labour and other partners working together to ensure Canada’s response reflects national priorities and promotes long-term economic growth,” reads a Sept. 4 news release.

Fréchette is not the first political leader to temporarily step away from an election campaign because of the tariff dispute.

During the 2025 federal election, Prime Minister Mark Carney paused his campaign three times to resume his official duties as the federal government prepared its response to the trade war with the United States.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa and Thomas Laberge in Gatineau
