stories.title: How to help your child navigate back-to-school anxiety
stories.summary: Psychotherapist Lori Griffith shares tips on how families can manage nerves ahead of the first day of school
stories.author: Travis Dolynny
paragraphs: Psychotherapist Lori Griffith shares tips on how families can manage nerves ahead of the first day of school
The countdown to the new school year can trigger a mix of excitement and stress.

Psychotherapist Lori Griffith, a director at the Canadian Mental Health Association (Cmha) Thames Valley, offers insight into why students and parents experience back-to-school nerves, how to validate those feelings, and when it might be time to seek professional support.
Griffith spoke with London Morning host Matt Allen.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Matt Allen: What are some of the emotions kids might be feeling as summer winds down?

Lori Griffith: It's completely normal for students of all ages to feel some level of anxiety about going back to school. A new teacher, new routine, social pressures, academic expectations, and uncertainty can all create stress.

The goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety. Anxiety is a normal human emotion. The goal is helping students to learn that they can cope with it. What we might see before going back to school is some butterflies before the first day, worrying if friends will be in their class, feeling nervous about a new school or teacher.
LISTEN | How to help your child:
Media Audio | London Morning :
MA: Is it just the kids who are nervous right now, or parents too?

LG: I think it's everybody. Every time you're starting a new challenge or an event, it's normal to feel a little bit anxious. The normal thing is to feel uncomfortable, but try to manage through it. As long as something's not interfering significantly with daily life, we do normally see routines and the anxiety will improve once they settle into their routine.
MA: Why do kids get so nervous heading into a new grade?

LG: I think it's the fear of the unknown. I mean, I think that's common with all of us. Also, we get this idea of this anticipatory anxiety. Often kids aren't struggling with the event itself, they're struggling with imagining the event. Maybe they're worrying all weekend about Monday, or worrying all summer about school, and thinking about every possible thing that could potentially go wrong.
MA: What are some tips for parents who are trying to psych their kids up to enter a new environment?

LG: I think it's really important to acknowledge the feeling. We're not looking to avoid or remove the feeling. We're wanting to acknowledge and then express confidence in the children and encourage gradual exposure.

As an example, if a child misses school because they're nervous, they May feel better that day, but then their brains will learn, "I survived it because I avoided it." The next time, the anxiety May come back a little bit stronger.
Instead of saying, "Don't worry, there's nothing to be nervous about," we want to say things like, "I can see you're nervous. New things can feel scary, but I know you can handle this."
MA: How can parents support their children if they don't have all the answers?

LG: One of the nice things is when we're kind of exposing ourselves to a new routine is to keep routines predictable. Children feel safer when expectations are clear. Consistent sleep schedules (sleep is one of the most important things that we can do in terms of relieving some of that worry), regular meals, and then preparing. Whether that looks like preparing on the weekend for the upcoming week, or preparing that night for the school the next day.

Focus on coping, not certainty. Parents often try to reassure away anxiety. Instead of saying that "Nothing bad will happen," try saying something to your youth or your child that says, "Whatever happens, we'll figure it out." This will teach the resilience rather than dependence on certainty.
MA: How do parents know if anxiety is normal or if professional help is necessary?

LG: Anxiety, it May be there for a couple weeks as they're adjusting to that schedule. When we want to look for more support is if it's persisting for more weeks, it's getting worse rather than better, it's causing significant distress, or if it's interfering with their school attendance, their sleep patterns, their friendships, family life, or other activities.
One kind of way of thinking about it is when anxiety starts running a child's life instead of simply visiting it from time to time, that's when we become more concerned.

When we want to look for more support is if it's persisting for more weeks, it's getting worse rather than better, it's causing significant distress, or if it's interfering with their school attendance, their sleep patterns, their friendships, family life, or other activities.

One kind of way of thinking about it is when anxiety starts running a child's life instead of simply visiting it from time to time, that's when we become more concerned.

stories.title: How Howard Lutnick became Donald Trump’s ‘ultimate disrupter’ in Canada’s trade war
stories.summary: Sometimes the U.S. commerce secretary has been described as charming and pleasant to deal with. Other times, his bare-knuckled bargaining style has been called "bananas." Everyone agrees that he's a
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Americans weren’t happy. But Howard Lutnick seemed furious.

It was early March 2025, the final days of Justin Trudeau’s prime ministership, and the trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump had only just begun. Ottawa had struck back with retaliatory tariffs against the first volley of U.S. import duties. Two days later, Trudeau and his advisers gathered in his office for a phone call with the American president, according to two Canadian officials with knowledge of what happened, who agreed to speak about sensitive discussions on the condition they weren’t identified.

During the conversation, which both officials described as heated, Trump brought in Vice President JD Vance and Lutnick, the New York billionaire who serves as commerce secretary. The Americans spoke of how they would now exempt goods from tariffs if they complied with the North American trade deal that Trump had signed during his first term.

Shouldn’t the Canadians be grateful?

As it turned out, Ottawa still saw the remaining tariffs as an unjustified violation of the trade deal, and would therefore still retaliate. This, according to both officials, is what offended the Americans — and nobody more so than Lutnick.

One of the officials said Lutnick sounded shocked and angry, expressing fury that Canada had the gall to strike back when the U.S. was softening its position. The second official described Lutnick as “losing his s — t,” and said his tone became “bananas” over the course of the call.

“He’s a guy whose basic instinct is to revert to anger,” they said. “He’s been an ultimate disrupter.”

That perception of Lutnick has hardened since Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with the Trump administration in August, declaring the U.S. had “attacked” Canada with last-minute demands that would have eroded the country’s independence.

Sources have told the Star and other media that Lutnick was a factor in the collapse of negotiations , particularly over the exclusion of trucks made in Oshawa and Oakville from American tariff relief that was on the table, while the commerce secretary and other American officials blamed the Canadian side for unreasonably pushing too hard and walking away from the best deal in Trump’s new world of tariffs and trade transactions.

The latest U.S. tariffs on more than 700 Canadian products took effect last month.

Regardless of what happened, observers — including some with direct knowledge of Lutnick as an American interlocutor — see in the commerce secretary the embodiment of the Trump administration’s transactional negotiating approach. Brash, slick-haired, cocksure, the erstwhile Manhattan financier was a key player in jockeying over the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which saw the U.S. extract further concessions from Canada allowing the opening of the $6.4-billion structure, which was financed entirely by Ottawa. Last year, behind closed doors at a conference in Toronto, Lutnick declared Canada should find something else to build in Ontario’s car-making heartland, since the U.S. planned to dominate the auto sector and “there is nothing Canada can do about it.”

Portraying Lutnick as the villain in the relationship would be simplistic, however. He can be charming and pleasant to deal with, said one Canadian official, adding that Lutnick’s bluster can also be read as a performance, and a tactic to accomplish his goals. But the official said it’s also true that Lutnick can turn on a dime, and show the edge and intensity of a ruthless New York dealmaker.

“He’ll stab you in the stomach while smiling in your face,” the official said.

Lutnick’s office did not respond to requests for comment from the Star.

It’s getting harder to believe that the president is a symptom rather than the cause of what’s gone off the rails in the U.S., Susan Delacourt writes.

Lutnick, 65, came to politics after a long career in the New York financial world. He helped raise money for Trump’s 2024 presidential run, and co-chaired his transition back to the White House as Trump met with petitioners at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. A profile in The New Yorker described him as “the most Trumpian member of Trump’s cabinet,” and Lutnick has seemed to embrace the president’s style and mercantilist world view. On a podcast in 2025, he echoed Trump’s notion of a halcyon era of high tariffs in the U.S., when taxes on imports filled government coffers in the absence of personal income tax.

Accounts of Lutnick’s past describe his ascent in the 1980s and 1990s at the New York investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald. By his mid-thirties he had control of the firm following a bitter succession battle with the widow of the company’s founder, in which Lutnick was accused in the New York Times of staging a “palace coup.”

One Canadian official said that Carney’s lead cabinet minister on U.S. trade, Dominic LeBlanc, established a solid relationship with Lutnick in early 2025. The pair texted often and got along well, the official said, even as the trade war heated up.

But Canadians have observed Lutnick’s forcefulness in trade talks. He has been seen as trying to assert dominance through his oversight of sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos — import duties the Trump administration justifies on “national security” grounds.

“He’s outrageous. He is mercurial. He yells. The way he talks in public is like he talks in private. He can be extremely aggressive, unlike Trump, who in private is never really aggressive,” one former official said.

“I think he is driven by the desire to be the top dog, be admired by the president, to always come out on top.”

Lutnick’s life has been marked by death and tragedy. His mother, an art teacher, died of cancer when he was 16 in 1978, and his father died the following year after he was given the wrong dose at his first chemotherapy treatment for lung cancer, Lutnick told a U.S. Senate committee after he was nominated to Trump’s cabinet.

Cantor Fitzgerald’s Manhattan offices took up the top five floors of the north tower of the World Trade Center. When hijacked planes struck the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001, 658 Cantor Fitzgerald employees were killed, including Lutnick’s younger brother Gary, who had lived with him in his college dorm room after their parents died. Lutnick told the Senate hearing that the only reason he wasn’t also killed is that he was taking his son to his first day of kindergarten when the attacks occurred.

Kevin O’Leary, the Canadian TV personality and investor, said Lutnick’s response to the disaster and efforts to support victims’ families and rebuild the company are “legendary” in the business community.

“He’s actually a nice guy. You know, he’s an entertaining guy with a lot of energy,” O’Leary said, describing how he last ran into Lutnick in a hotel lobby in Washington, D.C.

“You May or May not like his negotiating style,” O’Leary added. “Everybody’s got their own thing.”

And that rubs some people the wrong way. Last winter, when Lutnick gave the final speech at a dinner during the World Economic Forum in Davos, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde walked out.

Lutnick “just bashed Europe, right, left and centre,” she told the Wall Street Journal . “That was just too much and just unnecessarily offensive.”

The commerce secretary has also faced pressure and scrutiny from fellow Americans. Steve Bannon, the right-wing commentator and former Trump adviser, panned Lutnick’s defence of Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs last year as an “unmitigated disaster.”

Washington (AP) — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, in an interview with House lawmakers, backed away from a previous claim that convicted se…

Last May, after Lutnick admitted he and his family visited the Caribbean island of the disgraced late financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2012, members of the U.S. Congress accused him of lying about his interactions with Epstein — who had been Lutnick’s neighbour in New York City — and called on him to resign immediately.

One Canadian official said a big challenge in dealing with the Trump administration is reading who has more influence at any given time in what they described as a “chaotic” and at times “unclear” dynamic inside the White House.

Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and member of Carney’s advisory council on economic relations with the U.S., said that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer took the leading role in recent talks that almost landed with a deal in late August. But in the final days before talks fell apart, Lutnick got more involved, and it soon became clear to the Canadians that the U.S. would not include medium and heavy duty trucks in any tariff relief, Volpe said — something that could doom factories in Ontario.

“I know for sure that wasn’t the case going into Wednesday night,” Volpe said, citing the evening two days before the negotiations collapsed.

“We were in contact, semi-regular contact, with the negotiating team … The clarity that medium and heavy trucks were excluded came in after Canada repeatedly sought clarity on Friday,” he added. “Whether it came directly from Lutnick or not, it came after Lutnick became directly involved.”

Given Lutnick’s comments last year that Canada must surrender auto manufacturing to the U.S., Volpe said he believes the commerce secretary was responsible for this aspect of the disagreement.

“I don’t believe in coincidences,” he said.

Lutnick, meanwhile, has blamed Canada for adding last minute changes to the deal, and the U.S. maintains that medium and heavy trucks were never part of the deal. On Wednesday, a smiling Lutnick told the U.S. broadcaster Cnbc that the Carney government “blew it up for political reasons only” ahead of separatist concerns in the Quebec election and Alberta referendum in October.

“We were treated disrespectfully,” Lutnick insisted.

“It’s just sad the way Canada has treated us.”

With files from Tonda MacCharles

stories.title: How Canada’s border offices are facing a major security gap
stories.summary: The audit examined the security controls at border agencies including airports, land border crossings, mail processing centres, warehouses, telephone reporting sites and office buildings.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) is woefully behind when it comes to protecting its only facilities at airports, ports of entry and offices from security threat and risk, an audit found.

A recent effort to catch up on that work has exposed major shortcomings: Unauthorized people walked into secure areas through “piggybacking.” Surveillance cameras were missing or too blurry to be useful to guard the facilities. And official stamps used to process travellers and goods at ports of entry couldn’t be accounted for.

The report examined the security controls at premises of the border agency, which operates in more than 1,000 facilities across the country, including airports, land border crossings, mail processing centres, warehouses, telephone reporting sites and office buildings.

Of the 410 sites classified as “critical facilities,” 312 or 75 per cent had no records of threat and risk assessments or had one that was more than five years old — and only 69 or 40 per cent of 162 “medium and high-risk” premises had a valid evaluation, the internal audit found.

“This indicates that the agency does not have a comprehensive or up to date baseline understanding of the risks and vulnerabilities present in most of its facilities,” said the report, released on Monday.

Advocates say they are alarmed by the pushback of immigration authorities against migrants trying to exercise their right to protest.

Security and intelligence expert Wesley Wark said it’s incumbent on every federal department and agency, especially those with a role in national security, to protect their data and infrastructure.

“That level of seriousness in terms of responding to a potential threat is not there for Cbsa and improvements have to be made,” said Wark, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation. “This is an important responsibility that needs to be done in a better, more rigorous way.”

The Cbsa audit, covering the period between April 2022 and September 2025, focused on its physical security rules and oversight, internal controls and processes such as risk management, as well as monitoring and reporting of physical security activities.

Auditors reviewed more than 300 documents, interviewed over 75 people involved and affected by these measures and visited 18 sites with walk-throughs in facilities in Ontario, the Pacific and Quebec regions.

They pored over 180 physical security recommendations issued during the audit period but found only 25 per cent had been implemented, while the rest were either not carried out or could not be confirmed, indicating the identified vulnerabilities May have persisted, the report warned.

The border agency’s management attributed the lacking valid threat and risk assessments to other priorities and limited human and financial resources. Reasons for lagging implementations included insufficient funding, infeasibility and no clear order of priority.

In an email, Cbsa said it’s on track to complete all ongoing threat and risk assessments by March 2027, at which time it will establish annual compliance monitoring of threat risk assessment recommendations.

“We treat this matter seriously and take immediate action whenever gaps in physical security are identified,” said the agency, which has conducted an internal analysis to ensure its physical security data is accurate and up to date.

“The Cbsa has worked to address these issues over recent years by investing in physical security elements such as alarm systems, distress alarms, lighting, fences, barriers, signage, doors and windows.”

During a number of walk-throughs in various locations, audit team members were able to access all secure and non-secure floors unannounced, at various times of day, without access cards or visible Cbsa identification. They were let in by occupants of the floors or entered through “piggybacking” — following an authorized person. They were only questioned on one of the six secure floors and two of the nine non-secure floors.

On two occasions, employees were found to be away from their workstations, with computer screens unlocked and unattended. Sensitive documents were left at printers, including financial documents and documentation containing personal traveller data such as names, passage dates, passport numbers and dates of birth.

“In some instances, the audit team was also able to consult paper documents with Protected B and C information, in cabinets that were left open, without being questioned,” said the report, referring to classified information pertaining to private personal data and business records.

Although all 18 inspected sites had some form of electronic surveillance or Cctv infrastructure, problems were identified at half of them, including no coverage in key operational areas and low-quality resolution:

There was no Cctv installed at one primary inspection lane that processes millions of crossing vehicles yearly;

Three other locations had no Cctv coverage in areas such as the bond rooms, where seized goods are held;

The remaining five locations had Cctv cameras with such poor resolution that in some cases images were not visible.

“The most significant deficiencies were noted in one facility that had no electronic access management system; the entire Port of Entry (POE) leveraged locks with a pin code and/or keys with the same code for the entire facility,” the audit noted.

“This facility had no intrusion alarm, although the audit notes that it is manned 24/7 with officers. Another three POE had access management systems which were deemed to be at a very high risk of failure.”

The team also audited the management of port stamps that are used to identify the date, location, purpose and duration of a traveller’s authorized stay, or the personal and commercial goods entering and exiting Canada. They authenticate documents and identify the issuing officers with their unique numbers.

They found that the government’s database was consistently out of date and didn’t match the actual stamps on hand at border crossings, while others in the system were missing, damaged, moved, reassigned or unaccounted for. There were also stamps in storage that were not in the inventory data.

“Compromise, such as a lost or stolen stamps, can directly impact the integrity of Canada’s border,” the report cautioned.

Throughout his nine years in Canada, the Egyptian man has gone through — and passed — three extensive security checks by multiple federal agencies.

Security expert Wark believes the gaps identified in the audit have more to do with what he calls the “security culture” at Cbsa, rather than lacking resources because infrastructure such as access controls and Cctv cameras are not “a big money pit.”

He said a lot of people don’t understand the threat and risk until they are convinced to take it seriously, but more often than not major changes only happen after there’s a security crisis.

“The security culture at Cbsa is a little more lax than they should be comfortable with,” said Wark. “It’s an important reminder that physical security matters and that there are practices and policies in place that need to be followed as rigorously as possible.”

The border agency said many historical Cctv issues have been rectified and it’s working to address known deficiencies as quickly as possible.

Following the audit, it said it conducted further review of its port stamps inventory and located some missing stamps at a different port of entry, and the records have since been updated to reflect the stamps’ actual location.

The agency said a new step-by-step guide will be ready by the end of September for how to do a yearly check across the country to make sure all security-sensitive items are accounted for, and a five-year program of work will replace access control systems at a number of sites every year.

“The Cbsa maintains a safe and secure operational environment where its personnel, facilities, information and assets are guarded from security threats and vulnerabilities,” it said.

The Customs and Immigration Union, which represents more than 9,000 Cbsa employees, said it’s still reviewing the audit and declined to comment.

stories.title: Athletics Canada says mountaineer goes missing attempting Matterhorn record
stories.summary: Canadian mountain runner Kalie McCrystal has gone missing while preparing for a record attempt on the Matterhorn along the Switzerland-Italy border.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
Athletics Canada says one of its members has gone missing while attempting to break a mountain-running record in the Alps along the Switzerland-Italy border.

The national sport governing body says in a statement that Kalie McCrystal was last seen Tuesday.

It says the skyrunner and mountaineer was climbing Italy’s Matterhorn, a roughly 4,481-metre-tall, horn-shaped peak overlooking the Swiss town of Zermatt.

The statement says McCrystal has many years of experience in technical, high-altitude environments, and has climbed the Matterhorn before.

“This was therefore not her first ascent of the mountain,” it said.

The statement did not give details on the record she was trying to break.

“Kalie is a highly respected athlete and a valued member of the worldwide skyrunning community,” it said.

“Our thoughts are with Kalie, her family and everyone close to her at this extremely difficult time. We are hoping for her safe return and are grateful to those involved in the ongoing search.”

Riley Webb, a close friend from McCrystal’s hometown of Squamish, B.C., said he has known her for about five years and described her as an accomplished mountain runner, lawyer and deeply caring friend.

“She was very thoughtful and compassionate. Always there for you. Truly always there for you,” he told Global News.

Webb said McCrystal’s disappearance and the uncertainty surrounding the search have been difficult for those close to her.

“As a friend and someone very close to her, it’s almost unbearable,” he said.

The two began pursuing mountain and trail running around the same time, training and heading into the mountains together.

Webb said McCrystal’s passion and dedication to the sport stood out, as did her desire to champion women in mountain running.

“I think she was a very inspiring person.”

– With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Quebec parties target health care, affordability and debate referendum as election looms
stories.summary: Fréchette claimed St-Pierre Plamondon avoided the word ‘referendum’ at a major PQ campaign rally in Quebec City the previous night
stories.content:
With one month to go before Quebec’s provincial election, parties on Saturday pitched voters on health care, government spending and daycare, while their leaders also debated the prospect of another referendum on Quebec independence.

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette promised to expand access to reduced-fee daycare, while accusing Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon of hiding his commitment to hold a referendum.

Speaking at a news conference Saturday morning in Lorraine, north of Montreal, Fréchette claimed St-Pierre Plamondon avoided the word “referendum” at a major PQ campaign rally in Quebec City the previous night.

“Yesterday, he gathered his supporters. Not once did he use the word referendum,” she said. “That’s hiding things from Quebecers.”

Fréchette also argued this is the worst time to hold a referendum, pointing to the trade conflict with the United States, and she also accused her rivals of not talking enough about U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs .

“We’re in an economic war with our main trading partner, and for the other parties, it’s as though it were a minor news story,” she said.

However, St-Pierre Plamondon rejected Fréchette’s accusation he was avoiding referendum talk, saying he uses “popular consultation” and “referendum” interchangeably.

“I’ve used the word at times. I use popular consultation, referendum,” he told reporters in Quebec City. “Popular consultation and referendum mean exactly the same thing.”

Fréchette on Saturday also pledged 25,000 additional reduced-fee daycare spaces at a cost of $750-million over four years. But only 5,000 would be entirely new spaces.

Of the 25,000, 15,000 were part of previous commitments, while another 5,000 would come from converting existing unsubsidized spaces into subsidized ones.

The CAQ would also offer newly qualified daycare workers a $10,000 bonus if they commit to working for at least two years in a subsidized daycare or early childhood centre.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard accused Fréchette of playing with the numbers during a campaign stop in Lévis, across the St. Lawrence River from Quebec City.

“This isn’t 25,000 new spaces being announced this morning. It’s a maximum of 5,000 spaces,” he told reporters.

The Parti Québécois, meanwhile, proposed a series of measures aimed at accountability at the highest levels of government, including freezing the salaries of legislature members, cabinet ministers and heads of Crown corporations until Quebec returns to a balanced budget, which the party expects in 2028-29.

The PQ would also require candidates selected to lead Crown corporations to appear before a legislative committee, set performance targets for their CEOs and review executive bonuses.

“We can’t ask the public and broader public sectors to go on a certain diet while we don’t set an example ourselves,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.

At a campaign stop in Chicoutimi, about 200 kilometres north of Quebec City, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal proposed 400 primary-care access points inspired by Quebec’s Clsc community health centre model, at an estimated cost of $1.8-billion a year.

The party would open 200 during a first mandate and another 200 during a second. Ghazal said the centres would make it easier for Quebecers to enter the health system and help relieve pressure on emergency rooms.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, meanwhile, unveiled his party’s digital plan in Inverness, about 100 kilometres southwest of Quebec City, aimed at making nearly all Quebec government services available online.

His party says the plan would save $3.45-billion in administrative costs over five years. It also calls for reducing regulatory requirements by 30 per cent over four years and using artificial intelligence in government operations with human oversight.

“The Quebec government has to enter the 21st century, and quickly,” Duhaime said.

stories.title: Snowbirds roar over Toronto in near-final flight before jets grounded until 2030s
stories.summary: Negotiations are underway with the manufacturer of the team’s new jets, Defence Minister McGuinty said in May while Canada has increased military spending
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
Jets roared over downtown Toronto on Saturday as the Canadian International Air Show featured one of the final flights of the Snowbirds over Ontario’s capital until at least the 2030s.

Crowds whistled and waved their hats as the Snowbirds appeared in the skies overhead, flying in tight formation and trailing clouds of smoke behind them. Some broke into applause as two of the jets flew in a barrel roll, tracing a corkscrew path over the lakeshore in tandem.

The nine-jet aerobatic team of the Canadian Armed Forces will be grounded at the end of the 2026 season as their signature CT-114 Tutor jets are replaced by the CT-157 Siskin II.

The team is scheduled to perform twice more at the Canadian International Air Show, hosted annually on the Toronto’s lakeshore, over the Labour Day long weekend before heading to northern Ontario.

Pierre Gionet, an aviation enthusiast at the air show on Saturday, said the Snowbirds are a symbol of Canadian pride.

“I do stream a lot of air shows online and whenever the Snowbirds are there, I get a little feeling I don’t get for the other acts,” he said.

While Gionet has mixed feelings about the grounding of the Snowbirds, he said it’s more important for the Canadian military to update its aging equipment than prioritize the air force’s flight demonstration team.

Canada's famous military aerial fleet, the Snowbirds, will be grounded as the fleet is renewed. New planes won't be ready until an undetermined date in the 2030s.

The Canadian Press

Sandy Seymour, an air show spectator decked out in a Snowbirds hat and shirt, said she’s disappointed the federal government didn’t find a way to replace the Snowbirds’ jets without grounding them.

She said the Canadian National Exhibition fair, whose final weekend coincides with the air show, won’t be the same without the Snowbirds performing their high-flying stunts. She said it’s a yearly tradition for her to go to the fair and watch the jets soar over the exhibition grounds.

Seymour was joined by hundreds others on the CNE grounds who had their eyes and cameras trained to the sky as fighter jets dating from the Second World War to the modern day careened over the banks of Lake Ontario.

Other air show demonstrations featured military and police aircraft and performances by civilian aviators, including a father-and-son duo piloting homebuilt planes.

The exact timeline of the Snowbirds’ return is unclear. Defence Minister David McGuinty said in May negotiations are underway with the manufacturer of the team’s new Siskin jets.

The Snowbirds have performed some 2,700 times in the Tutor jets since 1971, becoming staples of national events and celebrations.

The Snowbirds’ final show is set for Nov. 15 at the Grey Cup in Calgary.

Canada rapidly increased its military spending last year before announcing the Snowbirds would be grounded.

After years of criticism from allies, Canada met its Nato commitment to spend two per cent of GDP on defense by shelling out over $63 billion on national security in 2025.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has also said Canada will spend five per cent of GDP on defence by 2035, a commitment the NDP has criticized as an “extraordinary” sum better spent on affordable housing and healthcare.

The commander of the Canadian Army, Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright, said earlier this year that the military will forge ahead with investments to modernize the Armed Forces, including purchasing new weapons and air defense systems and recruiting more soldiers.

stories.title: Woman airlifted to hospital after bear attack near Whistler, B.C.
stories.summary: A woman was airlifted to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries after a bear attacked a group of hikers in the backcountry near Whistler, B.C.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
A woman was taken to hospital after being attacked by a bear while hiking in the backcountry near Whistler, B.C., ON Friday evening.

A group of three hikers encountered two bears near Conflict Lake in the Callaghan Conservancy at around 5 p.m., the B.C. Conservation Officer Service said in a social media post Saturday afternoon.

One of the bears attacked the woman before disengaging, officials said.

The Conservation Officer Service’s Predator Attack Team, Squamish RCMP and Squamish Search and Rescue responded to the area by helicopter.

The woman received first aid at the scene before she was airlifted to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Conservation officers said an adult male black bear found at the attack site was killed due to safety concerns.

However, officials said they have not determined whether a black bear or grizzly bear was responsible for the attack.

Officers returned to the area Saturday to continue their investigation.

Trail access in the area is now closed, and officials are asking people to stay away while the investigation continues.

stories.title: Nova Scotia town lifts water conservation limits first issued after dam break
stories.summary: Lunenburg - A Nova Scotia town has lifted water conservation restrictions originally put in place after a dam breach earlier this week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Town of Lunenburg says conservation efforts were helpful and significant progress was made to restore its water reserve.

The town’s drinking water supply was endangered by a breach in the Dares Lake dam earlier this week that flooded the pump station.

Article continues below

The Lunenburg Regional Emergency Management Organization said in its update Friday the dam was stabilized with berms and trenches diverting water away from the pumps.

The organization says two of the three pumps at the site are now functional, but not at full capacity, while a third will need to be replaced.

Lunenburg Mayor Jamie Myra says businesses have re-opened and the town has largely returned to normal operations.

Myra on Saturday said he wasn’t willing at this point to lay blame at the feet of any company or individual for the dam break.

“I just know that whatever happened wasn’t supposed to happen and we’re going to get to the bottom of it sooner or later,” he said by phone Saturday.

stories.title: Quebec courts say generative AI cannot replace judges’ reasoning
stories.summary: Quebec's courts have issued new guidelines restricting judges' use of generative artificial intelligence, stressing that judging must remain a fundamentally human responsibility.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Quebec’s courts have issued new guidelines restricting judges’ use of generative artificial intelligence, stressing that judging must remain a fundamentally human responsibility.

The guidelines, jointly adopted by the Quebec Court of Appeal, Superior Court, Court of Quebec and the province’s municipal courts, say generative AI can be used for certain supporting tasks but cannot replace judicial reasoning, the assessment of evidence or deliberation.

Judging, they say, must remain the exclusive responsibility of judges.

“Generative AI, however sophisticated, possesses neither judgment nor conscience and is not subject to any form of accountability,” states the 10-page document. “It cannot understand the human, social and legal context specific to each case.”

The move comes months after questions were raised about whether a Quebec judge May have used generative AI in preparing a decision.

La Presse reported in March that a decision contained references to case law that did not exist, raising the possibility that generative AI had been used. The episode helped create a sense of urgency within the judiciary as it worked to establish rules for the technology.

The courts say there is currently no approved, secure institutional generative AI tool available to judges. They also warn that existing tools rely on algorithms whose workings remain largely opaque.

“Judging cannot be reduced to a technical exercise,” the guidelines say. “It is an intrinsically human function, based on deliberation, consideration of context, respect for dignity, the requirement of fairness and the exercise of moral responsibility.”

The courts acknowledge that generative AI can be useful, but say it cannot be used as a source of legal authority or reasoning, to assess evidence or to make decisions.

Judges May use it for limited tasks such as correcting, revising, rephrasing or translating text they have already written, certain administrative work, or locating information within specified sources.

Any such use must remain under human control, and AI-generated material must be independently verified.

The guidelines make clear that judges remain fully responsible for their legal reasoning, the contents of their decisions, and the accuracy of the facts, references, quotations and legal authorities they cite.

“No error can be attributed to the tool used,” the document says. “The use of a generative AI tool does not diminish the judge’s obligation to verify or their full responsibility for the final result.”

The guidelines say AI cannot be used for substantive legal reasoning, analyzing or characterizing facts, assessing evidence or credibility, determining the outcome of a dispute, or drafting those parts of a decision.

“If the use of AI has the effect or purpose of determining the legal outcome, assessing credibility or interpreting disputed facts, interpreting the relevance of facts, or formulating the reasons for a decision, it must not be used,” the guidelines say.

The courts also warn judges about confidentiality risks.

Judges should not provide AI tools with draft judgments, notes about ongoing cases or information protected by law or a court order.

Until an authorized institutional system is available, judges using an AI tool for permitted purposes must also ensure its settings prevent information they enter from being used to train or improve the system.

When in doubt, the guidelines recommend judges refrain from using generative AI.

The guidelines are intended to protect principles including judicial independence, impartiality, fairness, human rights and access to justice, while ensuring confidentiality, security and data protection.

content_blocks.text: The guidelines, jointly adopted by the Quebec Court of Appeal, Superior Court, Court of Quebec and the province’s municipal courts, say generative AI can be used for certain supporting tasks but cannot replace judicial reasoning, the assessment of evidence or deliberation.
content_blocks.html: The guidelines, jointly adopted by the Quebec Court of Appeal, Superior Court, Court of Quebec and the province’s municipal courts, say generative AI can be used for certain supporting tasks but cannot replace judicial reasoning, the assessment of evidence or deliberation.

content_blocks.text: Judging, they say, must remain the exclusive responsibility of judges.
content_blocks.html: Judging, they say, must remain the exclusive responsibility of judges.

content_blocks.text: “Generative AI, however sophisticated, possesses neither judgment nor conscience and is not subject to any form of accountability,” states the 10-page document. “It cannot understand the human, social and legal context specific to each case.”
content_blocks.html: “Generative AI, however sophisticated, possesses neither judgment nor conscience and is not subject to any form of accountability,” states the 10-page document. “It cannot understand the human, social and legal context specific to each case.”

content_blocks.text: The move comes months after questions were raised about whether a Quebec judge May have used generative AI in preparing a decision.
content_blocks.html: The move comes months after questions were raised about whether a Quebec judge may have used generative AI in preparing a decision.

content_blocks.text: La Presse reported in March that a decision contained references to case law that did not exist, raising the possibility that generative AI had been used. The episode helped create a sense of urgency within the judiciary as it worked to establish rules for the technology.

content_blocks.text: The courts say there is currently no approved, secure institutional generative AI tool available to judges. They also warn that existing tools rely on algorithms whose workings remain largely opaque.
content_blocks.html: The courts say there is currently no approved, secure institutional generative AI tool available to judges. They also warn that existing tools rely on algorithms whose workings remain largely opaque.

content_blocks.text: “Judging cannot be reduced to a technical exercise,” the guidelines say. “It is an intrinsically human function, based on deliberation, consideration of context, respect for dignity, the requirement of fairness and the exercise of moral responsibility.”
content_blocks.html: “Judging cannot be reduced to a technical exercise,” the guidelines say. “It is an intrinsically human function, based on deliberation, consideration of context, respect for dignity, the requirement of fairness and the exercise of moral responsibility.”

content_blocks.text: The courts acknowledge that generative AI can be useful, but say it cannot be used as a source of legal authority or reasoning, to assess evidence or to make decisions.
content_blocks.html: The courts acknowledge that generative AI can be useful, but say it cannot be used as a source of legal authority or reasoning, to assess evidence or to make decisions.

content_blocks.text: Judges May use it for limited tasks such as correcting, revising, rephrasing or translating text they have already written, certain administrative work, or locating information within specified sources.
content_blocks.html: Judges may use it for limited tasks such as correcting, revising, rephrasing or translating text they have already written, certain administrative work, or locating information within specified sources.

content_blocks.text: Any such use must remain under human control, and AI-generated material must be independently verified.

content_blocks.text: The guidelines make clear that judges remain fully responsible for their legal reasoning, the contents of their decisions, and the accuracy of the facts, references, quotations and legal authorities they cite.

content_blocks.text: “No error can be attributed to the tool used,” the document says. “The use of a generative AI tool does not diminish the judge’s obligation to verify or their full responsibility for the final result.”
content_blocks.html: “No error can be attributed to the tool used,” the document says. “The use of a generative AI tool does not diminish the judge’s obligation to verify or their full responsibility for the final result.”

content_blocks.text: The guidelines say AI cannot be used for substantive legal reasoning, analyzing or characterizing facts, assessing evidence or credibility, determining the outcome of a dispute, or drafting those parts of a decision.
content_blocks.html: The guidelines say AI cannot be used for substantive legal reasoning, analyzing or characterizing facts, assessing evidence or credibility, determining the outcome of a dispute, or drafting those parts of a decision.

content_blocks.text: “If the use of AI has the effect or purpose of determining the legal outcome, assessing credibility or interpreting disputed facts, interpreting the relevance of facts, or formulating the reasons for a decision, it must not be used,” the guidelines say.

content_blocks.text: The courts also warn judges about confidentiality risks.
content_blocks.html: The courts also warn judges about confidentiality risks.

content_blocks.text: Judges should not provide AI tools with draft judgments, notes about ongoing cases or information protected by law or a court order.

content_blocks.text: When in doubt, the guidelines recommend judges refrain from using generative AI.

stories.title: Man arrested after safe stolen during break-and-enter through roof of Rona in St. Thomas
stories.summary: A 45-year-old St. Thomas man has been arrested on reasonable grounds for the recent break and enter and theft of a safe from Rona.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A 45-year-old St. Thomas man has been arrested on reasonable grounds for the recent break-and-enter and theft of a safe from Rona.

Those charges include break and enter to commit indictable offence, wear disguise with intent, and mischief.

On Wednesday, CTV News learned a person entered the store through a hatch in the roof and made their way down to the office.

They left out the back door of the store with a safe and did not close the hatch of the roof which lead to serious water damage from a heavy storm.

In a news release Saturday, the Stps revealed a search incident to arrest the male had cocaine on his person and was further charged with possession of a controlled substance.

A search warrant was further conducted at the residence where the male had been staying with evidence being seized as well as a large quantity of oxycodone, 55.4 grams of cocaine, and 21.8 grams of fentanyl.

Total value of drugs seized was estimated at $5,690. More charges are pending.

stories.title: Love Lake Ontario? Here’s how to enjoy it this fall
stories.summary: Autumn colours delight during these excursions both in and on the water
stories.author: Diana Ballon
stories.content:
Lake Ontario, not to be mistaken for Lake America, is one of our country’s great treasures. Autumn is one of the best times to explore it — when green leaves share branches with gold, orange and red ones, summer crowds have dispersed and temperatures are comfortable.

Whether you’re in the water or on the water, there are endless ways to enjoy the lake this fall. Here are some to try before winter comes.

Visit Toronto Islands: Take the ferry from downtown Toronto at the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal or, for a speedier trip, buy tickets to a water taxi (multiple locations along the waterfront). Taxis run frequently until the end of September and then continue less regularly through October. Most take bikes and strollers. Once you’re there, there’s lots to do . Have a picnic. Take the kids to Centreville Amusement Park (open weekends until September 27). Play disc golf on Ward’s Island. Rent a kayak or stand-up paddleboard (until Sept. 30 through Toronto Island SUP, or inquire about their lessons, tours and experiences at torontoislandsup.com .) You can also enjoy the islands’ many beaches: Ward’s Island Beach and Gibraltar Point Beach are my personal favourites.

Explore quieter Lake Ontario islands Amherst Island, reached by ferry from Millhaven, is about a 20-minute drive south of Kingston. Wolfe Island connects the edge of Lake Ontario with the St. Lawrence River (it’s technically part of the Thousand Islands) and is a short ferry ride from Kingston. Explore each island’s small communities, visit the shops and check online calendars for dates and times of events, from music festivals to cultural celebrations. There’s the Wolfe Island Garden Party , running from Sept. 17 to Sept. 27 with music, art and more, and the Wolfe Island Gravel Grinder (a non-competitive gravel cycling ride) on Sept. 19. Amherst Island has their annual harvest festival on Sept. 12 and an Indigenous Drum Circle & Cultural Experience on Sept. 26.

Take a boat tour: There are many to choose from. Several cruise lines explore Lake Ontario as part of a wider Great Lakes tour (Viking’s eight-day Niagara and the Great Lakes itinerary has three more sailings leaving from Toronto in September). Other, shorter tours, many leaving from Toronto’s harbourfront, or the Port Dalhousie Cruise Line in St. Catharines, Ont., offer dinner and evening sunset cruises on Lake Ontario exclusively.

Cycle Lake Ontario: The Lake Ontario section of the Great Lakes Waterfront trail is just under 600 kilometres and runs from Niagara-on-the-Lake to the mouth of the St. Lawrence River. Toronto to Port Credit with lunch is a fun half-day cycling trip, but you can connect to many sections of this trail by car or GO Transit stations. For downloadable maps that you can print or view on your smartphone, see waterfronttrail.org .

Spend a weekend in Prince Edward County. Visitors to the County can stop at its many wineries and cideries, explore cycling trails, relax at high-end boutique hotels, cabins and B&Bs or go camping. Sandbanks Provincial Park has three popular beaches and enormous shifting dunes to play in. Outlet Beach has shallow waters and is great for kids. Nearby you can also enjoy a picnic at North Beach Provincial Park . Read more at: visitthecounty.com

Visit Niagara-on-the-Lake. Often ranked as one of the prettiest destinations in Canada, Notl is a great weekend getaway. Go for a wine tasting. ( Konzelmann Estate Winery prides itself on being Niagara’s only lakefront winery.) Go for a picnic before the theatre at Queen’s Royal Park. Play golf at the Niagara-on-the-Lake Golf Club , which runs along the lake. Or learn more about the War of 1812 at Fort George, a national historic site. Skip the drive and take the year round GO Transit train service, which connects to a local bus network in Niagara on the Lake.

Enjoy birdwatching. Spring migration gets birdwatchers excited but fall is a good time to watch birds leave. At Presqu’ile Provincial Park in Northumberland County (two hours drive east of Toronto), small birds start heading south from mid-August to mid-September, while waterfowl and shorebirds (easier to spot) can be seen until early November. Tommy Thompson Park (which extends into Lake Ontario at the bottom of Leslie Street in Toronto) is also a good spot.

Go camping. For waterfront camping, choose between Sandbanks Provincial Park, or Presqu’ile Provincial Park, both open until October 26. (Presqu’ile has the second-oldest operating lighthouse in Ontario.)

Take a hike — or a leisurely walk . The Scarborough Bluffs and Tommy Thompson Park offer sweeping views of Lake Ontario, as does Rattray Marsh Conservation Area in Mississauga (between Toronto and Burlington) and Darlington Provincial Park near Oshawa. Presqu’ile Park also has 16 kms of paths and trails.

stories.title: Nova Scotia flooding forces road closures, while 40,000 report power outages
stories.summary: ‘Your best route right now might be no route at all,’ warned provincial authorities
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Authorities are warning against unnecessary travel in northeastern Nova Scotia due to widespread flooding caused by torrential rainfall.

The province’s Department of Emergency Management said Saturday afternoon that heavy rain damaged dozens of roads in Cape Breton Island and the Eastern Mainland.

“Your best route right now might be no route at all,” the department said in warnings posted to social media.

It also warned that conditions can change quickly and drivers should turn back if they come across a submerged street.

Cape Breton Regional Municipality reported several roads in the Sydney and Glace Bay areas were closed due to flooding.

Nova Scotia’s provincial road conditions map showed at least 13 road closures across the Island and nearby mainland.

A slow-moving weather system brought heavy downpours and thunderstorms to Nova Scotia’s northeast region on Friday, with over 200 millimetres of rain recorded in some areas on Saturday morning.

Several videos posted to social media from the region on Saturday showed water rushing over roadways and breaking through barriers. Residents in Sydney were also recorded paddling down flooded streets in kayaks.

Environment and Climate Change Canada issued an orange alert level rainfall warning for all of Cape Breton early Saturday morning. It warned of rainfall rates of up to 20 millimetres an hour in some areas.

Nova Scotia Power reported nearly 40,000 customers were without power on Saturday afternoon. The private utility company listed high winds and rain as the reason for most of the outages in Cape Breton.

The national weather service also issued yellow rainfall alerts for large areas of northern Nova Scotia and all of Prince Edward Island.

The alerts say the rain isn’t expected to let up until Monday morning.

The ferry service between Wood Islands, P.E.I., and Caribou, N.S., was cancelled for Saturday due to high winds, Northumberland Ferries Ltd. said.

Nova Scotia RCMP said Saturday afternoon they were unaware of any deaths related to the flooding.

It also warned that conditions can change quickly and drivers should turn back if they come across a submerged street.
Cape Breton Regional Municipality reported several roads in the Sydney and Glace Bay areas were closed due to flooding.
Nova Scotia’s provincial road conditions map showed at least 13 road closures across the Island and nearby mainland.
A slow-moving weather system brought heavy downpours and thunderstorms to Nova Scotia’s northeast region on Friday, with over 200 millimetres of rain recorded in some areas on Saturday morning.

Several videos posted to social media from the region on Saturday showed water rushing over roadways and breaking through barriers. Residents in Sydney were also recorded paddling down flooded streets in kayaks.

Environment and Climate Change Canada issued an orange alert level rainfall warning for all of Cape Breton early Saturday morning. It warned of rainfall rates of up to 20 millimetres an hour in some areas.

Nova Scotia Power reported nearly 40,000 customers were without power on Saturday afternoon. The private utility company listed high winds and rain as the reason for most of the outages in Cape Breton.
The national weather service also issued yellow rainfall alerts for large areas of northern Nova Scotia and all of Prince Edward Island.
The alerts say the rain isn’t expected to let up until Monday morning.
The ferry service between Wood Islands, P.E.I., and Caribou, N.S., was cancelled for Saturday due to high winds, Northumberland Ferries Ltd. said.
Nova Scotia RCMP said Saturday afternoon they were unaware of any deaths related to the flooding.

stories.title: Missing man found alive after 6-day search near Squamish, B.C.
stories.summary: A man missing near Squamish, B.C., for nearly a week has been found alive after what rescuers described as an extensive six-day search.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
A man who had been missing near Squamish, B.C., for nearly a week has been found alive, police and search and rescue officials say.

Stanislav Volo, who was reported missing on Aug. 30, was located after an extensive search involving multiple agencies, Sea to Sky RCMP said in a news release.

Police said Volo was taken to hospital with what are believed to be minor injuries.

“It looks like a very good outcome, very strong young man, he’ll be fine,” said Sue Nicholson with Squamish Search and Rescue in an interview with Global News.

Volo walked out on his own and was located on the Indian Arm Forest Service Road, in a remote area behind the mountain range above Squamish.

“We have fantastic news today. Staz has been found,” Tyler Duncan, operations director and search manager with Squamish Search and Rescue, told Global News.

“It has, honestly, in almost 20 years of search and rescue, been one of the most involved searches I’ve ever been involved in,” he said.

Resources were brought in from across B.C., including search and rescue teams from Pemberton to Mission and teams from Vancouver Island.

Duncan said crews conducted operations throughout the night and used tools including infrared and cellphone detection technology in their efforts to find Volo.

RCMP said its police dog services, Lower Mainland Emergency Response Team and Air Services were involved in the search, along with Squamish Search and Rescue and the Sea to Sky Gondola team.

“A heartfelt thank you to every SAR team, first responder, volunteers and everyone else who played a part in the search — and to everyone who shared, supported, and kept hope,” a social media post from the Squamish Search and Rescue team said.

Police said no further information would be released out of respect for Volo’s privacy.

stories.title: Mountaineer missing while climbing near Switzerland-Italy border, Athletics Canada says
stories.summary: Kalie McCrystal, whose hometown is Squamish B.C., has climbed the Matterhorn before
stories.content:
Athletics Canada says one of its members went missing while attempting to break a mountain-running record in the Alps along the Switzerland-Italy border.

The national sport governing body says in a statement Kalie McCrystal was last seen on Tuesday.

It says the skyrunner and mountaineer was climbing Italy’s Matterhorn, a roughly 4,481-metre-tall mountain that’s horn-shaped peak also overlooks Zermatt, a town in Switzerland.

The statement says McCrystal has many years of experience in technical and high-altitude environments, and has climbed the Matterhorn before.

“This was therefore not her first ascent of the mountain,” it said.

The statement did not give details on the record she was trying to break.

“Kalie is a highly respected athlete and a valued member of the worldwide skyrunning community,” it said.

“Our thoughts are with Kalie, her family and everyone close to her at this extremely difficult time. We are hoping for her safe return and are grateful to those involved in the ongoing search.”

Athletics Canada’s website lists the hometown of an athlete with McCrystal’s name as Squamish, B.C.

stories.title: Quebec parties target health care, affordability as election nears
stories.summary: Montreal - With one month to go before Quebec's provincial election, parties are pitching voters on health care, government spending and daycare, while their leaders are also debating the prospect of another referendum on Quebec independence.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - With one month to go before Quebec’s provincial election, parties on Saturday pitched voters on health care, government spending and daycare, while their leaders also debated the prospect of another referendum on Quebec independence.

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette promised to expand access to reduced-fee daycare, while accusing Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon of hiding his commitment to hold a referendum.

Speaking at a news conference Saturday morning in Lorraine, north of Montreal, Fréchette claimed St-Pierre Plamondon avoided the word “referendum” at a major PQ campaign rally in Quebec City the previous night.

“Yesterday, he gathered his supporters. Not once did he use the word referendum,” she said. “That’s hiding things from Quebecers.”

Fréchette also argued this is the worst time to hold a referendum, pointing to the trade conflict with the United States, and she also accused her rivals of not talking enough about U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

“We’re in an economic war with our main trading partner, and for the other parties, it’s as though it were a minor news story,” she said.

However, St-Pierre Plamondon rejected Fréchette’s accusation he was avoiding referendum talk, saying he uses “popular consultation” and “referendum” interchangeably.

“I’ve used the word at times. I use popular consultation, referendum,” he told reporters in Quebec City. “Popular consultation and referendum mean exactly the same thing.”

Fréchette on Saturday also pledged 25,000 additional reduced-fee daycare spaces at a cost of $750 million over four years. But only 5,000 would be entirely new spaces.

Of the 25,000, 15,000 were part of previous commitments, while another 5,000 would come from converting existing unsubsidized spaces into subsidized ones.

The CAQ would also offer newly qualified daycare workers a $10,000 bonus if they commit to working for at least two years in a subsidized daycare or early childhood centre.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard accused Fréchette of playing with the numbers during a campaign stop in Lévis, across the St. Lawrence River from Quebec City.

“This isn’t 25,000 new spaces being announced this morning. It’s a maximum of 5,000 spaces,” he told reporters.

The Parti Québécois, meanwhile, proposed a series of measures aimed at accountability at the highest levels of government, including freezing the salaries of legislature members, cabinet ministers and heads of Crown corporations until Quebec returns to a balanced budget, which the party expects in 2028-29.

The PQ would also require candidates selected to lead Crown corporations to appear before a legislative committee, set performance targets for their CEOs and review executive bonuses.

“We can’t ask the public and broader public sectors to go on a certain diet while we don’t set an example ourselves,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.

At a campaign stop in Chicoutimi, about 200 kilometres north of Quebec City, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal proposed 400 primary-care access points inspired by Quebec’s Clsc community health centre model, at an estimated cost of $1.8 billion a year.

The party would open 200 during a first mandate and another 200 during a second. Ghazal said the centres would make it easier for Quebecers to enter the health system and help relieve pressure on emergency rooms.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, meanwhile, unveiled his party’s digital plan in Inverness, about 100 kilometres southwest of Quebec City, aimed at making nearly all Quebec government services available online.

His party says the plan would save $3.45 billion in administrative costs over five years. It also calls for reducing regulatory requirements by 30 per cent over four years and using artificial intelligence in government operations with human oversight.

“The Quebec government has to enter the 21st century, and quickly,” Duhaime said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Mayors push to turn Oliver correctional centre into mandatory care facility
stories.summary: Mayors in the Okanagan are specifically pointing to unused capacity at the Oliver facility as a potential location for mandatory care.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Okanagan mayors and regional leaders, including First Nations, are pressing the B.C. government to turn unused space at the Okanagan Correctional Centre in Oliver into a mandatory and secure care facility.

A handful of leaders gathered outside the correctional centre Friday, renewing calls on the provincial government to take action as communities across the region continue to grapple with the ongoing drug, mental health and social disorder crises.

“The need continues to grow on a daily basis. What is missing is action,” said Kelowna Mayor Tom Dyas.

Penticton Mayor Julius Bloomfield said communities need to focus on getting people the help they need.

“Let’s start helping the people that need help,” Bloomfield said. “Let’s do it with compassion because leaving people on the streets is not compassionate.”

The mayors are specifically pointing to unused capacity at the Oliver facility as a potential location for mandatory care.

Martin Johansen, the mayor of Oliver, said he understands the centre is operating at less than half capacity.

“It’s not anywhere near the capacity it could be,” Johansen said.

The Okanagan Correctional Centre has 401 cells.

The Ministry of Public Safety says the number of inmates varies, but the facility had an average daily inmate count of approximately 200 last year.

The calls come amid growing pressure on the province to address the complex intersection of addiction, mental health and public safety.

Bloomfield warned that continued inaction could have serious consequences.

“People are going to die,” he said. “There’s going to be a lot more suffering and there’s going to be a lot more unrest for the general public.”

2:03 Vancouver mayor calls for involuntary care beds

While the mayors see the correctional centre as a potential solution, the province says converting part of the facility into a mandatory care site requires a lot more than just a change in use of space.

“It’s not about simply holding people,” said Ravi Kahlon, B.C.’s health minister. “It’s about having infrastructure that helps enable the care that we need.”

He also said health-care professionals would need to be available at the site to provide the necessary support services.

The push will continue next week at the Union of B.C. Municipalities convention, where municipal leaders from across the province will meet with provincial ministers.

For the Okanagan mayors, the convention provides another opportunity to put the proposed use of the Oliver correctional centre directly in front of provincial decision-makers.

“I believe this is a viable solution,” Johansen said.

3:58 B.C.’s forced treatment laws ruled unconstitutional

stories.title: Dairy farmer turned Liberal MP vows to be voice for tariff-hit Quebec region
stories.summary: Ottawa - Newly elected Liberal MP Daniel Gobeil says his experience as a dairy farmer and agricultural leader will help him be a voice in Ottawa for a Quebec region on the front lines of the Canada-U.S. trade war.
stories.author: Émilie Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Newly elected Liberal MP Daniel Gobeil says his experience as a dairy farmer and agricultural leader will help him be a voice in Ottawa for a Quebec region on the front lines of the Canada-U.S. trade war.

The former president of Quebec’s dairy producers says he May already have contributed to Canada’s approach to the Trump administration, even before voters in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord elected him to Parliament in an Aug. 31 byelection.

“My opinion was taken into account, even when I was still a candidate,” Gobeil said in an interview on Friday with The Canadian Press.

Gobeil, who also served as vice-president of Dairy Farmers of Canada, said Prime Minister Mark Carney gave him a “receptive ear” during the campaign as Canada negotiated with the United States.

And Gobeil said he spoke with Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, as Washington pressed Canada over its supply-management system, particularly in the dairy sector.

Canada’s supply-management system regulates production and prices for dairy, poultry and eggs and uses import quotas and tariffs to protect domestic producers.

A federal law adopted last year, which originated as a Bloc Québécois bill, prevents Ottawa from making trade commitments that would increase import quotas or lower tariffs protecting supply-managed dairy, poultry and egg sectors.

“There were discussions,” Gobeil said of his exchanges with LeBlanc, adding, “I knew what was going on — not all of the demands, but certainly those within my area of expertise, the dairy sector.”

Protecting supply management became a major issue during Gobeil’s byelection campaign. A Canada-U.S. trade agreement appeared within reach for several days, with reports suggesting Canada was considering changes to how it administers dairy import quotas.

But Carney suspended the talks and ordered Canada’s negotiating team home, saying Washington had introduced last-minute demands Canada could not accept.

Gobeil said that decision was a “game changer” for his campaign.

“It happened on a Friday night,” he said. “Saturday morning, we saw Carney’s polling, he was at 85 per cent in Quebec. People were behind that ‘Maîtres chez nous’ position.”

The phrase, which translates roughly as “Masters in our own house,” was popularized by former Quebec premier Jean Lesage during the Quiet Revolution of the 1960s and has recently been invoked by Carney.

The win flipped a seat previously held by the Conservatives and was part of a three-byelection sweep for Carney’s Liberals on Aug. 31.

Gobeil repeatedly said he had been reassured that Ottawa was not considering concessions that would undermine the supply-management system.

Asked whether he had played a role in the negotiations, Gobeil said his influence was more limited, with LeBlanc, Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette and Carney’s inner circle leading the talks.

“I would say perhaps more of a role in their position, but I wouldn’t go so far as to say I had a role in the negotiations,” he said.

Gobeil heads to Ottawa at a difficult time for Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean, about 200 kilometres north of Quebec City, where the aluminum and forestry industries have been hit by U.S. tariffs.

The region is also home to Canadian Forces Base Bagotville, which is hoping to benefit from increased federal defence spending.

With speculation circulating about a possible cabinet shuffle, Gobeil said he would be willing to take on a larger role.

“Clearly, if the prime minister sees an additional role for me on the team, I’ll be there,” he said.

But Gobeil said he is also happy to begin his work as an MP and bring a regional perspective to the Liberal caucus.

“I have a lot of people, friends of mine, who work in forestry and are facing challenges, and people in aluminum,” he said.

Back home in La Baie, Gobeil has begun handing over more responsibility for Ferme du Fjord, his family’s dairy and grain farm, to his son, daughter and nephew.

Their help, he said, allowed him to take on other roles over the years and eventually make the jump into federal politics.

For Gobeil, farming also prepared him for the demands of a political campaign.

“On the farm, the days are long,” he said. “The days are long in a campaign, too. That’s part of my everyday life. And I think people recognized that we work hard. That’s part of the values we carry with us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Saturday Sports Notes: Majors open playoffs with win, Knights lose preseason game in Victoria, B.C.
stories.summary: The London Majors won their Canadian Baseball League playoff opener in dramatic fashion Friday.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Majors won their Canadian Baseball League playoff opener in dramatic fashion Friday.

Ryder Hancock raced home from second base to score the game winning run on Jarrett Burney’s single in the 11th inning at Labatt Park to give London a 6-5 win over Welland.

“I’m feeling awesome, that was the way to get back on track right there,” Burney told London Majors TV after the game.

“We came in with a little skid (four straight losses), but we knew that the playoffs is a reset. We just had to get back out there, get a win and get the train rolling again.”

Burney says he lost his grandmother the day before, so the game winning hit was emotional one for the Majors star.

Luis Perez (1-0) struck out one in a scoreless inning to get the win in relief.

London will travel to Welland for game two Saturday at 7:05 p.m before returning home to London for game three Sunday at 6:05 p.m.

Game 1 walk off win from 2 different angles! #londonmajors #MajorsCity pic.twitter.com/kW3aftEWzR — London Majors (@londonmajors) September 5, 2026

Victora Royals beat London Knights in ‘Clash of the Kingdoms’

Game one of a two-game exhibition series between the London Knights and Victoria Royals in Victoria, B.C. went to the hosts.

The final score was 7-1, and then Knight Ryan Brown added a goal in a 3-on-3 overtime period, which was included in the game.

Cameron Schmidt – who led the WHL in goals last season – scored three times for the Royals.

“It felt a little more intense, it was physical. I think our goalie masked the score as at the end of the night it was 7-1, and it feels a lot better to win than not, but I thought Vladdy (Vladimir Proskurin) was really good.”

The game will be streamed free on Youtube .
