content_blocks.text: But feeble Idiotius need not have worried. For what a voyage the movie was! More engaging in Imax 70mm – see it if you can – than in every other format, and way more vivid than page after page of the original text, with its endless cast of gods and Greeks and superfluous details, even in Wilson’s transmutation. The film’s ambition was as astonishing as its score was deafening, the theatre’s air conditioning as chilling as Odysseus’s visit to Hades and the land of the dead, the zombie graveyard of his regrets. (Nolan’s Odyssey was all about remorse, And how impossible it is to stay free of.) The special effects were especially special: Circe’s real-time massage of Odysseus’s men into living pigs was super-creepy. So was Polyphemus, “the reckless Cyclops, lacking in customs” (as Homer has it), whose lawless ways and awkward pulpy body brought to mind – of all people – Donald Trump (surely Idiotius was not alone in this?). The frightening gullibility of the mob, so easily led, the claustrophobia of drowning, the shameful thrill – but what a rush! – of Odysseus’s murderous revenge on Penelope’s entitled suitors: all of it came alive. Yes, some of the writing was pretentiously empty (“the power of the sacrifice is the cost to the person making it”), but the non-stop suspense, so skillfully built as the Ithacans unlocked the gates of Troy, made up for it: a beta blocker would have been in order. True, the dialogue was sometimes indecipherable, as it often is in a Nolan flick: everybody says this. And yes, it’s true, Troy is only a memory in the ancient poem, not a central plot point, as was the case in Nolan’s movie. But the tragic consequences of the sack of Troy are the same: Homer gave us these stories, and Homer’s dilemmas, Homer’s agonies, are on the screen, however re-ordered.

content_blocks.text: Nolan’s movie pulled modern truth from ancient matter: the challenge of love, despite our longing for impossible faithfulness; the pain of facing who we once were, and how abominably we behaved; the unintended consequences of our every decision. Because try as we might we cannot control our fates, much less the fate of the world. Modesty would so become us. The Trojans and the Ithacans and then Odysseus and his men in turn offended Zeus’s Law, a.k.a xenia – that dictum that hosts must treat strangers as they expect to be treated themselves, generously and kindly. Which became the Judeo-Christian Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. It is still the unreachable longing of our godless modern world – one torn by hatred and mistrust, floods and heat waves, warmongers and billionaires, smart machines and fearsome apps. We need each other more than ever, but can never admit it. Was that Homer’s point? Maybe not. Would he – or she, or they, there’s some debate – mind if a moviegoer, watching a smackdown adaptation of the poems composed 3,000 years ago, came to that conclusion? I seriously doubt it. As Odysseus says in the movie: “The clearest vision of a man is from below,” from the depths of the failed self. It’s the most recognizable place we humans know.

content_blocks.text: It was only afterwards, as his brain raced and his ears rang and his eyes adjusted to the light, as Idiotius made his way from the Imax palace to his parked Prius, that he spied Daniel again. The youthful engineer-in-training was bus-bound to bucolic Burlington. He was abuzz, and thrilled. The Odyssey had in a moment replaced Dune as his favourite flick of all time. Why, Idiotius asked, still shaking. “Without the story,” Daniel replied, “it still would have been a cool experience. But the story makes it a spiritual experience.” And what is it about the story that does that? Idiotius asked. “I think,” the youth declared, “I think it’s about the fact that human experience has so many levels we can’t describe. The Odyssey’s a myth. And a myth is something we hand down to make sense of human experience. Because we have so little information about who we are.” The myth, the work, lives in service to the humans who read it, not the other way around (dear Emily). The lad paused and shook his head in wonder at the spectacle he had seen. “Our minds are so much bigger than our experience. And we are so much bigger than our experience, too.” With that Idiotius bade Daniel farewell and took his leave, and searched for his car for 20 minutes in the colossus of the Square One parking lot. Torrential rain was falling from the sky like heavy curtains of reproach. He climbed aboard, and pressed the starter button, And began his long, watery trek home, to his waiting wife. He was eager to return, for it was his night to cook the dinner.

stories.title: CBL Playoffs: London Majors beat Welland Jackfish 6-5 to take Game 1
stories.summary: The best-of-seven Canadian Baseball League playoff series opened on Friday night at Labatt Park.
stories.author: Geoff Robins
stories.content:
London Majors player Jarrett Burney scores during the third inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series against the Welland Jackfish at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

It took 11 innings but the London Majors beat the Welland Jackfish 6-5 on Friday night at Labatt Park, winning the opening game of their best-of-seven series in the first round of the Canadian Baseball League playoffs. The teams had identical records (31-17) in the regular season. Game 2 is set for Saturday night in Welland. Photos by Lfp’s Geoff Robins.

Welland Jackfish second baseman Jonah Weisner misses the tag on London’s Jarrett Burney during the third inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London Majors starting pitcher Victor Payano throws a pitch during the fourth inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoffs series against the Welland Jackfish at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London Majors first baseman Trent Lenihan tags out Welland’s Carson Johnson during the fourth inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London’s Maikol Escotto tags out Welland’s Justin Gideon during the second inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press) grobins@postmedia.com

stories.title: Where is the ‘common sense’ here?
stories.summary: Ripping out Toronto bike lanes is more than just a waste of money
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
With nearly half a trillion dollars in debt and vast spending commitments for transit, highways, health and other urgent needs, the government of Ontario cannot afford to waste any money. So why on earth would we want to spend tens of millions to rip out a bunch of bicycle lanes in Toronto?

Under the past few mayors, the city has built a substantial network of lanes so that cyclists can navigate the city in relative safety. It lagged behind other cities in this effort – Montreal took the lead years ago – but it has been catching up. A cyclist can now get around most of the central city in marked and protected lanes, a huge improvement on the days of jockeying shoulder to shoulder with speeding cars.

Cities around the world have been building out their biking networks. London’s has grown fivefold since 2016, reaching 450 kilometres – more than the whole Tube system. An ambitious cycling plan introduced under former mayor Anne Hidalgo has transformed Paris into a pedalling paradise, with a vast bike-share fleet and tens of thousands of bike-rack spaces. New York, Vancouver, San Francisco, Shanghai, Amsterdam – all now have extensive cycling networks.

The result is not just safer and smoother cycling but calmer, healthier and more livable cities. Paris has a whole new feel, with streams of bikes replacing the throngs of belching cars that used to choke the streets. Those streams are as much the symbol of progressive 21st-century cities as hosts of gleaming automobiles were of 20th-century ones.

All of this seems to have sailed right over the head of Ontario’s Progressive Conservative premier, Doug Ford. Since the days he and his brother Rob ruled the roost at Toronto City Hall, he has been fixated on ending the so-called “war on the car.” Putting bike lanes on big Toronto streets such as Bloor, Yonge and University was, to him, part of that grand conspiracy against the long-suffering motorist.

He vowed that they must go, even though it cost the city $27-million to put them in and, according to a city report, would cost nearly double that to pull them out. He went as far as to bring in a law requiring cities to get a green light from Queen’s Park before building a bike lane that takes away a lane of traffic. The province also gave itself the power to rip out the offending lanes on Bloor, Yonge and University. That thwarted the clearly expressed will of Toronto’s city council, which had studied, debated and approved the lanes and was elected to make precisely this sort of local decision.

After an appeal-court ruling on Aug. 14 that said the government was within its rights to remove the lanes, Mr. Ford started revving up the bulldozers. In a social media video released this week, he told viewers that officials were already starting to hire contractors for the removal work. “We’re not wasting any time,” he said. “We’re moving fast.”

His government, he said, “was elected with a clear mandate from the people of Ontario to fight gridlock and get drivers moving again, including by taking bike lanes off our busiest streets and putting them on secondary roads.”

That sounds sensible enough: cars on big roads, bikes on smaller ones. But in fact, no efficient bike system works this way. Most big-city networks put major bike routes on bigger roads to connect to transit hubs and business or entertainment districts. Lanes on smaller streets complete the grid, linking up to major corridors and routing cyclists through quieter neighbourhoods when possible.

Paris has installed lanes on both small streets and major ones. It even put a big cycling corridor on the famous Rue de Rivoli, which runs past the Louvre and once had seven lanes for parking and traffic. New York has good, recently improved bike lanes on Sixth and Seventh Avenues in the heart of Manhattan. One of Vancouver’s busiest goes over the heavily trafficked Burrard Bridge. With good design and engineering, cars and bikes can co-exist on even the biggest roads.

Mr. Ford’s campaign against the bike lanes seems based more on animus against bike-riding pinkos – as Don Cherry described them at the inauguration of Rob Ford as Toronto’s mayor in 2010 – than any foundation of fact. Documents filed in court during the legal battle revealed that his government was shown research that removing the lanes could make collisions more likely and might not even reduce traffic congestion in the end.

But there was the premier this week, standing next to a bike lane and pledging more “common sense infrastructure decisions that will keep people moving.” If spending nearly $50-million to destroy something that already exists is his idea of common sense, we had all better hold onto our wallets.

stories.title: Braids and beers: Dads learn to do their daughters’ hair at events across Canada
stories.summary: As millennial and Gen X dads take on a larger share of child care, many are learning new skills
stories.author: Ann Hui, Photography by Gabriel Hutchinson
stories.content:
A couple years ago, Justin Podur was left to care for the kids on his own while his wife was away.

The 49-year-old Mr. Podur is, by all accounts, a very competent person. He’s a professor at York University in Toronto, and has written several books on geopolitics and social movements around the world. He’s calm, collected and, as a parent, considers himself to be hands-on.

Still, in those few days with his wife away, Mr. Podur quickly realized there was a glaring hole in his competencies.

His now-eight-year-old daughter is a gymnast, and her hair had to be up and out of her face for practice. It was supposed to be in a braid, but he had no idea where to start. He did his best.

Even now, years later, the look of pity on the coach’s face during drop-off is burned into his memory. “She was like, ‘Dad did your hair today, didn’t he?’” he said, shaking his head.

Workshops like these help dads learn techniques for styling their daughters’ hair in a relaxed setting.

That experience was what brought Mr. Podur to a west-end Toronto brewery one evening last month, sitting at a table with a set of pink hair tools neatly laid out in front of him. This was Braids and Brews, a workshop where dads learn the basics of how to style their daughter’s hair.

Over the past year, such events – often held in traditionally “masculine” spaces such as pubs and breweries – have taken off in popularity around the world. Similar events have popped up in Vancouver, Winnipeg and Ottawa. And this one, organized by local hairstylist and educator Amanda McCrea, is just one of several in the Toronto area.

It’s the consequence of millennial and Gen X dads taking on an increased share of the work of child care. In their pursuit of becoming more “hands-on” parents, many of these dads are finding themselves having to learn new and sometimes surprising skills – oftentimes subverting traditional gender norms and expectations along the way.

Mr. Podur was one of a small group taking the course that evening. There were finance dads wearing backward baseball caps, sensible dads in Under Armour gear and fashion dads with chunky sneakers and full-sleeve tattoos. Each of them had a mannequin head with a long mane of rainbow-coloured hair in front of them as they watched Ms. McCrea begin her lesson.

She started with a series of questions.

“Has anyone done a ponytail before?” A few of the men nodded.

“Has anyone done pigtails?” A few more nods.

“Has anyone tried braids?” The room was quiet. From his seat, Mr. Podur remained silent.

One hand finally shot up. It was Mark Donatelli, a 39-year-old dad who works in finance.

“I’ve dabbled,” he said.

The others looked on, impressed.

Mr. Donatelli hesitated, then reconsidered. “One dabble.”

Ms. McCrea began running these workshops a few months ago. She’d begun to realize how much of the morning routine was left to her, between waking up her two daughters, getting them fed, dressed and out the door each day. She decided she could off-load more of it to her husband.

“That was the big one,” she said. “Stepping back and letting him do it. And empowering him.” She wanted to pass that empowerment on to other families.

Ronak Gandhi, a dad who attended the class that evening, saw it as an opportunity to learn a skill that would allow him to bond with his daughter. She turns five in September.

“She’s very girly. She’s like, ‘I want to be a princess,’” he said. She loves makeup, dresses and painting his nails. “So this is a way for her and I to build a stronger relationship and connection.”

The 38-year-old Mr. Gandhi said the class is a signal of the generational shift he sees among his fellow millennial dads who want to be more hands-on, more present and ready to take on traditionally “feminine” sides of caregiving.

Growing up, he saw his own dad – an immigrant from India – having to adhere to much stricter gender roles. “Different time, different culture,” he said.

Still, he acknowledged that masculinity today has its own challenges.

Earlier this year, a similar hairstyling workshop in the U.K., called “Pints and Ponytails,” drew the attention of social media influencer Andrew Tate, a self-proclaimed misogynist. The podcaster publicly derided the dads as “cucks.” (The U.K. organizers, in response, cheekily renamed their club Cucks and Ponytails).

As a teacher, Mr. Gandhi said he often hears such messages parroted by the tween and teen boys at school. So for him, part of the interest in attending that night’s workshop was to reclaim the concept of masculinity and to reject the “toxic” ideas that have gained so much prominence.

“As a guy who has a daughter, I need to show her that not all guys are like that,” he said.

“This is my little piece, I guess, of fighting back.”

Ms. McCrea’s lesson that day began with the basics. She taught the men how to brush the mannequin’s hair, and to remove tangles without pain. After that, she had them practise on a moving target – mimicking the challenge that every parent faces when their child begins squirming, bouncing and trying to get away.

As Mr. Podur worked on the mannequin’s hair, another dad, Ernesto Barahona, began slowly bobbing it up and down in front of him. “Sorry man,” Mr. Barahona said, as he waved the head around, forcing Mr. Podur to grit his teeth and chase it around with his comb.

Beside them, Rhys Mohun said he’d been sent with a long list of requests from his daughters: French braids. Half braids. He paused – what was the name of the one that’s inverted?

Dutch braids, someone called out.

“Dutch braids. Right. I don’t understand half of it,” he said. “I thought there was only one type of braid. But I’ve learned there are all sorts of braids.”

Rhys Mohun, 40, has learned there is not just one, but many types of braids.

From the front, Ms. McCrea called out the next step. It was time for the dads to divide the hair not only into vertical sections, but horizontal ones, too.

There were groans from across the room. “Whoa,” one of the guys muttered. “Whoaaaa.”

“This is level one?” asked Mr. Donatelli.

But beside him, Mr. Mohun rallied the group. He pumped his fist in the air and clapped his hands together.

“Let’s go, fellas,” he called out. “We got this.”

By the end of the evening, all of the men had managed – some more shakily than others – to pull off basic braids. As they sat back in their chairs, they appraised one another’s work, slapping each other’s backs and taking photos with their phones.

“I have an appreciation now for what my wife has been doing all these years,” said Mr. Gandhi, leaning back to snap a pic. “It’s a challenge.”

Next to him, Mr. Podur looked spent. He was sitting backward in his chair, Dangerous Minds style – “so if I’m tired I can lean my chin on this rest here” – and the station in front of him was a mess.

His combs were askew, the brushes turned this way and that. Hair ties littered the table in front of him. A few tufts of blue mannequin hair lay on the ground beside his feet.

“Pure chaos,” he said, shaking his head.

Still, in front of him on his mannequin was a single, neat braid. He’d made a few small mistakes. It wasn’t perfect. But it was a massive improvement over what he’d done before.

“It’s good,” he said. “I’m already better.”

The podcaster publicly derided the dads as “cucks.” (The U.K. organizers, in response, cheekily renamed their club Cucks and Ponytails).

As a teacher, Mr. Gandhi said he often hears such messages parroted by the tween and teen boys at school. So for him, part of the interest in attending that night’s workshop was to reclaim the concept of masculinity and to reject the “toxic” ideas that have gained so much prominence.
“As a guy who has a daughter, I need to show her that not all guys are like that,” he said.
“This is my little piece, I guess, of fighting back.”

Ms. McCrea’s lesson that day began with the basics. She taught the men how to brush the mannequin’s hair, and to remove tangles without pain. After that, she had them practise on a moving target – mimicking the challenge that every parent faces when their child begins squirming, bouncing and trying to get away.

As Mr. Podur worked on the mannequin’s hair, another dad, Ernesto Barahona, began slowly bobbing it up and down in front of him. “Sorry man,” Mr. Barahona said, as he waved the head around, forcing Mr. Podur to grit his teeth and chase it around with his comb.
Beside them, Rhys Mohun said he’d been sent with a long list of requests from his daughters: French braids. Half braids. He paused – what was the name of the one that’s inverted?
Dutch braids, someone called out.
“Dutch braids. Right. I don’t understand half of it,” he said. “I thought there was only one type of braid. But I’ve learned there are all sorts of braids.”
Rhys Mohun, 40, has learned there is not just one, but many types of braids.
From the front, Ms. McCrea called out the next step. It was time for the dads to divide the hair not only into vertical sections, but horizontal ones, too.
There were groans from across the room. “Whoa,” one of the guys muttered. “Whoaaaa.”
“This is level one?” asked Mr. Donatelli.
But beside him, Mr. Mohun rallied the group. He pumped his fist in the air and clapped his hands together.
“Let’s go, fellas,” he called out. “We got this.”

By the end of the evening, all of the men had managed – some more shakily than others – to pull off basic braids. As they sat back in their chairs, they appraised one another’s work, slapping each other’s backs and taking photos with their phones.
“I have an appreciation now for what my wife has been doing all these years,” said Mr. Gandhi, leaning back to snap a pic. “It’s a challenge.”
Next to him, Mr. Podur looked spent. He was sitting backward in his chair, Dangerous Minds style – “so if I’m tired I can lean my chin on this rest here” – and the station in front of him was a mess.
His combs were askew, the brushes turned this way and that. Hair ties littered the table in front of him. A few tufts of blue mannequin hair lay on the ground beside his feet.
“Pure chaos,” he said, shaking his head.
Still, in front of him on his mannequin was a single, neat braid. He’d made a few small mistakes. It wasn’t perfect. But it was a massive improvement over what he’d done before.
“It’s good,” he said. “I’m already better.”

stories.title: Learning Lab brings Vancouver Chinatown’s history to life
stories.summary: The Learning Lab, opened in May, revives heyday of city’s Chinatown with immersive exhibits, artifacts and stories
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
As Henry Young remembers it, Nina Simone was in a bad mood when she arrived at the Marco Polo theatre restaurant in Vancouver’s Chinatown that spring evening in 1968.

Ms. Simone was then nearly a decade into commercial success as a singer, composer and pianist and had just received her first Grammy nomination weeks earlier. But a series of civil-rights flashpoints in the U.S. was transforming the musician both personally and politically, turning her live performances into platforms for protest, her songs into rallying cries for justice. It sometimes made for unpredictable appearances; Ms. Simone was as likely to banter with an audience as she was to scold it.

But Mr. Young, then 25 and the house guitarist for the popular supper club, didn’t know enough about Ms. Simone to feel intimidated by her presence. Recognizing only her arresting cover of Screamin’ Jay Hawkins’s I Put a Spell On You , he asked to play a song with her.

“You don’t know my music,” Ms. Simone said tersely.

“Well, I’ve always had good pitch,” Mr. Young responded.

The young guitarist ended up sitting in for Ms. Simone’s whole set. Before sunrise, she would invite him to join her on tour.

Mr. Young, now 84, recounted the story at Marco Polo Memories, which sold out both of its June performances at the Learning Lab, which opened in May at Vancouver’s Chinatown Storytelling Centre.

To mark the cultural hub’s fifth anniversary, organizers transformed a 4,000-square-foot basement space into a journey to Chinatown’s heyday through recreated façades of restaurants and curio shops, and colourful neon signs that evoke the vibrancy of the neighbourhood from the 1950s through the 1980s.

Carol Lee, chair of the Vancouver Chinatown Foundation, which operates the centre, said her team had from the outset avoided calling the storytelling centre a museum so as not to focus solely on the past. While the main floor exhibits confront difficult chapters of Chinese-Canadian history – including the treacherous working conditions faced by those building the Canadian Pacific Railway and the escalating head tax and Chinese Exclusion Act – Ms. Lee also wanted to spotlight the community that emerged in the decades that followed.

“Upstairs is kind of the challenge of what we faced when we got here, but, despite that, they created a very vibrant community,” she said in an interview. “And that’s what we wanted to show with the Learning Lab: This is what we created, despite all the hardship and obstacles.”

Guests enter the space by descending a flight of stairs, under neon lights in a plum blossom motif and past walls of chipped green paint that are ubiquitous in the neighbourhood. They continue through a hallway adorned with historic Hong Kong movie posters, flyers for “authentic Chinese cuisine” and covers of the English-language Chinatown News magazine from the 1950s. Inside, digital walls and carefully curated artifacts further tell the story of what once was.

On this June evening, Mr. Young is perched on a stool on a small stage in front of a brick wall façade bearing the Marco Polo’s retro wordmark, his audience on folding chairs. A faint smell of spring rolls wafts through the space – a snack offered to guests along with Dragon Tail Slings, the signature cocktail of the defunct nightclub. It’s an intimate setting, not unlike an old friend telling stories over dinner.

After Ms. Simone’s set, Mr. Young continued, he drove across town to his second job, starting at 2 a.m., playing guitar at an after-hours club owned by his friend and fellow musician, Tommy Chong.

“All of a sudden, the room hushed. Nina was in the crowd,” he told a rapt audience. “We played, she listened for an hour and a half and said, ‘Send him a plane ticket and a contract. I want him in New York.’”

Mr. Young ended up touring internationally with Ms. Simone for two years, ON and off, including a date at Carnegie Hall.

Alex, Victor and Harry Louie – brothers from one of the region’s most successful Chinese-Canadian families – opened the Marco Polo in 1964 and operated it in Vancouver until 1982. The nightclub quickly set itself apart from the city’s other live entertainment venues with its smorgasbord buffet, yo-yo champion emcee and capacity for 500 guests.

Despite being known as “Canada’s only Oriental nightclub,” the Marco Polo drew a diverse mix of both audiences and performers, the name itself a nod to exploration. Racial tensions at the time also kept the two other big Vancouver nightclubs from bringing in Black artists, Mr. Young recalled.

“The idea was when they brought in minority acts, like Redd Foxx and Sly and the Family Stone, they would not draw the rich Shaughnessy people they wanted,” he said, referencing a tony Vancouver neighbourhood. “So they would shoot down to the Marco Polo. Thank god, we had some good music.”

Comedian Richard Pryor and musicians the Platters and the 5th Dimension were among other acts who performed at the Marco Polo.

Karen, Jari and Mark Louie, Alex Louie’s adult children, joined Mr. Young on stage that evening and regaled the audience with childhood memories of the nightclub. Karen Louie spoke of its famous lemon chicken and whole barbecued pig, and the elaborate dragon art on the walls. She described the frantic activity in the kitchen downstairs, the clanging of utensils, hot oil sizzling at the wok stations and the line of cooks wielding meat cleavers over huge wooden blocks.

“It was marginally controlled chaos at best, and it was very noisy, but whenever we would venture down to the kitchen, the cooks would stop what they were doing and greet us like family,” Ms. Louie said, flipping through slides of photos and old menus on a projector. “And then dad would tell them to get back to work.”

Jari Louie told the crowd that preparing for the exhibit was an unexpected gift for the siblings, who, in preparation, pored through old photographs and memorabilia and swapped memories of growing up at the nightclub, “trying to approximate some kind of truth out of all of this crazy.”

“We passed these stories around like a basket of bread between us, and it was really joyful at times,” she said. “It was really hilarious at times, and at times, it was really emotional.”

The Learning Lab, accessible through a guided tour, includes a media studio and workshop space that can be used for hands-on activities. The venue can also be rented for private functions.

Beginning this month, Family Saturdays, with arts and crafts activities, will be held on the second Saturday of each month. A fifth anniversary celebration is also planned for November.

Agatha Sit, archivist at the Chinatown Storytelling Centre, said the design of the space is semi-permanent, and that displays and artifacts can be periodically updated.

“We believe that archives are not to be stored, but to be seen,” she said in an interview. “And from seeing, people know.”

Ms. Lee told the crowd at the Marco Polo event that she was heartened by the response the space had received in its first few weeks of opening.

“I think that many people had forgotten about the vibrancy of Chinatown,” she said. “What we’re trying to do is show them what once was – and what we hope can be again.”

They continue through a hallway adorned with historic Hong Kong movie posters, flyers for “authentic Chinese cuisine” and covers of the English-language Chinatown News magazine from the 1950s. Inside, digital walls and carefully curated artifacts further tell the story of what once was.

On this June evening, Mr. Young is perched on a stool on a small stage in front of a brick wall façade bearing the Marco Polo’s retro wordmark, his audience on folding chairs. A faint smell of spring rolls wafts through the space – a snack offered to guests along with Dragon Tail Slings, the signature cocktail of the defunct nightclub. It’s an intimate setting, not unlike an old friend telling stories over dinner.
After Ms. Simone’s set, Mr. Young continued, he drove across town to his second job, starting at 2 a.m., playing guitar at an after-hours club owned by his friend and fellow musician, Tommy Chong.

“All of a sudden, the room hushed. Nina was in the crowd,” he told a rapt audience. “We played, she listened for an hour and a half and said, ‘Send him a plane ticket and a contract. I want him in New York.’”
Mr. Young ended up touring internationally with Ms. Simone for two years, ON and off, including a date at Carnegie Hall.

Alex, Victor and Harry Louie – brothers from one of the region’s most successful Chinese-Canadian families – opened the Marco Polo in 1964 and operated it in Vancouver until 1982. The nightclub quickly set itself apart from the city’s other live entertainment venues with its smorgasbord buffet, yo-yo champion emcee and capacity for 500 guests.

Despite being known as “Canada’s only Oriental nightclub,” the Marco Polo drew a diverse mix of both audiences and performers, the name itself a nod to exploration. Racial tensions at the time also kept the two other big Vancouver nightclubs from bringing in Black artists, Mr. Young recalled.

“The idea was when they brought in minority acts, like Redd Foxx and Sly and the Family Stone, they would not draw the rich Shaughnessy people they wanted,” he said, referencing a tony Vancouver neighbourhood. “So they would shoot down to the Marco Polo. Thank god, we had some good music.”
Comedian Richard Pryor and musicians the Platters and the 5th Dimension were among other acts who performed at the Marco Polo.

Karen, Jari and Mark Louie, Alex Louie’s adult children, joined Mr. Young on stage that evening and regaled the audience with childhood memories of the nightclub. Karen Louie spoke of its famous lemon chicken and whole barbecued pig, and the elaborate dragon art on the walls. She described the frantic activity in the kitchen downstairs, the clanging of utensils, hot oil sizzling at the wok stations and the line of cooks wielding meat cleavers over huge wooden blocks.

“It was marginally controlled chaos at best, and it was very noisy, but whenever we would venture down to the kitchen, the cooks would stop what they were doing and greet us like family,” Ms. Louie said, flipping through slides of photos and old menus on a projector. “And then dad would tell them to get back to work.”

Jari Louie told the crowd that preparing for the exhibit was an unexpected gift for the siblings, who, in preparation, pored through old photographs and memorabilia and swapped memories of growing up at the nightclub, “trying to approximate some kind of truth out of all of this crazy.”
“We passed these stories around like a basket of bread between us, and it was really joyful at times,” she said. “It was really hilarious at times, and at times, it was really emotional.”
The Learning Lab, accessible through a guided tour, includes a media studio and workshop space that can be used for hands-on activities. The venue can also be rented for private functions.
Beginning this month, Family Saturdays, with arts and crafts activities, will be held on the second Saturday of each month. A fifth anniversary celebration is also planned for November.
Agatha Sit, archivist at the Chinatown Storytelling Centre, said the design of the space is semi-permanent, and that displays and artifacts can be periodically updated.
“We believe that archives are not to be stored, but to be seen,” she said in an interview. “And from seeing, people know.”
Ms. Lee told the crowd at the Marco Polo event that she was heartened by the response the space had received in its first few weeks of opening.
“I think that many people had forgotten about the vibrancy of Chinatown,” she said. “What we’re trying to do is show them what once was – and what we hope can be again.”

stories.title: Latvian citizens training with drones amid tensions with Russia
stories.summary: Riga - On a Thursday morning in August, about 20 executives from Latvia's largest companies gathered in a former plywood factory.
stories.author: Stéphane Blais The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Riga - On a Thursday morning in August, about 20 executives from Latvia’s largest companies gathered in a former plywood factory.

The business leaders were not there to discuss market opportunities of market growth. Instead, they learned how to fly drones and familiarize themselves with the latest technology redefining modern warfare.

The old factory, in Latvia’s capital city of Riga, is now known as the Drone House.

It provides a glimpse into local efforts by citizens organizing to strengthen their defences against growing threats from Russia in the context of a Nato mission that is led by Canada.

Local residents are learning how to fly and operate drones at the centre, which includes a 2,500-square-metre indoor hall and a 10,000-square-metere outdoor training area.

While taking a break from the training, businesswoman Laura Pica said she believes Latvians have a responsibility to defend their country.

“Look what we see in Ukraine, if civil citizens would not help, then probably Ukraine would be occupied,” she told The Canadian Press inside the training centre. “This is why we need to help our country to strengthen their forces.”

Being Russia’s neighbour is like standing next to “a monkey juggling with grenades,” she said.

“You can never know when it falls down,” she added.

Pica’s concerns are widespread in the Baltic country. Nato shot down a drone loaded with explosives in eastern Latvia three days prior.

Latvian authorities believe the drone was a Ukrainian aircraft that got diverted into Latvian airspace by Russian jamming.

“(Russia is) testing our limits and Nato limits,” said Maris Bruza, one of the four founders of the Drone House.

Testing those limits could include an operation to seize a portion of Latvian territory, just to see how Nato will react, he added.

The ambitious civilian project aims to train 50,000 citizens in the use of drones, including high school students who receive free training.

Even Ukrainian soldiers made their way to Drone House to provide training on the use of interceptor drones. The machines are designed to detect, track and neutralize enemy drones.

“At the moment, Ukrainians are the best in the world,” said Viesturs Silenieks, a co-founder of the Drone House. “No doubt that the best knowledge, expertise and practice comes from Ukraine.”

He explained that members of his team regularly travel to Ukraine, while Ukrainian military personnel frequently visit the Drone House to train and exchange information on the latest technologies developed on the front lines.

Among those training at the Drone House was Daiga Auzina, who has worked as a financial services manager for 20 years.

While she joked she does not have the skills to be a drone pilot, she stressed that investing in security and defence is crucial for Latvians.

“It’s on everybody’s mind today, it is our reality,” she said. “It’s not realistic to expect that governments will be able to help and cover every area.”

Auzina became emotional talking about the presence of Canadian soldiers, who have crossed the ocean to provide military support.

“I’m crying now because I think it’s just so great that Canadians are helping us,” she said.

Canada is leading a mission to “reassure, deter and defend” the Baltic states. But the situation is becoming increasingly complex.

With cyberattacks, armed drones, infrastructure sabotage, and disinformation campaigns, Latvia is facing threats that blur the line between war and peace.

Latvia’s new defence minister, Raivis Melnis, was appointed last May during a political crisis triggered by repeated drone attacks. The crisis led to the resignation of former prime minister Evika Silina.

Melnis, a former military officer, told The Canadian Press that Latvia is taking a proactive approach to the conflict that involves younger generations.

For example, the country reinstated conscription and added a mandatory national defence education course to school curriculums in 2024.

The 112-hour course, spread over two years, allows students to develop military skills and includes drone pilot training, according to the minister.

In Murjani, about 50 kilometres from Riga, volunteers aged 16 to 20 are preparing to participate in a drone-piloting competition using machines they assembled themselves.

The competition is the culmination of a two-week camp attended by members of the “Jaunsardzes,” the youth national guard.

Alesa Maza, 16, said it’s important to educate young people about drones “to demystify their intimidating aspect” and prevent panic when, for example, a drone enters the country’s airspace.

She said students are learning about the size of drones, their capabilities, what the aircraft can achieve and what to do when a drone is shot down.

After all, the teenager lucidly explained, drones are becoming an increasingly common part of Latvians’ lives, and “we’re going to be seeing them more so it’s just good to understand what it actually is.”

For many Latvians, defence is no longer just a matter for the military — it is everyone’s responsibility.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 5, 2026.

This report was produced with a grant from the Fonds québécois en journalisme international.

stories.title: What the menopause gap in the labour force is costing Canada
stories.summary: Stigma, silence and unmanaged symptoms are taking an immense toll on women – and on the economy
stories.author: Tavia Grant
stories.content:
Aimee Debow was giving a major presentation about a multibillion-dollar telecom merger to her executive team when words suddenly failed her.

She had been working on the project for months. She had a full team behind her. She had lived and breathed the material and knew it inside out.

“I went to present – and I could remember nothing,” she said, recalling that moment four years ago. “Like, I could not give the presentation, and it was so difficult and so embarrassing. And that was the moment I said, ‘Okay, things have to change at work. I can’t be the only one.’”

It wasn’t just the momentary loss for words. She had suffered from sleeplessness for more than a decade – at times getting just three hours a day. Through her early 40s to early 50s, she was exhausted. She had heart palpitations, joint pain, night sweats, frozen shoulders (causing excruciating pain and stiffness), and, for the first time in her life, anxiety. And the brain fog. She worried she had dementia.

She eventually left her Toronto job in 2022 after 26 years in the corporate world, at the height of her career. It was only later that she learned, through her own research, that she was among the 25 per cent of women who suffer from severe menopausal symptoms.

“At the time, I would have said the word burnt-out, but really it was I was just physically and emotionally overtaken by menopause,” Ms. Debow said.

Though menopause marks a year since the last menstrual period, which happens at the average age of 51, the term is often used to refer to the entire, multistep phase of life. It begins with perimenopause in a woman’s 30s or more often her 40s. After menopause comes postmenopause.

Symptoms hit the majority of women between the ages of 45 and 55, when they are at the top of their game in skills, experience and seniority – and for those with children, just as child-care pressures May be easing up. There are dozens of different symptoms, and their average duration is about seven years, though the effects can last for 10 years or more.

It’s not just about hot flashes. Many symptoms, such as depression and anxiety, are profound but not visible. And half of women in Canada, according to one survey by the Menopause Foundation of Canada , say they are unprepared for this transition in life.

Some are trying to change that. It is a growing topic in public discussions – in workplaces, governments and homes, in Canada and beyond. Gen X and older millennial women have been bringing new prominence to the topic through online discussions, group chats, support groups and public events, putting their feet down after watching their mothers and grandmothers suffer in silence. They include high-profile people such as Naomi Watts, Michelle Obama, Shania Twain – and Melinda French Gates, who recently called for systemic change in menopause care in a New York Times op-ed .

The toll is massive: One estimate from the Menopause Foundation puts the cost of unmanaged symptoms at $3.5-billion a year to the Canadian economy.

Five million women in Canada’s labour market are over the age of 40 – one-quarter of the working population.

Menopause symptoms cause some to reduce their hours, avoid promotions, change careers or drop out of the labour force altogether, according to the foundation, causing ripple effects for their financial security and retirement savings.

But the scale of the problem is hard to measure. A dearth of research, awareness and workplace supports is affecting labour-market outcomes, said Pnina Alon-Shenker, an associate professor at Toronto Metropolitan University’s department of law and business. She is the co-author of a study on menopause, work and legal protections that is soon to be published in the Dalhousie Law Journal.

“Think about the talent and the expertise and the institutional knowledge – that’s our loss. It’s the loss for employers, but it’s a loss for society, and for the economy,” she said.

Britain and Australia are ahead of Canada in addressing the issue. The U.K. recently became the first country in the world to write menopause into employment law, explicitly naming it in legislation. Australia just started its first-ever national campaign on menopause.

Canada doesn’t have any national strategy on menopause. It hasn’t had a national health campaign. Funding for research is still scant.

Federal politicians are starting to take note, though. In June, a House of Commons standing committee on the status of women began hearings for its study on the labour-force impacts of menopause and perimenopause, mirroring a parliamentary inquiry Britain concluded in 2022. (That committee’s report warned the impact of menopause was causing the economy to “haemorrhage talent.”)

Canada’s parliamentary committee has tasked itself with looking at access to treatments and workplace policies. These could include offering flexible or hybrid work options, improving ventilation in office spaces, paid sick days and communicating more openly with employees to reduce stigma. The study will make recommendations to the federal government.

In her expert testimony, Élise Brunot, director of the Montreal-based Quebec Women’s Health Action Network, noted that two out of three women don’t dare to talk about their symptoms with their supervisor. Half feel embarrassed to ask for accommodations, she said – requests like more frequent breaks, access to cold water or modified clothing requirements.

“This silence has real consequences: shame, presenteeism, gradual disengagement and premature departures. Above all, it represents a daily affront to the dignity of millions of women.”

Menopause is not a disease, nor is it a weakness, she said. It is a normal stage of life, “and our collective tendency to ignore this at work speaks volumes about the values that still shape the workplace.”

Janet Ko was 48 and at the peak of her career as a senior vice-president in Mississauga when she was, as she puts it, blindsided: Out of nowhere, she became exhausted and couldn’t sleep. She had brain fog and night sweats. Heart palpitations sent her to the emergency room.

She tried to power through it. But convinced she was burnt out, she stepped back from her senior role in 2016.

“It took years for me to understand that what I was experiencing were simply very common symptoms of perimenopause. Had I known, had I been treated, my career would have looked very different,” she said.

“We’re actually losing women in the prime of their working lives, and I know this personally.”

It took years to figure out what was happening, and to get effective treatment. Menopause hormone therapy, she said, was a game-changer. She feels great now. And the experience spurred her to co-found the Menopause Foundation of Canada in 2022, where she is president.

“I just thought this was a tremendous injustice for women,” she said. The foundation provides online tools for workplaces and evidence-based resources for women seeking information.

There have been few definitive studies in Canada on the effects of untreated menopause symptoms among women at work. The federal government does not publish data on the topic.

Labour-force participation rates do show a shift among women in their fifties, however; menopause could be one factor, in addition to others including having to care for aging parents, stress or other health issues. In 2025, the participation rate for women aged 55 to 59 years old was 73.3 per cent, compared with 82.8 per cent among men of the same age, according to Statistics Canada survey data.

This data doesn’t capture the impact of menopause specifically. Questions are broader, covering illness, disability or job satisfaction. The survey doesn’t track information on workplace accommodations or reflect who is getting promoted or why.

The British government cites more specific figures, with estimates that £1.7-billion is lost each year owing to missed days, lost productivity and women leaving the work force because of menopause. In Britain, estimates show that a 5-per-cent increase in female employment overall could boost its economy by up to £125-billion a year.

Its government’s recent review of 42 studies said there is “clearly evidence” of women’s progress at work being hampered by their experiences of menopause, and said further research is needed.

A study based on Norwegian and Swedish data showed lasting drops in earnings and employment after menopause. The 2025 Nber paper, called the Menopause Penalty, said its findings showed the hidden economic toll of menopause, and said better support policies can reduce these economic losses.

In the U.S., a 2023 Mayo Clinic study found menopause costs American women an estimated US$1.8-billion in lost working time each year.

In Canada, some non-government groups have tried to quantify the impact of menopause in a similar way. The Menopause Foundation and Deloitte Canada estimate that about 540,000 work days are lost each year in Canada owing to managing symptoms. The foundation’s survey also found that 70 per cent of those experiencing symptoms don’t feel comfortable speaking with their HR departments about them.

In Sudbury, Roberta Heale is conducting a survey about menopause symptoms and workplace impacts in Canada. Preliminary results, based on 184 respondents so far, show one-third are considering leaving their jobs owing to symptoms, with fatigue as the top symptom. Two-thirds reported diminished confidence at work, and four in 10 said it reduced their ability to advance in roles.

Prof. Heale, a professor at Laurentian University’s School of Nursing, gives presentations and runs a virtual menopause clinic for professionals from teachers to real estate agents to lawyers. “Just in the last month, I’ve talked to several women who’ve had absences from their jobs or gone on leaves,” she said.

Experiences of symptoms and access to care can differ depending on a woman’s circumstances. U.S. surveys have shown that Black women experience hot flashes and night sweats over a longer duration than other groups, and are more likely to report adverse work outcomes. Women in lower-income or more precarious jobs are less likely to be able to access treatment , and have fewer job protections.

Evidence shows that, for many women, hormone replacement therapy is an effective option for alleviating symptoms. However, it is not covered in every province.

Amy Flood, executive director of Women’s Health Collective Canada, said the costs of unmanaged symptoms go well beyond the day to day.

“The first cost is to the woman herself. Her health [both physical and mental], her confidence, her career progression, and her earning power. And still, women just continue powering through because their financial stability depends on it,” she said.

Any time away from work will also affect pension contributions, benefits and future earnings, she said.

And there are consequences for employers: reduced productivity, increased turnover and training and recruitment costs. Knowledge and skills go out the door when a senior-level woman leaves.

Cooke Aquaculture is one of the Canadian companies educating workers about menopause. Women make up about a third of its work force, from Diana Baranetska and Tetiana Aksonenko at the hatchery in St. Alban’s, N.L., to Tanya Cook and Stacey Tucker on the packaging line in St. George, N.B. Courtesy of Cooke Aquaculture

Blacks Harbour, N.B.-based Cooke Aquaculture Inc. has 3,100 employees in Canada, about one-third of whom are women. The aquaculture company held a webinar on menopause earlier this year. About 150 workers took part – men and women – who learned about the stages of menopause, common symptoms, myths and misconceptions and insights on workplace impacts.

The intent “was to normalize the topic and be a springboard for a more sustained conversation around menopause as part of well-being in the workplace,” said Catherine McBride, chief human resources officer, in an e-mail.

One of the employees who participated was Monica Wheaton, who works in IT. “It was reassuring to hear other women’s experiences and know that many of us share similar challenges,” she said. ”I especially appreciated that men participated in the session as well.”

Since that webinar, the company says some participants have used a workplace checklist to evaluate and alter their workspaces, based on what they learned in the session. The seafood company is now planning a follow-up webinar for more information sharing.

Some large employers are stepping up efforts. Sun Life, Canada’s second-largest life insurer, is one of them. Thirty-five per cent of its Canadian work force are women aged 40 and up.

“Menopause is one of the most overlooked health and workplace challenges today, quietly affecting women’s well-being, productivity and career progression,” said Helena Pagano, chief people and culture officer at Sun Life, in an e-mail. “For employers, this is not only a health issue, it’s a culture and talent issue.”

It runs programs to build awareness of menopause. In 2024, it started a menopause training for all employees globally. The company also offers accommodations, such as hybrid work, to those who need them. And its benefits include a service that offers personalized care plans, with treatment options that can include the prescription of hormone therapy.

It’s still rare for employers in Canada to have such policies – “and they should,” said Erin Porter, founder and partner at Protea LLP, a Toronto-based labour and employment firm. This May be as simple as amending current workplace accommodation policies to explicitly include mention of menopause.

Some are forcing the issue in tribunal cases . In one 2016 B.C. human-rights tribunal case , a worker said she experienced overheating and a racing heart owing to mandatory, wool PPE required for her job as a painter. Her doctor said she had “menopause heat exhaustion symptoms” and the complaint was allowed to proceed. In another tribunal case , a manager allegedly told a worker her “hormones were making her overreact”; this complaint, too, was allowed to proceed.

In a well-publicized 2023 case in Britain that some in Canada are pointing to as an example, an insurance company was forced to pay a former employee more than £64,000 after a tribunal found it failed to make reasonable adjustments for her menopause symptoms.

“It’s not a matter of if; it’s just a matter of when” more of these cases are filed in Canada, Ms. Porter said.

As of this year, the British government is encouraging large employers to have action plans that support people experiencing menopause. It will become mandatory in 2027. A women’s employment ambassador to champion women’s health in the workplace has also been appointed.

Last year in the U.S., Rhode Island became the first state to require workplace accommodations for women experiencing menopause. A state news release on the announcement noted that “menopause is not something that women choose to experience.”

As part of Australia’s national campaign, its federal government recently expanded services for women experiencing menopause and perimenopause by adding supports and treatment options in clinics.

In Canada, “in terms of what the government is doing to protect workers experiencing menopause – not much, as far as I can tell,” said Prof. Alon-Shenker of TMU. She points to the need for better legal protections, awareness campaigns and flexible work arrangements – and is looking forward to the recommendations that the committee will make.

But there is a lot that companies can do in the meantime. For employers, it is advantageous to develop a policy, she said, not just to avoid litigation, which could be costly, but also to attract and retain talent.

The kind of accommodations that can help people thrive are often not very expensive, Prof. Alon-Shenker said. Workplaces that find ways to accommodate this stage of life have a competitive advantage. And more inclusive policies have been shown to be healthier workplaces for everyone – men and women, younger and older.

In Toronto, Ms. Debow now runs a business called Menovate that educates and trains workplaces on how to respond. She founded it last year because she didn’t want to see other women, including her own daughter’s generation, have to go through the same long struggles without support as she did.

“It’s such a small investment to invest in a women’s health who’s going through menopause,” she says, “and the payback is huge.”

Labour-force participation rates do show a shift among women in their fifties, however; menopause could be one factor, in addition to others including having to care for aging parents, stress or other health issues. In 2025, the participation rate for women aged 55 to 59 years old was 73.3 per cent, compared with 82.8 per cent among men of the same age, according to Statistics Canada survey data.

This data doesn’t capture the impact of menopause specifically. Questions are broader, covering illness, disability or job satisfaction. The survey doesn’t track information on workplace accommodations or reflect who is getting promoted or why.

The British government cites more specific figures, with estimates that £1.7-billion is lost each year owing to missed days, lost productivity and women leaving the work force because of menopause. In Britain, estimates show that a 5-per-cent increase in female employment overall could boost its economy by up to £125-billion a year.
Its government’s recent review of 42 studies said there is “clearly evidence” of women’s progress at work being hampered by their experiences of menopause, and said further research is needed.

A study based on Norwegian and Swedish data showed lasting drops in earnings and employment after menopause. The 2025 Nber paper, called the Menopause Penalty, said its findings showed the hidden economic toll of menopause, and said better support policies can reduce these economic losses.
In the U.S., a 2023 Mayo Clinic study found menopause costs American women an estimated US$1.8-billion in lost working time each year.

In Canada, some non-government groups have tried to quantify the impact of menopause in a similar way. The Menopause Foundation and Deloitte Canada estimate that about 540,000 work days are lost each year in Canada owing to managing symptoms. The foundation’s survey also found that 70 per cent of those experiencing symptoms don’t feel comfortable speaking with their HR departments about them.

In Sudbury, Roberta Heale is conducting a survey about menopause symptoms and workplace impacts in Canada. Preliminary results, based on 184 respondents so far, show one-third are considering leaving their jobs owing to symptoms, with fatigue as the top symptom. Two-thirds reported diminished confidence at work, and four in 10 said it reduced their ability to advance in roles.

Prof. Heale, a professor at Laurentian University’s School of Nursing, gives presentations and runs a virtual menopause clinic for professionals from teachers to real estate agents to lawyers. “Just in the last month, I’ve talked to several women who’ve had absences from their jobs or gone on leaves,” she said.

Experiences of symptoms and access to care can differ depending on a woman’s circumstances. U.S. surveys have shown that Black women experience hot flashes and night sweats over a longer duration than other groups, and are more likely to report adverse work outcomes. Women in lower-income or more precarious jobs are less likely to be able to access treatment , and have fewer job protections.
Evidence shows that, for many women, hormone replacement therapy is an effective option for alleviating symptoms. However, it is not covered in every province.
Amy Flood, executive director of Women’s Health Collective Canada, said the costs of unmanaged symptoms go well beyond the day to day.

“The first cost is to the woman herself. Her health [both physical and mental], her confidence, her career progression, and her earning power. And still, women just continue powering through because their financial stability depends on it,” she said.
Any time away from work will also affect pension contributions, benefits and future earnings, she said.
And there are consequences for employers: reduced productivity, increased turnover and training and recruitment costs. Knowledge and skills go out the door when a senior-level woman leaves.

Cooke Aquaculture is one of the Canadian companies educating workers about menopause. Women make up about a third of its work force, from Diana Baranetska and Tetiana Aksonenko at the hatchery in St. Alban’s, N.L., to Tanya Cook and Stacey Tucker on the packaging line in St. George, N.B. Courtesy of Cooke Aquaculture

Blacks Harbour, N.B.-based Cooke Aquaculture Inc. has 3,100 employees in Canada, about one-third of whom are women. The aquaculture company held a webinar on menopause earlier this year. About 150 workers took part – men and women – who learned about the stages of menopause, common symptoms, myths and misconceptions and insights on workplace impacts.

The intent “was to normalize the topic and be a springboard for a more sustained conversation around menopause as part of well-being in the workplace,” said Catherine McBride, chief human resources officer, in an e-mail.

One of the employees who participated was Monica Wheaton, who works in IT. “It was reassuring to hear other women’s experiences and know that many of us share similar challenges,” she said. ”I especially appreciated that men participated in the session as well.”

Since that webinar, the company says some participants have used a workplace checklist to evaluate and alter their workspaces, based on what they learned in the session. The seafood company is now planning a follow-up webinar for more information sharing.
Some large employers are stepping up efforts. Sun Life, Canada’s second-largest life insurer, is one of them. Thirty-five per cent of its Canadian work force are women aged 40 and up.

“Menopause is one of the most overlooked health and workplace challenges today, quietly affecting women’s well-being, productivity and career progression,” said Helena Pagano, chief people and culture officer at Sun Life, in an e-mail. “For employers, this is not only a health issue, it’s a culture and talent issue.”

It runs programs to build awareness of menopause. In 2024, it started a menopause training for all employees globally. The company also offers accommodations, such as hybrid work, to those who need them. And its benefits include a service that offers personalized care plans, with treatment options that can include the prescription of hormone therapy.

It’s still rare for employers in Canada to have such policies – “and they should,” said Erin Porter, founder and partner at Protea LLP, a Toronto-based labour and employment firm. This May be as simple as amending current workplace accommodation policies to explicitly include mention of menopause.

Some are forcing the issue in tribunal cases . In one 2016 B.C. human-rights tribunal case , a worker said she experienced overheating and a racing heart owing to mandatory, wool PPE required for her job as a painter. Her doctor said she had “menopause heat exhaustion symptoms” and the complaint was allowed to proceed. In another tribunal case , a manager allegedly told a worker her “hormones were making her overreact”; this complaint, too, was allowed to proceed.

In a well-publicized 2023 case in Britain that some in Canada are pointing to as an example, an insurance company was forced to pay a former employee more than £64,000 after a tribunal found it failed to make reasonable adjustments for her menopause symptoms.
“It’s not a matter of if; it’s just a matter of when” more of these cases are filed in Canada, Ms. Porter said.

As of this year, the British government is encouraging large employers to have action plans that support people experiencing menopause. It will become mandatory in 2027. A women’s employment ambassador to champion women’s health in the workplace has also been appointed.

Last year in the U.S., Rhode Island became the first state to require workplace accommodations for women experiencing menopause. A state news release on the announcement noted that “menopause is not something that women choose to experience.”
As part of Australia’s national campaign, its federal government recently expanded services for women experiencing menopause and perimenopause by adding supports and treatment options in clinics.

In Canada, “in terms of what the government is doing to protect workers experiencing menopause – not much, as far as I can tell,” said Prof. Alon-Shenker of TMU. She points to the need for better legal protections, awareness campaigns and flexible work arrangements – and is looking forward to the recommendations that the committee will make.

But there is a lot that companies can do in the meantime. For employers, it is advantageous to develop a policy, she said, not just to avoid litigation, which could be costly, but also to attract and retain talent.

The kind of accommodations that can help people thrive are often not very expensive, Prof. Alon-Shenker said. Workplaces that find ways to accommodate this stage of life have a competitive advantage. And more inclusive policies have been shown to be healthier workplaces for everyone – men and women, younger and older.

In Toronto, Ms. Debow now runs a business called Menovate that educates and trains workplaces on how to respond. She founded it last year because she didn’t want to see other women, including her own daughter’s generation, have to go through the same long struggles without support as she did.
“It’s such a small investment to invest in a women’s health who’s going through menopause,” she says, “and the payback is huge.”

stories.title: Food influencer gets to know B.C. by eating flora and fauna
stories.summary: From starfish gonads to Dungeness crab, West Coast foraging has become a hit on social media
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
After a purple starfish is barbecued, its yellow gonads look a bit like scrambled eggs and they taste a little like them too, except with a bit of a bitter “pop.”

That’s one of the many revelations social media influencer Justin Park relayed during his quest to fish and forage for dozens of different species of flora and fauna from across British Columbia.

Some of the tapas the amateur chef has profiled for his tens of thousands of online followers include globally renowned favourites such as spot prawns and Dungeness crab. But his creations often skew more obscure and eye-popping, such as making crostini with acorn and oak weevils, fashioning fruit roll-ups out of salal berries and pickling bull kelp.

The 30-year-old from Honolulu said he gave himself just under a year to see how much of B.C. he could find and eat after free-diving for fish and shellfish around Victoria, where the U.S. naval veteran recently completed a two-and-a-half-year contract working on submarines for the Royal Canadian Navy. The challenge is now over, but he said he is still editing videos chronicling the up to 70 different species he ate during that period.

Anecdotally, it appears more and more North Americans are finding and fixing their own meals from the wild as an antidote to a variety of modern ills: Inflating grocery store prices, the ecological and health harms of industrial agricultural systems and the tiny screens monopolizing our free time.

Data are scarce on people who are using snorkels or shovels in order to secure their next meal. Results from the last census, in 2021, show only three per cent of Canadian households reported hunting close to home, with that number reaching as high as seven per cent for those living outside larger cities. In B.C., the province has issued 13-per-cent more fishing licences to residents over the past decade ending in 2023, the last year for which data is available.

Tom Cervenka, a Vancouver computer programmer who sells field guides to berry and mushroom picking in various provinces, said he believes the COVID-19 pandemic and our increasing dependence on social media created an uptick in Canadians becoming more interested in self-sufficiency.

“How can I look after myself without relying on food distribution chains that could fail conceivably?” said Mr. Cervenka, who also leads mushroom tours of Pacific Spirit Regional Park, which surrounds the University of British Columbia’s sprawling campus.

Mr. Park said he took to social media to share his exhilaration with the province’s natural bounty, as well as to challenge people to get outside their comfort zones and consider trying to catch and prepare their own meals – as long as they obey the rules and avoid species in peril.

“I was just so excited to discover these things: I didn’t know you could just dig in the sand and catch a Dungeness crab and go home with a $30 crab,” Mr. Park said during a recent phone interview from Ecuador, where he travelled this summer.

“I was just like blown away by how much food there was, not only in the sea, but on land as well.”

Still, he is keen to get people to pivot from the popular meats of crab, salmon and halibut and embrace lesser-known foods that Indigenous people have consumed for millennia.

Dr. Jennifer Grenz, a member of the Lytton First Nation and a food systems scientist with Ubc’s Department of Forest Resources Management, said it is great that Mr. Park is sharing how to access the abundance Western Canada has to offer.

She added that an increasing number of Indigenous influencers are posting their own videos online to share traditional knowledge, referencing chef and educator Jared Qwustenuxun Williams, who also refers to himself as the Indigenous Forest Punk.

Among the traditional practices seeing a resurgence are “sea gardens,” which First Nations often built by piling rock walls along intertidal zones to trap sediment and make a healthy habitat for shellfish, Dr. Grenz said.

“Humans are inherently lazy, right?” she added of the common misconception that Indigenous peoples were constantly hunting and gathering to survive, explaining that this method of sustainable aquaculture offered minimal effort and maximum returns.

Dr. Grenz, author of Medicine Wheel for the Planet: A Journey Toward Personal and Ecological Healing , said the erasure of traditional knowledge was rammed home when she was called into the principal’s office after her twin daughters got in trouble during a class hike. The pair were showing their classmates how to pick and eat salmon berries when their teacher found out and “flipped out.”

The school explained that teaching people to eat wild berries was against its rules.

“I’m like, ‘well, they know their plant identification, they’re teaching them: This is food. They’re just teaching their friends to find food out in the places they go all the time,’ ” she said. “And then that’s when I was like, ‘do you want this to be a news story or do you want to apologize to them?’”

“They apologized to them.”

stories.title: More than half of Canadians support rejecting proposed trade deal and countertariff measures, poll finds
stories.summary: About two-thirds also said they were worried or somewhat worried about the impact that tariffs will have on them and their families
stories.author: Olivia Grandy
stories.content:
Most Canadians support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States and instead impose retaliatory countertariffs, even if it means paying more for goods, a new poll suggests.

A Nanos Research survey conducted for The Globe and Mail found that 85 per cent of more than 1,000 respondents said they support or somewhat support Mr. Carney’s rejection of the proposed trade deal with the Trump administration.

The survey also found that 80 per cent of respondents said they support or somewhat support Ottawa’s plan to retaliate with dollar-for-dollar countertariffs on a range of U.S. products, scheduled to take effect on Tuesday.

Negotiations to avoid additional U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods fell apart last month when Mr. Carney ordered his officials to withdraw from talks and return home. He later said the Americans introduced unreasonable demands on a range of issues, from French-language requirements to tariffs on trucks .

Nik Nanos, the chief data scientist for Nanos Research, said support for retaliatory tariffs is as high as the early days of the trade war at the beginning of last year, when American policies fuelled antipathy toward the United States and consumer boycotts of U.S. goods and travel.

“We’re back to a situation where the temperature is about as hot as it got when Donald Trump first said that Canada should be the 51st state,” Mr. Nanos said.

About seven in 10 survey respondents said they were willing or somewhat willing to pay higher prices for everyday goods as part of Canada’s response to U.S. tariffs.

Yet, only time will tell how many Canadians will hold on to these views when “economic causalities start piling in” from the trade war, Mr. Nanos said. He added the near-consensus could be short-lived, mirroring the common trend of public opinion during wars.

“That’s the risk for the Carney administration,” he said.

The online random survey sampled 1,037 Canadians from Aug. 30 to Sept. 2 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The margin of error for regional results is higher.

Respondents from the Prairies were comparatively less likely to support Canada rejecting the possible trade deal, at about 17 per cent. Similarly, about 19 per cent of respondents from the region opposed Canada implementing countertariffs.

“Albertans and folks in the Prairies, specifically, are more likely to have an affinity with the United States in terms of the importance of the bi-national relationship and the importance of the trade talks,” Mr. Nanos said. Still, he flagged that even in this region, nearly 77 per cent somewhat rejected the potential U.S.-Canada deal.

Overall, respondents expressed high levels of support for the country’s elbows-up posture: More than three in four said they had both sought out purchasing Canadian goods and avoided purchasing American goods or services in response to Mr. Trump’s comments.

Six in 10 Canadians are either confident or somewhat confident that Canada can protect its economic interests if a new agreement with the U.S. is reached, the poll found.

Meanwhile, about two-thirds also said they were worried or somewhat worried about the impact that tariffs will have on them and their families.

These coinciding views seem to reflect the “clear-headed” understanding Canadians have about the effects of a trade war, Mr. Nanos said.

“They know that you’re not going to enter into a tariff war with the United States without suffering.”

Three-quarters of Canadians disagreed in some way that the U.S. is a trustworthy ally of Canada. The lowest level of agreement (4.7 per cent) came from Quebeckers. Mr. Carney has said that the U.S. tried to influence Canada’s language protections during the August trade talks.

Despite the lack of trust, polling did suggest that some Canadians still believe there is a chance the relationship between the two countries could rebound. More than three in five expected Canada’s relationship with the U.S. to be better (22 per cent) or somewhat better (39 per cent) five years from now.

Put another way, Mr. Nanos pointed out that only one in five respondents firmly said the relationship would improve after this time period.

“Even the hope that Canadians have that things will get better to one extent or another in the next five years is tepid,” he said.

stories.title: In B.C.’s busy waters, coast pilots guide ships into safe harbour
stories.summary: Skilled mariners, dispatchers, and Talon Helicopter crews work together to cover the largest pilotage district in the world
stories.author: James MacDonald
stories.content:
Spend enough time on Dallas Road in Victoria, B.C., and you’ll see it: A small yellow vessel sailing out to meet the hulking bulk carriers, container ships, cruise ships and car carriers that ply the Salish Sea.

Whether during the calm, warm days of a B.C. summer, or the cold, rain-whipped nights of a coastal winter storm, the Pacific Guardian makes the trip. It has a crucial mission: to deliver ship pilots to the vessels that transit in and out from the Pacific.

The ship pilot’s job is to board vessels travelling the immense coast of the province, helping them to safely navigate unfamiliar waters and busy ports.

Ship pilots are professional mariners with decades of experience on the water. While ship captains and crew know their own vessel, they are less familiar with local waterways, tides, coastlines, and ports.

At more than 25,000 kilometres, the BC coastline is the largest pilotage district in the world. The BC Coast Pilots and PPA are responsible for territory from the southern tip of Vancouver Island to the southern tip of Alaska, as well as the length of the Fraser River.

In 2025, more than 140 pilots – along with launch captains, deckhands, dispatchers, and Talon Helicopter crews – responded to 15,200 ship assignments.

Talon Helicopter crews transfer ships pilots on and off of vessels in the pilotage district along the coast.

Ship pilots are some of the most skilled and knowledgeable mariners on the water.

“They need between 700 and 1,000 days at sea on the BC coast [as] the prerequisites to entry,” explained John Wilson, CEO of the PPA.

“Then they do a very comprehensive examination on navigation chart knowledge of the coast. That normally takes them a year or two of ... almost full-time preparation. If they’re successful on the exam, then they have an oral board [exam] that’s between four and five hours in length.”

It takes another seven years to become an unrestricted pilot, able to navigate the largest of vessels.

Joe McDonugh, small vessel machinery operator and deckhand on the PPA pilot vessel the Pacific Guardian, stands watch on deck after the crew dropped off a ships pilot for the cruise ship Anthem of the Seas' final approach and docking at the Port of Victoria.

Pilot Michel Drouin speaks to the challenges of the job.

“No two [ship] bridges are alike. You must not let things bother you too much, just go along with it.”

Mr. Drouin is among the most experienced BC Coast pilots, and the only BC Coast pilot to navigate a submarine, the Hmas Collins, through Seymour Narrows, a notoriously challenging and treacherous stretch of water between Vancouver Island and the mainland.

Mr. Drouin’s deep knowledge of the ports, tides, and corners of the coast are the hallmark of the skill set these ship pilots bring to shipping traffic around British Columbia.
