Cibc spokesperson Tom Wallis said the lease at The Well will consolidate several spaces and teams currently spread across the city into one new, modernized space.

Scotiabank BNS-T took out three large leases in downtown Toronto. It took out 159,073 square feet at 1 Adelaide St. East, 128,278 square feet at 33 Yonge St. and 122,347 square feet at 351 King St. East (The Globe and Mail’s Toronto office is located in the same building). Scotiabank would not comment on whether it had enough office space to accommodate its employees except to say that its teams have been working together on-site four days per week in all locations that space allows.

Stripe LLC , a financial services company, took out 223,229 square feet at 530 Front St. West. Stripe declined to comment.

National Bank of Canada NA-T renewed its lease at 130 King St. West for 203,111 square feet. Spokesperson Alexandre Guay said the bank increased its office footprint when it renewed its lease as the bank is growing nationally. He said: “Some teams work entirely on-site, while others follow a hybrid model that combines in-person and remote work.”

Other cities have had a much more mixed recovery in office building vacancies than downtown Toronto, according to CoStar data.

Vacancy rates have fallen back to pre-pandemic levels, but the city was already grappling with empty buildings in early 2020 because of fallout from last decade’s collapse in oil prices. The city’s recovery has also been helped by office-to-residential conversions, which took a lot of empty inventory off the market, said CoStar’s Mr. Haythornthwaite. “In many respects, Calgary was quicker to pursue large-scale interventions because the market’s challenges were already evident before the pandemic,” he said.

While employers in the two cities have embraced return-to-office mandates, both markets are still adjusting to a world in which many tenants require less office space than they did in 2019, even as more office space has come online.

While large, premium office buildings in the downtown core have recovered, office space across the broader Greater Toronto Area is still suffering. The GTA office vacancy rate sits at roughly 8 per cent, according to CoStar, down from roughly 11.5 per cent last year, but still double where it was in 2019.

The Globe and Mail spoke with workers and businesses about the downtown Toronto revival, and the pros and cons of returning to the office. As told to Sophia Bertuzzi.

“This might be a really unpopular opinion for our generation, but I actually love coming into the office. I find that it just helps me be a lot more productive to be around other people. I get to engage with my coworkers, make friends, be motivated by the people around me, and I find that when I’m sitting at my desk, it’s often that things will happen and I’ll get to up, move around, talk to people. But at home, I can sit and not leave my desk for eight hours straight.

“Overall, I think it’s just better for my mental health and my productivity to be surrounded by other people. My office is quite young, fun, collaborative, so it might not be the same for everyone.”

“I like being in office – it’s the commute that I don’t like. I live in Kleinberg, so my commute is pretty far. Of course, return to work means certain parts of your budget increase. It does cost to come downtown. I do read a lot more to go on the train, listen to a lot of audiobooks. You have to make the best use of your time.”

“I like being in office three days a week. I feel like that’s almost the perfect amount to go in the office, and I have a really great team who works in Toronto as well. Once a month, I would say we try to co-ordinate our days and go to the same office. [Her company has multiple offices in the city.]

“It’s nice to be able to collaborate, bounce off ideas in person. It’s nice to be able to still have two days at home, so I get a little break whenever I need it.”

“There’s been drastic change. I feel like due to summer, especially in the last few months, more people want to work from the office itself rather than being at home. With winter coming, we might expect people going back to working from home.”

“A lot of people worked from home. That was three years of no customers, but to be honest, during those three years, a lot of dry cleaners shut down and I got lucky because of the location. My businesses work together, so it helps me survive. I got Elite [her dog, a French Bulldog mix] in 2022. I’m super lucky because she’s like a mascot for the store, people come to see her.

“In 2024, slowly more and more people came back to the office, starting at two days a week, and then three. Every year they come back more and more days. Slowly we’ve built up our new customers, those who were looking for new dry cleaners.”

Vacancy rates have fallen back to pre-pandemic levels, but the city was already grappling with empty buildings in early 2020 because of fallout from last decade’s collapse in oil prices. The city’s recovery has also been helped by office-to-residential conversions, which took a lot of empty inventory off the market, said CoStar’s Mr. Haythornthwaite. “In many respects, Calgary was quicker to pursue large-scale interventions because the market’s challenges were already evident before the pandemic,” he said.

While employers in the two cities have embraced return-to-office mandates, both markets are still adjusting to a world in which many tenants require less office space than they did in 2019, even as more office space has come online.

While large, premium office buildings in the downtown core have recovered, office space across the broader Greater Toronto Area is still suffering. The GTA office vacancy rate sits at roughly 8 per cent, according to CoStar, down from roughly 11.5 per cent last year, but still double where it was in 2019.
The Globe and Mail spoke with workers and businesses about the downtown Toronto revival, and the pros and cons of returning to the office. As told to Sophia Bertuzzi.

“This might be a really unpopular opinion for our generation, but I actually love coming into the office. I find that it just helps me be a lot more productive to be around other people. I get to engage with my coworkers, make friends, be motivated by the people around me, and I find that when I’m sitting at my desk, it’s often that things will happen and I’ll get to up, move around, talk to people. But at home, I can sit and not leave my desk for eight hours straight.
“Overall, I think it’s just better for my mental health and my productivity to be surrounded by other people. My office is quite young, fun, collaborative, so it might not be the same for everyone.”

“I like being in office – it’s the commute that I don’t like. I live in Kleinberg, so my commute is pretty far. Of course, return to work means certain parts of your budget increase. It does cost to come downtown. I do read a lot more to go on the train, listen to a lot of audiobooks. You have to make the best use of your time.”

“I like being in office three days a week. I feel like that’s almost the perfect amount to go in the office, and I have a really great team who works in Toronto as well. Once a month, I would say we try to co-ordinate our days and go to the same office. [Her company has multiple offices in the city.]
“It’s nice to be able to collaborate, bounce off ideas in person. It’s nice to be able to still have two days at home, so I get a little break whenever I need it.”

“There’s been drastic change. I feel like due to summer, especially in the last few months, more people want to work from the office itself rather than being at home. With winter coming, we might expect people going back to working from home.”

“A lot of people worked from home. That was three years of no customers, but to be honest, during those three years, a lot of dry cleaners shut down and I got lucky because of the location. My businesses work together, so it helps me survive. I got Elite [her dog, a French Bulldog mix] in 2022. I’m super lucky because she’s like a mascot for the store, people come to see her.

“In 2024, slowly more and more people came back to the office, starting at two days a week, and then three. Every year they come back more and more days. Slowly we’ve built up our new customers, those who were looking for new dry cleaners.”

content_blocks.text: Calgary
content_blocks.html: Calgary

content_blocks.text: Vacancy rates have fallen back to pre-pandemic levels, but the city was already grappling with empty buildings in early 2020 because of fallout from last decade’s collapse in oil prices. stories.title: Inside Canadian newsrooms’ triumphs — and regrets — while covering the 9/11 attacks
stories.summary: Toronto — Like every other journalist working in a Canadian newsroom on Sept. 11, 2001, Michelle Shephard recalls the moment she learned a plane had struck the World Trade Center in New York City.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Elissa Mendes, The Canadian Press

Posted September 4, 2026 4:01 am.

Last Updated September 4, 2026 5:56 am.

Toronto — Like every other journalist working in a Canadian newsroom on Sept. 11, 2001, Michelle Shephard recalls the moment she learned a plane had struck the World Trade Center in New York City.

Then a crime reporter at the Toronto Star, she barely stopped to grab her passport and a notebook before rushing to the airport, which had already grounded flights and switched off television screens.

Shephard quickly switched gears and jumped into a car headed for New York with other Star reporters, joining scores of other journalists and volunteers hustling toward Ground Zero as thousands were trying to escape it.

Reporting on the 9/11 attacks required an extraordinary collective effort at a time when verifiable facts and explanations were scarce and the world was gripped with fear. The attacks also pushed journalists to their physical and emotional limits, exposing the risks of reporting on traumatic events.

Twenty-five years later, prominent journalists reflected on their triumphs and regrets in covering 9/11, and how newsroom decisions shaped Canadians’ understanding of the events that changed global security and international politics.

Reporting from a traumatized city

During their “crazy fast” drive to New York, Shephard and her colleagues got lucky.

She said her laminated Toronto Star press pass “looked like it was made in someone’s basement,” but it was enough for one official to let them into a lane marked for emergency responders.

They arrived in the eerily quiet city that night and the sight of a firefighter slumped over on the ground, weary after digging for bodies in the rubble, stopped Shephard in her tracks.

Other details from the scene are still seared in her mind a quarter-century later. The mountain of papers that fell in a blizzard from the collapsed office towers, which Shephard initially mistook for a snowbank. Thousands of eyes staring out from posters of missing people plastered across Manhattan. The repulsive, metallic smell hanging in the air.

“It was an entire city that was traumatized,” Shephard said in a recent interview.

Every other aspect of her life quickly fell by the wayside.

Shephard’s husband, fellow Star reporter Jim Rankin, had rushed off to Boston, where the flights that crashed into the towers originated. The pair realized within a few hours that in the chaos, neither had made plans for someone to look after their new kitten.

For three days, Shephard wore the same shirt and pants she had arrived in, washing off thick dust in the sink each night and blasting the clothes dry with a hotel hair dryer in the morning.

Shephard, who subsequently authored the book “Decade of Fear” about national security since 9/11, said she is proud of her coverage but might make some small changes if she could go back.

She recalled there being pressure in the newsroom to get emotionally charged photos, such as of a grieving wife crying. The journalism industry has since become more mindful of retraumatizing sources, she added.

Shephard believes that meeting people who became victims of post-9/11 policies early in her national security reporting career strengthened her journalism. She said many of her early stories about Islamophobia were relegated to the back of the paper, but eventually “the pendulum swung the other way.”

Despite covering funeral after funeral in the days after 9/11, Shephard said she found solace knowing her reporting was a public service.

She believes some journalists who weren’t reporting from New York May have been even more traumatized, including editors who had to watch footage of people jumping from the towers over and over.

She recalled breaking down at the end of an interview with a Red Cross official, who asked Shephard who was looking after the reporters.

“I remember that when I would put my head down, I would be teary about all that I had seen,” she said.

The voice mail that changed peter mansbridge’s perspective

CBC News anchor Peter Mansbridge was at his doctor’s office when he got a call about the 9/11 attacks.

As the veteran journalist drove toward CBC headquarters in Toronto, not yet knowing that day would be the biggest of his 50-year career, he turned the fundamentals of reporting over and over in his mind: “You’re going to hear all kinds of things. There are going to be all kinds of rumours. You have to deal with fact.”

Forty-four hours of wall-to-wall coverage from the public broadcaster would follow.

Mansbridge said he was running on adrenalin and he got his first “real break” around 4 a.m. on Sept. 12, when he ducked into his private dressing room to change and take a shower.

A short voice mail from his daughter, then a university student in Winnipeg, was waiting for him.

“I just want you to know that I’m watching you,” she told her father. “And I love you.”

Hearing her voice, Mansbridge felt the emotional weight of the attacks for the first time since he sat down behind the anchor desk the day before.

“Sometimes, when you sit in the studio, it’s almost like watching a movie,” he said. “You’re watching a monitor, and sometimes as real as you know it is, it doesn’t feel real.”

The voicemail “was one of the things I used that night to remind me how big the impact of this thing was for families literally around the world — wanting to reach out and connect with each other.”

Mansbridge said the CBC’s 44 hours of intensive coverage weren’t perfect, but overall he is proud of what the broadcaster achieved.

He said the network was careful not to hazard guesses about the death toll and was judicious about replaying footage of the plane crashes.

Mansbridge said the CBC relied on experts to “keep feeding the beast” and find new ways to convey information to audiences as interns sprinted back and forth through the newsroom, hands full of marked-up scripts.

One especially helpful person was introduced as a retired pilot, and he gave detailed explanations of cockpit operations to fill airtime, inferring the planes had been hijacked.

Mansbridge said he found out weeks later that the man’s background in aviation was fabricated. Perhaps just as strangely, he recalled, “everything he said was right.”

The CBC apologized to viewers, and Mansbridge said the incident was another reminder of the importance of verification in a chaotic situation.

Mansbridge said he barely left the newsroom for a week after the attacks.

“The world would never be the same after that,” he said.

Few journalists, including those at the CBC, adequately covered the rampant Islamophobia following the attacks, Mansbridge said.

“I’m not sure that enough of us in Western journalism understood what was happening (with Islamophobia),” he said. “Some did, but they were kind of lonely voices in the midst of all this.”

How the canadian press covered the unfathomable

The bustling Canadian Press newsroom in downtown Toronto fell completely silent as journalists watched on live television another plane crash into the second tower, sending ash and debris onto the streets below.

“It was a ‘holy s—‘ moment,” recalled Scott White, then the news agency’s editor-in-chief. “You’re seeing it happen, right in front of you, and it just changed everything.”

Reporters mobilized as quickly as they could, hurtling south by car in fear that the border would close. The Canadian Press even paid for a traffic ticket that one reporter incurred as he sped through Pennsylvania, White said.

In New York City, Canadian Press journalists arrived at a hellscape where the iconic World Trade towers were now a tangle of steel, and watched as workers shovelled mountains of sludge and knee-deep ash.

“We saw the bodies come out and we cheered because we thought they were alive,” one worker told The Canadian Press at the time.

“But then they brought in the chaplain to read his last rites.”

In one frightening moment, a panicked Canadian Press reporter phoned a colleague to say she had heard a rumour that another plane attack was imminent. It was quickly confirmed to be a hoax, but she ran for her life for several minutes, White said.

“She was terrified, and rightly so,” he said. “That was the first time I remember worrying that something was going to happen to one of our reporters.”

As the dust at Ground Zero settled, one of the iconic post-9/11 images came from Canadian Press photojournalist Andrew Vaughan.

The photo shows Rachel Uchitel pleading for information about her fiancé, who was working on the 104th floor of the second tower when it was obliterated. Her face contorted with grief, Uchitel is almost unrecognizable from the beaming picture of her pressed against James Andrew O’Grady on his missing person poster.

Twenty-five years later, White no longer works in journalism but he’s still haunted by a correction the wire had to issue on the day of the attacks. The Canadian Press reported that borders were closing based on a tip from an official that turned out to be inaccurate.

White said it was a reminder that being right is always more important than being first.

“It still, to this day, bothers me that we misreported that element,” White said. “I don’t think we were the only ones who did it, but that’s still no excuse.”

White, who led the wire’s transition to multimedia journalism, added there were many 9/11 storylines and not enough reporters and resources to cover them all.

White said he was in constant discussions with various bureau chiefs at CP to ensure the wire avoided speculation or fearmongering at a time when even military and government officials were flailing in the same information vacuum.

“These are high-stress times, the terrible things and emotions — seeing people fall out of the World Trade Center,” White said.

“But you have to press on. You have a job to do.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

Elissa Mendes, The Canadian Press

Mansbridge said he found out weeks later that the man’s background in aviation was fabricated. Perhaps just as strangely, he recalled, “everything he said was right.”
The CBC apologized to viewers, and Mansbridge said the incident was another reminder of the importance of verification in a chaotic situation.
Mansbridge said he barely left the newsroom for a week after the attacks.
“The world would never be the same after that,” he said.
Few journalists, including those at the CBC, adequately covered the rampant Islamophobia following the attacks, Mansbridge said.
“I’m not sure that enough of us in Western journalism understood what was happening (with Islamophobia),” he said. “Some did, but they were kind of lonely voices in the midst of all this.”
How the canadian press covered the unfathomable

The bustling Canadian Press newsroom in downtown Toronto fell completely silent as journalists watched on live television another plane crash into the second tower, sending ash and debris onto the streets below.
“It was a ‘holy s—‘ moment,” recalled Scott White, then the news agency’s editor-in-chief. “You’re seeing it happen, right in front of you, and it just changed everything.”

Reporters mobilized as quickly as they could, hurtling south by car in fear that the border would close. The Canadian Press even paid for a traffic ticket that one reporter incurred as he sped through Pennsylvania, White said.

In New York City, Canadian Press journalists arrived at a hellscape where the iconic World Trade towers were now a tangle of steel, and watched as workers shovelled mountains of sludge and knee-deep ash.
“We saw the bodies come out and we cheered because we thought they were alive,” one worker told The Canadian Press at the time.
“But then they brought in the chaplain to read his last rites.”

In one frightening moment, a panicked Canadian Press reporter phoned a colleague to say she had heard a rumour that another plane attack was imminent. It was quickly confirmed to be a hoax, but she ran for her life for several minutes, White said.
“She was terrified, and rightly so,” he said. “That was the first time I remember worrying that something was going to happen to one of our reporters.”
As the dust at Ground Zero settled, one of the iconic post-9/11 images came from Canadian Press photojournalist Andrew Vaughan.

The photo shows Rachel Uchitel pleading for information about her fiancé, who was working on the 104th floor of the second tower when it was obliterated. Her face contorted with grief, Uchitel is almost unrecognizable from the beaming picture of her pressed against James Andrew O’Grady on his missing person poster.

Twenty-five years later, White no longer works in journalism but he’s still haunted by a correction the wire had to issue on the day of the attacks. The Canadian Press reported that borders were closing based on a tip from an official that turned out to be inaccurate.
White said it was a reminder that being right is always more important than being first.
“It still, to this day, bothers me that we misreported that element,” White said. “I don’t think we were the only ones who did it, but that’s still no excuse.”
White, who led the wire’s transition to multimedia journalism, added there were many 9/11 storylines and not enough reporters and resources to cover them all.

White said he was in constant discussions with various bureau chiefs at CP to ensure the wire avoided speculation or fearmongering at a time when even military and government officials were flailing in the same information vacuum.
“These are high-stress times, the terrible things and emotions — seeing people fall out of the World Trade Center,” White said.
“But you have to press on. You have a job to do.”

stories.title: Meet the Indigenous lawyer who's shaking up Alberta's independence movement
stories.summary: Indigenous lawyer Leighton Grey was the surprise star of an Alberta independence rally in Edmonton over the weekend.
stories.author: Rahim Mohamed
stories.content:
Ottawa — Indigenous lawyer Leighton Grey was the surprise star of an Alberta independence rally at the provincial legislature in Edmonton over the weekend.

Grey, a criminal defence attorney and Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation member based in Cold Lake, Alta., delighted the pro-independence crowd when he laid out his vision for a future Alberta where all citizens are treated equally under the law.

“To the government, (and) I’m talking about the federal government now, I’m the other. I’m an Indian,” said Grey. “Which is to say I live in an apartheid state. That’s what Canada is.”

“If we’re going to create the greatest society, a new Alberta that’s free and prosperous, that society has to be one that unifies Indigenous peoples and, as Albertans, invites them into the community that ends the otherness,” he finished to applause.

Grey made the case, through his 20-minute speech, that the Indian Act of 1876 set the Indigenous on a separate, and inferior, path from the non-Indigenous.

“They call us the First Nations, but I find we’re first in all the wrong things and we’re last in all the good things,” said Grey.

“What I would say to these chiefs who are pleading and going to court and trying to stop Alberta independence, explain to me how this relationship is good for our people. Because I’m just a dumb country lawyer, but it goes way over my head,” said Grey to another round of applause.

His self-assessment as a “dumb country lawyer” undersells his impressive resume , which includes, among many other accolades, becoming Alberta’s youngest lawyer appointed to the King’s Counsel in 2010 and being named one of Canada’s Top 50 Lawyers in 2024.

National Post spoke to Grey about his support for Alberta independence. This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

I was not personally involved in the referendum drive. I’ve just, more or less, been a speaker who’s invited to attend various events. What’s pushed me to jump into the fray a bit more has been the oppositional attitude toward the referendum that’s been taken by the premier (Danielle Smith). If I had known, say six or nine months ago, that she’d be taking this stance, I probably would have done things differently.

Well, I have a lot of respect for what people like Mitch Sylvestre and Jeff Rath have done to bring this issue to the forefront, and I’d never want to disparage those guys. But one of the things the independence movement lacks right now is a clear leader that can set the tone and establish message discipline. There’s no question that the other side has used this against us.

No. I don’t have any aspiration to be an out-in-front political leader. That isn’t in my DNA right now. I would see myself more as maybe a key advisor. Someone who could help develop policy for, for example, Indigenous peoples.

Absolutely. When I connect with Indigenous people, either through my podcast or when I go out and speak, I generally find that they want the same things as everyone else does: safe streets, proper health care, good schools for their kids. It’s hard to argue that Canada is succeeding in these areas, especially when you look at the living conditions on reservations. Many don’t even have potable water!

I think the best we can hope for is to send Ottawa a message. Unlike some in the movement, I happen to think that we already have a pretty good Constitution. The problem is that we’re not governing ourselves in accordance to it. It was never intended for us to have this all-powerful federal government, with really all effective lawmaking power concentrated in the prime minister’s office. I’m more in the line of seeing the independence movement as a way of showing Albertans, and indeed the rest of Canada, that there’s a better way to govern ourselves.

National Post rmohamed@postmedia.com

stories.title: Joe Rogan: Trump trying to rename Lake Ontario ‘doesn’t make any sense’
stories.summary: The popular American podcaster and Trump supporter said the U.S. president’s order renaming the Great Lake is to distract “from the fact that we’re in a war that we can’t win in Iran.”
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
Lake Ontario is garnering support from an unlikely source.

Joe Rogan took time on his highly popular podcast earlier this week to question U.S. President Donald Trump’s efforts to rebrand Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

“Lake Ontario has been Lake Ontario forever. Isn’t it connected to Ontario?” the American host asked his guest, comedian Brian Simpson, ON Tuesday’s episode of “The Joe Rogan Experience.”

Simpson later asked Rogan if he knew the purpose of Trump’s renaming efforts.

“To distract you from the fact that we’re in a war that we can’t win in Iran,” Rogan said.

“It doesn’t make any sense,” the influential host continued, laughing. “Like who cares (if) it’s Lake Ontario? It’s a good name. We’ve had that name forever.”

Rogan is a longtime Trump supporter who endorsed the president’s campaign on the eve of the 2024 election and then attended the inauguration last January. But the former “Fear Factor” host, actor, UFC commentator and comedian has criticized Trump more recently .

In March of last year, during the previous Trump tiff with Canada, Rogan called the feud “stupid” and bemoaned the fact that Canadians “booed us over tariffs” during pro sports events featuring teams from both countries. Earlier that year, Rogan also broke with Trump on other issues including wide-ranging deportations, calling an operation to detain immigrants “horrific.”

In 2022, Rogan drew the ire of Canadians for calling the country “communist” and for referring to then-prime minister Justin Trudeau as a “dictator” over the leader’s response to the pandemic.

Rogan’s podcast has more than 21 million subscribers.

Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 27 to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” following a bitter public spat with Ontario Premier Doug Ford , which stemmed from the latest round of tariffs Trump imposed on Canada.

Apple and Google have changed the body of water’s name to “Lake America” in the U.S. , while MapQuest refused to change the name for users on either side of the border.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Mike Wilner: Jays fans defy Trump’s trade war threats and renaming of Lake Ontario. Here’s why they went to Cleveland
stories.summary: Cleveland — If you closed your eyes, you might have thought the Blue Jays were playing at home.
stories.author: Mike Wilner
stories.content:
CLEVELAND — If you closed your eyes, you might have thought the Blue Jays were playing at home.

Over a three-game series with huge playoff implications , every Jays’ run was met with loud cheers and there were several spontaneous chants of “Let’s go Blue Jays!” that rained down from the seats at Progressive Field in Cleveland, which sits at the corner of Ontario Street and Carnegie Avenue.

Spencer Arrighetti will start Tuesday’s opener in Cleveland, September reinforcements on the way.

On occasion, especially during the Guardians’ 6-1 win on Tuesday night, the locals attempted to shout down the Jays fans, but often there was no response.

In the fourth inning Thursday, when the Jays scored their first run in what wound up a 6-3 victory over the Guardians, the chants were so loud that the stadium’s public address system tried to get some crowd activation started to drown them out.

Even in these days of Donald Trump ‘s tariff wars , annexation threats and his renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” Canadians keep heading south to support their baseball team. The Star wandered through the stands and spoke to several before Thursday’s series finale.

They were all aware of the political climate , but most didn’t consider it important enough to change their plans.

Steve and Brenda Reinecke, who were there for the Jays’ World Series victories in 1992 and ‘93, made the drive in from Sarnia.

Steve and Brenda Reinecke drove from Sarnia to see the Jays play the Guardians on Thursday. “It’s about seeing the Blue Jays and trying to forget about all that other stuff,” said Brenda.

“The American situation hopefully does not interfere with baseball,” said Steve. “I still think baseball fans are baseball fans and coming here and hanging out with these other baseball fans, Guardians fans, it’s still baseball and hopefully politics doesn’t play into that.”

The other Reinecke felt some reluctance in making the trip, though.

“That was me, for sure,” said Brenda. “I feel like, uhhhhhhhhhhh, but I’m here for the Blue Jays, not about, ‘Oh, I’m coming to the States.’ It’s about seeing the Blue Jays and trying to forget about all that other stuff.”

Melissa, who didn’t want to provide her last name for safety reasons, made the 4-1/2-hour drive to Cleveland on Thursday morning, leaving at 6:30 a.m. with Jonathan Nava. She wasn’t entirely thrilled about the trip.

“After the whole ‘Lake America’/Lake Ontario thing,” said Melissa. “You kind of get numb to the whole ‘We’re going to charge you tariffs’ and everything like that, but as it just escalates now you just kind of get turned off from wanting to come, but I’m going to love the game. We’ve gone to other stadiums this season and people have been pretty welcoming.”

“You’re never alone,” said Jonathan Nava. “There are so many Jays fans in every stadium you go to when they’re on the road.”

Nava, who has family in Texas and plans to head down there when the Jays visit the Rangers later this month, said he shares Melissa’s trepidation, but finds strength in numbers.

“You’re never alone,” said Nava. “There are so many Jays fans in every stadium you go to when they’re on the road.”

“I’m going to be here no matter what. Until they close the border, that is,” said Jays fan Joshua Glass.

Joshua Glass, travelling with a friend who gracefully exited the conversation when he heard what the topic was going to be, doesn’t share his fellow fans’ hesitance.

“I’m not going to pay attention to the rantings of a petulant child, quite frankly,” said Glass, referring to Trump. “It’s not going to keep me from going to see my team fight for a wild-card spot. I think the whole thing is a bit ridiculous, but it’s not going to prevent me from coming ... I’m going to be here no matter what. Until they close the border, that is.”

Jennifer Espensen, from Hamilton, who came with husband Chad, feels the same way.

“Honestly, we have a bucket list and we’re sticking to our bucket list,” said Espensen. “We were supposed to do the (American) west coast in July and we derailed that (with) everything that was going on then, so we stuck with our plan for September. We weren’t going to let any changes happen because everything keeps changing by the minute.”

Including, at least on this side of the border, the name of a Great Lake.

“Honestly, that’s a joke, that’s a joke,” said Espensen. “We’re all going to call it Lake Ontario for the rest of our life. That will never ever change.”

Toronto’s Jon and Kellie Van Dyk made the snap decision to drive from London, Ont. to Cleveland on Thursday morning for the big game.

Kellie and Jon Van Dyk drove from London, Ont. to see Thursday’s game in Cleveland. Donald Trump “doesn’t define who Americans are,” said Jon.

“There’s a pretty good heat for the wild-card race that’s going on, so that’s pretty fun,” said Kellie. “It’s a driveable distance, we like to travel together. Tickets are cheaper here than in Toronto, and they’re available.”

That last point hits hard. The Blue Jays are averaging 41,055 fans per night, with the overwhelming majority of home games being sold out. The biggest crowd of the three games in Cleveland was Thursday’s 18,186.

There was zero reluctance for the Van Dyks to cross the border given the political climate.

“It’s a sideshow that’s meaningless,” said Jon. “Some of the politics and the economics that’s going on is unfortunate, but Americans are just like Canadians, they’re people. We’ve got a lot of friends that are Americans.

“I don’t dislike Canadians because the prime minister is an idiot. I still like my fellow citizens,” added Jon. “On the same side, Trump is a buffoon, but he doesn’t define who Americans are.”

stories.title: Seth Meyers says Trump’s push to rename Lake Ontario is ‘nothing that anyone can be proud of’
stories.summary: Meyers and his video podcast co-host, Sal Gentile, had no shortage of material lambasting the president over the lake controversy.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
The late-night host called out the U.S. president and his staff over their efforts to rebrand the Great Lake that borders Canada.

“This is some real dork sh—,” Meyers said to supervising writer and producer Sal Gentile on Thursday’s episode of his video podcast “A Closer Look: Proof of Life And/Or Out of Office.”

“They’re just such dorks,” the host continued. “It is a real reminder that they can’t actually accomplish anything. Then … they take to social media (and) they have an army of people that are good at sort of flexing over this news that … Google Maps is calling it ‘Lake America,’ but nobody cares. They are flexing, but nobody cares.”

Meyers and Gentile then played a clip of Trump crossing out Lake Ontario on a map and writing “Lake America” over it with a Sharpie.

Gentile compared the attempted name change to a bodybuilder flexing on Muscle Beach in Santa Monica, Calif., to the indifference of passersby.

“But it’s like a scrawny guy who’s flexing and wrote with Sharpie on his arm, ‘Big Muscle.’” Meyers replied, as both laughed. “Everybody can see it for what it is.”

The show then played a clip of Trump talking about how he previously tried to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” In the clip, the president says, “So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.”

“‘So if you think about it, we have a lake and a gulf,’ as if you have to think about it,” Meyers quipped.

“All right, everybody, this is a real thinker,” Gentile said, mockingly. “We’re going to get the chalkboard out here.”

Meyers also joked that the move changes nothing for Americans who swim in the lake when it comes to Canadian customs.

“I also like that nothing is gained, right? Nobody is like, ‘That’s so great. Every time we’d go swimming in Lake Ontario, we had to bring our passport.’”

He then shared an idea for 2028 Democratic presidential nominee.

“I think the next candidate for president on the Democratic side should just start saying things they’re going to rename,” Meyers said. “Like that they’re going to rename it ‘Trumpa Bay’ for Tampa Bay … like name things after Trump that Trump wouldn’t want named after him.”

Gentile eventually pointed out that the president’s efforts to rename the lake are indicative of a larger point.

“This is a great example of exactly what we’re talking about, which is his helplessness the second he doesn’t get exactly what he wants … he doesn’t think about things even half a step ahead,” Gentile said.

“His first move when he doesn’t get exactly what he wants in this completely unnecessary trade war with a close ally neighbour that’s going to affect the midterm elections that are coming up (and) have major economic and political consequences … his first retaliatory move is, ‘Well, I’m renaming a lake.’”

Meyers agreed and implied that it’s shameful.

“This is nothing that anyone can be proud of,” he said. “No work went into this.”

Last week, ON the same video podcast series, Meyers called Trump’s trade war with Canada “lunacy” and joked that Ontario Premier Doug Ford looked like a dollar store version of the president.

Trump is trying to rename Lake Ontario after getting into a trade-related war of words with Ford, who told the president to kiss his ass before toning down his language and saying he hoped Canada and the U.S. could reach a trade deal.

Google and Apple both changed the name within their map apps to “Lake America” in the U.S., while Mapquest refused to do so on either side of the border.

stories.title: Welcome home, Mustangs and Falcons!
stories.summary: Tips for living, learning, and exploring the cityAs post-secondary students settle in, the Ci
stories.content:
As post-secondary students settle in, the City of London welcomes new and returning students to London for the upcoming school year.

Moving to a new city and starting school at the same time can be challenging, but there are lots of tips and resources to help students feel right at home.

Make the most of your time here! There are plenty of ways to get involved and be a part of the community.

The City of London’s website london.ca is a great tool to learn about services and programs, including information about your City Councillor , your neighbourhood , or even your water bill.

We offer many different recreation and sport opportunities at community centres, pools, and arenas. View our programs and courses online to see what’s being offered this fall and winter. Looking for activities on Labour Day? The City is offering free recreation activities across London on September 7, including recreational swimming, Zumba, badminton, yoga, and pickleball.Enjoy the last few days of summer with us!

Looking to gain work experience? We post several internships and student opportunities throughout the year. All current employment opportunities are available online – check back frequently for updates!

Get Involved is our online engagement platform for residents to participate in City projects and initiatives. Your feedback helps us develop new plans and programs for London.

In between studying and classes, be sure to make time to explore all that London has to offer. Visit Tourism London for a guide to things to do and places to see.

In a band and looking to get into the music scene in London? Or just looking to enjoy some live local music? Check out the London Music Office for events, networking opportunities and programming to help make your mark on London’s music scene.

Do you love nature? London has designated Environmentally Significant Areas , which offer many different trails and paths to help you explore local forests, wetlands, and meadows.

With concerts, pop-up markets, cultural events, food and art festivals, there's something for everyone on Dundas Place. Check out the events calendar and join in on the fun!

Looking to hit your step goal or go for a bike ride?

Our bike and walk map can help you discover more than 350 km of pathways, bike lanes and cycle tracks in London, including London’s primary multi-use recreational trail, the Thames Valley Parkway .

Bike lockers are available downtown where you can securely store and lock your bike. Download the Movatic app to begin to use this bike parking.

If you’re using a personal e-scooter, learn more on our website about where they can be used in London.

If you’re taking public transit:

Review your schedule ahead of time and familiarize yourself with LTC routes and service updates that help us ride safely together.

The Transit app can help you plan your trip, check transit routes and get real-time information. As part of a one-year pilot, London Transit riders can access enhanced features at no additional cost, including more trip-planning options and customizable settings such as personalized walking times.

If you’re driving:

If a school bus is displaying flashing red lights, traffic in both directions must stop. You are also required to stop at pedestrian crossovers where people are crossing the street. London also has red light cameras at a number of intersections to make streets safer.

Bus-only lanes separate buses from mixed traffic to help reduce congestion. Do not drive in these bus-only lanes, and watch for signs, red paint, diamonds and arrows to recognize them.

Slow down, follow road and parking signage, and be mindful of others traveling. Help us keep our roads safe .

Construction is underway on Western Road and Philip Aziz Avenue, including road, watermain, sewer, sidewalk and cycling improvements.

Philip Aziz Avenue is currently closed at Western Road and will remain closed until the end of July 2027. Traffic is reduced through the construction area.

Students are invited to a drop-in session on September 9 from noon to 2 p.m. at the UCC to learn about the project, upcoming work and impacts to travel around campus.

The East London Link is a Rapid Transit project connecting Downtown to Fanshawe College, with new transit lanes, road improvements and upgraded infrastructure along the corridor.

As students return to campus in September, construction and lane restrictions on Oxford Street and Highbury Avenue may affect travel to and from Fanshawe. Plan ahead, allow extra time and follow posted detours and signs.

London Transit service will return to London Lane at the Fanshawe College terminal on September 6, following completion of the remaining work at the location.

Check london.ca/roadconstruction for current road construction and closures that may affect your trip to campus, and to see the City’s top 10 construction projects.

Get settled in London by reviewing this important information for your new home.

Service London is the City’s customer service portal. You can report different issues and book a furniture pick-up online at service.london.ca

To report a missed recycling collection or ask a recycling-related question, please contact Miller Waste . Recycling collection is no longer managed by the City.

Put waste in the right place and find your home’s garbage and Green Bin collection dates if you’re living off-campus this year. The Recycle Coach app can also provide you with a personalized collection schedule and reminders about collection dates.

Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are your landlord’s responsibility to install and maintain. Your responsibility is to flag it if they are not working properly. Take the Saved by the Beep pledge and receive a monthly reminder to check your alarms.

The City’s by-laws are in place to keep your new home safe and make sure you’re protected as a tenant. Review some of these common City of London by-laws that can help you and your new home:

The Property Standards By-law addresses property maintenance, pests such as cockroaches, and access to vital services such as heat, hydro or water.

The Yard and Lot Maintenance By-law helps ensure that refuse is not being hoarded, dumped, or poorly contained on properties.

The Sound By-law addresses noise complaints.

The Municipal Waste & Resource Materials Collection By-law requires owners and occupants to keep the boulevard (the grassy portion between the sidewalk and curb) next to their property free of garbage and recyclables.

The Open Air Burning By-law regulates when, where and how you can have outdoor fires. Following these regulations ensures you do not create a nuisance for neighbours.

Have questions about a particular by-law or looking to register a complaint? Connect with our Enforcement team at 519-661-4660 or by email at enforcement@london.ca .

stories.title: Fanshawe prepares to welcome students back to residence
stories.summary: Media are invited to join Fanshawe as the College prepares to welcome students back to residence
stories.content:
Media are invited to join Fanshawe as the College prepares to welcome students back to residence this weekend in time for the start of the fall semester.

More than 1,600 students will live in one of the College's residence buildings at the London Campus. Just over 1,300 of these students are beginning their first year of post-secondary education.

"For many students, moving into residence is their first big step into college life and, for many of our first-year students, their first time living away from home," says Erica Robertson, general manager of Fanshawe's Residence and Conference Centre. "There’s always a lot of excitement on move-in weekend, along with some nerves for both students and parents. Our goal is to make the experience feel organized, welcoming and supportive from the moment they arrive."

Move-in takes place on Saturday, September 5 and Sunday, September 6. Students will be greeted by a large group of volunteers along with residence staff and residence advisors who will help students get settled in their new home away from home.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.ca

stories.title: Jason Kenney calls for investigation into Alberta separatist party after a mysterious $190,000 surge in donations
stories.summary: Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney urges elections watchdog to investigate a mysterious $190,000 surge flowing into a provincial separatist party.
stories.author: Emma McIntosh
stories.content:
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney is calling on police and the province’s election regulator to investigate the finances of a separatist political party.

Kenney’s comments follow a Star investigation into a mysterious surge in donations into the coffers of the Republican Party of Alberta (RPA), a provincial group that advocates for the province to separate from Canada.

The Star’s analysis found the party received a sudden influx of $190,000 in 2025 despite having reported no donations the year before. The cash came from fewer than 50 people, with more than half of them giving $5,000, the maximum amount allowed under Alberta rules.

The RPA’s donations soon dried up after that initial flood: the party reported just $6,000 in donations in the second half of 2025, and $1,000 in the first quarter of this year.

In an interview with the Star, Kenney said it’s highly unusual for that percentage of donors to give the max amount — especially to a young, populist party, which would typically be fuelled by larger numbers of ordinary people giving smaller amounts of money. Very few people can afford to give thousands of dollars to a political party, he said.

“It just doesn’t add up,” said Kenney, whose call for an investigation was first posted to the social media site X last week. “At the very best, something highly unusual is going on here.”

The RPA and its leader, Cameron Davies, did not answer questions from the Star for this story.

In a statement, Elections Alberta said it cannot publicly comment on what it may or may not be investigating. The agency also pointed to a 2025 change to its governing legislation, which Elections Alberta says raised its threshold for launching a probe. Now, it can only do so if it has “reasonable grounds to believe an offence has occurred.”

“This is a very high threshold, much higher than the threshold imposed on other administrative regulators,” Elections Alberta said. “This is the threshold required by police to arrest someone following an investigation.”

Alberta RCMP spokesperson Fraser Logan said the law enforcement agency can’t comment on whether it has received a complaint or started an investigation. “Further to that, the Alberta RCMP are unable to take these complaints either online or via email,” Logan said. “We encourage anyone with concerns regarding this matter to reach out to their nearest RCMP detachment or their local police.”

The Star also found $18,000 of the donations appear to have been made by four interconnected people based in British Columbia, a violation of Alberta election rules that require donors to legally reside in the province at the time they contribute.

Apollo Chung

One of the four was Apollo Chung, a longtime political operative who has worked for three political parties in B.C., and in 2025 served as executive director of the Alberta Republican Party.

Public records viewed by the Star connected Chung to a Vancouver address. He has not answered questions from the Star, but this week he told the online media outlet PressProgress that he recently lived in Alberta. He did not specify exactly when or how long he lived there.

Most recently, Chung had been director of operations for the B.C. Conservative party, but leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay announced last week that he had been fired. Findlay did not give a reason for the move, but Chung’s departure came after audio recordings were posted online of an unidentified Findlay staffer talking about monetizing their work in politics.

The Star cannot independently verify the authenticity of the audio. Chung told PressProgress that he was speaking in the audio, but that it was “doctored,” presented without context and part of an exaggerated conversation about fundraising. Findlay’s office has not responded to questions from the Star.

In his post, Kenney expressed concern about one of the alleged recordings, pointing out that Chung had also recently held a top role at the RPA. The combination of the alleged audio recording and the unusual fundraising patterns at the RPA raises questions, Kenney said.

“I just, connecting the dots, think that there’s a lot of smoke,” Kenney told the Star. “It all looks to me like something that demands an investigation.”

The RPA’s Davies has previously said that to his knowledge, the party did not accept out-of-province donations.

Kenney was Alberta’s premier from 2019 until he resigned in 2022, under siege from far-right and populist forces within the United Conservative Party he helped create. Over the last year, he has been an outspoken critic of Alberta separatism, which remains a minority opinion on the province as it heads to a referendum on the issue this fall.

The Alberta Republican Party leader previously had an ownership stake in the same polling company that reported support for his new party was surging.

That stance has, at times, appeared to make him a target. Earlier this year, his home address was allegedly revealed to a group of separatist volunteers as part of a massive voter data breach that is now under investigation by Elections Alberta, the RCMP and the province’s privacy commissioner.

The voter data involved in the breach was publicly posted by a separatist group called the Centurion Project, but Elections Alberta said it had originated with the RPA. Neither Davies nor the RPA responded to questions from the Star about the breach.

Kenney, who has repeatedly alleged there are “dodgy” characters in the separatist movement, has history with some of those involved, especially Davies, a longtime conservative political operative in Alberta.

Davies was previously fined by Elections Alberta after the watchdog investigated purported irregularities in the 2017 leadership race that made Kenney the leader of the provincial United Conservative Party. Among them were allegations that senior members of Kenney’s campaign had co-ordinated with another candidate to sling mud at a key rival.

Davies worked on that alleged ‘kamikaze’ campaign, and Elections Alberta later concluded he helped fuel it with illegal donations. The watchdog never accused Kenney of any wrongdoing in the scandal, and Kenney has said he did not know how the ‘kamikaze’ campaign was funded.

Speaking to the Star for this story, Kenney said he attended a meeting with the political operative in 2017 “against my better judgment.”

“I’ve never trusted the guy,” Kenney said.

paragraphs: Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney is calling on police and the province’s election regulator to investigate the finances of a separatist political party.

Kenney’s comments follow a Star investigation into a mysterious surge in donations into the coffers of the Republican Party of Alberta (RPA), a provincial group that advocates for the province to separate from Canada.

The Star’s analysis found the party received a sudden influx of $190,000 in 2025 despite having reported no donations the year before. The cash came from fewer than 50 people, with more than half of them giving $5,000, the maximum amount allowed under Alberta rules.
The RPA’s donations soon dried up after that initial flood: the party reported just $6,000 in donations in the second half of 2025, and $1,000 in the first quarter of this year.

In an interview with the Star, Kenney said it’s highly unusual for that percentage of donors to give the max amount — especially to a young, populist party, which would typically be fuelled by larger numbers of ordinary people giving smaller amounts of money. Very few people can afford to give thousands of dollars to a political party, he said.
“It just doesn’t add up,” said Kenney, whose call for an investigation was first posted to the social media site X last week. “At the very best, something highly unusual is going on here.”
The RPA and its leader, Cameron Davies, did not answer questions from the Star for this story.

In a statement, Elections Alberta said it cannot publicly comment on what it may or may not be investigating. The agency also pointed to a 2025 change to its governing legislation, which Elections Alberta says raised its threshold for launching a probe. Now, it can only do so if it has “reasonable grounds to believe an offence has occurred.”

“This is a very high threshold, much higher than the threshold imposed on other administrative regulators,” Elections Alberta said. “This is the threshold required by police to arrest someone following an investigation.”

Alberta RCMP spokesperson Fraser Logan said the law enforcement agency can’t comment on whether it has received a complaint or started an investigation. “Further to that, the Alberta RCMP are unable to take these complaints either online or via email,” Logan said. “We encourage anyone with concerns regarding this matter to reach out to their nearest RCMP detachment or their local police.”

The Star also found $18,000 of the donations appear to have been made by four interconnected people based in British Columbia, a violation of Alberta election rules that require donors to legally reside in the province at the time they contribute.

stories.title: Welcome Back, Thames Valley!
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

Dear Parents and Caregivers,

We are excited to welcome you back to Thames Valley for the 2026-2027 school year!

My name is Kevin Auckland, and it is both a privilege and an honour to serve you, and every student throughout Thames Valley, in the role of Chief Executive Officer.

In this role, I am motivated by the opportunity to help guide the system forward with clarity, purpose and an unwavering focus on equity, student achievement and well-being. As we begin another exciting school year, my commitment as your CEO is to listen deeply, communicate transparently and lead alongside you, in service of students. I look forward to sharing monthly updates with you throughout this school year.

We have prepared helpful resources below and on our website to support your family during the transition back to school. You will also receive further information from your child’s school before classes begin, to ensure every student has a great first day.

Thames Valley welcomes and values parents and caregivers as partners in your student’s education. I encourage you to explore the many ways you can be involved in your school community this year, and to reach out to the school directly for support.

Whether you are new to Thames Valley or back for another fulfilling year, I wish your family a strong start this September!

Kevin Auckland Chief Executive Officer Thames Valley District School Board

Elementary and Secondary 2026-2027 School Year Calendars are available on our website. Classes begin on Tuesday, September 8. We look forward to welcoming you back!

View the School Year Calendars

Everyone has a role to play in creating positive school and work environments that are safe, caring and inclusive. The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) Code of Conduct ensures that the rights and responsibilities of all members of the school and Thames Valley community are clearly communicated and understood.

Read the TVDSB Code of Conduct

The beginning of a new school year can be both an exciting and challenging time for many students and will impact their well-being in different ways. Thames Valley has resources available for parents and caregivers to support student mental health and well-being.

Family Well-being Community Workshop Series – Watch pre-recorded webinars presented by local community service providers on a wide variety of topics, including school anxieties and back-to-school worries.

"By Your Side" Parent/Caregiver Resources – Check out School Mental Health Ontario's free online resource hub for parents and caregivers, designed to support mental health learning and well-being for every family.

As part of our ongoing commitment to student account security, the TVDSB student password guidelines require students to reset their passwords at least once a year. Beginning September 1, 2026, all students will be prompted to change their password when they log in to board systems.

Students in Kindergarten to Grade 2 will enter their default password first, then the new password with support from the classroom teachers.

Students in Grades 3 to 12, Continuing Education, and Remote Learning programs will enter their current password, then the new password.

To assist families and students, information about the password reset process, password requirements, and student password guidelines will be available through the TVDSB Parent Portal before school resumes. School staff will also be available to assist students with password resets. Students are encouraged to complete their password change as soon as possible after returning to school. Thank you for supporting safe and secure use of digital learning tools at TVDSB.

content_blocks.text: Everyone has a role to play in creating positive school and work environments that are safe, caring and inclusive. The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) Code of Conduct ensures that the rights and responsibilities of all members of the school and Thames Valley community are clearly communicated and understood.
content_blocks.html: Everyone has a role to play in creating positive school and work environments that are safe, caring and inclusive. The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) Code of Conduct ensures that the rights and responsibilities of all members of the school and Thames Valley community are clearly communicated and understood.

content_blocks.text: Read the TVDSB Code of Conduct
content_blocks.html: Read the TVDSB Code of Conduct

content_blocks.text: Mental Health Resources to Support Students
content_blocks.html: Mental Health Resources to Support Students

content_blocks.text: The beginning of a new school year can be both an exciting and challenging time for many students and will impact their well-being in different ways. Thames Valley has resources available for parents and caregivers to support student mental health and well-being.
content_blocks.html: The beginning of a new school year can be both an exciting and challenging time for many students and will impact their well-being in different ways. Thames Valley has resources available for parents and caregivers to support student mental health and well-being.

items.text: Family Well-being Community Workshop Series – Watch pre-recorded webinars presented by local community service providers on a wide variety of topics, including school anxieties and back-to-school worries.
items.html: Family Well-being Community Workshop Series  – Watch pre-recorded webinars presented by local community service providers on a wide variety of topics, including school anxieties and back-to-school worries.

items.text: "By Your Side" Parent/Caregiver Resources – Check out School Mental Health Ontario's free online resource hub for parents and caregivers, designed to support mental health learning and well-being for every family.
items.html: "By Your Side" Parent/Caregiver Resources  – Check out School Mental Health Ontario's free online resource hub for parents and caregivers, designed to support mental health learning and well-being for every family.

content_blocks.text: Student Password Reset
content_blocks.html: Student Password Reset

content_blocks.text: As part of our ongoing commitment to student account security, the TVDSB student password guidelines require students to reset their passwords at least once a year. Beginning September 1, 2026, all students will be prompted to change their password when they log in to board systems.
content_blocks.html: As part of our ongoing commitment to student account security, the TVDSB student password guidelines require students to reset their passwords at least once a year. Beginning September 1, 2026, all students will be prompted to change their password when they log in to board systems.

items.text: Students in Kindergarten to Grade 2 will enter their default password first, then the new password with support from the classroom teachers.
items.html: Students in Kindergarten to Grade 2 will enter their default password first, then the new password with support from the classroom teachers.

items.text: Students in Grades 3 to 12, Continuing Education, and Remote Learning programs will enter their current password, then the new password.
items.html: Students in Grades 3 to 12, Continuing Education, and Remote Learning programs will enter their current password, then the new password.

content_blocks.text: To assist families and students, information about the password reset process, password requirements, and student password guidelines will be available through the TVDSB Parent Portal before school resumes. School staff will also be available to assist students with password resets. Students are encouraged to complete their password change as soon as possible after returning to school. Thank you for supporting safe and secure use of digital learning tools at TVDSB.
content_blocks.html: To assist families and students, information about the password reset process, password requirements, and student password guidelines will be available through the TVDSB Parent Portal before school resumes. School staff will also be available to assist students with password resets. Students are encouraged to complete their password change as soon as possible after returning to school. Thank you for supporting safe and secure use of digital learning tools at TVDSB.

content_blocks.text: We look forward to welcoming you back on Tuesday, September 8!
content_blocks.html: We look forward to welcoming you back on Tuesday, September 8!

stories.title: Conservative MP launches ‘stay’ campaign in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Dane Lloyd, the Conservative MP for the Edmonton-area riding of Parkland, is spearheading the initiative to convince Albertans that the province can do better within Canada.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — With a little more than six weeks before Albertans decide on a question of independence, a new campaign has emerged on the “stay” side targeting the province’s largest voting bloc: Conservatives.

More specifically, the 1.4 million Albertans who cast ballots for Conservative candidates in last year’s federal election.

Dane Lloyd, the party’s MP for the Edmonton-area riding of Parkland, is spearheading the initiative. He says the reason for that focus is “self-evident” in a province historically awash in Conservative blue.

“We are the largest political demographic in Alberta,” he told the Star on Friday. “We have a critical voice that needs to be heard and needs to be engaged.”

Lloyd says the campaign will involve Conservatives from Alberta and beyond, with the focus on getting people engaged ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum through social media, lawn signs, canvassing and phone calls.

It is launching as champions of independence argue that the referendum is less about secession than it is about Alberta’s place within Canada.

“We’re trying to get as many people to understand that Alberta can do better,” said constitutional lawyer and independence advocate Keith Wilson.

Albertans who vote in next month’s referendum will have their choice of two options: “Alberta should remain a province of Canada,” or “The government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

Lloyd was tapped by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre earlier this summer to lead their party’s response to the referendum. He told the Star he has spent the past two months hosting round tables and speaking with Albertans in both the “pro-Canada” and separatist camps.

“What was universal was that every single one of those people viewed themselves as a patriotic Canadian,” Lloyd said.

“What that made clear to me is that this needs to be a campaign that’s focused on reminding people of our love for our country, that it’s fundamental and that, yes, there needs to be change to the status quo,” he said.

“Ottawa does need to change, but that doesn’t mean leaving Canada.”

While Lloyd notes that there are campaigns similar to his, he says they aren’t speaking specifically to Conservative voters.

“It’s a campaign that recognizes that the status quo is not all right. We don’t support the status quo, but fundamentally it’s not a problem with Canada. It’s a problem with Ottawa and that’s where we need to see the change,” he said.

“There’s many campaigns out there talking to many different audiences and our campaign’s focused on reaching that audience — but not just that audience, all Albertans — to try and get them out to vote for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada.”

Wilson, who is among the leaders of the independence group “Let Alberta Decide” and helped write a 214-page report outlining a separatist vision for what an independent Alberta could look like, argues the federalist side has “no plan” to deal with what he and others say are the structural issues that constrain Alberta.

While Wilson says “many” supporters of Alberta independence are also support the federal Conservatives, including those who live in Poilievre’s own deep-blue riding of Battle River—Crowfoot, the issue runs deeper than frustrations over seeing the party shut out of power in Ottawa for more than a decade.

He says past attempts to remedy those grievances — from the rise of the populist Reform Party to the election of Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, who famously declared after his first victory that the “West is in” — have failed.

“Many have come to the conclusion that Canada is structurally broken,” Wilson said.

For whatever frustrations exist, Lloyd argues that change is possible, pointing to past battles Alberta has won and ways the province and Conservatives have “been moving the needle” in Ottawa.

“We’re talking about pipelines again as a country,” he said, “and it’s not a conversation about whether or not to have pipelines — it’s about when and how fast we can get pipelines built.”

stories.title: Former Metrolinx CEO Phil Verster joins federal government’s Alto high-speed rail project
stories.summary: Once-embattled Metrolinx CEO Phil Verster is joining the federal government’s $90 billion Alto high-speed rail project. Read about his new role.
stories.author: Andy Takagi
stories.content:
Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Nick Lachance Toronto Star File Photo[](http://www.thestar.com/news/gta/former-metrolinx-CEO-phil-verster-joins-federal-government-s-alto-high-speed-rail-project/article_19bf830c-b844-4ff1-b40d-50ceb7ffe71e.html)

ByAndy Takagi Transportation Reporter

Phil Verster, the once-embattled CEO of provincial transit agency Metrolinx, is making his return to Canadian transit.

Verster will be joining the federal government’s Alto high-speed rail project as a consultant, the Crown corporation confirmed to the Star.

“His work mainly focuses on helping us better understand GTA intermodal and regional transit dynamics, and how to integrate Alto’s HSR service with the existing local transit network,” said Alto spokesperson Caroline Des Rosiers.

Article continues below

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

“His experience also helps us draw lessons from past transit projects in the region as we advance the planning and development of Alto.”

Alto would not say how much Verster would be paid. In his final year at Metrolinx, he was paid $837,097.

Verster did not respond to the Star’s request for comment.

During his seven years at the helm of Metrolinx, Verster oversaw the construction of the Eglinton Crosstown and Finch West LRTs, both of which missed several opening dates promised by Verster and Metrolinx, and ended up costing billions more than initially budgeted.

Originally appointed to the role under then-premier Kathleen Wynne in 2017, Verster — as previously reported by the Star — maintained a contentious relationship with the private contractors that worked on the Eglinton Crosstown.

Verster left the agency in December 2024 and was replaced by current Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay.

According to his LinkedIn, Verster worked as an executive adviser for the Royal Commission of Riyadh City from January to November of 2025.

stories.title: Leaders of B.C.’s centre-right movements struggling to come together
stories.summary: A void is growing in the province with nine MLAs recently leaving the provincial Conservative party
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Two efforts to build a more centrist alternative to the B.C. Conservatives are emerging from the party’s turmoil, but their leaders are unable to agree on which one should unite voters disillusioned with both the governing NDP and the embattled opposition.

CentreBC Leader Mike Bernier and Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar, who quit the Conservative caucus last month and announced his intention to start a new party, are friends who share many of the same values and much of the same policy agenda. CentreBC was founded in March, 2025, as an option for voters dissatisfied with the Conservatives.

But after several discussions, the two remain at an impasse on forging a united centre-right alternative, raising the prospect of a fractured vote in the future. The next provincial election is scheduled for October, 2028, but could be called much sooner.

“We’re in that weird spot that we’ve got to figure out how to work together, otherwise we’re splitting the vote,” Mr. Bernier said.

Mr. Bernier, a former BC Liberal cabinet minister and MLA for Peace River South, became leader of CentreBC in July, feeling a Conservative party under Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay didn’t represent most British Columbians. CentreBC, founded by former BC United MLA Karin Kirkpatrick in 2025, presents itself as a “socially progressive, fiscally responsible choice.”

Mr. Milobar left the Conservative caucus on Aug. 14, saying his values don’t align with Ms. Findlay’s. Delta South MLA Ian Paton followed suit 10 days later, and the two announced their intention to form a new party with Mr. Milobar as interim leader.

Since Mr. Milobar’s departure, a total of nine sitting MLAs have quit the Conservative caucus, all citing issues with leadership, communication and differences over the party’s direction. The Conservative exodus has fuelled a growing push for a more centrist political option, with defectors and other politicos largely agreeing on the need but not the vehicle.

Ms. Findlay, meanwhile, is doubling down on her leadership, attributing her party’s challenges and disagreements to its rapid growth, while vowing to bring positive change.

The B.C. Conservatives went from having less than 2 per cent of the vote in 2020 to coming within three seats of forming government four years later. Ms. Findlay became the party’s leader in late May.

“I was elected to lead this party, and I intend to lead it with determination, with humility and with the experience to know that strong leaders listen, learn and make changes when changes are needed,” she said in a statement to media on Thursday.

Ms. Findlay has not responded to interview requests from The Globe and Mail.

Mr. Bernier said CentreBC has spent 18 months building the infrastructure of an established party, including its constitution, databases and website. At least 20 candidates have said they want to run for the party, he said.

Lakhwinder Jhaj will be CentreBC’s first candidate in the Sept. 26 Abbotsford-Mission by-election, where Ms. Findlay is vying for a seat. The Conservative leader will face off against Ms. Jhaj, a community advocate and businessperson, and NDP candidate Pam Alexis, a former cabinet minister who represented the riding from 2020 to 2024.

Ms. Jhaj previously ran for the BC Liberals and the NDP, as well as the Liberal Party of Canada.

Mr. Bernier said he made the case to Mr. Milobar that he could build on the organization CentreBC had already put in place.

“I’ve had sit-down meetings with Peter and said, ‘Why would you start up something new and compete against something we’ve already started doing when we should all just be working together on a path to keep that centre, centre-right all in one tent?’ ” he said.

Mr. Bernier added that he has “no ego” in the venture and no attachment to being the one at the helm.

“If we’re able to work together and Peter or somebody else wanted to be the leader of the party, by all means, let’s do that,” he said.

For Mr. Milobar, the question came down to which vehicle could attract enough sitting MLAs to give a new party a foothold in the legislature.

“There just wasn’t traction within the MLAs I was talking to, and others that were contemplating leaving, around CentreBC,” he said. “Some have felt that some of their policy, or where they were headed, is a little left of centre for their liking.”

Having sitting MLAs was important to establish the new party as a viable political force from day one, Mr. Milobar said.

“That revolves around having as many sitting MLAs as possible within a new upstart party so that you can generate the news, you can be recognized inside the legislature and you can get that extra credibility and attention that comes with being an official party with seats inside of the legislature,” he said.

Mr Milobar said he is working with lawyers on the party’s constitution and expects the new organization to be up and running when the legislature’s fall session begins Oct. 5.

Randy Hawes, the former Conservative riding association president for Abbotsford-Mission, is among those trying to get the parties to work together, arguing that anything else is “just handing the NDP the government again.”

Mr. Hawes resigned from his position on Aug. 24 after learning through media reports that MLA Reann Gasper had given up her seat to give Ms. Findlay a chance to run.

“I don’t see this going anywhere unless they unite,” he said. “That’s an absolute must.”
