stories.title: Ottawa issues comprehensive climate report that reflects country’s physical transformation
stories.summary: From retreating glaciers to wildfires and marine heat waves, climate change will likely become even more pronounced, assessment finds
stories.author: Jenn Thornhill Verma, Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Canadians are feeling the effects of climate change to a greater degree and facing more serious consequences than federal scientists projected less than a decade ago.

That’s the message in a comprehensive federal report released on Thursday. It details how climate change is physically transforming the country and how those trends are likely to become more pronounced in the future, from floods, wildfires and heat waves to vanishing glaciers and permafrost.

A striking feature of the report is the high degree of certainty that ties so many diverse effects to fossil-fuel emissions as the primary driver of climate change.

“Warming temperatures have driven wide-ranging, interconnected, and sustained changes across Canada,” the report notes unequivocally in one of its headline statements .

Running nearly 1,500 pages, Canada’s Changing Climate Report 2026 is the country’s definitive statement on the physical state of the climate. Only the second such document ever issued by the federal government, it is the product of more than 100 experts working over a three-year period.

But unlike its predecessor, whose release in 2019 was widely publicized and accompanied by minister-led press conferences and technical briefings to help the public grasp its implications, the second edition was quietly posted online ahead of a late-summer holiday weekend.

The report arrives at a sharply different political moment. In late June, Prime Minister Mark Carney conceded Canada will not meet its 2030 greenhouse-gas emissions targets.

A statement from Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin’s office did not address the report’s findings. It said the government is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 through “a pragmatic and durable approach,” citing clean-energy investments, $2.1-billion committed to the National Adaptation Strategy and a new goal of $13-billion in international climate finance over five years.

The minister was not available for an interview.

Even so, the report requires little interpretation: Much of what was anticipated in 2019 has now come to pass, plus more that was not yet on climate scientists’ radar then.

Canada has warmed about two degrees since 1948 and Northern Canada about 2.6 degrees. Since 1970, the country has warmed nearly twice as fast as the global average, and the Canadian Arctic three times as fast. Precipitation is up 9.7 per cent nationally since 1949, and 18.9 per cent in the North. Human influence, the report finds, is the only explanation for the collective changes observed.

“We have fundamentally altered our climate system, and even if we do succeed at limiting warming to a certain threshold, there are parts of our environment that will continue to change,” said Chris Derksen, director of the Climate Modelling Research Division at Environment and Climate Change Canada.

A hotter and wetter North

Average annual temperature and precipitation increased measurably in Canada from the late 1940s to 2023, with the trend growing more pronounced after 1970. The Arctic has experienced the most rapid change and is now 2.6°C warmer on average than it was less than a century ago, especially in the northwest during winter months. The averages do not capture weather extremes, which have also increased in severity during the same time period.

Change in annual temperature (1948–2023)

Dotted areas indicate statistically insignificant changes

Change in annual precipitation (1949–2023)

The globe and mail, source:

Environment and climate change Canada

Some of the changes are fixed: Sea level rise, glacier melt and permafrost thaw will continue even if temperatures stabilize. Western Canada’s glaciers will largely disappear by the end of this century. Other changes are a choice. Under current global policies, Canada warms five degrees above preindustrial levels by century’s end. Under a scenario with no climate policies, warming reaches 6.9 degrees and the area burned by wildfire climbs 287 per cent. Under net zero, warming stabilizes after 2050 and reaches 3.5 degrees.

Extremes are where warming is already being felt, and the rarer the event, the more it changes: A once-in-50-years heat extreme occurs nearly four times as often at two degrees of global warming. Droughts and flash floods will become more frequent and severe. Fire seasons are already longer.

“Every increment of warming will cost us more in damages,” Dr. Derksen said. “It will cost us more to adapt to those changes.”

And on comparable scenarios, the warming now projected for Canada is greater than the last assessment estimated.

This week, a United Nations Environment Programme report concluded the world will cross 1.5 degrees of warming within the next few years – the tougher of the two limits nearly 200 countries, including Canada, set in Paris a decade ago.

If the 2019 edition made the predictions, then the 2026 report provides the receipts. The inaugural report warned of more intense heat, heavier rain, deeper drought and worsening fire risk. Canada then experienced the 2021 B.C. heat dome, the floods that levelled the province’s highways that November, years of drought on the Prairies and the record 2023 fire season. The current edition puts those risks in plainer language – heat extremes, flooding, drought, fire weather – and adds marine heat waves.

Summer sea surface temperatures have risen everywhere in Canada, but most sharply in Atlantic Canada and Hudson Bay, by as much as 2.5 degrees. Off Nova Scotia, marine heat wave conditions have persisted more than 100 days annually on the Scotian Shelf almost every year since 2012. The ocean is also acidifying and losing oxygen below the surface.

The report is clear that Canadians are stuck with some of these changes, said Sabine Dietz, executive director of CLIMAtlantic, one of five regional climate service providers. However, she said, “every point of a degree that we can bring the temperature back down or we can reduce the increase, we will benefit from it.”

Christina Caron and Glen Hodgson: Not addressing climate change costs the economy more. When will we finally get this?

That Canada can see these changes coming at all is a function of its own capacity. Dr. Derksen said his department runs one of roughly 15 Earth system models in the world.

And while much of what Canadians can expect from the climate over the next 10 to 20 years is largely a given because of past choices, the scenarios diverge more widely when projected further into the future.

“We made a lot of effort to show that end-of-century climate changes are still very much dependent on political decisions that are made now,” said Damon Matthews, a professor and climate scientist at Concordia University in Montreal who was co-lead author on the chapter of the report that deals with future projections.

Similar to the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change physical science volume, the report describes the changes under way and what the models project, but stops short of prescribing what to do about them.

“The big question is, so what? So what do we do with this?” said Alain Bourque, head of Ouranos, the Quebec climate services consortium whose scientists contributed to the assessment.

That question is also the agenda of Adaptation Canada 2026, a national conference in Toronto later this month where the report’s authors will meet practitioners.

For Mr. Bourque, the answer must involve policies that drive toward carbon neutrality. Short of that, the report lays a foundation for those seeking to understand the effects on individuals and communities.

“Canadians and Ontarians must prepare for a hotter future and act now to avoid the worst impacts,” said Ewa Jackson, director of the Ontario Resource Centre for Climate Adaptation.

“Ultimately, warming in Canada will stop only when global emissions reach net zero,” said Sherilee Harper, a professor and Canada Research Chair in climate change and health at the University of Alberta. “Until then, every fraction of a degree we avoid will quite literally save lives.”

stories.title: “It just picked the shed up and put it in the neighbour’s field”: Shocked residents picking up pieces following massive storm
stories.summary: A large shed used to cover the Eedy family’s farm machinery, but now that shed is a rolled up ball of metal and wood.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A large shed used to cover the Eedy family’s farm machinery, but now that shed is a rolled up ball of metal and wood.

“It was a tornado. A tornado came through late yesterday afternoon,” said Sandra Eedy, who lives and farms near Winthrop.

While the Eedy’s themselves walked away unscathed, a mechanic working on their combine in the shed, held onto that combine for dear life, as the storm rolled through Huron and Perth counties, around 5:30 p.m. Wednesday.

“He did come out unscathed, but not without a lot of bad memories. The walls just fell out. But, I assume that’s after the roof came off. So ,that’s the mess. The steel is everywhere. It went right across the county road. How nobody was in the path of that when it was coming through, is amazing, It’s probably best, because there could have been actually more people hurt from it, as it was going through the air,” said Eedy.

A few concessions away, Kevin Murray’s family got hit with a double whammy, damage to their home, and the entire loss of their family’s century old barn.

“The grain bin, it moved from it’s foundation, and our barn next door, it’s down, and a bunch of the neighbors sheds and barns are down, too. It’s pretty bad,” said the Winthrop area farmer.

On Sawmill Road near Winthrop, more than six sheds or barns were flattened by the violent storm. Further east, towards Monkton, a 5 storey high steel grain bin bent in half, by Wednesday’s strong winds.

In Seaforth, the local golf course lost more than 50 trees, and is closed indefinitely. All told, damage stretches from as far west as Bayfield, and as far east as Cambridge. The hardest hit areas of Midwestern Ontario, appear to be concentrated on an area from Seaforth, Egmondville, and Clinton, through Kinburn, Winthrop, Brodhagen, Bornholm, and south of Monkton.

Hydro remains out for thousands of residents in Huron and Perth Counties.

“I was just moving my truck from underneath those trees there, and I put it in the back yard, and then the wind came up, and I couldn’t even see the highway for the rain. Some lady pulled in my laneway because she couldn’t see. And so I sat there till it let up a bit, and my neighbor ran across the road to me and said, your tree fell down on your house. I never even seen it. I never heard it. So, I come out here, and there it is,” said Tony McDonald, cleaning up a tree leaning on his house in Kinburn.

Tornado investigators with the Northern Tornadoes Project are in the region, combing through the damage. With no visible funnel clouds caught on camera, they’re not yet able to say the damage in Huron and Perth Counties is from a tornado, but whatever it was, it left a swath of field and property damage across a vast area.

“Scott, it’s just like it picked it up, picked the shed up, and put it in the neighbor’s field. That’s essentially what happened,” said Eedy.

“The trampoline took out our hydro wire to the house. I have never seen anything like that. We had hail come in ‘91, but nothing like this at all. The fields are flat, the corn’s flat. It’s not nice, at all,” said Murray.

stories.title: Stps launches e-scooter safety and enforcement initiative
stories.summary: St. Thomas Police Service launched an initiative Thursday focused on violations involving e-scooters and e-bikes.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
St. Thomas Police Service launched an initiative Thursday focused on violations involving e-scooters and e-bikes.

According to police the initiative comes after several residents voiced their concerns.

They said it will focus on e-bikes and e-scooters being operated dangerously or contrary to provincial and municipal laws on local roads, side walks, and trails.

“We’re trying to just get ahead of this,” said Matthew Lobsinger with St. Thomas Police Services. “This is equal parts of an education as it is enforcement, and really just making sure that people understand the rules around these things, to keep everyone safe before something bad happens.”

stories.title: Trump had nothing to do with U.S. fighter jets pulling out of Toronto air show: organizers
stories.summary: Organizers said U.S. Air Force demo team won't be at this weekend's Canadian International Air Show in Toronto due to 'scheduling issue.'
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
A “scheduling issue,” not deepening political friction or American barbs at Canada’s military, is to blame for a U.S. Air Force demo team pulling out of the Canadian International Air Show in Toronto this weekend, organizers said.

In a social media post earlier this week, organizers of “North America’s longest running air show” held each year on Toronto’s waterfront announced that the U.S. Air Force’s F-16 Viper Demonstration Team would no longer be participating in this year’s show. “Last-minute schedule changes are a reality of real time Air Show operations, and these decisions remain outside of our control,” the Cias said.

“Our full remaining lineup, including celebrating the 55th Anniversary of the CF Snowbirds, Rcaf CF-18 Hornet and our Wwii Heritage Flight, remains set for an incredible weekend” the post read . “Transparency with our fans is a top priority, and we will always keep you informed of any updates.”

Speculation ran high over whether the abrupt call-off was down to the trade war, U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” or U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s taunts this week that Canada’s navy lacks military firepower. “I mean, we’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada,” Bessent said on Cnbc. “What, are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?”

“It was a scheduling issue,” Cias executive director Lori Duthie told reporters at the air show’s media day. “We work very closely, our Canadian Forces and the United States Air Force across North America.”

In a statement to the Sun, a spokesperson for the F-16 Viper Demonstration team also blamed a double booking.

U.S. Treasury secretary taunts Canadian navy's lack of firepower: 'Two submarines from the Edmonton mall'

Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America

The team “sincerely regrets to announce that, due to a scheduling conflict, they are unable to participate in this weekend’s Canadian International Air Show,” Staff-Sgt. Steven Cardo said.

The U.S. Air Force demo team is scheduled to perform at an air show in Batavia, New York Sept. 5 and 6. The Toronto air show takes place Sept. 5 to 7 during the final weekend of the CNE (Canadian National Exhibition).

“Decisions to withdraw from the scheduled appearances are never made lightly,” Cardo said. “We understand the anticipation surrounding this event and extend our deepest apologies to the air show organizers, our Canadian partners, and the aviation fans who looked forward to our performance.”

stories.title: Venice Lagoon provides living laboratory for Western researchers studying climate change
stories.summary: Alina Shchepetkina and her students studied tiny organisms that leave behind traces of their lives, providing a record of how a changing environment is affecting the ecosystem.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Venice really is sinking. Sort of.

The home of gondolas, bridges and canals is built across a collection of islands, and the sediments beneath them are gradually compacting, causing the ground to subside. But while the land moves down, climate change is pushing the water up – making the shallow lagoon surrounding the Italian city an increasingly vulnerable environment.

To understand what that change means for the lagoon, a team of Western researchers led by Earth sciences professor Alina Shchepetkina dug into the mud this summer, studying the murky waters surrounding the historic city.

Shchepetkina, along with graduate students Martina Duarte and Tess Gates-Flaherty, studied tiny organisms that burrow, feed and move through the sediment, leaving behind traces of their lives and providing a record of how a changing environment is affecting the ecosystem.

These clues also help scientists understand how similar changes played out in Earth’s not-so-distant past.

“These tiny organisms are very sensitive to their environment, so changes in their behaviour can give us clues about changes in the ecosystem,” said Duarte, a geology master’s student. “By analyzing sediment cores layer by layer, we can look back roughly 70 years and see how those changes are recorded in the traces they leave behind.”

During 12 weeks in Italy, the research team collected and analyzed sediment cores, working layer by layer with University of Padua professor Massimiliano Ghinassi and the scientists, technicians and students in his lab to reconstruct how the lagoon’s environment and its organisms have changed over the past several decades. This work was supported by a Mitacs Globalink Research Award.

The field study is a continuation of research that began last year in Canada, when Shchepetkina and Gates-Flaherty studied sediments and burrowing organisms in the Bay of Fundy on the east coast, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The two locations could hardly be more different.

The Bay of Fundy is one of the world’s great tidal environments, with a difference of as much as 16 metres between high and low tide in some areas. The Venice Lagoon is microtidal, with a tidal difference closer to one metre. But that contrast is exactly what makes the two places useful for this research.

“The Venice Lagoon is much warmer, with finer, muddier sediment and more extensive marshes, while the Bay of Fundy has stronger waves, much more sediment movement and a wider range of sediment, from mud to pebbles and gravel,” said Gates-Flaherty, a geology master’s student. “We found some similar organisms in both places, but also clear differences in the species and the traces they leave behind.”

The Venice Lagoon is particularly vulnerable to climate-driven environmental change. It is shallow, connected to the sea and heavily influenced by human activity. Rising sea levels are putting additional pressure on an ecosystem already altered by centuries of development and more recent industrial activity.

The result is a landscape where the city appears to be moving down as the water moves up.

stories.title: Calgary mayor claims confidential budget docs show ‘wishlist’ as whistleblower revealed
stories.summary: 'This is a wishlist. Everybody comes out of the woodwork around budget time and asks for all of the stuff,' Mayor Jeromy Farkas told reporters Thursday.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Any spending requests for city council to consider are simply part of a “wishlist,” according to Calgary’s mayor, as fallout continues at city hall over the leak of preliminary budget documents.

It comes after Global News obtained the confidential documents , which indicated revenue from property taxes would need to increase by 20.2 per cent next year alone to fund an additional $510 million in operating spending required to cover every single spending request from across city departments and partners.

According to the documents, which were presented to council during a closed session on July 28, property taxes would also need to increase by 8.5 per cent in 2028, nine per cent in 2029 and 8.9 per cent increase in 2030, if all the spending requests got council approval this fall.

However, city council directed administration to narrow the scope of those requests within a 15 per cent property tax increase next year, followed by a 12.5 per cent increase in 2028, a nine per cent jump in 2029 and a six per cent increase in 2030.

Those updated figures will be presented to council during a closed session on Sept. 22, Global News has learned.

“At this time, city council hasn’t adopted any tax increase, we haven’t even adopted a proposed tax increase,” Mayor Jeromy Farkas told reporters Thursday.

“We’re still pencils to paper to really make sure we’re focusing on the needs over the wants.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We're still pencils to paper to really make sure we're focusing on the needs over the wants."

According to Farkas, the slew of spending requests up for council consideration do not represent what the final number taxpayers could face when the budget is finalized in November; he noted his objectives are to prioritize infrastructure and public safety.

“This is a wishlist. Everybody comes out of the woodwork around budget time and asks for all of the stuff,” Farkas said.

“If you were to add and tally all the requests… it comes out to a real big number.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "If you were to add and tally all the requests… it comes out to a real big number."

However, the documents show many of the funding requests to be debated during budget talks in November have already been in front of and endorsed by city council throughout the year.

Those figures for 2027 include:

$44.3 million to help secure sustainable funding for infrastructure maintenance

$16.9 million to increase the number of Transit Peace Officers on the transit system

$20 million to improve transit service frequency as part of RouteAhead

$27.5 million to fund the low-income transit pass, $28 million to fill the gap in fine revenue from photo radar rule changes

$25.1 million for the city’s Safer Together plan

“That’s not a wishlist — that’s a council that has trouble saying no,” said Ward 14 Coun. Landon Johnston. “I’m not okay with that. I don’t think taxpayers should be okay with the mayor (being) unable to make difficult decisions.”

Typically, the budget documents and discussions remain behind closed doors until the spending plan is finalized and released in early November for public feedback, ahead of deliberations later that month.

Johnston argued releasing the “unconstrained” insight into the budget process would be in the public interest, and that “deep” spending cuts would be required.

“I’m hardly the first person to release confidential information, I was just the first person not to be a coward about it,” he told reporters.

“This gives us a reason to come back and attack the priorities Calgarians want.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This gives us a reason to come back and attack the priorities Calgarians want."

Farkas accused Johnston of “click baiting, rage farming, and trying to provoke a reaction.”

Farkas defended the confidential nature of the discussions to date, and added he is concerned about the legal risk for the city if third-party information is released.

Ward 3 Coun. Andrew Yule told reporters he was disappointed the information was released, but isn’t confident there will be any repercussions, as the council code of conduct was eliminated by the provincial government last year.

“Every leak is inappropriate and every leak should be investigated, but without a framework to do that, we’re just left hanging,” Yule said.

“Whether people think this is a big deal or a nothingburger — it is a breach of trust of this council and our oath of office.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Whether people think this is a big deal or a nothingburger — it is a breach of trust of this council and our oath of office."

Calgary city council will deliberate the next four-year budget on Nov. 23 after the proposed spending plan is released publicly in early November.

Global News reached out to the Ministry of Municipal Affairs for comment but did not receive a response before publishing.

stories.title: Polar bear, beluga conservation, education in Churchill, Man.
stories.summary: Churchill, Man. is home to thousands of beluga whales this time of year, and soon hundreds of polar bears will also gather around the community.
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
The pristine, subarctic wilderness of Churchill, Man. is home to thousands of beluga whales this time of year, and soon hundreds of polar bears will also gather around the community, waiting for the sea ice to form.

“It’s really incredible, we get this big migration, thousands of beluga whales migrate here and they spend the summer in the estuary,” said Kieran McIver, the manager of Churchill field operations for Polar Bears International.

The non-profit organization just wrapped up its ‘beluga boat’ season, which launched on July 15 to coincide with Arctic Sea Ice Day. Throughout the summer and until the end of August, the beluga boat heads out on the water daily, capturing and livestreaming underwater images of the beluga whales in the Churchill River estuary and along the shores of the Hudson Bay.

McIver says the beluga whales are curious of the boat and cameras and often follow them, something that is relatively unique to the belugas in the Churchill-area, he says.

“They seem to just be really curious,” he said.

“Something that kind of makes them unique as well is their cervical spine is not fused vertebrae, so that gives them the ability to move their heads and necks around. So when they are coming and approaching the paddle boarders or kayakers or us on the beluga boat, you can see them physically looking up at you – so it’s a pretty neat experience.”

Polar Bears International is the only non-profit organization in the world dedicated solely to polar bear conservation through research and education.

“Our goal is to keep polar bears in the Arctic for a long time and to do that we need to understand the species,” Polar Bears International director of science Alysa McCall told Global News.

The organization does a variety of research on the bears, aiming to better understand their physiology, genetics, behaviour, and the coexistence between humans and bears.

“We want to keep polar bears around for a long time, and we also know more polar bears are spending a longer time on-land, especially in Canada, so we have this obligation to support the people that now have to increasingly live with this very large predator,” McCall said.

Polar Bears International also supports tracking research in conjunction with Environment & Climate Change Canada and the University of Alberta. Each year, tracking collars are put on about ten female bears in the Churchill area.

McCall said that research is useful in understanding the bear’s patterns as they deal with their biggest threat; sea ice loss caused by climate change.

“I like to call them blubber-hunting ice bears,” McCall said. “They’re really out there to hunt seals, eat blubber, they’re mainly focused on fat, they’re on the ice – but within that, there is so much individual variation of where the females move – It might depend on their age, what their mom taught them, but the patterns we see our really cool.”

stories.title: Man who fatally stabbed dad of toddler on Vancouver Starbucks patio guilty of manslaughter
stories.summary: Inderdeep Singh Gosal had been charged with second-degree murder but was found guilty of the lesser charge of manslaughter.
stories.author: Susan Lazaruk
stories.content:
A man who stabbed the father of a toddler after a fight on a busy Vancouver Starbucks patio has been found guilty of manslaughter.

But Justice Kathleen Ker found him guilty instead of the lesser charge of manslaughter.

Second-degree murder carries with it an automatic life sentence with no chance of parole for at least 10 years. With manslaughter, there is no mandatory minimum except for gun crimes.

Gosal, who remains in custody since his arrest, will be sentenced at a later date. He returns to court later this month to set a date for sentencing.

The stabbing at the café on Georgia and Granville streets followed a complaint by Schmidt that Gosal had been smoking near his toddler. That led to a short fight before Schmidt was stabbed six times within metres of many onlookers.

The prosecutor said the evidence, especially the 24 seconds of the security footage of the stabbing and events leading up to it, support conviction on the second-degree murder charge.

Gosal’s lawyer argued for manslaughter because he was in an “unmedicated medical state,” due to a failure to take his antipsychotic medicine, and because he suffered from fear and paranoia.

Gosal also testified that Schmidt attacked him first, and that he was defending himself because he thought Schmidt was going to kill him.

'I stabbed him': Vancouver Starbucks killing accused tells court he was afraid for his life

Father stabbed to death outside Vancouver Starbucks after asking man to not vape near his toddler

But prosecutor Karin Blok said the evidence shows Gosal attacking Schmidt first, physically and verbally. Blok recounted several inconsistencies in his testimony and statements to police.

The stabbing took place on a Sunday at around 5:30 p.m. and its aftermath was captured by onlookers on cellphone cameras. Several versions had been posted to the web that day, despite pleas by family and police to remove the graphic videos.

Schmidt was at the coffee shop with his daughter and fiancée and he handed the toddler to her before the fight.

Bryan Tepper, the B.C. Conservative opposition critic for the solicitor general, said the manslaughter conviction did not fit the crime.

“It’s ludicrous that a judge could find that someone who violently stabbed a father outside a coffee shop didn’t understand that death could follow,” Tepper said.

“This is about more than one terrible incident. British Columbians are watching public disorder become normalized while violent crime continues to threaten ordinary families. People should not have to wonder whether asking someone to follow the rules could put their lives at risk.”

stories.title: Parts of 1986 report on Nazis in Canada must be made public, court rules
stories.summary: The decision follows years of attempts to obtain an uncensored version of the study, Nazi War Criminals in Canada.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
A 618-page report from 1986 examining the postwar arrival in Canada of those alleged of Nazi war crimes still hasn’t been fully declassified, but certain segments must now be made public, according to a recent Federal Court ruling.

In a 21-page ruling issued Tuesday, Justice Simon Fothergill said the public interest in preserving the historical record, the many decades that have passed and the weakness of the government’s reasons for continued secrecy all weighed in favour of increased disclosure of historian Alti Rodal’s report.

“We deserve the opportunity to learn from our past and to come to terms with the shortcomings of Canada,” Richard Robertson, B’nai Brith Canada’s Director of Research and Advocacy said.

The decision follows years of attempts to obtain an uncensored version of the study, Nazi War Criminals in Canada: The Historical and Policy Setting from the 1940s to the Present, commonly called the Rodal Report.

Prepared for the Commission of Inquiry on War Criminals in Canada — the Deschênes Commission — the report examined the circumstances under which alleged Nazi war criminals and collaborators came to Canada after the Second World War. Although substantial parts of the previously unpublished study have become public, significant passages remained concealed.

Rodal concluded that weak screening procedures enabled some perpetrators of Nazi crimes to enter Canada.

Robertson told the National Post that it was his organization’s advocacy that pushed the case, as it was in February 2024, when Library and Archives Canada released new segments in response to an access-to-information request from B’nai Brith. The release revealed numerous passages that had previously been censored, but redactions remained on seven pages in one section and in RCMP file references contained in 14 endnotes.

The contents of newly declassified materials are as yet unknown, he said.

The still-withheld section concerned Canadian officials’ 1954 discovery of a covert U.S. intelligence initiative that allegedly helped Nazis and Nazi collaborators settle in Canada while bypassing normal security procedures.

Library and Archives Canada argued that the withheld text was protected by section 15(1)(a) of the Access to Information Act, which permits the government to refuse disclosure where release could harm Canada’s international relations. It also relied on section 13 for one passage: a U.S. official’s assessment of American immigration law that Canada had allegedly received in confidence from the United States.

The agency also withheld RCMP file numbers under section 15(1)(d)(ii), which covers intelligence information whose release could undermine efforts to detect, prevent, or suppress subversive or hostile activity.

Justice Fothergill dismissed all but one of Library and Archives Canada’s exemption arguments. He found that the institution had not established that releasing information of clear historical importance would, today, damage Canada’s international relations or national security.

Greater public knowledge of the country’s past, he added, promotes informed discussion and reinforces democratic life.

The judge allowed the continued withholding of the quoted U.S. official’s remarks under section 13, because the material had been received from a foreign government in confidence. Still, he described the contents as apparently “innocuous” and said Canada should continue seeking U.S. permission to disclose them.

“Frankly, I think the opening of the report, if that actually happens any time soon, is a non-event. There’s likely nothing in the report that’s not already known, or at least suspected by the Jewish community. I think the bigger story is how hard over the years the Canadian government has fought the Jewish community on every level regarding this issue. The non-release of this report until now is just a symptom of that,” said Steven Rambam, founder and CEO of Pallorium, Inc., a Brooklyn-based licensed investigative agency.

In the mid-1990s, Rambam and his associates compiled a list of 2,000 possible Nazi war criminals living in Canada, and winnowed them down to 200 of the worst to investigate. He located 170 suspected Nazi war criminals and collaborators living in Canada, and interviewed about 70 of them undercover.

“I can personally attest to the fact that all the war criminals were known decades ago. The Canadian government could have done much, much more,” he told the Post. “There’s no war criminal that entered Canada that wasn’t known to the RCMP. That I feel confident in saying.”

The federal government has 30 days to appeal the Sept. 1 ruling, and Robertson said that “it’s a real possibility” that they could do so, to delay even further.

“What will the unsealing of the few remaining portions of this report, if it happens, actually reveal to Canadians or to the Jewish community in particular? Nothing that hasn’t already been known for decades,” Rambam said. Complete accountability, in Robertson’s view, would look like “full disclosure of Canada’s Nazi past, the full release of the Rodal Report, the full release of the Deschenes Commission Part 2, and turning this into part of Canadian education, so that Canadians can learn from the mistakes of our past and can understand them and come to grips with them.”

He added: “Rather than try to sweep that history under the rug and to fight about whether or not that history should be disclosed to the public, our government should be exercising its ability in acting with moral fortitude, and leadership.”

The issue of Canada’s allowing in of suspected former Nazis returned sharply to public attention in September 2023, when MPs in parliament gave a standing ovation to Yaroslav Hunka, who had served in the Waffen-SS Galicia Division. The controversy prompted renewed scrutiny of Canada’s immigration, vetting, and historical-record practices concerning alleged Nazi war criminals and collaborators.

paragraphs: A 618-page report from 1986 examining the postwar arrival in Canada of those alleged of Nazi war crimes still hasn’t been fully declassified, but certain segments must now be made public, according to a recent Federal Court ruling.

In a 21-page ruling issued Tuesday, Justice Simon Fothergill said the public interest in preserving the historical record, the many decades that have passed and the weakness of the government’s reasons for continued secrecy all weighed in favour of increased disclosure of historian Alti Rodal’s report.
“We deserve the opportunity to learn from our past and to come to terms with the shortcomings of Canada,” Richard Robertson, B’nai Brith Canada’s Director of Research and Advocacy said.

The decision follows years of attempts to obtain an uncensored version of the study, Nazi War Criminals in Canada: The Historical and Policy Setting from the 1940s to the Present, commonly called the Rodal Report.

Prepared for the Commission of Inquiry on War Criminals in Canada — the Deschênes Commission — the report examined the circumstances under which alleged Nazi war criminals and collaborators came to Canada after the Second World War. Although substantial parts of the previously unpublished study have become public, significant passages remained concealed.
Rodal concluded that weak screening procedures enabled some perpetrators of Nazi crimes to enter Canada.

Robertson told the National Post that it was his organization’s advocacy that pushed the case, as it was in February 2024, when Library and Archives Canada released new segments in response to an access-to-information request from B’nai Brith. The release revealed numerous passages that had previously been censored, but redactions remained on seven pages in one section and in RCMP file references contained in 14 endnotes.
The contents of newly declassified materials are as yet unknown, he said.

The still-withheld section concerned Canadian officials’ 1954 discovery of a covert U.S. intelligence initiative that allegedly helped Nazis and Nazi collaborators settle in Canada while bypassing normal security procedures.

Library and Archives Canada argued that the withheld text was protected by section 15(1)(a) of the Access to Information Act, which permits the government to refuse disclosure where release could harm Canada’s international relations. It also relied on section 13 for one passage: a U.S. official’s assessment of American immigration law that Canada had allegedly received in confidence from the United States.

The agency also withheld RCMP file numbers under section 15(1)(d)(ii), which covers intelligence information whose release could undermine efforts to detect, prevent, or suppress subversive or hostile activity.

Justice Fothergill dismissed all but one of Library and Archives Canada’s exemption arguments. He found that the institution had not established that releasing information of clear historical importance would, today, damage Canada’s international relations or national security.
Greater public knowledge of the country’s past, he added, promotes informed discussion and reinforces democratic life.

The judge allowed the continued withholding of the quoted U.S. official’s remarks under section 13, because the material had been received from a foreign government in confidence. Still, he described the contents as apparently “innocuous” and said Canada should continue seeking U.S. permission to disclose them.

“Frankly, I think the opening of the report, if that actually happens any time soon, is a non-event. There’s likely nothing in the report that’s not already known, or at least suspected by the Jewish community. I think the bigger story is how hard over the years the Canadian government has fought the Jewish community on every level regarding this issue. The non-release of this report until now is just a symptom of that,” said Steven Rambam, founder and CEO of Pallorium, Inc., a Brooklyn-based licensed investigative agency.

In the mid-1990s, Rambam and his associates compiled a list of 2,000 possible Nazi war criminals living in Canada, and winnowed them down to 200 of the worst to investigate. He located 170 suspected Nazi war criminals and collaborators living in Canada, and interviewed about 70 of them undercover.

“I can personally attest to the fact that all the war criminals were known decades ago. The Canadian government could have done much, much more,” he told the Post. “There’s no war criminal that entered Canada that wasn’t known to the RCMP. That I feel confident in saying.”
The federal government has 30 days to appeal the Sept. 1 ruling, and Robertson said that “it’s a real possibility” that they could do so, to delay even further.

“What will the unsealing of the few remaining portions of this report, if it happens, actually reveal to Canadians or to the Jewish community in particular? Nothing that hasn’t already been known for decades,” Rambam said. Complete accountability, in Robertson’s view, would look like “full disclosure of Canada’s Nazi past, the full release of the Rodal Report, the full release of the Deschenes Commission Part 2, and turning this into part of Canadian education, so that Canadians can learn from the mistakes of our past and can understand them and come to grips with them.”

He added: “Rather than try to sweep that history under the rug and to fight about whether or not that history should be disclosed to the public, our government should be exercising its ability in acting with moral fortitude, and leadership.”

The issue of Canada’s allowing in of suspected former Nazis returned sharply to public attention in September 2023, when MPs in parliament gave a standing ovation to Yaroslav Hunka, who had served in the Waffen-SS Galicia Division. The controversy prompted renewed scrutiny of Canada’s immigration, vetting, and historical-record practices concerning alleged Nazi war criminals and collaborators.

stories.title: Beacon of history returns: St. Thomas locomotive light finds new home
stories.summary: A significant piece of St. Thomas’ rich railway heritage, long thought lost, has returned to the city shedding new light on its industrial past. A historic headlight, once belonging to one of two locomotives actually assembled in St. Thomas, is now on display at the Caso Station, a testament to the city’s former prominence as a railway manufacturing hub.
stories.content:
A significant piece of St. Thomas’ rich railway heritage, long thought lost, has returned to the city shedding new light on its industrial past. A historic headlight, once belonging to one of two locomotives actually assembled in St. Thomas, is now on display at the Caso Station, a testament to the city’s former prominence as a railway manufacturing hub.

The artifact’s journey home was orchestrated by longtime city historian Steve Peters, who recently brought the recovered headlight back to St. Thomas after a lengthy acquisition process.

These locomotives, numbered 1290 and 1291, were completed in July and October of 1900, respectively, at the Michigan Central shops located on land south of the M.C.R. mainline.

Manufactured as 4-6-0 configuration engines, each tipped the scales at a massive 45 tons and cost approximately $18,537.82. Engine #1290, specifically, weighed 146,700 pounds with 112,900 pounds on its wheels, boasting a wheelbase of 24 feet 7 inches and an overall length of 61 feet 6 inches.

These behemoths had a substantial capacity, holding 6,000 gallons of water and 12 tons of coal. Their construction, overseen by Divisional Master Mechanic Mr. Michael Flynn, would have provided steady employment for railway workers at the St. Thomas shops, where building a locomotive from scratch typically took about two years.

Originally, Engine 1290 bore the number #449 and was used for passenger service. Both locomotives later served on “way freight trains” along local branches of the Michigan Central and New York Central lines, including the St. Clair and Fort Erie/Niagara Falls branches, serving the rail line between St. Thomas and Courtright (near Sarnia) from their assembly until their final runs.

Locomotive 1291 concluded its service on Jan. 15, 1957, followed by Locomotive 1290 on April 27, 1957, after nearly 60 years of operation.

However, the city leadership at the time declined the offer, and the locomotive was sent to the scrap yard, with an estimated scrap value of $4,928.57.

Despite the fate of the locomotives themselves, the headlight from one of them survived. It was given to a railway brakeman and eventually served as a beacon on his dock. Learning of its availability, Steve Peters set his sights on bringing this piece of history back to its origins.

“A lot of back and forth,” Peters recounted, describing the headlight’s journey from Peterborough to Grand Bend, and finally, home to St. Thomas about three weeks ago. “The whole intent was to make sure that it was repatriated and became part of the local collection.”

The recovered headlight has now found its permanent home on the second floor of the historic Caso Station, the very building that now houses the North America Railway Hall of Fame. The Caso Station, completed in 1873, was instrumental in connecting St. Thomas to a continent-wide rail system, fostering growth and prosperity.

Fully restored, it serves as a popular venue for events and houses various business offices, while also offering visitors a glimpse into the past through its exhibits.

The North America Railway Hall of Fame was established to promote and raise awareness of significant figures, equipment, and historical pieces within the railway industry across the continent.

The headlight will soon be placed in the hands of an electrician to ensure it is safe and in good working order. A suitable light bulb will be installed, along with a dimmer switch, allowing the artifact to be illuminated and appreciated without overwhelming the display space.

Cole stated that this artifact will be one of the most prominent pieces in the museum, celebrating a unique chapter in St. Thomas’ industrial legacy.

Visitors can explore the Caso Station and learn more about local railway history, including Hall of Fame inductees, during self-guided tours Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

stories.title: Beleaguered Rogers Stadium suffers Toronto storm damage
stories.summary: Photos of the open-air Downsview Park stadium show blue bleachers strewn across partially collapsed grandstands.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The beleaguered Rogers Stadium suffered “significant” damage after a powerful storm swept through Toronto on Wednesday evening.

Photos of the open-air Downsview Park stadium show blue bleachers strewn across partially collapsed grandstands.

The sign outside the open-air venue also looked to be damaged, partially stripped of its red cover.

Live Nation Canada, which operates the stadium, said the venue sustained “significant damage” but no one was hurt. It did not immediately provide details about the extent of the damage.

It’s the latest setback for a stadium beset by issues since it opened last summer.

Live Nation said it would make adjustments after concertgoers initially complained the 50,000-person venue seemed ill-prepared to handle crowds and local officials raised noise complaints.

The venue last hosted a show on Aug. 23 for K-pop superstars BTS and is next scheduled to welcome AC/DC on Sept. 16.

Wednesday’s storm walloped Toronto with strong winds and dumped more than 100 millimetres of rain on some hard-hit neighbourhoods, prompting widespread power outages and flooding.

stories.title: Everything we know about Carney’s investment summit
stories.summary: The high-profile nature of the event has many on Bay Street keeping close tabs on its agenda
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
In April, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the federal government would host a summit for global business executives and leaders to attract more foreign direct investment to Canada.

The high-profile nature of the event has many on Bay Street keeping close tabs on its agenda. Here’s everything we know so far about the 2026 Canada Investment Summit.

The summit will take place between Sept. 14 and 15 at a luxury hotel in downtown Toronto.

The government said it was deliberately scheduled while the Toronto International Film Festival, another event that draws a global crowd, is taking place.

Ottawa promised in its most recent federal budget to spur more than $1-trillion in total investment from public, private and institutional partners over five years.

The summit is part of the Carney government’s plan to promote the country’s resources and major projects , with a focus on showcasing Canada’s energy, critical minerals, defence sector and advanced technologies. It is being co-organized by the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

The government, along with Canadian executives, plan to emphasize the country’s stability – even in the midst of a trade war – and frame investing in Canada as an option to reduce risk in portfolios that are heavily tilted toward the U.S., Europe and Asia.

The Prime Minister has invited Canada’s top CEOs from targeted sectors to meet with financiers and business heavyweights from around the world, who collectively oversee nearly $120-trillion in assets.

The guest list includes 26 of Canada’s largest investors, including 11 major pension funds, as well as more than 45 of the country’s most prominent corporations.

So far, The Globe has confirmed the following people and organizations will be attending:

Stephen Harper, former prime minister and current chair of AIMCo

Deborah Orida, CEO of PSP Investments

Nicolle Butcher, CEO of Ontario Power Generation

Rich Kruger, CEO of Suncor Energy

François Poirier, CEO of TC Energy

John Graham, CEO of CPP Investments

Tim Gitzel, CEO of Cameco

Jonathan Price, CEO of Teck Resources

Aidan Gomez, CEO of Cohere

Christian Weedbrook, CEO of Xanadu

Matthew Bromberg, CEO of CAE

Daniel Goldberg, CEO of Telesat

Linda Hasenfratz, executive chair of Linamar

Éric Martel, CEO of Bombardier

International :

Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock

Jon Gray, president of Blackstone

Dilhan Pillay, CEO of Temasek

Annette Mosman, manager of Amsterdam-based APG

Berkshire Hathaway

KKR & Co.

Mubadala Investment Co.

Norges Bank Investment Management

Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.

Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund

Hong Kong Monetary Authority

IFM Investors

Macquarie Group

The high-profile nature of the event has many on Bay Street keeping close tabs on its agenda. Here’s everything we know so far about the 2026 Canada Investment Summit.
The summit will take place between Sept. 14 and 15 at a luxury hotel in downtown Toronto.
The government said it was deliberately scheduled while the Toronto International Film Festival, another event that draws a global crowd, is taking place.
Ottawa promised in its most recent federal budget to spur more than $1-trillion in total investment from public, private and institutional partners over five years.

stories.title: NDP MP Dick Proctor overheard an inflight conversation that sparked a national scandal
stories.summary: In addition to his time as a member of Parliament, he worked as a journalist for The Globe and Mail, a union organizer and an aide to such NDP luminaries as Ed Broadbent, Jack Layton and Stephen Lewis
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
A chatty traveller bending the ear of his seatmate on a flight caught the attention of a man sitting across the aisle.

The prolix passenger was Andy Scott, the federal solicitor-general, who maintained an apparently voluble conversation with his seatmate about matters of public interest.

The nearby eavesdropper was former reporter Dick Proctor, an NDP member of Parliament, who furiously scribbled verbatim notes from a conversation he could scarcely believe.

He would use the notes to challenge the minister during Question Period, accusing him of having prejudged the outcome of an inquiry into security at an Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Vancouver in 1997. Mr. Scott categorically denied having done so. Furious Liberals decried the ethics of sharing the contents of an overheard conversation. Mr. Scott, who at first denied being able to remember even the gender of his seatmate on the flight, questioned Mr. Proctor’s veracity.

In the end, Mr. Proctor, who has died at 85, was vindicated when the resulting furor led to Mr. Scott’s resignation from cabinet eight weeks after the flight.

What happened on Air Canada Flight 8876 from Ottawa to Fredericton on Oct. 1, 1998, would be settled when the seatmate, Frederick Toole, a well-regarded New Brunswick lawyer, swore an affidavit for the RCMP’s Public Complaints Commission into Apec security.

As it turned out, Mr. Toole was a fellow Liberal and an acquaintance of about 15 years when they were seated together on the flight. He had told the solicitor-general he had seen disturbing images during an Apec protest of an older RCMP officer, who turned out to be RCMP Staff-Sergeant Hugh Stewart, using pepper spray on peaceful protestors.

“To this, Mr. Scott said, ‘Oh, Hughie,’ or ‘Oh, you mean Hughie,’ and commented to the effect that ‘Hughie’ might have to take ‘a,’ or ‘the,’ ‘hit’ or ‘fall’ for that,” Mr. Toole stated in his affidavit.

Mr. Proctor also overheard the two men discuss the RCMP’s investigation of the sale of Airbus airplanes to Air Canada in 1988. He said he overheard Mr. Scott describe former Newfoundland premier Frank Moores as being “crooked as a snake.”

Both Mr. Scott and prime minister Jean Chrétien accused Mr. Proctor of fabricating the story.

Outside the House, Mr. Proctor declared Mr. Scott to be a liar, goading him into launching a defamation suit so the matter could be settled under oath.

Meanwhile, various privacy and government experts weighed in, most saying it was unacceptable for a minister to be so indiscreet as to be overheard in the first place.

When he resigned, Mr. Scott told a news conference that his inflight conversation “made me vulnerable to accusations that I had prejudged the outcome” of the inquiry. He also insisted he could not remember his seatmate though “it May seem hard to believe.” Mr. Scott was reappointed to cabinet six years later in a different portfolio by prime minister Paul Martin.

Mr. Proctor had a long career as a journalist, union organizer and strategist and aide to such NDP luminaries as federal leaders Ed Broadbent and Jack Layton, Saskatchewan premier Allan Blakeney and Ontario opposition leader Stephen Lewis. He liked to joke that he wrote speeches for Mr. Lewis, widely regarded as the greatest orator of his generation, before adding a knowing “nobody writes Stephen’s speeches.”

Mr. Proctor also worked as a publicist for the Canadian Union of Public Employees and as a researcher for the National Union of Public and General Employees. He was based for several years in Cuernavaca, Mexico, where he ran a Canadian Labour Congress project to assist independent trade unions throughout Latin and South America.

After the NDP took a drubbing in the 1993 federal election, he decided to contest a seat for the party in the next federal election. He defeated seven other contenders to win the party’s nomination for Palliser, a new riding encompassing Moose Jaw and part of Regina. “Dick Proctor is moving from the shadows to the limelight,” the Regina Leader-Post reported.

He then defeated Alene Tanner of Reform and controversial lawyer Tony Merchant of the Liberals in the 1997 general election even while acknowledging “I’m not a household name.” He won re-election three years later before losing the seat in 2004 by 132 votes to Dave Batters of the Conservatives.

While in the House, Mr. Proctor served as his party’s critic for labour and agriculture.

Years later, he acknowledged a preference for the backroom.

“Public speaking is something I have never really been enamoured with,” he once said. “I have preferred to be the one loading the gun rather than pulling the trigger.”

John Richard Proctor was born in Toronto on Feb. 12, 1941, to the former Jacqueline Adele Jolly, known as Jackie, a cashier at the time of her marriage, and Clement Hudgin Proctor, an assistant superintendent with North York Hydro in the township’s Willowdale neighbourhood. (The elder Mr. Proctor died suddenly at the age of 59 in 1969 when accidentally electrocuted while installing a fuse box at a factory in Whitby, Ont.)

When the boy was 10, the family moved to a dairy farm in Prince Edward County, where Dick handled farm chores, joined the local 4-H club and attended classes in a one-room schoolhouse. He was high-school quarterback and part of a record-setting 440-yard relay team. In winter, he was a top goal-scoring forward for area hockey teams, including the Wellington Juvenile Dukes and the junior Picton Merchants.

Mr. Proctor studied journalism at Carleton University in Ottawa, playing hockey for the varsity Ravens. He also contributed to the student newspaper. During his tenure as news editor, he published an unsolicited opinion article written by the school’s interdenominational chaplain suggesting sex out of wedlock was not necessarily sinful. The article included the sentence: “If premarital sexual intercourse is all right in Samoa it can’t be so bad in Ottawa.” The subsequent controversy landed on the front page of the city’s two dailies.

Mr. Proctor then worked for the Edmonton Journal in the summer of 1965 before becoming a sports reporter for the Toronto Telegram the following year after graduating with a journalism degree. He eventually became the newspaper’s Action Line columnist, handling thousands of requests and complaints as a readers’ ombudsman who promoted tenant’s rights and advised on such matters as the proper way to register a purebred dog.

As a sports reporter for The Globe and Mail for four years, Mr. Proctor’s assignments included junior hockey, football’s Toronto Argonauts and the Indianapolis 500 car race.

In 1977, he travelled to Moscow with the Don Mills Flyers, a team of teenagers whose roster included future Hockey Hall of Fame defenceman Larry Murphy. While overseas, he filed stories about players and their parents likely violating Soviet currency laws by trading rubles on the black market and selling blue jeans, T-shirts and other clothes to local teenagers. He noted a set of a jean jacket, pants and coveralls sold for 220 rubles, almost five times as much as the spending money the Soviets had gifted each player as spending money for the entire tour.

“Not only are such transactions illegal,” he wrote, “but that represents far more money than most players declared when they cleared Soviet Union customs last week.”

Years later, Jim Bronskill of Southam News reported the Canadian embassy in Moscow spied on Mr. Proctor during that Cold War exhibition tournament, obtaining a copy of his Globe article after he sent it to the Reuters news agency in London for transmission to Canada.

“You always think it was the other guys that were doing all the spying, and we weren’t,” Mr. Proctor told Mr. Bronskill in 1999. “But I guess two can play the same game.”

Mr. Proctor also contributed articles to the Hockey News, circumventing a Globe ban on freelancing by using the pseudonymous byline Mike Gamble, thus making his bylines Proctor and Gamble after the prominent consumer goods company.

He retired to Victoria in 2005. He died there on Aug. 13 about six weeks after getting a diagnosis of cancer. He leaves his second wife Merran (née Moreau), a former deputy labour minister in Saskatchewan, whom he married in 1986. He also leaves a son and a daughter from their marriage, as well as a son and three daughters she brought to their union; six grandchildren; four great-grandchildren and a brother and a sister. An earlier marriage for Mr. Proctor ended in divorce without children.

Oddly enough, Mr. Proctor had an earlier instance of noteworthy airplane eavesdropping many years prior to overhearing Mr. Scott’s conversation.

“I sat on an airplane flying from Ottawa to Toronto once and I heard two insurance guys talking about a rate increase they were going to be suggesting to a company in North Gower, which is just outside Ottawa,” he told Anne McIlroy of the Globe in 1998. “And one of them made the point that they were going to demand x as the rate, but would settle for y .

“When I got off the plane I phoned the company and I told them I had heard this.”

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

When he resigned, Mr. Scott told a news conference that his inflight conversation “made me vulnerable to accusations that I had prejudged the outcome” of the inquiry. He also insisted he could not remember his seatmate though “it May seem hard to believe.” Mr. Scott was reappointed to cabinet six years later in a different portfolio by prime minister Paul Martin.

Mr. Proctor had a long career as a journalist, union organizer and strategist and aide to such NDP luminaries as federal leaders Ed Broadbent and Jack Layton, Saskatchewan premier Allan Blakeney and Ontario opposition leader Stephen Lewis. He liked to joke that he wrote speeches for Mr. Lewis, widely regarded as the greatest orator of his generation, before adding a knowing “nobody writes Stephen’s speeches.”

Mr. Proctor also worked as a publicist for the Canadian Union of Public Employees and as a researcher for the National Union of Public and General Employees. He was based for several years in Cuernavaca, Mexico, where he ran a Canadian Labour Congress project to assist independent trade unions throughout Latin and South America.

After the NDP took a drubbing in the 1993 federal election, he decided to contest a seat for the party in the next federal election. He defeated seven other contenders to win the party’s nomination for Palliser, a new riding encompassing Moose Jaw and part of Regina. “Dick Proctor is moving from the shadows to the limelight,” the Regina Leader-Post reported.

He then defeated Alene Tanner of Reform and controversial lawyer Tony Merchant of the Liberals in the 1997 general election even while acknowledging “I’m not a household name.” He won re-election three years later before losing the seat in 2004 by 132 votes to Dave Batters of the Conservatives.
While in the House, Mr. Proctor served as his party’s critic for labour and agriculture.
Years later, he acknowledged a preference for the backroom.
“Public speaking is something I have never really been enamoured with,” he once said. “I have preferred to be the one loading the gun rather than pulling the trigger.”

John Richard Proctor was born in Toronto on Feb. 12, 1941, to the former Jacqueline Adele Jolly, known as Jackie, a cashier at the time of her marriage, and Clement Hudgin Proctor, an assistant superintendent with North York Hydro in the township’s Willowdale neighbourhood. (The elder Mr. Proctor died suddenly at the age of 59 in 1969 when accidentally electrocuted while installing a fuse box at a factory in Whitby, Ont.)

When the boy was 10, the family moved to a dairy farm in Prince Edward County, where Dick handled farm chores, joined the local 4-H club and attended classes in a one-room schoolhouse. He was high-school quarterback and part of a record-setting 440-yard relay team. In winter, he was a top goal-scoring forward for area hockey teams, including the Wellington Juvenile Dukes and the junior Picton Merchants.

Mr. Proctor studied journalism at Carleton University in Ottawa, playing hockey for the varsity Ravens. He also contributed to the student newspaper. During his tenure as news editor, he published an unsolicited opinion article written by the school’s interdenominational chaplain suggesting sex out of wedlock was not necessarily sinful. The article included the sentence: “If premarital sexual intercourse is all right in Samoa it can’t be so bad in Ottawa.” The subsequent controversy landed on the front page of the city’s two dailies.

Mr. Proctor then worked for the Edmonton Journal in the summer of 1965 before becoming a sports reporter for the Toronto Telegram the following year after graduating with a journalism degree. He eventually became the newspaper’s Action Line columnist, handling thousands of requests and complaints as a readers’ ombudsman who promoted tenant’s rights and advised on such matters as the proper way to register a purebred dog.
As a sports reporter for The Globe and Mail for four years, Mr. Proctor’s assignments included junior hockey, football’s Toronto Argonauts and the Indianapolis 500 car race.

In 1977, he travelled to Moscow with the Don Mills Flyers, a team of teenagers whose roster included future Hockey Hall of Fame defenceman Larry Murphy. While overseas, he filed stories about players and their parents likely violating Soviet currency laws by trading rubles on the black market and selling blue jeans, T-shirts and other clothes to local teenagers. He noted a set of a jean jacket, pants and coveralls sold for 220 rubles, almost five times as much as the spending money the Soviets had gifted each player as spending money for the entire tour.
“Not only are such transactions illegal,” he wrote, “but that represents far more money than most players declared when they cleared Soviet Union customs last week.”

Years later, Jim Bronskill of Southam News reported the Canadian embassy in Moscow spied on Mr. Proctor during that Cold War exhibition tournament, obtaining a copy of his Globe article after he sent it to the Reuters news agency in London for transmission to Canada.
“You always think it was the other guys that were doing all the spying, and we weren’t,” Mr. Proctor told Mr. Bronskill in 1999. “But I guess two can play the same game.”

Mr. Proctor also contributed articles to the Hockey News, circumventing a Globe ban on freelancing by using the pseudonymous byline Mike Gamble, thus making his bylines Proctor and Gamble after the prominent consumer goods company.

He retired to Victoria in 2005. He died there on Aug. 13 about six weeks after getting a diagnosis of cancer. He leaves his second wife Merran (née Moreau), a former deputy labour minister in Saskatchewan, whom he married in 1986. He also leaves a son and a daughter from their marriage, as well as a son and three daughters she brought to their union; six grandchildren; four great-grandchildren and a brother and a sister. An earlier marriage for Mr. Proctor ended in divorce without children.
Oddly enough, Mr. Proctor had an earlier instance of noteworthy airplane eavesdropping many years prior to overhearing Mr. Scott’s conversation.

“I sat on an airplane flying from Ottawa to Toronto once and I heard two insurance guys talking about a rate increase they were going to be suggesting to a company in North Gower, which is just outside Ottawa,” he told Anne McIlroy of the Globe in 1998. “And one of them made the point that they were going to demand x as the rate, but would settle for y .
“When I got off the plane I phoned the company and I told them I had heard this.”

stories.title: Canada 'affirms sovereignty' with new vertical $20 bill featuring King Charles
stories.summary: Amid bitter trade tensions with the Trump administration, a redesigned Canadian $20 bank note was officially unveiled.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Amid bitter trade tensions with the Trump administration, a redesigned Canadian $20 bank note was officially unveiled Thursday featuring a portrait of King Charles, who hailed Canada as “indeed strong and free” amid hostility from the U.S.

“It’s also a reflection of the strength and stability of Canada’s financial system, one of the most trusted in the world and an important foundation of our economic resilience,” said Liberal MP Wayne Long, secretary of state for the Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions.

In addition to being “a beautiful work of art,” the new bank note, like all Canadian currency, is a “symbol of confidence,” Long said. “Confidence in our institutions, confidence in our economy and confidence in our future.”

The unveiling might seem a strategically timed move to shore up support from the King, who, during his official visit to the White House in April reminded U.S. President Donald Trump, who’d been taunting Canadians with “51st state” rhetoric and references to Prime Minister Mark Carney as “governor,” that the monarch is Canada’s official head of state.

The U.S. and Canada were set to host the Fifa World Cup. “So in one sense, Mr. President, as heads of state, we are joint hosts,” the King said at the time.

Last year, the King declared “the True North is indeed strong and free” during an historic throne speech opening Parliament.

In addition to featuring distinctive symbols of Canadian identity, Canada’s currency “affirms our sovereignty and our determination to define ourselves in the eyes of the world on our own terms,” Governor General Louise Arbour said.

The new vertical $20 bill is “both visually stunning and more secure than ever,” Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said at Thursday’s unveiling (the new note won’t enter circulation until February 2027).

The “dynamic features” on the new, and still predominantly green bill are “easy to check, and hard to fake,” Macklem said.

For example, tilting the purple security stripe makes images of maple leaves, poppies and 20s pulse, spin and move, features to help thwart counterfeiters and allow Canadians to easily authenticate the new note.

The portrait of King Charles on the front is surrounded by a “floral and leafy tapestry inspired by the King’s lifetime dedication to the environment,” reads a Bank of Canada press release.

It is the first bank note to feature a portrait of the King since his accession to the throne following the death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, ON Sept. 8, 2022.

The image on the back features the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in northern France, a war memorial commemorating Canadians who served during the First World War, “particularly those whose final resting place is unknown,” Macklem said.

The bank note features the official flower of every province and territory, gold maple leaves and raised ink on the King’s portrait. A circular window features plants that are culturally important to Indigenous Peoples — wild strawberries, Western red cedar, braided sweetgrass and Arctic cotton.

The first bank note in the vertical series, a $10 note, features the civil rights pioneer Viola Desmond.

Canadians use the $20 bank note more than any other denomination.

Since 1937, when King George VI first appeared on the $20 bill, Canada’s banknotes “have borne the likenesses of Canada’s sovereign monarchs,” Arbour said.

Queen Elizabeth II was featured on Canada’s bank notes for more than seven decades, “first as a young princess and then as the reigning sovereign,” Arbour said.

“Her image became one of the most recognizable in our currency for generations of Canadians.”

“Today, this tradition continues with His Majesty King Charles III,” she said.

stories.title: Carney chooses senior bureaucrat Scott Jones to head cyberspy agency
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has named senior bureaucrat Scott Jones as the next head of the Communications Security Establishment, Canada's cyberspy agency.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney has named senior bureaucrat Scott Jones as the next head of the Communications Security Establishment, Canada’s cyberspy agency.

Jones, most recently the president of Shared Services Canada, is set to replace the retiring Caroline Xavier at the CSE.

The CSE uses cutting-edge technology to gather foreign intelligence in the online world and protect Canada from cyberthreats.

Jones led the Cse’s Canadian Centre for Cyber Security from 2018 to 2021.

From 2008 to 2018, he held a variety of positions at the cyberspy agency.

In a media statement, Carney thanked Xavier for her dedication and service to Canadians.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tornado watch ends for Chatham-Kent
stories.summary: A warm and humid day is in store for southern Ontario Thursday, with scattered showers and thunderstorms expected to develop through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Another round of severe weather is moving through southern Ontario, with several severe thunderstorm watches.

Radar indicated a tornado in Wheatley Provincial Park.

A large storm system moving through Michigan has prompted tornado warnings in the U.S., while storms are moving through Lambton County, Western Middlesex and Western Elgin, where weather watches and warnings are in effect.

The main threats include torrential downpours, damaging wind gusts and hail.

Photo Gallery: Sept. 2, 2026 storm damage

CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison says the storms are developing along a stalled frontal boundary across southern Ontario.

“Unfortunately, rain back in the forecast Friday morning,” Atchison said.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected to move into the London area over the next couple of hours before the risk of storms comes to an end overnight. The skies will remain mainly cloudy, with another chance of showers Friday.

Rainfall totals Friday are expected to be under 2 mm, although 10 to 20 mm could fall in areas hit by heavier thunderstorms.

Some sunshine is expected Saturday, although there will still be a 40 per cent chance of showers. Daytime highs over the holiday weekend are expected to be around 25 C.

Sunday is expected to be mostly good, with Monday shaping up to be a beautiful day for the Labour Day holiday.

stories.title: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy set to visit Canada soon: source
stories.summary: is planning to visit Canada as soon as next week.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is planning to visit Canada as soon as next week.

A non-government source says the exact timing of the visit is being adjusted, possibly due to the funeral of Norway’s King Harald, scheduled for Sept. 9 in Oslo.

Both governments generally do not confirm Zelenskyy’s travel plans until the immediate days before departure, though he might visit more than one province, the source says.

Prime Minister Mark Carney visited Kyiv a year ago, while Zelenskyy last visited Canada in Halifax last December amid ongoing efforts to end Russia’s full-scale invasion.

MPs across party lines have put Ukraine at the centre of their foreign policy platforms and Canada has joined an agreement to learn from Ukrainian drone producers.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is preparing to host a Toronto summit later this month focused on the return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russian officials.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press
