stories.title: As Toronto Tempo fandom hits fever pitch, brands sense an opportunity
stories.summary: Women’s sports are using brand sponsorships – from Tampax to Sephora Canada – to push for progress beyond the court
stories.author: Lesa Hannah
stories.content:
On a Tuesday night in mid-August, Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena drew a sold-out crowd of more than 19,000 fans to see the Toronto Tempo face off against the Indiana Fever.

In the four months since Canada’s first Wnba team started its inaugural season, numbers have proven that an interest in women’s sports is here to stay. According to an August report , all home games at Coca-Cola Coliseum have sold out, and in July, 21,000 fans attended a Montreal game against the Dallas Wings, breaking a Wnba regular season record . On that Tuesday night in Toronto, Tempo fever was palpable, ON par with anything you’d see at a Raptors game.

The unquestionable momentum in women’s sports in Canada goes beyond sports fandom. Yes, there’s the athleticism, as well as the unpredictability and excitement of watching the competition unfold. But there’s also something more – with a new fan base comes new marketing opportunities, tied into brand activism.

Allison Sandmeyer-Graves, CEO of Canadian Women and Sport, a non-profit that advocates for equity and inclusivity in sport, said that for spectators, there’s an underlying sense of purpose. “They see [women’s sport] as connected to women’s empowerment,” she explained. “They see it as a space that is women-coded and women-celebrating.”

That makes it an appealing draw for brands looking to leverage a highly engaged audience and align themselves with women-centred causes such as reducing stigma about menstruation and raising awareness of the declining number of teenage girls in sport.

“I think it’s one of the unique and exciting things about the development of women’s professional sport here in Canada,” said Sandmeyer-Graves. “Brands get to show up in a different way, and different brands get to show up.”

Tampax, the Tempo’s official period partner – yes, players have to compete while on their period – is prominently featured on the scoreboard and around the stadium with the phrase, “Protect the home court.” Its logo also pops up on the jumbotron during the “De-fense” chant. The brand’s product is also handed out to the loudest-cheering section every game. Lisa Ferkul, the Tempo’s chief revenue officer, remarked that she loves seeing men leaving the stadium with a box of tampons.

“Ultimately for us, this partnership was really about continuing to allow conversations about periods and about women’s health to be normalized,” said Chelsey Harshman, senior director for North America Tampax.

Then there’s Sephora, a founding sponsor of the team. The beauty retailer had been looking at women’s sports for some time after noticing how its audience was growing . “Our brand ambition is to really expand the way the world sees beauty and drive more inclusivity of who belongs in beauty and who belongs at Sephora. So getting into women’s sport really helped us do that,” said Allison Litzinger, senior vice-president and chief marketing officer at Sephora Canada.

This idea is the focus of the brand’s “Pretty Badass” campaign featuring Tempo players Marina Mabrey, Kiki Rice, Temi Fágbénlé and others. It pokes at a tension that exists for many women, not just in sports but in life: the way women are often put into one-dimensional boxes. “It’s ‘brainy or beautiful,’ ‘strong or feminine,’” said Litzinger. “We intentionally wanted to challenge these outdated stereotypes to show that you can actually embrace this multidimensionality that women are.”

Cathal Kelly: Will uncomplimentary coverage of the Wnba cost you your seat in the Toronto Tempo’s press box?

Outside of basketball, beauty brands Clinique and Dove have joined forces with AFC Toronto, a professional women’s soccer club, to combat declining numbers of teenage girls in sports ( according to Canadian Women and Sport , 62 per cent of teen girls do not play sports at all, a drop of 14 per cent in the last decade). Clinique’s messaging emphasizes individuality and highlights the benefits of being part of a team, while Dove’s “Keep Her Confident” campaign features jerseys with images of the AFC players as kids and the individuals who helped them stay in the game.

“What women’s sports offers [brands] is commercial impact and social impact going hand-in-hand,” said Sandmeyer-Graves.

Seeing women excel at their sport feels meaningful because of how long and hard they have had to fight for the opportunity to play at all, she added.

“For the opportunity to play at that level. For the right to be respected. And celebrated.”

stories.title: High winds flatten farm shed, as family scrambles into basement in Huron East
stories.summary: A family at a farm in Huron East hand to quickly dash to the basement after Wednesday's sudden storm arrived with heavy winds that wound up damaging their house and destroying a shed.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Video
A family at a farm in Huron East hand to quickly dash to the basement after Wednesday's sudden storm arrived with heavy winds that wound up damaging their house and destroying a shed.
· Posted: Sep 03, 2026 5:14 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
When the weather alert sounded on her phone, Helen Oldsfield had just stepped out of her swimming pool at her family cattle farm in Huron East.
Storm that hammered south, southwestern Ontario leaves 'significant' damage, outages as cleanup continues
It was just before 5 p.m. She'd seen the weather reports and knew at least a thunderstorm was likely.

"I went in the house ... and then the tornado warnings came on," she said. "We got in the house, we moved a bit of stuff downstairs ... and really within two minutes it hit. It was pretty terrifying."
While hunkering down in the basement with her family, Oldfield couldn't see what was happened outside but could hear the wind scream and trees smack against the house.
"All I heard was crashing and splintering wood and just real chaos," she said. "I was sure the house was gone but as it turned out, it was just trees on the house."
Once the storm passed, she emerged from the basement and went outside to inspect the damage.

A 60 by 100 foot drive-in shed, used to house farming equipment, had been completely flattened. The side walls had collapsed, and much of the shed's framing and chunks of its roof had been strewn into an adjacent cornfield.
"It picked up all the trusses, and the roof and all the steel that part popped off all at once and blew into the next field and all the sidewalls collapsed," she said. "It's a total loss."
The family's cattle were grazing in a field, and one cow suffered a gash.
"She'll be fine, but we'll be having the vet look after her," said Oldsfield.

She said the farm has been in her husband's family since the 1840s and while summer rainstorms and thunder happen almost every year, no one can recall anything on a similar scale hitting the property.
The house has suffered some damage caused by trees landing on its roof. Oldsfield said she's worried if more rain comes, it could get into spots where the roof is damaged.
"It's something I never expected to see in our lifetime, we're winding down our farming career," said Oldsfield. "We've never had anything like this before, it's one for the history books."

stories.title: Free transit pass program for Halifax students to continue after funding uncertainty
stories.summary: After months of uncertainty, it was announced the day before the school year began that students in grades 7 to 12 will once again receive the passes.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Eligible junior high and high school students across Halifax Regional Municipality will be able to ride public transit for free after the provincial government and municipality came to an agreement to continue its Student Transit Pass Program.

After months of uncertainty following the province’s decision to cut funding to the program, it was announced Wednesday — the day before the school year began — that students in Grades 7 to 12 will once again receive the passes.

According to the municipality, the Halifax Regional Centre for Education will hand out transit passes for students attending five Halifax schools where public transit is “more practical than school buses.”

2:13 Nova Scotia budget cuts funding for Halifax student bus pass program

The province’s Department of Opportunities and Social Development (OSD) is funding passes for youth aged 13 to 18 who are connected to Employment Support and Income Assistance, which amounts to more than 1,700 students.

The municipality said it is funding transit passes for all remaining grades 7 through 12 students as well.

“We’re excited that the program will now be expanding to include private schools as well as homeschooled students and (students at) public schools who were included in the program last year,” said Anthony Edmonds, Halifax Transit’s acting director of planning.

The province announced in February it was cutting its $1.2-million contribution to the program.

At the time, the municipality was uncertain whether it could shoulder the burden .

Education Minister Brendan Maguire told reporters Thursday it was never the province’s plan to cut the program entirely. He said $600,000 of that funding, for example, was redirected to OSD to provide passes to eligible youth connected to income assistance.

“What we were going to pay for, and always were going to pay for, is any access that those kids needed to (get to) school and our OSD clients. So I think it just became who’s responsible for what,” he said.

“On our end, we continue to provide what we’ve always provided: $600,000 will be coming from OSD for income assistance clients, and then the five high schools (…) where the students need school bus passes, we’ll provide them with $500,000. So we’re still providing the same amount of money. “

With the uncertainty around the future of the program, Coun. Kathryn Morse said it reveals a problem with how transit is funded and supported in Nova Scotia.

“Most other provinces provide predictable operational funding for transit systems. Here in Nova Scotia, we don’t have that from the province,” she said.

“So I think that’s something we need to work on in the future just to get that more continuity, more predictability into our transit programs.”

The province’s opposition leaders said they were glad to see the program funded, but called into question Maguire’s narrative.

“So they can call it whatever they want, but they are reinstating the thoughtless and cruel cut that they made in the spring,” said NDP Leader Claudia Chender.

Iain Rankin, the interim leader of the Liberal Party, called it a “strange communications exercise.”

“It’s just a strange communications exercise to not just admit that they were wrong and just say that they’re wrong and that they are bringing it back,” he said.

The student passes will be valid until Aug. 31, 2027 and will be delivered through Halifax Transit’s mobile fare payment app, Hfxgo.

Physical passes will be available upon request.

stories.title: Alberta government touts Oct. 1 launch of $14 solar panel recycling fee, landfill ban
stories.summary: Brooks - Albertans purchasing new solar panels next month will face a hefty fee for recycling them, the government says.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Albertans purchasing new solar panels next month will face a hefty fee for recycling them.

Environment Minister Grant Hunter announced Thursday a ban on landfill disposal for the panels and the $14 recycling fee per panel beginning Oct. 1.

Hunter said the move will protect municipalities and taxpayers from future costs. He estimated that by 2045, most of the solar panels currently installed in the province will reach the end of their lives and could produce nearly 73,000 tons of material.

“We’re creating the opportunity for new made-in-Alberta recycling programs and industries that recover valuable materials instead of burying them,” he told reporters in Brooks.

The government estimates a typical household of 20 panels.

But industry associations and advocates have said the $14 price tag is far too steep, punitive and being imposed without clear accounting to back it up.

They note it’s nearly five times the $2.75 cost of recycling a large television set in the province.

Heather MacKenzie, executive director of renewables advocate Solar Alberta, said for a typical panel, a $14 fee is like adding a 10 per cent tax.

In an interview, she said it’s yet another hit to the solar sector from a provincial government that appears intent on undermining it.

“It appears that the government of Alberta is artificially increasing the cost of solar, and that will enable natural gas to compete more easily in our marketplace,” she said.

She added that the impact will be significant.

“It’ll hurt all the small solar installation companies. It’ll hurt the electricians, and we will see job losses as a result.”

When word of the fee trickled down to stakeholders from the Alberta Recycling Management Authority earlier this summer, MacKenzie said they pushed back, and asked how the $14 figure was reached.

“They are not willing to show how they came to that number, which means that nobody can really critique the assumptions that are embedded in it,” said MacKenzie.

Independent research commissioned by the Canadian Renewable Energy Association put the cost of recycling a solar module at about $5.

Hunter, when asked how the province arrived at its cost, said the actual cost of shipping old panels to the United States for processing is $40 per panel.

He said it will also take time for recyclers to develop “economies of scale,” and if they can do it for cheaper, then that price will be passed on to consumers.

The announcement comes after a string of rule changes affecting renewable energy development from Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservatives.

In 2023, the UCP put a short-term moratorium on renewable energy project development before introducing strict new rules on where they can go. Subsequent reclamation fees for decommissioned projects were later criticized as too high.

Business Renewables Centre Canada — which works to help businesses and institutions reduce their emissions by connecting buyers and sellers of renewable power — said it supports a recycling fee but Alberta’s is higher than those of any other jurisdiction in the world.

“We’re disappointed to see the government saddle the industry with another disproportionate burden,” said director Jorden Dye in a Thursday news release.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

“They are not willing to show how they came to that number, which means that nobody can really critique the assumptions that are embedded in it,” said MacKenzie.
Independent research commissioned by the Canadian Renewable Energy Association put the cost of recycling a solar module at about $5.
Hunter, when asked how the province arrived at its cost, said the actual cost of shipping old panels to the United States for processing is $40 per panel.
He said it will also take time for recyclers to develop “economies of scale,” and if they can do it for cheaper, then that price will be passed on to consumers.
The announcement comes after a string of rule changes affecting renewable energy development from Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservatives.

In 2023, the UCP put a short-term moratorium on renewable energy project development before introducing strict new rules on where they can go. Subsequent reclamation fees for decommissioned projects were later criticized as too high.

Business Renewables Centre Canada — which works to help businesses and institutions reduce their emissions by connecting buyers and sellers of renewable power — said it supports a recycling fee but Alberta’s is higher than those of any other jurisdiction in the world.
“We’re disappointed to see the government saddle the industry with another disproportionate burden,” said director Jorden Dye in a Thursday news release.

stories.title: Owner of two dogs that mauled boy to death in Edmonton gets community sentence
stories.summary: Judge sentences Crystal MacDonald to two years less a day for criminal negligence causing death in April, 2024 attack that killed Kache Grist
stories.author: Daniela Germano
stories.content:
The owner of two dogs that killed an 11-year-old boy wiped away tears Thursday as she was given a conditional sentence to be served in the community.

Crystal MacDonald otherwise stared straight ahead during sentencing by Justice Eric Macklin in Court of King’s Bench in Edmonton.

The term is two years less a day.

“A sentence served in the community still denounces the crime of criminal negligence causing death and, more specifically, keeping dangerous animals and failing to properly ensure the protection and safety of others, especially children,” Macklin said.

“Ms. MacDonald is fully aware of the consequences of her actions and inactions, and there is no suggestion that she might engage in future behaviour such as that which brought her before the court in this case.”

MacDonald’s two cane corsos fatally attacked her roommate’s son, Kache Grist, in her Edmonton home in April 2024.

Macklin allowed MacDonald to serve her sentence in Penticton, B.C., where she has been living with her mother. He imposed a lifetime ban on dog ownership but said she could bring forward an application in 10 years to try to remove it.

The Crown sought a five-year prison sentence for MacDonald and a lifetime ban on dog ownership. The defence asked for the conditional sentence of two years less a day.

Outside court, MacDonald’s lawyer said they were pleased with the judge’s decision and that she has filed an appeal challenging the conviction.

“The issue in this case has never been whether the dogs caused Kache’s death,” Evan McIntyre said. “The issue is whether she was legally responsible for that death.”

He said it is not contradictory for her to feel “incredibly remorseful” for Kache’s death while exercising her legal right to ask a higher court to overturn the conviction. Her appeal had been raised by the Crown prosecutor as evidence MacDonald has little remorse.

MacDonald, 46, was found guilty of criminal negligence causing death in May.

At trial, court heard Kache, who lived in British Columbia with his mother, was in Edmonton visiting his father Wesley Grist for spring break. Wesley Grist was living in MacDonald’s home.

MacDonald testified during trial that she repeatedly told Wesley not to leave the boy alone with her dogs. She said she didn’t approve of Kache staying at her home and tried to get the dogs into a boarding kennel, but they lacked the required vaccinations.

Before Kache’s death, the dogs had killed two pets and injured three adults, including MacDonald.

Wesley Grist later testified that on that fateful day that he was in the garage when his son was killed. He had allowed the boy to go inside to play a new video game while he finished cleaning up tools.

About 45 minutes later, he found his son lying in a pool of blood surrounded by the dogs on the kitchen floor. An autopsy found he died from bite injuries to the neck. The dogs were later euthanized.

The judge told MacDonald that simply warning Grist about the dogs was not enough. Macklin said there were many things MacDonald could have done, such as keeping the dogs leashed or chained in the backyard, locking them in their kennels or finding another place for the boy to stay.

MacDonald said Wednesday during her sentencing hearing that she thinks about Kache every single day.

“There is no sentence that this court could impose on me that could make me feel the weight of this loss more than I already do,” she said.

stories.title: Snowbirds to make final flight at Grey Cup in Calgary
stories.summary: The Canadian Forces Snowbirds will make their final flight at the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary on Nov. 15, the CFL announced Thursday.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
The iconic Canadian Forces Snowbirds will make their final performance at the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary this fall.

The iconic military aerobatics team will take to the skies on Nov. 15 as part of the championship celebration at McMahon Stadium , the Canadian Football League announced Thursday on social media.

The final flight had previously been scheduled to take place in Sacramento, Calif., where the Snowbirds are set to perform at the California Capital Airshow on Oct. 10 and 11.

2:23 ‘Bittersweet’: Snowbirds wrapping up final season with aging jets

The Snowbirds, officially known as 431 Air Demonstration Squadron based out of Moose Jaw, Sask., have been performing with the CT-114 Tutor aircraft since 1971.

The jets are being retired following the 2026 season, ahead of transitioning to new planes in the early 2030s.

“As we close out the Snowbirds’ 55th anniversary, I want to thank all Canadians for celebrating our team over this past season,” said said Major-General Denis O’Reilly, deputy commander of the Royal Canadian Air Force.

The legendary team has previously performed at three Grey Cups — the 101st, 106th and 109th. This year’s championship game is the 113th edition.

The 113th Grey Cup is scheduled for Nov. 15 at McMahon Stadium in Calgary.

— With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: A gorgeous and affordable elbows-up destination
stories.summary: Head to Northern Ontario for available campgrounds, beautiful scenery and inexpensive attractions
stories.author: Erica Alini
stories.content:
The problem with elbows-up vacations is that they can be quite expensive. Flying within Canada is notoriously costly and food, accommodation and attractions can also add up.

Camping is a lot cheaper, of course, but it is also quite hard to book at popular national and provincial parks, as I wrote about a few weeks ago .

If you’ve been running up against the same issues, here’s a hack: Head north.

My family and I just came back from a week around Lake Superior and, let me tell you, it was beautiful and quite affordable.

Another perk: Booking campgrounds is less competitive. We managed to get several nights at Sleeping Giant Provincial Park on a prime lakefront campsite during the peak summer camping period.

Sure, it takes at least two days in the car to get there from Toronto, but there is barely any traffic once you get past Sault Ste. Marie, Ont. And driving through Superior country is in itself quite a treat, at least if you like road trips. Think lake, forest and Canadian Shield, with everything growing progressively more majestic as you go further north. Meanwhile, overnight accommodation along the way was around $175 a night for three people. (I don’t remember the last time I found a hotel room for less than $200 in Southern Ontario.)

Sleeping Giant itself was everything I’d hoped for. (It was gorgeous. It really does look like the photos ).

But the biggest surprise was Thunder Bay. The city wasn’t initially part of our itinerary, but we ended up spending a day there after the weather turned and we decided we weren’t prepared to put up with 12 hours of thunderstorms in a tent.

I wasn’t expecting the food scene. Croissants from Swell Bakery were on par with the best I’ve had in Toronto. So were the smash burgers at the Tilted Turret Pinball Pub . A double burger there is $17.95 before tax, which is $5 to $7 less than your typical craft burger in Southern Ontario.

Then there are the Kakabeka Falls, known as the Niagara of the North for good reason. It costs $6.50 for a two-hour vehicle permit, which is all you need to walk around the site.

We also made a pit stop at one of the several amethyst mines just outside the city that lets people dig up their own minerals. The entrance fee was a reasonable $12.50 a person and for $12 more we got to take home two pounds of the shiny purple quartz. (If you also have a rock-obsessed kid, you know you can easily spend that much on a couple of pebbles of polished minerals.)

Finally, there was Fort William Historical Park . I don’t know how I hadn’t heard about it before.

It’s a massive living history site featuring a reconstruction of the wilderness headquarters of the North West Company and a nearby Anishinaabe encampment as they existed in 1815. It’s staffed by actors who play the part of various fur-trade-era characters, including a variety of artisans who are baking bread, crafting cups and lanterns out of tin or making barrels.

I’ve been to live history sites before, but this was on another level. Not only was the acting impeccable, it also required meticulous historical training. We asked all sorts of questions and never caught anyone unprepared. And the best part was everyone always stayed in character.

And the cost? Just $50 for the three of us.

There are mega-houses and then there are mega-mortgages. Nearly 50 per cent of Canadian homeowners who renewed their mortgages this year say their housing costs swelled to more than half of their household budget when they had to give up their ultra-low COVID-era rates, according to a recent survey.

My family and I just came back from a week around Lake Superior and, let me tell you, it was beautiful and quite affordable.
Another perk: Booking campgrounds is less competitive. We managed to get several nights at Sleeping Giant Provincial Park on a prime lakefront campsite during the peak summer camping period.

Sure, it takes at least two days in the car to get there from Toronto, but there is barely any traffic once you get past Sault Ste. Marie, Ont. And driving through Superior country is in itself quite a treat, at least if you like road trips. Think lake, forest and Canadian Shield, with everything growing progressively more majestic as you go further north. Meanwhile, overnight accommodation along the way was around $175 a night for three people. (I don’t remember the last time I found a hotel room for less than $200 in Southern Ontario.)

stories.title: Pedestrian dies after collision with vehicle in London: Police
stories.summary: The driver remained at the scene, police said.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
A pedestrian has died after a collision with a vehicle in northwest London on Wednesday night, police say.

Emergency crews responded to the “serious” motor vehicle collision around 11:20 p.m. to the collision in the area of Sarnia Road and Chapman Court, just west of Wonderland Road North.

The pedestrian was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died, police said.

The driver remained at the scene, police said.

The investigation has been turned over to the London police Road Safety Section and is ongoing.

A police spokesperson told The Free Press that the collision did not occur in the dedicated pedestrian crosswalk at the intersection, which is equipped with traffic lights for Sarnia Road traffic controlled by a button.

Anyone who was in the area between 11 p.m. and 11:30 p.m. and May have witnessed the collision, or has dashcam, residential or business surveillance footage, is asked to contact investigators at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477).

Ontario Provincial Police continue to investigate after a man was found dead late Wednesday evening in Kingsville.

Officers were called to the 500 block of Road 11, between Graham Side Road and the Albuna Townline, shortly before midnight Wednesday.

A 43-year-old man was found and pronounced dead at the scene, police said.

The investigation is continuing and nearby residents were warned to expect an increased police presence Thursday.

Police also said there is no threat to public safety but provided no other information.

Photos taken by a Windsor Star reporter Thursday show a yellow ATV lying in a ditch between two downed hydro poles. Several other damaged poles could be seen farther down the road.

Investigators would not say whether the ATV was involved in the man’s death.

A nearby resident, however, said an officer at the scene Thursday morning told her there had been a “terrible” accident.

“My heart just sank,” Laura Lanoue said. “I don’t know if the person was trying to get home or if something struck the pole and knocked it.

“All I know is that it was a horrific accident.”

With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: Montreal cat returns home after 2 weeks on loose at Toronto Pearson airport
stories.summary: Abir Batikhi said Caramel was one of four cats she had travelling with her from Jordan to Montreal on Aug. 17.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A Montreal woman says it’s a “miracle” her cat was found after more than two weeks in Toronto Pearson Airport.

Abir Batikhi said Caramel was one of four cats she had travelling with her from Jordan to Montreal on Aug. 17.

When she arrived at Montreal’s Pierre Trudeau Airport, only three cats were in their cages.

“I received the four cages. One cat was missing,” Batikhi previously told Global News.

The owner was told Caramel had been seen in the cargo hold when the aircraft arrived at Toronto Pearson International Airport, where the flight stopped before continuing to Montreal.

Airport officials informed her the cat escaped onto the airport ramp area near Terminal 3 and ran toward gates 29 and 30, she said.

Batikhi told Global News Thursday that Caramel has been found alive and is expected to arrive in Montreal on Friday.

“It was a big relief,” she said. “It was a miracle honestly.”

Caramel was located Wednesday night in a cargo facility at the airport and was safely captured, a spokesperson for Pearson Airport told Global News.

“Information provided by an airport worker about the cat’s last known location helped the wildlife team focus search efforts in the area where Caramel was ultimately found,” they said.

Now that Caramel is safe, Batikhi is able to marvel in the adventure the cat has had over the past two weeks.

“She’s been escaping to the food,” she chuckled. “She’s been eating good, she knows where to go. She’s a survivor.”

Batikhi said Caramel was in the rain for a bit and was wet when she was captured but once she dries up she will be the same as before.

The Montreal woman had made a plea on social media for anyone travelling through Pearson Airport to keep an eye out for Caramel.

On Thursday, she delivered the anticipated update many were hoping for.

“The amount of care, kindness, and support we received while searching for our beloved cat meant more to me than I can put into words,” she wrote. “Every suggestion, message, prayer, and share gave me hope during such a stressful and emotional time.”

Darcia Rohlehr, CEO of pet transportation company Paws En Route, previously told Global News that a case like Caramel’s is extremely uncommon.

“There are about four million pets that travel annually, and out of those four million pets, about 0.01 per cent experience an issue,” she said.

Gates and doors on animal carriers are secured with a zip tie, Rohlehr said, to ensure animals are well secured and cannot escape during flight. She said strict regulations are in place to reduce the risk of animals getting lost in transport.

After perhaps the most daring adventure of the cat’s life, despite never leaving the airport, Batikhi said she is patiently awaiting Caramel’s scheduled arrival at 1 p.m. Friday.

“I can’t wait to see her,” she said.

– With files from Phil Carpenter, Global News

stories.title: Eby blames OpenAI for new Tumbler Ridge lawsuits, says it walked away from mediation
stories.summary: Prince George - British Columbia Premier David Eby says new lawsuits against OpenAI from witnesses to the deadly Tumbler Ridge mass shooting are a result of the tech firm walking away from a mediation process, calling it inexcusable and disgraceful.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prince George - British Columbia Premier David Eby says new lawsuits against OpenAI from witnesses to the deadly Tumbler Ridge mass shooting are a result of the tech firm walking away from a mediation process, calling it inexcusable and disgraceful.

Eby, who was speaking at an unrelated event in Prince George, B.C., ON Thursday says the plaintiffs in 30 new lawsuits that were announced this week have the provincial government’s full support and the province intends to join the litigation, so long as it doesn’t interfere with the families’ ability to access justice.

stories.title: Ottawa needs to be more transparent about major projects, think tank says
stories.summary: The government needs to be more transparent in identifying which types of major projects are national priorities, says a leading think tank.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government needs to be more transparent in identifying which types of major projects are national priorities, says a leading think tank on the eve of a major Canadian investment summit.

In an open letter to be released Friday, the C.D. Howe Institute said Canada also needs to be clearer about processes and timelines for major projects, which have been identified by the federal government as a key building block in efforts to build a stronger economy.

After almost a decade under former prime minister Justin Trudeau where infrastructure investments waned, Prime Minister Mark Carney opened up a major projects office in Calgary a year ago to try to speed up regulatory approvals and financing. A number of projects have since been approved but some of those were already in the works, while others have been approved but are not yet under construction.

“This is how we give investors the certainty they need, complete projects more efficiently, and create lasting economic growth,” the institute wrote in a document obtained by National Post.

The letter, from the institute’s chief executive Jeremy Kronick, also says that if Canada is to attract more investment, the country needs to better leverage its abundant energy resources, while using both conventional and renewable energy to better diversify the economy.

C.D. Howe also argues that the government needs to cut both business and individual taxes so that Canada is more attractive to new capital.

The Canada Investment Summit is to be held in Toronto on Sept 14-15 and is expected to attract about 250 investment and financial services leaders from around the world. The event is seen as an important opportunity for Canadian political and business officials to sell Canada as a place to invest.

Achieving that goal became more difficult late last month, however, when trade talks with the United States broke down, leaving access to the world’s largest market uncertain in some sectors.

The summit is a key piece of Ottawa’s effort to attract at least $1 trillion in investments — at least half of that new and from the private sector — over the next five years in areas such as infrastructure, mines, energy, defence, housing and artificial intelligence.

Many of the summit’s events are led by Canadian political or business leaders who are expected to present Canada’s case. Carney is scheduled to open the event with a keynote speech.

stories.title: Montreal’s LaSalle College will open its doors as judge renews creditor protection
stories.summary: Montreal - A Montreal judge has prolonged LaSalle College’s creditor protection as the school faces close to $30 million in fines from the Quebec government.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Students at LaSalle College said they were relieved and excited as they learned they would be able to return to school on Friday following a week of uncertainty during which the fate of their school hung in limbo.

“I feel ecstatic. I’m just super happy. I don’t know, I felt like I was holding back tears almost for the past five days,” said Dominique Goulet, a second-year fashion design student, outside Montreal’s courthouse.

About a dozen students, teachers and administrative staff chatted on the steps of the courthouse next to a quilt students had been sewing to read “No school, no future. Keep our doors open.”

On Thursday, a judge prolonged LaSalle College’s creditor protection as the school faces close to $30 million in fines from the Quebec government. Government subsidies to the college will also be reinstated as the school negotiates a payment plan with the province.

The fines stem from a 2022 language law passed by the provincial government, which imposed limits on the number of students in English-language college programs.

In the 2023-24 school year — the first year the new limits were applied — LaSalle College exceeded its quota by 716 students and received a fine of $8.8 million. The following year, the college surpassed its quota by 1,066 students, and was fined an additional $21 million.

Last year, the college delayed the beginning of classes by one day because of these fines.

LaSalle College is a subsidized private school and one of the few institutions in Quebec offering both English-language and French-language programs.

On top of these fines, LaSalle College must reimburse $17.9 million in subsidies it received last year, bringing the total debt to close to $48 million.

During the hearing, Judge Martin Castonguay, who presided over the case, accused the provincial government of failing to give LaSalle College an exit ramp to repay its debts and of trying to “create new rules of the game.”

“Why would the government be above the rest of the world?” he questioned.

He highlighted the need to consider the 3,000 students and the college employees whose lives would be affected by a potential closure.

“I’m being asked to throw out the bathwater and the baby with it. After only 10 days. I won’t do that,” he said.

The Quebec Superior Court had first granted the college a 10-day window of protection on Aug. 24. That protection has been extended to Sept. 24, at which time the school and government will have to provide an update on a payment agreement.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette kept her remarks short from the campaign trail.

“We’re going to take the time to analyze the judgment, but we will follow up on it,” she told reporters.

Outside the courtroom, Camille Dorvilier-Schell, a student who had been attending the hearing, said she was excited to go back to class.

“It’s absolutely incredible, and it’s what we’ve been asking for since the beginning. We want to keep going to class while the government and the college negotiate behind the scenes,” she said.

Nathalie Simard and Lara Jaber, president and vice-president of the Lasalle College teachers union, said they were relieved and that teachers were ready to start the school year.

“We’re also happy for students who have been in some kind of uncertainty for the last two weeks, that at last they’ll get their peace,” said Jaber.

The question of the money owed by LaSalle College to the provincial government remains up in the air. On Thursday, Claude Marchand, director of LaSalle College, once again called the fine “disproportionate.”

“But for what is the most important — delivering our core mission, our students going back to the classrooms — that’s assured until the end of the school year,” he said.

Dorvilier-Schell said she isn’t nervous that she and her classmates might go through this again next year. In her eyes, the judge’s language against the fines, as well as the surge of support the students have received, should shield them going forward.

Outside the courthouse, Goulet, the fashion student, said she was still worried about what would happen at the next back-to-school.

“I’m ready to fight again next year if we need to,” she added.

And if it comes down to it, their protest quilt will be ready to go.

“We can just reuse it again next year, add some stitching,” she said, laughing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

— with files from Patrice Bergeron

stories.title: Western School of Health Studies director named to U.K. academy
stories.summary: Rachel Forrester-Jones, director of Western's School of Health Studies, has been elected to the Fellowship of the Academy of Social Sciences.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
Rachel Forrester-Jones, professor and director of the School of Health Studies in Western’s Faculty of Health Sciences, has been elected to the Fellowship of the Academy of Social Sciences in the United Kingdom.

Forrester-Jones is the only individual from a Canadian institution among the 74 new fellows announced Sept. 3.

As a newly elected fellow, she joins a prestigious community of leading professionals in the social sciences.

Forrester-Jones’ research focuses on social inclusion, social support networks and protection for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, including autism, as well as people with mental health issues. Her work across the lifespan, including palliative and end-of-life care, has helped change policy and practice to improve individuals’ quality of life.

In a release announcing the latest inductees, Academy president Will Hutton lauded the incoming fellows as “the most influential voices in social science today,” whose work is “expanding knowledge, challenging assumptions and generating insights that are informing and even redefining decision making across government, business, education and civil society.”

Shaun Boe, dean of the Faculty of Health Sciences, spoke to the impact and merit of Forrester-Jones’ work.

“It is wonderful to see Professor Forrester-Jones recognized for her extensive contributions shaping social policy, working on behalf of people with intellectual disabilities and mental health issues,” he said. “Her breadth of expertise reflects the strength of scholarship within the Faculty of Health Sciences’ School of Health Studies, and we extend our deepest congratulations on this well-deserved honour.”

Forrester-Jones is also cross-appointed to the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry. There, working with a team that included Dr. Saverio Stranges, Amadeep Thind and Victoria Smye, director of the Arthur Labatt Family School of Nursing, she developed the certificate in Critical Public Health. She also worked with Stranges, Cheryl Currie and other Schulich and health studies colleagues to develop the bachelor of science in public health .

Rachel Forrester-Jones

The primary focus of Forrester-Jones’ research is to further the inclusion of vulnerable adults through social networks and support.

“I’ve had the opportunity to help change policy and practice to improve people’s quality of life, and in doing so, also impact their health and wellbeing,” she said.

It’s experience she brought to Western five years ago, arriving from the University of Bath, with extensive knowledge as a social scientist, social policy expert and barrister.

In the U.K., she also performed stand-up comedy – a pursuit seemingly off the path of an academic career launched through a joint honours degree in sociology and American studies. But it wasn’t a stretch.

“My jokes were based on social policy material,” said Forrester-Jones, noting her stand-up gigs drew a loyal following of fans and colleagues in her field.

Comedy is also a central theme in her latest book, Tourette’s Syndrome, Stigma, and Society’s Jests . Co-authored with Melina Aikaterini Malli, from the University of Oxford, the book explores how the mass media and humour both reinforce and challenge the social prejudices around Tourette’s Syndrome. It features narratives by comedians living with Tourette’s.

Forrester-Jones has long incorporated lived experience of those with disabilities into her work.

As part of her PhD research tracing the closure of large psychiatric institutions in Wales in the early 1990s, she lived in a hospital alongside patients with long-term mental health problems, before following them out into the community.

In 2002, she became the first female master of Rutherford College at the University of Kent, overseeing the welfare and conduct for 4,500 students across four departments.

While working as a professor of social inclusion and as director of the Tizard Centre, a facility internationally renowned for its pioneering research and teaching in intellectual and developmental disabilities, Forrester-Jones developed an interest in legal issues related to vulnerable adults.

“People with intellectual disabilities tend to acquiesce and are more liable to make false confessions,” she said. “It can lead to this terrible situation where you have innocent people in prison.”

That concern drove her to become trained and qualified as a barrister – while working full-time as an academic.

She’s since offered her legal services pro bono, choosing to remain in academia, where she’s made a significant impact, not only for those living with intellectual disabilities, but those caring for them as well.

“One of the challenges is older parents caring for adult children with intellectual disabilities. That can be very difficult if they don’t have the social support,” Forrester-Jones said.

Forrester-Jones’ research, combining health, social and policy sciences, has taken her across Canada, Europe, the U.K., South America and most recently, North Africa and the Middle East.

Her past work includes advising U.K. government bodies on combating social exclusion and providing consultancy to NGOs in Brazil and Spain, helping to bring social-network-based approaches to services across continents.

“I would argue social networks are the apex of social inclusion,” she said. “Even though we like to think we are a society that is very keen on equality and equity, stigmatization is still an issue. That leads to prejudice against the group being stigmatized, which then leads to discrimination.”

Social networks help remove fear of the unknown and lessen the stigma, Forrester-Jones said.

“People begin to realize that individuals with intellectual disabilities have the same feelings they do – they love, they want romance, to work and retire. They want all the same experiences but are thwarted.” – Rachel Forrester-Jones, director of Western’s School of Health Studies

Forrester-Jones counts working at Western, where she oversees roughly 2,000 health sciences undergraduate students and, together with colleagues, introduced the master’s in health equity and sustainability program, as “one of the best jobs I’ve ever had.”

“I love that our school is truly interdisciplinary and this makes a difference to how we teach students to understand health and health care,” she said.

Under her leadership, the school has grown substantially and increased its research funding.

Forrester-Jones remains an honorary professor in social policy at the University of Bath, where, before joining Western, she saw the opportunity to set up a partnership between the two schools, facilitating research and learning opportunities such as internships and practicums abroad for students at both institutions.

She is also the co-chair of the European Task Force on Palliative care for intellectual disability.

Later this month, Forrester-Jones heads to the University of Verona, developing a new comparative project exploring community social inclusion of people with intellectual disabilities and their caregivers in Italy and Canada.

She said she was honoured to have her work recognized in a field that is making meaningful advances to benefit society.

“Social science really matters because it helps us to understand people, the economy and manage the many issues individuals and society face. Social science theories about stigma help explain how prejudice and discrimination lead to inequalities in health and social care. Health and social science combined can make tangible differences, through the innovations they facilitate and by guiding good policy decisions,” she said.

“If we get it right for the most vulnerable, disabled people and their caregivers, we get it right for everyone.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all .

stories.title: Two beluga whales die at Chicago aquarium, including one recently rescued from Marineland
stories.summary: Rain, a 20-year-old female, was relocated from shuttered Niagara Falls water park in mid-August
stories.author: Cybele Mayes-osterman
stories.content:
Two more beluga whales have died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium, including one that was rehomed at the facility just weeks earlier as part of an international effort to rescue Canada’s last captive whales, the aquarium announced Wednesday.

Rain, a 20-year-old female, was the second to die out of a group of four whales that were moved to the Chicago aquarium in mid-August from a shuttered water park in Ontario. A whale named Peekachu died last week as caretakers tried to revitalize it.

The third whale to die, a 34-year-old male named Beethoven, had lived at Shedd Aquarium for decades, the aquarium said in an announcement.

The aquarium did not indicate the cause of the whales’ deaths in its announcement. “Necropsies, blood tests and additional exams” of their bodies are in process, it said.

“These deaths were unexpected and there is still much we do not know about what led to them,” officials said in the statement.

Shedd Aquarium accepted 10 beluga whales as part of the mission to rescue 30 of them and four dolphins at Marineland, a water park in Ontario that closed its doors years ago and lost the ability to care for the animals. The Chicago aquarium announced Tuesday it welcomed the last two of those 10 – young males named Gimli and Yukon – from the Canadian park.

Twenty whales – 19 belugas and one killer whale – had died at Marineland since 2019, according to provincial government data obtained through Freedom-of-Information laws and official statements.

Officials at Shedd Aquarium previously told The Associated Press that moving the beluga whales was a complex, meticulously monitored process. The whales were hoisted in custom-made slings and held in temperature-controlled containers. Since they arrived, their health and behaviour have been monitored on a minute-to-minute basis, they said.

Canadian Minister of Fisheries Joanne Thompson said she was “saddened” to hear of Rain’s death. Canada’s government “has taken reasonable steps to ensure the safe rescue of the whales,” she said in a statement to AP.

“My thoughts are with the care staff who worked tirelessly to support Rain and the other belugas.”

Georgia Aquarium, SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, and Oceanogràfic Valencia in Spain are also taking in the animals rescued from Marineland.

The two beluga whales rehomed at Georgia Aquarium are “settling in nicely,” although it will take months before they are fully adjusted, the aquarium said in an email to AP. paragraphs: Two more beluga whales have died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium, including one that was rehomed at the facility just weeks earlier as part of an international effort to rescue Canada’s last captive whales, the aquarium announced Wednesday.

Rain, a 20-year-old female, was the second to die out of a group of four whales that were moved to the Chicago aquarium in mid-August from a shuttered water park in Ontario. A whale named Peekachu died last week as caretakers tried to revitalize it.
The third whale to die, a 34-year-old male named Beethoven, had lived at Shedd Aquarium for decades, the aquarium said in an announcement.
The aquarium did not indicate the cause of the whales’ deaths in its announcement. “Necropsies, blood tests and additional exams” of their bodies are in process, it said.
“These deaths were unexpected and there is still much we do not know about what led to them,” officials said in the statement.

Shedd Aquarium accepted 10 beluga whales as part of the mission to rescue 30 of them and four dolphins at Marineland, a water park in Ontario that closed its doors years ago and lost the ability to care for the animals. The Chicago aquarium announced Tuesday it welcomed the last two of those 10 – young males named Gimli and Yukon – from the Canadian park.
Twenty whales – 19 belugas and one killer whale – had died at Marineland since 2019, according to provincial government data obtained through Freedom-of-Information laws and official statements.

Officials at Shedd Aquarium previously told The Associated Press that moving the beluga whales was a complex, meticulously monitored process. The whales were hoisted in custom-made slings and held in temperature-controlled containers. Since they arrived, their health and behaviour have been monitored on a minute-to-minute basis, they said.

Canadian Minister of Fisheries Joanne Thompson said she was “saddened” to hear of Rain’s death. Canada’s government “has taken reasonable steps to ensure the safe rescue of the whales,” she said in a statement to AP.
“My thoughts are with the care staff who worked tirelessly to support Rain and the other belugas.”

stories.title: Producer Perry Rosemond created the Canadian TV classic King of Kensington
stories.summary: After dropping out of law school to become an actor, he instead found success working behind the scenes on variety shows, comedies and hockey broadcasts in Canada
stories.author: Frank B. Edwards
stories.content:
In the mid-1950s, when Perry Rosemond was a student at the University of Manitoba, his interest in campus theatre was hurting his academic marks but winning such good reviews that director John Hirsch invited him to join the newly launched Manitoba Theatre Centre in 1958.

A year later at age 22, Mr. Rosemond hatched a new plan that ultimately changed his life.

“I would drop out of law school. I would go to join my Catholic actress girlfriend in Toronto, and I would become a huge television star,” he deadpanned to an audience of retired Toronto executives in 2018 before delivering his punchline. “Well, one can only imagine my Jewish parents’ surprise and delight. ‘Now why didn’t we think of that?’”

In 1959, he headed to Toronto with one of his Manitoba Theatre Centre castmates, 28-year-old Gordon Pinsent, a displaced Newfoundlander who was boarding at the Rosemond home while moonlighting as a dance instructor after a stint in the Canadian Army.

In Toronto, the pair rented rooms at a University of Toronto fraternity and launched their professional careers. Mr. Pinsent’s first part was as a corpse in a TV show after Mr. Rosemond was promoted from dead body to a two-line role and a new actor was needed for the slab.

But the friends’ acclaim on the stage in Winnipeg did not lead to easy success in Toronto, and Mr. Rosemond returned home alone to the Manitoba Theatre Centre a year later after credited roles in two CBC television series, Hudson’s Bay and General Motors’ Theatre . Unable to live off his acting, he took a job with Winnipeg’s CBC station as a television producer/director for $4,200 a year.

His duties included producing both Winnipeg metro news and a popular weekly country and Western variety show called Red River Jamboree that was beamed across Canada. While the work schedule was gruelling, it proved to be good training for a career spent working on big-time variety programs and sitcoms.

Over the next 55 years, he worked with such stars as Dean Martin, Johnny Cash, Donny and Marie Osmond and David Steinberg, and gave breaks to dozens of gifted young comedians including Martin Short, John Candy, Howie Mandel and Mike Myers. Millions of Canadians regularly tuned into his 1970s hit series, King of Kensington , and, later, The Royal Canadian Air Farce, which ran on CBC-TV for 16 seasons. In 2003, he was named to the Order of Canada for his contribution to CBC television.

Mr. Rosemond died in Toronto on Aug. 20 at the age of 89.

Born Nov. 15, 1936, to Max and Mona (Magid) Rosemond in Winnipeg’s ethnically diverse North End neighbourhood, Perry Rosemond was raised in a bustling household shared with a dozen cousins, aunts and uncles.

His father’s family had immigrated from Russia and his mother’s came from Ukraine. The couple worked together in Winnipeg’s thriving garment trade. He used to joke that his parents were so poor when he was born that they couldn’t afford to give him a middle name.

As their business grew, the Rosemonds were able to send their only child to university. After earning a Bachelor of Arts degree, he dropped out of law school in his first year.

By the time CBC’s hugely popular Red River Jamboree ended in 1965, Mr. Rosemond was back in Toronto looking for work at CBC Television. His first success there was an innovative current affairs program hosted by teenagers called Through the Eyes of Tomorrow that ran from early 1966 to 1969. Topics included birth control, LSD, the Ku Klux Klan and John Lennon.

Busy as always, he served as executive director of Mr. Dressup in 1967 and, in 1968, produced Children of the World in co-operation with Unicef, portraying humanitarian projects through the eyes of children in 11 different countries. An episode of that series, The Trumpet , won the Unicef Prize at Japan’s prestigious educational broadcasting awards in 1968. In 1972, Mr. Rosemond became the first executive producer of the Canadian segments created for CBC’s edition of Sesame Street .

Despite being told by his agent, Sandy Werner, that “you won’t make a dime” with documentaries, Mr. Rosemond dabbled with news and documentary programs throughout his career. Between 1967 and 1969, he directed nine episodes of CBC’s Telescope biography series including a profile of his old friend Mr. Pinsent, who had stuck with acting and starred in Quentin Durgens, M.P. for four years, launching himself into Canadian stardom.

In that same period, Mr. Rosemond worked as a segment producer for CBC’s The Way It Is, where he collaborated with hosts Barbara Frum, Peter Desbarats and Patrick Watson. The big-budget Sunday night newsmagazine folded in 1969 after two seasons.

A decade later, he directed several episodes of Pbs’s Steve Allen’s Meeting of Minds where four actors portraying important historical figures from different eras, such as Karl Marx and Catherine the Great, discussed current affairs. The program won an Emmy for outstanding informational series and several acting/writing nominations. Mr. Allen also won a personal Peabody Award.

Perhaps Mr. Rosemond’s best-loved series was a sitcom he created for his early theatre mentor Mr. Hirsch, who had become CBC’s head of drama in 1974. Both he and Mr. Hirsch knew Winnipeg’s North End well, so the multiethnicity and themes of King of Kensington were familiar territory.

Running from 1975 to 1980, the series starred Al Waxman who had grown up in Toronto’s Polish-Jewish community. To gain a wider audience, they set it in Toronto’s Kensington Market rather than Winnipeg. (Mr. Waxman and Mr. Rosemond already knew each other. They attended the same acting workshops in 1959 and appeared together on a General Motors Presents production of The Apprenticeship of Duddy Kravitz. )

Although Mr. Rosemond used to claim the show’s premiere “got the worst review in the history of TV Guide,” King of Kensington quickly became a Canadian television icon for its portrayal of Larry King, a well-meaning neighbourhood mensch who befriended everyone.

Fifteen years after it ended in 1980, The Globe and Mail’s John Haslett Cuff wrote, “ King of Kensington was a traditional domestic comedy, exceptional only in that it was overtly Canadian, full of topical references and marked by a geographical and cultural specificity that was fresh and endearing to domestic viewers.”

Mr. Rosemond’s role as producer and occasional director of the series’ 111 episodes did not prevent him from taking on production jobs on other successful television productions. Constantly flying between Toronto and Los Angeles, he produced and directed Abc’s gala 50th anniversary special in 1979 that featured a range of the network’s stars from Tony Bennett to John Travolta, 24 episodes of The David Steinberg Show (the uber successful comic was another North Winnipeg alum), 19 episodes of Donny & Marie (1975 to 1979), and about half a dozen episodes of comedian Norm Crosby’s The Comedy Shop (1978 to 1980) that introduced many young standups to a large American audience.

One of his proudest innovations was bringing live theatre to television. In 1983 he taped Cold Storage , a successful Broadway play starring Martin Balsam and Len Cariou, at Toronto’s Ryerson Theatre. When The Globe’s Rick Groen watched rehearsals, Mr. Rosemond explained, “The constant is that there has to remain some element of theatricality in the televised production. … As you can see, we’re groping with the genre.”

But the 47-year-old director still had his theatrical chops, and the production won him an ACE Award from the National Cable Television Association for “excellence in national performance and craft.” He proudly displayed the trophy in his living room for the rest of his life.

On one of his countless flights between Canada and L.A., he met Toronto-born realtor Nora Niddery who was unhappily stuck in the plane’s smoking section. His charming manner overcame Ms. Niddery’s aversion to his smouldering cigarette and the pair married in the early eighties. They moved back to Toronto in 1985 when Mr. Rosemond began a five-year stint as president of Molstar Productions, a sports and entertainment consortium led by brewer The Molson Companies Ltd.

His most prominent program was Hockey Night in Canada to which he added the 26-year-old referee Ron MacLean as a level-headed counterbalance to the more abrasively flamboyant Don Cherry .

Ms. Rosemond remembers her husband’s love of sports, explaining with a laugh, “Perry liked anything that had a ball. … We were always right at the glass with the pucks smashing it.”

Even as a sports producer, Mr. Rosemond found time to dabble in comedy, launching the American sitcom Starting from Scratch with Connie Stevens in 1988, and then co-creating (and writing) a British spin-off, Close to Home , the following year. He also found time to sit in at Mark Breslin’s crowded and smoke-filled Toronto comedy club, YukYuk’s.

“It was pretty hard to be involved in comedy and not know Perry Rosemond,” says Mr. Breslin, who expanded his original 1976 Church Street cellar into a national comedy club franchise. “He was a legend. … He was one of the greatest variety producers in the golden age of TV.”

Mr. Rosemond was particularly fascinated by the young comic actors on stage at Second City. In 1979, he produced a failed pilot for the Second City Comedy Show with host John Candy. Mr. Candy, along with Martin Short and Andrea Martin, also made appearances on episodes of The Comedy Shop and The David Steinberg Show . As well, Ms. Martin, Eugene Levy and Mike Myers appeared in King of Kensington , and in the early 90s, Mr. Rosemond directed Sctv cast member Joe Flaherty in 15 episodes of Maniac Mansion .

Mr. Rosemond’s greatest comedy challenge was the adaptation of CBC’s beloved 20-year-old radio program, Royal Canadian Air Farce , for television. A New Year’s Eve TV special in 1992 proved that he could work with the tight-knit, four-person troupe and the show was launched in fall 1993, running for 15 years with Mr. Rosemond at the helm. Its weekly audience never fell below one million viewers.

“He faced the challenge of coming into a tight group,” founding member Don Ferguson recalls. “We trusted him and he later said it was the best gig of his career.

“He was good at analyzing the script and had a fabulous eye for the core of comedy. His laughter was genuine.”

Calvin, Mr. Rosemond’s second son, born in 1990 in Toronto, appeared on stage with the cast in Grade 2 and later became a grip and worked in catering. “I never heard a negative word. Everyone just admired him. … They said he was the best director they ever worked with,” he says.

Mr. Rosemond and his earlier wife Annie Rosemond had a son, Michael, born in 1971 in L.A. Mr. Rosemond leaves his wife, Nora; his two sons (both lawyers); and a grandson, Maxwell.

stories.title: Ottawa lays out plan for AI data centres as community backlash grows
stories.summary: A.I. Minister Evan Solomon says the government understands Canadians are concerned about noise, electricity and water use of large-scale data centres.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The federal Liberals are attempting to address Canadian concerns over the impact of large-scale artificial intelligence data centres by introducing a set of voluntary industry-backed “principles” that they say will guide new facilities’ construction.

At the same time, the government is acknowledging that “we don’t have the jurisdiction” to enforce those principles.

In Markham, Ont., Thursday, AI Minister Evan Solomon unveiled the federal government’s five-point “national framework” for how data centres should be built across the country. The move comes after high-profile opposition to new AI-servicing facilities in multiple Canadian cities.

The set of principles are entirely voluntary, backed by some of the largest international companies pursuing generative artificial intelligence programs, and are not binding in any way. Solomon stressed that decisions on data centre approvals and locations will still be up to provinces and municipalities.

The proposals suggest the federal government would prefer data centres create “lasting local benefits,” not shift electricity costs onto Canadians, minimize water use and “environmental impacts,” be transparent about their “local impacts” and bring strategic value to the country.

“All the questions Canadians are asking about how are we going to build the digital infrastructure of the future are excellent questions … we get them,” Solomon told reporters at a press conference.

“What will AI do for my community? Who is it going to benefit? Where is it going to be built? How much water will it use? Is it going to affect my power bill? Is there going to be a net benefit to my community?”

The federal framework has the endorsement of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, and “signatories” include U.S. web giants Amazon, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, as well as Bell Canada and Telus.

Are there any teeth to the plans?

Asked if the federal government would monitor whether companies are complying with the framework, Solomon suggested they would not.

“Any data centre first requires power allocation, that’s the provincial regulator, then they’re going to go to a municipality and say ‘we’d like to locate here,’” Solomon said.

“And what we are saying in the (federal) framework … is to provide reliable and verifiable information on the standards that they set. Those are going to be enforced by the municipalities or the provinces, because that is their enforcement, we don’t have the jurisdiction.”

A July study released by York University researchers Lyndsey Rolheiser and Alexander Carlo found that while there are just four active AI-specific data centres operating in Canada, there are an additional 49 facilities either announced or currently under construction.

The rapid proliferation of AI data centres — required by U.S. companies locked into an artificial intelligence arms race against their rivals — has led to significant opposition in America.

Community concerns generally revolve around the massive water and electricity consumption used to run the facilities, as well as noise pollution inflicted on nearby homes from backup diesel generators, constantly running electronics, and cooling fans.

The massive amount of power used by AI data centres have also put additional stress onto aging North American energy infrastructure, increasing the risk of blackouts.

AI security intelligence company 10a Labs tracks local opposition to data centre construction. In the company’s most recent Data Centre Watch Report, they estimate that at least 75 projects marketed as worth $130 billion U.S. were “disrupted” by “local opposition” to the projects in the first quarter of 2026 alone.

What's driving AI data centre backlash in Canada?

Canada hasn’t seen that level of widespread opposition, largely because the country hasn’t seen the same scale of proposed data centre projects to date.

Opposition to new data centre construction in Hamilton, Ont., became a flashpoint earlier this year — but that city’s council voted in July to reject a one-year moratorium on development.

There are signs, however, that Canadians are souring on the prospect of AI products in their lives.

Ipsos’ annual AI Monitor report, released in June, found that Canadians are among the least enthusiastic populations for the technology out of 32 countries surveyed.

The reported noted that the share of Canadians who expressed excitement about AI products and services was just 26 per cent, down five percentage points from the year before. Canadians are among the most nervous when it comes to the technology — with 67 per cent saying so, a full 17 percentage points higher than the international average.

Few Canadians believe AI will improve their country’s economy (14 per cent) or the job market (11 per cent) in the medium term, and just 27 per cent trust companies that use AI will protect their personal data.

All that makes for an uphill battle for Solomon, tasked by Prime Minister Mark Carney to pitch the broader adoption of AI tools across the public and private sector.

“There’s a big rush to build because of this new technology, and you gotta build right,” Solomon said.

“We want to attract the investment, but be transparent about it. Though we need to build at speeds we haven’t seen before, (that’s) not at the expense of our values.”

As Solomon was making his announcement Thursday, the website Downdetector reported outages affecting OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and X.com’s Grok artificial intelligence services.

With files from Global News’ Sean Boynton.

stories.title: Trump says his threat to tariff Canadian aircraft started from a conversation with a wealthy friend
stories.summary: The unprompted remark appeared to be a glimpse into what was behind his threat to tariff Canadian aircraft by 50 per cent back in January
stories.author: Swikar Oli
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said 50 per cent tariffs targeting Canada’s aircraft industry was prompted by a complaint from a friend who couldn’t buy the corporate jet of his choosing.

Trump made the remark during a six-minute-long rant about Canada in the Oval Office on Wednesday.

“I had a case about a week ago, where a friend of mine was buying a Gulfstream jet, and he said, ‘You know, it’s a crazy thing. We’re not able — that Canada won’t certify Gulfstream,’” Trump said.

“Gulfstream is the best private jet, you know, the best of the best,” he noted, adding that Canada “won’t certify it because they make a competitor, Bombardier Global Express.”

The unprompted remark appeared to be a glimpse into what was behind his threat to decertify Canadian-made aircraft and impose 50 per cent tariff on sales back in January.

The friend was close to Gulfstream, Trump said, and had asked the head of the company to arrange a call with him and explain the situation.

“We called, we spoke,” he said, adding that the head of Gulfstream told him the American manufacturer had spent $60 million trying to get certified in Canada for “nine years without success.”

“So I immediately said, ‘I’m putting a major tariff on Bombardier and other things that they sent until they’re certified,'” Trump said.

“They got certified in two hours.”

He had spoken to the prime minister, Trump said, without naming Mark Carney directly.

“Essentially (Gulfstream) can’t sell any plane in anything having to do with Canada, but Bombardier has free rein over the United States,” Trump said, while noting they were both “very good planes.”

“I said, ‘So what we’re going to do is, we’re going to charge you tariffs on various products, including Bombardier,’” he added. “We put a nice big tariff. And within 30 minutes, I guess it took maybe less, everything got certified.”

In February, Transport Canada granted regulatory approval to two business jets produced by Gulfstream. It came nearly four weeks after Trump had threatened to decertify Bombardier and impose 50 per cent tariffs on all aircraft sold by Canada to the United States.

Trump’s anecdote was part of a litany of complaints he had about Canada’s trade practices amid a trade war between the two countries covering roughly 5 per cent of Canadian exports. Trump was answering a question on his plans to renew trade talks with Ottawa.

In his response, Trump said the U.S. does not need “anything” from Canada, adding that its leaders were “emboldened,” and was “toughest” to deal with. The remarks were made during a meeting with travel executives to mark the end of the summer season.

“We can’t lose 60 to $100 billion dollars for the privilege of allowing them to make cars; we don’t want their cars,” Trump added. However, in reality, the U.S. runs a trade surplus with Canada in the auto sector, according to RBC.

Trump also seemingly voiced displeasure at Doug Ford, who he referred to as a “slob” without naming the Ontario premier directly.

He also repeated an unfounded claim that Canada barred U.S. banks from operating within its borders. ”I think they have six or seven major banks here, (but) we don’t have our banks there,” Trump said.

That assertion has been contradicted by the Canadian Bankers Association, which pointed out in 2025 that 16 U.S. based bank subsidiaries and branches operate in Canada.

stories.title: Alberta independence ballot count expected to run deep into morning after vote
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says results from separation question will be reported before others
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Elections Alberta says much of the country will likely be asleep when it finishes tabulating millions of expected ballots and announces the results of the province’s independence vote next month.

The results from the separation question – which asks voters whether they wish to remain in Canada or lay the legal groundwork for a second, binding secession referendum – are expected on Oct. 20 between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. local time, the agency said.

Results from the other nine referendum questions, about issues such as immigration and the Constitution, likely won’t be publicly reported until the next morning, ON Oct. 21.

Elections Alberta on Thursday provided some details on how it expects the 10-question referendum will unfold. It is the first time a vote in Alberta has been solely dedicated to referendum questions.

The gargantuan task has stressed the electoral agency, which has been forced to respond to a tsunami of changes to provincial elections law in recent years under Premier Danielle Smith’s government. Many of those have focused on making it easier for Albertans to take part in what she calls “direct democracy.”

Elections Alberta says it has received 290,000 applications for mail-in ballots for the Oct. 19 referendum, which is four times higher than in the 2023 general election. The ballots list 10 questions, including one asking if Alberta should stay in Canada or if there should be a second, binding referendum on separation.

The Canadian Press

“Not only has Alberta never done anything like this – nowhere in Canada has done anything like this before,” Dallas Stoesz, deputy chief electoral officer, told reporters at a news conference.

“Yes, we’ve had referendums. Yes, there’s been millions of ballots. But not concentrated like this, or across a 10-question event.”

While Ms. Smith’s question on secession has dominated the conversation in recent months, she is also hoping voters will endorse nine additional questions that propose dramatically curtailing the public services Alberta offers certain immigrants and starting conversations with other provinces about lobbying for changes to the Canadian Constitution.

Elections Alberta will first count and report the votes for the secession question and then move to counting ballots for the nine others, the agency said.

Ballots will be reported live from each of Alberta’s 87 electoral districts after polls close at 8 p.m. on Oct. 19, Jennifer Maskoske, the agency’s director of elections operations, said.

Smaller, less populous ridings will likely report results earlier in the night, Ms. Maskoske said. Voter turnout will also determine how long the count takes, she added.

The referendum will be Alberta’s first provincewide vote to be hand-counted since Ms. Smith banned the use of electronic tabulators for vote counting, arguing the machines have failed to produce faster results or increase confidence in elections.

The extreme workload facing Elections Alberta has fuelled concern over the agency’s ability to run a smooth referendum. The agency said roughly 35,000 people have applied to work the referendum – still well short of its target of hiring 60,000 people. The Globe reported last month that the agency is recruiting a pool of skilled, experienced election staff from other provinces to help.

Elections Alberta will have 48 hours to count the ballots, though provincial law doesn’t dictate the consequences for failing to meet that deadline. If turnout matches that of Alberta’s 2023 election at 1.7-million people – roughly 60 per cent of all eligible voters – the agency will be forced to count at least 17-million ballots in that window.

This week, the first special ballots – otherwise known as mail-in ballots – were sent to some of the roughly 290,000 Alberta residents who have requested them. Until last year, special ballots required voters to sign a declaration form testifying that they couldn’t otherwise vote in-person.

Ms. Smith’s government removed that requirement last year. Now, any voter in Alberta can request a special ballot in lieu of going to the polls.

Yet, despite the change, voters this week reported that their special ballots include a section requiring signed testimony that they’re unable to vote in-person, underlined by the threat of a fine up to $50,000 or prison time.

Ms. Stoesz, the deputy chief electoral officer, said electors can strike out that specific declaration without being penalized, and it will be removed from all ballot packages that haven’t already been sent.

“If electors are uncomfortable, if electors want, they can strike that out on their declaration,” she said. “[If] they complete the rest of the declaration, sign it, send it back, we will accept those.”

Elections Alberta did not say how much it will cost to run the election, but a former Alberta chief electoral officer recently estimated the vote will cost roughly $120-million. (The 2023 provincial election cost about $37-million.)

Ms. Stoesz said Elections Alberta will send the final budget to a government committee after the referendum.
