stories.title: New vertical $20 bill featuring King Charles III unveiled by Bank of Canada
stories.summary: This is the first Canadian paper currency to feature King Charles III, whose image replaces that of his mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada has unveiled a new vertical $20 banknote featuring King Charles III.

In keeping with tradition, the $20 note features a portrait of Canada’s Head of State, with King Charles’s “advocacy of sustainable action and his commitment to the environment are reflected in the many botanical elements on the note,” the national bank said in a news release.

Canada’s 13 provinces and territories are represented on the note with their respective “floral emblems,” along with several culturally significant flowers among the country’s Indigenous population, including wild strawberries, Western red cedar, braided sweetgrass and arctic cotton.

The notes also reference the country’s “natural heritage” and “Canadian ingenuity,” Governor General Louise Arbour said in a statement Thursday .

Quotes from artists that recognize Canada’s bilingualism, and celebrations of social advancements and scientific discoveries that have “helped define our place in the world,” also appear beside the King.

“Our currency affirms our sovereignty and our determination to define ourselves in the eyes of the world on our own terms,” Arbour said.

As is traditional on Canadian currency, the maple leaf appears in several design elements, some of which serve as key security features, making this banknote “unmistakably Canadian” and easy to authenticate.

The note also pays tribute to Canadian troops who served during the First World War, with an illustration of the Canadian National Vimy Memorial and poppies etched on it.

“The creation of a bank note involves a tremendous amount of collaborative work. Congratulations to all of the partners and professionals who have contributed to this effort over the past few years,” Arbour said.

“From the multidisciplinary team at the Bank of Canada to its various partners and other organizations, notably the Indigenous Advisory Circle, Veterans Affairs Canada and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, many people have lent their expertise and dedication to this project,” Arbour continued.

“You can all be proud of the result: a new note that is safe, accessible and meaningful for Canadians,” she added.

Canada’s bank notes have featured portraits of the sovereign for decades. Queen Elizabeth II first appeared on a series of $20 bills at just eight years old, when she was still Princess Elizabeth and was honoured over her 70-year reign on numerous iterations of notes.

Her childhood bill is the only portrait of the future queen as a young girl to appear on a bank note.

The Royal Canadian Mint first started circulating coins with King Charles’s face on them in 2023.

Other Canadian figures appearing on currency include former prime minister Wilfred Laurier, Nova Scotian civil rights activist Viola Desmond, and eventually Terry Fox, who was selected to appear on a new version of the $5 bill , which is yet to be released.

The government said when Fox was announced, it hoped it would inspire more Canadians to give $5 to the cause Terry Fox championed.

Laurier will move from the $5 banknote to appear on the next version of the $50 note.

stories.title: Canada’s Auger-Aliassime eliminated in second round of US Open
stories.summary: Félix Auger-Aliassime's run at the 2026 US Open was unexpectedly short.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Félix Auger-Aliassime’s run at the 2026 US Open was unexpectedly short.

Auger-Aliassime, the third seed in the men’s draw, was soundly defeated 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2, 6-2 by Russia’s Karen Khachanov in second-round action Thursday at the hardcourt Grand Slam.

The 26-year-old Canadian struggled with his serve throughout the match. He was accurate on just 58 per cent of first serves and faced 20 break points, surrendering seven.

Auger-Aliassime also had eight double faults and had 47 unforced errors to Khachanov’s 30. Both players had 12 aces.

Auger-Aliassime advanced to the semifinals of last year’s US Open before losing to runner-up Jannik Sinner. His early exit this year puts his career-high world ranking of No. 4 in jeopardy.

In first-round women’s doubles action, Leylah Fernandez of Laval, Que., and partner Janice Tjen of Indonesia cruised to a 6-1, 6-1 win over Slovenia’s Nika Radisic and Isabelle Haverlag of the Netherlands. Second seeds Gabriela Dabrowski of Ottawa and Luisa Stefani of Brazil faced Russia’s Irina Khromacheva and Anastasia Detiuc of Czechia in a later match.

Fernandez was set to return to singles action Friday with a third-round match against third-seed Jessica Pegula of the United States. In Friday’s third-round men’s action, Denis Shapovalov of Richmond Hill, Ont., was set to take on eight-seeded American Ben Shelton.

stories.title: Ontario court denies Toronto woman with bipolar disorder emergency access to Maid
stories.summary: Claire Brosseau’s legal battles underscore debate over whether patients with mental illness should be able to access medical help to die
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
An Ontario court has denied a Toronto woman living with bipolar disorder emergency access to medical assistance in dying.

In May, Claire Brosseau requested an emergency stay from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to immediately end her life with medical help. She is also suing the federal government over its decision to bar Maid in cases of mental illness.

In a written decision Thursday, Justice Carissima Mathen described how Ms. Brosseau presented compelling evidence of the harm she has suffered and will likely continue to endure.

Justice Mathen also noted the considerable interests on the other side including “Parliament’s role to make policy decisions on sensitive social issues and the proper interpretation of the Charter rights in play.”

Advocacy organization Dying With Dignity Canada said Ms. Brosseau and her legal team will take some time to review the court’s decision. In a statement on Thursday, it shared her reaction.

“I am disappointed yet not surprised that my emergency motion was denied,” Ms. Brosseau, 49, said in the statement, adding that it amounts to an additional barrier extending her suffering.

“This is not living – I do not have a life.”

Maid remains against the law for patients whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness.

Ms. Brosseau, who has bipolar 1, a form of bipolar disorder, has said that she must be able to access Maid because she endures “constant pain and unrelenting torment.”

An Ontario judge denied an emergency motion that would have allowed Claire Brosseau, who suffers solely from mental illness, to apply for a medically assisted death. But the judge insisted the Attorney-General of Canada promptly respond to Brosseau's constitutional challenge that she launched two years ago.

The Canadian Press

In August, 2024, Ms. Brosseau and Dying With Dignity Canada sued the federal government for barring Maid access to patients like herself. That matter remains before the courts.

Justice Mathen ordered the Attorney-General of Canada and Ms. Brosseau to take steps toward an urgent case conference on that suit within 14 days.

Ms. Brosseau’s legal battles – to die with the help of medical professionals – underscores a complex policy debate over whether patients with mental illness should be able to access medical help to die.

In July, Joseph Cheng, senior counsel for the Attorney-General of Canada, urged the Ontario Superior Court of Justice to consider findings from a special parliamentary committee.

A majority of the special committee’s members recommended this spring that the federal government disallow patients with mental illness from being able to access Maid early next year.

Maid access for patients with mental illness is currently set to become legal in March, 2027, but the timeline could change if the federal government introduces legislation.

Three sources told The Globe and Mail in May that the government is open to introducing such a bill. The Globe did not identify the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the government’s plans.

The following month, Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the matter was serious and that he planned to take time to review the parliamentary committee’s report, as well as dissenting opinions.

Maid first became legal a decade ago, in June, 2016. The law established access to the procedure for Canadians whose deaths were deemed “reasonably foreseeable.”

In 2021, the country’s Maid law was expanded after a Quebec Superior Court decision two years earlier found that the original law was unconstitutional.

The amended law expanded criteria to allow patients with incurable conditions to seek to end their lives, known as “track two” Maid.

A two-year temporary exclusion was put in place to give time to study the delivery of Maid for patients with mental illness, but implementation has been twice delayed.

This spring, the special parliamentary committee held hearings to determine if Canada is ready to allow Maid for patients with mental illness.

A report produced by a majority of its members said the committee heard “significant complexities and risks, grave concerns and deep divisions that continue to accompany this issue.”

It also recommended that Ottawa amend the Criminal Code to indefinitely exclude patients from becoming eligible for Maid if their sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness.

In July, Ms. Brosseau’s lawyer, Michael Fenrick, argued before Justice Mathen that the parliamentary committee’s findings should not be considered as part of Ms. Brosseau’s request.

He said the findings did not reflect the will of Parliament and that Ms. Brosseau’s motion to seek Maid was brought on an “urgent basis.”

stories.title: Toronto’s Rogers Stadium suffers storm damage
stories.summary: Wednesday’s storm dumped more than 100 millimetres of rain on some neighbourhoods, causing power outages and flooding
stories.content:
The beleaguered Rogers Stadium suffered “significant” damage after a powerful storm swept through Toronto on Wednesday evening.

Photos of the open-air Downsview Park stadium show blue bleachers strewn across partially collapsed grandstands.

The sign outside the open-air venue also looked to be damaged, partially stripped of its red cover.

Live Nation Canada, which operates the stadium, said the venue sustained “significant damage” but no one was hurt. It did not immediately provide details about the extent of the damage.

It’s the latest setback for a stadium beset by issues since it opened last summer.

Live Nation said it would make adjustments after concertgoers initially complained the 50,000-person venue seemed ill-prepared to handle crowds and local officials raised noise complaints.

The venue’s most recent show was on Tuesday with singer Chris Stapleton and it’s next scheduled to welcome AC/DC on Sept. 16.

Wednesday’s storm walloped Toronto with strong winds and dumped more than 100 millimetres of rain on some hard-hit neighbourhoods, prompting widespread power outages and flooding.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Rogers Stadium last hosted a show on Aug. 23 with K-pop band BTS. The venue’s most recent show was on Tuesday, Sept. 1 with singer Chris Stapleton.

stories.title: Incumbent Quebec minister directs F-word at Trump in radio interview
stories.summary: Montreal - An incumbent Quebec minister is being compared to Ontario Premier Doug Ford after directing the F-word at American President Donald Trump in a radio interview on Wednesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - An incumbent Quebec minister is being compared to Ontario Premier Doug Ford after directing the F-word at American President Donald Trump in a radio interview on Wednesday.

“F — k you, e — i,” said Bernard Drainville bluntly, combining English and French swear words while discussing the breakdown of trade negotiations between Canada and the United States.

The incumbent economy minister said he found it infuriating that the American president would try to undermine Canadian sovereignty.

He was referring to reports that the United States wanted to prohibit Canada from entering into trade agreements with other countries, and said he believes the Trump administration had a “genuine desire to say, ‘Canada is mine,’” with its final offer in the negotiations.

Drainville later said on social media that his choice of words was inappropriate but his indignation remains.

Before his post, Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette had told journalists she wanted Drainville to walk back his comment.

Drainville vied for the Coalition Avenir Québec leadership earlier this year, but lost the race to Fréchette.

On social media, Drainville’s comments drew comparisons to Ford, who told Trump to “kiss (his) ass” in late August.

Daniel Béland, a McGill University political science professor, said it’s possible Drainville took a cue from Ford, since Fréchette’s party has been emphasizing the trade war with the United States during the electoral campaign.

He said he wasn’t surprised to see Fréchette call Drainville to order.

“Christine Fréchette did not seem to appreciate Drainville’s slip of the tongue and called him to order. Fréchette’s style is very different from Ford’s, so her reaction is understandable,” he said.

However, Danielle Pilette, a political science professor at Université du Québec à Montréal, said there are major differences between Drainville and Ford’s comments.

While Ford is the premier of Ontario, Drainville is in campaign mode.

Pilette said she believes Drainville is trying to reignite anger and fear toward Trump through personal attacks and that it could benefit the party as a whole. She said the Coalition Avenir Québec is relying on “typical CAQ doublespeak.”

“Fréchette gives no indication that she disagrees with Drainville’s remarks because it could be advantageous and give the campaign fresh momentum,” she said.

Fréchette herself took the stage and declared Trump her “real opponent” on the first day of the electoral campaign.

However, Fréchette wants to maintain a clean image by asking Drainville to retract his comments, Pilette added.

She said the incumbent premier has been benefiting from her proximity to Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has been more temperate in his approach to the American president.

“Fréchette is asking to project an image that is compatible with Carney’s, but that doesn’t mean the CAQ isn’t benefiting … from (Drainville)‘s more populist attacks against Trump,” said Pilette.

The professor believes the difference in their approach isn’t simply one of personality, but also reflects the ridings they want to represent.

“It’s not just a good cop, bad cop situation,” Pilette said.

Drainville is running in Lévis, ON the south shore of Quebec City, which Pilette said is largely made up of entrepreneurs who sell and export to the United States.

Meanwhile, Fréchette has been representing the riding of Sanguinet and is running in Trois-Rivières, two metropolitan areas.

“It’s a matter of targeting districts that might try to vote differently, and bombarding them with this kind of doubletalk tailored to specific district profiles — that is, the ridings — that are essential to the CAQ,” Pilette said.

When former premier François Legault stepped down in January, the Coalition Avenir Québec had tanked in the polls and was on its way to being erased from the legislature.

But recent polls show the Coalition Avenir Québec catching up to the Parti Québécois, which has been leading in public opinion since 2023.

Quebecers will be heading to the polls for the election on Oct. 5.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

stories.title: I left the U.S. for Canada a decade ago. These plays and musicals taught me what it means to be Canadian
stories.summary: These works made me fall in love with the Great White North
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
On a steamy September morning a decade ago, my mother and I crammed her car full of everything we figured I’d need for a Canadian theatre degree. My mom had bought me a winter coat I was certain would be too warm – I discovered by October that it wasn’t – and I had carefully packed a considerable collection of Broadway songbooks.

No part of me thought I would someday write about theatre for The Globe and Mail. At age 18, ON the 10-hour drive from suburban Baltimore to the University of Ottawa, I hardly thought I’d stay in Canada long enough to finish the degree.

But the longer I spent in Ottawa’s arts scene – in theatre classes, in auditions, at the National Arts Centre – the more I learned what it means to thrive in this country. My first year in Canada, I took a theatre exam in a University of Ottawa ice rink, an experience so surreally Canadian that I half-expected the final to be proctored by a beaver or some human embodiment of the word “sorry.”

Indeed, my experience of Canada is inseparable from my experience of its theatre. Sure, I measure my adulthood by the usual milestones – birthdays, apartments, jobs – but as someone who sees 220-plus shows a year, I also measure it in plays. I remember vividly the first time I read Infinity by Hannah Moscovitch, sticky with sweat in a Gatineau studio; I remember, too, the way I wept when I saw Kat Sandler’s adaptation of Anne of Green Gables .

Here are the 10 plays and musicals that have taught me what it means to be Canadian. They’re not necessarily the best shows I’ve seen, or even my favourites – that’s what end-of-year lists are for – but they’re the works that made me fall in love with this country and with its extraordinary community of theatre-makers.

‘da Kink in My Hair by Trey Anthony

This enduring play about a hair salon on Eglinton Street West was the first show I saw in Canada, at the National Arts Centre’s Babs Asper Theatre. I remember I admired the way the work peeled back how it feels to exist as a Black woman in this country; with each additional character, I felt myself learning something new about the place I had chosen to call home.

The Assembly by Alex Ivanovici, Annabel Soutar and Brett Watson

For my first few years in Ottawa – coincidentally, also the first few years of Donald Trump’s presidency – I somewhat avoided political theatre, not feeling the need to see the vitriol of my Twitter feed replicated on stage.

The Assembly , however, was formative for me as an American still finding my sea legs in Canadian discourse. As a devotee of verbatim theatre, I appreciated seeing North American politics debated with so much nuance – the play’s script, assembled from a transcript of four real-life Montrealers discussing a number of hot-button issues, felt like a juicy conversation, rather than a lecture or rant. As a fledgling critic, I loved, too, that the performance I saw in Ottawa responded directly to J. Kelly Nestruck’s review of the show in Toronto.

Come From Away by David Hein and Irene Sankoff

I often joke that, as The Globe’s theatre reporter, I could write exclusively about Come From Away and never run out of stories. Come From Away , about the diverted flights that landed in Newfoundland on Sept. 11, 2001, was the first show I saw in Toronto, and as a critic, it’s the show I’ve seen most often – and in the most places. Travelling to Gander to see where Come From Away takes place was particularly meaningful; so too was seeing the show in a massive American amphitheatre during Trump’s trade war.

PlayMe , hosted by Chris Tolley and Laura Mullin

For a theatre student in Ottawa – and, once the pandemic hit, a theatre critic without access to theatres – CBC’s PlayMe was the ultimate boon.

A podcast that sees Canadian scripts transformed into fully produced (and Foley-produced) audio dramas, PlayMe continues to ensure that audiences from coast to coast can enjoy this country’s hottest new plays, no matter where they might be running. My favourite episodes: Hannah Moscovitch’s What a Young Wife Ought to Know and Leanna Brodie’s translation of Wildfire by David Paquet.

The Master Plan by Michael Healey

Need a crash course on a slice of Canadian history, distilled into its funniest, most absurd form? Michael Healey’s your guy. The Master Plan , Healey’s adaptation of Sideways: The City Google Couldn’t Buy (by my Globe colleague Josh O’Kane), added fascinating historical context to the work I was doing at the time as a breaking news reporter at Toronto’s CP24. I appreciated, too, that the script gave me a fresh understanding of the city I now know better than Baltimore.

A Christmas Carol , directed by Stafford Arima

A hazard of my job is the endless stream of Christmas Carol s that clog my calendar every December. After seeing at least 20 productions in half as many years, I am sick of Scrooge; I care little if Tiny Tim makes it to New Year’s Day.

But Theatre Calgary’s annual production of the classic tale, performed by an enormous cast, is the exception to this rule. Stafford Arima’s staging, which I saw in 2023 on my first-ever trip to Alberta, was jaw-dropping: Its costumes, music and sets were lavish and rich, expansive in ways I had not yet experienced outside of Broadway. I still think often of the festive dance scene – it was utter theatre magic.

William Shakespeare’s As You Like It , a Radical Retelling by Cliff Cardinal

In 2021, Cliff Cardinal’s take on As You Like It was advertised innocuously enough – you’d be forgiven for thinking you’d purchased a ticket to Shakespeare’s famous pastoral comedy – but in reality, the show was a monologue about Canada’s thorny relationship with land acknowledgments, with very little digression into the Bard. Cardinal’s experiment was gutsy and provocative, exactly what this city needed after 18 months of lockdown; even the walkouts from angry patrons who realized they’d been duped were thrilling.

Theatre can be so delightfully punk-rock, and Cardinal’s solo show was an electric reminder of that during an otherwise uncertain time for performing arts in Canada.

Prince Faggot by Jordan Tannahill

I must confess I had to return to my home country to see this one – Canadian playwright Jordan Tannahill’s Lucille Lortel Award-winning play has not yet been produced in Canada. But, trade war aside, I’m profoundly grateful I made the trip to New York to see it in 2025. Tannahill’s script, about what might happen if Prince George of Cambridge were to come out as a gay man, was risky and taut, and one of my favourite evenings in a theatre since starting at The Globe and Mail last January.

It’s worth adding that when I was in theatre school, Tannahill was all but proselytized during my classes – the writer is something of a hometown hero in Ottawa – and his book Theatre of the Unimpressed was central to my decision to become a critic in 2019. To see one of his plays produced so thoughtfully, and at such a large scale, felt like the ultimate full-circle moment.

Casey and Diana by Nick Green

Nick Green’s Casey and Diana , first produced at the Stratford Festival in 2023, was special. A Canadian story of queer inheritance and destiny, the play’s premiere was directed sensitively and artfully by Andrew Kushnir, and its starry cast couldn’t have been better-calibrated to Green’s sardonic – yet hopeful – tone.

You don’t get many Casey and Diana s in a career; the play is my unofficial benchmark for new works at the Stratford Festival, and one special show aside (more on that below), nothing has come close to surpassing it.

Anne of Green Gables , adapted by Kat Sandler

If there were only one production on this list, the Stratford Festival’s 2025 production of Anne of Green Gables would be it. Kat Sandler’s adaptation – my first encounter with Prince Edward Island’s most famous redhead – was a coming-of-age tale when I needed it most, a warm hug of a story about fighting for what’s right and accepting life’s many changes with grace.

I still can’t quite believe I had never read or seen Anne of Green Gables before (hey, blame my parents!), but perhaps more than any on this list, this play showed me that being Canadian isn’t just paying Canadian taxes or enjoying maple syrup. As made clear by Anne Shirley, being Canadian is caring for your friends; it’s enjoying meals and treats made from Canadian ingredients; it’s frolicking in this country’s oceans, lakes and dells.

And, for me, to be Canadian is to spend time in this country’s theatres. It’s the thing I love most, the way I bond with my friends, the way I spend my weekends and holidays.

Yes, after a decade in this country, my elbows are proudly up – or, most nights, tucked politely by my side in the darkness, taking notes on the plays that have shaped not only this country’s mythology, but my own, too.

I still think often of the festive dance scene – it was utter theatre magic.

content_blocks.text: William Shakespeare’s As You Like It , a Radical Retelling by Cliff Cardinal
content_blocks.html: William Shakespeare’s As You Like It, a Radical Retelling by Cliff Cardinal

content_blocks.text: In 2021, Cliff Cardinal’s take on As You Like It was advertised innocuously enough – you’d be forgiven for thinking you’d purchased a ticket to Shakespeare’s famous pastoral comedy – but in reality, the show was a monologue about Canada’s thorny relationship with land acknowledgments, with very little digression into the Bard. Cardinal’s experiment was gutsy and provocative, exactly what this city needed after 18 months of lockdown; even the walkouts from angry patrons who realized they’d been duped were thrilling.

content_blocks.text: Prince Faggot by Jordan Tannahill
content_blocks.html: Prince Faggot by Jordan Tannahill

content_blocks.text: I must confess I had to return to my home country to see this one – Canadian playwright Jordan Tannahill’s Lucille Lortel Award-winning play has not yet been produced in Canada. Tannahill’s script, about what might happen if Prince George of Cambridge were to come out as a gay man, was risky and taut, and one of my favourite evenings in a theatre since starting at The Globe and Mail last January.

stories.title: Internal data reveals 726 Quebecers waiting in hospital for long-term care beds
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - Hundreds of Quebecers are occupying hospital beds while waiting for a spot in a long-term care facility, and the number is on the rise, reveals data released by Santé Québec through an access to information request.
stories.author: Katrine Desautels The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - Hundreds of Quebecers are occupying hospital beds while waiting for a spot in a long-term care facility, and the number is on the rise, reveals data released by Santé Québec through an access to information request.

It’s a situation that raises concerns for patients rights advocates who warn many elderly people now living in an unsuitable living environment and tying up hospital resources.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through an access to information request shows there were 726 hospitalized patients awaiting a spot in a long-term care facility as of Aug. 3.

These are patients who don’t need hospitalization but are waiting in hospital for a long-term care bed because they can no longer live at home due to a medical condition.

At Pierre-Le Gardeur Hospital in Lanaudière, north of Montreal, 43 patients are on the long-term care waiting list. At Charles-Le Moyne Hospital in Montérégie, east of Montreal, there are 37 such patients, and at the Jewish General Hospital in Montreal, there are 30.

The data show an upward trend. There were 568 hospitalized patients awaiting a long-term care facility bed in the 2023—2024 fiscal year. Each year since then, approximately 50 more patients have found themselves in this situation.

According to patients’ rights advocate Paul Brunet, the increase was to be expected given an aging population.

Both Brunet’s organization and the head of a network representing non-profit domestic home care service providers believe the solution lies in better care and services in the home.

“One solution that (local health authorities) have found is for a caregiver to visit seniors regularly in their homes,” explains Brunet, who is executive director of the Conseil pour la protection des malades.

He says people who receive care at home stay healthier for longer and are less likely to spend time in hospital and waiting for care beds.

“Since they’re better off at home, they’re doing well and aren’t overburdening either the emergency room or the (long-term care facilities), because we’re taking care of them,” he said.

Brunet says that while home support is being offered to a greater number of people, the number of hours provided has been reduced.

J. Benoit Caron, the executive director of a network of dozens of non-profit businesses that provide home care services, says provincial data shows an increase in the use of domestic help and personal assistance services.

“When there’s a loss of independence, the first service people need is help to continue living comfortably, hygienically, and safely in their immediate environment,” Caron said.

He’s pleased that the government announced a few weeks ago that it was expanding a pilot project for simplified home support to six new regions. The initiative allows people to hire domestic help directly through the more than 85 non-profit businesses in the network, rather than having to go through local health centres.

“Until now, when someone experienced a loss of independence that required personal assistance services … they would call the (health clinic) in the public system and wait for some time — often several months,” he said. “Now, with the initiative we launched earlier this year with the Government of Quebec, the person calling will receive services immediately. Much more quickly,” explained Caron.

People receiving in-home care will be eligible for reduced rates, based on their income. “It’s important to note that the services were already available; it was the financial assistance that was lacking, or it involved a major detour through the public system,” Caron said.

Brunet criticizes the hospital-centric approach that prevails in Quebec. He says more places should follow the example of a health clinic in Montreal’s Verdun neighbourhood, which offers an acute home care support team. He says more than 60 per of patients are able to avoid hospitalization or emergency room visits thanks to the team.

Caron believes older adults have a hard time asking for help — for example, with household chores — even though they aren’t necessarily sick.

“In Quebec, we have a culture where, when you’re old, you move — whether you’re a caregiver or a senior. The concept of in-home care — the idea of receiving services without being part of the health care system, without being sick — is a concept that isn’t well-known in Quebec,” he states.

He points out that his network complements the health care system. “We can intervene early on to extend independence, as long as it’s possible and appropriate for the user,” he says. When a health condition becomes too severe, the health care system takes over.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Global Affairs working to collect DNA from families of missing Canadians in Nepal
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal government says it is working to collect DNA samples from the families of Canadians still missing in Nepal and China after a flash flood ripped through the border region last week.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Federal government officials said Global Affairs Canada is working to collect DNA from the families of Canadians still missing in Nepal and China after a flash flood ripped through the border region last week.

Senior government officials, briefing reporters on background, said they are starting to collect the samples from the families of 29 people still considered missing, with assistance from the RCMP and police forces in Nepal and China.

The flooding on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,100 people and left roughly 4,400 missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.

One Canadian was found safe, while the remaining 29 are believed to have been in the region where the flash flood occurred.

The Nepal Tourism Board reported on Sept. 1 that more than 580 foreign nationals and tourists were still unaccounted for, while another 330 had been rescued.

Federal officials said the situation is changing by the day and they continue to work with local authorities and the families of the missing.

Global Affairs has 10 officials in Kathmandu and has established points of contact with the families of the missing Canadians.

Search, recovery and identification efforts are being led by Nepali and Chinese authorities and Canada has offered assistance, the federal officials said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

— With files from Ian Bickis in Winnipeg

The Canadian Press Staff

stories.title: N.S. woman says her family has lost hundreds of relatives, friends in Nepal floods
stories.summary: One N.S. resident says she has lost hundreds of relatives and friends after Nepal's deadly flash floods in her home district of Rasuwa.
stories.author: Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
A Nepalese woman in Nova Scotia has been living a nightmare ever since the Aug. 26 deadly flash floods in Nepal.

Ang Faulkner grew up in one of the affected districts — Rasuwa — and says she is missing hundreds of family members, neighbours and childhood friends.

“I just blame myself for not being there in the worst time of their life,” said Faulkner from her home in Bedford, N.S.

Ever since she heard the news, Faulkner says she has struggled to eat or sleep.

It took her two desperate days to make contact with her parents back home.

She says her father had to use a friend’s solar panel just to charge his phone enough to make the two-minute call she was anxiously waiting for.

“All he could say is, ‘I’m safe, your mom is safe. But we have lost a lot of people from here,'” she said. “He could just hear screams and cries from the people of my village.”

Faulkner says many of her missing relatives are now presumed dead.

Among them is her cousin’s wife, who ran a hotel in Syabrubesi, a village that once sat on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River.

“They were just having coffee together, husband and wife, and all of a sudden all he could hear was like a lot of loud noises,” Faulkner said.

“So, they ran out and everyone was running, like ‘Run! Run!’ And they were running without knowing what was happening.”

She says her cousin managed to grab and pull himself up.

“He looked back. All he could he was a big, massive wave, almost as high as maybe five, six-storey-high building,” she said.

She says his wife was behind him.

“He literally had to see his wife washed away from the flood,” Faulkner said.

Her cousin made it to the mountainside with other survivors where she says they went about 24 hours without any food or water.

“I remember he’s saying, ‘I have nothing left. Like my whole life, my hometown, my wife, my life savings — everything is gone.'”

Faulkner’s aunt and uncle, who ran another hotel in Syabrubesi, are also still unaccounted for.

She’s heard through family members that they were doing housekeeping when the water came.

A video has surfaced on multiple broadcast channels, showing what Faulkner identified as their hotel, succumbing to the massive wave.

She says the mountain village of Syabrubesi has been completely washed away.

Experts say a glacial collapse likely triggered the flooding.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and Tibet, an autonomous region of China, ON Aug. 26 at 8:37 a.m. local time.

Initially reported as an earthquake, the event is now believed to have been caused by a falling glacier, resulting in the flow of debris.

The focus in Nepal remains on rescue and recovery in the primarily affected districts, with the death toll surpassing 1,200 and more than 4,000 still missing.

But for families searching for their missing loved ones, the mud makes closure hard to come by.

“It’s almost like concrete,” Faulkner said. “How are you going to find their bodies?”

She adds that a common practice in Nepal is to send children away to Kathmandu for boarding school once they’re around age five.

This means that many of the flood victims were adults, Faulkner says, and their children are now orphans who will need all the support they can get.

“They have lost a lot, but we can save their future.” Faulkner said. “Support Nepal, stand with us, and try to get answers that families are waiting for.”

Those looking to donate to the relief effort can do so through the Government of Nepal Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

stories.title: Construction begins on major B.C. transmission line aimed at powering northwest
stories.summary: Prince George - Construction is underway on a major electricity transmission project in British Columbia's north, a project the federal and provincial governments say will contribute nearly $10 billion a year to B.C.’s economy.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Construction is underway on a major electricity transmission project in northern British Columbia that the federal and provincial governments say will inject billions into the provincial economy, drive new industrial development and assert Canada’s sovereignty in the face of U.S. threats.

The North Coast Transmission Line expansion will link Prince George to Terrace near the North Coast, and is expected to more than double electricity supply to that region.

The transmission line, which was referred to the federal major projects office in November 2025 for possible fast-tracking, is expected to power big initiatives in the works such as the Ksi Lisims liquefied natural gas facility and mines in B.C.‘s Golden Triangle near the Alaskan border.

“This has gone from a concept to shovels in the ground in an incredibly short period of time,” Tim Hodgson, the federal natural resources minister, said in an interview.

“It’s showing what happens when the federal, the provincial and local government, in partnership with First Nations, agree on a shared strategy to build Canada.

“It shows what Canadians can do, and that’s so important at this challenging time in the world.”

The governments estimate the power expansion will contribute $10 billion a year to B.C.‘s economy, spur 9,700 jobs and generate $950 million in municipal and provincial revenue.

It can also help strengthen Canada’s position as the trade turmoil intensifies with its southern neighbour, B.C. Premier David Eby and Hodgson told a news conference in Prince George, B.C., ON Thursday.

“It’s a significant part of the kind of country that we are trying to build,” Eby said, adding the U.S. government has made clear it would like to “break us economically so that they can take us over as the 51st state.”

That’s why, the premier said, “we’re going to use our resources and our strength and what we do well to ensure that we are growing and prospering and diversifying not just away from the United States ... but building the kind of country that delivers what the world wants and needs.”

The Canadian and U.S. power grids are deeply integrated and, ON any given day, a region can be an importer or an exporter. The ability for B.C. mines and other industrial players to source more of its electricity domestically provides for more cost certainty and reduces reliance on imported diesel to fuel their operations, Eby said.

Hodgson said that when it comes to the trade war with the United States: “I always live by the motto of ‘don’t get mad, get even.’”

“Nothing would make me happier than when the United States asks us for more electricity to say, ‘You know what? We’ve got a lot of mines we need to develop in northern British Columbia. We have a lot of the cleanest LNG in the world.

“Nothing would make me happier than to say, ‘You know what? We’re going to use all our electricity here.’”

Charlotte Mitha, chief executive of BC Hydro, said the provincial utility is sourcing all the materials it can from Canada during construction, though some specialty equipment May have to come from Asia.

“No stone will go unturned on that, and we expect to have almost everything supplied from Canadian sources, from a materials and equipment perspective,” she said.

“We are anticipating very, very, high Canadian content — as high as we can get — and we’re prepared to make the tough decisions on that, even if it means having to re-look at schedules.”

The power line expansion’s first phase consists of a 165-kilometre stretch from Prince George to near Fraser Lake, which is targeted for completion in 2030. A second phase connecting to Terrace is set to be completed in 2032.

The federal and provincial governments agreed in July to commit a combined $3.9 billion to the project. The project has also been supported by a loan of close to $140 million from the Canada Infrastructure Bank to BC Hydro for fast-tracking preconstruction work to expedite the groundbreaking.

The B.C. government said in a news release that co-ownership agreements with First Nations are expected to be finalized by the end of this year.

“Today represents a new beginning for our region, our shared economy and our shared alignment of values that move strong economy-building projects forward,” said Chief Dolleen Logan of the Lheidli T’enneh First Nation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Survey says Saskatchewanians support social media limits for youth: province
stories.summary: The majority of households who responded to the government's survey supported limiting social media for children and teenagers younger than 16, the province said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
More than 80 per cent of Saskatchewanian households support social media limits for children and teenagers, according to the provincial government’s survey responses.

The mailout surveys were launched in May , with postcards sent to every household in Saskatchewan. The card posed a yes or no question, asking residents if they would support social media limits for children younger than 16.

More than 26,000 households, approximately five per cent of those polled, responded, according to Saskatchewan’s Mental Health and Addictions Minister Lori Carr.

“The results of those surveys were pretty overwhelming (and said) that 86 per cent of Saskatchewan residents believe that there should be some sort of social media limits for youth within the province,” she told reporters at a news conference Thursday.

Slightly more than 13 per cent said no, according to the Saskatchewan government. Of them, 68 per cent said there should be parental consent for kids to access the apps, Carr said.

A news release from the provincial government noted that the majority of respondents agreed with 16 being the cut-off age for any potential constraints.

The postcards also asked about exemptions for some specific mainstream social media platforms, including TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Snapchat and Facebook. Most households supported imposing restrictions on all, but some respondents told the province YouTube should be shielded from such limitations, it said.

Carr said the survey results have already been forwarded to the federal government to help advise them on what Saskatchewanians believe, adding that “it’s important they get the information from Saskatchewan.”

The mailouts cost the province approximately $180,000, the mental health minister added.

stories.title: Western student turns everyday challenges into entrepreneurial impact
stories.summary: Dual degree student Enya Law found entrepreneurship at Western University and discovered it was a way to merge her passions.
stories.author: Shana Dalby Althaus
stories.content:
Entrepreneurship is often described as the pursuit of big ideas, but Enya Law is more interested in the smaller problems that go unnoticed – and yet, shape everyday life.

Law was drawn to health care, business and work that builds community. Rather than choosing between them, a dual degree at Western University allowed her to explore how all three can work together.

“It’s a strange intersection,” said Law, now heading into the fourth year of her dual degree in health science and honours business administration at Ivey Business School. “But that’s what I love about it. It keeps every door open.”

Looking for ways to merge her passions, Law sought out theFounders Program at the Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship, Powered by Ivey. The Founder’s program builds skills and empowers entrepreneurs through education, mentorship, a $20,000 tuition bursary and the opportunity to grow networks on campus.

Initially, she was intimidated. She didn’t come from a traditional business background. But Law said she found that entrepreneurship thrives on different perspectives. Her background in health sciences gave her a unique way of approaching challenges.

“People think entrepreneurship is just tech and startups, but there’s so much of it in community work, in art, in food – aspects that don’t always get recognized.”

Within the Founders Program, entrepreneurship was not just framed around outcomes, but around a willingness to try, adapt and continue pushing despite hurdles.

### “Your first idea probably won’t work. It’s about whether you’re willing to keep going anyway.” – Enya Law, fourth-year dual degree student and Founders Program president

Recently elected president of the Founders Program, she’s now helping to lead and support future student entrepreneurs who are starting the same journey she did just a few years ago. Her focus is on creating a supportive community for all.

“Becoming president feels a little surreal because I’m now helping shape a program that once gave me an opportunity I wasn’t sure I was ready for,” Law said. “I think some of the most meaningful entrepreneurial journeys start before someone even considers themselves an entrepreneur, and I’d love for the Founders Program to be the place that sparks that realization for someone else.”

In high school, Law surveyed student perceptions of women’s health. Many of her peers were uncomfortable discussing it or lacked basic information. She realized it could be an opportunity to make a change.

That moment led to the creation of the Purple Project, a nonprofit initiative focused on raising awareness around women’s health through community events and social media campaigns. When Law brought the project to Western, its scope expanded.

At Western, she continued to look for small, overlooked issues. As a Residence Don, Law noticed piles of clothing, bedding and kitchen supplies being left behind when students moved out. She organized a Fashion and Food Drive across Western’s 12 residence buildings with colleague Peter Dani. The first drive collected more than 700 pounds of clothing, 200 bedding items and over 1,000 kitchen supplies for those in need.

She took the same approach in other facets of her life.

During a summer internship with a luxury hotel chain in Hong Kong, Law developed a colleague recognition initiative designed to strengthen the workplace. The idea came from observing gaps in connection and recognition within the organization.

As a research assistant in the Faculty of Health Sciences, she’s tackled projects on gender-based humanitarian studies and investigated how misinformation on social media influences perceptions of women’s health. The research pushed her to think more critically about the platforms and systems behind the issues she cares about.

“It has made me aware of my own biases,” she said. “You start to think about what might be missing – who isn’t being considered – and how that affects the outcome.”

Law is now pursuing new entrepreneurship-focused research under Ivey professor Laurel Steinfield. She is helping to map the entrepreneurship ecosystem in South Africa and studying why women-led ventures fail at higher rates than those led by men.

“I’m especially interested in understanding where entrepreneurs are falling through the cracks and why those gaps continue to exist,” Law said. “Ultimately, I want this work to contribute to a more inclusive entrepreneurial ecosystem where someone’s gender, race, background or circumstances don’t determine how far their idea can go.”

Through all her experiences at Western, Law has learned that entrepreneurship is not limited to starting a business. More important is the mindset: seeking out solutions to problems big and small.

Through the Founders Program, she’s learned how to apply those skills in everyday situations, approaching challenges with curiosity.

“You never really know where you’ll find your passion,” she said. “Just try things; you might be surprised by what you discover.”

stories.title: U.S. abandonment of Cusma would be severe but survivable for Canada, report finds
stories.summary: Study from Deloitte predicts big hit unevenly spread across sectors and recommends more free trade with other nations and between provinces.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A U.S. withdrawal from the Canada-United-States-Mexico trade agreement (Cusma) would have a “severe but not cataclysmic impact on Canada’s overall economy, although perhaps cataclysmic for some sectors,” according to a new report released this week by Deloitte Canada.

The report is titled “ Tariffs: A rough road leads to new destinations,” and imagines two broad scenarios in the near future.

In the first, the “Cusma Withdrawal Scenario,” the U.S. opts out of Cusma entirely. “Trade resets at Most-Favoured-Nation rates that apply to member countries in the World Trade Organization,” the report says. It assumes a 10 per cent global tariff imposed by the U.S. affects previously Cusma-exempt sectors, including oil and gas.

“There is potential for much worse if the Trump administration imposes further punitive tariffs on Canadian goods, as it has stated will happen in January,” the report notes, but it’s uncertain how long they would last and whether they would withstand legal and political challenges.

Even without a worst-case-scenario, however, the outlook is rough. The report predicts Canadian GDP would fall 1.6 per cent by 2036 relative to where it was last July, representing $402 billion in lost GDP over the coming decade.

“Domestic investment in things like infrastructure and machinery take a hit and employment is also projected to shrink by 163,000 jobs annually on average,” it says. “Average wages would likely decline, cutting into domestic consumption and household purchasing power.”

The pain would not be shared equally, with sectors that rely heavily on exports suffering the most. Manufacturing could see a 28 per cent drop in GDP over the decade, while electronics, machinery and equipment could lose 21 per cent, rubber and plastics products 20 per cent, and chemicals 13 per cent.

Oil and gas would fare better, with a loss of 0.4 per cent in GDP for oil and 0.9 per cent for natural gas — the “severe, not cataclysmic” part of the forecast.

The second scenario is called “Accelerated diversification” and paints a somewhat rosier picture. In this “best-case scenario,” Canada maintains all its existing free trade agreements while successfully negotiating new ones elsewhere.

Here the report predicts GDP growth of 0.6 per cent by 2036, representing $141 billion and the creation of 53,000 jobs a year. The gains aren’t as large as the losses under the first scenario, but at least they’re positive.

“Agriculture … represents one of our highest potential growth sectors, particularly to the extent markets open in China and India,” the report finds, predicting a possible increase in crop exports to non-U.S. markets of $4 billion by 2036, and food manufacturing increases of $16 billion.

Manufacturing of electronics, machinery and equipment could grow by $3 billion or 5 per cent, while motor vehicles and parts could increase by $1.1 billion or 3 per cent, and transportation equipment manufacturing and chemical manufacturing by about $1 billion, representing 4 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively.

Matthew Stewart, a partner in the Economics and Financial Advisory group at Deloitte Canada and one of the report’s co-authors, told National Post that, while the numbers are relatively easy to calculate, the future is hard to predict.

“It’s so tough to tell lately,” he said when asked for the odds of America actually walking away from Cusma. “Every day I hear different things from our government negotiators and the contacts I have. So it’s so tough to tell. It just seems to change direction on a regular basis.”

As to whether the next U.S. administration might behave differently, he’s cautiously optimistic. “I t’s clear that trade benefits both economies,” he said. “ But it’s clear that there’s increased protectionism across both parties.”

He added: “ I’m hopeful that we’ll get back to the table, whether it’s soon or after the (next U.S.) election, and then we’ll be able to restore some normalcy to the trade agreement. But it’s likely that we’re going to continue to see some increased tariffs .”

As to what can be done, Stewart sees several tactics beyond inking more free-trade deals with other partners.

“ I t’s also transportation capacity,” he said. “I f we can build better transportation capacity, we can get more of our oil and raw materials to market.”

Major projects around critical minerals are also vital, “ so that we can develop new markets … to try and offset some of this downside.”

He added: “The final piece that we can do, that is completely within our control, is interprovincial trade barriers. A nd we have been talking about this for years. And I know we made some effort to reduce them, but there’s still substantial barriers.”

Research by Deloitte found that interprovincial exports’ share of the Canadian economy has remained largely unchanged for more than 30 years, standing at 18.1 per cent of GDP in 2023.

“If Canada is to be tariffed by the U.S. and is looking for offsetting economic gains, it can start at home,” the report says. A Deloitte analysis from last year found that completely phasing out interprovincial trade barriers over five years would generate $881 billion in economic output by 2040 — a 2.4 per cent GDP increase — and create 133,000 new jobs.

Interprovincial trade involves workers as well as goods, Stewart added. “If we can’t move construction workers from B.C. into Manitoba, where we’re building a major project, because of health and safety regulations on those construction workers, it makes it much more expensive.”

content_blocks.text: A U.S. withdrawal from the Canada-United-States-Mexico trade agreement (Cusma) would have a “severe but not cataclysmic impact on Canada’s overall economy, although perhaps cataclysmic for some sectors,” according to a new report released this week by Deloitte Canada.
The report is titled “ Tariffs: A rough road leads to new destinations,” and imagines two broad scenarios in the near future.
content_blocks.html: The report is titled “Tariffs: A rough road leads to new destinations,” and imagines two broad scenarios in the near future.

content_blocks.text: In the first, the “Cusma Withdrawal Scenario,” the U.S. opts out of Cusma entirely. “Trade resets at Most-Favoured-Nation rates that apply to member countries in the World Trade Organization,” the report says. It assumes a 10 per cent global tariff imposed by the U.S. affects previously Cusma-exempt sectors, including oil and gas.

“There is potential for much worse if the Trump administration imposes further punitive tariffs on Canadian goods, as it has stated will happen in January,” the report notes, but it’s uncertain how long they would last and whether they would withstand legal and political challenges.

Even without a worst-case-scenario, however, the outlook is rough. The report predicts Canadian GDP would fall 1.6 per cent by 2036 relative to where it was last July, representing $402 billion in lost GDP over the coming decade.

“Domestic investment in things like infrastructure and machinery take a hit and employment is also projected to shrink by 163,000 jobs annually on average,” it says. “Average wages would likely decline, cutting into domestic consumption and household purchasing power.”

The pain would not be shared equally, with sectors that rely heavily on exports suffering the most. Manufacturing could see a 28 per cent drop in GDP over the decade, while electronics, machinery and equipment could lose 21 per cent, rubber and plastics products 20 per cent, and chemicals 13 per cent.
Oil and gas would fare better, with a loss of 0.4 per cent in GDP for oil and 0.9 per cent for natural gas — the “severe, not cataclysmic” part of the forecast.

The second scenario is called “Accelerated diversification” and paints a somewhat rosier picture. In this “best-case scenario,” Canada maintains all its existing free trade agreements while successfully negotiating new ones elsewhere.

Here the report predicts GDP growth of 0.6 per cent by 2036, representing $141 billion and the creation of 53,000 jobs a year. The gains aren’t as large as the losses under the first scenario, but at least they’re positive.

“Agriculture … represents one of our highest potential growth sectors, particularly to the extent markets open in China and India,” the report finds, predicting a possible increase in crop exports to non-U.S. markets of $4 billion by 2036, and food manufacturing increases of $16 billion.

Manufacturing of electronics, machinery and equipment could grow by $3 billion or 5 per cent, while motor vehicles and parts could increase by $1.1 billion or 3 per cent, and transportation equipment manufacturing and chemical manufacturing by about $1 billion, representing 4 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively.

Matthew Stewart, a partner in the Economics and Financial Advisory group at Deloitte Canada and one of the report’s co-authors, told National Post that, while the numbers are relatively easy to calculate, the future is hard to predict.

“It’s so tough to tell lately,” he said when asked for the odds of America actually walking away from Cusma. “Every day I hear different things from our government negotiators and the contacts I have. So it’s so tough to tell. It just seems to change direction on a regular basis.”

So it’s so tough to tell. It just seems to change direction on a regular basis.”

content_blocks.text: As to whether the next U.S. administration might behave differently, he’s cautiously optimistic. “I t’s clear that trade benefits both economies,” he said. “ But it’s clear that there’s increased protectionism across both parties.”

content_blocks.text: He added: “ I’m hopeful that we’ll get back to the table, whether it’s soon or after the (next U.S.) election, and then we’ll be able to restore some normalcy to the trade agreement. But it’s likely that we’re going to continue to see some increased tariffs .”

content_blocks.text: As to what can be done, Stewart sees several tactics beyond inking more free-trade deals with other partners.
“ I t’s also transportation capacity,” he said. “I f we can build better transportation capacity, we can get more of our oil and raw materials to market.”

content_blocks.text: Major projects around critical minerals are also vital, “ so that we can develop new markets … to try and offset some of this downside.”

content_blocks.text: He added: “The final piece that we can do, that is completely within our control, is interprovincial trade barriers. A nd we have been talking about this for years. And I know we made some effort to reduce them, but there’s still substantial barriers.”
content_blocks.html: He added: “The final piece that we can do, that is completely within our control, is interprovincial trade barriers. And we have been talking about this for years. And I know we made some effort to reduce them, but there’s still substantial barriers.”

content_blocks.text: Research by Deloitte found that interprovincial exports’ share of the Canadian economy has remained largely unchanged for more than 30 years, standing at 18.1 per cent of GDP in 2023.

content_blocks.text: “If Canada is to be tariffed by the U.S. and is looking for offsetting economic gains, it can start at home,” the report says. A Deloitte analysis from last year found that completely phasing out interprovincial trade barriers over five years would generate $881 billion in economic output by 2040 — a 2.4 per cent GDP increase — and create 133,000 new jobs.

Interprovincial trade involves workers as well as goods, Stewart added. “If we can’t move construction workers from B.C. into Manitoba, where we’re building a major project, because of health and safety regulations on those construction workers, it makes it much more expensive.”

stories.title: Bank of Canada unveils new $20 bill featuring King Charles, Vimy memorial
stories.summary: Circulation of the redesigned banknote, which includes unique security features, is set to begin next February
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
For the first time in more than 70 years, a new monarch will appear on Canada’s $20 bill.

The Bank of Canada unveiled the new banknote on Thursday during a ceremony in Ottawa.

The bill features a linework image of King Charles III executed by Canadian engraver Jorge Rodrigo Peral based on a 2024 photograph taken by Andrew Parsons, a British photographer, for the currency. The King’s portrait is displayed vertically on the bill.

Charles became King after the 2022 death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, whose time on the $20 banknote has now exceeded the length of her record-breaking 70-year reign. Work on the new banknote began on the day of King Charles’ coronation, May 6, 2023, according to a Bank of Canada official speaking on background ahead of the unveiling.

The Bank of Canada has unveiled the design for the country's newest $20 note, which features King Charles III for the first time.

The Canadian Press

The back of the bill features an image of the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in France. About 3,600 Canadians died at the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 1917 during the First World War.

Circulation of the new $20 bill is scheduled to begin next February.

It’s the second vertical banknote produced by the Bank of Canada after the $10 note, which features Viola Desmond, a civil-rights pioneer and businesswoman from Nova Scotia. It was unveiled in 2018.

Since 1937, when King George VI first appeared on the $20 banknote early in his reign, all of Canada’s $20 bills have featured likenesses of Canada’s monarchs.

As an eight-year-old princess, the future Queen Elizabeth was first featured on the Bank of Canada’s inaugural $20 banknote in 1935, before her portrait was replaced by her father’s. She returned to the $20 bill in 1954, after ascending to the throne in 1952.

“Her image became one of the most recognizable on our currency for generations of Canadians. Today, this tradition continues with His Majesty King Charles III, who is appearing on a Canadian banknote for the first time,” Governor-General Louise Arbour told the unveiling ceremony on Thursday.

Ms. Arbour said Canadian banknotes are more than just a form of payment.

“They reflect our history, our realities and the significant achievements of our collective journey,” she said. “Our currency affirms our sovereignty and our determination to define ourselves in the eyes of the world on our terms.”

Tiff Macklem, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, said at Thursday’s unveiling that the bill will feature new security features to prevent counterfeiting.

These include a purple security stripe that appears to spin and transform when the bill is moved. The stripe, which is difficult to reproduce, has been used elsewhere in the world but is making its debut in Canada with the new $20 banknote.

“Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever,” Mr. Macklem said.

Ahead of the bill’s rollout in 2027, the bank will hold discussions with law enforcement agencies and financial institutions to raise awareness of its security features, Mr. Macklem said.

Of the Vimy Ridge imagery on the banknote, Mr. Macklem noted that his grandfather, also named Tiff, was a lieutenant in the Canadian military who served as a liaison officer during the battle.

“Fortunately – as evidenced by my standing here before you – my grandfather returned home to Canada. Many did not,” he said.

He noted that the Vimy Memorial, which he personally saw during a visit to France earlier this summer, is a symbol of sacrifice.

“The soaring pillars and solemn sculptures honour those who gave their lives to protect freedom, peace and democracy,” he said.

stories.title: Childhood Cancer Awareness Month highlights advances in care and research at London hospital
stories.summary: September is Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, and London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is highlighting advances in treatment and research that are helping improve care for children and families across southwestern Ontario.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
September is Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, and London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) is highlighting advances in treatment and research that are helping improve care for children and families across southwestern Ontario.

For Nia Tsangaris, the past year has been a journey from cancer treatment back to the life she loves.

“When I was diagnosed with Lymphoma, I never imagined how many people would be cheering me on.”

“Being here and then being out all the treatment and then coming out and going back to school after all this… it’s like just crazy”

Her story is one example of the care being provided at Children’s Hospital, which serves families across the region.

Dr. Alexandra Zorzi, division head of paediatric hematology oncology at Children’s Hospital, says childhood cancer is rare and more awareness is needed to support patients and their families.

“Childhood cancer is rare. Less than seven per cent of Canadian research dollars go to childhood cancer research, and so raising awareness of children and families within our own home community that are struggling with this disease, and not only during their illness but afterwards as long term survivors, is important.”

The hospital is also part of a national research collaboration exploring liquid biopsy technology.

The approach uses samples such as blood or spinal fluid to help doctors learn more about a patient’s tumour and how it is responding to treatment.

Dr. Chantel Cacciotti, a paediatric hematologist-oncologist at Children’s Hospital, says the technology could help doctors identify changes in a tumour and determine whether treatment is working.

“It’s the concept that we take liquid from a patient, so either fluid from their spinal cord so CSF or liquid like blood. And through a process of evaluating that liquid we’re actually able to get information about what kind of tumor they have, whether their tumor is responding to the treatment that we’re giving them, or in cases if the tumor is coming back and no longer responding.”

LHSC says researchers across Canada are working to standardize how those samples are collected and analyzed, helping lay the groundwork for future clinical trials.

The goal is to make emerging research more accessible to patients while improving care for children and families.

For Nia, the progress is personal. She says she’s grateful for the care that helped her get back to school, volleyball and the people she loves most.

stories.title: 2 men charged after stolen vehicle reaches 180 km/h in Regina: police
stories.summary: Two men are facing charges after a stolen vehicle reached speeds of up to 180 km/h before crashing off an embankment near Regina, police say.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
Two men are facing charges after a stolen vehicle was driven at speeds of up to 180 km/h through Regina before crashing off an embankment, police say.

Patrol officers located a reported stolen vehicle being driven dangerously near Victoria Avenue and Athol Street shortly after midnight on Wednesday, Regina police said in a news release.

“Due to safety concerns related to the high rate of speed, Patrol officers on the ground did not pursue the vehicle. ASU took over and tracked it from the sky,” police said in the release. ASU refers to a police aerial support unit.

The driver headed south of Regina, speeding along several grid roads before travelling toward Lumsden, police said.

Once in the town, police say the vehicle was driven dangerously through the streets and nearly collided head-on with several motorists.

The driver then turned onto railway tracks and attempted to continue driving along them before losing control and going off a steep embankment, police said.

Police said the suspect was also arrested on outstanding warrants.

A 32-year-old has been charged with possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000 and resisting arrest.

Both men appeared in Regina provincial court on Wednesday.

stories.title: Ontario court denies Toronto woman’s motion to apply for Maid for mental illness
stories.summary: An Ontario judge has dismissed a motion that would have allowed a woman who suffers solely from a mental illness to apply for a medically assisted death.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — An Ontario judge has denied a motion that would have allowed a woman who suffers solely from mental illness to apply for a medically assisted death, while insisting the Attorney General of Canada respond to a constitutional challenge launched by the same plaintiff two years ago.

Claire Brosseau, a 49-year-old former actress and comedian who lives in Toronto, filed a motion in May seeking a constitutional exemption from a law that currently prevents people from applying for Maid on the basis of mental illness alone.

Justice Carissima Mathen said although Brosseau’s evidence of decades of suffering is credible, the consequences of granting her an exemption from the law cannot be overlooked.

Brosseau said Thursday’s decision forces her to continue suffering.

“(It is) yet another example of governmental systems telling people with mental illnesses that we do not have the same rights nor the same autonomy as others,” she said in a statement.

“Canada is clearly delivering a message. Despite its promise to be a country with equal rights, it is not. It doesn’t value bodily autonomy, or at least not for a certain kind of person, and it appears that I am one.”

Brosseau’s legal team argued in court on July 20 that she required emergency relief from persistent mental anguish that began when she was a child and has only intensified over the last 35 years.

She said she’s been treated for bipolar disorder, an eating disorder, substance use disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Brosseau said that for decades she has been trapped by a whiplash of manic and depressive states, likening it to standing on the ledge of a building and wanting to jump, but also believing she can fly.

When Maid legislation was first passed in 2016, it required someone’s death to be reasonably foreseeable in order to qualify. In 2021, the federal government revised the legislation to include people who are suffering intolerably with a serious and incurable illness or disability but whose death was not reasonably foreseeable.

It put a temporary exclusion in place for people whose suffering was solely from mental illness. The exclusion has been repeatedly extended, most recently until March.

As a result, Canadians are not eligible to apply for Maid on the basis of mental illness alone.

Mathen said in her decision that although she is dismissing Brosseau’s motion, she is ordering the federal attorney general to respond to a constitutional challenge she launched in August 2024, arguing that Maid’s exclusion of Canadians whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness is a breach of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The case has not commenced in court, which ultimately led Brosseau to launch a separate urgent motion.

Mathen said Brosseau and the attorney general must schedule next steps for the Charter challenge within 14 days.

She also said Brosseau’s evidence of suffering is credible and compelling.

“Over the months and, perhaps, years that this litigation will endure, she is at risk of significant harm,” Mathen said.

However, the judge said that the interests on the other side are considerable.

“They include Parliament’s role to make policy decisions on sensitive social issues, and the proper interpretation of the Charter rights in play.”

Brosseau said she has tried electroconvulsive therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy, rehabilitative treatment, and continues to see two psychiatrists, but none of the treatments have meaningfully addressed her constant pain.

Her lawyer Michael Fenrick argued in July that granting his client access to Maid is the “only meaningful solution” to her advanced state of irreversible decline. In its absence, he said, “her choice is between continuing to suffer – suffer intolerably – or to choose suicide.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said Thursday that while it acknowledges “the difficult circumstances that led to this motion,” it agrees with the court’s decision that the legal requirements for granting a special exemption or pause of the law were not met in this case.

Joseph Cheng, senior counsel for the Attorney General of Canada, acknowledged at the onset of his arguments on July 21 that he does not dispute Brosseau’s suffering, but rather the legal principles of her motion and its potential implications.

Cheng argued that the court was being asked to make a policy decision on Maid eligibility, “one of the most contentious, complex and sensitive policy issues” at exactly the same time as Parliament is determining the course it will take.

A special parliamentary committee recommended in June that people with mental illness as the sole reason for seeking Maid should be “indefinitely” excluded from the life-ending procedure, and the government has not yet said whether it will heed that advice.

In essence, Cheng said, the judge was asked to “go and stand out there and be bold and take a move that parliament is unwilling to take.”

Helen Long, chief executive officer of Dying With Dignity Canada, said in a statement that while the decision was not what she was hoping for, it did place urgency on pushing forward the Charter challenge.

“It is time for the government to take action on this larger case so the systemic challenges in Maid access for all eligible persons across Canada can finally be addressed,” Long said.

Sonia Patel, a member of Brosseau’s legal team, said it had always been their intention to move ahead with the Charter challenge.

“We will continue to push that forward in hopes that eventually the law will allow Claire and others in her situation to make the kinds of fundamental decisions we think they should be allowed to under the Charter,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press
