stories.title: Ford's $25K Lake Ontario sign a costly way to send Trump a message: Taxpayers Federation
stories.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford spent $25,000 on a Lake Ontario sign erected just days before a byelection was set to take place in the same area.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford spent $25,000 on a new Lake Ontario sign. And while there are many reasons to be angry with the Trump administration, “there are a lot cheaper ways to send a message to the president,” Noah Jarvis, Ontario director at the Canadian Taxpayers Federation (CTF), told National Post.

“The president himself does it all the time with his tweets and his posts on Truth Social,” Jarvis added.

The sign, which reads “Lake Ontario, now and always” in both English and French, was unveiled in Winona, Ont. — one of the areas covered by the Hamilton East—Stoney Creek byelection taking place on Thursday.

It was erected just days after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in U.S. government records and maps, which has also since been adopted by both Google and Apple Maps for users in the U.S.

Just this past weekend, Trump shared several posts criticizing Canada, including claiming that the U.S. loses $60 billion a year to Canada, that Canada is “ripping off” the U.S. and suggesting that all Canadian companies doing business with America should move to the U.S.

He also shared a screenshot of the new “Lake America” name on Google Maps and an AI video of himself replacing a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign with one that reads “Welcome to Lake America” underneath a U.S. flag.

Meanwhile, voters in the area where Ford’s $25,000 sign was erected have started heading to the polls to elect a new MPP, after Progressive Conservative Neil Lumsden retired on Aug. 4. It’s one of three provincial byelections held on the same day, with the others in the Toronto ridings of Scarborough Southwest and York—Simcoe. They come after the Liberals won three byelections that took place on Monday.

When asked if the new Lake Ontario sign might be a strategic move by Ford ahead of the vote, Jarvis said he couldn’t comment on the motivation, but that “when public funds are being used for advertising, the government in power needs to make sure that it is not being used for political reasons.”

It’s an issue the Canadian Taxpayers Federation has previously commented on, after the Ontario government spent a record $103.5 million on advertising in 2023-24. Federal director Franco Terrazzano said at the time that “the rules need to change because politicians shouldn’t be allowed to spend taxpayer money on ads to promote themselves.”

National Post has reached out to the PC Party of Ontario for comment.

The sign’s price tag was first reported by Global News on Tuesday and later confirmed in an email from the premier’s office Wednesday morning to CTV News .

Unveiling the sign in a video posted on X on Saturday, the Ontario premier said, “You May have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake all because he doesn’t like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves.”

Ford continued: “Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”

“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he added.

And several U.S. politicians condemned Trump’s executive order , too, including former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton, who simply wrote, “It’s Lake Ontario,” in a post on X , and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who said, “The American people don’t want to rename Lake Ontario Lake America.”

The new sign is the latest move in Ford’s combative stance against the U.S. and its president after trade negotiations collapsed last month.

He previously told Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010 that Trump could “kiss my ass,” to which the U.S. president responded with a Truth Social post in which he called Ford “flunky” and compared him unfavourably to his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford.

Later that day, while speaking at a press conference in Hamilton, Ford refused to back away from his blunt language, saying that he had “plenty of real estate” on his behind for Trump to find a place to kiss.

When asked about Trump’s criticism, Ford said: “I’ve dealt with guys like that my whole life,” before directing a blunt message to the U.S. president: “You’re a loser.”

However, the Ontario premier said at a news conference later that week that things had since “simmered down” between himself and Trump, adding that “it was a heated day for both him and I.”

Nevertheless, Ford’s tough stance on the trade war appears to have lent him a boost in support , with a recent Liaison Strategies poll showing that his approval rating has sharply rebounded from 24 per cent in July to 36 per cent at the end of August. The poll also found that Ontario’s Progressive Conservatives now lead the Liberals in the province by four points.

But the national picture is very different. A separate Liaison Strategies poll published Aug. 31 showed the Liberals opening a 17-point lead over the Conservatives, with Carney’s approval rating rising by five points to 64 per cent.

Conservative support, however, had fallen below 30 per cent nationally.

It was erected just days after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in U.S. government records and maps, which has also since been adopted by both Google and Apple Maps for users in the U.S.

Just this past weekend, Trump shared several posts criticizing Canada, including claiming that the U.S. loses $60 billion a year to Canada, that Canada is “ripping off” the U.S. and suggesting that all Canadian companies doing business with America should move to the U.S.

He also shared a screenshot of the new “Lake America” name on Google Maps and an AI video of himself replacing a “Welcome to Lake Ontario” sign with one that reads “Welcome to Lake America” underneath a U.S. flag.

Meanwhile, voters in the area where Ford’s $25,000 sign was erected have started heading to the polls to elect a new MPP, after Progressive Conservative Neil Lumsden retired on Aug. 4. It’s one of three provincial byelections held on the same day, with the others in the Toronto ridings of Scarborough Southwest and York—Simcoe. They come after the Liberals won three byelections that took place on Monday.

When asked if the new Lake Ontario sign might be a strategic move by Ford ahead of the vote, Jarvis said he couldn’t comment on the motivation, but that “when public funds are being used for advertising, the government in power needs to make sure that it is not being used for political reasons.”

It’s an issue the Canadian Taxpayers Federation has previously commented on, after the Ontario government spent a record $103.5 million on advertising in 2023-24. Federal director Franco Terrazzano said at the time that “the rules need to change because politicians shouldn’t be allowed to spend taxpayer money on ads to promote themselves.”
National Post has reached out to the PC Party of Ontario for comment.
The sign’s price tag was first reported by Global News on Tuesday and later confirmed in an email from the premier’s office Wednesday morning to CTV News .

Unveiling the sign in a video posted on X on Saturday, the Ontario premier said, “You May have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake all because he doesn’t like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves.”

Ford continued: “Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”
“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he added.

And several U.S. politicians condemned Trump’s executive order , too, including former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton, who simply wrote, “It’s Lake Ontario,” in a post on X , and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who said, “The American people don’t want to rename Lake Ontario Lake America.”
The new sign is the latest move in Ford’s combative stance against the U.S. and its president after trade negotiations collapsed last month.

He previously told Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010 that Trump could “kiss my ass,” to which the U.S. president responded with a Truth Social post in which he called Ford “flunky” and compared him unfavourably to his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford.

Later that day, while speaking at a press conference in Hamilton, Ford refused to back away from his blunt language, saying that he had “plenty of real estate” on his behind for Trump to find a place to kiss.
When asked about Trump’s criticism, Ford said: “I’ve dealt with guys like that my whole life,” before directing a blunt message to the U.S. president: “You’re a loser.”
However, the Ontario premier said at a news conference later that week that things had since “simmered down” between himself and Trump, adding that “it was a heated day for both him and I.”

Nevertheless, Ford’s tough stance on the trade war appears to have lent him a boost in support , with a recent Liaison Strategies poll showing that his approval rating has sharply rebounded from 24 per cent in July to 36 per cent at the end of August. The poll also found that Ontario’s Progressive Conservatives now lead the Liberals in the province by four points.

But the national picture is very different. A separate Liaison Strategies poll published Aug. 31 showed the Liberals opening a 17-point lead over the Conservatives, with Carney’s approval rating rising by five points to 64 per cent.
Conservative support, however, had fallen below 30 per cent nationally.

stories.title: Prime Video unveils Wednesday Night Hockey schedule
stories.summary: The 27-game national package begins Sept. 30 with the Toronto Maple Leafs hosting the New York Islanders
stories.content:
Amazon’s Prime Video has unveiled the schedule for its first season of Wednesday Night Hockey .

The 27-game national package begins Sept. 30 with the Toronto Maple Leafs hosting the New York Islanders.

Montreal leads Canadian teams with seven appearances, followed by Toronto with six and Edmonton with five. Calgary, Winnipeg and Ottawa each appear four times, while Vancouver is featured twice.

Marquee matchups include Brady Tkachuk’s return to Ottawa with the Florida Panthers on Oct. 21 and a Battle of Alberta between the Oilers and Flames a week later.

The games will stream in English and French to Prime subscribers in Canada at no additional cost.

The package is part of a 12-year sub-licensing agreement with Rogers that also gives the streaming service two first-round and one second-round Stanley Cup playoff series each season.

stories.title: Audit flags reports of abuse, missing patients in N.L. long-term care
stories.summary: ST. John's - Newfoundland and Labrador's auditor general found reports of abuse, medication errors and missing residents in the province's long-term care homes.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Newfoundland and Labrador’s auditor general is calling for more accountability in the province’s system of long-term care homes after documenting a series of alleged deficiencies, including reports of abuse, medication errors and missing residents.

In an audit released Thursday, Denise Hanrahan’s office says facilities received complaints of unexplained bruising and aggression between residents, including a reported incident of strangulation.

Newfoundland and Labrador is home to the most rapidly aging population in Canada, and people aged 65 or older could make up more than 30 per cent of the province’s population by 2043, Hanrahan noted. She said it was critical for the government and the health authority to ensure residents of long-term care homes are safe and well cared for.

“Overall, there is a lack of accountability within the long-term care system, including weaknesses in governance, oversight, monitoring and operational practices,” her report said.

“This increases the risk that vulnerable residents are not receiving safe, high-quality care that they deserve.”

Hanrahan and her team analyzed 39 of 43 long-term care facilities in the province, all but one of which were owned and operated by Newfoundland and Labrador Health Services. Her team also visited 15 care homes in the audit period, which ran from April 2024 to March 2026.

In some cases, they found holes in flooring, exposed heating equipment and tripping hazards, the report said. The document also flagged concerns with food safety and staffing levels.

They found no records of criminal background checks among hiring documents for nearly a fifth of 150 employees analyzed. More than a quarter were missing vulnerable sector checks, Hanrahan said.

Citing patient safety legislation, the provincial health authority would not share details with the auditors about more than 21,000 occurrence reports, which are filed when “an undesired or unplanned event” could have or did cause harm to a patient, the report said. However, the authority provided a summary, showing that at least 16 per cent of those — more than 3,400 — resulted in temporary harm to a resident.

The team did manage to see reports of 37 incidents which included verbal abuse by staff, resident abuse, medication errors and missing patients, the report said.

Hanrahan’s team did not have enough information to determine whether officials reported any incidents to the police, if such reporting was warranted, she told reporters on Thursday.

Her team’s report also chided the health authority’s handling of wait-lists, saying that as of March, there were 730 people waiting for spots in a province with roughly 3,200 beds.

The audit report says the government spent about $482 million on long-term care in the 2025-26 fiscal year, which works out to about $151,000 per publicly funded bed.

The audit came with 22 recommendations for the province and the health authority, including that Newfoundland and Labrador Health Services ensure all long-term care staff meet hiring requirements.

Though the report details flaws, Hanrahan told reporters her team also found “good people doing good work” in the province’s long-term care system.

“There are a lot of good things also happening, but you need to have the specifics to fix the things that aren’t (working),” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Federal Court orders release of some secret material in Nazi war crimes study
stories.summary: The Federal Court has ordered the release of some long-concealed passages of a September 1986 study prepared for a landmark federal commission of inquiry on war crimes.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Federal Court has ordered the release of some long-concealed passages of a September 1986 study prepared for a landmark federal commission of inquiry on war crimes.

In a ruling made public today, Federal Court Justice Simon Fothergill ordered the government to disclose previously redacted portions of the study on the resettlement of alleged Nazi war criminals in Canada after the Second World War.

B’nai Brith Canada has fought for years to see more of the report by researcher Alti Rodal.

In February 2024, Library and Archives Canada released some additional portions of the report in response to an Access to Information request from B’nai Brith.

Library and Archives continued to withhold other elements, including passages that discuss the role of American intelligence agencies in facilitating the settlement of Nazi collaborators in Canada.

In his ruling, Fothergill rejected the federal argument that the release of certain additional information would harm Canada’s international relations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney rejects U.S. claim that Canadian politics ended trade talks
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney rebuffed U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s recent comments.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Prime Minister Mark Carney rebuffed U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s recent comments that Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to political reasons.

“I don’t think, with all respect, appointed, unelected cabinet members in the United States are experts on Canadian politics,” said Carney, during an announcement in Thunder Bay, Ont., ON Thursday.

Carney was in the northern Ontario city announcing a $4.7-billion contract to build over 300 new Via Rail passenger rail cars.

The prime minister’s comments come after Lutnick claimed the reasons Canada blew up trade talks last month were “manufactured” and had to do with the Quebec provincial election and Alberta’s referendum.

Both the Canadian and American governments have blamed each other for the breakdown in negotiations.

Carney said several last-minute conditions on the U.S. side of negotiations made accepting a deal untenable.

He cited the addition of language on auto industry tariffs, such as a failure by the U.S. to reduce tariffs on heavy-duty trucks like the ones produced in auto plants in Southern Ontario. He also cited “efforts to restrict our protections of our language, our culture, and in effect, our sovereignty.”

Lutnick and United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have both said the French language provisions were not a red line for American negotiators.

On Wednesday, Lutnick told Cnbc a Canadian minister did not deny it when asked if Canadian negotiators were trying to “blow up” trade talks on Aug. 21.

Lutnick also claimed Canada had made several last-minute demands of its own.

The key to winning the Canada-U.S. trade war is not retaliating, says think tank

A Republican senator could be one of the first political victims of Trump's tariff war

Carney said the Americans have changed their stances since negotiations halted.

“I’ll say one other thing, which is that there are a few issues that the United States was arguing right up to the last hour, red lines weren’t going to change, boom, it’s in there, you know, our way or the highway, take it or leave it, you know, attitude,” he said.

“Some of what they’re saying now is different than what they were drawing the line on, and we are always going to stand up for what’s in the best interest of Canada workers, Canadian families,” Carney added.

The prime minister said his government is not looking for an easy win, but said a deal is still possible with the U.S.

“The deal that’s possible, that’s in the interests of Canadian workers, families, and businesses, is also the deal that is in the interests of American families, American businesses, American consumers,” said Carney.

“We’re ready to sit down and strike that deal when the Americans are ready,” he added.

In addition to the Section 232 tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, Canada also faces a 50-per-cent tariff under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which applies to $28 billion worth of Canadian exports to the U.S.

In response to the Section 338 tariffs, Canada has promised to retaliate with tariffs ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. products, effective Sept. 8.

stories.title: NBA waiting for Raptors, Clippers to submit Kawhi Leonard trade for approval
stories.summary: The NBA is still waiting for the Toronto Raptors and Los Angeles Clippers to submit the Kawhi Leonard trade for approval.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — The NBA is still waiting for the Toronto Raptors and Los Angeles Clippers to submit the Kawhi Leonard trade for approval.

NBA spokesperson Tim Frank said Thursday it’s up to the teams when to present the deal.

The trade that would send Leonard to Toronto for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and a package of draft picks paused in July while the league investigated salary-cap circumvention allegations involving Leonard and the Clippers.

The NBA announced Wednesday that it would not suspend Leonard or void his contract, seemingly clearing the way for the all-star forward to return to Toronto, where he won an NBA championship in 2019.

The league stripped the Clippers of five first-round picks and fined the team US$30 million for multiple violations, while Leonard was fined $700,000. Owner Steve Ballmer and team president of business operations Gillian Zucker were each suspended one year, while president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank was banned for six months.

The Clippers will forfeit a first-round pick in five straight NBA drafts starting in 2029. Los Angeles would recoup some draft capital in the Raptors trade, as Toronto is reportedly sending the Clippers unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and second-round picks in 2030 and 2033. The trade also includes a first-round pick swap in 2027.

Under NBA rules, teams must formally present an agreed-upon trade to the league office on a conference call. The deal is not considered complete until its conditions are satisfied and the league provides written confirmation.

While the trade has not been finalized, it appears Leonard is starting to move forward with a Raptors return. He was in Toronto for the retirement announcement of former teammate Kyle Lowry and also attended the National Bank Open last month.

“As I return to Toronto, I am focused on what I can control, closing this chapter, and moving forward with a clean slate,” he said in a statement issued Wednesday.

The Raptors acquired Leonard before the 2018-19 NBA season in a deal that saw popular star forward DeMar DeRozan and centre Jakob Poeltl head to the San Antonio Spurs.

Leonard, who is from the Los Angeles area, led the Raptors to their only NBA title that season, earning his second NBA Finals MVP award in the process, before signing a three-year, US$103 million deal with the Clippers.

The NBA began investigating the Clippers in September 2025 after journalist Pablo Torre reported on a $28 million endorsement contract between Leonard and Aspiration Fund Adviser LLC, a company that filed for bankruptcy last year. The league investigated whether the agreement broke its rules.

Earlier this year, Aspiration co-founder Joseph Sanberg was sentenced to 14 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to defrauding investors and lenders of at least $248 million.

The league said Ballmer knowingly sought to help Leonard obtain off-court income deals, approved a business deal that he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter into an endorsement contract with Leonard, and failed to create conditions under which his team followed league rules.

“I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family,” Leonard said.

The NBA said Leonard, through his former business manager and uncle Dennis Robertson, “violated the circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtaining those opportunities, and failing to reimburse payments by the Clippers for personal expenses.”

Robertson was banned from conducting business with NBA teams and their affiliates for five years.

— With files from The Associated Press.

stories.title: Ontario paper cup and bowl maker sees demand surge from local foodservice customers
stories.summary: Number of so-called tariff winners May be small and could shift as the U.S. trade dispute unfolds
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
A Canadian paper cup and bowl manufacturer is seeing growing demand from foodservice customers across the country as tariffs prompt coffee chains and fast-food restaurants to seek out more Canadian-made take-out packaging.

Eco Guardian Inc., which makes compostable and recyclable cups and bowls in Aurora, Ont., is one of a number of Canadian manufacturers poised to expand domestic business amid the escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S.

The company has received so many requests from potential new customers in the past two weeks that even if only half turn into orders it will be extremely busy, Eco Guardian founder and CEO Anil Abrol said in an interview.

“This has fast-tracked our growth,” said Abrol. “We’re bringing the equipment on faster and building up our capacity.”

The situation highlights the effect of the trade war on Canadian manufacturers, with some companies emerging as potential beneficiaries.

However, the slate of so-called tariff winners May be small, and could shift as the trade tussle unfolds.

Eco Guardian recently opened its new facility north of Toronto with the capacity to produce more than a billion paper cups a year.

The company was in talks with a U.S. manufacturer of paperboard when the first round of tariff threats hit last year, prompting the company to change course and source its raw material from Asia and Europe instead.

That shift means the company makes its products in Canada without U.S.-origin inputs, shielding it from Canadian retaliatory tariffs and making its cups and bowls more attractive to the domestic foodservice industry.

Despite becoming more appealing to Canadian restaurants and cafes, Eco Guardian has dealt with challenges in the U.S. due to tariffs.

“There’s a 50 per cent tariff that started,” Abrol said. “My team told me there’s one container which they have shipped ... the container value might be $25,000 (and) there’s a tariff of $14,000.”

One of the company’s machines, which was producing paper packaging exclusively for a U.S. customer, was switched off this week and will be converted to a new customer’s product, he said.

However, Eco Guardian has managed to maintain sales to the U.S. customer by distributing a similar product made in Asia rather than made in Canada, he said.

While Eco Guardian manufactures paper cups and bowls in Ontario, it also distributes compostable and recyclable packaging including fibre plates, clamshells and cutlery made overseas.

“Our supply from Asia will continue to them,” Abrol said. “We will not suffer any sales loss.”

Still, the company’s plan to grow its U.S. market share is on pause.

“We May see our exports to U.S.A. reducing a bit or not increasing the way we have planned it,” he said. “But the Canadian large customers for whom we built this factory ... we’ll be able to service them Canadian-made products without any exposure to either Sept. 8th (tariffs) or anything which might be looming ahead.”

The company is also positioned to benefit from an ongoing anti-dumping investigation by the Canada Border Services Agency involving Chinese-made paper cups and containers, Abrol said.

If the Cbsa finds the paper packaging – used to serve hot or cold take-out drinks and food – is being sold at unfair prices in Canada, the packaging could face large duties.

Those potential anti-dumping duties could send the price of paper cups and containers from China skyrocketing.

“Some of the large customers ... especially some of their distributors who are buying it directly from Asia ... they’re in panic mode,” Abrol said. “And that’s why we’re in discussions with them.”

stories.title: 2026 Eli Palfreyman Memorial Tournament
stories.summary: The annual Eli Palfreyman Memorial Tournament is back for another year. 6 teams will compete in Ayr.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Thursday, 3 September 2026 12:25

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The annual Eli Palfreyman Memorial Tournament is back for another year. 6 teams will compete in Ayr.

AYR - The Ayr Centennials are once again hosting the Eli Palfreyman Memorial Tournament.

Six teams will participate in the tournament at the North Dumfries Community Complex. Games begin today, with the first game starting at 1 p.m. The Brantford Titans will take on the Ridley College Tigers. The Woodstock Navy Vets will also take part in the tournament, and they will have their first game tonight at 7 p.m. against the host Ayr Centennials. The other teams in the tournament include the Pittsburgh Penguins Elite and Strathroy Rockets.

Focusing on the Navy Vets, they will also have games tomorrow at 4 p.m. against Ridley College, then on Saturday at 1 p.m. against Pittsburgh.

Tickets are $10 for adults, seniors, and students, while kids under 12 are $5. When you purchase a ticket for the day, you will be able to watch all three games that are played.

The full schedule is below.

Thursday, September 3, 2026

1 p.m. - Brantford Titans vs. Ridley College Tigers

4 p.m. - Pittsburgh Penguins Elite vs. Strathroy Rockets

7 p.m. - Woodstock Navy Vets vs. Ayr Centennials

Friday, September 4, 2026

1 p.m. - Pittsburgh Penguins Elite vs. Brantford Titans

4 p.m. - Ridley College Tigers vs. Woodstock Navy Vets

7 p.m. - Ayr Centennials vs. Strathroy Rockets

Saturday, September 5, 2026

1 p.m. - Woodstock Navy Vets vs. Pittsburgh Penguins Elite

4 p.m. - Strathroy Rockets vs. Brantford Titans

7 p.m. - Ayr Centennials vs. Ridley College Tigers

Sunday, September 6, 2026

1 p.m. - Consolation #1

4 p.m. - Consolation #2

7 p.m. - Finals

Stolen Motorcycles Recovered by Woodstock Police An ongoing investigation by Woodstock Police has resulted in charges and the recovery of stolen motorcycles.

Blandford-Blenheim Candidate Profile - Crystal Wymenga There is a fifth name on the ballot when Blandford-Blenheim residents cast their ballots for councillor on Township Council.

Last Call for Road Safety Survey! Oxford residents have until Tuesday to provide input for a Road Safety Strategy.

Possible Tornado in Tavistock The Northern Tornadoes Project has evidence that a tornado may have occurred in Tavistock on Wednesday.

Another Supplies4Students in the Books Over 1,300 local students will be supported by United Way Oxford's Supplies4Students program this year.

Ingersoll Candidate Profile - Sherry Ashby The ballot for Ingersoll Town Council has another name on it, as Sherry Ashby has come forward as a candidate.

Tree Planting Coming to Ingersoll A joint project will see trees and shrubs planted in six Ingersoll parks.

Summer Storm Rolls Through Oxford We had wind gusts between 90 to 100 kilometres per hour, along with about 10 to 35 milimetres of rain.

United Way Launches Workshops for Older Adults United Way Oxford says the workshops will help form social connections.

Power Outages Reported in Oxford County Most of the power outages appear to be in the north end of Oxford County.

Morning Fog Advisory for Oxford County Environment Canada says it could be hard to see on the roads out there.

Ingersoll Candidate Profile - Fred Freeman Fred Freeman served on Ingersoll Town Council for 19 years and he's looking to add four more as a councillor.

UPDATE: Fog Advisory Cancelled but Heat Warning Remains We're currently under a yellow warning for heat.

Theatre Woodstock Celebrates 80 Years Theatre Woodstock is celebrating it's 80th anniversary with a special event at South Gate Centre.

Operation Safe Start Hitting Oxford County The start of another school year is right around the corner, and police want to make sure everyone is safe.

Landfill Not Accepting Blue Box Materials The Oxford County Waste Management Facility in Salford is no longer accepting blue box recycling materials starting today.

Yellow Warning for Heat Issued in Oxford County High temperatures and humidex values are expected in Oxford County, causing Environment Canada to issue a yellow warning for heat.

Norwich Candidate Profile - Lacey Hird Lacey Hird would like to be a voice for residents living in Oxford Centre.

Final Whales Transferred from Marineland Tofino was the last captive whale to be transferred out of Canada.

SWPH Investigating Dog Scratch in Tavistock Officials say a dog scratched someone close to the gazebo in Tavistock Optimist Park.

stories.title: London Knights trade opens up import roster spot. Will an NHL first-rounder fill it?
stories.summary: The London Knights have opened up one of their three precious import spots.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The London Knights have opened up one of their three precious import spots.

The Ontario Hockey League club dealt Swedish defenceman Linus Funck Thursday to the Oshawa Generals for Guelph’s second-round pick in 2027 and Sudbury’s third-rounder in 2028. That paves the way for London to sign Anaheim first-rounder Marcus Nordmark, the Swedish scoring star who the Knights picked in the third round (180th overall) in the 2025 Canadian Hockey League import draft.

The 6-foot-4, 206-pound Funck scored four goals and 22 points with a plus-18 rating in 65 games as an 18-year-old rookie with the Knights. The Colorado Avalanche fourth-rounder spent the season adjusting to the smaller North American ice and Dale Hunter’s systems before a strong off-season.

“He had a real good summer in the gym and his training,” London associate GM Rob Simpson said. “He took the feedback we gave him and took a big step forward. He had a great world junior summer camp with Sweden and it looks like he’ll have a real good year.”

The Knights needed a second-round pick to replenish their 2027 draft board. They have also built the framework for the best import depth in junior hockey if Nordmark joins Flyers first-rounder Maksim Sokolovskii and Finnish newcomer Luca Santala, a forward prospect expected to be picked early in the next National Hockey League draft.

“We know what Maksim brings at the back end and Santala has had a good start in camp,” Simpson said. “It really helps your lineup to have that level of players.”

The 18-year-old Nordmark has spent the past few weeks working out with the Swedish men’s national hockey team. The 6-foot-2, 180-pounder from Stockholm is a world junior-level talent and should he join London, would be one of the most explosive point producers in the OHL ranks.

The Ducks picked him 28th overall at the draft at Buffalo in June.

“He has high-end offence and his hockey sense and skill is right up there,” Simpson said. “Any time you can add a player of his calibre who can create offence every night, that would help to produce goals and (add) to the power play.”

The Knights are currently in British Columbia preparing for two exhibition games against the Western Hockey League’s Victoria Royals Friday and Saturday. Their flight was delayed due to Wednesday’s inclement weather and the team finally landed at 11:30 p.m. Pacific time – a half-half before the airport in Victoria was set to close due to curfew.

RCMP in Richmond, B.C., say police were called to the McArthurGlen Designer Outlet at Vancouver airport early on Aug. 15.

stories.title: Campground closed due to bear activity
stories.summary: The Bruce Peninsula National Park has taken the rare step of closing a section of its campground, due to a habituated bear that has lost its fear of humans.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The Bruce Peninsula National Park has taken the rare step of closing a section of its campground, due to a habituated bear that has lost its fear of humans.

The Cyprus Lake campground, within the sprawling Bruce Peninsula National Park, near Tobermory, is closed until Sept. 7 due to a black bear that has been getting close to campers.

Parks Canada staff says while bears are common on the Bruce Peninsula, they’ve never had to close a campground during the busy summer camping season due to bear activity.

While no injuries have been reported, campers have reported seeing the bear very close to the campground over the past few weeks. Park staff say they’ve tried bear management strategies to try and separate the bear from campers, but it hasn’t worked, so they’ve had to close the campground.

Parking at the Grotto was also closed Wednesday afternoon and evening, as a result of the bear roaming the area.

Parks Canada staff say they’ll continue to monitor the situation, in hopes of reopening Cyprus Lake campground, after Sept. 7.

stories.title: Dutch central bank moves billions in gold to U.K. from Ottawa, New York
stories.summary: The Dutch bank owns 612.4 metric tons (675 tons) of gold that was worth 72.2 billion euros (about $83.6 billion) at the end of 2025.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Dutch central bank announced Wednesday that it has moved billions of dollars worth of its gold reserves out of North America in a move it described as “crisis preparedness” in a time of global political unrest.

It said that between March and August, some 86 metric tons (94.8 tons) of gold were transferred to London from the combined total of around 313 metric tons (345 tons) held in New York and Ottawa, Canada.

Before the move, New York housed 31.3 per cent of the Dutch gold and Ottawa held 19.7 per cent. After the move, both cities now hold 18.5 per cent, the bank said.

The bank owns 612.4 metric tons (675 tons) of gold that was worth 72.2 billion euros (about $83.6 billion) at the end of 2025.

“With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves,” the bank’s governor, Olaf Sleijpen, said in a written statement. “We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.”

More than 27 metric tons (30 tons) of gold were “physically transferred” from the United States and Canada to the Dutch bank’s heavily guarded vault on a military base near the central town of Zeist, the bank said, without elaborating on exactly how the gold bars got across the Atlantic Ocean. A similar quantity of gold was transferred from Zeist to London.

The rest of the relocation was achieved by selling around 59 metric tons (65 tons) of gold in New York and using the proceeds to buy gold in London.

The Dutch bank, known by its acronym DNB, said that gold held at the Bank of England “must meet modern international trade standards and is regarded as the world’s most easily tradable gold and will therefore be the most readily available for DNB in a crisis situation.

The gold reserves held in New York and Ottawa cannot be utilized as quickly and directly in such a situation.”

stories.title: N.B. and N.S. gaming Crown corps fined for lax money laundering reports
stories.summary: Canada’s money laundering watchdog has fined the Crown corporations in charge of gaming in N.B. and N.S. for failing to submit reports regarding suspicious activity.
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Canada’s money laundering watchdog has fined the Crown corporations in charge of gaming in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia for failing to submit reports regarding suspicious activity.

Fintrac said in a news release Thursday that it has fined the New Brunswick Lotteries and Gaming Corporation almost $400,000 and the Nova Scotia Gaming Corporation almost $232,000.

Fintrac says both organizations failed to submit suspicious transaction reports when there were reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering or terrorist activity.

In addition, Fintrac says Nova Scotia Gaming failed to document the risk of money laundering or a terrorist activity financing offence.

Fintrac and the provincial Crown corporations did not immediately respond to requests for more information on Thursday.

In a statement, Fintrac’s acting director and CEO, Stéphane Sirard, said regulated businesses have obligations under Canadian law to file reports to deter criminals and terrorists from operating in the legitimate economy.

“We will take firm action, when it is required, to ensure that businesses do their part and fulfil these obligations,” Sirard said in the statement.

stories.title: Toronto begins recovery after ‘100-year storm’ leaves behind massive flooding
stories.summary: A massive thunderstorm swept into Toronto on Wednesday afternoon, dropping two months of rain over the course of a few hours.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Officials in Toronto say cleanup operations are well underway and many services are returning to normal after homes and streets was soaked by a “100-year storm ” that battered the city on Wednesday evening.

A massive thunderstorm swept into Toronto on Wednesday afternoon, dropping hail and rain over the course of a few hours.

At its peak, the city said tens of thousands of people lost power, while the Don River burst its banks, closing portions of the Don Valley River. Homes flooded, trees and power lines came down, and both subway and Toronto island ferry service were suspended.

By Thursday morning, the sun had returned and the city began to dry off.

“The storm has passed,” Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said at an event Thursday morning.

“I want to assure the people of Toronto, we were prepared, ours teams were coordinated and we will keep work-in until every road is clear and every resident has power back.”

The mayor said roughly 90 per cent of homes had had their power restored, while the Don Valley Parkway has reopened. She urged anyone with flooding or other storm-related issues to call 311 for help.

City manager Paul Johnson said the quantity of rain that fell qualified the event as a “100-year storm” by Toronto’s definition.

“The Don River took the brunt” of the storm,” he told reporters.

While there will be sewage impacts and some pools remain closed, Johnson said the city was quickly returning to normal service.

“By and large, the City of Toronto today, all of our services and operations are back to normal,” he told reporters.

“We encourage people who have issues with city services or things that have happened, whether it is trees down in the neighbourhood or whatever, call 311.”

stories.title: VIA Rail cars to be made in Canada for 1st time in 40 years, Carney says
stories.summary: The prime minister says the country is being 'tested' by Donald Trump’s trade war, but that Canadians will not be divided by American tariffs.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Amid ongoing trade tensions with the United States, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Thursday that Ottawa will spend $4.7 billion to build and maintain 313 VIA Rail passenger cars domestically in Canada.

Flanked by ministers and factory workers in Thunder Bay, Carney noted it will be the first time in four decades that the VIA cars will be produced “right here in Canada” — rather than the U.S.

“For the first time in four decades, those cars will be produced and assembled and maintained in our country. Cars that used to be built in the United States will be built right here in Thunder Bay at Alston,” Carney said, adding that amid the U.S. trade war, “ Our country is being tested.”

“Two weeks ago, we made the right decision to suspend our trade negotiations with the United States. We couldn’t accept what they’d offered. We wouldn’t give what they asked. As a result, the U.S. has imposed new tariffs designed to hurt and divide us.”

“That’s a miscalculation because Canadians will always take care of each other. And it’s a miscalculation because we have everything we need to build the country we want,” Carney added.

Carney said the construction of the fleet, which will be done by Alstom, will directly support 700 jobs in Ontario and Quebec. The prime minister said Alstom will “maximize” the use of Canadian steel in the work.

More to come.

stories.title: Season preview: What to expect from Michael Faulds' Western Mustangs
stories.summary: The Michael Faulds hiring healed a lot of the scars from last year’s late-season meltdown. But not all of them.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The Michael Faulds hiring healed a lot of the scars from last year’s late-season meltdown. But not all of them.

The Western football veterans don’t forget the 60-13 blowout loss to Wilfrid Laurier while their new coach guided the Golden Hawks or the bizarre one-point playoff loss to Guelph after botching a missed field goal at the buzzer.

“The sour taste of the end of last season is still in,” Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt said. “It’s not going to go away. We know these are not the Western expectations. We still went 7-1 (in the regular season), which for every other team is great. But we lost in the first round, which basically means nothing at this point.

“We know where we fell short and where we have to improve on offence, defence, specials and leadership.”

It was an unpleasant way to close the book on Greg Marshall’s 20 years of success. Did Faulds ever address it in the lead-up to the new season, which begins Sunday (7 p.m.) against York at Western Alumni Stadium?

“I don’t think it’s something that needs to be,” returning defensive lineman Conner Franzisi said. “We all know what’s expected and what should be happening on the field. When something like that happens, everybody is aware of what needs to be done and I think we’ve done a good job of addressing that and getting ready for this season to right the wrongs.”

The Mustangs kept working out while the other 10 Ontario university teams kicked off last week. A first-week bye is a bummer, but Western got a good look on video at the Lions, who beat Carleton 35-34 at home.

Western hasn’t lost to York in football in 46 years, but the new boss isn’t taking anything for granted.

“I was a player the last time there was a coaching transition,” Faulds said. “It started out ugly. 0-4 would be shockingly ugly. That’s exactly how that 2007 season – Coach Marshall’s first season – did start out. Our guys will respect every opponent and we’re going to have to play our best.”

That fabled ’07 team rallied to win the Yates Cup. Faulds would take that ending this fall, minus those growing pains if possible.

DUAL THREAT: The Mustangs expect to score a lot of points again.

Record-setting Ethan Dolby is back running the ball, but they’re going to have to balance his output with a lot of graduated firepower. Strong-armed quarterback Evan Hillock spent his first pro season with the Paris Lights, a team in the American Football League of Europe.

Rancourt, the former backup and short-yardage specialist, brings a different dimension to the field.

“Of course, I’ll be running the ball and extending the play,” the 6-foot-5, 270-pound engineering student from Quebec said. “I’m still a quarterback passing first. It will be more explosive getting more guys involved as well as still keeping our identity and running the football, too.”

Dasani McIntosh slots into a top ball-catching role due to the graduation of Brayden Misseri and Seth Robertson. He noted the difference in Hillock and Rancourt’s approach.

“One thing I can say about Jerome is I’m excited to play with him,” the Ajax native said. “Any time we needed him to step up where Evan went down, Jerome came in and made big plays. We know he’s a bit more of an athlete and can do more with his legs. But coming from me and speaking for the guys, we have full confidence in Jerome this season.”

It was hard to recruit quarterbacks in Marshall’s final few seasons. That was a product of Hillock winning the Vanier Cup in his first year, essentially establishing himself as the clear No. 1.

Now, Rancourt gets his long-awaited opportunity. Ben Casselman, a third-year pivot from Whitby, is ready if needed, too.

OUTLOOK: Faulds has set the expectation that Western is a Vanier Cup contender – this fall and every year moving forward. That isn’t misplaced faith because he has become one of university football’s top recruiters.

But it isn’t going to be easy to replace OUA rookie of the year Jackson Mackay, the free safety who transferred to Arkansas to focus on his track and field career. It takes time to build up the linebacking corps again and re-establish the pass rush.

If Western has been able to do that through transfers, in-house development and coaching strength, then expect big things. Faulds called on his old Mustangs teammate Craig Butler to assist defensive co-ordinator Paul Gleason and the early returns have been overwhelmingly positive.

“It’s made a difference,” Franzisi said. “Coach Butler brings a wealth of CFL experience.”

That was one of the more shocking developments in the fallout of Western’s disappointing 2025 season. Not a single player was drafted.

That shouldn’t be an issue moving forward.

The hope is Faulds’ presence will quickly restore Western’s grip on best-in-conference status.

The coach is resolved and the players are determined.

It’s a good place to start.

York (1-0) at Western (0-0)

When: Sunday, 7 p.m. at Western Alumni Stadium.

The matchup: Western pounded the Lions 65-28 on Oct. 10, 2025, which marked the Mustangs’ final win of the Greg Marshall Era.

stories.title: Carney pushes back on Trump administration claims about collapse of trade talks
stories.summary: Tensions between the United States and Canada have escalated since the breakdown in trade talks last month.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is pushing back against senior members of the Trump administration who have been claiming his government tanked trade talks in the eleventh hour for political reasons.

At an unrelated news conference in Thunder Bay, Ont., ON Thursday, Carney said he doesn’t think “appointed, unelected” cabinet members in the United States are experts on Canadian politics.

Carney said a deal with the United States that works to the benefit of both countries is still possible.

Tensions between the United States and Canada have escalated since the breakdown in trade talks last month.

U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was on multiple U.S. news stations this week claiming Canada added “crazy ideas” in the final hours of negotiations in order to terminate trade talks for domestic political reasons.

Lutnick told Bloomberg he asked his Canadian counterpart if they were trying to blow up the deal on purpose and claimed they responded, “I’m not allowed to say that.”

Carney also said that he’ll tell Russian President Vladimir Putin to “get out of Ukraine” if they speak at the G20 summit in December.

U.S. President Donald Trump will host world leaders in Miami for the summit and there are signs he might allow Putin to attend, despite the arrest warrant issued against the Russian leader by the International Criminal Court.

Ottawa says the Trump administration’s decision to host Russia’s finance minister at a G20 meeting this week caused discomfort among allies.

Carney says it’s up to Trump to decide who attends the summit but Putin “only understands strength and directness.”

He says if he speaks with Putin in December, he’ll tell him to give Ukraine back all of the territory Russia took after its 2014 capture of Crimea and the 2022 full-scale invasion.

The United States has barred South Africa from multiple G20 events and Trump has falsely claimed the country is pursuing a genocide against white people.

With files from Dylan Robertson of The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney says Russia’s ejection from G20 was ‘valid’ as officials return
stories.summary: The Canadian prime minister says it’s up to U.S. President Donald Trump which world leaders get an invite to G20 meeting in Miami.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he believes Russia’s ejection from the G7 and G20 was for “very valid reasons” amid concerns about U.S. President Donald Trump welcoming Kremlin officials back to the international forum.

“It’s the host prerogative who to invite,” Carney told reporters in Thunder Bay, Ont., Thursday morning when asked about Russia’s finance minister attending the group’s meeting this week and about reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin could attend the meeting set for Miami later this year.

“Russia’s unprovoked attack (of Crimea) in 2014 was why they were ejected from the G7 and then the further attacks (on Ukraine) of almost five years ago now was why they were rejected from the G20. And Canada stands steadfastly with Ukraine.”

Carney said his message to Putin, should the Russian president attend the G20 leaders meeting in Miami this December, would be simple: “Get out of Ukraine.”

“He only understands strength and directness,” Carney said.

“Get out of Ukraine, give back all of Ukraine to Ukraine, end this war which is killing more than 30,000 of your people every single month. And I’d leave it at that.”

More to come.

stories.title: Canada’s new Heritage Minute honours Gander as 9/11 anniversary nears
stories.summary: The commemorative celebration precedes a visit to Gander by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra and other officials and plane passengers on Sept. 11.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
Almost 25 years after the town of Gander , Newfoundland, took in nearly 7,000 stranded travellers whose planes were diverted due to the Sept. 11 , 2001, terrorist attacks, a new Heritage Minute is commemorating the Canadian community that welcomed them with open arms.

Historica Canada , in its latest Heritage Minute, a 60-second film series highlighting significant stories from Canadian history, honoured the small community for its humanitarian efforts, which went on to capture the attention of the world when the story was retold through the stage musical Come From Away, which became a major Broadway and West End hit.

Locals who remember the events, along with community members and supporters, attended a celebration at Gander International Airport earlier this week, which Historica Canada described as “a special evening celebrating a remarkable story of generosity, compassion, and community.”

The event precedes a visit by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra and other officials to Gander that is set to take place on Sept. 11. The town has hosted commemorative events every year since the terror attacks that killed almost 3,000 people when Al-Qaeda terrorists hijacked and crashed four commercial aircrafts into the Twin Towers, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania.

Gander Mayor Percy Farwell said Tuesday, “We also acknowledge the connection that transpired with our little neck of the woods here and how meaningful that turned out to be.”

“(We were) responding to people that were in distress and needed a lot of life’s necessities like food and shelter. Mostly they needed love and compassion because it was a very distressing time,” he added.

The town of about 9,500 people became eternally linked to the 9/11 attacks when its tiny airport took in 38 passenger planes grounded by air traffic control in the immediate aftermath of the coordinated hijackings.

The people of Gander rallied around what they called the “plane people,” converting schools and church halls into shelters and taking many passengers into their own homes while providing food, hot showers, clothing and phones so stranded folk could contact their families.

Twenty-five years later, those taken in by the town continue to express their gratitude.

Every September, Sue Riccardelli and her wife, Maureen Murray, fly a large flag combining a maple leaf and America’s stars and stripes outside their New Jersey home to honour the people of Newfoundland who cared for them and their fellow passengers.

The couple were on their way home from France when their plane was grounded in Gander. They stayed for four days, with more than 230 other passengers from their flight.

During their stay in Gander, the couple made lifelong friends and have since returned at least 10 times to visit them.

Last year, as relations between the U.S. and Canada soured amid a reignited trade war, the couple began bringing their flag to local performances of “ Come From Away ,” as a symbol of solidarity.

Riccardelli, 65, and Murray, 67, are among a group of Americans expected to return to Gander next week for the 25th anniversary of 9/11.

The couple told The Canadian Press they were horrified by U.S. President Donald Trump’s treatment of Canada and plan to bring their flag to Gander and hold it high.

“As Americans, our country was at war, we were far away from home, and here were these people — Canadians, people from Gander — who just gave us their all,” Riccardelli said from their home in New Jersey.

— with files from the Canadian Press

stories.title: Legendary jewels on display in Quebec City after a century hidden in suitcase
stories.summary: The exhibition tells of close historical ties between Canada and Europe, and of the remarkable story of the last empress of Austria-Hungary’s journey to safety in Quebec City with nothing but a battered suitcase in hand.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Quebec City -- In a world premiere, a Quebec museum will display a pocket watch that once belonged to Marie-Antoinette and the legendary 137-carat Florentine diamond. The precious jewels are among a collection once thought lost or stolen, that had been hidden in a suitcase and kept secret for over a century in a Canadian bank vault.

The jewels will be on display to the public at the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec (Mnbaq) as of Friday, Sept. 4.

The exhibition tells of close historical ties between Canada and Europe, and of the remarkable story of the last empress of Austria-Hungary’s journey to safety in Quebec City with nothing but a battered suitcase in hand.

“The city of Quebec offered my family safety, respect and hope during a time of great uncertainty,” said Empress Zita’s grandson Karl von Habsburg in a statement shared in a Thursday press release. “Showing these jewels at the Musée is an expression of profound gratitude to Quebec and Canada for welcoming and sheltering my grandmother and her eight children during World War II.”

Near the end of the First World War , and the abolition of the Austria-Hungarian Empire, the jewellery owned by the Habsburg family was transported to Switzerland and eventually to Belgium, where Emperor Charles I and his wife Empress Zita were in exile.

After the death of her husband, Empress Zita had to flee once again during the Second World War to escape Nazi troops. The Germans bombed the Habsburg family’s house two days after her escape. The empress made her way to Quebec City in October 1940 with her eight children and priceless family jewels packed in the same small suitcase.

The Sisters of Sainte-Jeanne d’Arc, a Quebec congregation, offered the empress and her children a modest home, with the blessing of the then-Archbishop of Quebec, where she stayed for a decade. When she returned to Europe, she left the collection of 15 jewels behind for safekeeping where they remained for decades with the Saint Joseph Trust, an entity entrusted with holding the jewels.

“More than 80 years later, it is deeply moving to see this story continue in Quebec and to be able, in turn to share these treasures with the public,” said Saint Joseph trustee Andrew Molson.

It was Empress Zita’s wish that the location of the jewels remain secret until the 100th anniversary of her husband Charles’ death in 1922. The fate of the jewels had long been a mystery, with newspapers speculating as early as the 1920’s that they had likely been lost, stolen, or recut.

The empress died in Switzerland in 1989 at the age of 92 but had passed along the Habsberg family secret to two of her sons. They, in turn, revealed the fate of the jewels to only two of their children.

In the fall of 2025, the family publically announced the items had been kept in Quebec City and would, as was Empress Zita’s wish, be displayed in that city. In December 2025, the Austrian government established a commission of experts to establish whether the country has any claims on some of the jewels. That process is ongoing.

Among the treasures, is a pocket watch once owned by Marie Antoinette. The museum describes it on its website as a “sumptuous accessory that is a rare intersection of fine jewellery and watchmaking.”

The museum added that the watch had been placed in safekeeping during the French Revolution and in a locket on its backside is a lock of hair that May have belonged to Marie Antoinette’s mother.

The centrepiece of the collection is the Florentine Diamond. It is one of the largest known diamonds, described as “remarkably pure” and of light-yellow colour. The museum describes it as a double rose cut that adds a second layer of facets on the underside of the gem to create more sparkle. It once belonged to the Medici family, rulers of Florence.

Its mysterious disappearance became a plot point in novels, and films including a 2014 French movie called Le Dernier Diamant (The Last Diamand) in which a fictional character attempts to steal the Florentine Diamond.

“For the first time, we are inviting the public to see these extraordinary masterpieces of European jewellery, whose brilliance, elegance, and story echo through history,” said Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec Director General Jean Luc Murray in a statement.

Empress Zita’s descendants say they are “delighted” that heir grandmother’s wish to have the family jewellery on display to people from around the world fulfilled.

“She was acutely aware of our family’s cultural and historical responsibility, and it was deeply important to her that this significant private collection would once again be seen and appreciated at the right time, as is now the case at the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec,” Karl von Habsburg added in his statement.

One of her grandsons will be in Quebec City for the unveiling of the exhibit designed and produced in collaboration with the Saint Joseph Trust called Hidden Treasure: A Century of Mystery.

Visitors will need to buy a plus admission ticket to be able to view the exhibition.

Near the end of the First World War , and the abolition of the Austria-Hungarian Empire, the jewellery owned by the Habsburg family was transported to Switzerland and eventually to Belgium, where Emperor Charles I and his wife Empress Zita were in exile.

After the death of her husband, Empress Zita had to flee once again during the Second World War to escape Nazi troops. The Germans bombed the Habsburg family’s house two days after her escape. The empress made her way to Quebec City in October 1940 with her eight children and priceless family jewels packed in the same small suitcase.

The Sisters of Sainte-Jeanne d’Arc, a Quebec congregation, offered the empress and her children a modest home, with the blessing of the then-Archbishop of Quebec, where she stayed for a decade. When she returned to Europe, she left the collection of 15 jewels behind for safekeeping where they remained for decades with the Saint Joseph Trust, an entity entrusted with holding the jewels.
“More than 80 years later, it is deeply moving to see this story continue in Quebec and to be able, in turn to share these treasures with the public,” said Saint Joseph trustee Andrew Molson.

content_blocks.alt: Empress Zita surrounded by six of her children in Quebec City Courtesy: Darius Consulting GMBH
content_blocks.caption: Empress Zita surrounded by six of her children in Quebec City Courtesy: Darius Consulting GMBH

content_blocks.text: It was Empress Zita’s wish that the location of the jewels remain secret until the 100th anniversary of her husband Charles’ death in 1922. The fate of the jewels had long been a mystery, with newspapers speculating as early as the 1920’s that they had likely been lost, stolen, or recut.

The empress died in Switzerland in 1989 at the age of 92 but had passed along the Habsberg family secret to two of her sons. They, in turn, revealed the fate of the jewels to only two of their children.

In the fall of 2025, the family publically announced the items had been kept in Quebec City and would, as was Empress Zita’s wish, be displayed in that city. In December 2025, the Austrian government established a commission of experts to establish whether the country has any claims on some of the jewels. That process is ongoing.
Among the treasures, is a pocket watch once owned by Marie Antoinette. The museum describes it on its website as a “sumptuous accessory that is a rare intersection of fine jewellery and watchmaking.”
The museum added that the watch had been placed in safekeeping during the French Revolution and in a locket on its backside is a lock of hair that May have belonged to Marie Antoinette’s mother.

The centrepiece of the collection is the Florentine Diamond. It is one of the largest known diamonds, described as “remarkably pure” and of light-yellow colour. The museum describes it as a double rose cut that adds a second layer of facets on the underside of the gem to create more sparkle. It once belonged to the Medici family, rulers of Florence.

Its mysterious disappearance became a plot point in novels, and films including a 2014 French movie called Le Dernier Diamant (The Last Diamand) in which a fictional character attempts to steal the Florentine Diamond.

“For the first time, we are inviting the public to see these extraordinary masterpieces of European jewellery, whose brilliance, elegance, and story echo through history,” said Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec Director General Jean Luc Murray in a statement.
Empress Zita’s descendants say they are “delighted” that heir grandmother’s wish to have the family jewellery on display to people from around the world fulfilled.

“She was acutely aware of our family’s cultural and historical responsibility, and it was deeply important to her that this significant private collection would once again be seen and appreciated at the right time, as is now the case at the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec,” Karl von Habsburg added in his statement.
One of her grandsons will be in Quebec City for the unveiling of the exhibit designed and produced in collaboration with the Saint Joseph Trust called Hidden Treasure: A Century of Mystery.
Visitors will need to buy a plus admission ticket to be able to view the exhibition.

stories.title: ‘It’s not just me’: Cyclists carry memories of fallen paramedics across P.E.I.
stories.summary: For Riley MacKenzie, the inside of an ambulance is both a workplace and a raw reminder of the father he lost in the line of duty less than two months ago.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Tracadie, P.E.I. - For Riley MacKenzie, the inside of an ambulance is both a workplace and a raw reminder of the father he lost in the line of duty less than two months ago.

Riley is an equipment supply technician with Island EMS, the same service where his dad, Mike MacKenzie, worked as a paramedic. He and colleague Jenna Croucher died July 7 when their ambulance collided head-on with a transport truck in New Brunswick. The patient in their care, Anne Martell, also died.

This week, the pair are among the fallen paramedics being honoured by roughly 40 cyclists travelling about 300 kilometres across P.E.I.

“Times are tough, but we know that Mike is here with us every step of the way and wouldn’t want us to be sad over it,” Riley said. “So we’re making the best out of what these moments have brought us.”

The three-day Tour Paramedic Ride is bringing together locals and others from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario, and highlights the risks of answering emergency calls, from dangerous roads and scenes to the emotional toll of the job.

Among the cyclists is Ryan O’Meara, a policy analyst and planner with the province’s Emergency Health Services division, riding to remember those who have made the ultimate sacrifice.

“The total to date is 58, which I think is surprising to a lot of people,” O’Meara said, adding that he knew some personally.

“It’s heartwarming to know that we as a profession can come together in times of tragedy to comfort one another and to hold one another up,” he said. “That’s the only way we’re really going to get through it.”

Participants are also raising money for a national monument in Ottawa. Firefighters and police officers already have their own.

More than $500,000 has been raised over 13 years, according to Tour Paramedic Ride President Mike Janczyszyn. But the project is expected to cost up to $6 million, and the group hopes the federal government will help close the gap.

“Their co-workers, their family, their friends, they can go to honour the people that they’ve known that have been part of the profession,” Janczyszyn said.

He believes part of the reason a monument hasn’t already been built is that paramedicine is a relatively newer profession, but the growing network of participants helps give paramedics a stronger voice.

The turnout was even more moving than Riley expected.

His father was an integral member of the ride’s planning committee and a dedicated ambassador for Island EMS, encouraging children and teenagers to consider the field.

“I know that it’s not just me out there,” he said. “Other people have had these losses in their lives.”

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Ottawa spending $4.7B on new made-in-Canada Via Rail passenger cars
stories.summary: Carney says he'll make the announcement in Thunder Bay on Wednesday morning.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Thunder BAY - Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a $4.7 billion contract to build 313 new passenger cars for Via Rail on Thursday.

Carney made the announcement at the Alstom plant in Thunder Bay, Ont., where the cars will be built.

“Our rail cars on our long-distance and remote routes are more than 70 years old. They were built when the NHL had six teams. Goalies wouldn’t wear masks. The Leafs would win the (Stanley) Cup,” Carney said.

“Those old cars have served our country well, but they’re long overdue for retirement. It’s time to build new ones, to build them here at home.”

Carney emphasized the fact that the new cars are being built in Canada.

“For the first time in four decades, those cars will be produced and assembled and maintained in our country. Cars that used to be built in the United States will be built right here in Thunder Bay at Alstom, by the best workers in the world,” Carney said.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon called the investment the single largest in Via Rail’s history and said the project will lead to 700 new jobs.

“This is a truly Canadian project. Canadian supply chains, workers, and it’s a renewed investment in that passenger rail service that connects us all,” MacKinnon told The Canadian Press following the announcement.

He said the first new car should be delivered in 2031.

In the 2024 federal budget, the previous Liberal government announced new funding for VIA Rail to replace its aging fleet on routes outside the Québec City-Windsor Corridor.

MacKinnon said the procurement process has been ongoing since then and the work is “long overdue.”

“That we’ll be able to replace it with Canadian-made equipment is an unbelievably good bonus,” he said.

Via Rail last imported passenger cars in August 2025 through a 2018 contract with Siemens Canada to replace locomotives and cars in the Windsor-Quebec City fleet, the company told The Canadian Press.

The cars and locomotives were manufactured at Siemens’ facility in Sacramento, California.

The contract is for nine different types of passenger cars: 78 sleepers, 58 coaches, 38 panorama cars, 29 baggage cars, 26 accessible sleepers, 25 dome cars, 20 dining cars, 20 prestige sleepers and 19 berth cars.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office said the average age of passenger cars along Via’s long distance and remote routes is 77 years.

In July, the government announced plans to spend $1.6 billion to replace 45 of Via Rail’s aging locomotives and another $357 million to build a new assembly plant and maintenance facility.

The locomotive contract was awarded to Stadler, a Swiss company which will use its facility in Valencia, Spain to design and manufacture much of the fleet. The government said 36 of the 45 locomotives will be completed in Canada.

Those new trains are also expected to be delivered in 2031.

At the time of the announcement, the federal government said the new locomotives would improve Via Rail’s reliability and on-time performance, which Canada’s auditor general found had dropped to a dismal 30 per cent in the first three months of 2025.

Conservative transport critic Dan Albas said in a media statement that Conservatives have pushed the Carney government to ensure taxpayer dollars support Canadian workers and industries using Canadian sourced materials.

“We expect that the Liberals will have put in place safeguards in the contracts to ensure these rail cars are built on time and on budget,” said Albas. “As the auditor general has reported, the fundamental issue is Via Rail’s reliability. Having new passenger cars does not address this.”

Albas also said the Conservatives call on the government to “stop paying Via Rail executive bonuses and address the deterioration of service.”

“While the Liberals are good at spending taxpayer money, they are not good at fixing problems,” he said.

MacKinnon said Via Rail will run the contract management, adding there are safeguards in place.

Addressing concerns about Via’s reliability, MacKinnon said the Crown corporation will be under new leadership soon.

“There are things they don’t control, meaning they run on someone else’s tracks, and that’s a very hard obstacle to get over, although I’m also hoping that we can get to a better running arrangement with CN,” he said.

“But on the things that Via can control, customer service, reliability, we have set high expectations for the things they can control, and I don’t think I’ve made any secret of either my impatience or concern for some of these problems to get resolved.”

After the announcement, Carney met with pop star Bryan Adams, who was scheduled to perform in Thunder Bay on Wednesday and Thursday. The pair went to a bakery to try a local pastry before visiting the Terry Fox National Historic Monument.

Carney later toured the Thunder Bay Fire Management facility.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa.

stories.title: Bank of Canada to unveil new $20 bill featuring King Charles
stories.summary: The bank was directed by former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government to feature the King in its next redesign process.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Bank of Canada is set to unveil a new bill today featuring an image of King Charles.

This is the first Canadian paper currency to feature Charles, whose image replaces that of the late Queen Elizabeth II.

The bank was directed by former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government to feature the King in its next redesign process.

The reigning monarch has been featured on Canadian bills since 1935.

The Royal Canadian Mint has produced coins featuring King Charles since 2023.

The King ascended to the throne in September 2022 after the death of his 96-year-old mother, who reigned for 70 years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.
