stories.title: ‘New hazards:’ Nepal disaster highlights emerging risks in Canada, researcher warns
stories.summary: A catastrophic rock-and-glacier collapse in Nepal is drawing attention to the risks posed by Canada’s own changing mountain landscapes, with a leading Canadian researcher warning that melting glaciers and thawing permafrost are creating new hazards.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
A catastrophic rock-and-glacier collapse in Nepal is drawing attention to the risks posed by Canada’s own changing mountain landscapes, with a leading Canadian researcher warning that melting glaciers and thawing permafrost are creating new hazards.

John Pomeroy, director of the Global Water Futures Observatories project at the University of Saskatchewan, said there is concern about similar types of mountain hazards occurring in Canada, which he says has more glaciers than any other country and vast areas of permafrost and snow.

“All this is melting and it’s melting faster and faster every year,” said Pomeroy, who is also the Unesco Chair in Mountain Water Sustainability. “So it’s creating new hazards that we haven’t seen before.”

The warning comes a week after catastrophic flash floods swept through parts of Nepal and neighbouring Tibet. At least 1,100 people have been killed and thousands remain missing, including 30 Canadians.

Search and rescue efforts continue as authorities grapple with the scale of the destruction.

Pomeroy said the disaster began high in the Himalayas, where a massive collapse sent rock and a sizeable portion of glacier plunging roughly a kilometre into the valley below.

He said the failure involved a slab of rock that had likely previously been frozen. When it fractured, the rock and glacier collapsed together, releasing vast amounts of meltwater stored in the ice.

“This then formed, like a tsunami of water and ice and rock and sediment that, within minutes, ran downstream over the border station on the China-Nepal border,” Pomeroy said.

It then “carried on at speeds over 160 km/h,” he said, with the wave reaching tens of metres high — “as high as 50 metres in some places.”

Pomeroy said warming in the Himalayas has been particularly rapid in recent years, contributing to glacier retreat and thawing permafrost that can destabilize mountain slopes.

Changing mountain environments

While an event on the scale of the Nepal disaster is extreme, he said Canada has already experienced smaller examples of hazards involving changing mountain environments.

In Jasper National Park in 2012, a rock-and-glacier collapse at Mount Edith Cavell sent a tsunami-like wave through the water below.

“It was in the middle of the night, so nobody was there,” Pomeroy said. “If that had been in the afternoon, there could have been a thousand people.”

Pomeroy also pointed to Canmore, Alta., as one of the mountain communities researchers are watching.

The town, about 100 kilometres west of Calgary, sits at the base of steep mountain terrain.

“We had the flood of a lifetime in 2013 and another pretty big flood — two floods in June this year involving debris movement in Cougar Creek,” Pomeroy said.

“A lot of that debris comes out of solid ground in the upper Cougar Creek basin and thawing permafrost up there. And we’re getting more extreme rainfall events.”

Pomeroy said a debris-control structure has since been built to help protect Cougar Creek, but added: “There’s many other mountain creeks around here that are very hazardous.”

Those changes are also being noticed by people who spend their working lives in the mountains.

Tim Ricci, director of operations with Yamnuska Mountain Adventures in Canmore, said changing conditions can be apparent over surprisingly short periods of time.

“We spend so much time in this terrain and we see the effects of the change season to season, and sometimes week to week, given huge temperature fluctuations,” Ricci said.

“As guides and mountain guides, we’re definitely adapting to those changes and thinking about how to best manage the risk side of things and safely move people through the mountains, given what we’re seeing with respect to climate change.”

Another type of glacier-related threat has already forced Canadians from their homes.

Near Pemberton, B.C., residents in the Poole Creek and Gates Lake area have experienced flooding for three years in a row, according to resident Nancy King.

This year, residents were placed under an evacuation order over the threat of an outburst flood from Place Glacier.

“What we know is that this is expected to be a yearly occurrence, as long as the glacier is still there,” King said.

“As residents, the concern is, do we have to leave our home every year? Are we going to lose our home? What is it going to look like?”

King said the uncertainty has taken a toll.

“We all put a lot of value into our homes,” King said. “It’s intended to be our safe space and our safe haven. And it doesn’t feel that way.”

Pomeroy said one of the challenges facing scientists is that many potentially hazardous areas are remote and difficult to continuously observe.

He said the Nepal event was large enough to register as a seismic event and was initially interpreted as an earthquake. Six minutes later, he said, the flood wave reached the Nepal-China border.

Pomeroy said better monitoring will be critical as mountain environments continue to change.

“Our early warning systems have to go beyond stream gauging,” he said. “We need satellites, new satellites and repurposing of existing satellites to be monitoring high risk areas.”

stories.title: Newfoundland welcomed them after 9/11. They’re heartbroken by Trump’s trade war
stories.summary: Canada's relationship with the United States began crumbling last year when U.S. President Donald Trump started making threats of annexation and tariffs on Canadian goods.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie
stories.content:
Every September, Sue Riccardelli and her wife, Maureen Murray, fly a large flag composed of Canada’s Maple Leaf and America’s Stars and Stripes outside their New Jersey home.

The flag honours the people of central Newfoundland who cared for them and more than 6,500 other passengers aboard 38 planes grounded in Gander, N.L., for days after the terrorist attacks in the United States on Sept. 11, 2001.

It is also a reminder of how important Canada and the United States are to each other, they said.

Last year, as relations between the countries grew strained, the couple started bringing the flag to local performances of “Come From Away,” a musical about the stranded passengers and the people in Gander who gave them food, clothing, shelter and friendship.

Riccardelli, 65, and Murray, 67, are among a group of Americans expected to return to Gander next week for the 25th anniversary of 9/11, an event that changed the world and their lives.

They are horrified by their president’s treatment of Canada, they said, and they plan to bring their flag and hold it high as a message of love and solidarity.

“As Americans, our country was at war, we were far away from home, and here were these people — Canadians, people from Gander — who just gave us their all,” said Riccardelli in a video interview from their home in New Jersey.

“That’s what the message needs to be, that Americans are not Trump, Americans are not this government,” Riccardelli added. “We are Americans who love Canada. That’s my message.”

Canada’s relationship with the United States began crumbling last year when U.S. President Donald Trump started making threats of annexation and tariffs on Canadian goods.

Tensions erupted into an all-out trade war last month when Prime Minister Mark Carney walked out of negotiations with the United States. Trump introduced 50 per cent levies on billions of dollars of Canadian exports and Carney has retaliated with tariffs beginning next week.

All this just weeks before an anniversary of a horrific event that brought thousands of Americans and Canadians together.

Kerry Derringer-Cashin was flying home to New Jersey from Dublin when hijackers slammed two planes into the World Trade Center in New York on Sept. 11, 2001, killing nearly 3,000 people. Her plane was the first to make an emergency landing in Gander when officials closed U.S. airspace that day.

She and her fellow passengers had to wait on the plane for hours, wondering what was happening. Strangers finally hustled them into the small Gander airport, where locals offered them sandwiches.

Local school bus drivers stopped a labour strike to shuttle the so-called “plane people” to churches, schools and community centres in towns throughout the area. Derringer-Cashin got off a bus at around 5 a.m. on Sept. 12, 2001, in Glenwood, about 20 kilometres west of Gander, where residents had set up cots and blankets in a church in the community.

They had even set up television sets, so the frightened passengers could watch the morning news and finally understand what was happening in the United States, she said. People offered phones and computers so passengers could contact their families. Some offered their homes for showers.

Some even offered the plane people their guest rooms, she said.

“I’m hoping that the message (of care and kindness) still somehow comes through,” said Derringer-Cashin, now 63, about the upcoming anniversary of 9/11. “People always say here, ‘I wish it was Sept. 12 again,’ because that’s when everybody in America came together, they put their differences aside.”

“We’re not happy with the relationship with the U.S. and Canada these days. We’re hoping that it will change and this will just be a blip in time,” she added. “I apologize on behalf of my country.”

Riccardelli and Murray were on their way home from France when they landed in Gander on 9/11. They stayed at the local College of the North Atlantic campus for four days, with more than 230 other people from their flight.

They made lifelong friends in Gander, and they’ve been back at least 10 times since to see them.

They first brought their flag to a local production of “Come From Away” in Morristown, N.J., a few months after Trump’s inauguration last year. He had already begun threatening to make Canada the 51st state.

They sat in the audience, nervous and clutching the fabric. When the show ended, Riccardelli said she stood up and opened the flag, turning to face the crowd.

Someone threw a spotlight onto her and the crowd erupted in applause.

“They went wild,” Murray said.

She said it’s important to remember that airports and towns all over Canada welcomed planes on 9/11.

“This was a Canada-wide effort to shelter people during this really hard time, to support them and support our country. And I’m hoping that is the takeaway,” she said. “Whatever is happening now between the U.S. and Canada is not deserved.”

Local school bus drivers stopped a labour strike to shuttle the so-called “plane people” to churches, schools and community centres in towns throughout the area. Derringer-Cashin got off a bus at around 5 a.m. on Sept. 12, 2001, in Glenwood, about 20 kilometres west of Gander, where residents had set up cots and blankets in a church in the community.

They had even set up television sets, so the frightened passengers could watch the morning news and finally understand what was happening in the United States, she said. People offered phones and computers so passengers could contact their families. Some offered their homes for showers.
Some even offered the plane people their guest rooms, she said.

“I’m hoping that the message (of care and kindness) still somehow comes through,” said Derringer-Cashin, now 63, about the upcoming anniversary of 9/11. “People always say here, ‘I wish it was Sept. 12 again,’ because that’s when everybody in America came together, they put their differences aside.”
“We’re not happy with the relationship with the U.S. and Canada these days. We’re hoping that it will change and this will just be a blip in time,” she added. “I apologize on behalf of my country.”

content_blocks.caption: Stranded passengers start waking up on Thursday morning Sept. 13, 2001, in Gander, N.L., in the gymnasium at Gander Academy, an elementary school. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Scott Cook

content_blocks.text: Riccardelli and Murray were on their way home from France when they landed in Gander on 9/11. They stayed at the local College of the North Atlantic campus for four days, with more than 230 other people from their flight.
They made lifelong friends in Gander, and they’ve been back at least 10 times since to see them.

They first brought their flag to a local production of “Come From Away” in Morristown, N.J., a few months after Trump’s inauguration last year. He had already begun threatening to make Canada the 51st state.
They sat in the audience, nervous and clutching the fabric. When the show ended, Riccardelli said she stood up and opened the flag, turning to face the crowd.
Someone threw a spotlight onto her and the crowd erupted in applause.
“They went wild,” Murray said.
She said it’s important to remember that airports and towns all over Canada welcomed planes on 9/11.

“This was a Canada-wide effort to shelter people during this really hard time, to support them and support our country. And I’m hoping that is the takeaway,” she said. “Whatever is happening now between the U.S. and Canada is not deserved.”

stories.title: Thousands remain without power, roads closed across southwestern Ontario after severe storms hit region
stories.summary: Thousands of customers remain without power, and several roads are closed across southwestern Ontario Thursday morning, after severe thunderstorms and high winds swept through the region Wednesday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Thousands of customers remain without power, and several roads are closed across southwestern Ontario Thursday morning, after severe thunderstorms and high winds swept through the region Wednesday afternoon.
· Posted: Sep 03, 2026 6:46 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Hydro One is reporting power outages across southwestern Ontario following severe thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon.(Hydro One)
Thousands of people across southwestern Ontario remain without power Thursday morning after severe thunderstorms and high winds swept through the region Wednesday afternoon.
Hydro One says crews are working to restore power, with some of the largest outages reported in lakeside communities from Grand Bend to Goderich.

"Currently across the province we have just over 50,000 customers out," said Hydro One spokesperson Bianca Pizzo. "Outages are being caused by severe winds overnight that caused downed tree limbs and branches onto power lines and in some cases have broken poles."
Crews are out in full force, said Pizzo, working as safely and quickly as they can to restore power.
Tornado watch lifted for London and Middlesex County, power outages remain across the region
As of early Thursday morning, the largest outages in the region included:
About 4,500 customers in the Grand Bend area
About 4,500 in the Bayfield area
About 3,500 near Goderich
About 3,600 in the Huron East area
About 900 near Ailsa Craig
About 1,100 near Woodstock
Smaller outages were also reported elsewhere across the region with restoration times unknown.
London Hydro reported no power outages as of early Thursday.
Updated Cleanup underway after severe GTA thunderstorm causes flooding, power outages

Hydro One's outage map and other outage tools are updated every 10 minutes. Customers can report an outage by texting 92887 (Watts), through the company's outage map or app, or by calling 1-800-434-1235.
West Region OPP said a number of roads remain closed Thursday morning because of fallen trees and downed hydro lines.
Among the affected roads are:
Perth Line 55 between Highway 23 and Road 166
Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140
Perth Line 44 from Road 150 to Road 179
Hensall Road from Highway 8 to Hydro Line Road
Front Road in Clinton between Victoria Boulevard and Highway 8
Ontario Street in Clinton between East Street and Smith Street
Road 11 in Essex between Graham Sideroad and County Road 31
McTaggart Line in Exeter
Victoria Street in Simcoe at Homewood Avenue
Highway 21 in Zurich between Zurich-Hensall Road and Sararas Road
Police are advising motorists to use caution and watch for debris and other hazards.
Hydro One is reminding people to stay at least 10 metres away from any downed power line and to call 911 and Hydro One to report it.
People using generators should operate them outside and away from windows, doors, and vents to prevent carbon monoxide from entering a home.

Environment Canada is also advising people to continue monitoring weather alerts as conditions can change quickly. The weather agency has issued a yellow fog advisory for the London region Thursday morning.

Travel will likely be hazardous in some locations, with visibility potentially reduced suddenly at times. Drivers should be prepared for areas of near-zero visibility and allow extra time to reach their destination.

Environment Canada is forecasting cloudy skies on Thursday with a 60 per cent chance of showers and a risk of a thunderstorm. Winds will become west at 30 km/h, gusting to 50 km/h late this afternoon with a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35 with the humidity.

stories.title: Canadian citizen confirmed safe after Nepal floods but 29 still missing
stories.summary: The search for missing individuals in Nepal is ongoing despite treacherous terrain, damaged infrastructure and dangerous weather conditions.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
A Canadian citizen previously reported missing in flash flooding in Nepal has been located and is safe, Global Affairs Canada said in an update Wednesday.

The agency said it is aware of 29 other Canadians and permanent residents in Nepal and Tibet whose whereabouts remain unknown.

“This number May fluctuate as new information becomes available, and as officials are able to establish contact with people in affected areas,” the agency said.

The search for missing individuals is ongoing despite treacherous conditions and damaged infrastructure, it added.

Nepal police are asking families of the missing individuals to share any information about the Canadian, foreign, or local phone numbers of their missing loved ones, as it May help with geolocation.

Efforts to collect DNA samples are also underway to assist with identification efforts; those who need to provide samples will be contacted directly by Global Affairs.

Canada is sending more than 18,000 supply kits to Nepal from its emergency stockpiles, including shelters, tools, hygiene products, and solar lights.

It has also provided $5 million in funding to support emergency relief efforts in Nepal.

Nepal’s foreign ministry said Thursday that 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while another 590 from 39 countries remain missing following the Aug. 26 floods.

At least 1,204 people have been killed, and more than 4,200 are missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency.

— with files from the Associated Press

stories.title: Analysts raise Canadian dollar forecasts, expecting trade tensions to ultimately fade
stories.summary: Medium projection is for the Canadian dollar to edge 0.4 per cent lower to 1.39 per U.S. dollar
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
Canada’s dollar will edge lower in ​coming months before notching moderate ‌gains in a year if a resolution is reached in the trade conflict with the United States, a Reuters poll showed.

The median forecast of ⁠32 foreign ​exchange analysts in an August 31 to September 2 poll was for the Canadian dollar to edge 0.4 per cent lower to 1.39 per U.S. dollar, or 71.94 U.S. cents, in three months, compared ​with a 1.40 forecast in a ‌survey last month.

In 12 months, the Canadian currency is expected to strengthen 1.8 per cent to 1.36, versus 1.3660 in the previous forecast.

“While we are bearish on the loonie in the short term, we expect many of the factors ‌currently weighing ​against the Canadian dollar ‌to fade,” said Nick Rees, head of macro research at Monex ​Europe.

“Trade tensions with the U.S. should eventually ⁠be resolved with a deal, regardless of present posturing, allowing ⁠domestic macro data to recover.”

Last month, the U.S. imposed new 50 per cent tariffs ​on at least $20 billion of imports from Canada after talks between the two countries collapsed.

The Bank of Canada said on Wednesday it does not expect the tariffs to have a large direct impact on the economy as it left its ⁠benchmark interest rate on hold at 2.25 per cent, adding that the ongoing Middle East conflict had raised upside risks to the inflation outlook.

“We do expect a modest strengthening to 1.35 by end of next year,” said Mirza Baig, a foreign exchange strategist at Desjardins. “We believe ⁠this will come about as the gap ​between U.S. and Canadian interest rates will narrow, and investment spending in ⁠Canada will accelerate.”

Investors expect about 100 basis points in tightening from the BoC by the ‌end of 2027, which would move the policy rate toward the top of ​the central bank’s estimated 2.25 per cent to 3.25 per cent range for the neutral interest rate — the rate at which borrowing costs are neither slowing nor boosting the economy.

stories.title: Randy Boyagoda’s new novel puts the university campus on a global stage
stories.summary: Lords of Serendipity, Boyagoda’s first international release, has the makings of a breakout
stories.author: Emily Donaldson, Photography by Randy Boyagoda
stories.content:
Randy Boyagoda, novelist and career academic, has satirized university life before. But in his latest, Lords of Serendipity, he takes the campus novel global.

Boyagoda is hardly an unknown quantity in Canada. His first novel, Governor of the Northern Province , was longlisted for the Giller Prize; his second, Beggar’s Feast , for the International Dublin Literary Award.

Lords of Serendipity has the makings of a breakout. It’s Boyagoda’s first international release, with simultaneous publication in Canada, the U.S. and Britain, among other countries. When I met with him at his 10th-floor office in the University of Toronto’s Jackman Humanities Institute, where he was recently appointed director, he was getting ready to leave for an Australian book tour.

Over the decade it took him to write Lords of Serendipity, the contemporary university was a moving target. But Boyagoda proved prescient in several respects. He tells me, with some pride, that encampments were in the novel well before 2024.

By the time he submitted Lords to publishers, in early 2025, reality had caught up with the novel. The war in Gaza had thrown universities into political turmoil, and the second Trump administration had just taken office. The timing was, if you will, serendipitous.

Boyagoda was born in Oshawa, Ont., in 1976, the eldest of three children of Sri Lankan parents who immigrated to Canada in the late 1960s. His father was a high-school chemistry teacher, his mother a medical secretary. He describes his upbringing as “pretty straightforward middle-class Canadian.”

Before there was Randy, there was Soharn – an identifiably Sri Lankan name that did not pass unnoticed in 1980s Oshawa. Taunted for it, he eventually traded it in for his middle name. The irony, as Boyagoda sees it, is that his father was militantly assimilationist. When the family visited Sri Lankan relatives, the latter made curries. The Boyagodas brought Shake ‘n Bake chicken and mashed potatoes.

Boyagoda might have filed the childhood ridicule under injury. Instead, he says, it taught him something about irony: how a situation can be painful or strained yet funny, double vision that would serve him well as a writer.

Books had him early. By 15, writing was already serious business. After a game of 500 Up with buddies in an Oshawa field, there was a plan to go to the mall. Boyagoda declined to go. His friends, most from families who worked at the local GM plant, couldn’t understand why. Strict immigrant parents, perhaps? The badgering continued until, finally, he cracked: “I’m writing a novel.” They howled.

Boyagoda studied English at the University of Toronto, then did a PhD at Boston University, where he met his wife, Anna, a fellow doctoral candidate from Milwaukee.

He entered academia , in part, because he knew “professor” would be a more acceptable profession to his parents than “novelist.” But he kept writing, setting himself the goal of publishing his first short story by 21, the age at which he knew Hemingway had done it. He met the deadline.

After stints at Notre Dame and Ryerson University (now Toronto Metropolitan University), Boyagoda arrived at U of T in 2016. Though he enjoys teaching, he discovered that leading and running things came naturally to him, and moved into administration at the earliest opportunity.

It’s not hard to see why. Boyagoda is warm, articulate and has a knack for putting people at ease. He also has a strong sense of what he wants to accomplish. Until recently, one of those accomplishments was pursued under the grand-sounding title of provostial adviser on civil discourse.

Doing a PhD convinced him that he didn’t want to spend his life writing for other academics. He wanted to bring books and ideas into a wider public conversation. Fiction, he believes, is uniquely suited to this: Novelists have a rare capacity to offer readers a larger vision of human experience.

Boyagoda grew up Catholic and remains devout . His two Prin novels – comic satires centred on a middle-aged Catholic English professor – are steeped in Catholic themes (the trilogy’s third book is forthcoming).

Lords of Serendipity has more in common with the Catholic tradition of Graham Greene, Evelyn Waugh (to whom Boyagoda has been compared) and Flannery O’Connor. Greene, in fact, has been strongly on Boyagoda’s mind lately. The English author’s “sense of people trying to do the good in spite of themselves and in spite of the world around them,” resonates strongly with him. For the past few years, he’s given papers at the annual Greene Festival in Berkhamsted, England.

Catholic novels, in this tradition, aren’t necessarily pious novels. They’re often populated by adulterers, drunks, hypocrites and people who are terrible at being Catholics (Exhibit A: the alcoholic “whisky priest” who fathers a child in Greene’s The Power and the Glory ). What ties Boyagoda to it is precisely that ability to combine comic social observation with serious moral stakes. He describes his approach as that of a “morally minded take-no-prisoners satirist.”

His character Prin is hardly a model believer. He’s vain, professionally ambitious, frequently self-absorbed and capable of spectacular failures as a husband and father, even as he keeps trying to understand what his faith requires of him. His misadventures take him, first, to the Middle East on a quixotic mission to save his Toronto college, then to small-town Indiana, where he helps an evangelical millionaire develop an Inferno -themed (as in Dante) amusement park.

Lords of Serendipity follows a cast of characters scattered across a globalized university system. Among them is Devi, a girl from a poor Sri Lankan village whose family is staking much of its future on her getting into a Western university.

Unless you count Devi’s regular trips to the local cathedral to steal its Wi-Fi for video calls with Johannes, the tutor helping with her university applications, Lords is less overtly Catholic than the Prin books. Still, something of the same moral architecture remains. Sacrifice runs through the novel. To pay for Devi’s hoped-for university education, her father cleans hotel toilets and, with the rest of the family, works weekends as a professional mourner at a funeral home.

In the U.S., Jack, a widowed statistician, struggles to afford his daughter’s education at Haven College while teaching an overloaded schedule at Arcadia Tech, where a “Compassionate Grading Protocol” gives everyone in a class an automatic A minus after an extreme event – an active shooter, a terrorist attack or a “credible threat of class-specific violence.”

Others get by in less honourable ways. Johannes, who purports to attend “a prestigious uni overseas,” repeatedly wheedles Devi for more money. Boyagoda tends to be forgiving even of his more rapacious characters, like Johannes, who are often victims of a gig economy that has pushed them to the margins.

His Catholic sensibility May help explain one of Boyagoda’s favourite fictional manoeuvres: dropping his characters into strange, sometimes far-flung worlds where they don’t quite belong. “Ultimately it’s religious,” he tells me. “Christianity proposes to be in the world but not of the world.” He points to Saint Augustine’s distinction between the City of God and the Earthly City, which leaves the believer with an abiding sense that “this is not finally where I’m supposed to be.”

Growing up both Catholic and “a Sri Lankan kid from Oshawa” gave Boyagoda a more personal version of that experience. “I think it translates imaginatively into an interest in putting people in unexpected situations and seeing what’s going to happen,” he says.

Lords of Serendipity is ultimately a campus novel that’s less about campus life than the global market that feeds it. Here is the university reduced to a ticket, a brand, a status symbol. Devi has set her sights on getting into Ochyps (OxfordCambridgeHarvardYalePrincetonStanford). What she wants to study is beside the point. She wants to study at Harvard because she wants to go to Harvard.

The universities of Lords have effectively become borderless, drawing students from across the world even as their own substance and history are being hollowed out. Chapels become wellness centres, library stacks give way to meditation zones, a century-old Gothic quadrangle is “a beautiful front for hedge fund investments.” Employees are made to train the artificial-intelligence bots designed to replace them.

Boyagoda has, as ever, a sharp eye for the absurdities of university politics and pieties. After Jack uses the example of an eagle catching a pigeon’s wing in midair to illustrate probability, he gets reprimanded for subjecting his students to “graphic acts of animal cruelty.” Later, when he uncovers a grade-fixing scandal tied to a student suicide, however, the school is less solicitous, performative compassion giving way to damage control.

By Lords’ end, Jack finds himself in a particularly Greeneian predicament. Any which way he turns, he’s compromised. Someone will suffer, but he still has to act. In a fallen world, the best he can hope for is to do good rather than great.

When I ask if he’s worried about how students or staff might react to his novel’s skewerings, Boyagoda gives a wry smile. “I’ll be gratified if enough people read the book that they find themselves in there.”

For all his poking fun at university life, Boyagoda clearly loves it. He entered academia at 19 and never left. I ask him about the stories out there: of English students graduating without ever having read an entire book. He answers by telling me about the Intro to the Novel survey course he’ll teach this fall, whose reading list consists of just three books: George Eliot’s Middlemarch , Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man and Kiran Desai’s The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny , which together run to about 2,200 pages.

To keep the AI hounds at bay, he’ll administer oral exams to all 80 students. “It’s going to take me two days. And it’s going to be a conversation. All they’re going to have is a glass of water, a box of Kleenex and M&Ms. And we’re going to sit there, and I’m going to ask them about the books.

“The world says you don’t want to do this, you can’t do this, you’re not capable of this,” he continues. “But I don’t believe that. I believe that if people keep telling you that, it might be true. But come live inside the world of a novel with me.”

What ties Boyagoda to it is precisely that ability to combine comic social observation with serious moral stakes. He describes his approach as that of a “morally minded take-no-prisoners satirist.”

They’re often populated by adulterers, drunks, hypocrites and people who are terrible at being Catholics (Exhibit A: the alcoholic “whisky priest” who fathers a child in Greene’s The Power and the Glory). What ties Boyagoda to it is precisely that ability to combine comic social observation with serious moral stakes. He describes his approach as that of a “morally minded take-no-prisoners satirist.”

content_blocks.text: His character Prin is hardly a model believer. He’s vain, professionally ambitious, frequently self-absorbed and capable of spectacular failures as a husband and father, even as he keeps trying to understand what his faith requires of him. His misadventures take him, first, to the Middle East on a quixotic mission to save his Toronto college, then to small-town Indiana, where he helps an evangelical millionaire develop an Inferno -themed (as in Dante) amusement park.

content_blocks.text: Lords of Serendipity follows a cast of characters scattered across a globalized university system. Among them is Devi, a girl from a poor Sri Lankan village whose family is staking much of its future on her getting into a Western university.

content_blocks.text: Unless you count Devi’s regular trips to the local cathedral to steal its Wi-Fi for video calls with Johannes, the tutor helping with her university applications, Lords is less overtly Catholic than the Prin books. Still, something of the same moral architecture remains. Sacrifice runs through the novel. To pay for Devi’s hoped-for university education, her father cleans hotel toilets and, with the rest of the family, works weekends as a professional mourner at a funeral home.

content_blocks.text: In the U.S., Jack, a widowed statistician, struggles to afford his daughter’s education at Haven College while teaching an overloaded schedule at Arcadia Tech, where a “Compassionate Grading Protocol” gives everyone in a class an automatic A minus after an extreme event – an active shooter, a terrorist attack or a “credible threat of class-specific violence.”

content_blocks.text: Others get by in less honourable ways. Johannes, who purports to attend “a prestigious uni overseas,” repeatedly wheedles Devi for more money. Boyagoda tends to be forgiving even of his more rapacious characters, like Johannes, who are often victims of a gig economy that has pushed them to the margins.

content_blocks.text: His Catholic sensibility May help explain one of Boyagoda’s favourite fictional manoeuvres: dropping his characters into strange, sometimes far-flung worlds where they don’t quite belong. “Ultimately it’s religious,” he tells me. “Christianity proposes to be in the world but not of the world.” He points to Saint Augustine’s distinction between the City of God and the Earthly City, which leaves the believer with an abiding sense that “this is not finally where I’m supposed to be.”

content_blocks.text: Lords of Serendipity is ultimately a campus novel that’s less about campus life than the global market that feeds it. Here is the university reduced to a ticket, a brand, a status symbol. Devi has set her sights on getting into Ochyps (OxfordCambridgeHarvardYalePrincetonStanford). What she wants to study is beside the point. She wants to study at Harvard because she wants to go to Harvard.

What she wants to study is beside the point. She wants to study at Harvard because she wants to go to Harvard.

content_blocks.text: The universities of Lords have effectively become borderless, drawing students from across the world even as their own substance and history are being hollowed out. Chapels become wellness centres, library stacks give way to meditation zones, a century-old Gothic quadrangle is “a beautiful front for hedge fund investments.” Employees are made to train the artificial-intelligence bots designed to replace them.

content_blocks.text: Boyagoda has, as ever, a sharp eye for the absurdities of university politics and pieties. After Jack uses the example of an eagle catching a pigeon’s wing in midair to illustrate probability, he gets reprimanded for subjecting his students to “graphic acts of animal cruelty.” Later, when he uncovers a grade-fixing scandal tied to a student suicide, however, the school is less solicitous, performative compassion giving way to damage control.

content_blocks.text: By Lords’ end, Jack finds himself in a particularly Greeneian predicament. Any which way he turns, he’s compromised. Someone will suffer, but he still has to act. In a fallen world, the best he can hope for is to do good rather than great.

content_blocks.text: For all his poking fun at university life, Boyagoda clearly loves it. He entered academia at 19 and never left. I ask him about the stories out there: of English students graduating without ever having read an entire book. He answers by telling me about the Intro to the Novel survey course he’ll teach this fall, whose reading list consists of just three books: George Eliot’s Middlemarch , Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man and Kiran Desai’s The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny , which together run to about 2,200 pages.

All they’re going to have is a glass of water, a box of Kleenex and M&Ms. And we’re going to sit there, and I’m going to ask them about the books.

stories.title: Pool, basketball court and elevator lure buyer to North York home
stories.summary: The house has more land and luxuries than most homes have in the area between Downsview and Earl Bales parks
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
20 Sunbeam Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $3,999,995 (July, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $4,550,000 (May, 2026); $4,799,995 (January, 2026); $5,499,995 (October, 2025)

Selling price: $3,950,018 (July, 2026)

Taxes: $20,496 (2025)

Days on the market: 16

Property days on market: 216

Listing agent: Jordan Glaser, Re/Max Realtron Realty Inc.

This five-year-old house has more than 5,500 square feet of living space, as well as a basketball court, an in-ground pool, a hot tub and a cabana at the back of the 65- by 170-foot lot. With more land and luxuries than most homes have in the area between Downsview and Earl Bales parks, it floated an asking price of nearly $5.5-million last fall.

“It’s an absolutely amazing house with features and benefits you don’t really see in this neighbourhood; like a Forest Hill or Bridle Path type of house,” agent Jordan Glaser said.

“There was no direct comparable to this because it’s so much bigger and different than other stuff on the market.”

Despite its allurements, there were no serious offers and the asking price for the four-bedroom home was adjusted downward twice. When the price dipped again this summer, this time below $4-million, a return guest made an offer of $3,950,018, which the seller accepted.

It May not have met its highest aspirations, but the home still made its mark, Mr. Glaser said. “It officially became the highest reported sale on MLS in Clanton Park’s history.”

“If this house was five kilometres south or east, it would cost double the price. It really provided a huge value for what it was and what you’re getting in this neighbourhood.”

This two-storey house has an attached, double garage and a heated, circular driveway.

There is an elevator, two laundry rooms and seven bathrooms, including four ensuites with heated floors upstairs.

There are two offices, a dining room and three entertaining areas, including one in the basement.

The eat-in kitchen has 12-foot doors to a covered patio with a fireplace and a barbecue station.

“Rounded driveways are unique enough in the area, let alone a heated one,” Mr. Glaser said.

“The backyard is like a resort. You don’t need to have a cottage or go away for the summer; you can just spend it there.”

stories.title: New homes HST rebate cramps sale of dated townhouse in Toronto’s Hillcrest Village
stories.summary: The three-bedroom home near Don Mills Road and Steeles Avenue had less than 20 viewings over nearly three months
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
191 Jenny Wrenway, No. 11, Toronto

Asking price: $799,000 (March, 2026)

Selling price: $700,000 (June, 2026)

Taxes: $3,838 (2025)

Days on the market: 84

Listing agent: Bill Thom, Re/Max Realtron Realty Inc.

Agent Bill Thom thought an affordable asking price of $799,000 might attract buyers to this three-bedroom townhouse, built near Don Mills Road and Steeles Avenue in the 1970s. Over nearly three months, it had less than 20 viewings, a low turnout Mr. Thom attributes to buyers skipping older homes for brand-new ones eligible for a recently announced HST rebate.

“Usually townhouses like that, I expected a lot more showings,” Mr. Thom said. “The market was bad, and one reason May be, ON April 1, the government came out with an HST rebate for new homes up to about $1.8-million. That affected prices for anything [older] below $1.8-million.”

Once these sellers received a viable offer for the property, they accepted a $700,000 deal.

“We did okay, even though the price was not what we anticipated,” Mr. Thom said. “There was one other [seller in the area] competing with us, and they tried all kinds of price strategies … and ended up giving up and not selling.”

This condominium townhouse has an attached garage, a street-level entrance and 1,600 square feet of living space spread across multiple levels, plus a finished basement.

The living room has vaulted ceilings, sliding patio doors and stairs to a dining area and an eat-in kitchen.

There are three bedrooms on the top floor, and two bathrooms.

Monthly fees of $601 cover water, cable and use of a common pool.

“The house is in a very good school catchment area,” Mr. Thom said. “You can walk to the TTC, take one bus to the subway, and it has convenient access to Highway 404 and 401.”

stories.title: Toronto Area home sales down 2% in August, prices dip below $1M: board
stories.summary: The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board says 5,057 homes changed hands last month, down 2.1 per cent year-over-year, while sales also fell 1.3 per cent from July.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area were down in August compared with a year ago as prices also continued to fall.

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board says 5,057 homes changed hands last month, down 2.1 per cent year-over-year, while sales also fell 1.3 per cent from July on a seasonally adjusted basis.

The average selling price stood at $993,410, down 2.7 per cent year-over-year, while the composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.5 per cent.

It’s the second time this year that the average selling price has dipped below the $1-million level, after January marked the first instance of that happening in five years.

There were 12,075 new listings on the market in August, down 14.1 per cent from last year.

Trreb president Daniel Steinfeld says that if inventory tightens and home prices begin to rise, some buyers May face a trade-off between waiting for greater economic certainty and purchasing before prices move higher.

stories.title: From folk rock to fundamental research: Dupras leads Quebec science
stories.summary: Dupras comes from farming families on both sides and said an uncle interested in genealogy traced about 16 generations of farmers on his father’s side.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Jérôme Dupras spent much of his twenties on the road, playing bass guitar across Quebec and beyond.

In 1997, he joined a band with friends. That summer, the folk rock group anonymously released 500 cassettes of its first album. Over the next few years, it would become Les Cowboys Fringants, one of Quebec’s most popular musical acts.

Their songs tell stories about Quebec and its people, mixing humour and nostalgia with a critical look at society.

“(Touring) made me love music, but also really love Quebec, and want to talk about it elsewhere in the world,” Dupras said in an interview.

All the while, he pursued a second career in science, studying biochemistry and eventually becoming a researcher specializing in biodiversity and ecological economics. He became Quebec’s chief scientist in June, tasked with advising the government and championing research in an era of disinformation.

Now, as Quebecers prepare to elect a new government this fall, Dupras faces a challenge that brings his two sides as a musician and scientist together.

His ability to communicate beyond the scientific community could prove particularly valuable in his new job, according to members of Quebec’s research community.

One of Les Cowboys Fringants’ songs, “Plus rien,” which translates to “nothing left,” imagines a future devastated by climate change, while “8 secondes” takes aim at overconsumption and the environmental cost of modern life. Other songs explore inequality and Quebec identity — and an attachment to a place they worried was changing.

Luc-Alain Giraldeau, director general of the Institut national de la recherche scientifique, a Quebec university institution devoted to research and graduate education, said Dupras “combines scientific rigour and creativity.”

His scientific credibility and ability to reach a broad public are “an undeniable asset,” Giraldeau said, particularly at a time when disinformation is gaining ground worldwide.

Sophie Montreuil, executive director of the Association francophone pour le savoir, a Canadian organization based in Montreal that promotes French-language science and research, called Dupras’s unusual background “a great strength.”

The bassist succeeded Rémi Quirion, who held the chief scientist position since it was created in 2011.

Dupras says Quebec is at an “important crossroads,” and that its position as a research leader cannot be taken for granted.

As chief scientist and head of the Fonds de recherche du Québec, Dupras must remain politically neutral. But he is watching the election closely: “I’m curious to see what place innovation, research and science will have.”

After the election Oct. 5, his organization plans to brief the incoming government on the sector and its priorities. Among them is protecting fundamental research, which can take decades to produce practical results.

“We have areas of excellence that are recognized internationally,” he said, pointing to artificial intelligence, aerospace and environmental sciences.

But there’s no guarantee Quebec can remain a leader in those areas, Dupras said, noting how public institutions and science are coming under increasing political pressure in the United States.

“We shouldn’t think that we’re immune,” he said.

He also said the province faces a challenge in ensuring discoveries made in Quebec translate into intellectual property, companies and economic benefits that remain here.

“We really have a brain drain and capital flight,” Dupras said.

When an idea developed in Quebec attracts investment from elsewhere, and the company commercializing it ends up outside the province, he said, “the talent will follow, the products will follow, and the wealth will follow.”

Dupras also wants scientists to play a greater role in public life as social media and algorithms transform how people receive information. If researchers fail to keep pace with those changes, he said, “we risk losing ground.”

Thus, reaching young people is particularly important to him.

“Young people are a priority for me,” Dupras said. “A path in science is inspiring.”

His own path began in a family that valued education. Dupras comes from farming families on both sides and said an uncle interested in genealogy traced about 16 generations of farmers on his father’s side.

His grandfather was a farmer who emphasized education, and Dupras grew up seeing higher education as a natural possibility. He wants that opportunity to extend to everyone.

“We have to make sure everyone has the same equal chances, whether we’ve been here for 15 generations or we’re a newcomer,” he said.

He said teachers helped spark his fascination with biology and led him to biochemistry. Science became another outlet for the curiosity and creativity he had found in music, he added.

“Music and science are channels for dreaming, for being creative, for communicating with people,” Dupras said.

The two passions sometimes overlapped. In the mid-2000s, Dupras and his bandmates created the Fondation Cowboys Fringants, which supports nature conservation and the protection of threatened ecosystems in Quebec. The band’s lead singer, Karl Tremblay, died in 2023.

Both careers also took Dupras abroad and gave him a platform to promote Quebec.

Dupras sees public service as another way of giving back, and he embraces a vision that puts science at the heart of Quebec’s future.

“I’ve received so much in my life,” he said. “If, very humbly, I can give back to Quebec by serving it as a public servant, as part of the state, it’s a source of pride and a privilege.”

stories.title: Voters head to polls in three Ontario by-elections amid trade war with U.S.
stories.summary: Progressive Conservatives are looking to hold on to two seats in York and Hamilton, while NDP is hoping to keep Scarborough-Southwest
stories.author: Laura Stone, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives held on to two seats in Thursday’s Ontario by-elections while the NDP retained a third, results that leave the status quo in the provincial legislature unchanged.

The races happened at a critical time in Canada-U.S. relations and after the Ontario Premier engaged in a war of words with President Donald Trump. The contests were seen as the first political test for Mr. Ford’s majority government since trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed last month.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals swept three federal by-elections across the country, including winning a Quebec seat that was previously Conservative.

Thursday’s results were a blow the Ontario Liberals, who are set to name a new leader on Nov. 21.

Ontario’s by-elections were held in York-Simcoe, Hamilton East-Stoney Creek and Scarborough Southwest.

Going into the vote, Mr. Ford’s Progressive Conservatives held the two seats in York and Hamilton, which were vacated when former cabinet ministers Caroline Mulroney and Neil Lumsden resigned.

The Scarborough seat in Toronto’s east end was previously held by Doly Begum, who resigned her position as NDP deputy leader to run for the federal Liberals.

In Hamilton East—Stoney Creek, PC candidate Jeff Beattie won with about 39 per cent of the vote. The Ndp’s Monique Taylor came in second with almost 33 per cent, and Liberal Heino Doessing was in third with 23 per cent.

In York-Simcoe, PC candidate Susan Lahey won almost 50 per cent of the vote, with Liberal Naomi Davison in second at 39 per cent, and the NDP candidate a distant third with 4 per cent. The Liberals did significantly better than they did in the 2025 vote, when they won only 24 per cent.

In Scarborough Southwest, the NDP held onto its seat, with candidate Fatima Shaban garnering about 40 per cent of the vote - well ahead of Liberal Ahsanul Hafiz at about 30 per cent and PC candidate Noor Tarun at 23 per cent.

Speaking alongside Mr. Beattie outside his victory party in Hamilton, Mr. Ford congratulated his candidate and thanked the opposition parties for their campaigns.

The Premier vowed to keep up his fight against Mr. Trump’s tariffs: “The enemy isn’t each and every one of us, all of us together. The enemy is Donald Trump. And we’re going to fight against Donald Trump.”

The victory in Scarborough was a rare bit of good news for NDP Leader Marit Stiles, after the loss of her deputy leader, which sparked the by-election race, and a series of polls that have shown her party behind Ontario’s leaderless Liberals.

She told cheering organizers in Scarborough that Thursday’s victory belonged to them – and that the results showed that her party was the one that could eventually defeat Mr. Ford.

“You delivered a message today to Doug Ford,” Ms. Stiles said, flanked by her candidate and several of her MPPs. “You said, ‘You better watch your back, because we are coming for you.’”

Mr. Ford’s popularity took a hit earlier this spring after a series of controversies, including his government’s purchase of a $28.9-million private jet and a hotel-expenses scandal that resulted in the resignation of one of his cabinet ministers. But the Premier has since rebounded in some polls amid a public spat with Mr. Trump, who has personally attacked the Premier. Last week, Mr. Ford told Mr. Trump to “kiss my ass” and called him a loser.

The PCs used the conflict with the U.S. President as part of their campaign materials, saying the Premier is the only one who can “stand up to Trump.” But political opponents accused Mr. Ford of deflecting from his own government’s record, including on health care and education.

Political observers expected the PCs to hold rural York-Simcoe, north of Toronto, long a Conservative stronghold. But the Hamilton seat was seen as being in play for the opposition parties. NDP candidate Ms. Taylor was a former long-time MPP from a neighbouring area, and the Liberals were hoping to make inroads with Mr. Doessing, who placed second in the 2025 provincial election.

The Scarborough seat was seen as the most unpredictable. Both Ms. Stiles and Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser watched the by-election results roll in at candidate events in Scarborough.

The NDP saw the seat, which was won three times by Ms. Begum, as a must-win for candidate Ms. Shaban. But the Liberals were looking to take it back, after a nomination battle in which former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith accused the party of wrongdoing after he narrowly lost to candidate Mr. Hafiz.

The Ontario PC Party, meanwhile, barred journalists from attending their candidates’ by-election parties, which are traditionally open to media.

Voter turnout for the races was low: 29 per cent in Hamilton-Stoney Creek, 26.5 per cent in Scarborough and 21 per cent in York-Simcoe, according to Elections Ontario.

Mr. Ford’s popularity took a hit earlier this spring after a series of controversies, including his government’s purchase of a $28.9-million private jet and a hotel-expenses scandal that resulted in the resignation of one of his cabinet ministers. But the Premier has since rebounded in some polls amid a public spat with Mr. Trump, who has personally attacked the Premier. Last week, Mr. Ford told Mr. Trump to “kiss my ass” and called him a loser.

The PCs used the conflict with the U.S. President as part of their campaign materials, saying the Premier is the only one who can “stand up to Trump.” But political opponents accused Mr. Ford of deflecting from his own government’s record, including on health care and education.

Political observers expected the PCs to hold rural York-Simcoe, north of Toronto, long a Conservative stronghold. But the Hamilton seat was seen as being in play for the opposition parties. NDP candidate Ms. Taylor was a former long-time MPP from a neighbouring area, and the Liberals were hoping to make inroads with Mr. Doessing, who placed second in the 2025 provincial election.
The Scarborough seat was seen as the most unpredictable. Both Ms. Stiles and Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser watched the by-election results roll in at candidate events in Scarborough.

The NDP saw the seat, which was won three times by Ms. Begum, as a must-win for candidate Ms. Shaban. But the Liberals were looking to take it back, after a nomination battle in which former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith accused the party of wrongdoing after he narrowly lost to candidate Mr. Hafiz.
The Ontario PC Party, meanwhile, barred journalists from attending their candidates’ by-election parties, which are traditionally open to media.
Voter turnout for the races was low: 29 per cent in Hamilton-Stoney Creek, 26.5 per cent in Scarborough and 21 per cent in York-Simcoe, according to Elections Ontario.

stories.title: Saskatchewan sees another overpass strike near Borden Bridge
stories.summary: A new month, a new overpass strike in Saskatchewan. This time, just West of Saskatoon near the Borden Bridge where a semi was hauling agriculture equipment.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
By Ashley Beherns Global News

Posted September 3, 2026 7:13 am

Another overpass has been hit in Saskatchewan, except this time, just outside of Saskatoon near the Borden Bridge about half an hour northwest of the city.

It happened just before noon on Sept. 2 on the Yellowhead Highway heading west.

This is at least the seventh time a vehicle has struck an overpass or train bridge in the province this year.

Saskatoon alone has seen five of those incidents, with the last strike happening in July, when a semi hauling a grain bin hit the 51st Street overpass on Idylwyld Drive.

The most expensive was the first one on March 5, when a semi hauling an excavator slammed into the Highway 16 overpass above Highway 11, causing more than $280,000 in damages.

Crews were on scene shortly after this incident near Borden, bringing in a crane to help move the equipment.

The Saskatchewan Highway Patrol is assisting the RCMP with the investigation.

People are asked to check highway hotline for any road restrictions and use caution in the area.

Watch the video above for more on the series of Saskatchewan overpass strikes.

stories.title: Kelowna asks Ottawa to help shut down the downtown’s supervised consumption site
stories.summary: Mayor Tom Dyas has written to the federal health minister asking that the facility’s 2027 renewal be denied.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The City of Kelowna is pushing to have the supervised consumption site in the city’s downtown shut down when its current authorization expires.

Mayor Tom Dyas has written to the federal health minister asking that the facility’s 2027 renewal be denied.

“We feel collectively that, as you know, myself, council, and I think many individuals within this community, that the current system is not working,” Dyas told Global News.

The letter, dated Aug. 26, states, “the status quo of outreach urban health is not working, and the impacts concentrated around this specific location have become unsustainable.”

It goes on to say, “The city, RCMP and public safety partners continue to respond to serious and recurring incidents near the site, including gang activity, weapons-related assaults, intimate partner violence, drug trafficking, fencing of stolen property, arson, overdoses and other medical emergencies.”

“We have had over 3,500 RCMP calls. We have had 371 different medical emergencies that our fire department has had to deal with,” Dyas said. “We’ve had over 450 bylaw occurrences.”

The incidents have been an ongoing concern for businesses and residents near the site.

In June, the adjacent alley was fenced off in an effort to mitigate impacts around the facility.

1:44 City of Kelowna fences off problem-plagued alley

Global News spoke with half a dozen business operators near the site.

None wanted to appear on camera, citing concerns about potential retribution, but they were largely supportive of efforts to shut the site down.

Advocates, however, say closing the facility could put other services offered at the Outreach Urban Health Centre at risk, including primary health care, at time when more services are needed, not less.

“It just does not make any sense because all those services will be lost,” said Wes Zawertailo, executive director of People Lived Experience Society.

“And so often things are shut down with the idea that we’re going to make it bigger and better and offer more services, but they never come to fruition.”

According to Interior Health, the site recorded approximately 37,000 visits last year.

“It’s a life-saving health service for people who are using drugs,” said Dr. Sue Pollock, Interior Health’s chief medical health officer. “We are starting to see a decline in the number of overdose deaths in Kelowna.

“So there was a peak in overdose deaths in 2023 coming off the pandemic and now we’re starting to see a slow decline in the number of deaths, so we are encouraged that we are able to reach people and provide them the supports they need.”

Dyas said council ultimately went to Ottawa after what he describes as a lack of timely action from the provincial government and Interior Health (IH) in addressing the city’s concerns.

He says the city had previously sent letters to both organizations.

But Pollock said discussions about the concerns raised by the city are continuing.

“Conversations are ongoing and we recognize that the issues and challenges faced by the City of Kelowna in the downtown core, in particular, need to be addressed by all of us,” Pollock said. “It’s not going to be solved by one organization.”

B.C.’s health minister confirmed to Global News that the province had received a letter from the city several weeks ago.

“We have received the letter from the City of Kelowna and are responding to Mayor Dyas directly very soon,” said health minister Ravi Kahlon. “I also greatly look forward to meeting with Mayor Dyas and the City of Kelowna at Ubcm, and working together to address his concerns and improve care for people in Kelowna.”

The federal health ministry, which received the latest letter from the city, was unable to provide a response before time of publication.

stories.title: Toronto poet and educator offers lifeline to Afghan girls barred from school under Taliban rule through online classes
stories.summary: Since 2021, the Taliban regime has been excluding women from every aspect of public life, including education
stories.author: Sharif Hassan
stories.content:
On a recent summer Friday, nearly a dozen students logged on for their online literature class. It was a group of mostly young women joining from different parts of Afghanistan , eagerly waiting for their turn to discuss a story they had read the week before.

Before the Taliban’s return to power five years ago, the women were studying in high school or university, hoping education would give them a better future. Some had just obtained their undergraduate degrees. But their plans were put on hold when, like millions of other Afghan girls, they were barred from going to school.

Once a week, the group gathers in a Google Meet room for a 90-minute class hosted by Toronto-based poet and educator Hazrat Wahriz. In this lesson attended by a reporter, they discussed a short story about a teenage boy’s journey fleeing the Taliban.

The story’s author, Shams Erfan, joined the virtual class from Toronto and listened attentively throughout the session. Then he had a few words for the women.

“I hope you continue ... writing, critiquing, reading, protesting, attending online classes,” he said in Persian.

“These activities are a fight,” he continued, “a fight against the Taliban ideology that is trying to remove you all.”

Since 2021, the Taliban regime has been excluding women from every aspect of public life by imposing what international human rights groups call a system of “gender apartheid.” It has issued sweeping edicts to restrict women’s right to work, education and freedom of movement.

In a report published last month, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization estimated that 2.4 million Afghan girls have been barred from secondary education, a number that could increase to four million by 2030.

The Taliban also banned education for girls and women during its first rule in the late 1990s, before the regime was toppled in 2001 by a U.S-led international coalition in response to the 9/11 attacks.

Canadian troops spent 13 years in the country as part of a Nato stabilization mission. More than 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel were deployed to Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014.

Girls and women returned to classrooms in 2001, and Canadian military and aid organizations invested heavily in women’s education and empowerment projects over the years.

But the Taliban waged a bloody insurgency that paved their way back to power in 2021. Soon after seizing Kabul, the regime renewed its ban on women’s education.

As the ban continues, virtual and underground schools operating from overseas – including the one founded by Wahriz in Toronto – have become a lifeline for many.

In addition to online literature, photography and critical thinking courses, Wahriz’s non-profit, the Network of Community Schools for Girls in Afghanistan, runs a web of secret schools across the country.

“Our first school was established in one of the faraway provinces of Afghanistan and since then, we gradually expanded our activities,” he said

More than 1,600 girls are now being taught in his underground classrooms by female teachers turning their own homes into learning centres, he said.

Under current rules, girls are only allowed to go to school up to Grade 6, meaning those attending secondary and higher education are violating the Taliban’s strict religious code. If caught, they could face severe punishment including physical violence and imprisonment.

Despite those risks, Wahriz said, girls are showing up in classrooms every day to learn math, physics, chemistry and history in a fight against the “darkness.”

“We are challenging that darkness just by our existence,” he said.

Wahriz said funding for the network mostly comes from “kind-hearted” people he knows, including his Canadian friends and an organization based in the United Kingdom.

The teachers are paid US$100 a month when funding is available, he said.

“They are dedicated, committed enough not to expect every month to get paid, but are sure that whenever we find something, they get paid,” Wahriz said.

He said even though his efforts are like a “small drop in the desert” given the magnitude of the crisis, he is optimistic because others are also doing the same.

“Drop by drop, it becomes a sea,” he said, referring to a Persian proverb.

A number of similar organizations in other countries are also working to bypass the Taliban ban on girls’ education.

Women’s rights was a central issue during the 2020 peace talks between the Taliban and the former U.S.-supported Afghan government.

Taliban negotiators repeatedly said they would no longer oppose women’s right to education and employment, but “within the framework of Islamic law,” a vague promise they immediately broke after seizing power. They have since issued more than 100 edicts targeting women, according to the United Nations.

The group’s top leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and his chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani are now wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in their treatment of women and girls.

The Canadian government said it has been backing efforts to expand education opportunities for all Afghans, including girls and women, for over two decades, and has provided more than $143-million to fund education and health-care programs in the past five years while avoiding any investments through the Taliban.

“Canada strongly condemns the ongoing repression, systematic human rights abuses and erosion of fundamental freedoms under Taliban rule in Afghanistan, and is deeply concerned by the worsening humanitarian situation,” Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Brittany Fletcher said in a statement.

For Murwarid Ziayee, the devastating impact of the ban on women’s education was a “painful” experience.

She was in her last semester of law school when the Taliban took power in 1996 and closed the doors of Kabul University to female students. But she didn’t give up on her dreams, she said.

Ziayee self-studied, learned English and computer skills, and even found a job at an underground non-profit that helped educate women at the time. She was able to complete her studies and obtain her degree after the Taliban were overthrown in 2001.

Ziayee, now the senior director of Calgary-based Right to Learn in Afghanistan, said she is trying to do her part to help girls and women who have once again been banned from school.

“It’s better to be in front seat and have the wheel and move forward and do what can be done,” she said in interview.

The non-profit, formerly known as Canadian Women for Women in Afghanistan, was founded in 1998 and has been working to empower women through education ever since.

Ziayee said more than 700 students, mostly in Afghanistan, are attending the organization’s virtual school and 92 per cent of them are girls.

The first cohort will graduate from high school next year, she said. “Once you provide these girls with the education . . . the doors to many opportunities will open for them.”

She said students from Grade 7 to Grade 9 study the former government’s curriculum before taking Canadian and internationally accredited courses during the three years of high school.

Once the students graduate, they obtain internationally accepted diplomas so they can apply for postsecondary education abroad. Most of the funding comes from the federal government or individual Canadians, while people living in other countries also support some students.

But even though many other organizations are involved, they cannot fulfill a state’s job to provide education, Ziayee said.

“The gap is huge and that’s why we are obviously impatiently waiting and praying and advocating for the day that things change in Afghanistan,” Ziayee said.

Until then, Ziayee said the group wants to see the international community step up to fund alternative ways to support more Afghan women and girls “who are left behind and waiting for opportunities to be enrolled.”

stories.title: Damaging storms across southern Ontario flood streets and leave thousands without power
stories.summary: It also caused flight delays and cancellations at Toronto’s Pearson airport, and left some serious damage to Rogers Stadium
stories.content:
Cleanup and power restoration efforts continued in Toronto on Thursday after a severe storm battered the city and surrounding areas, drenching some neighbourhoods in more than 100 millimetres of rain and knocking down trees as well as utility lines.

Toronto Hydro said it had restored power to about 90 per cent of those who lost it during the storm, with roughly 4,500 still in the dark Thursday night. The outage map of provincial power supplier Hydro One showed that around 10,000 customers, including some near Hamilton and Kitchener, remained offline late Thursday.

Localized flooding forced the closure of some major roadways, including parts of Yonge Street and the Don Valley Parkway, at the height of the storm and suspended subway service in some areas during the Wednesday afternoon rush hour.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow praised public servants and emergency responders who fielded an “overwhelming” number of calls and reassured residents that the city had planned and co-ordinated its response ahead of the storm.

“The storm has passed and I want to assure the people of Toronto that we were prepared. Our teams were co-ordinated and we will keep working until every road is clear and every resident has power back,” she said at a news conference at city hall.

The Don Valley Parkway and the Canadian National Exhibition were open Thursday morning, and transit was running as scheduled, as were city-run summer camps, she said.

Crews will be working hard to ensure parks, outdoor pools and public beaches are safe and ready for the Labour Day long weekend, the mayor said.

“To everyone who sheltered in place, checked in on a neighbour, or stayed off flooded roads last night: thank you,” she said. “That’s what got us through this safely together.”

Toronto officials said they received roughly 1,000 requests for service, while fire officials reported just shy of 1,500 calls over a 24-hour period, which they said was their second-highest call volume in a day, after the 2013 ice storm.

Toronto crews worked to restore power and clear roads after a torrential Wednesday storm led to one the busiest days in the fire service’s history, with dispatchers at one time fielding more than 400 active calls.

The Canadian Press

City manager Paul Johnson said the storm was unique in that it dumped large amounts of rain across the city rather than in isolated areas.

“We’ve not seen an event like this that’s brought this amount of water across the city of Toronto,” he said.

“Yes, there was some wide variation, anywhere from about 11 millimetres through to 110 millimetres of rain, but wide areas of the city received large amounts of rain,” along with hail and powerful winds, he said.

“Just to put it into context, that’s what we would declare as a 100-year storm.”

A similar storm hammered the city in 2005, spurring work around flood mitigation and protection, and “those have been working,” he added.

Crews were also out in nearby Vaughan to deal with flooding, water ponding, downed trees and other storm-related issues, the city said in a statement.

“Some roads remain closed, and we ask everyone to continue to use caution and avoid affected areas,” Mayor Steven Del Duca said on social media.

The intense weather brought torrential rain, large hail and the risk of a tornado to wide swaths of southern Ontario as skies darkened over downtown Toronto and hail pummelled neighbourhoods further north.

Video on social media showed large hail falling and downpours flooding vehicles and bus stations, sending people running for cover.

The storm also caused flight delays and cancellations at Toronto’s Pearson airport, and left some serious damage to Rogers Stadium, a 50,000-capacity music venue in the city’s north end. The airport said operations were “returning to normal” Thursday morning but encouraged travellers to check with their airline.

David Sills, director of the Northern Tornadoes Project at Western University, said there was “no credible evidence” at this stage that a tornado occurred as part of Wednesday’s storms, but the organization continues to receive reports and analyze them.

A survey team was heading Thursday for the community of Brodhagen, in the municipality of West Perth about 60 kilometres north of London, Ont., where the worst damage appeared to have occurred, Sills said.

“The team will have a lot of area to cover in the next couple of days,” he wrote in an email.

A few minutes down the road from Brodhagen, Laura Leybourne said she went through a “surreal” experience driving home in the storm.

She was picking up her daughter from daycare when she saw the storm approach in her rearview mirror. Leybourne said she could feel the wind pushing her car forward as branches came down around her, ricocheting off her SUV.

“I have my four-year-old in the back seat so I’m trying to tell her, ‘It’s fine we’re gonna make it home.’ And internally I was panicking because I didn’t know what was going to happen,” she said.

As she neared her home in Rostock, Leybourne said she saw a tree come down and snap the power line running along her street.

Leybourne and her daughter got home safely, but the family’s gazebo didn’t survive the storm. Nor did their trampoline, which Leybourne said she later found about a kilometre away in a corn field.

The family’s home was still without power nearly 24 hours after the storm hit.

Leybourne said she took her daughter to have breakfast at her brother-in-law’s house Thursday morning and took stock of the destruction on the drive over.

“Seeing what that storm had done, it was an indescribable feeling,” she said.

The downed trees and power lines littering the area made her consider just how narrowly she and her daughter had avoided disaster, she said.

“It just gave me a real wake-up call to see how severe storms can really be. I always kind of liked thunderstorms, but after yesterday, I’m really not so sure anymore,” she said.
