stories.title: Canadians are happier than they've been in years, poll finds
stories.summary: Canadians are at their cheeriest and most optimistic place in several years, according to a new Leger poll.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
By self-reporting their happiness at greater than seven out of 10 on average, a significant increase over last year, Canadians are at their cheeriest and most optimistic place in several years, according to a new poll .

It is a tricky thing to measure, but these findings are the latest in the novel science of happiness studies, which has grown rapidly from a niche academic interest into a major factor in economic policy development, including an important new priority of Statistics Canada.

“I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that things in the country overall are closer to the pre-pandemic norm,” said Andrew Enns, executive vice-president, Central Canada, for Leger, which conducted the new poll.

It found the happiest provinces are Quebec, by a wide margin of almost five points, followed by Newfoundland and Labrador and New Brunswick.

“There’s something about Quebec, they love the moment,” Enns said. “It’s a cultural trait.”

The happiest cities are Montreal, Brampton, and Toronto. The least happy provinces are Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and the least happy of the ten largest cities are Winnipeg, Edmonton, and Ottawa.

Financial pressure was the most common barrier to happiness that people reported, at 57 per cent of respondents, followed by physical health at 32 per cent, and mental health and uncertainty about the future, both at 23 per cent. The political situation, work-life balance, the cost of leisure activities, and loneliness were also common answers.

But with such robust findings of widespread happiness, buoyed by a comparable sense of optimism for the future, the poll suggests that happiness for Canadians rests on “deeply human dimensions,” as Leger’s report calls them, such as caring for one’s health, maintaining close friendships, trusting neighbours, having a sense of purpose, and feeling secure.

The comparison with last year’s version of the same poll is particularly revealing for how the state of the world at large can affect individual happiness, Enns said.

Canadians need an income of $155,850 to be happy, researchers say

Happiest city to live in Canada is in Ontario but it's not Toronto, survey finds

“When you look at what 2025 was presenting the country, we had (U.S. President Donald) Trump in full flight, we had a federal election under way, we had gone from a very unpopular prime minister to one who turned out to be very popular,” Enns said in an interview.

But the poll also shows people tend to evaluate their own happiness on an extremely local level. “People May think the world is going to hell in a handbasket,” Enns said, “but the closer your perspective gets, the better it seems.”

“Happiness to some degree is reflected by your community around you, your local group of peers, whether neighbours, colleagues. There’s a sense of trust, reliance, comfort in that support,” Enns said. Being able to say hello to a neighbour when you take out the garbage, or feeling that you trust the people around you, “some of those things bring as much happiness as having money left over from a paycheque…. That’s how people can report high happiness, while also expressing pessimism about the world.”

Asked to give a maximum of three factors that contribute to their happiness in their community, the most common response was a sense of safety and security at 46 per cent.

The next most common answer was green spaces, parks and access to nature, at 40 per cent, which was significantly higher than any of the other less common factors, such as quality of neighbourhood life (27 per cent), cleanliness and attractiveness of the area (22 per cent), and affordability, shops transit, infrastructure.

Enns said this shows that “as citizens, we’re actually sending mixed messages here, and that makes it hard for policy makers.” Voters tend to downplay the importance of the “soft sides” of life in a city, like parks and walking trails, “but their presence makes people happy, it improves their quality of life.”

This sort of counterintuitive finding is typical of the scientific field of happiness studies, which has a colourful history that runs through Canada.

Books about “hedonic psychology,” about what truly makes people happy, were all the rage in publishing in the early 2000s, and policy makers soon took note.

The most famous and quirkiest example was Bhutan, the tiny Himalayan country, which made itself into a unique science experiment by becoming the first country to track its Gross National Happiness, and it was reporting interesting results.

Until then, to economists, happiness had seemed mostly separate from the central goals of fiscal governance, such as gross domestic product. In contrast, happiness and well-being seemed either irrelevant or impossible to measure or both.

But this interest in happiness caught on at the highest levels, thanks largely to the work of John F. Helliwell, a professor emeritus at the University of British Columbia, who ran a seminal research program on Social Interactions, Identity and Well-Being at the Canadian Institute For Advanced Research.

He had shown, for example, that rising income has only a limited and relative effect on happiness, and that one of the best predictors of a random person’s happiness is how much they trust their neighbours. If happiness and well-being were going to be primary goals of governments, some of the old purely financial metrics would have to be updated.

People May think the world is going to hell in a handbasket but the closer your perspective gets, the better it seems

Economists and policy makers started to take notice. In 2012, the first World Happiness Report had Canada ranked fifth overall.

The newest World Happiness Report 2026, of which Helliwell remains an editor, ranks Canada 25th, its lowest place ever since tracking began in 2010. Historically, Canada’s average life evaluation score has shown a modest but steady decline over the last 15 years.

Now, the field boasts a robust track record of data, and a generation of policy makers who have grown up with happiness in the forefront of their minds.

Statistics Canada started a Quality of Life program in 2021 to track life satisfaction among Canadians, and in its most recent review said it “has made substantial progress in establishing itself as a truly horizontal effort with clear links to the federal policy cycle.”

StatCan does not have a prepandemic measure, but it began in 2021 with a quite low initial measure of 42 per cent of Canadians saying they had a high life satisfaction.

This rose above 50 per cent and stayed there before plunging ten points to 45 per cent in the fourth fiscal quarter of 2022. Then it returned to the 50 per cent baseline again before falling to 40 per cent in the second quarter of 2024, and since then has stayed a few points below 50 per cent.

The same chart for people reporting a high sense of meaning and purpose follows a similar historical shape, with coinciding dips in 2022 and 2024, but with numbers about ten points higher. The most recent measure shows 55.7 per cent of Canadians report a high sense of meaning and purpose.

“All those things can provide a sense of how a person feels about their current situation,” Enns said

The online survey was conducted by Leger in June of this year among 63,710 Canadians, of whom about half were in Quebec, and the results have been weighted according to age, gender and region. A true margin of error cannot be calculated for this kind of online panel poll, but to compare, this many respondents in a probability sample would give a margin of error of plus or minus 0.39 per cent 19 times out of 20.

This sort of counterintuitive finding is typical of the scientific field of happiness studies, which has a colourful history that runs through Canada.
Books about “hedonic psychology,” about what truly makes people happy, were all the rage in publishing in the early 2000s, and policy makers soon took note.

The most famous and quirkiest example was Bhutan, the tiny Himalayan country, which made itself into a unique science experiment by becoming the first country to track its Gross National Happiness, and it was reporting interesting results.

Until then, to economists, happiness had seemed mostly separate from the central goals of fiscal governance, such as gross domestic product. In contrast, happiness and well-being seemed either irrelevant or impossible to measure or both.

But this interest in happiness caught on at the highest levels, thanks largely to the work of John F. Helliwell, a professor emeritus at the University of British Columbia, who ran a seminal research program on Social Interactions, Identity and Well-Being at the Canadian Institute For Advanced Research.

He had shown, for example, that rising income has only a limited and relative effect on happiness, and that one of the best predictors of a random person’s happiness is how much they trust their neighbours. If happiness and well-being were going to be primary goals of governments, some of the old purely financial metrics would have to be updated.

The newest World Happiness Report 2026, of which Helliwell remains an editor, ranks Canada 25th, its lowest place ever since tracking began in 2010. Historically, Canada’s average life evaluation score has shown a modest but steady decline over the last 15 years.
Now, the field boasts a robust track record of data, and a generation of policy makers who have grown up with happiness in the forefront of their minds.

Statistics Canada started a Quality of Life program in 2021 to track life satisfaction among Canadians, and in its most recent review said it “has made substantial progress in establishing itself as a truly horizontal effort with clear links to the federal policy cycle.”
StatCan does not have a prepandemic measure, but it began in 2021 with a quite low initial measure of 42 per cent of Canadians saying they had a high life satisfaction.

This rose above 50 per cent and stayed there before plunging ten points to 45 per cent in the fourth fiscal quarter of 2022. Then it returned to the 50 per cent baseline again before falling to 40 per cent in the second quarter of 2024, and since then has stayed a few points below 50 per cent.

stories.title: Carney set to announce ‘historic investment’ in Canadian manufacturing
stories.summary: PM visiting northern Ontario as the country prepares to impose countertarrifs on a range of U.S. goods
stories.content:
The federal government will spend $4.7-billion to build and maintain more than 300 Via Rail passenger rail cars in Canada, using facilities in Quebec and Thunder Bay, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Thursday.

At a news conference in the northwestern Ontario city, Mr. Carney said the move represents a shift away from importing trains from south of the border.

“For too long, we bought from abroad what we were more than capable of building right here at home. We’re bringing that work back, and we’re turbocharging it,” Mr. Carney said.

The Prime Minister framed the train car announcement as an example of how the federal government is encouraging more domestic manufacturing at a time when its largest trading partner is taking a protectionist turn with waves of new tariffs.

“For the first time in four decades, those cars will be produced and assembled and maintained in our country. Cars that used to be built in the United States will be built right here in Thunder Bay, at Alstom, by the best workers in the world,” he said.

The announcement said design and engineering work for the 313 new cars will take place in Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville, Que., while some manufacturing will also happen in La Pocatière, Que.

Via’s most recent trainsets are from Siemens Canada and were built in Sacramento, Calif. Siemens received a $989-million contract in 2018 to build 32 trainsets for the Quebec-City Windsor corridor. Those trains began to enter service in 2022.

The trains currently operating outside of the Windsor-Quebec City corridor have an average age of 77 years old. The new replacements are scheduled to begin entering service in 2031. They will include sleeper cars, dining cars and cars with panorama views.

In July, the Prime Minister announced $1.6-billion for the production of 45 new locomotives for Via Rail by Switzerland-based Stadler, as well as $357-million for a new assembly and maintenance facility in Montreal.

The new trains announced Thursday will serve Via Rail’s long-distance and remote routes.

Trade tensions between Canada and the United States could escalate next week as Ottawa plans to impose new countertariffs on Tuesday. They are in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s new 50-per-cent tariffs on about $28-billion worth of Canadian goods.

The President announced those new tariffs after trade negotiations between the two countries collapsed last month.

Senior U.S. officials have said Canada should expect an additional response if the Sept. 8 countertariffs go ahead.

When asked about the state of trade relations with the U.S., Mr. Carney said a deal remains possible provided that the Americans accept Canada’s positions related to protecting the French language, manufacturing and retaining its sovereignty with respect to trade deals with other countries.

“We’re ready to sit down and strike that deal when the Americans are ready,” he said.

Mr. Carney was also asked to respond to recent criticism from U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has said he believes Mr. Carney’s team deliberately derailed the negotiations to gain political advantage ahead of October votes on a sovereignty-related referendum question in Alberta and the Quebec provincial election, where the sovereigntist Parti Québécois has been leading in the polls.

Mr. Lutnick has predicted that Canadian negotiators will want to resume talks after those two elections.

Mr. Carney dismissed that analysis.

“I don’t think, with all respect, appointed, unelected, cabinet ministers in the United States are experts on Canadian politics,” Mr. Carney said.

He said talks between the two countries will resume at the appropriate time.

“But the most important thing we can do is not to spend all our time waiting by the phone, waiting for a call ... refreshing on social media to see what’s coming across. No, it’s building. It’s building here,” he said.

Mr. Trump commented on Canada again Thursday on Truth Social.

“It is very good for Canadian Politicians like Prime Minister Carney to make President Donald J. Trump “the enemy,” until their Economy collapses, then it will prove to be very bad for Politics – Worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian Politician. Just watch!” he said.

The Prime Minister also said Thursday’s announcement is a show of support for passenger rail in Canada, with traditional trains supporting plans for a new high-speed rail line between Quebec City and Toronto.

A recent report from Alto, the Crown corporation leading the high-speed rail project, said ridership on the existing Via Rail service has declined to 4.4 million passengers a year in 2025 from about eight million in the 1980s.

Via Rail has long said its ability to provide faster and more dependable service is hindered by the fact that it primarily operates on privately-owned tracks where slower-moving freight traffic is prioritized.

Alto estimates that ridership on its planned high-speed rail line, which would operate on new tracks dedicated exclusively to passenger rail, will reach 24 million passengers a year by 2055 and up to 43 million by 2084.

Alto has estimated that the project will cost between $60-billion to $90-billion.

The Globe and Mail reported this week that an internal estimate shows the total cost will be much higher when operational and maintenance expenses are included.

Alto’s regularly stated cost range only accounts for the capital cost of building the line. An internal 2023 draft obtained by The Globe showed operating and maintenance costs over 40 years are projected to be between $62.6-billion and $67-billion. The cost of rolling stock is estimated at around $2-billion over that same period.

The document said the total cost, including capital and operating expenses, over 40 years will be between $148.1-billion and $152.7-billion.

The document also says total revenue over that period will be $105-billion, which would more than fully cover the operational expenses.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Siemens Canada built 32 passenger cars for Via, after receiving a contract in 2018. Siemens built 32 trainsets.

stories.title: Driver suffers life-threatening injuries in Perth South crash
stories.summary: A 40-year-old Thames Centre resident suffered life-threatening injuries following a single-vehicle collision involving a farm tractor in Perth South on Wednesday night.
stories.content:
A 40-year-old Thames Centre resident suffered life-threatening injuries following a single-vehicle collision involving a farm tractor in Perth South on Wednesday night.

Emergency crews responded to the crash on Perth Road 151 at about 9:30 p.m.

Police said the collision involved a farm tractor that was pulling a trailer.

The injured driver was transported to hospital with injuries described as life-threatening.

The Stratford Police Service Traffic Unit was called in to investigate and reconstruct the collision. Officers remained at the scene Wednesday night.

Perth Road 151 is expected to remain closed for several hours between Line 2 and Whalen Line as the investigation continues.

Police have not released further details about the circumstances surrounding the crash.

stories.title: Advocates push for better education on dangerous currents
stories.summary: The gentle sound of waves rolling onto the shore can create a sense of calm, but water safety experts say the conditions beneath the surface can be far more dangerous than many beachgoers realize.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The gentle sound of waves rolling onto the shore can create a sense of calm, but water safety experts say the conditions beneath the surface can be far more dangerous than many beachgoers realize.

For Nathan MacIntyre , founder of the Rip Current Information Project, improving public understanding of lake currents has become a personal mission.

“We don’t paint every current with the same brush of undertow,” MacIntyre said. “There’s several different currents at play.”

MacIntyre launched the organization following a series of drownings in the region, including the death of a young boy near the Port Stanley pier in 2024.

The issue also hits close to home. As a teenager, MacIntyre lost a friend to a drowning in Lake Erie and later spent years working as a lifeguard on Port Stanley’s main beach.

“There was information that the public needs to know,” he said. “I feel like we’ve been living with an old system that’s a bit fragmented and outdated.”

Using the beach itself as a teaching tool, MacIntyre demonstrated how wind direction and wave action can create what is known as a structural rip current. According to him, prevailing southwest winds can funnel water along man-made structures such as piers, creating powerful currents capable of pulling swimmers into dangerous situations.

“It is a relentless current that doesn’t stop until the wind and the waves stop,” MacIntyre said.

Following the fatal drowning in 2024, safety measures were enhanced near the Port Stanley pier. Buoys have been installed to discourage swimmers from entering hazardous areas, and warning signs along the beach now alert visitors to the risks.

But advocates say physical barriers and signage alone are not enough.

The dangers posed by rip currents, drop-offs and other water conditions can be especially challenging for newcomers to Canada or visitors unfamiliar with the Great Lakes. The boy who drowned near the pier had recently arrived in Canada from Syria.

Scott Ruddle , a longtime lifeguard who spent decades working on beaches in Grand Bend and Port Stanley, said several recent drowning victims on Lake Huron were also newcomers or tourists.

“With that comes the dangers of not having any swim lessons, not understanding the dangers of currents and drop-offs that our sandbars might have,” Ruddle said.

Ruddle believes water safety education should become a regular part of school curricula.

“We mandate that people are supposed to graduate from school with a first aid and a CPR class,” he said. “Why not another life skill?”

The Rip Current Information Centre hopes to bring greater attention to the issue at the upcoming Great Lakes Risk Communication Summit. The event is scheduled for Sept. 17 at the Caso Station in St. Thomas and will bring together leaders from communities across the Great Lakes region to discuss strategies for improving public awareness and preventing future tragedies.

For MacIntyre and other advocates, the goal is simple: ensuring that everyone who comes to enjoy the Great Lakes returns home safely.

stories.title: 15-year-old murder suspect to be sentenced this October
stories.summary: A 15-year-old Huron County boy who stabbed an 11-year-old girl to death, will most likely be sentenced for his crime this October.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A 15-year-old Huron County boy who stabbed an 11-year-old girl to death, will most likely be sentenced for his crime this October.

The 15-year-old, who cannot be named because they are a young offender, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in June, for the brutal killing of an 11-year-old girl in Holmesville.

The incident happened on July 2, 2024. Court heard that the murder suspect and victim knew each other, and the 15-year-old was interested in having sex with the girl.

A psychologist assessment has not been completed, as of yet, but court expects it to be completed before the next court appearance, ON Sept. 29.

At that point, a sentencing date is expected to be set for Oct. 13,14, or 16.

The maximum sentence for a young offender found guilty of first-degree murder is 10 years, six of which would be served behind bars. The 15-year-old boy, who was 13 at the time of the murder, has already served 26 months in custody awaiting his sentence.

stories.title: Fog advisory in effect, warm, humid conditions bring risk of thunderstorms Thursday
stories.summary: A warm and humid day is in store for southern Ontario Thursday, with scattered showers and thunderstorms expected to develop through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A warm and humid day is in store for southern Ontario Thursday, with scattered showers and thunderstorms expected to develop through the afternoon, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“We will remain under this warm, humid air mass. Lots of moisture to tap into and significant amounts of rain if we get under one of these heavier storms,” Atchison said.

The day will start mainly cloudy, with breaks of sunshine expected through the afternoon. Temperatures will reach a high of 27 C, but will feel closer to 35 with the humidity.

Photo Gallery: Sept. 2, 2026 storm damage

Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected to redevelop Thursday, with the potential for torrential downpours and damaging wind gusts associated with some storms.

Friday will be mainly cloudy with a high of 25 C and a 30 per cent chance of thunderstorms and rainfall.

The chance of rain will ease heading into the Labour Day weekend. Saturday and Sunday are expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud, with daytime highs between 23 and 25 C.

More sunshine and a more stable air mass are expected to move into the region for the holiday weekend.

stories.title: Habsburg family jewels to go on display in Quebec City this week
stories.summary: Storied gemstones were smuggled out of Europe at outset of Second World War and presumed lost for decades, stashed all the while in a Quebec vault
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
A pale yellow diamond as large as a quail’s egg. A glittering watch worn by Marie Antoinette. Rubies and emeralds fit for a coronation.

A trove of storied imperial gemstones is emerging from a cloak of secrecy and legal fog this week to go on display in Canada, the improbable country where they lay hidden for more than 80 years.

The Habsburg family jewels were smuggled out of Europe at the outset of the Second World War by Zita of Bourbon-Parma, Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary, and presumed lost for decades. Only last year did her grandchildren reveal that, all along, they had been stashed in a vault in Quebec – the same province where Zita and her children sheltered during the war.

It has been a long journey for an array of jewellery that adorned Medicis and included the 137-carat Florentine Diamond, through the chaotic dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, to the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec, where they will star in a public exhibition opening Friday.

The family wanted to display the treasures in Quebec City, the quiet Catholic government town where the former imperial family found a fitting refuge from their Nazi persecutors.

“Showing these jewels at the Musée is an expression of profound gratitude to Québec and Canada for welcoming and sheltering my grandmother and her eight children during World War II,” Karl von Habsburg, Zita’s grandson, said in a statement.

The museum show also comes at a time when the Austrian government is awaiting the results of a commission on the legal ownership of the jewels, which it says will determine whether the modern state has a claim to the heirlooms of a family that once ruled its territory.

Last November, the remaining Habsburg grandchildren announced that the precious collection would be held in a Canadian trust with Andrew Molson, scion of the Canadian brewing dynasty, as trustee.

The family hired eminent British historian Richard Bassett to study the provenance of the jewels and he found the Florentine Diamond, among others, had always remained the personal property of the Habsburgs.

Meanwhile, as the grandchildren were preparing to reveal the whereabouts of the gems, the Louvre heist in Paris last October massively heightened security concerns. Anxiety about the safety of the treasures prompted the museum to forgo publicity of its landmark exhibition until the day before its grand opening.

For all the hype around the jewels, one of the most striking exhibits on display is the flimsy suitcase Empress Zita used to carry her priceless cargo across the Atlantic – not made of cardboard, as family lore had it, but the somewhat flashier material of crocodile leather.

Empress Zita and Emperor Charles were effectively on the run, until he died of pneumonia on the Portuguese island of Madeira in 1922.

Zita and her children wandered Europe through the interwar period, notably emerging as staunch opponents of the Nazis. In retaliation, the Luftwaffe descended on the Belgian castle where Zita had been living at the outbreak of the Second World War.

Again, the Habsburgs had already fled with their jewels, as a confluence of factors drew them to Quebec. It was Catholic, like them, and the children were already being educated in French. Canada’s government welcomed them and arranged for accommodation in the Quebec City area.

Despite their secret bounty, the Habsburgs were cash poor and lived modestly. Zita wore a widow’s black habit and made soup from dandelion leaves. The family hunted moose and went cross-country skiing. After two decades on the run, the Empress was happy.

“She felt she had some of the best times of her life in Quebec,” Karl von Habsburg said in an interview on Thursday.

The family eventually left Canada after the war, but the jewels remained in a Quebec vault whose location her children were sworn to keep secret until 100 years after her husband’s death.

The Florentine Diamond, especially, developed an extensive lore. After its disappearance in the 1920s, rumours spread that it had been stolen by a servant and spirited to South America. Truth was stranger than fiction: The stone was wrapped in yellowing paper inside a crocodile-skin suitcase, burrowed deep within a Canadian bank.

There are other remarkable treasures in the exhibition, including a diamond and yellow sapphire brooch that the 18th-century Habsburg ruler Maria Theresa wore on “festive sleigh rides, attached to the ribbon of her muff,” and a jewel-studded pocket watch that belonged to her daughter, the doomed Queen of France Marie Antoinette.

The Austrian culture ministry did not respond to a request for comment about the jewellery, but Karl von Habsburg dismissed any rival claims as “political chit-chat.”

Jean-Luc Murray, director general of the museum, is treading more carefully. He is “conscious of questions around” ownership and has been in contact with the government of Quebec about them.

Diplomatic concerns are hardly his only stressor. The specter of the Louvre heist has prompted the museum to take extraordinary security measures whose details he would not discuss.

“It hasn’t been easy!” he acknowledged.

Then again, nothing about the saga of the Habsburg jewels ever has been.

A trove of storied imperial gemstones is emerging from a cloak of secrecy and legal fog this week to go on display in Canada, the improbable country where they lay hidden for more than 80 years.

Last November, the remaining Habsburg grandchildren announced that the precious collection would be held in a Canadian trust with Andrew Molson, scion of the Canadian brewing dynasty, as trustee.

stories.title: Ontario’s high-school attendance policy isn’t a guaranteed solution
stories.summary: It remains to be seen that assigning marks for showing up will help solve the high-school attendance problem all that much
stories.author: Daryl Sneath
stories.content:
Daryl Sneath is a teacher and novelist.

There is no shortage of clichés when it comes to the importance of “showing up.” “Showing up is half the battle.” “Success is not about being the best, but rather showing up when others choose to stay home.” “Every day we show up we invest in our future selves, so don’t underestimate the power of attendance.”

The power of attendance is something the Ontario government is taking very seriously come the new school year. When high-school students return to their hallowed halls this month, a portion of their final grade in every class (15 per cent for grades 9 and 10; 10 per cent for grades 11 and 12) will be determined by their attendance and participation.

Many readers might agree with this policy. It used to be, after all, that if we made absence too much of a habit, a truancy officer would show up at our door. But it also used to be that we scratched out our lessons on slate tablets, not digital ones. An argument based on tradition is not argument enough. And it remains to be seen whether assigning marks for showing up will help solve the attendance problem all that much.

Let’s look at some numbers. Only 40 per cent of Ontario high-school students meet the provincial expectation of 90-per-cent attendance, which means 60 per cent of students miss more than nine days per semester. More troubling are the statistics we don’t have an accurate handle on: By how much do these students miss the standard? Ask a high-school teacher you know and they will likely say many students miss the standard by a lot more than nine days. For the two Grade 12 courses I taught this past spring, it became commonplace, a mere month into the semester, to have at least a third of the students absent – every day. Colleagues cite similar numbers.

The new attendance rule has historical precedent: In the 1990s, students who accrued 10 unexcused absences in a course ran the risk of losing that credit, regardless of the mark they had attained. The problem with the new policy, though, lies in the implementation. As soon as poor attendance lowers a student’s overall mark such that it’s not what a student (or their parents) say they need or want, such that scholarships and acceptances to university programs fall into jeopardy, it will be nearly impossible to make the poor attendance mark stick. Unexcused absences, for many, will magically become excused.

According to the Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario, 52 per cent of graduating students receive and accept offers to university programs. When we consider the number who do not meet the provincial standard for attendance but still manage to earn grades high enough to be accepted into university, the lesson being scratched out here becomes very clear: Being present, for too many students, doesn’t really matter.

Aside from excused absences due to illness or participation in extracurricular activities, one of the major causes of the absenteeism problem comes from what the Grade 12 cohort affectionately calls “senioritis”: a severe decline in motivation, engagement, effort and quality of work as the end of high school draws ever nearer. Some wear their senioritis like a badge of honour; some see it as a rite of passage; some see it, quite plainly, as a right. It used to be that this condition arrived some time in May, with the nice weather and the school year’s end actually being near. Now it begins before spring has sprung. More troubling is the spread of the condition to and through the younger grades.

But let’s say the new policy has a positive effect. Say we inch toward the prepandemic success rate of 60 per cent of students attending 90 per cent of the time. The problem is that for too many students (including those who are already meeting the provincial attendance standard), their physical presence does not, by a long shot, guarantee their mental presence. Much of the time, the culprit for this problem is the cellphone.

Although much was made of Ontario’s cellphone “ban,” introduced in 2024, the plain truth is that cellphones still accompany students to class. Many students still resist giving up their phones, vehemently. Parents, too. If teachers made a situation out of every student who didn’t comply with the “phones away” rule, teachers and principals alike would have time to do little else.

But perhaps the most important word in the new attendance policy – not to mention the trickiest to define, track and assess – is “participation.” Physical attendance in the classroom is objective: a student is either there or not. Participation is far more varied and nuanced.

The Ministry of Education’s foundational document, “Growing Success,” implemented in 2010, states that “teachers must use practices and procedures that ... relate to the interests, learning styles and preferences, needs, and experiences of all students.” This means, to take only one example, that if a student’s learning style or preference tends toward active listening and away from traditional methods of participation, such as hand-raising or contributing to class discussion, they cannot be penalized for that. But assessing active listening, just to stick with this example, is not so easy to do.

In short, measuring participation – which is an equal part of the 10 per cent to 15 per cent cited above, inasmuch as the rule states attendance and participation – becomes potentially as varied in its implementation as every student in every class for every teacher.

It’s easy to throw stones, as the saying goes, and also not very productive. The solution to the attendance problem is not an easy one. The intention behind the new rule does seem to be fair and thoughtful. The inevitably varied execution, though, May skew how fair and thoughtful the results.

For the two Grade 12 courses I taught this past spring, it became commonplace, a mere month into the semester, to have at least a third of the students absent – every day. Colleagues cite similar numbers.

content_blocks.text: The new attendance rule has historical precedent: In the 1990s, students who accrued 10 unexcused absences in a course ran the risk of losing that credit, regardless of the mark they had attained. The problem with the new policy, though, lies in the implementation. As soon as poor attendance lowers a student’s overall mark such that it’s not what a student (or their parents) say they need or want, such that scholarships and acceptances to university programs fall into jeopardy, it will be nearly impossible to make the poor attendance mark stick. Unexcused absences, for many, will magically become excused.

content_blocks.text: According to the Higher Education Quality Council of Ontario, 52 per cent of graduating students receive and accept offers to university programs. When we consider the number who do not meet the provincial standard for attendance but still manage to earn grades high enough to be accepted into university, the lesson being scratched out here becomes very clear: Being present, for too many students, doesn’t really matter.

Some wear their senioritis like a badge of honour; some see it as a rite of passage; some see it, quite plainly, as a right. It used to be that this condition arrived some time in May, with the nice weather and the school year’s end actually being near. Now it begins before spring has sprung. More troubling is the spread of the condition to and through the younger grades.

content_blocks.text: But let’s say the new policy has a positive effect. Say we inch toward the prepandemic success rate of 60 per cent of students attending 90 per cent of the time. The problem is that for too many students (including those who are already meeting the provincial attendance standard), their physical presence does not, by a long shot, guarantee their mental presence. Much of the time, the culprit for this problem is the cellphone.

Many students still resist giving up their phones, vehemently. Parents, too. If teachers made a situation out of every student who didn’t comply with the “phones away” rule, teachers and principals alike would have time to do little else.

content_blocks.text: But perhaps the most important word in the new attendance policy – not to mention the trickiest to define, track and assess – is “participation.” Physical attendance in the classroom is objective: a student is either there or not. Participation is far more varied and nuanced.

content_blocks.text: The Ministry of Education’s foundational document, “Growing Success,” implemented in 2010, states that “teachers must use practices and procedures that ... relate to the interests, learning styles and preferences, needs, and experiences of all students.” This means, to take only one example, that if a student’s learning style or preference tends toward active listening and away from traditional methods of participation, such as hand-raising or contributing to class discussion, they cannot be penalized for that. But assessing active listening, just to stick with this example, is not so easy to do.

content_blocks.text: In short, measuring participation – which is an equal part of the 10 per cent to 15 per cent cited above, inasmuch as the rule states attendance and participation – becomes potentially as varied in its implementation as every student in every class for every teacher.

The intention behind the new rule does seem to be fair and thoughtful. The inevitably varied execution, though, May skew how fair and thoughtful the results.

stories.title: New poll finds Toronto viewed as one of Canada’s least safe cities
stories.summary: The study tested 15 cities and found Toronto ranks second‑lowest on net safety at –18, ahead only of Winnipeg at –28.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto

Posted September 3, 2026 5:58 am.

Toronto is facing the largest safety‑reputation penalty of any major Canadian city, according to a new national public‑perception study that suggests the country’s biggest urban centre is viewed as far less safe than its crime‑severity data would indicate.

A new Liaison Strategies survey , released Thursday, finds 57 per cent of Canadians consider Toronto somewhat or very unsafe, compared with 39 per cent who say it is safe.

Only Winnipeg fares worse, with 59 per cent calling it unsafe. The results also concluded that Toronto’s negative rating has also worsened over time — up five points from 52 per cent in 2017.

The study looked at 15 Canadian cities and found Toronto ranks second‑lowest in net safety, at –18, ahead only of Winnipeg at –28.

But when you look at official Crime Severity Index (CSI) data, Toronto sits much lower on the national list, meaning its crime severity is not among the worst. That contrast creates what researchers call Canada’s largest “reputational penalty”; the gap between Toronto’s relatively moderate crime‑severity ranking and the far more negative way Canadians perceive the city’s safety.

Liaison says the gap is politically and economically significant: only 12 per cent of respondents say crime statistics are the main factor shaping their impression of city safety. Instead, perceptions are driven by news coverage, personal experience, word of mouth, and national image.

Among the cities tested, negative perceptions cluster around the country’s largest urban centres:

Winnipeg — 59 per cent unsafe

Toronto — 57 per cent unsafe

Vancouver — 52 per cent unsafe

Edmonton — 50 per cent unsafe

Saskatoon — 45 per cent unsafe

Montreal — 41 per cent unsafe

Regina — 37 per cent unsafe

Calgary — 35 per cent unsafe

At the other end of the spectrum, Quebec City (+57), Ottawa (+56) and Charlottetown (+51) lead the country in net safety.

David Valentin, Principal at Liaison Strategies, says Toronto’s perception gap is the defining feature of the study.

“Toronto has a public‑safety reputation problem. It is not just that 57 per cent of Canadians call Toronto unsafe. It is that Toronto is being perceived almost the same way as Winnipeg, even though the official crime‑severity picture is not the same.”

Valentin says Winnipeg’s perception aligns with its crime‑severity data, while Toronto’s does not — creating the largest reputational penalty among all cities tested.

“Residents, visitors, investors, students, and businesses do not respond only to police‑reported crime statistics. They also respond to what they think a city feels like.”

stories.title: Bank of Canada set to unveil redesigned $20 bill featuring King Charles
stories.summary: Royal Canadian Mint has produced coins featuring King Charles since 2023
stories.author: The Canadian Press staff
stories.content:
For the first time in more than 70 years, a new monarch will appear on Canada’s $20 bill.

The Bank of Canada unveiled the new banknote on Thursday during a ceremony in Ottawa.

The bill features a linework image of King Charles III executed by Canadian engraver Jorge Rodrigo Peral based on a 2024 photograph taken by Andrew Parsons, a British photographer, for the currency. The King’s portrait is displayed vertically on the bill.

Charles became King after the 2022 death of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, whose time on the $20 banknote has now exceeded the length of her record-breaking 70-year reign. Work on the new banknote began on the day of King Charles’ coronation, May 6, 2023, according to a Bank of Canada official speaking on background ahead of the unveiling.

The Bank of Canada has unveiled the design for the country's newest $20 note, which features King Charles III for the first time.

The Canadian Press

The back of the bill features an image of the Canadian National Vimy Memorial in France. About 3,600 Canadians died at the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 1917 during the First World War.

Circulation of the new $20 bill is scheduled to begin next February.

It’s the second vertical banknote produced by the Bank of Canada after the $10 note, which features Viola Desmond, a civil-rights pioneer and businesswoman from Nova Scotia. It was unveiled in 2018.

Since 1937, when King George VI first appeared on the $20 banknote early in his reign, all of Canada’s $20 bills have featured likenesses of Canada’s monarchs.

As an eight-year-old princess, the future Queen Elizabeth was first featured on the Bank of Canada’s inaugural $20 banknote in 1935, before her portrait was replaced by her father’s. She returned to the $20 bill in 1954, after ascending to the throne in 1952.

“Her image became one of the most recognizable on our currency for generations of Canadians. Today, this tradition continues with His Majesty King Charles III, who is appearing on a Canadian banknote for the first time,” Governor-General Louise Arbour told the unveiling ceremony on Thursday.

Ms. Arbour said Canadian banknotes are more than just a form of payment.

“They reflect our history, our realities and the significant achievements of our collective journey,” she said. “Our currency affirms our sovereignty and our determination to define ourselves in the eyes of the world on our terms.”

Tiff Macklem, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, said at Thursday’s unveiling that the bill will feature new security features to prevent counterfeiting.

These include a purple security stripe that appears to spin and transform when the bill is moved. The stripe, which is difficult to reproduce, has been used elsewhere in the world but is making its debut in Canada with the new $20 banknote.

“Our new $20 note is both visually stunning and more secure than ever,” Mr. Macklem said.

Ahead of the bill’s rollout in 2027, the bank will hold discussions with law enforcement agencies and financial institutions to raise awareness of its security features, Mr. Macklem said.

Of the Vimy Ridge imagery on the banknote, Mr. Macklem noted that his grandfather, also named Tiff, was a lieutenant in the Canadian military who served as a liaison officer during the battle.

“Fortunately – as evidenced by my standing here before you – my grandfather returned home to Canada. Many did not,” he said.

He noted that the Vimy Memorial, which he personally saw during a visit to France earlier this summer, is a symbol of sacrifice.

“The soaring pillars and solemn sculptures honour those who gave their lives to protect freedom, peace and democracy,” he said.

stories.title: Guerrero Jr. looks like himself again as Blue Jays win big over Guardians
stories.summary: Finally, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. got under one and hit it a long way. Beside home plate at Progressive Field, Guerrero Jr. stood and watched as the ball soared down the left-field line. It stayed fair, clearing the wall by a wide margin, and Guerrero Jr. could begin his first home run trot in nearly a month. More […]
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Finally, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. got under one and hit it a long way.

Beside home plate at Progressive Field, Guerrero Jr. stood and watched as the ball soared down the left-field line. It stayed fair, clearing the wall by a wide margin, and Guerrero Jr. could begin his first home run trot in nearly a month.

More importantly, the three-run homer gave the Blue Jays a 6-0 lead and some reason for optimism as they push for the playoffs. That swing — one of three big ones for Guerrero Jr. Wednesday — helped the Blue Jays beat the Guardians 11-0 and climb back to within 1.5 games of Cleveland in the American League wild-card standings.

“That was nice,” said manager John Schneider. “I’ve been behind him the entire year and will continue to be, but I think that was a little bit of a deep breath for him and a deep breath for everyone. Hopefully he can stay right there.”

Dylan Cease lowered his season ERA to 2.25 with six innings of scoreless baseball, and Josh Smith added a solo home run in the eighth as the Blue Jays improved to 69-71 on the season, but this game was all about Guerrero Jr.

In a season of many lows for the 27-year-old, this game was a high point. To this point, the production just hasn’t been there — and ultimately, he’s accountable for those results. Within the last week, he’s heard boos at Rogers Centre.

Still, that doesn’t mean it’s been easy for Guerrero Jr. Midway through the season, he tried to work his way out of the slump, taking upwards of 300 swings per day. Later, he opted for rest, skipping the All-Star Game to help with lingering back and hamstring soreness.

All the while, the questions about his performance intensified. That’s part of the job at this level — but in ways it’s a new challenge for Guerrero Jr., who has never struggled like this before. Along the way, he’s had to learn new ways to handle these struggles.

“He talks to his teammates about it,” Schneider said recently. “He’s open about it.”

And the way Schneider sees it, the more Guerrero Jr. talks to his teammates about it, the better. They’re all pulling for him. They all respect him. Lean into it.

“And Vlad’s good at lying,” Schneider continued. “He’s good at saying, ‘No, I’m good.’ And you have to keep asking and break down that wall a little bit.”

Once you do?

“He’s way more honest with me and the guys than probably he leads on to the media,” Schneider said. “But yeah, he’s frustrated for sure. (And) he’s more aware of it probably than you guys know.”

If so, the swings Guerrero Jr. took Wednesday must have offered him plenty of relief. Along with the no-doubt home run, he contributed an RBI double that nearly left the park, as well as an opposite-field RBI single.

While Guerrero Jr. declined to speak to writers after the game, Schneider expressed confidence that a game like this could provide some momentum for his first baseman.

“You never know where the mental game takes you in this long season, you know?” Schneider said Wednesday. “Mentally, you have to be tough, and mentally, you have to focus on what’s important in the moment. And I think Vlad’s doing a good job right now of working on that.”

It was the first three-hit game since July 25 for Guerrero Jr., who drove in five, a season best. It’s hard to quantify, but he looked like himself again.

Meanwhile, it was with games like this in mind that Cease chose to sign in Toronto, and he enjoyed his first taste of September baseball with his new team.

“It felt great,” the right-hander said. “I’m not really trying to think about all that when I pitch. I’m just going out and trying to execute, but yeah, the result definitely makes us happy.”

While Cease could have pitched deeper into the game if needed, the Blue Jays removed him after 83 pitches. Not only has he thrown 156.1 innings already, the Blue Jays hope he’ll be pitching many more.

“I’m probably still learning how to manage workloads and all that, but that’s why we’ve got Max (Scherzer) here who’s done it for 25 years,” Cease said. “You’ve just got to ask him how to do it.”

Most importantly, the Blue Jays won, setting up a massive series finale on Thursday between Tanner Bibee and Jose Soriano. At this point in the season, it’s about the team rather than any individual player.

But it’s impossible not to dream about the kind of difference Guerrero Jr. can make if he can stay locked in for a few more weeks. A night like this reminds everyone of the immense potential he still offers.

“Whatever has happened isn’t important,” Schneider said. “And what’s going to happen is the most important. So I think Vlad having a firm grasp on that is really, really big for him and really big for us.”

stories.title: Saab intensifies pitch to sell Gripen jets to Canada, promising assortment of benefits
stories.summary: Behind the scenes, Swedish defence company is pulling out all the stops to secure major order and deepen ties
stories.author: Gavin John
stories.content:
In the final-assembly hall for the Saab Gripen fighter jet in the Swedish city of Linkoping, the flags of Saab’s eight customer countries hang above the production line. A ninth spot holds a white banner reading, in red capital letters, Reserved.

Asked whether it was for Canada, a Saab official smiled, shrugged and said nothing.

Behind the scenes, though, Saab is pulling out all the stops in order to put Canada’s name on the banner.

At a recent briefing at Saab’s Linkoping headquarters that included The Globe and Mail, company officials laid out a range of benefits that Canada can expect should it go ahead with a major order for Gripen jets.

Saab had already promised a Canadian assembly line for the Gripen but had yet to detail the scope of that promise. The company is proposing to build the fighter jets in Canada from parts to finished aircraft, across a network of roughly 10 prime partners and some 250 suppliers in several provinces.

Canada would be the first start-to-finish Gripen production line outside Sweden, provided the order is large enough to justify it, Saab officials say. Canada has also been invited by Saab and the Swedish government to join Sweden’s next combat-aircraft program in the future, if the Gripen is selected.

It’s not clear at what stage and how detailed talks are between Saab and the federal government. The company’s promises come amid a growing trade rift between Canada and the U.S., traditionally this country’s largest military supplier. And Ottawa is still determining whether to forge ahead with a deal to buy additional U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets.

Saab’s previously announced partners include Bombardier, CAE, IMP Aerospace & Defence, Arcfield Canada and Cohere.

Beyond that, a document viewed by The Globe showed plans for half a dozen “Saab innovation hubs” across Canada for R&D, AI, cybersecurity and Arctic innovation.

Saab, which manufactures the JAS 39E Gripen, lost a competitive bid in 2022, when Canada, looking to replace its aging fleet of F-18s, chose U.S.-based Lockheed Martin to buy 88 F-35s.

The deal locked in the purchase of the first 16 planes, which are now in production, but when American tariffs were first introduced a year and a half ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review of the contract for the remaining 72 planes.

After trade talks collapsed late last month, Canada announced that it would fight U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest levies with countertariffs that are set to take effect next week.

The F-35 review, and any potential decision on the Gripen, are now caught up in the intensifying trade war, with Washington reportedly demanding that Canada complete the full F-35 buy while calls mount for the federal government to cancel the rest of the order.

At the same time, Saab continues its comprehensive multiyear campaign to woo Canada with no assurances that it will bear fruit.

In an interview, Saab CEO Micael Johansson put the decision in larger terms. “Canada has to decide, [does it] want the sovereign aerospace industry and is that important to them? That’s the first decision,” he said. “And then if they take that decision, Sweden and Saab is the best choice.”

He does not expect the F-35 to disappear; Canada has 16 under contract and has paid long-lead costs on 14 more. “I don’t think Canada will give up F-35 completely,” he said. “I have no clue how many.”

Mr. Johansson insists that Saab is not asking Canada to choose between suppliers. “We’re not trying to replace F-35. That’s a Canadian sovereign decision to go F-35,” he said. And a minute later: “It’s not replacing F-35. It’s both.”

A spokesperson for the office of Industry Ministry Mélanie Joly said in a statement that the minister has been in constant contact with Saab, as well as Lockheed Martin. “Her objective remains to create good-paying jobs for Canadians, especially at a time where Canada’s manufacturing sector is dealing with the impacts of the trade war,” said Gabrielle Landry, deputy director of media relations.

Mr. Carney vowed last spring that “the days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the United States are over” and has already made moves to diversify its purchases, including Canada’s continuing negotiations with Saab for a separate program: six GlobalEye early-warning aircraft.

Mr. Johansson said in the recent interview that a term sheet for the GlobalEye was due to be signed by the end of August.

The Defence Investment Agency, the federal body negotiating the purchase, said in a statement that, “The term sheet has not been signed.” The statement added that “Canada has been in constant and productive discussions with Saab regarding the GlobalEye” and that “these negotiations are not related to trade discussions between Canada and the U.S.”

The company’s ambitions, however, are much larger than that, and include the sale of at least 40 Gripen fighters, which Saab says is the number it would need to make building the aircraft in Canada viable. Saab says it needs a third final-assembly line, in addition to those in Sweden and Brazil, for its Gripen E fighter to meet demand.

Canada can maintain sovereign control over the aircraft’s military software, Saab says, and keep a classified program office in Montreal under Canadian control.

Saab officials offered a breakdown of estimated regional benefits. A document dividing production of both Gripen and GlobalEye by region shows that 50 per cent will go to Quebec, 26 per cent to Ontario, 14 per cent to the West and 10 per cent to Atlantic Canada.

Slightly less than half the work would be production and mechanics; the rest would be research and development, and program management.

In addition to establishing groundwork on the supply side, Saab has also moved to try to overcome one of the biggest hurdles. The Gripen’s one American part is its most important: the F414 engine, made by General Electric. Its export is governed by the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or Itar, the U.S. rules that allow Washington to approve, restrict or refuse the export of American military technology and dictate where it is repaired.

“Every contract that we secure is also backed by a licence from the U.S.,” Mr. Johansson said. So far, it has held: “It’s never been a problem, GE supporting us tremendously, and GE is also supporting doing things in Canada.”

On July 22, GE Aerospace and Canadian company Magellan Aerospace signed a memorandum of understanding to overhaul the engines in Mississauga if Canada buys the Gripen, so the engines would be fixed in Ontario rather than shipped to the United States. The hedge was negotiated by Saab and GE, its American supplier; Ottawa has said nothing publicly about seeking such assurances itself.

The office of Stephen Fuhr, the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement, said in a statement that it “regularly engage[s] with defence-industry representatives including from Saab.”

However, it noted: “Engagement does not constitute the launch of a procurement process, a commitment to procure or an assessment against requirements.” The F-35 procurement, the statement said, “is currently under review,” and the DIA “does not comment on the receipt of solicited or unsolicited proposals from industry.”

Mr. Carney vowed last spring that “the days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the United States are over” and has already made moves to diversify its purchases, including Canada’s continuing negotiations with Saab for a separate program: six GlobalEye early-warning aircraft.
Mr. Johansson said in the recent interview that a term sheet for the GlobalEye was due to be signed by the end of August.

The Defence Investment Agency, the federal body negotiating the purchase, said in a statement that, “The term sheet has not been signed.” The statement added that “Canada has been in constant and productive discussions with Saab regarding the GlobalEye” and that “these negotiations are not related to trade discussions between Canada and the U.S.”

Canada can maintain sovereign control over the aircraft’s military software, Saab says, and keep a classified program office in Montreal under Canadian control.

Saab officials offered a breakdown of estimated regional benefits. A document dividing production of both Gripen and GlobalEye by region shows that 50 per cent will go to Quebec, 26 per cent to Ontario, 14 per cent to the West and 10 per cent to Atlantic Canada.
Slightly less than half the work would be production and mechanics; the rest would be research and development, and program management.

In addition to establishing groundwork on the supply side, Saab has also moved to try to overcome one of the biggest hurdles. Its export is governed by the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or Itar, the U.S. rules that allow Washington to approve, restrict or refuse the export of American military technology and dictate where it is repaired.

“Every contract that we secure is also backed by a licence from the U.S.,” Mr. Johansson said. So far, it has held: “It’s never been a problem, GE supporting us tremendously, and GE is also supporting doing things in Canada.”

The office of Stephen Fuhr, the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement, said in a statement that it “regularly engage[s] with defence-industry representatives including from Saab.”

However, it noted: “Engagement does not constitute the launch of a procurement process, a commitment to procure or an assessment against requirements.” The F-35 procurement, the statement said, “is currently under review,” and the DIA “does not comment on the receipt of solicited or unsolicited proposals from industry.”

stories.title: Virtual classrooms organized in Canada offer lifeline to girls under Taliban rule
stories.summary: On a recent summer Friday, nearly a dozen students logged on for their online literature class. It was a group of mostly young women joining from different parts of Afghanistan, eagerly waiting for their turn to discuss a story they had read the week before.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
On a recent summer Friday, nearly a dozen students logged on for their online literature class. It was a group of mostly young women joining from different parts of Afghanistan, eagerly waiting for their turn to discuss a story they had read the week before.

Before the Taliban’s return to power five years ago, the women were studying in high school or university, hoping education would give them a better future. Some had just obtained their undergraduate degrees. But their plans were put on hold when, like millions of other Afghan girls, they were barred from going to school.

Once a week, the group gathers in a Google Meet room for a 90-minute class hosted by Toronto-based poet and educator Hazrat Wahriz. In this lesson attended by a reporter, they discussed a short story about a teenage boy’s journey fleeing the Taliban.

The story’s author, Shams Erfan, joined the virtual class from Toronto and listened attentively throughout the session. Then he had a few words for the women.

“I hope you continue ... writing, critiquing, reading, protesting, attending online classes,” he said in Persian.

“These activities are a fight,” he continued, ”a fight against the Taliban ideology that is trying to remove you all.”

Since 2021, the Taliban regime has been excluding women from every aspect of public life by imposing what international human rights groups call a system of “gender apartheid.” It has issued sweeping edicts to restrict women’s right to work, education and freedom of movement.

In a report published last month, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization estimated that 2.4 million Afghan girls have been barred from secondary education, a number that could increase to four million by 2030.

The Taliban also banned education for girls and women during its first rule in the late 1990s, before the regime was toppled in 2001 by a U.S-led international coalition in response to the 9/11 attacks.

Canadian troops spent 13 years in the country as part of a Nato stabilization mission. More than 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel were deployed to Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014.

Girls and women returned to classrooms in 2001, and Canadian military and aid organizations invested heavily in women’s education and empowerment projects over the years.

But the Taliban waged a bloody insurgency that paved their way back to power in 2021. Soon after seizing Kabul, the regime renewed its ban on women’s education.

As the ban continues, virtual and underground schools operating from overseas — including the one founded by Wahriz in Toronto — have become a lifeline for many.

In addition to online literature, photography and critical thinking courses, Wahriz’s non-profit, the Network of Community Schools for Girls in Afghanistan, runs a web of secret schools across the country.

“Our first school was established in one of the faraway provinces of Afghanistan and since then, we gradually expanded our activities,” he said

More than 1,600 girls are now being taught in his underground classrooms by female teachers turning their own homes into learning centres, he said.

Under current rules, girls are only allowed to go to school up to Grade 6, meaning those attending secondary and higher education are violating the Taliban’s strict religious code. If caught, they could face severe punishment including physical violence and imprisonment.

Despite those risks, Wahriz said, girls are showing up in classrooms every day to learn math, physics, chemistry and history in a fight against the “darkness.”

“We are challenging that darkness just by our existence,” he said.

Wahriz said funding for the network mostly comes from “kind-hearted” people he knows, including his Canadian friends and an organization based in the United Kingdom.

The teachers are paid US$100 a month when funding is available, he said.

“They are dedicated, committed enough not to expect every month to get paid, but are sure that whenever we find something, they get paid,” Wahriz said.

He said even though his efforts are like a “small drop in the desert” given the magnitude of the crisis, he is optimistic because others are also doing the same.

“Drop by drop, it becomes a sea,” he said, referring to a Persian proverb.

A number of similar organizations in other countries are also working to bypass the Taliban ban on girls’ education.

Women’s rights was a central issue during the 2020 peace talks between the Taliban and the former U.S.-supported Afghan government.

Taliban negotiators repeatedly said they would no longer oppose women’s right to education and employment, but “within the framework of Islamic law,” a vague promise they immediately broke after seizing power. They have since issued more than 100 edicts targeting women, according to the United Nations.

The group’s top leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and his chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani are now wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in their treatment of women and girls.

The Canadian government said it has been backing efforts to expand education opportunities for all Afghans, including girls and women, for over two decades, and has provided more than $143 million to fund education and health-care programs in the past five years while avoiding any investments through the Taliban.

“Canada strongly condemns the ongoing repression, systematic human rights abuses and erosion of fundamental freedoms under Taliban rule in Afghanistan, and is deeply concerned by the worsening humanitarian situation,” Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Brittany Fletcher said in a statement.

For Murwarid Ziayee, the devastating impact of the ban on women’s education was a “painful” experience.

She was in her last semester of law school when the Taliban took power in 1996 and closed the doors of Kabul University to female students. But she didn’t give up on her dreams, she said.

Ziayee self-studied, learned English and computer skills, and even found a job at an underground non-profit that helped educate women at the time. She was able to complete her studies and obtain her degree after the Taliban were overthrown in 2001.

Ziayee, now the senior director of Calgary-based Right to Learn in Afghanistan, said she is trying to do her part to help girls and women who have once again been banned from school.

“It’s better to be in front seat and have the wheel and move forward and do what can be done,” she said in interview.

The non-profit, formerly known as Canadian Women for Women in Afghanistan, was founded in 1998 and has been working to empower women through education ever since.

Ziayee said more than 700 students, mostly in Afghanistan, are attending the organization’s virtual school and 92 per cent of them are girls.

The first cohort will graduate from high school next year, she said. “Once you provide these girls with the education ... the doors to many opportunities will open for them.”

She said students from Grade 7 to Grade 9 study the former government’s curriculum before taking Canadian and internationally accredited courses during the three years of high school.

Once the students graduate, they obtain internationally accepted diplomas so they can apply for post-secondary education abroad. Most of the funding comes from the federal government or individual Canadians, while people living in other countries also support some students.

But even though many other organizations are involved, they cannot fulfil a state’s job to provide education, Ziayee said.

“The gap is huge and that’s why we are obviously impatiently waiting and praying and advocating for the day that things change in Afghanistan,” Ziayee said.

Until then, Ziayee said the group wants to see the international community step up to fund alternative ways to support more Afghan women and girls “who are left behind and waiting for opportunities to be enrolled.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.

Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: On a recent summer Friday, nearly a dozen students logged on for their online literature class. It was a group of mostly young women joining from different parts of Afghanistan, eagerly waiting for their turn to discuss a story they had read the week before.

Before the Taliban’s return to power five years ago, the women were studying in high school or university, hoping education would give them a better future. Some had just obtained their undergraduate degrees. But their plans were put on hold when, like millions of other Afghan girls, they were barred from going to school.

Once a week, the group gathers in a Google Meet room for a 90-minute class hosted by Toronto-based poet and educator Hazrat Wahriz. In this lesson attended by a reporter, they discussed a short story about a teenage boy’s journey fleeing the Taliban.
The story’s author, Shams Erfan, joined the virtual class from Toronto and listened attentively throughout the session. Then he had a few words for the women.
“I hope you continue ... writing, critiquing, reading, protesting, attending online classes,” he said in Persian.
“These activities are a fight,” he continued, ”a fight against the Taliban ideology that is trying to remove you all.”

Since 2021, the Taliban regime has been excluding women from every aspect of public life by imposing what international human rights groups call a system of “gender apartheid.” It has issued sweeping edicts to restrict women’s right to work, education and freedom of movement.

In a report published last month, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization estimated that 2.4 million Afghan girls have been barred from secondary education, a number that could increase to four million by 2030.

The Taliban also banned education for girls and women during its first rule in the late 1990s, before the regime was toppled in 2001 by a U.S-led international coalition in response to the 9/11 attacks.
Canadian troops spent 13 years in the country as part of a Nato stabilization mission. More than 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel were deployed to Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014.
Girls and women returned to classrooms in 2001, and Canadian military and aid organizations invested heavily in women’s education and empowerment projects over the years.
But the Taliban waged a bloody insurgency that paved their way back to power in 2021. Soon after seizing Kabul, the regime renewed its ban on women’s education.
As the ban continues, virtual and underground schools operating from overseas — including the one founded by Wahriz in Toronto — have become a lifeline for many.

In addition to online literature, photography and critical thinking courses, Wahriz’s non-profit, the Network of Community Schools for Girls in Afghanistan, runs a web of secret schools across the country.
“Our first school was established in one of the faraway provinces of Afghanistan and since then, we gradually expanded our activities,” he said
More than 1,600 girls are now being taught in his underground classrooms by female teachers turning their own homes into learning centres, he said.

Under current rules, girls are only allowed to go to school up to Grade 6, meaning those attending secondary and higher education are violating the Taliban’s strict religious code. If caught, they could face severe punishment including physical violence and imprisonment.
Despite those risks, Wahriz said, girls are showing up in classrooms every day to learn math, physics, chemistry and history in a fight against the “darkness.”
“We are challenging that darkness just by our existence,” he said.
Wahriz said funding for the network mostly comes from “kind-hearted” people he knows, including his Canadian friends and an organization based in the United Kingdom.
The teachers are paid US$100 a month when funding is available, he said.
“They are dedicated, committed enough not to expect every month to get paid, but are sure that whenever we find something, they get paid,” Wahriz said.
He said even though his efforts are like a “small drop in the desert” given the magnitude of the crisis, he is optimistic because others are also doing the same.
“Drop by drop, it becomes a sea,” he said, referring to a Persian proverb.
A number of similar organizations in other countries are also working to bypass the Taliban ban on girls’ education.
Women’s rights was a central issue during the 2020 peace talks between the Taliban and the former U.S.-supported Afghan government.

Taliban negotiators repeatedly said they would no longer oppose women’s right to education and employment, but “within the framework of Islamic law,” a vague promise they immediately broke after seizing power. They have since issued more than 100 edicts targeting women, according to the United Nations.

The group’s top leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and his chief justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani are now wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in their treatment of women and girls.

The Canadian government said it has been backing efforts to expand education opportunities for all Afghans, including girls and women, for over two decades, and has provided more than $143 million to fund education and health-care programs in the past five years while avoiding any investments through the Taliban.

“Canada strongly condemns the ongoing repression, systematic human rights abuses and erosion of fundamental freedoms under Taliban rule in Afghanistan, and is deeply concerned by the worsening humanitarian situation,” Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Brittany Fletcher said in a statement.
For Murwarid Ziayee, the devastating impact of the ban on women’s education was a “painful” experience.
She was in her last semester of law school when the Taliban took power in 1996 and closed the doors of Kabul University to female students. But she didn’t give up on her dreams, she said.

Ziayee self-studied, learned English and computer skills, and even found a job at an underground non-profit that helped educate women at the time. She was able to complete her studies and obtain her degree after the Taliban were overthrown in 2001.
Ziayee, now the senior director of Calgary-based Right to Learn in Afghanistan, said she is trying to do her part to help girls and women who have once again been banned from school.
“It’s better to be in front seat and have the wheel and move forward and do what can be done,” she said in interview.
The non-profit, formerly known as Canadian Women for Women in Afghanistan, was founded in 1998 and has been working to empower women through education ever since.
Ziayee said more than 700 students, mostly in Afghanistan, are attending the organization’s virtual school and 92 per cent of them are girls.
The first cohort will graduate from high school next year, she said. “Once you provide these girls with the education ... the doors to many opportunities will open for them.”
She said students from Grade 7 to Grade 9 study the former government’s curriculum before taking Canadian and internationally accredited courses during the three years of high school.

Once the students graduate, they obtain internationally accepted diplomas so they can apply for post-secondary education abroad. Most of the funding comes from the federal government or individual Canadians, while people living in other countries also support some students.
But even though many other organizations are involved, they cannot fulfil a state’s job to provide education, Ziayee said.
“The gap is huge and that’s why we are obviously impatiently waiting and praying and advocating for the day that things change in Afghanistan,” Ziayee said.

Until then, Ziayee said the group wants to see the international community step up to fund alternative ways to support more Afghan women and girls “who are left behind and waiting for opportunities to be enrolled.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 3, 2026.
Sharif Hassan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: A pediatric emergency physician on the risks of e-scooters
stories.summary: Fractures, head and brain injuries among most common e-scooter injuries
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland
stories.content:
The popularity of e-scooters on Canadian roads has exploded in recent years. But new data from health officials and the Canadian Paediatric Society shows that the risks of e-scooters can lead to hospitalization and death. Has policy and regulation kept up with how readily available the transportation has become?

Dr. Daniel Rosenfield , pediatric emergency physician at SickKids Hospital in Toronto and chair of the Injury Prevention Committee for the Canadian Paediatric Society, joins The Decibel to talk about the trauma cases he’s seen first-hand, why e-scooters can be deadly and how to balance regulation with medical safety.

Questions? Comments? Ideas? E-mail us at thedecibel@globeandmail.com
