stories.title: Montreal West parents want crossing guard back at troubled intersection near school
stories.summary: Reconfiguration of the intersection is expected to begin Wednesday with the new layout expected to be completed by the first week of October.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Parents of students at a Montreal West high school are urging police to bring back a crossing guard to an intersection that’s been the source of concerns after collisions in recent years.

The corner of Ainslie Road and Westminster Avenue is a commonly-used path by students of Royal West Academy.

“It is very frustrating. I feel we have gone a step backwards from where we were last year,” said Joanna Duy, the chair of the Royal West Parent Safety Subcommittee.

In the past two years, three students from the school have been struck by vehicles and injured at the intersection.

Back in April, Montreal police stationed a crossing guard at the roadway. It was in place until the end of the school year.

The guard was temporarily assigned with the expectation the municipality of Montreal West would be making changes, including reducing the number of lanes from four to two, according to the subcommittee. The work was to take place during this past summer, along with road changes at the nearby level train crossing.

When the school year ended, the guard was no longer in place, but the subcommittee went to the Montreal Agglomeration Council to ask for the crossing guard to return this school year.

A pilot project is underway to narrow the roadway, and remove left-hand turns to make the area safer.

2:03 Parents demand crossing guard at dangerous intersection

“With these improvements, we really think that this will be some kind of calming measures and that there will be more space for kids to cross safely,” said Montreal West Mayor Jonathan Cha.

Though improvements are on the way, parents and advocates say a crossing guard would still be important to have.

Duy said as the intersection changes, driver frustration could increase and create more concerns.

“We are asking for a school crossing guard for one other year. That would give the city the chance to make the improvements that it wants to make, but also to give the time for the dust to settle a little bit,” said Duy.

“We’re all a little concerned that with bringing the number of lanes down from four to two, that driver frustration is actually going to increase and that might have an effect on this intersection.”

Cha echoed Duy’s call for a crossing guard, saying he’s been speaking with Montreal city officials about the urgent need to improve safety.

“We really hope the city will provide us a crossing guard at least until the end of the school year,” he said.

In a statement to Global News, Montreal police said the crossing guard assigned last year was done so “on an exceptional and temporary basis for the 2025-2026 school year.”

Police said the temporary measure was put in place as an “interim solution” while Montreal West assessed the situation and reconfigured the roadway.

Reconfiguration of the intersection is expected to begin Wednesday with the new layout expected to be completed by the first week of October.

paragraphs: Parents of students at a Montreal West high school are urging police to bring back a crossing guard to an intersection that’s been the source of concerns after collisions in recent years.
The corner of Ainslie Road and Westminster Avenue is a commonly-used path by students of Royal West Academy.
“It is very frustrating. I feel we have gone a step backwards from where we were last year,” said Joanna Duy, the chair of the Royal West Parent Safety Subcommittee.
In the past two years, three students from the school have been struck by vehicles and injured at the intersection.
Back in April, Montreal police stationed a crossing guard at the roadway. It was in place until the end of the school year.

The guard was temporarily assigned with the expectation the municipality of Montreal West would be making changes, including reducing the number of lanes from four to two, according to the subcommittee. The work was to take place during this past summer, along with road changes at the nearby level train crossing.
When the school year ended, the guard was no longer in place, but the subcommittee went to the Montreal Agglomeration Council to ask for the crossing guard to return this school year.
A pilot project is underway to narrow the roadway, and remove left-hand turns to make the area safer.

stories.title: London home sales slide as average price hits three-year low
stories.summary: Realtors say more lower-priced homes changed hands as the region slipped back into buyer’s-market territory.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The London region’s real estate market took a hit in August, with home sales down from the same period last year and the average sale price falling to its lowest level in more than three years, newly released figures show.

A total of 526 homes sold last month across the London area – which also includes St. Thomas, Strathroy and parts of Elgin and Middlesex counties – according to statistics from the London and St. Thomas Association of Realtors (LSTAR).

That’s a 14.3 per cent decline compared with August last year and a 23 per cent drop from the 686 homes sold in July.

LSTAR chairperson Robin Tiller said August is typically a slower month, with people on vacation and families getting ready for the school year. But she said uncertainty surrounding trade and tariffs with the United States may also have contributed to the drop.

“There’s been so much news out and in this world news, it’s economic stuff that Canadians can’t do anything really about to this larger point,” she said. “It weighs on people’s minds. I mean, we’re all following the news to see what’s going on.”

The average home price also declined in August, falling to $590,550, down 9.3 per cent from a year earlier. It was the lowest average sale price in the region since January 2023, when the average was $585,252.

Tiller said the average price is more reflective of the types of homes sold, with more lower-priced properties changing hands in August.

“This is just an average, so it’s the type of home that’s selling, not just the total number sold,” she said.

The sales-to-new-listings ratio was 37.5 per cent, down from 44.5 per cent in July. It compares the 526 homes sold with 1,403 new listings in August.

“We started off (this year) in a buyer’s market. We have climbed steadily into just below a balanced market, and then in August again we’ve slid back into that buyer’s market territory,” Tiller said.

London plot, ready to add 28 townhomes, listed for $3.3M

Advertisement 1Story continues below

But Tiller noted there are signs of stability, with interest rates holding steady at 2.25 per cent.

LSTAR also reported 6.3 months of inventory in August, the highest level this year. Tiller said that gives buyers more choice, while sellers should not be overly concerned because the median number of days on market fell from 30 a year ago to 28 this August.

The sales-to-list-price ratio was 97.1 per cent, with homes selling slightly below their listed price, though Tiller said the difference was not significant.

“Be patient. The market will be fine. Let August sit, and look forward to September because there is stability coming,” she said. “Municipal elections will be focusing on housing issues, my advice to buyers and sellers is stay educated on what your municipal leaders are talking about and how it relates to housing.”

stories.title: MP Lori Idlout contravened conflict of interest code, ethics commissioner says
stories.summary: Idlout claimed reimbursement for more than $1,700 in gifts purchased from a business owned by herself and her spouse, commissioner’s office reports
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
MP Lori Idlout contravened the House of Commons conflict of interest code, Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein announced today.

The commissioner’s office reports that Idlout last year claimed reimbursement for more than $1,700 in gifts she purchased from a business owned by herself and her spouse.

MPs aren’t allowed to act in a way that furthers their private interests.

Von Finckenstein said while Idlout made errors in judgment, he believed she acted in good faith since she repaid the House of Commons as soon as the issue was raised.

He recommended that no sanctions be imposed.

Idlout made the purchases while sitting as an NDP member of Parliament before crossing the floor to the Liberals back in March.

stories.title: Holocaust orphan Saul Reichert built a prosperous life in Edmonton
stories.summary: ‘Stubbornly optimistic’ Auschwitz survivor immigrated to Canada through War Orphans Project and launched successful career in restaurants and real estate
stories.author: Alan Freeman
stories.content:
In January of 1948, Saul Reichert landed at Pier 21 in Halifax, alone in the world. He was 17, with one English pound and a few U.S. dollars in his pocket. He was a survivor of Auschwitz and had lost his mother and five sisters in the Holocaust. There was no question of returning to his hometown in Poland.

Mr. Reichert was a participant in the War Orphans Project, the product of an agreement between the Canadian Jewish Congress and the Canadian government that ultimately saw 1,123 Jewish survivors under the age of 18 immigrate to Canada. It was also the first crack in the notorious Canadian immigration policy that had shut out Jews fleeing the Nazis before and during the Second World War.

Most of the orphans were sponsored by Jewish families in Montreal and Toronto, but Saul was one of 28 headed for Alberta, travelling across the country to Edmonton, where he was welcomed by a sponsoring family. Within two years, he owned a lunch counter and spoke English, launching a successful business career in restaurants and real estate and becoming an active member of Edmonton’s Jewish community, showing a remarkable resilience and positive attitude that continued throughout his life.

“He didn’t look back, he looked forward and lived in the present,” said David Margolus, an Edmonton lawyer whose parents sponsored young Saul on his arrival in the city in 1948. Mr. Margolus was born two years later and Mr. Reichert became a presence in his life that continued until Mr. Reichert’s death. “He was in every sense a part of our family. He was like an older brother to me.”

Mr. Reichert, who died in Toronto on July 24 at 95, never stopped being thankful for his chance at a new life. “To come to a country like Canada was really the difference between day and night,” he recalled in a 1985 video testimony produced for the Jewish Archives and Historical Society of Edmonton and Northern Alberta.

“He was a very optimistic person, stubbornly optimistic,” said Bonny Reichert, a Toronto food writer and the youngest of Mr. Reichert’s four daughters, who chronicled her father’s life in her own memoir, How to Share an Egg, published in 2025. “He didn’t expect to survive and when he did, he saw it as a marvellous second chance.”

“Seeing things in a positive way and thinking things would get better soon, that was Saul to a T,” said his eldest daughter, Rochelle, who recalled that her father didn’t dwell on what he lived through as a child and teenager. “He didn’t want to burden his children and didn’t want us to experience what he had,” she said.

Shlomo Reichert was born on Dec. 17, 1930, in Pabianice, a small city adjacent to Lodz in central Poland, the only son of Betzalel Reichert and his wife, the former Udel Rotblat, who also had four daughters together. A fifth girl, Saul’s half-sister, was the daughter of Betzalel’s first wife, who had died.

The family owned a paint-supply shop and lived a middle-class life, though they were affected by the Depression. In the video, Mr. Reichert recounts that he had a wonderful childhood, surrounded by a warm and loving family. That childhood ended in 1939, with the death of his father from natural causes and the Nazi invasion of Poland. He was 8.

In 1940, the family was forced into Pabianice’s Jewish ghetto, where he was nevertheless able to continue some schooling. Two years later, they were forcibly sent to the ghetto in Lodz where conditions were much more difficult. There was no school and hardly any food. “People were sitting in the streets waiting to die and nobody could help them,” he recalled.

Then Saul managed to get work as a sorter in a church where the authorities had sent pillows, duvets and other bedding taken from Jewish families. Workers like Saul would slash them open, and then separate the feathers and down, which were ultimately shipped off to Germany.

Reacting to Saul’s inherent charm, a supervisor named Mr. Sharp took a liking to the boy and found a job for Saul’s mother distributing food, giving the family better access to scarce rations. “All of a sudden, our fate in the ghetto became better,” Saul said.

There was another advantage to the sorting job. Desperate Jews would occasionally hide jewellery or cash which would emerge when the bedding was ripped open and could be traded for something of immediate value. “For a diamond ring, you’d be lucky if you got two or three loaves of bread,” Saul said.

In the fall of 1944, the Lodz ghetto was emptied. Saul and his family were loaded into rail cars and sent to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Arriving at the camp, they were surrounded by armed German guards screaming at them, accompanied by dogs. “All of a sudden, they separated the women and the men.” It was the last time Saul saw his mother and sisters.

“You could see the crematorium in the background,” Mr. Reichert recalled in 1985. “The people who looked sick and were very thin went to the other side and were never seen again.” But Saul, despite his small stature, was nevertheless selected for forced labour and ended up in a sub-work camp called Gleiwitz, where he hauled railway ties.

As the Red Army advanced in early 1945, the Nazis sent the remaining concentration camp inmates north on the infamous death marches. Saul and a cousin ended up on a train that took them to Germany, where they were liberated by U.S. soldiers in May of 1945. Hiding in a barn, he was initially skeptical but when he heard the troops speaking English, he was elated. “I was so excited. I’m going to live. I’m not going to die,” he recalled later.

Saul survived over the next two years working in a kitchen for American troops and made a brief foray into cigarette smuggling. Then he and his cousin heard about the opportunity to get a visa. He told officials he wanted to go to New York, not knowing he would be heading for Canada. His cousin, who was already 18, was excluded from the Canadian program.

When he arrived in Edmonton, the Margolus family helped Mr. Reichert get started, finding him a job at Teddy’s Lunch, a deli and grocery store known for its corned beef sandwiches and chili con carne. Working seven days a week, he ended up buying the business two years later with help from the Margolus family. He soon paid off the loan.

Mr. Reichert bought a couple of other luncheonettes and opened the Carousel, a 250-seat dining room and bar. He expanded Teddy’s and with partners bought stakes in other restaurants and a hotel. As Edmonton grew, Mr. Reichert bought farmland in nearby Beaumont and became a house builder and developer. A street in the town bears his name.

Mr. Reichert married in 1956 and with his wife, Toby, had four girls. As teens, the sisters ended up working the cash or acting as a hostess or server at one of the restaurants.

Saul and Toby were keen card players, particularly bridge, and Saul enjoyed poker as well. When they became more prosperous, they began to winter in Arizona but still felt most at home in Edmonton. After retiring, they eventually moved to Toronto, to be closer to their daughters. Mrs. Reichert died in 2021.

In 2004, the Reicherts endowed the Toby and Saul Reichert Holocaust Lecture at the University of Alberta’s Wirth Institute for Austrian and Central European Studies. The series features an annual lecture at the university by a prominent scholar of the Holocaust.

Though he didn’t harp on it, Mr. Reichert did have his views on the causes of the Holocaust. He lay the blame firmly at the feet of the German people. “Look at the newsreels of 1933 to 1944. They were cheering him [Hitler] on,” Mr. Reichert said in his video testimonial, blaming the German people for failing to rebel against the Nazi regime.

“There must never be a nation who can do what the Germans did and get away with it,” he said in the video.

Mr. Reichert leaves his daughters, Rochelle, Jerell, Adell and Bonny, as well as 10 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren.

Mr. Reichert was a participant in the War Orphans Project, the product of an agreement between the Canadian Jewish Congress and the Canadian government that ultimately saw 1,123 Jewish survivors under the age of 18 immigrate to Canada. It was also the first crack in the notorious Canadian immigration policy that had shut out Jews fleeing the Nazis before and during the Second World War.

Most of the orphans were sponsored by Jewish families in Montreal and Toronto, but Saul was one of 28 headed for Alberta, travelling across the country to Edmonton, where he was welcomed by a sponsoring family. Within two years, he owned a lunch counter and spoke English, launching a successful business career in restaurants and real estate and becoming an active member of Edmonton’s Jewish community, showing a remarkable resilience and positive attitude that continued throughout his life.

“He didn’t look back, he looked forward and lived in the present,” said David Margolus, an Edmonton lawyer whose parents sponsored young Saul on his arrival in the city in 1948. Mr. Margolus was born two years later and Mr. Reichert became a presence in his life that continued until Mr. Reichert’s death. “He was in every sense a part of our family. He was like an older brother to me.”

stories.title: ‘Keep human culture alive’: Halifax music venue takes a stand against AI posters
stories.summary: Gus' Pub in Halifax has decided it will no longer be accepting AI event posters. Staff say they want to promote and support local artists and 'human culture.'
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
A popular Halifax music venue is taking a stand against event posters generated by artificial intelligence.

Gus’ Pub in the city’s north end has been supporting local artists for years. Going beyond just the music itself, the walls of the pub are littered with event posters crafted by local graphic designers.

But when show fliers generated by AI started creeping in, the bar pushed back.

“It just reflects our values as musicians and as the pub. This place is very artist-run, artist-centric. We have a really strong community of artists that come here of all different kinds, not just music,” said TJ Ploughman, who is a bartender at the pub and a musician.

“As a staff, we’re all musicians. We’re all artists. So we decided to just basically be the landmark for purely human artistry.”

Gus’ Pub recently shared a post on its Instagram page, announcing the venue will no longer be accepting AI event posters. Instead, if performers submit one for their booking, they’ll opt for a “No Name” template, which was created as a parody of Loblaws’ brand.

“We will give them resources. Sometimes even the manager, CJ, is very good at just whipping up a poster for somebody,” Ploughman added.

“It’s either do it yourself or get someone artistic to do it for you.”

The message struck a nerve and has generated thousands of online responses.

Halifax artist, Gabriela Warlet, is one of many applauding the move.

“There’s no soul in art created by AI because it looks all the same,” said Warlet.

The musician and graphic designer says she started losing clients as AI use became more prevalent. However, she believes more musicians have reached out to her for design work since Gus’ Pub took a stand.

“I feel like after AI, I stopped having commissions as much as I did years ago,” she said.

“I started doing this when I was like 16 and I was selling more art frequently. And after AI came to be, a lot of people stopped commissioning.”

One organization representing Nova Scotian visual artists says AI adoption in art and commercial spaces is a top concern for many in the industry.

“It really does devalue the artist in so many ways,” explained Therese Cruz, executive director of Visual Arts Nova Scotian.

Cruz says she’d like to see more businesses take a stand similar to Gus’ Pub and encourage more people to seek out original work created by humans.

“Their careers in the arts are actually supported by doing so and taking a strong stance against technology that is not helpful,” she said.

paragraphs: A popular Halifax music venue is taking a stand against event posters generated by artificial intelligence.

Gus’ Pub in the city’s north end has been supporting local artists for years. Going beyond just the music itself, the walls of the pub are littered with event posters crafted by local graphic designers.
But when show fliers generated by AI started creeping in, the bar pushed back.

“It just reflects our values as musicians and as the pub. This place is very artist-run, artist-centric. We have a really strong community of artists that come here of all different kinds, not just music,” said TJ Ploughman, who is a bartender at the pub and a musician.
“As a staff, we’re all musicians. We’re all artists. So we decided to just basically be the landmark for purely human artistry.”

Gus’ Pub recently shared a post on its Instagram page, announcing the venue will no longer be accepting AI event posters. Instead, if performers submit one for their booking, they’ll opt for a “No Name” template, which was created as a parody of Loblaws’ brand.
“We will give them resources. Sometimes even the manager, CJ, is very good at just whipping up a poster for somebody,” Ploughman added.
“It’s either do it yourself or get someone artistic to do it for you.”
The message struck a nerve and has generated thousands of online responses.
Halifax artist, Gabriela Warlet, is one of many applauding the move.
“There’s no soul in art created by AI because it looks all the same,” said Warlet.

The musician and graphic designer says she started losing clients as AI use became more prevalent. However, she believes more musicians have reached out to her for design work since Gus’ Pub took a stand.
“I feel like after AI, I stopped having commissions as much as I did years ago,” she said.
“I started doing this when I was like 16 and I was selling more art frequently. And after AI came to be, a lot of people stopped commissioning.”
One organization representing Nova Scotian visual artists says AI adoption in art and commercial spaces is a top concern for many in the industry.
“It really does devalue the artist in so many ways,” explained Therese Cruz, executive director of Visual Arts Nova Scotian.

stories.title: Hit series Heated Rivalry skates into London for second-season filming
stories.summary: Sources confirmed filming at Canada Life Place and Museum London, while social media reports pointed to other locations.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us May earn us a commission, which supports our work.

A scorching-hot television series hit the ice in London this week.

Heated Rivalry, the Crave streamer series that became a breakout hit in its first season, filmed part of its second season in London recently, sources close to the production confirmed.

Social media also lit up with reports of filming at Canada Life Place and elsewhere in the city.

“Pretty exciting! Nice that we’ll be able to see something local in a huge show,” one Reddit user wrote.

The X account Toronto Filming posted: “Filming Update! It sounds like #HeatedRivalry was filming at Canada Life Place in London.”

Another X user, Kathrynne Martin, wrote: “I can confirm it WAS ‘HR’ filming in London for a few days. I know people that were on set.”

The series follows professional hockey stars Shane Hollander, played by Hudson Williams, and Ilya Rozanov, portrayed by Connor Storrie, who have a passionate relationship that defies the taboo of gay love in professional sports.

The show created fictional teams for the characters, with Hollander playing for the Montreal Metros and Rozanov for the Boston Raiders.

The series has become a viral sensation and earned acclaim for its queer sports romance and Lgbtq+ representation.

Entertainment publication Variety reported the series averaged 10.6 million viewers per episode in the U.S., according to Warner Bros. Discovery. Heated Rivalry also became HBO Max’s most-watched non-animated acquired series since the platform launched in 2020.

On Rotten Tomatoes, the film and television review website, the series has a 97 per cent critics score and an 88 per cent audience score.

After just one season, Heated Rivalry has racked up 42 wins, including a record 16 Canadian Screen Awards and the Television Critics Association’s Program of the Year honour.\

In London, sources confirmed the series filmed at Canada Life Place and Museum London. Social media reports also suggested scenes were filmed in Wortley Village.

Museum London and Canada Life Place could not be reached for comment. Sources said those involved with the production were required to sign non-disclosure agreements.

The series is an adaptation of Canadian writer Rachel Reid’s bestselling novels and was brought to the screen by Jacob Tierney, its writer, director and executive producer.

The first season was filmed largely in Ontario, including Hamilton, Toronto, Guelph and the Muskoka area.

One London Reddit user wrote: “This is going to sound crazy but I was dropping a package off at the Delta (hotel) earlier today . . . and I swore I saw Connor Storrie.”

Another fan added: “There’s so many great actors here this week, it’s exciting for the city!”

stories.title: Conservation authorities warn of potential flooding as severe storm approaches
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 6:12 PM | Last Updated: 8 hours ago
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 6:12 PM | Last Updated: 8 hours ago
Up to 60 millimetres of rain is possible Wednesday afternoon
Conservation authorities are warning of a heightened risk of flooding as a severe storm moves through the London region Wednesday afternoon.
Environment Canada says the heaviest rain is expected between 4 and 8 p.m., with up to 60 millimetres possible.
The Kettle Creek Conservation Authority, which covers the watershed south of London to Lake Erie, is urging residents to use extra caution around creeks and streams as the rain moves through.
Water levels have already risen slightly following rainfall earlier Wednesday.
Jennifer Dow, the authority's water resources supervisor, said the wet conditions mean much of the new rainfall could run off into waterways rather than being absorbed by the ground.

hat has saturated the ground, so that means any extra rain that we get, we're going to see probably significant runoff into the creeks and streams in the watershed, which could result in elevated water levels and flows," she said.
The Kcca says areas that receive more than 50 millimetres of rain are at increased risk of flash and localized flooding. It also warns that intense downpours could overwhelm local drainage systems.
Dow said residents can reduce the risk around their homes by clearing leaves and debris from storm drains.
And people living near waterways or in floodplains should move property to higher ground where possible.
"If you do live next to water courses or are in the floodplain, it's always good to move property out of that area so that it is less likely to be impacted by flooding," she added.
The Upper Thames River Conservation Authority, which covers the watershed north of London, issued its own flood outlook Monday.
The region received about 150 millimetres of rain in August, leaving the ground saturated and less able to absorb more water, according to Utrca spokesperson Eleanor Heagy.
She says that could lead to overland flooding if parts of the region get a particularly heavy downpour.
"We want people to be aware that if there's any really heavy downpour, if there's some localized thunderstorms that dump a lot of water, then there May be some overland flooding," she said.
Heagy says drains and culverts could also become overwhelmed.
But she emphasizes that the situation is still uncertain until the storm arrives.
"Since none of the rain has happened yet, it's really a watch and wait," she said.

Dow said residents can reduce the risk around their homes by clearing leaves and debris from storm drains.

And people living near waterways or in floodplains should move property to higher ground where possible.

"If you do live next to water courses or are in the floodplain, it's always good to move property out of that area so that it is less likely to be impacted by flooding," she added.

The Upper Thames River Conservation Authority, which covers the watershed north of London, issued its own flood outlook Monday.

The region received about 150 millimetres of rain in August, leaving the ground saturated and less able to absorb more water, according to Utrca spokesperson Eleanor Heagy.

She says that could lead to overland flooding if parts of the region get a particularly heavy downpour.

"We want people to be aware that if there's any really heavy downpour, if there's some localized thunderstorms that dump a lot of water, then there May be some overland flooding," she said.

Heagy says drains and culverts could also become overwhelmed.

But she emphasizes that the situation is still uncertain until the storm arrives.

"Since none of the rain has happened yet, it's really a watch and wait," she said.

stories.title: Severe afternoon thunderstorm could 'pack a punch' for London and area
stories.summary: A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario that left thousands of people in the dark in parts of Huron, Lambton and Perth counties.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario that left thousands of people in the dark in parts of Huron, Lambton and Perth counties.
· Posted: Sep 02, 2026 7:01 AM EDT | Last Updated: 4 hours ago
A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario.

A severe thunderstorm watch and yellow heat warning remained in place for the London area as of 8 p.m. A yellow severe thunderstorm warning was also active for St. Thomas and Elgin County and areas between London and Chatham-Kent.
Thousands of people were left without power in Huron, Lambton, Oxford and Perth counties after a major storm that crossed Lake Huron from Michigan battered the region around 5 p.m.
Nearly 5,000 were offline in the Grand Bend and Lambton Shores areas, while nearly 3,500 were without power near Goderich, in Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, Central Huron and North Huron.

Several roads in the region have also been impacted by fallen trees and downed power lines, according to Ontario Provincial Police, including Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140, Highway 23 near Road 165, and Perth Line 55 from Highway 23 to Road 166.
Power had been expected to return to most areas by 7:30 or 7:45 p.m., but remained out as of 8 p.m., according to the Hydro One outage map. Roughly 2,000 people were also impacted near Woodstock.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro, who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.
The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.
A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.
It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.
Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."
One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.
"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.
The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.
Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.
People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.
The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.
The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.
It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.
A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the Middlesex-London Health Unit website.
There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.
It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.
Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

stories.title: U.S. admiral compares military action against Canada to fighting extraterrestrials
stories.summary: Calling question "preposterous," Admiral Samuel J. Paparo adds: "Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?"
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A question to a U.S. admiral about the possibility of military action against Canada was met with incredulity from the military leader, who called it “preposterous” and added: “Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?”

Gen. Jennie Carignan, Canada’s chief of the defence staff, and Admiral Samuel J. Paparo, commander of the U.S. Pacific Command, were holding a joint news conference on Wednesday as the three-day annual Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defence conference came to a close.

Most of the questions dealt with cooperation between Canada and U.S. military forces and the upcoming decision about the potential purchase of F-35 fighter jets, as well as issues both countries face in the Western Pacific region.

However, midway through the event, a reporter asked, “With all due respect, under what circumstances would you obey an order to launch military action against Canada?”

Paparo looked flustered and stammered for several seconds before replying: “I find that scenario to be absolutely and utterly preposterous.” He added: “I follow the orders of the commander-in-chief, but that is a needlessly emotional question,” before concluding that “Canada is a close ally.”

The reporter replied: “You didn’t answer the question.”

Paparo started to repeat his earlier remarks before adding: “Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?”

The reporter then responded: “If you want to dismiss it, by all means.”

Paparo said: “Yes, sir. I don’t dismiss you, but I do dismiss the question.”

The reporter continued: “You belittle it, and I don’t think that’s the right approach at all. This is a serious question about a serious issue. We’ve had threats of annexation. I know it’s a hypothetical, but nonetheless if you’ve not thought about it, maybe you should.”

At this point, the event moderator thanked the reporter and moved on to another question. The press conference wrapped up several minutes later.

U.S. President Donald Trump has spoken openly of making Canada the “51st state,” even insinuating during trade talks that it was something Canada wanted. He has also talked about annexing Greenland and “taking back” control of the Panama Canal.

Trump also recently threatened to attack Oman, an ally of the United States for more than 200 years , saying last month that if Oman “gets in the way” of his efforts to reach an agreement with Iran, “we’ll bomb the shit out of them.”

In 1840, Oman sent an emissary to the United States, the first Arab diplomat accredited there. In 1980, it became the first Gulf Arab state to formally allow U.S. military access to its airfields and ports, allowing it to operate and resupply without relying on the Strait of Hormuz.

The president has also talked recently about pulling back military support from South Korea, a major U.S. partner in the Asia-Pacific region.

stories.title: Police issue warning after London man charged with child sexual abuse offences on bail
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 6:11 PM | Last Updated: September 2
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 6:11 PM | Last Updated: September 2
The Crown opposed the man's release, but a judge granted bail

London police are asking people with information about a 39-year-old man charged with multiple sexual offences involving children to contact investigators after he was released on bail while awaiting trial.
Investigators are asking anyone who believes the man May be breaching his release conditions to contact police.

Londoner Kyle Vanderheiden was arrested July 26. He's charged with buying or attempting to buy sexual services from a person under 18, luring a person under 18, and making sexually explicit material available to a person under 18.
He also faces charges related to publishing and distributing child sexual abuse material, and using telecommunications to commit criminal offences involving someone under 16.
The Crown opposed Vanderheiden's release, but he was granted bail Aug. 21.
His conditions include living in London with his surety and remaining on the property at all times.
He's also prohibited from being in the company of, or communicating directly or indirectly with, anyone under 18.
He cannot go within 10 metres of a school, community centre, park, daycare, swimming pool or other location where children are known to be.
He's also prohibited from possessing weapons.
Police said people May have information relevant to the investigation, including those who believe they May have had contact with Vanderheiden in similar circumstances.
Police are asking anyone with information to contact investigators.
"The LPS recognizes that coming forward in matters involving sexual violence can be difficult and support is available," police said in a statement.
Vanderheiden's next court appearance is scheduled for Oct. 1.
The charges have not been proven in court.

Investigators are asking anyone who believes the man May be breaching his release conditions to contact police.

Londoner Kyle Vanderheiden was arrested July 26. He's charged with buying or attempting to buy sexual services from a person under 18, luring a person under 18, and making sexually explicit material available to a person under 18.

He also faces charges related to publishing and distributing child sexual abuse material, and using telecommunications to commit criminal offences involving someone under 16.

The Crown opposed Vanderheiden's release, but he was granted bail Aug. 21.

His conditions include living in London with his surety and remaining on the property at all times.

He's also prohibited from being in the company of, or communicating directly or indirectly with, anyone under 18.

He cannot go within 10 metres of a school, community centre, park, daycare, swimming pool or other location where children are known to be.

He's also prohibited from possessing weapons.

Police said people May have information relevant to the investigation, including those who believe they May have had contact with Vanderheiden in similar circumstances.

Police are asking anyone with information to contact investigators.

"The LPS recognizes that coming forward in matters involving sexual violence can be difficult and support is available," police said in a statement.

Vanderheiden's next court appearance is scheduled for Oct. 1.

The charges have not been proven in court.

stories.title: Federal government admits two trans inmates charged with sexual assault after transfer to women's prisons
stories.summary: The federal government acknowledged that two transgender inmates in women's prisons have faced sexual-assault charges following complaints.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The federal government has acknowledged that two transgender inmates incarcerated in women’s prisons faced sexual-assault charges following complaints made by female inmates.

On Monday, the government filed its statement of defence in an ongoing constitutional challenge to Correctional Service Canada’s (CSC) policy allowing some “gender diverse” inmates to be transferred to women’s prisons. The CSC uses the term “gender diverse” to describe identities or expressions that differ from expectations based on sex assigned at birth, including non-binary, transgender and two-spirited.

According to the filing, one inmate was charged with one count of sexual assault and one count of criminal harassment in May 2020 after a female inmate filed a complaint. Another inmate was charged with two counts of sexual assault after a female inmate filed a complaint in October 2024.

The inmate charged in 2020 was alleged to be an instigator in an additional five incidents against three women inmates, but the government said in its filing that they were not involved in four of these, while a “cisgender woman” inmate was also found to be an instigator in the fifth.

The government uses the term “cisgender women” to refer to “individuals whose gender identity corresponds to the gender assigned to them at birth.”

The inmate charged in the 2024 complaint was also identified in another incident, but this was a false allegation, the government said.

Responding to a demand for particulars, the plaintiff in the case identified 45 cisgender women inmates who were allegedly impacted in 59 incidences of harm. For 45 of the 59 alleged incidences, the government says, “insufficient particulars were provided to allow Canada to respond.”

Of the remaining 14 claims, 10 took place at Grand Valley Institution for Women in Kitchener, Ont., three took place at Fraser Valley Institution, in Abbotsford, B.C., and one at the Okimaw Ohci Healing Lodge on the Nekaneet First Nation, Sask. These include a 2018 complaint that led to a police investigation but no charges, a 2019 report of sexual assault, and a 2021 complaint alleging sexual and physical assault.

Transgender inmate with history of sex crimes loses bid to be transferred to women's prison

Transfers of trans prisoners in Canada have fallen. An upcoming case will test gender policies

The constitutional challenge brought against the federal government concerns Csc’s Commissioner’s Directive 100: Gender Diverse Offenders , and was launched in 2025 by the Justice Centre for Constitutional Freedoms (Jccf).

CSC introduced its policy on “gender diverse” offenders in May 2022. The directive states: “Throughout their sentence, offenders May apply for a voluntary transfer to a men’s or a women’s institution according to their gender identity or expression.” It adds that all transfers are assessed on a case-by-case basis, and that the Deputy Commissioner for Women is the final decision-maker for transfers to women’s institutions.

Data previously obtained by the Investigative Journalism Bureau found that, between 2017 and 2025, 57 transgender women made 129 requests to transfer to a women’s prison. During that period, 35 requests were approved, and more than 70 requests were denied by CSC.

As of October 2025, there are 90 transgender women in federal prison — 73 in men’s prisons and 17 in women’s prisons. Of the 17, eight have had gender-affirming surgery.

Lawyers funded by the Jccf brought the lawsuit on behalf of Canadian Women’s Sex-Based Rights (Cawsbar), arguing that allowing transgender inmates to be housed in women’s prisons exposes female inmates to physical and psychological harm and violates their Charter rights.

Ottawa denies that its policy violates female inmates’ Charter right to life, liberty, and security of the person, stating: “In each specific factual context, CD 100 has been implemented in good faith and consistent with the principles of fundamental justice, including not being arbitrary, overbroad, or grossly disproportionate.”

Also in the filing, the federal government “wholly denies that any alleged harm to inmates housed in women’s institutions flowed from the implementation of CD 100” and maintains that its individualized assessment process provides an appropriate framework for managing risks.

In a Jccf news release Tuesday, constitutional lawyer Chris Fleury said the government’s defence shows that female inmates have raised serious complaints about their experiences in women’s prisons, some of which resulted in sexual-assault charges.

“Female inmates are being exposed to real risks and real harm,” he said. “This case is about protecting their safety, dignity and constitutional rights.”

In total, the government responded to allegations involving 13 gender diverse inmates who are alleged to have “taken and will continue to take advantage of CD 100.” For four of these inmates, there were no specific allegations provided, with the statement of defence reading: “rather, it is their mere presence in a women’s institution that is alleged to cause harm to cisgender women inmates.”

In May 2026, the Federal Court rejected the government’s attempt to strike the lawsuit and granted Cawsbar public interest standing, allowing the constitutional challenge to proceed. The federal government is now asking the court to dismiss the claim with costs.

The case follows a separate Federal Court decision in July, which saw a transgender inmate lose a bid to be transferred to a women’s prison.

Amanda Joy Cooper, 59, has been incarcerated since 2001 and is convicted of four sexual assaults, forcible confinement and other crimes against adult women and one girl, mostly in Montreal. All those crimes were committed long before Cooper’s 2020 diagnosis of gender dysphoria and 2024 surgery to construct female genitalia and breasts.

Cooper was at the Atlantic Institution in New Brunswick before asking to be moved to a women’s prison, and instead was moved last October to Millhaven Institution in Ontario, a maximum-security prison for men.

Justice Janet Fuhrer ruled that CSC had not acted unreasonably in refusing the transfer request.

stories.title: An island is floating around a B.C. reservoir — and it keeps disappearing
stories.summary: The floating forest, which is 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, was first spotted in July near Finlay Bay in the middle of Williston Reservoir in the northern interior of B.C.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
A bizarre phenomenon is drawing international attention to the shores of British Columbia’s largest body of water: a floating island of densely woven vegetation keeps appearing, disappearing, and then showing up elsewhere in the water.

The floating forest, which is 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, about the size of a soccer field, was initially spotted in July near Finlay Bay in the middle of Williston Reservoir in the northern interior of B.C.

Satellite imagery first confirmed its position, but by August it had vanished.

B.C. Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer told Global News that his staff were alerted to the island in a Facebook post, but that because of its size and movement, it was tricky to follow and was likely “flimsy” and “dangerous.”

Williston Reservoir is the world’s seventh-largest artificial reservoir, measuring 250 km north to south and 125 km east to west. Gammer described tracking the nomadic island as like looking for “a needle in a haystack.”

But weeks after it was first seen bobbing along the shore, the travelling bulk of trees showed up again, this time resting on the banks of the reservoir, pushed northwards by blustering winds.

The government agency believes the island began as a collection of decaying logs that, over time, became tethered by tree roots and broke free from land as water levels rose, which are at their highest in 14 years. Gammer said the man-made lake was effectively “full,” creating the perfect conditions for the island to be lifted off the land.

John Clague, an earth sciences professor at Simon Fraser University, likened the appearance of the woven mass of trees to a “fairytale,” explaining that islands supporting forests aren’t supposed to “float around in a lake” and noting that visitors are safest admiring it from afar, advising them not to set foot on the self-supporting structure.

Rocky Avery, a lifelong McKenzie, B.C., resident living near the reservoir who posted a video of the island on social media last month, told Global News he had never seen anything like the floating island before, but planned to fly over it for a better view.

“It’s remarkable to see it sitting there floating around; who knows how long it’ll be out there,” Avery said.

The island is moving north, away from the W.A.C. Bennett Dam , the largest in British Columbia. B.C. Hydro does not believe it’s a threat to the dam, Gammer assured, and is confident it would never be a problem, even if it ended up nearby.

Gammer said the island would have taken many years to form and told The Guardian it likely hosted diverse species of fish, birds, trees and small animals, all living among a web of branches that keep the structure afloat.

These types of islands are studied and have been spotted before in other lakes across the globe, including Forty Acre Bog in Wisconsin, a large drifting island on Lake Chippewa bound together by mud roots and trees. It appeared more than 100 years ago when the area was flooded to create the Chippewa Flowage.

stories.title: Republicans split on Canada as Trump’s trade war escalates: polls
stories.summary: While polling data shows some Americans. particularly Republicans, are turning on Canada, most still view the northern neighbours positively.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Americans are becoming increasingly divided on their feelings about their northern neighbours and the freshly stoked trade war, according to new polls released this week.

Polling conducted by YouGov for The Economist found that 38 per cent of Republican voters “now view Canada as unfriendly or an enemy, by far the highest level in the past decade” and up from 22 per cent in February polling. Only 12 per cent of Republicans felt the same way in April 2024, before U.S. President Donald Trump began his second term.

Meanwhile, only eight per cent of self-identified Democrats viewed Canada in the same light, up from three per cent this February.

Overall, a majority of Americans (net 64 per cent) describe Canada as either an ally (39 per cent) or friendly (25 per cent). Less than a quarter (net 22 per cent) now see Canada as unfriendly (19 per cent) or an enemy (three per cent) — “a new high since 2016.”

YouGov also polled respondents about Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America in the U.S., finding most citizens (68 per cent) strongly or somewhat disapproved of the move.

The 17 per cent who strongly or somewhat approved were predominantly Republicans, but Republicans more broadly were divided, with 41 per cent disapproving and 37 per cent endorsing it.

“The exception is Maga Republicans: 47 per cent approve of the renaming and 29 per cent disapprove,” YouGov wrote, “while non-Maga Republicans disapprove by 67 per cent to 22 per cent.”

A similar pattern emerged on a question regarding Canada’s trade treatment of the U.S.

Asked whether they felt Canada was treating the U.S. unfairly in trade, 45 per cent said no, 28 per cent said yes and the remaining 27 per cent were unsure. Republicans (49 per cent) were more likely than Democrats (11 per cent) to say Canada was being unfair.

But fewer Republicans who identified as non-Maga (33 per cent) judged Canada to be unfair, compared to 58 per cent of Maga Republicans.

Nearly half want a federal election if new Canada-U.S. trade agreement is reached: poll

Most Canadians oppose concessions as response to looming 50% U.S. tariffs: poll

Polling by Ipsos also explored Americans’ feelings on the new 50 per cent tariffs enacted by the Trump administration last month, finding more Republicans support (44 per cent) than oppose (33 per cent) the sanctions, with 22 per cent unsure.

Republicans were similarly split on who was most responsible for the trade hostilities — Canada (31 per cent), the U.S. (19 per cent) or both equally (30 per cent). A fifth of respondents (20 per cent) were unsure.

And when it comes to ending the trade dispute, the majority of respondents (68 per cent) said the U.S. should be willing to “make tradeoffs with Canada even if it means it doesn’t get most of what it wants.” Only a quarter of respondents (25 per cent) want team Trump to “take a tough stance with Canada and insist on getting most of what it wants.”

Across political lines, while Democrat voters are overwhelmingly (88 per cent) in favour of concessions that would leave the U.S. short of its desires, Republicans were largely split on the matter — 47 per cent on the side of trade-offs and 50 per cent in support of holding firm.

Ipsos also asked about the contentious Lake Ontario-Lake America issue, garnering results similar to Leger’s.

More Republicans oppose (43 per cent) than support (33 per cent) the change, but 24 per cent remain unsure. Across the board, 63 per cent of Americans are against Trump’s executive order.

A third poll, conducted by Abacus Data , explored “the political consequences of the trade war in the five states most likely to determine Senate control” following the upcoming U.S. midterm elections — Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, Maine and South Carolina, where 500 people were polled, respectively.

It found that those “voters have not turned on Canada.”

Positive impressions of Canada are highest in Maine (81 per cent), “where cross-border ties are part of daily life,” but even the low water mark was still high at 66 per cent in Ohio.

Their “feelings toward the Canadian people are warmer still,” landing between a low of 74 per cent in South Carolina to 87 per cent in Michigan and 88 per cent in Maine.

“Americans are drawing a line between a government dispute and a neighbouring people they continue to like,” Abacus wrote. “For Canadian readers, the audience on the other side of the border is not hostile, it is more conflicted about its own government’s policy.”

Data also indicated that Trump’s own approval rating in every state is higher than approval of how he’s handled trade with Canada — even in the red state of South Carolina, where his approval reaches 46 per cent.

“When one of the president’s signature economic initiatives polls behind the president himself in his strongest state, the initiative is not building his coalition. It is borrowing from it,” the pollster wrote.

Most respondents also predicted the tariffs will be “mostly bad” and hurt the American economy, workers, farmers, their own states and their own households.

“Across 25 combinations of measure and state, ‘mostly bad’ beats ‘mostly good’ every single time, usually by wide margins,” Abacus said.

And given the chance to have the Canada-U.S. relationship return to what it was before Trump, three times as many respondents said they would prefer that to the present fracturing.

“The current state of relations with Canada is not an equilibrium Americans in these states have accepted,” they wrote. “It is a condition most of them want reversed.”

South Carolinans were the only ones on side with the current White House strategy, and only by two points (33 to 35 per cent), “a policy defended likely out of loyalty and a weaker bond with Canada.”

The overall sample of YouGov’s poll, conducted among 1,592 U.S. citizens between Aug. 28-31, has a margin of error of roughly 3.5 per cent, as did Ipsos’ poll of 1,023 people, conducted Aug. 28-30.

Abacus’s survey of 2,500 voters was conducted Aug. 26-28. The overall sample carries a margin of error of 4.4 per cent, while the margin for a probability sample of 500 is two per cent.

stories.title: Private company to take over New Brunswick veterinary services next year
stories.summary: Starting next year, Hartland-based company Carleton AgriSolutions will take the reins of providing care for the province's livestock.
stories.author: Johnny James, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Five months after provincial veterinary services fell victim to budget cuts in New Brunswick, a new private service will be taking over.

As of April 1, 2027, Hartland-based company Carleton AgriSolutions will take the reins of providing care for the province’s livestock. The company will work in collaboration with the province’s current provincial veterinarians.

Carleton AgriSolutions was formerly known as NB Seed Grower Coop and is a seed wholesaler that also supplies feed and farm supplies.

Peter Carpenter, the company’s vice-president of sales and marketing, says they don’t have experience delivering this kind of veterinary care, so their role in the partnership will be facilitative.

“Just on the management side to make sure they have the equipment and the facilities that they need to perform the duties that they do and let them look after that side,” he said.

During the unveiling of the provincial budget in March, New Brunswick’s Liberal government announced it would phase out provincial veterinary and veterinary laboratory services over three years.

The province said the cuts will save $4 million annually as it tries to address a $1.4-billion deficit. The announcement sparked backlash and a protest from industry members and supporters.

2:08 N.B. extends deadline for field vet service cuts after ‘productive’ meeting with advocates

Carpenter says many moving pieces remain to ensure a successful transition but the company decided to make the announcement now so the industry can prepare.

“We can’t wait until February to make an announcement,” he said. “It’s not fair to industry, so we want to get it out that this is what we are looking at doing, what we are collaborating on and everyone’s intention is to get there.”

Lisa Freeze, the current provincial field veterinarian supervisor, says the majority of the current provincial veterinarians have agreed to stay on while the transition process is ongoing.

“There have been a couple of veterinarians who have left the province since March, but the majority of the rest of the people are planning to stay on until the end of March 2027 with the government,” said Freeze.

“So long as this process is figured out by then, (they) hopefully (will) transition to Carleton AgriSolutions at that point.”

Agricultural Alliance of NB’s president, Danielle Connell, says while maintaining a government-funded service would have been best, the sector had to find a solution that addressed the reality it faced.

“In a perfect world, government would have appropriately resourced and funded veterinary services from the get-go, but over the last 20 years it’s been death by a million cuts and there is just a skeleton left,” she said.

Connell isn’t worried about Carleton AgriSolutions having a monopoly on these services, because she says the company has enough motivation to keep prices reasonable.

“If they charge too much, no one will call. If they charge too much, we’ll have dead animals, and that’s not good for their business,” Connell added.

In a news release, the province says it will contribute up to $1.2 million to support the transition.
paragraphs: Five months after provincial veterinary services fell victim to budget cuts in New Brunswick, a new private service will be taking over.

As of April 1, 2027, Hartland-based company Carleton AgriSolutions will take the reins of providing care for the province’s livestock. The company will work in collaboration with the province’s current provincial veterinarians.
Carleton AgriSolutions was formerly known as NB Seed Grower Coop and is a seed wholesaler that also supplies feed and farm supplies.
Peter Carpenter, the company’s vice-president of sales and marketing, says they don’t have experience delivering this kind of veterinary care, so their role in the partnership will be facilitative.
“Just on the management side to make sure they have the equipment and the facilities that they need to perform the duties that they do and let them look after that side,” he said.
During the unveiling of the provincial budget in March, New Brunswick’s Liberal government announced it would phase out provincial veterinary and veterinary laboratory services over three years.
The province said the cuts will save $4 million annually as it tries to address a $1.4-billion deficit. The announcement sparked backlash and a protest from industry members and supporters.

Carpenter says many moving pieces remain to ensure a successful transition but the company decided to make the announcement now so the industry can prepare.

“We can’t wait until February to make an announcement,” he said. “It’s not fair to industry, so we want to get it out that this is what we are looking at doing, what we are collaborating on and everyone’s intention is to get there.”
Lisa Freeze, the current provincial field veterinarian supervisor, says the majority of the current provincial veterinarians have agreed to stay on while the transition process is ongoing.

“There have been a couple of veterinarians who have left the province since March, but the majority of the rest of the people are planning to stay on until the end of March 2027 with the government,” said Freeze.
“So long as this process is figured out by then, (they) hopefully (will) transition to Carleton AgriSolutions at that point.”

Agricultural Alliance of NB’s president, Danielle Connell, says while maintaining a government-funded service would have been best, the sector had to find a solution that addressed the reality it faced.

“In a perfect world, government would have appropriately resourced and funded veterinary services from the get-go, but over the last 20 years it’s been death by a million cuts and there is just a skeleton left,” she said.
Connell isn’t worried about Carleton AgriSolutions having a monopoly on these services, because she says the company has enough motivation to keep prices reasonable.
“If they charge too much, no one will call. If they charge too much, we’ll have dead animals, and that’s not good for their business,” Connell added.
In a news release, the province says it will contribute up to $1.2 million to support the transition.

stories.title: London man facing child-exploitation charges released on bail
stories.summary: Police are asking anyone with information, including potential additional complainants, to contact investigators.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
A London man facing multiple child-exploitation charges has been released on bail, police said Wednesday as they appealed for information that could identify potential additional complainants.

Police are asking anyone with information, including potential additional complainants, to contact investigators.

The man was released from custody on Aug. 21 after a contested bail hearing and is subject to several conditions, police said in a release on Wednesday.

The conditions include remaining at his residence at all times, not communicating with anyone under 18, staying at least 10 metres from schools and other places children are known to frequent, and not possessing weapons.

He is scheduled to reappear in London court on Oct. 1.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the London police’s Internet Child Exploitation Unit at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477).

Two firefighters suffered minor injuries and a resident was taken to hospital Tuesday following a rapidly changing house fire in downtown Windsor.

Windsor Fire Chief James Waffle said crews rushed into the burning home in the 400 block of Vera Place but had to retreat after conditions worsened. Firefighters then launched a defensive attack from outside.

“Pretty extreme conditions as they made entry, rapidly changing conditions that caused a little concern initially,” Waffle said at the scene. “Pulled the crews out, defensive fire for a short period of time before we made reentry back into the fire.”

Three Londoners among seven charged in $913K drug seizure

London man formally charged with murder in fatal home stabbing

Advertisement 1Story continues below

Waffle said the fire displaced three people. Paramedics took one resident to hospital. The extent of the person’s injuries was unknown, but the victim was “conscious and breathing.”

Two firefighters were also treated at the scene for minor burns, Waffle said.

The cost of the damage was unknown Tuesday.

With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: Lutnick says Canadian minister didn't deny trying to 'blow up' negotiations
stories.summary: Howard Lutnick said a Canadian minister did not deny it when asked if Canadian negotiators were trying to "blow up" trade negotiations.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said a Canadian minister did not deny it when asked if Canadian negotiators were trying to “blow up” trade negotiations last month.

Lutnick, the brash Trump cabinet member who is a close advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, made the claim during an interview on Cnbc Wednesday morning when discussing the end of negotiations late Friday Aug. 21.

“Friday at 4 o’clock, the Canadians call. They start adding crazy ideas to the mix. So, I said to one of the ministers, ‘are you actually trying to blow this up?’ And his answer to me was, ‘I’m not allowed to say that.’ And they blew it up for political reasons only,” Lutnick said.

The only minister present at the negotiations with the U.S. was Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc. LeBlanc’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Canadian and U.S. governments have consistently blamed the other side for blowing up recent trade negotiations aimed at avoiding new tit-for-tat tariffs and reducing ongoing U.S. tariffs on key Canadian sectors.

The day after instructing Canadian negotiators to leave the table and come home, Carney told reporters the U.S. had added a series of last-minute unacceptable conditions to draft deal text that pushed him to cut negotiations.

He cited the addition of language on auto industry tariffs, such as a failure by the U.S. to reduce tariffs on heavy-duty trucks such as those produced in auto plants in Southern Ontario. He also cited “efforts to restrict our protections of our language, our culture, and in effect, our sovereignty.”

In response, U.S. Trade Representative Jameson Greer and Lutnick have accused the Canadians of cutting talks off for political reasons.

Days after talks ended, Greer attributed the collapse to Canada ultimately wanting more than what his administration was willing to give, noting that the proposed agreement included halving U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, reducing tariffs on Canadian autos and tariff relief on Canadian softwood lumber.

The Ustr said it was the best market access to the U.S. compared to any other country in the world.

“They wanted more,” said Greer. “I don’t know if it was political for them, it certainly doesn’t make economic sense, but perhaps for political reasons, they have some byelections coming up,” Greer said in reference to three federal by-elections that occurred Monday Aug. 31. The Liberals won all three.

National Post also recently reported a senior Canadian government official noting that the country’s negotiators pulled out because Ontario Premier Doug Ford “was not on board.” A key Canadian concession in the negotiations was that all provincial liquor boards would resume stocking U.S. alcohol.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Carney said “no” when asked if Doug Ford had any role in the failure of the negotiations.

“We consult with the premiers, take into account their views,” Carney said. “The decisions on trade are the decisions of the government of Canada. I’m the prime minister. Ultimately, I am responsible with the Cabinet for those decisions.”

“Those of us who are at the table, or next to the table if you will, know exactly why an accumulation of issues, each of them (were) serious enough… to not have a deal.”

National Post cnardi@postmedia.com

Washington - Apple is changing its Maps app to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the United States after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an order to change the name of the Great Lake.

“Apple Maps has just announced that it has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, so now that very important change of names, between Google Maps and Apple Maps, is complete, ratified, and binding” Trump posted on social media Wednesday. “Thank you for your attention to this matter!”

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told the Fox Business network Monday that Trump reached out directly to Apple to ensure the new name would be used on its service.

People in Canada who use Apple Maps still see the lake identified as Lake Ontario.

Trump signed the order to change the name last week as tensions between the United States and Canada escalated following a breakdown in trade talks.

Trump last month put 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods, from hockey sticks and cement to honey. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs are set to take effect next week.

Trump singled out Canada in the Oval Office again Wednesday, complaining about everything from the automobile industry and supply-managed dairy system to banks and aircraft certification.

Trump talked about the change of leadership from former prime minister Justin Trudeau to the “new guy” he described as “nice,” and alluded to another person he called “the slob.”

“I did change the name of a certain lake to Lake America, just like I changed the name of the Gulf of … Mexico to the Gulf of America,” he said. “And people in this country love it.”

Trump said he does things “like that” because he’s fighting for the United States.

“Canada has taken advantage of us, they have ripped us off for years, and now we’re turning the tables, very easily turning the table,” Trump said.

An Ipsos/Reuters poll published earlier this week suggested the lake renaming was not popular, with two-in-three Americans disapproving of the change, and fewer than one in six Americans polled supporting it.

Last year, Trump signed an executive order to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The geographic controversy led to the White House removing The Associated Press from certain duties covering the president after the news service did not use “Gulf of America” in its reporting.

The Associated Press took the White House to court, which led to then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt taking many authorities away from the White House Correspondents’ Association, the organization representing journalists who cover the president.

Google Maps updated its service to identify the body of water as “Lake America” over the weekend. The company said in a post on its corporate website the change was made because the U.S. government’s geographic names database had formally renamed the lake.

Users in Canada will still see it displayed as Lake Ontario on Google Maps, while people elsewhere in the world will see both names.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians know Lake Ontario will be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”

Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The name comes from the Wendat word Ontari:io, which means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The Canadian province is named after the lake.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign declaring “Lake Ontario, now and always” on Saturday.

Not all map services are following Trump’s orders. After MapQuest declared it won’t be changing Lake Ontario’s name, it surged to the top of Apple’s App Store in Canada and the United States.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press
