stories.title: George Clooney calls out Pete Hegseth for mocking Canadian military cadets
stories.summary: 'You see what the secretary of defense just tweeted out a picture about women in the military in Canada, and you're going, 'What's wrong with you?' George Clooney said.
stories.author: Katie Scott
stories.content:
Actor George Clooney is calling out U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for his recent comments mocking two female Canadian military cadets.

On Monday, Hegseth posted an image of two female cadets at a British Columbia training centre with the words “this is real” and a Canadian flag.

Clooney said he was “ashamed” of Hegseth’s post while attending the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday, where he received a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the opening ceremony.

2:58 Carney says Canada’s decision to walk away from U.S. trade talks wasn’t about any one issue

“The idea that cruelty is the base — that being cruel and unkind is part of the fun of all of this,” Clooney told reporters . “You see what the secretary of defense just tweeted out a picture about women in the military in Canada, and you’re going, ‘What’s wrong with you? Where’s the sense of decency in all of this?’

“And I’m ashamed of all of that, but we will get through it, and we will come out better on the other side.”

The 65-year-old actor also spoke about U.S. politics and the direction of the country under the leadership of U.S. President Donald Trump .

“I’m always very optimistic about things,” he said. “We’re at a moment in time that’s unfortunate…. That’s an understatement. I do believe that we’re going to get through all of this. I’m old enough to have been through 1968 in the States when every city in the United States was set on fire, and we lost Martin Luther King and Bobby Kennedy in the same year. There was tons of violence. The capital was surrounded with tanks. We’ve had some other difficult times, but this is one of them,” Clooney said.

He also suggested that the midterm elections in November could restore “some normalcy” to the United States.

“There’s a great word, kakistocracy, which is a country run by the least qualified people. I think maybe we have a kakistocracy right now, but we’ll get through it, and we will have an election in November that should be a check and balance, and then in 2028, with any luck, we’ll have some restoration into some normalcy,” he added.

Clooney is not the only person who has spoken out following Hegseth’s post on X.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the message was “beneath their office.”

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney said of U.S.-Canada trade talks. “It’s not constructive, but that’s their democracy.”

2:21 Carney says U.S. should ‘stop throwing shade’ amid escalating trade dispute

British Columbia Premier David Eby also responded , calling Hegseth’s post “an embarrassment” and saying that he was looking at the remarks in the context of the U.S.’s war in Iran, calling it “a war that was supposed to be over in a few days.”

“To think that in that context the elected leadership of the military has decided to attack cadets who have volunteered to serve their country selflessly as part of a military that has been an ally to the United States for generations, it tells you everything you need to know about the amateur hour.”

Defence Minister David McGuinty also said the recent social media post from Hegseth was “below the dignity of the office he holds.”

When asked about the backlash stemming from Hegseth’s post on Tuesday, Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss told The Canadian Press, “The X post speaks for itself.”

The Army Cadet League of Canada took to Facebook to speak out following Hegseth’s post, writing, “The Army Cadet League of Canada stands firmly behind cadets, adult staff, volunteers, and officers who dedicate their time to building stronger communities and developing the next generation of Canadian leaders.”

1:58 Trump administration continues to insult Canadian military

“The Canadian Cadet Programs provide world-class leadership, citizenship, and physical fitness opportunities to tens of thousands of young Canadians across the country, completely free of barrier. The dedicated officers of the Cadet Organizations Administration and Training Service and civilian volunteers go above and beyond every day to mentor, educate, and celebrate the genuine achievements of these young people,” the statement continued.

“The safety, dignity, and well-being of our members, cadet leaders, and especially cadets is our highest priority. We strongly condemn any online harassment, or mockery of cadets’ achievements. Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable.”

“We remain immensely proud of cadets and the leaders who support them, and we will continue to champion their hard work, resilience, and service to Canada,” the statement concluded, adding the hashtag #NoPlaceForHate.

— with files from Global News’ Alex Boutilier

stories.title: Conservative MLA Donegal Wilson quits caucus, citing Findlay’s leadership
stories.summary: Boundary-Similkameen MLA says she will sit as an Independent
stories.content:
British Columbia Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay said she was the victim of a “co-ordinated political attack” after she accepted the resignation of her chief of staff and two more legislators quit her caucus on Wednesday, both citing ethical concerns and Findlay’s reported connections to Alberta separatists.

Scott McInnis became the ninth MLA to defect in less than three weeks, announcing his departure a little over two hours after Donegal Wilson’s.

Their exits were swiftly followed by Findlay’s announcement that Chris Delaney had resigned as her chief of staff, adding to the chaotic reshaping of the party since Findlay narrowly won the leadership three months ago.

Delaney has been at the centre of allegations that legislators were improperly offered jobs in exchange for resigning so Findlay, who does not have a seat in the legislature, could run in a by-election now set for later this month.

One of the legislators who quit the caucus last week, Delta South MLA Ian Paton, has said Delaney offered him a job as an adviser in exchange for resignation as an MLA, and the RCMP had since arranged to interview him.

Findlay said accusations being levelled against her and her team were “baseless,” part of an effort to derail her campaign in Abbotsford-Mission, where Reann Gasper resigned as MLA. Gasper was then appointed Findlay’s deputy chief of staff last week, before being promoted to fill the vacancy left by Delaney on Wednesday.

“I have spent my career serving in positions of significant public trust,” Findlay said in a statement.

“I am a lawyer, a former Canadian Human Rights Tribunal judge, a King’s counsel and a member of the King’s Privy Council for Canada. I served British Columbians as a federal cabinet minister and later as chief Opposition whip in the Conservative caucus. I have been vetted numerous times to be given the highest security clearances.”

Findlay said her responsibilities had carried “serious ethical and professional obligations” and she had always “conducted myself accordingly.”

Both McInnis and Wilson cited Findlay’s reported connections to Alberta separatists as part of a series of concerns in their decisions to defect.

McInnis, who said he would sit as an Independent in Columbia River-Revelstoke, said there were “serious ethical questions” around Findlay’s team, as well as their reported connections to Alberta separatism, which Wilson also cited in a statement announcing she would sit as an Independent in Boundary-Similkameen.

Findlay’s communication with the caucus had broken down, experienced staff had been fired and more than one of her senior appointees “has been reported to have links to Alberta’s separatist movement,” Wilson said.

The MLA said she no longer believed Findlay could “bring Conservatives back together” and she could not honestly campaign for the leader in the by-election.

The party has been in a state of upheaval since former leadership contender Peter Milobar quit the caucus on Aug. 14. A parade of other MLAs followed, including Paton, who said RCMP had made an appointment to speak with him and he expected they would ask about his claim that Delaney offered him a job as an adviser if he would stand down as an MLA to allow Findlay to run in a by-election.

Wilson’s statement cited “mounting questions about alleged inducements” to secure Findlay a seat in the B.C. legislature.

She also made apparent reference to Apollo Chung, who was abruptly removed from his post as the party’s director of operations last week.

Her statement described “a recording attributed to (Findlay’s) own director of operations discussing forcing fundraisers, wanting half a million dollars and being able to ’steal everything.’”

Gasper’s resignation as an MLA came after a lengthy effort by Findlay to find someone willing to quit to make way for her. Paton said Delaney asked him to step down in July, saying he’d be given a job for two years with the same salary as an MLA.

“I was told I would be given some sort of a staff job as a party staffer and I would be an agriculture adviser or policy adviser,” Paton said in an interview Tuesday.

Paton rejected the offer but said he initially wasn’t aware that it could be an offence.

It is illegal under the Criminal Code to negotiate a reward or benefit related to resignation from political office.

Findlay has previously denied offering jobs in exchange for resignations and said suggestions that a recording released online shows she illegally did so were “preposterous.”

She said in a statement last week that the recordings were “normal political discussions” that did not constitute a criminal offence.

RCMP have said they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators, but the force does not confirm or deny any investigation or the identity of anyone who May be subject to an investigation until charges are laid.

McInnis said the party had increasingly become “an exclusive private club more concerned with ideological bona fides than building the broad coalition” needed to achieve government, calling it a “recipe for failure.”

He said he could no longer support Findlay’s “direction, judgment and decisions.”

Editor’s note: A previous version of this story misspelled the surname of Scott McInnis.

stories.title: Torrential rain, strong winds and tornado risk loom over southern Ontario
stories.summary: A severe thunderstorm watch has been issued for the Greater Toronto Area and much of southern Ontario as Environment Canada warns of heavy rain, large hail and the risk of a tornado.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Severe storms cut across the Greater Toronto Area on Wednesday, causing widespread power outages, flooding and serious damage to a major concert venue.

An intense weather system brought torrential rain, large hail and the risk of a tornado to wide swaths of southern Ontario.

The weather office issued multiple emergency alerts for extreme weather in parts of the GTA as skies darkened to almost nighttime levels over the city’s downtown and hail pummelled neighbourhoods further north.

Rogers Stadium, a 50,000-capacity music venue in the city’s north end, sustained “significant damage” in the storm, Live Nation Canada said in a statement.

“Fortunately, no one was injured during today’s extreme weather event,” the venue operator said late Wednesday. “We are currently assessing the extent of the damage.”

Video footage circulating on social media shows collapsed framing and torn off coverings on stadium grounds.

Subway service was suspended on a stretch of one of Toronto’s main lines during the afternoon and evening rush hours, as the sound of emergency alerts rang out inside train cars held up by flooding at multiple stations. The smell of sewage lingered at Union Station hours after flooding peaked at the busy transit hub.

Toronto police said they responded to multiple reports of fallen trees and downed power lines across the city.

Under one overpass in the downtown core, at least two partially submerged vehicles were abandoned in the floodwater Wednesday evening as police cordoned off the area. Police also issued a hazard alert on social media about flooding on the Don Valley Parkway, a major city artery.

Long stretches of Yonge Street in midtown Toronto were also flooded, with waves breaking over curbs and covering sidewalks in inches of water. In the east end, Michael Garron Hospital reported flooding in its emergency department but said the facility remained operational.

Outside the city, there were reports of damaged buildings, including a destroyed roof in Brampton, Ont.

Toronto Hydro said about 17,000 customers were still without power as of early Thursday, down from about 65,000 on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Hydro One, Ontario’s Crown-owned power utility, reported roughly 52,000 customers were in the dark as of early Thursday. Outages were concentrated mostly to areas west and southwest of the Toronto area, including Hamilton.

“We are responding to reported hazards, including downed power lines and damaged electrical equipment, while co-ordinating restoration efforts across the city,” Toronto Hydro said in a social media post.

“Given the scale of the storm and the number of outages, restoration efforts May take time and vary by location.”

The storm caused numerous flight delays and cancellations at Toronto’s Pearson airport, which urged passengers to check their flight status with the airline before heading there.

The Salt-N-Pepa concert at the outdoor RBC Amphitheatre in Toronto was also postponed due to severe weather, and the Canadian National Exhibition fair shut down early for the day.

Videos from across the region shared on social media showed large hail and downpours pummelling cars in parking lots, flooding buses and transit stations and sending people running for cover.

Environment Canada lifted most of the severe weather alerts across southern Ontario by 9 p.m. Wednesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

— With files from Jordan Omstead, John Chidley-Hill and Paola Loriggio

stories.title: Police seeking possible victims in ongoing child exploitation investigation
stories.summary: The London Police Service is seeking more potential victims in connection with a child exploitation investigation.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London Police Service is seeking more potential victims in connection with a child exploitation investigation.

On July 26, police said they arrested 39-year-old Kyle Vanderheiden on charges of:

Two counts of printing, publishing, or possessing for the purpose of publishing child sexual abuse and exploitation material

Telecommunications agreement to commit specific criminal offenses with another under or believed to be under 16 years

Possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation material

Obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18 years of age

Luring a person under 18 years of age by means of telecommunication

Making sexually explicit material available to a person under 18 years of age

Importing, selling, or distributing child sexual abuse material

On Aug. 21, the accused was released from custody on bail conditions.

Police are releasing a photo and information for any information and additional victims. Anyone with information or who is a potential victim is asked to contact investigation LPS Internet Exploitation Unit at 519-661-5670. Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 or online .

stories.title: Ottawa commits millions to help Nova Scotia companies weather U.S. tariffs
stories.summary: Package includes grants for 27 businesses and organizations, says Justice Minister Sean Fraser
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
When Ace Machining Ltd. president Ron Wallace needed a new piece of equipment for his Dartmouth, N.S., shop, he knew for certain it wouldn’t be coming from the United States.

“Our normal procurement process would have involved American manufacturers, but given the first wave of tariffs , we decided to remove them from consideration,” the company co-owner told reporters during a news conference Wednesday.

“This is a small move … in the big picture, it will have very little effect. But if more Canadians look to their day-to-day purchases, together, we can make a difference.”

Wallace went with a Japanese-made computer numerical control milling machine, designed to automatically remove raw material with precision as the company creates parts and products for clients in industries including the defence and marine sectors. The company employs 54 people and is proud that 25 of them are either new Canadians or the children of immigrants, said Wallace.

On Wednesday the federal government announced Ace was the recipient of a $400,000 federal grant, one of 27 Nova Scotian companies to receive $14.1-million in combined funding from the Regional Tariff Response Initiative. The $1.5-billion program is part of a $7.5-billion federal package designed to help Canadian businesses deal with the impacts of U.S. trade policy.

Last month, the U.S. introduced tariffs of 50 per cent on $28-billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries fell apart. Canada’s reciprocal tariffs on a similar amount of goods are set to come into effect on Tuesday.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser, also the Nova Scotian MP in charge of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, made the funding announcement Wednesday and thanked the company for excluding U.S. firms from its procurement. He said other business owners should do the same because the success of Canada’s trade war efforts won’t be decided in closed rooms on Parliament Hill, but by the decisions of Canadians across the county.

“People are not just buying Canadian, but they’re making sure that we’re not supporting someone who is actively attacking our economic well-being by buying an American product,” Fraser told reporters.

“What gives me a great deal of optimism is not just this one example, but that this one example is being repeated in communities big and small across Canada in every aspect of life.”

Fraser said Wednesday’s grants were among the first tranche of projects to receive tariff relief. He said another round of applications, with a greater dollar value, is expected to open in the coming weeks. He said similar funding is available in every region of the country.

The minister said in a perfect world Canada would preserve its trade relationship with the U.S., and business would be conducted purely on commercial terms.

“But that’s not the world we live in,” he said.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced $14.1-million in grants for Nova Scotia firms on Wednesday to help offset the impact of U.S. tariffs.

The Canadian Press

Fraser said Nova Scotia has certain trade vulnerabilities, pointing to the Michelin tire plant in Granton, N.S., about 10 minutes away from his home. Fraser said three-quarters of the plant’s products are shipped to the U.S., with other components shipped across the border and made into industrial tires that are then sold back to Canadian consumers.

“There are 300 households in my community who are at risk with one employer, this is a strategic vulnerability,” he said. “We have relied on the United States for too long … This goes back three-quarters of a century or more, based on the way that we have historically, extracted our resources, shipped them across the border, allowed the value-add to be done somewhere else and often buying those same products back at a higher price."

Wallace said Ace Machining is seeing a lot of volatility in the price of materials. He said the company’s pricing quotes used to be valid for 30 days, but now that’s down to just seven. Meanwhile, shipping charges are up, budgets are strained and companies are struggling with an uncertain business climate that seems to change every day.

“I have lots of friends in the U.S. and they’re not happy with what’s happening either,” he said. “They’re like cousins and brothers. It’s just an unfortunate situation that decisions were made way, way, way above my pay grade and the working people have to suffer the consequences.”

In a statement, Conservative critic for Atlantic economic development, Richard Bragdon, reiterated the party’s call for the federal government to release details of the U.S. trade deal it walked away from and called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to recall Parliament. “Today’s announcement is a temporary Band-Aid without a long-term solution. Local businesses in Nova Scotia are hurting and facing massive uncertainty. They need more than a renouncement of a short-term government program,” said Bragdon.

stories.title: Canada is an ‘indispensable’ ally despite political tensions: U.S. admiral
stories.summary: The commander of U.S. Pacific Command tells reporters military-to-military relations need to stay above the political fray, as relations between Canada and the U.S. remain tense.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The head of U.S. Pacific Command called Canada an “indispensable” partner in the Indo-Pacific and said military-to-military relations are removed from the current political and economic conflict between the two countries.

Speaking to reporters in British Columbia Wednesday, Adm. Samuel Paparo talked up the importance of Canada-U.S. military cooperation for the mutual defence of the continent’s Pacific coast.

Paparo’s comments come as U.S. President Donald Trump and his cabinet secretaries continue to attack Canada in media appearances and on social media after trade talks between the two countries fell apart last month.

“Military-to-military relationships are such a serious foundation, they’re executed without emotion, they’re executed on the facts on the ground of a requirement to defend our spaces together,” Paparo told reporters in Victoria.

“Militaries are designed to remain apolitical and ruthlessly focused on defence of the geography and the capability and the long term interests of the company. So while you do see political discussions take place, for military professionals, we’re always ruthlessly focused on the mission ahead.”

Canadians certainly have seen “political discussions take place” between the two countries over the last two weeks.

The two countries appeared close to a trade deal last month, but discussions fell apart on Aug. 21. The Trump administration accused the Canadian negotiators of altering the deal on the table in the last minute, while the Canadian government has said the U.S. brought forward a deal that differed from what was discussed.

Prime Minister Mark Carney reiterated Tuesday that the deal the U.S. side proposed included several non-starters — such as changes to French language and cultural rules, U.S. say over Canada’s trade deals with other nations, and changes that would threaten the long-term viability of the Canadian auto sector.

On Wednesday, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick suggested Carney blew up trade talks in order to “gain leverage” over sovereignty movements in Quebec and Alberta.

“They treat their biggest trading partner so, so poorly,” said Lutnick, whose government has imposed repeated rounds of sweeping tariffs against Canada and other allied nations since Trump returned to office in January 2025, during a Cnbc interview.

Paparo was speaking at the close of the annual Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defence conference, this year co-hosted by the U.S. and Canada.

The conference brings together senior military leadership from Indo-Pacific nations to discuss the security environment and military-to-military cooperation, and includes close American allies as well as adversaries, including China.

Paparo laughed off a question about the circumstances under which he would accept orders to take military action against Canada, given that his commander-in-chief — Trump — has openly mused about the country’s annexation.

“I find that scenario to be absolutely and utterly preposterous,” Paparo said.

“Would you ask me please also what my attack plans are for the Martians?”

stories.title: Zelensky plans to visit Canada next week, but trip yet to be finalized, sources say
stories.summary: Ukrainian President last visited Canada in December, when he met with the Prime Minister in Halifax
stories.author: Marieke Walsh, Mark MacKinnon
stories.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is planning a visit to Canada next week, but the trip is not yet finalized, sources from both countries said Wednesday.

Five sources with direct knowledge of the planning said Mr. Zelensky’s government is arranging a visit to Canada midweek.

Three of the sources said the travel will include business and community events in Toronto, for which invitations have already been issued.

However, some of the sources also cautioned that while plans are in the works, the high-level visit could still be called off. The trip is aimed at persuading Ottawa to provide more assistance to Kyiv as it fights off the Russian invasion.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources, who were not authorized to disclose Mr. Zelensky’s travel plans.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office declined to comment on the possible visit.

The plans were confirmed by a source in Mr. Zelensky’s office. Another source with knowledge of Mr. Zelensky’s travels said the intention was for the President to visit both Canada and the United States, and that the trip could be called off because of unspecified problems with the planned U.S. leg.

The Ukrainian President would make his visit at a pivotal moment for Europe, with fears growing that Russia is planning to widen the conflict with a direct assault on North Atlantic Treaty Organization member countries .

Mr. Zelensky last visited Canada in December , when he met with Mr. Carney in Halifax.

Ukraine is in its fifth year of the war, which started with a full-scale Russian assault in February, 2022. Against all expectations, the smaller country has held its own against Moscow’s forces. The lengthy war has come at a high cost for Ukraine, with widespread damage and tens of thousands of Ukrainians killed and injured.

Vadym Prystaiko, a former Ukrainian foreign minister, said Mr. Zelensky’s visit to Canada would aim to persuade the long-time ally that it can and must contribute more to Ukraine’s defence.

“We believe that you guys are flagging a bit. You could do more, you could do much more,” said Mr. Prystaiko, who is also a former Ukrainian ambassador to Ottawa.

He said many Canadians perceive the Russian invasion of Ukraine as something happening far away, rather than a hostile act carried out by a country with which Canada shares a border.

“You are good people, but you believe that you live outside of this world,” he said.

Ukraine relies heavily on financial and military support from other Western countries to sustain its defences.

Canada has provided $6.5-billion in military assistance to Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion, money that will be spent through 2029. However, Mr. Prystaiko noted that since 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump halted all direct military aid to Ukraine, the European Union has picked up the slack via the new €90-billion Ukraine Support Loan, which has allowed Kyiv to continue purchasing the weapons it needs.

Opinion: The question facing Ukrainians in Canada and abroad: Should they stay or should they go?

According to a federal website, Ottawa has also given $13-billion in direct financial support. It has not made any recent announcements of military assistance to Ukraine outside of one in May, when a joint venture between the Canadian company Sentinel R&D Inc. and Airlogix of Ukraine was announced to produce drones for the Ukrainian military at facilities in Canada.

An unspecified number of the new drones will be purchased by the Directorate of Military Assistance Coordination, which is part of the Department of National Defence, and then donated to Ukraine.

Mr. Prystaiko said Canada and Ukraine should work to rapidly deepen their defence co-operation, particularly on drones. He said that while Kyiv was happy with the level of support it received while Justin Trudeau was prime minister, it remains to be seen whether Mr. Carney will maintain the same level of commitment.

As the war drags on, Mr. Zelensky has faced increased domestic pressure for his government’s response to the conflict. This summer, the President bowed to days of protests over changes to senior military ranks and replaced his top general.

Ukraine last held elections in 2019. The country has been under martial law since Russia’s 2022 invasion .

stories.title: Police issue warning about London man charged with child sexual abuse offences
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 6:11 PM | Last Updated: 14 hours ago
stories.author: Kate Dubinski
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 6:11 PM | Last Updated: 14 hours ago
The Crown opposed the man's release, but a judge granted bail

London police are asking people with information about a 39-year-old man charged with multiple sexual offences involving children to contact investigators after he was released on bail while awaiting trial.
Investigators are asking anyone who believes the man May be breaching his release conditions to contact police.

Londoner Kyle Vanderheiden was arrested July 26. He's charged with buying or attempting to buy sexual services from a person under 18, luring a person under 18, and making sexually explicit material available to a person under 18.
He also faces charges related to publishing and distributing child sexual abuse material, and using telecommunications to commit criminal offences involving someone under 16.
The Crown opposed Vanderheiden's release, but he was granted bail Aug. 21.
His conditions include living in London with his surety and remaining on the property at all times.
He's also prohibited from being in the company of, or communicating directly or indirectly with, anyone under 18.
He cannot go within 10 metres of a school, community centre, park, daycare, swimming pool or other location where children are known to be.
He's also prohibited from possessing weapons.
Police said people May have information relevant to the investigation, including those who believe they May have had contact with Vanderheiden in similar circumstances.
Police are asking anyone with information to contact investigators.
"The LPS recognizes that coming forward in matters involving sexual violence can be difficult and support is available," police said in a statement.
Vanderheiden's next court appearance is scheduled for Oct. 1.
The charges have not been proven in court.

stories.title: Toronto Argonauts release Canadian kicker Lidster
stories.summary: It appears veteran Canadian Lirim Hajrullahu is ready to resume kicking duties with the Toronto Argonauts.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 2:03 pm

Toronto – It appears veteran Canadian Lirim Hajrullahu is ready to resume kicking duties with the Toronto Argonauts.

Toronto released Canadian rookie Brady Lidster on Wednesday. Lidster, 21, of St. Thomas, Ont., had been handling kicking duties for the Argos since their 24-23 home loss to the Hamilton Tiger-Cats on July 18.

Hajrullahu was unsuccessful on a game-ending 31-yard field goal try in that contest. He also missed a convert earlier.

stories.title: Recovering from Okanagan wildfires, Summerland’s wineries work toward the future
stories.summary: Wineries and other local businesses are recovering from a summer of wildfires, dry conditions and decreased tourism
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Alison Moyes, winemaker at Solvero in the Garnet Valley in Summerland, B.C., watched camera feeds from her home in Penticton as the fast-moving Bald Range wildfire bore down on the winery on Aug. 7, while her colleagues evacuated the property for safe accommodations in nearby Naramata.

“When the power cut out at midnight, we had no idea what would be left,” she said.

The Bald Range wildfire forced the evacuation of around 20,000 properties in and around Summerland in the central Okanagan last month, destroying about 150 structures.

Moyes joined winery owner Matt Sartor and the rest of the team on Aug. 16 when they were able to return to the site and calculate the damage. Using a temporary access permit available to agricultural operators, they returned to find the winery and other structures, including Sartor’s family home and a tasting room, still standing. But this year’s crop won’t be harvested to make wine.

Things could have been worse. Neighbours on both sides of the winery lost their homes to the blaze, while others in the surrounding area also lost barns and crops.

Wineries and other Okanagan businesses are working to overcome the effects of a harsh summer. Tourism numbers are down as the Okanagan and Similkameen valleys continue to face a high-risk wildfire season because of continuing drought, prolonged heat waves and windy weather, while some grapes have had to be harvested early because of the heat.

At Solvero, the irrigated grape vines helped to provide a buffer from wildfires. Grape leaves and vines don’t burn as easily as dry vegetation like the dense Ponderosa pine forest adjacent to the winery.

“It is remarkable to see the path the fire took,” Moyes said. “It burned the trees behind the winery, jumped the vineyard and continued through the forest.”

The irrigation system for the vineyard needed repair and a generator was brought in until power could be fully restored to the area. Some singed vines will need to be replaced.

Meanwhile, Moyes is hoping to find replacement grapes from vineyards in unaffected areas in the province such as Vancouver Island and the Fraser Valley. “We will be going through the crop insurance process,” she said.

Watering the vines that had survived the fire to keep them productive in the future was the priority, Moyes said. Solvero has another vineyard in Happy Valley, B.C., where this year’s crop will be tested for smoke damage.

“I’ve learned a lot about wildfires having gone through this,” Moyes said.

Hot and dry conditions have also led to an early grape harvest at some wineries. Vineyards across the region bloomed early, and the growth cycle has consistently been two weeks ahead of schedule, according to winemakers.

“From a seasonal perspective, we are well ahead of where we traditionally are,” said Ben Bryant, Western operations manager for wine producer Andrew Peller Ltd.

Peller started its harvest on Aug. 14, bringing in chardonnay grapes for sparkling wine and table wine. Grapes used for sparkling wine are typically harvested when they are less ripe so that the finished, fizzy wines have a refreshing acidity. They are usually the first to be harvested, while those used for table wine are picked when they have higher sugar levels and riper fruit flavours weeks later in the summer.

As for concerns about the effect of smoke on this year’s crop, Bryant said it’s too early to assess. There are localized challenges faced by the vineyards in Summerland, including smoke and ash concerns. (Tender fruit growers in the area, especially peach and plum orchards, face similar challenges. A portion of this year’s crop risks becoming worthless because it was ready for harvest as the evacuation orders were distributed.)

“Fire isn’t a new issue in the Okanagan, we’ve been here before,” said Bryant, who added there is greater awareness and understanding of the impact of smoke on vineyards because of continuing international research.

The issue for winemakers is the unpredictable nature of what smoke will do to a cluster of grapes. The threat is that volatile phenols from the airborne smoke can be absorbed through the grape skins and become bound to the sugars in the berry. Those acrid compounds are released during fermentation into the flavour of the wine. But smoke affects different grape varieties at different stages of ripening in different ways, so there isn’t a silver bullet to remedy the problem.

“Not all grape varieties are susceptible to smoke in the same way. Every winery will make decisions that give us the best outcome given the circumstances we are facing,” Bryant said. Continuing issues with wildfires in wine regions around the world have introduced new technology and treatments to mitigate the impact of smoke without stripping away desirable flavours, aromas, body or colour.

The devastating effect of last month’s wildfire is not confined to Summerland’s small agricultural community, said Jordan Kubek, winemaker and co-owner of Pamplemousse Jus Natural Winery, and chair of the Bottleneck Drive Association, which represents Summerland producers. Its timing during the peak tourism season resulted in cancellations at hotels, restaurants and wineries.

“This affects all of the Okanagan and all of British Columbia,” she explained.

The Okanagan Valley is home to 86 per cent of the grapes grown in British Columbia, which are cultivated in vineyards that stretch across 250 kilometres, from Vernon to Osoyoos, at the border with Washington state. The vineyards hug a system of six main lakes across a changing landscape of lakeside resorts, rolling benchlands and sagebrush-covered foothills.

It is a broad and diverse region that has been divided into 11 distinct grape-growing areas based on the variety of soils and landscape as well as other natural factors. Three of those sub-appellations are based in Summerland, namely Summerland Bench, Summerland Lakefront and Summerland Valleys, where Solvero’s high-elevation vineyards in Garnet Valley are located.

But even given the Okanagan’s expansive and varied nature, tourists aren’t likely to book a holiday while fires are burning anywhere in the region. The decline in visitation is a significant setback for an industry that relies on tourism from Easter to Thanksgiving.

Operators across British Columbia’s wine country are hoping for a strong finish to the season, said Kubek, who has lived in Summerland for 16 years.

“The fall is an amazing time to visit. It’s my favourite time of the year here,” she said.

stories.title: Fairway Fest gearing up for a full three-night lineup on Labour Day weekend in London, Ont.
stories.summary: East Park’s Fairway Fest is excited and ready for a full lineup for the 2026 Labour Day weekend, with three nights of live music planned for Sept. 4 to 6.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
East Park’s Fairway Fest is excited and ready for a full lineup for the 2026 Labour Day weekend, with three nights of live music planned for Sept. 4 to 6.

The festival will feature Canadian rock, East Coast music, and tribute acts, with performances scheduled each night at East Park.

Friday’s opening night, themed “Rewinding the Classics,” will feature Canadian rock band Glass Tiger, synth-pop group Men Without Hats, and DJ Alpha.

Saturday’s lineup, billed as “The East Coast Kitchen Party,” will include Alan Doyle, The Navigators and DJ Alpha.

The festival will wrap up Sunday with a “Rock Revival” featuring tribute acts Practically Hip and Full Petty Fever, along with DJ Enchanted.

Organizers say new Weekend Passes and Premium Passes have also been introduced this year for people who want to attend multiple nights.

“We can’t wait to welcome guests back to East Park for another three-day Labour Day weekend of music paired with our activities,” said East Park’s Justin Tiseo.

“Fairway Fest 2026 brings legendary talent and incredible tribute acts, and with our new Premium and Weekend Passes, it’s easier than ever to enjoy all three nights of the festival at an affordable price.”

New this year, the Wave Fest video party.

“On Sunday, from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m., with your water park access, you’ll get a live DJ as well as think of like video, dance party meets wave pool,” said Kayla Sibbald, event organizer.

“It’s going to be a lot of fun for all ages, so everybody is welcome. Anyone with a fairy fest ticket to gets discounted rates on all of our activities here at East Park.”

For tickets and more information: East Park Fairway Fest tickets .

stories.title: Kane Barch embraces family legacy with London Knights
stories.summary: The Knights head to Victoria for two exhibition games while key import and overage roster spots take shape.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Kane Barch already owns some battle scars on his face from the early Ontario Hockey League preseason.

“I got nailed in Watford at the end of the Erie game – a high stick as I shot the puck,” the new London Knights forward said. “Didn’t feel great, but all fine now.”

The second-generation Knight’s comfort level has been apparent from the day he signed two weeks ago. He scored three goals in his first two outings and is rocking the familiar No. 10 jersey his father Krys did nearly three decades ago at the Ice House.

“I want to continue the legacy here,” the 17-year-old said. “I felt that was a number that came to mind at the start.”

Kane Barch, who played minor hockey for his dad with the Huron-Perth Lakers, often made the trip to Canada Life Place to watch games. He was born in Plano, Tex., while Krys was in the Dallas Stars organization, was picked by Kitchener in the first round of the 2025 OHL draft and spent last season with the United States national team development program based in Plymouth, Mich.

Now, this feels like home again.

“It was a tough first year of junior hockey (with the U.S. team), but I got in the swing of things later in the season,” he said. “I got the hang of it. It’s a bit faster, more pace, but it’s all good now. These guys here are great and London is such a pro organization.

“I love it here.”

Krys Barch, who coached the Niagara IceDogs last season, will assist the Knights with some development work.

“He’s still in Grand Bend,” Kane said, “and it’s nice he’ll be around to help.”

VICTORIA TRIP: The Knights departed Wednesday for a whirlwind trip to play two exhibition games against the Western Hockey League’s Victoria Royals in British Columbia.

They play Friday night and Saturday afternoon on their historic trip out west before catching a red-eye flight home.

‘London’s always first’: Knights sign first-round pick Kane Barch

London Knights (and play-by-play man Mike Stubbs) find new radio home

Advertisement 1Story continues below

“We’re going to use it as a great team and bonding experience,” London assistant coach Rick Steadman said. “We’re bringing a few extra guys and treating it like exhibition games in who we normally bring. It just ends up being in Victoria.”

Forward Jaxon Cover will miss the first outing while serving a one-game suspension for fighting in the final 10 minutes of the Watford contest. Brody Cook was cleared because he was instigated upon in his fight.

“The guys have been playing hard and putting their noses to the grindstone,” Steadman said. “There is lots of compete out there.”

Defenceman Cooper McAslan, who is dealing with a foot injury, won’t play in Victoria, but the Knights are hoping to get him into action next week in the final two tuneups against Sarnia.

VITAL SPOTS: The fastest way to rebuild a contender in the OHL now is to hit on your three imports and three overagers. That’s worth a lot of wins if done properly.

The Knights currently have Flyers first-rounder Maksim Sokolovskii, top NHL prospect Luca Santala from Finland and Avalanche draft pick Linus Funck. There are also persistent rumours Anaheim first-rounder Marcus Nordmark, who has been working out with the Swedish national team, could be in London at some point.

There aren’t many junior teams that can match that depth of quality talent in their organization.

The club is also banking on consistent firepower from its three overage forwards – speedy Evan Van Gorp, United States Hockey League scoring star Thomas Zocco and former Green Bay Gambler Geno Carcone.

Van Gorp is a grizzled Knights vet, but Zocco and Carcone come with a lot of familiarity.

“I grew up playing against (Geno) my whole life,” Zocco said of his fellow New Yorker. “Always an enemy of mine, and now, he’s one of my close friends. I’m happy to be with him.”

If Zocco can come close to the 22-goal, 70-point output he produced last year in Sioux Falls, the Knights would happily take it.

“There is a lot of skill here and many offensive threats,” the 5-foot-11, 185-pounder said. “I’m excited to see what the season holds and how good we’ll do together.”

stories.title: Sean Fraser applauds exclusion of U.S. suppliers as he announces N.S. tariff relief
stories.summary: Dartmouth - When Ace Machining Ltd. president Ron Wallace needed a new piece of equipment for his Dartmouth, N.S., shop, he knew for certain it wouldn’t be coming from the United States.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Dartmouth - When Ace Machining Ltd. president Ron Wallace needed a new piece of equipment for his Dartmouth, N.S., shop, he knew for certain it wouldn’t be coming from the United States.

“Our normal procurement process would have involved American manufacturers, but given the first wave of tariffs, we decided to remove them from consideration,” the company co-owner told reporters during a news conference Wednesday.

“This is a small move … in the big picture, it will have very little effect. But if more Canadians look to their day-to-day purchases, together, we can make a difference.”

Wallace went with a Japanese-made computer numerical control milling machine, designed to automatically remove raw material with precision as the company creates parts and products for clients in industries including the defence and marine sectors. The company employs 54 people and is proud that 25 of them are either new Canadians or the children of immigrants, said Wallace.

On Wednesday the federal government announced Ace was the recipient of a $400,000 federal grant, one of 27 Nova Scotian companies to receive $14.1 million in combined funding from the Regional Tariff Response Initiative. The $1.5-billion program is part of a $7.5-billion federal package designed to help Canadian businesses deal with the impacts of U.S. trade policy.

Last month, the U.S. introduced tariffs of 50 per cent on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries fell apart. Canada’s reciprocal tariffs on a similar amount of goods are set to come into effect on Tuesday.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser, also the Nova Scotian MP in charge of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, made the funding announcement Wednesday and thanked the company for excluding U.S. firms from its procurement. He said other business owners should do the same because the success of Canada’s trade war efforts won’t be decided in closed rooms on Parliament Hill, but by the decisions of Canadians across the county.

“People are not just buying Canadian, but they’re making sure that we’re not supporting someone who is actively attacking our economic well-being by buying an American product,” Fraser told reporters.

“What gives me a great deal of optimism is not just this one example, but that this one example is being repeated in communities big and small across Canada in every aspect of life.”

Fraser said Wednesday’s grants were among the first tranche of projects to receive tariff relief. He said another round of applications, with a greater dollar value, is expected to open in the coming weeks. He said similar funding is available in every region of the country.

The minister said in a perfect world Canada would preserve its trade relationship with the U.S., and business would be conducted purely on commercial terms.

“But that’s not the world we live in,” he said.

Fraser said Nova Scotia has certain trade vulnerabilities, pointing to the Michelin tire plant in Granton, N.S., about 10 minutes away from his home. Fraser said three-quarters of the plant’s products are shipped to the U.S., with other components shipped across the border and made into industrial tires that are then sold back to Canadian consumers.

“There are 300 households in my community who are at risk with one employer, this is a strategic vulnerability,” he said. “We have relied on the United States for too long … This goes back three-quarters of a century or more, based on the way that we have historically, extracted our resources, shipped them across the border, allowed the value-add to be done somewhere else and often buying those same products back at a higher price.”

Wallace said Ace Machining is seeing a lot of volatility in the price of materials. He said the company’s pricing quotes used to be valid for 30 days, but now that’s down to just seven. Meanwhile, shipping charges are up, budgets are strained and companies are struggling with an uncertain business climate that seems to change every day.

“I have lots of friends in the U.S. and they’re not happy with what’s happening either,” he said. “They’re like cousins and brothers. It’s just an unfortunate situation that decisions were made way, way, way above my pay grade and the working people have to suffer the consequences.”

In a statement, Conservative critic for Atlantic economic development, Richard Bragdon, reiterated the party’s call for the federal government to release details of the U.S. trade deal it walked away from and called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to recall Parliament. “Today’s announcement is a temporary Band-Aid without a long-term solution. Local businesses in Nova Scotia are hurting and facing massive uncertainty. They need more than a renouncement of a short-term government program,” said Bragdon.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

The $1.5-billion program is part of a $7.5-billion federal package designed to help Canadian businesses deal with the impacts of U.S. trade policy.

Last month, the U.S. introduced tariffs of 50 per cent on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries fell apart. Canada’s reciprocal tariffs on a similar amount of goods are set to come into effect on Tuesday.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser, also the Nova Scotian MP in charge of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, made the funding announcement Wednesday and thanked the company for excluding U.S. firms from its procurement. He said other business owners should do the same because the success of Canada’s trade war efforts won’t be decided in closed rooms on Parliament Hill, but by the decisions of Canadians across the county.

“People are not just buying Canadian, but they’re making sure that we’re not supporting someone who is actively attacking our economic well-being by buying an American product,” Fraser told reporters.
“What gives me a great deal of optimism is not just this one example, but that this one example is being repeated in communities big and small across Canada in every aspect of life.”

Fraser said Wednesday’s grants were among the first tranche of projects to receive tariff relief. He said another round of applications, with a greater dollar value, is expected to open in the coming weeks. He said similar funding is available in every region of the country.
The minister said in a perfect world Canada would preserve its trade relationship with the U.S., and business would be conducted purely on commercial terms.
“But that’s not the world we live in,” he said.

Fraser said Nova Scotia has certain trade vulnerabilities, pointing to the Michelin tire plant in Granton, N.S., about 10 minutes away from his home. Fraser said three-quarters of the plant’s products are shipped to the U.S., with other components shipped across the border and made into industrial tires that are then sold back to Canadian consumers.

“There are 300 households in my community who are at risk with one employer, this is a strategic vulnerability,” he said. “We have relied on the United States for too long … This goes back three-quarters of a century or more, based on the way that we have historically, extracted our resources, shipped them across the border, allowed the value-add to be done somewhere else and often buying those same products back at a higher price.”

Wallace said Ace Machining is seeing a lot of volatility in the price of materials. He said the company’s pricing quotes used to be valid for 30 days, but now that’s down to just seven. Meanwhile, shipping charges are up, budgets are strained and companies are struggling with an uncertain business climate that seems to change every day.

“I have lots of friends in the U.S. and they’re not happy with what’s happening either,” he said. “They’re like cousins and brothers. It’s just an unfortunate situation that decisions were made way, way, way above my pay grade and the working people have to suffer the consequences.”

In a statement, Conservative critic for Atlantic economic development, Richard Bragdon, reiterated the party’s call for the federal government to release details of the U.S. trade deal it walked away from and called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to recall Parliament. “Today’s announcement is a temporary Band-Aid without a long-term solution. Local businesses in Nova Scotia are hurting and facing massive uncertainty. They need more than a renouncement of a short-term government program,” said Bragdon.

stories.title: OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits from witnesses to mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.
stories.summary: The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
stories.author: Chuck Chiang The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Artificial intelligence company OpenAI and founder Sam Altman are facing 30 new lawsuits from witnesses to the deadly mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., with plaintiffs including a teacher who described trying to protect pupils from the shooter, and a teenage student who recalled his classmates arming themselves “with kitchen knives and heavy tools.”

“My colleagues and I are haunted by the memory of shielding children with our own bodies as our ears rang from the sound of continual gunshots and high-pitched screams. An entire generation of young lives, gone in a second,” teacher Deidre Rushlow said in a statement provided by Vancouver-based law firm Rice Parson Leoni and Elliott.

“And for what? So OpenAI could get to an IPO? Were the lives of my students and educational assistant just the cost of doing business?”

The lawsuits were to be filed Wednesday in California on behalf of “injured and traumatized students and educators” at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in the northern British Columbia community, the law firm said. Six of the eight victims who died in the shootings were killed at the school.

“These students and teachers were eyewitnesses to gun violence, murder and emergency life-saving efforts rarely seen outside of a theatre of war, and only in the most lawless of places on Earth,” said John Rice, lead Canadian counsel.

He said in a statement that OpenAI had the chance to stop the attack after its staff identified the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, as a credible threat of imminent gun violence months beforehand, but police in Canada weren’t notified.

The company had banned Van Rootselaar’s account on its ChatGPT platform, but “nothing else was done,” the law firm’s statement said.

“Based on what we understand the shooter to have discussed with ChatGPT, this murderous rampage was specific, predictable and preventable,” Rice said.

The claims have not been tested in court.

In addition to compensatory and punitive damages over what Rice described as OpenAI’s “reckless disregard for public safety,” he said the plaintiffs are seeking Van Rootselaar’s messaging history with ChatGPT before the shooting.

They are also seeking OpenAI’s internal documents outlining the decision not to alert authorities, along with measures to prevent future mass shootings, including obligations for major online platforms to make safety reforms and mandatory reporting to law enforcement for foreseeable acts of violence.

The plaintiffs include a principal at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School as well as a teacher who shared a classroom and “the same moment of terror” with her nephew, the law firm said in a separate email.

Among the student plaintiffs are “siblings who were separated, each fearing the other had been killed,” it said.

The lawsuits are being filed in the Northern District of California, the same jurisdiction where seven previous lawsuits from victims’ families were filed.

The Feb. 10 attack began with Van Rootselaar killing her mother and brother in their family home before moving to the school and killing five students and an educational assistant. She then fatally shot herself.

OpenAI and Altman have been heavily criticized after the revelation that Van Rootselaar’s use of the company’s ChatGPT chatbot months before the attack was concerning enough for the account to be banned, yet police were not notified.

In a social media post, Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said the company was approaching litigation related to Tumbler Ridge “with respect for both the legal process and the families and victims” and would “continue to engage in good faith.”

“There isn’t a day that goes by that I don’t think about what happened at Tumbler Ridge, or the victims of this devastating tragedy and their families,” he said.

But Kwon said it was “completely untrue” those working at OpenAI don’t prioritize safety. They “work continuously to identify potential warning signals of serious violence,” while also protecting the privacy and security of ChatGPT users, he said.

Members of OpenAI’s legal department and intelligence and investigations team employ “hard-to-define standards and processes for when to report cases to law enforcement” in complex situations, he said in the statement issued Wednesday.

“They use automated systems that leave the toughest calls to human judgment, but within standards to minimize discretion and produce principled decisions that strive to balance security and privacy for the people who use our service and the public,” Kwon said.

“That judgment is not infallible, but it is always rooted in looking out for this balance for people.”

B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma issued a statement saying the province supported the latest claims filed against the company.

“We are deeply disappointed that OpenAI has made no meaningful efforts to address the harm suffered by those affected by this tragedy,” she said.

Sharma said the province would work with families and community members in Tumbler Ridge while it explores the potential for its own, separate legal action. Sharma had announced in July that B.C. had retained legal counsel in the matter.

“The commitments made by OpenAI’s leadership, including Sam Altman and Ann O’Leary (OpenAI’s vice-president of global policy), have yet to be matched by meaningful action for the people most affected by this tragedy,” Sharma said in her statement on Wednesday.

“It is not too late for the company to demonstrate a genuine commitment to survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community.”

Rushlow, a Grade 7 English and humanities teacher, said in her statement that she had sent her students to the library at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, where police have said most of the shootings would take place.

“I did not know, nor could I know, that when I sent them to the library with my educational assistant, they were living their final moments,” Rushlow said.

Another plaintiff, an unnamed Grade 10 student, said in an account provided by the law firm that he had to step over a victim’s body during the school’s evacuation.

The student said he had witnessed his teacher perform 45 minutes of CPR on the victim in an attempt to save her life, and other students taking refuge with the group in a small storage closet had “armed themselves with kitchen knives and heavy tools, ready to use them if the shooter came through the door.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Winnipeg woman saves father and child from drowning: WPS
stories.summary: Winnipeg police said the child entered the Red River first and started to drown, prompting their father to follow her. A bystander saved both.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Jayclyn Morrissette is a Winnipeg woman police are crediting for saving a father and his child from drowning in the Red River.

The child entered the Red River near St. John’s Park on Aug. 24 and began to drown, prompting the father to jump in and try to save them, according to the Winnipeg Police Service’s (WPS) news release.

Morrissette told Global News she jumped off the park bench she was sitting on when she saw the child, adding that she intervened after noticing the father – who entered the river before her – was starting to sink.

“I knew that I was about to save two people. My first thought was to get him (the father) first, since he’s closer. So, I threw everything out of my pockets and then I jumped in,” she recalled.

She described rescuing the father as “difficult” because he was struggling and trying to hold onto her, pulling her into the water. Her neighbour, who was nearby and on the phone with 911, helped pull Morrissette and the man out of the water.

Her attention then shifted to the man’s child, who Morrissette said was further in the water than their father, and “no longer moving” while face down in the water.

After reaching the child, the woman headed back toward the shoreline, police said.

Morrissette held the child on her chest as she helped them expel the water from their lungs. After returning to shore, she said others started trying to help the child, but did not know how to do CPR. She went back to help the family.

“I had kept performing it until I no longer could, my arms had given out. At that point of picking up the father and swimming back-and-forth, my arms could only handle so much,” she said. Her neighbour took over until the police arrived.

“I remained calm and just did what I thought anybody should do.”

Winnipeg police said her actions that day demonstrated “remarkable courage and selflessness.”

North district WPS officers arrived at the scene shortly before 7 p.m. and took over efforts to save the unconscious child. The child was taken to hospital in critical condition but has since stabilized and is expected to make a full recovery.

Police credited the bystander who swooped into action “for saving both the lives of the child and parent during this incident.”

Morrissette said she started to feel some of the emotional effects of her life-saving park visit when she saw her daughter and spoke with her mom at home.

“I still feel like what I did wasn’t that heroic. Anybody would do that. I would hope anybody would do that,” she said.

“I would only hope that if my child was in the same situation someone would do that too.”

The release reminded parents to supervise their children around water and to exercise caution when visiting parks and waterways.

stories.title: Rabies vaccine operation targets raccoons and skunks in Montreal parks
stories.summary: Workers will be spreading sweet-smelling baits containing a rabies vaccine through Montreal's parks in the coming weeks to head off an outbreak of the deadly disease.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 12:51 pm

Teams of workers will be spreading sweet-smelling baits containing a rabies vaccine through Montreal’s parks in the coming weeks in the hopes of heading off an outbreak of the deadly disease.

The provincial environment department said last month that it is leading an effort to distribute some 815,000 baits throughout the Estrie, Montérégie and Centre-du-Québec regions to the south and east of the city, as well as in nine Montreal-area parks.

The baits will be spread by hand and each one looks like a small piece of green ravioli in a packet.

The province has recorded 171 raccoon rabies cases since the beginning of the year, including two cases in cats.

There have also been seven cases of bat rabies, one of which was detected in Montreal in late July.

People are being asked to avoid handling the baits, and should wear gloves or use a shovel if they are forced to move one.

They should also wash their hands after touching one of the baits.

stories.title: Lake Ontario renamed 'Lake America' for U.S. users of Apple Maps
stories.summary: Move follows Google's similar change, even as majority of Americans remain opposed to changing the name of Lake Ontario.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Apple has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America on the web version of its Apple Maps, but only for U.S. users of the service.

The decision by the tech giant took place on Tuesday, the same day John Ternus officially took over as CEO, succeeding Tim Cook, who had led the company for 15 years.

It follows a move by Google’s parent company, Alphabet, to change the name of the lake on its Google Maps, also for U.S. users.

“These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now,” Google said in a statement announcing its change. “People using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names.”

U.S. President Donald ‌Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to rename the lake, which was given its original title, Ontari:io , millennia ago by Indigenous people and means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” European settlers in the 1600s started using the word, which also became the official name of the adjoining province in 1867.

In an ‌interview on Fox Business’ Mornings with Maria program on Monday, U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Trump had reached out to Apple directly, “so I’m sure that we May be seeing that change coming up soon to Lake America.”

This comes even as a new poll finds that almost two-thirds of Americans oppose the renaming.

The Ipsos poll reported that 63 per cent of Americans were against the new name, with only 14 per cent in favour and another 21 per cent unsure. Democrats and independents were most likely to be opposed (84 and 65 per cent respectively) but even among Republican voters, just 33 per cent were in favour and 43 per cent against.

The Google change caused confusion and consternation in Canada, as maps on sites run by Hydro One, Metrolinx, Infrastructure Ontario, the Lcbo and others all displayed the American name over the weekend.

Here are the Trump lakes, islands and an avenue Canada could consider renaming

'Sad and pathetic': U.S. politicians condemn Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario

However, Ontario government agencies have restored Lake Ontario to their websites, with Metrolinx telling National Post on Monday that “the issue has since been resolved, and our maps once again show Lake Ontario.”

The international boundary running between the U.S. and Canada means that about 52 per cent of the surface area of Lake Ontario is in Canada, with the remainder in New York State. However, Trump has pointed out that, due to the varying depth of the water, more of Lake Ontario by volume is on the American side.

The naming issue mirrors that of the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump ordered to be renamed the Gulf of America early last year. Both Google and Apple subsequently revised their map apps to reflect the change for U.S. users.

New York’s Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul responded to Trump’s latest renaming saying that her state would not follow the new naming, adding in a social media post : “An acronym for the Great Lakes used to be Homes. Thanks to Donald Trump, it’s now Shame.”

Trump has posted several AI-generated videos on social media, including a clip of him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with another that says “Welcome to Lake America.” Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded by placing a real sign on the shore, declaring the body of water “Lake Ontario now and forever.”

Meanwhile, MapQuest, a free web mapping service, said on social media : “We’re not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure.” It included an image with the lake labelled: “Lake Are We Doing This Again?”

News reports noted that MapQuest became one of the most-downloaded applications on both sides of the border following the change. Forbes reported it had “soared to the top of Apple’s App Store rankings,” while other reports said it had reached second-place among Canadian downloads over the weekend.

stories.title: Group prepares push for referendum on proposed downtown arena in Saskatoon
stories.summary: Saskatoon residents May soon get their say on the proposed downtown arena, a project that could become the largest in the city's history.
stories.author: Chris Carr
stories.content:
Saskatoon residents May soon get their say on the proposed downtown arena, a project that could become the largest in the city’s history.

Ken Wood, a retired arena manager, announced on Aug. 21 his plans to organize an effort to force a referendum on the proposed $1.2 billion Downtown Event and Entertainment District. At the same time, he launched voteondeed.CA , where people can find details on the petition to force that referendum.

“Right now, we’re concentrating on volunteers. We’re thinking that is going to be key, getting out there, door to door,” said Wood, former CEO of Credit Union Centre.

Wood said nearly 100 people are offering to canvass. Once they start, they will have 90 days to collect signatures from 10 per cent of eligible voters to force a referendum.

Based on information from the City of Saskatoon, the threshold for meeting this requirement is 26,615 valid signatures. Should the group gather the required signatures, the petition would need to be presented to the city clerk within 90 days after the first signature is collected. A referendum would then need to happen within nine months.

Wood said his group is still working with legal on how the ballot question would be worded.

While the question would be hypothetically structured, Saskatoon Mayor Cynthia Block sees the real question facing the community as something beyond a simplistic, binary ‘should the city proceed or not with the project.’

“We will be making a significant investment in one of two things: taking care of the infrastructure we already own, which will be expensive, or investing in new infrastructure that we will own,” said Block.

Wood sees that as a false argument. He believes renovations at SaskTel Centre could be made much cheaper than some are saying.

“People, when looking at SaskTel, when they are looking at the renovation, they are looking at bringing it up to NHL standards. To me, that’s a non-starter,” said Wood.

Wood said renovations at the existing facility could be done for much cheaper than that.

But Block believes Saskatoon requires a venue with a higher roof to accommodate acts that would otherwise end up in other cities.

“To me, one of the really big questions should be … are we going to invest in aging infrastructure that will not serve the future in the way that modern cities are able to serve and what does that do to our competitive edge?” said Block, noting the city’s responsibility to maintain infrastructure.

“The roof of the building has to be higher, or we can’t attract a lot of the events that a lot of cities are going to be able to attract, including, probably, Regina.”

Wood said we could know as soon as next week when the petition will be launched.

In July, the provincial government said it would match federal funding up to a third of the eligible project costs. So far, there has been no funding commitment to the project from the federal government.

Block said the direction of council has always been that the cost will not impact property taxes.

“If that were ever to change, that would come back to council and there would be a full public discussion at that time. And I am not anticipating that for a number of reasons,” Block said.

Wood said cost is an issue that has come up repeatedly with people he has spoken with.

“People are very concerned about the financial viability of this project. It’s [would be] 100 percent government-financed. And there is no case of a major arena being built like this in North America and being fully funded by government,” said Wood.

Back in June, the city of Saskatoon signed a Memorandum of Understanding to explore a possible partnership with Muskeg Lake Cree Nation.

Earlier this year, city council rejected a proposal from administration to enter into an agreement with U.S.-based Oak View Group 360 to manage the arena.

stories.title: Clinical trial patient says ketamine treatment for bipolar depression changed his life
stories.summary: Toronto — Greg Rennie says his bipolar depression was an eight out of 10 when he went in for his first ketamine infusion in April 2025.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 12:16 pm.

Last Updated September 2, 2026 1:53 pm.

Toronto — Greg Rennie says his bipolar depression was an eight out of 10 when he went in for his first ketamine infusion in April 2025.

He ranked it a zero out of 10 right afterward.

Rennie, who has had bipolar depression for almost 30 years, was one of the 68 participants in a University Health Network clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of repeated ketamine infusions for people with bipolar depression.

The 61-year-old was hooked up to an IV in a UHN hospital room. About 10 minutes after they turned on the ketamine he recalls feeling like he was floating, dissociated from his body, like he was in outer space. He began to envision himself in a dark room where at times light would shine through.

“I realized what it was showing me is that this is your depression. That I’m in this black box,” he said.

“It did change my life in the way that it made me realize how dark the depression is and that a lot of the time I live within this black room.”

Rennie wasn’t the only one who found his symptoms improved.

The clinical trial, published in Jama Psychiatry Wednesday, found the treatment reduced depressive symptoms for more than 35 per cent of participants, who received two 40-minute ketamine infusions over two weeks.

That’s compared with fewer than 12 per cent in the control group receiving a benzodiazepine medication as a comparison.

Psychiatrist and senior author Dr. Joshua Rosenblat said the ketamine infusions also didn’t trigger mania, psychosis or suicidality.

“That’s one of the most important takeaways, that it didn’t trigger mania, which is what a lot of people were concerned about,” Rosenblat said.

“What we found was that with each subsequent dose there were more and more benefits,” Rosenblat said.

People with bipolar depression have often been excluded from ketamine treatment due to the risk of bringing on a “switch” from depression to mania, said Dr. Jennifer Swainson, a psychiatrist in Edmonton who was not involved in the study.

“This randomized controlled trial suggests that this is not a significant concern, not more so than we May see with the course of the illness itself,” Swainson said.

Ketamine, an anesthetic used for decades to block pain during surgery, has been offered in small doses to treat severe depression, and other psychiatric disorders, over the past 20 years.

There is a need for a treatment that works for bipolar depression, as about one in three do not respond to standard treatments and many medications make people feel worse, Rosenblat said. Approximately three per cent of people in Canada will experience bipolar disorder, according to the federal government’s latest statistics.

There have been concerns about the risk of ketamine treatment leading to addiction in the wake of Matthew Perry’s overdose death. The former “Friends” star was receiving legitimate ketamine infusion treatments for depression but turned to a dealer for supplying him with illicit doses, according to court filings.

However, research shows that most people using ketamine for depression are not at high risk of abusing it or developing an addiction, Swainson said. In her experience of treating patients with ketamine for depression, she said many reported a neutral opinion or even a dislike of the drug’s effects, but kept using it as prescribed because it helped.

The barrier to ketamine treatment becoming more widely accessible is it’s not covered by most provincial health insurance. Some clinics cover the cost of a limited number of sessions or suggest patients join clinical trials like this one to get access to it. There are also private community clinics that offer treatment that can cost $4,200 for a full cycle of six treatments.

The study found patients’ symptoms returned after they stopped the infusions, suggesting they would need maintenance sessions to keep up the antidepressant effects.

That’s what Rennie has done. He was referred to a private clinic, where he gets infusions every couple months, for $500 for a session.

“That’s the sad part of it,” said Rennie, who believes the therapy should be covered and available across Canada. “I think that has to change.”
